papers.title: Authoritarianism and the Rule of Law
papers.abstract: Mr. Kayode-Idowu in the witness chair. Chairman examines Mr. Kayode-Idowu. Chairman: Where do you come from? Mr. Kayode-Idowu: I am a Yoruba. Q. What are you? A. A Freelance writer Q. Where do you live? A. 11 Issac Jones Street, Igbobi. Q. Tell us what you know about the incident. A. In the early part of January 1966, the Army came to power – Q. What are you saying? A. I am a member of the Young African pioneers. I want to brief you on some points. A. Did you see what happened on the 18th of February? A. Yes. Q. Why do you want to take me to 1966? Q. I will make my position clearer and you will see where I am coming from easily. Q. I cannot see where are coming from ten years ago (Laughter) A. The Army came into power and said they wanted to protect lives in this country. Q. I know that myself. What I do not know is what happened on the 18th of February, 1977. I am older than you are probably in a position better to know what you want to tell me. What I do not know is what happened on the 18th of February. If you do not want to talk about that, go and sit down but if you want, please go ahead. There must be a limit to all these jokes. Do you know what really happened on the 18th? A. Yes. For some time now in that area, we can see that members of the Armed Forces, especially the Army have us become “horrors”. For example, on Thursday 17th, February, I myself and my friend were looking for a taxi in front of the African Shrine. We saw a solider jumping in front of taxis trying to stop them. We too tried to stop the taxis but the solider said, “Who are you to stop the taxi I have stopped.” We told him that taxis cabs are public transport. My friend even went further to tell him that he was constituting a danger to us in the way he was behaving. The next thing he did was that he slapped my friend. I tried to ask him why he did this and he replied me with another slap. I then held on to that soldier. Luckily, the civilians and some members of the Young African Pioneers who were around came to my aid and this soldier had to run away. On the 18th, Sir, I was around Fela’s house around 10.30 a.m. because we have our Young African Pioneers’ office at the shrine. I happened to go to Fela’s house around 12.30 that day. I learnt that Fela was sleeping. I even met one Angus Okoli in the sitting room that day. Not quite ten minutes after I had gone back to the Shrine I heard people upstairs shouting “Soldiers have surrounded Fela’s house.” Knowing them before to have been coming to harass people like that, I ran along Kalakuta Close in order to call some of our members to see what help we could be. The next thing I saw was that solders started cordoning the whole area. We thought it as a joke. I had to leave my position because I saw that these people were really out for something because they were armed to the teeth, I went back to the Shrine. In the Shrine we have an open place where you can see everything that is happening within the distance of that area. The next thing I saw was a new consignment of soldiers coming and throwing stones and bottles at Fela’s house. They did this for about one hour or so. The whole area was filled up with solider. They stood across t roads driving all the civilians and even asking people to lock their doors. With the wave of violence, I did not know what to do. The situation was tense. Meanwhile they tried to enter the house but they could not because of the barbed wire fence. Some of them were shaking the fence while other threw stones inside the house. The next thing we saw was an Army vehicle, a Mercedes Benz 280S with Registration No. NA.56C parked in front of the Shrine. When this vehicle parked, an Amry officer came out—a short slimly built officer. I think he is a Colonel because he had a red band on his cap. He looked to me like Col. Tarfa. Ever since we released the YAP NEWS of November, second volume, and he wrote a letter to us, I have taken special note of Col. Tarfa and I can recognize him any where I see him. I think it was Major Daudu and some other officers who stood around the shrine while the boys carried on the operation after consultation with Col. Tarfa. Major Daudu, I am sure, gave the instruction by waving his hand. I was on the higher place and I could see them though I could not hear exactly want he said but I saw jerry cans and the boys went round the Ford that carried the generator and set it ablaze. They went on to the civilian bus, set it ablaze and then on to the Passat that was outside. At first Fela’s wagon was spared. That wagon looks like a bus it is a car and I saw Major Daudu pointing at it. The Army now have this type of bus and I am sure the way Major Daudu was pointing he seemed to be saying, Why did they leave that. The soldiers had left it originally while they sprayed the Ford, the Civilian bus and Beko’s Passat. I saw some soldier with some liquid, I did not know what it they were carrying. But it was this liquid that was used in spraying the car before it was set ablaze. The next thing they did was to cut the fence open and they went in and what followed had been described by people who have come before you, sir. Your Lordship, I must say that the action of the men in uniform that day debased us as Africans bearing in mind that they did not respect human beings. From their action on that day, one could see that they wanted to kill. Almost everybody that was brought out of Kalakuta Republic sustained injury on his or her head. These people, in fact, really mowed their victims because they did not spare them at all. They were taken away naked. After the incident, we stood and made sure we got down what happened. I took down some of the numbers of the cars that were around. There was a Landrover NA1563A, a Peugeot 504, NA AD.2499 and another 504 NA AD 2414 and another 504, NA 2312. These were cars belonging to the senior officers who were standing under the shrine that day. I was in a potion to see all what happened from where I was and I saw them as they parked their cars in front of the shrine watching their boys performing. What annoyed me most was that there was a top Army officer there. I saw him here yesterday. I do not know whether he is here today. He was standing there on the day and the way he stood I guessed he was coming out from the officers’ Mess. His belt was not properly on. He was standing in front of Lido Hotel. His “batsman”, I do not know what they are called in the Army, those who carry gun behind the officers, went into Fela’s house while the boys were looting the minerals in the kiosk that was inside the house. The batsman took three bottles of minerals one 7up and two bottles of Fanta. He opened one, gave a salute and gave it to his officer. The officer drank out of the looted property. I can identify this officer anywhere. I know him. A lot of them did the same thing. Your Lordship, as I was saying earlier on, the Army came to power with hope of protecting the lives of the citizens of this country. This was as a result of the political situation in this country then in 1966. Now, these people who are meant to protect lives of the citizens of this country are now destroying the lives of citizens. Now, how safe are we when members of the Armed Forces are looting and even robbing with arms, because they carried guns there and this portrayed them as armed robbers. There were Police men who could have arrested Fela if he had committed any offence. Your Lordship, the decision is yours, I hope the lives of innocent citizens of this country would be saved, because we hear of this attached everyday all over the place. Thank you. Mr. Kayode-Idowu in the witness chair. Chairman examines Mr. Kayode-Idowu. Chairman: How old are you? Kayode-Idowu: I am 21. Q. How old were you in 1966. A. I was about ten. Q. When did you become member of YAP? A. I am a foundation member. Q. What year did you start the YAP? A. Last year October. Q. What are the aims and objectives of the YAP? A. To spread economic and cultural awareness Q. Who is your president? A. Fela Anikulapo-Kuti. Q. Have you got a Vice President? A. We do not believe in Bureaucracy much. Q. You believe in the President but you – A. You see, Fela is a black President. Q. Who is your Secretary? A. We have a care-taker Committee. Q. Comprising how many people? A. Three members. Q. How often do you meet? A. Regularly. Q. How regularly? A. Everyday because we have an office at the shrine. Q. I understand your membership is at the moment about 25,000 strong? A. Yes, Sir. Q. From where do you draw your members? A. All over Africa. Q. In this party of yours – A. It is a movement and not a party. Q. All right, call it a movement, it teaches you to have courage. A. You do not fear anything. A. We learn how to defend our rights as citizens. Q. To muster all the courage you can? A. Yes, as far as you can sustain it. Q. On this day, you saw all these things happened, things that could disturb the conscience of everybody in your movement. You did not do anything, you stood with your arms folded. A. Like I said, I ran to Kalakuta Close. That was the first thing I did. Q. What positive action did you take, if any? A. The soldiers were too many for my members, at least, they were armed. Like it is said, once one section of the country is armed and the other section is not armed, the armed section constitutes a danger to the unarmed section. The soldiers who surrounded Fela’s house on that day had guns and dangerous weapons that could destroy human lives. Q. About how many of your members were present in the Kalakuta and around that day? A. We have YAP members who live – Q. About how many of you? A. I could not have estimated because there were over 50,000 Nigerians who saw what happened on that day. I could not say how many YAP members were there. The situation was so tense. I was trying to observe as much as possible and to survive so that I could testify against these people. Q. You said that about 50,000 Nigerians were around on the day? A. Yes, and they saw it as it happened on that day, Sir. Chairman: All right, thank you. Mr. Kayode-Idowu: Can I submit the car numbers? Chairman: They have been taken down by the Official Reporters. Testimony of Kayode Idowu, “Proceedings of the Administrative Board of Inquiry into the Disturbances at 14A Agege Motor Road, Idi-Oro, Held at Cinema Hall II, National Arts Theatre, Lagos, 16th March, 1977, Day 9.” Lagos State Research and Archives Board, LCE.A12C. In 1977, Nigeria’s military dictator tried to silence his most famous opponent. Since independence from Great Britain in 1960, Nigeria had gone through a brief period of democracy, a civil war, and a series of military coups. The latest of those coups had brought to power General Olusegun Obasanjo, an authoritarian who hoped military-style discipline would make the country more orderly and prosperous. His opponent was Fela Kuti, a famous Afrobeat musician with a silver tongue and a youth following that the military thought looked suspiciously like a militia (the “Young African Pioneers,” as they called themselves). He was popular, profane, and relentlessly critical of the army. He scorned both the military and the British colonizers who had come before them, and in one famous song, “Zombie,” he mocked soldiers for their blind obedience. He had many fans abroad, which made him especially threatening to Nigeria’s image-conscious dictatorship. The military wanted to silence Fela, but they knew that throwing him in jail might make him a martyr. Instead, they took an indirect approach—wearing him down through raids, investigations, and trials. In March 1977, the army burned down Fela’s house and nightclub during one of those raids. They then staged a “commission of inquiry” about the fire. Ostensibly its purpose was to determine how it had started, but really it was to drag Fela’s name through the mud. Like the United States, Nigeria has a common-law legal system where the judiciary’s role is not just to enforce the rules but to constrain what the other branches of government can do. Like many authoritarians, Nigeria’s military dictators thought that law was on their side, and they staged trials like this thinking that judges were their allies. But as they learned, what happens in a courtroom can be unpredictable. In this document, we see a young man who was part of Fela’s entourage using his day in court not to denounce Fela, but to go after the military. Ultimately, the inquiry did not come to much; Fela paid some fines, a few of his supporters went to jail, and the soldiers who burned his house down got off scot-free. So how meaningful was this young man’s testimony in court? It’s debatable. But the outcome of a case like this is less important than the questions it raises. On its own, this testimony is a good starting point for an in-class discussion about how dictators and their critics use law. The “rule of law” is an important but widely misunderstood concept, and you can use this source to invite students to start defining it. The rule of law is the principle that everyone, including the people in power, should be subject to clear, established laws that define what they can and cannot do. This trial illustrates what happens when that principle starts to fail. After giving some context, work through the document with your students. It is a transcript of one of Fela’s Young African Pioneers, Kayode Idowu, being questioned about the raid that burned down Fela’s nightclub (the African Shrine, also referred to as the Kalakuta Republic in the document). Idowu starts by trying to talk about the events that brought the military to power, which the judge impatiently shuts down. He then describes the raid, lingering on how the soldiers started the fire. He dwells on the image of some officers blithely drinking looted sodas while the nightclub burns. Then Idowu criticizes the military in general, which the judge now lets him do. They take a break, and when they reconvene the judge asks him about the Young African Pioneers. Idowu answers these questions tersely, and then he is dismissed. After figuring out what’s going on in the document, students can assess its values and limitations as a source. A transcript like this records what was said, but we shouldn’t necessarily trust that what was said in the courtroom was true. There are some clues that Idowu is exaggerating—did fifty thousand people really witness the blaze? A better way to think about the document is as a record of a power play. Who has the upper hand changes from one question to the next. The transcript alone doesn’t tell us everything. We don’t know the tone of the interrogation, for example, or its context in the trial transcript as a whole (which runs to several thousand pages). Nonetheless, you can interpret something about each party’s intent even in this little fragment. You might ask: What do you think Idowu is trying to do through his testimony? What about the judge? What rhetorical strategies does the judge use to discredit Idowu? Do they seem to work on him? Ultimately the judge lets Idowu speak his mind, which he does, seemingly without worrying that he might incriminate himself. Why would the judge let him? And why do you think Idowu chose to speak freely? Do you trust Idowu as a witness? After a close read of this testimony, and with a recommended group listening to some of Fela’s music–especially “Zombie”—students could engage in an inquiry discussion of the following questions: How can we tell when the rule of law has stopped working? Why do people make stands against a dictatorship in court, even if they’re unlikely to win? Even in a “show trial” with a predetermined outcome, legal proceduralism can end up giving people a soapbox to criticize those in power. Witnesses can speak their minds on the stand, and judges don’t always toe the political line. It’s easy to assume that “law and order” is naturally on the side of authoritarianism. Is it? Fela Anikulapo Kuti, “Zombie,” 1976, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qj5x6pbJMyU. Tejumola Olaniyan, Arrest the Music! Fela and His Rebel Art and Politics (Indiana University Press, 2004). This biography places Fela in the context of his times. Olaniyan describes the 1977 raid in detail, and his account is consistent with Idowu’s in some ways but not in others. This could be the basis for a debate about perspective: Whose version of events should we trust more, and why? Eboe Hutchful and Abdoulaye Bathily, editors, The Military and Militarism in Africa (CODESRIA, 1998). This collection of essays describes how Africa’s military dictatorships worked at a time when many of them were still in power. Depending on how you use it, it could be a primary source about how military regimes were viewed at the turn of the twenty-first century, or a secondary source about their structural characteristics in the decades prior. To hear Samuel Fury Childs Daly share more about the source and how to teach it, visit https://www.youtube.com/@AmericanHistoricalReview. Photo by Robert Salazar for Bob. Samuel Fury Childs Daly is an associate professor of history at the University of Chicago. He is the author of A History of the Republic of Biafra: Law, Crime, and the Nigerian Civil War (Cambridge University Press, 2020) and Soldier’s Paradise: Militarism in Africa After Empire (Duke University Press, 2024), which has a chapter about Fela Kuti and his legal troubles.

papers.title: Andrew Lipman. Squanto: A Native Odyssey
papers.abstract: In his Bancroft Prize–winning book, The Saltwater Frontier, Andrew Lipman presented a gripping account of the seventeenth-century American Northeast, centering maritime encounters and violence between the region’s Indigenous inhabitants and European arrivals. In that book, perhaps the most famous man from Patuxet makes a brief appearance. Named Squanto, or Tisquantum, Lipman explains that the man from Patuxet saved the Plymouth Colony through his role as translator in negotiations with neighboring Wampanoags and his willingness to teach the English colonists how to cultivate crops. Squanto’s appearance in the pages of The Saltwater Frontier was necessarily fleeting. Nor was Squanto an unknown figure in need of explaining when Lipman penned his first book—Squanto’s real-life efforts to ensure the survival of the English colony has earned him a larger-than-life place in the American imagination as the individual often credited with bringing about the first Thanksgiving. In his new book, Squanto: A Native Odyssey, Lipman turns back to the life and world of Tisquantum. As a contemporary and ally of the notoriously verbose Plymouth colonists, Squanto’s life was well documented and has been written about frequently by scholars ever since. Despite the attention paid to certain aspects of Squanto’s life, Lipman’s book represents the first stand-alone study of the Patuxet man. One reason for this lack of a detailed biography of Squanto is sources, which were predominantly penned by Englishmen who Lipman argues “were genuinely curious about Squanto and his people” but who wrote within a wider world in which “their motivation was to claim and rule Native land” (4). The documentary record has not allowed for a traditional biography of Squanto since basic biographical details, such as whether or not he ever married or had children, remain obscure. To counter the “blinkered perspectives” of colonial writers, Lipman draws from a multidisciplinary array of sources and methods to create a “mosaic of evidence” against which he critically and productively reads the colonial record (4, 5). The result is a compelling and important “new picture of a man too often rendered as a caricature” (6).

papers.title: Mary E. Hicks. Captive Cosmopolitans: Black Mariners and the World of South Atlantic Slavery
papers.abstract: Mary E. Hicks has produced an insightful and deftly nuanced study of Black mariners in 18th- and early 19th-century Bahia in the best intellectual traditions of both Atlantic and Brazilian history. She conceptualizes them as captive cosmopolitans: individuals mostly enslaved and often born in Africa who manned and piloted ships transporting enslaved individuals and trading goods across the South Atlantic, the space between the Bight of Benin and Northeastern Brazil. The conditions of their enslavement were substantially different from the plantation slave paradigm: They “demanded constant motion” (2) aboard transatlantic ships, leading to a historical trajectory characterized by mobility, autonomy, and access to manumission—but still within the legal boundaries of slavery. Hicks starts Captive Cosmopolitans by charting their historical origins in a genuinely transatlantic manner. Not only were Black mariners a well-known figure in late medieval Lisbon and Portugal, they were also instrumental to Portuguese commercial penetration in West Africa in the early modern era. They manned ships, practiced commerce—sometimes beyond the confines of what the Portuguese state allowed—and participated in the formation of a culturally ambidextrous populations in Elmina and other cities and trading posts along the West African coast. Meanwhile, in Bahia the ascent of sugar as an export crop led to an explosion in the slave, and later free Black, population. By 1700, the traditional West African dexterity and cultural traditions in maritime activities such as shipbuilding, fishing, and navigation quickly led to a Black predominance among Bahia’s watermen, including those employed in slaving expeditions to the African coast.

papers.title: An End to All Doubt and Disorder: Genealogy and Law in Spanish History
papers.abstract: This article argues that centuries of compilations of laws in Spain, and possibly elsewhere in Europe, were not evidence of a desire to make statutes more comprehensible or efficient, as is generally assumed by historians, but rather a statement of royal power and genealogy. What we call law today is a far cry from late medieval and early modern law, whose symbolic role outweighed its practical function. From the thirteenth to the early nineteenth centuries, Spanish monarchs in their prefaces to these enormous volumes always claimed the compilations would end disorder and confusion, seen as the enemies of good rule. These volumes provided an implicit history of rule, made visible through glosses, and in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries this implicit link became explicit, as laws and historical chronicles were the object of parallel compilation programs by the crown and the Cortes. There was good reason for monarchs and lawmakers to believe that fat volumes of law and history were part of the same project. It was not the content of either sort of book that mattered, but rather their physical existence and their proclamation of origins, authority, and completeness.

papers.title: Nations Behind Transnationalism: State Power and the Allegiances of Italian-Tunisians, 1920s–1940s
papers.abstract: This article examines the intricate historical currents that shaped the conflicting allegiances of Italian-Tunisians during the interwar years. Marked by multilingualism and cultural hybridity, these communities expressed radical forms of nationalist identification with their country of origin. Through an exploration of the diverse sociocultural facets of the Italian-Tunisian communities and their intricate interplay with the Italian state’s involvements in Tunisia, the article analyzes the mechanisms underlying the paradoxical coexistence between nationalism and transnationalism. The article shows that these divergent traits had common roots in the sociopolitical position occupied by Italian-Tunisians in the context of interwar Tunisia. Consequently, these Italian-Tunisian communities emerge as the basis for a rich case study, shedding light on the possible alliances and mutual reinforcement that can occur between national political projects and migrant transnational social formations.

papers.title: Beastly Ambiguity: Monkey Theater in Paris, 1600–1789
papers.abstract: This article examines live animals as symbolic media in early modern and eighteenth-century Europe. Animal performances had become a common phenomenon in European cities by the eighteenth century. Since the influential debate that Robert Darnton’s article “Workers Revolt: The Great Cat Massacre of the Rue Saint Severin” triggered in The Journal of Modern History, the extent to which historians could read accounts of such performances as anthropological “texts” and to thus decipher inherent “signs” and symbolism has remained highly controversial. Recent writing in the history of animals has questioned the validity of interpreting the presence of animals as passive stand-ins for their symbolic meaning. Rather, human-animal encounters are now seen increasingly in terms of the interspecies cooperation that made them possible in the first place. This article argues that the newer history of a shared human-animal world can be enriched by the analysis of cases of human-animal interaction that served symbolic purposes. It focuses on the history of the particularly well-documented case of live monkey performances in Paris. Between 1600 and 1789, performances of trained monkeys produced monkey stars who became famous across Europe. Monkeys could become celebrities because, as a medium, they were suited to addressing particular preoccupations of the eighteenth-century French public sphere: celebrity culture, divisions in the society of orders, and the human-animal divide. Moreover, they did so in a way that stayed just shy of censorship, allowing us to gauge more astutely the limits of public discourse during the Enlightenment.

papers.title: Seasonal Sedition: The Environmental Limits of Gunrunning across the Arabian Sea, 1899–1914
papers.abstract: Abstract: In recent years, historians have increasingly drawn attention to the myriad weaknesses that plagued colonial empires during the second half of the nineteenth century. One of these shortcomings was the ease with which contraband traversed their borders. In this regard, environmental knowledge has been highlighted as critical in helping smugglers to skirt attempts at regulation and repression. The challenges faced by these smugglers, however, have received less attention. Using gunrunning in the Arabian Sea as an analytical lens, the following article contends that smuggling networks evolved in response to environmental vulnerabilities as much as advantages. Topography, seasonality, and climate all imposed spatial and temporal constraints on gunrunning operations. In turn, these pressures influenced how imperial authority was contested and upheld along colonial frontiers.

papers.title: Mendel All the Way? Genetics and Plant Breeding in the British Cotton Belt
papers.abstract: Abstract: This article analyzes the impact of genetics on colonial agriculture in the British Empire, examining two case studies of cotton breeding in early twentieth-century Egypt and Uganda. Scholars have long been skeptical that genetics had any immediate impact on plant breeding. I argue that such skepticism is justified. Genetics made little practical difference to cotton breeding in the first decade of the twentieth century. Colonial administrators and agriculturalists in this period were concerned with longstanding biological problems rooted in persistent social and economic anxieties: notably the degeneration of plants and varietal mixing. In the early 1900s, colonial officials implemented programs of seed selection and—most dramatically—the complete destruction of mixed cotton stocks in Uganda, with the goal of restarting the industry from scratch. These schemes, however, relied not on genetics, but drew on established techniques or existing economic and eugenical principles.

papers.title: Nicki Kindersley. New Sudans: Wartime Intellectual Histories in Khartoum
papers.abstract: Nicki Kindersley’s book New Sudans: Wartime Intellectual Histories in Khartoum explores the intellectual, political, and educational lives of southern Sudanese displaced by the Second Sudanese Civil War (1983–2005) to the capital, Khartoum. One of the outcomes of the 2005 peace agreement that brought an end to the civil war was the independence referendum that brought about the secession of South Sudan in 2011, and thus the departure of many of those who had lived in Khartoum during the war years from the capital to join the new nation. Indeed, most of the research for this book was conducted in South Sudan in the years following secession. Yet the title speaks to alternative possibilities through its wink to the “New Sudan” vision most associated with John Garang, the leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army during the civil war. The New Sudan vision sought less to separate the south and more to emancipate all the marginalized populations in Sudan, who in the view of its advocates were being exploited by a hegemonic elite in Khartoum.

papers.title: Communications
papers.abstract: To the Editor: New Orleans, with its colonial roots in the Francophone Atlantic, its Latin European military and legal traditions, its complex religious culture, and its challenge to Anglo-America’s rigid color line, has long perplexed most United States historians. Andrew N. Wegmann proves this point in his review of my book, Creole New Orleans in the Revolutionary Atlantic, 1775-1877 (2023). Though the reviewer finds my use of the ethnic designation “Afro-Creole” a “potentially troubling term,” (American Historical Review 130, no. 2 [2025],956), it is widely used in academic discourse and in published works. In the essay, “Can the Church Evolve?” in the New York Review of Books (June 12, 2025:6), for instance, columnist Fintan O’Toole references Pope Leo XIV’s (Robert Francis Prevost) “Afro-Creole” roots in New Orleans as embodying the hybrid nature of the nation’s identity. My book, the reviewer also complains, “never productively defines the term and usage of ‘Creole,’” brushing aside or overlooking my discussion of its origins in Spanish America where colonial Black people coined the term “criollo” to apply to African-descended peoples born in the Americas (956). The Spaniards broadened the term’s usage to apply to all native-born colonists with the French, like the Spanish, applying “créole” to its colonial populations. With the arrival of Anglo-Americans in Louisiana, the designation came under increasing attack (Bell, 93).

papers.title: Grasping the Pencil: Polish Memoirs of Childhood on the Eastern Front, 1914–1921
papers.abstract: This article recovers the voices of civilian survivors of World War I in parts of today’s Ukraine, Lithuania, Belarus, and Poland. Drawing on a rare cache of retrospective accounts composed in 1930s Poland for memoir-writing competitions, it foregrounds the voices of peasants and poor people in villages and small towns at the front lines, particularly those who survived the war as children and young people. Surveying their narratives of violence, hunger, disease, and displacement, it asks how memoirists made sense of their wartime experience in an autobiographical context, considering the relationship between war, literacy, and knowledge, on the one hand, and trauma, “brutalization,” and resilience on the other. For all its horrors, the memoirs show that war could generate new mobilities, perspectives, and subjectivities; destruction and chaos could break open vistas of a wider world. The article concludes by considering how both nationalist frameworks and geospatial imaginaries have contributed to silencing this history of war from the margins. It argues that civilians’ experience on the Eastern Front should be centered not only in the history of World War I but also in the broader social history of twentieth-century warfare and state violence.

papers.title: On the Edge of Power: Peasants and Escape Ecologies in Eastern Europe, 1700–1850
papers.abstract: The article explores the impact of inaccessible landscapes (such as forests, swamps, and wastelands) on the relationship between subjects and centers of power (such as the nobility and the state) in Eastern Europe during the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. This region’s situation was unique because successive disasters, including the Little Ice Age, eighty years of continuous warfare, epidemics, and economic collapse, resulted in significant depopulation and the re-wilding of vast areas of Poland, Lithuania, and Ukraine in the early eighteenth century. The dominant historical narrative portrays this period in an unequivocally negative light. This text aims to present a more nuanced perspective. While the disasters at the turn of the eighteenth century affected all social classes, the weakening of the repressive apparatus due to the crisis, coupled with the growth of forests, floodplains, and wastelands, caused the eighteenth-century Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth to become a destination for mass migration, particularly from neighboring enlightened monarchies. For many people in Central and Eastern Europe, migrating to a country offering ample hiding places, easy access to the commons, and significant privileges for folk colonizers was more appealing than living under the often repressive systems introduced by modern states, such as compulsory conscription, high taxes, and the elimination of cultural or religious autonomy.

papers.title: Migration, Adaptation, and Innovation: Firearms and Franco-Ottoman Technological Dialogue in Eighteenth-Century Algiers
papers.abstract: Abstract: This article explores the mission of two French cannon founders, Dupont Sr. and his son François, to build a new foundry and produce cannons for the Ottoman Algerian authorities in 1772–1775. The analysis of consular correspondence and Arabic and Ottoman inscriptions on the cannons produced in Algiers between 1775 and 1782 challenges the preconceived notion of a mere technological transfer from Europe to an Islamic country. Focusing on Dupont’s experience as migrant-expert, it becomes clear that a successful technological enterprise requires a dialogue between foreign and local experts. This dialogue involved technical features as well as socio-religious matters concerning the migrant’s experience in a foreign place. Using the technologies of cannon making as a case study, this micro-global analysis examines the successful development of an innovative product by migrants coming from different parts of the Mediterranean world, such as Rochefort, Algiers, Switzerland, and Istanbul.

papers.title: China in African Americans’ Struggle for Equality, 1900–1919
papers.abstract: Abstract: The existing literature suggests that African Americans historically approached China either as a reliable ally or as a supplicant to white people. However, these perspectives mainly pertain to the post-1930s relationship. Prior to this period, African Americans ascribed a different significance to China in their quest for equality. They regarded it as an inadvertent destabilizer of America’s prevailing racial hierarchy, which marginalized African Americans as non-members of the nation. They asserted their claim to national inclusion by expressing pride in the supposed appeal of American civilization among the Chinese, protesting the neglect by white Americans, and pledging to adopt resistance strategies from China. These assertions, aimed at proving African Americans’ eligibility for full American identity, reflect complex attitudes toward a non-white Other as well as their resourcefulness in seeking pathways to achieve equality.

papers.abstract: Abstract: This article carries out a general analysis and quantification of the evolution of international coffee markets since the late 1980s, when the economic clauses of the International Coffee Agreement (ICA), in force since 1962, were suspended. These clauses assigned export quotas to different producing countries and established fluctuation bands for prices to keep them within a range that made them predictable for producers and consumers. In this article, the case of Mexico is used to exemplify these impacts on peasant economies.

papers.title: Bowl By Bowl: Black Women, Food Selling, and Survival in the Antebellum North
papers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the lives of Black women, free and enslaved, who hawked prepared foods like pepper pot stew on the streets and in the markets of northern cities between the late-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Though ubiquitous in their own time, evidence relating to female provisioners is scattered and thin. These women appear, fleetingly, in newspaper accounts, reminiscences, census records, legal documents, and visual culture. Stitching together these archival fragments reveals the importance of Black women to urban commerce. Food selling allowed them to evade the coercion associated with most kinds of work available to them but forced them into fraught negotiations in public space. Most Black women vendors earned meager incomes, but for a few of them, this selling offered relatively good compensation. By keeping a sharp focus on these petty entrepreneurs, this study offers a critical new perspective on northern urban life, labor, and racial hierarchies during the nineteenth century.

papers.title: Reading John Selden’s Titles of honor (1614) as a Work of Polemic
papers.abstract: Abstract First published in 1614, John Selden’s Titles of honor has long been ignored by historians of political thought. A large and compendious description of the various titles of Europe and the Near East; by its structure and tone, it resembles nothing more than a work of dusty antiquarianism. It attracted none of the controversy that would plague Selden’s Historie of tithes (1618); and it did not state its polemical purpose in such explicit terms as his Mare clausum (1635). If historians of political thought have remembered it at all, they have done so because Thomas Hobbes recommended the work in chapter 10 of Leviathan (1651). This article will treat Titles of honor as a work of political intention. Following Selden’s engagement with Roman Civil Law, it will argue that he composed the treatise to criticize sixteenth-century theories of resistance, and the medieval theories of divided sovereignty upon which they were founded. In short, this article will seek to reframe Titles of honor as a defence of state sovereignty against theories of noble resistance – and so explain Hobbes’s affection for the work.

papers.title: Galileo’s Three Repudiations of Copernicanism – Two Coerced and One Volunteered
papers.abstract: Abstract Up to 1616, when the Copernican theory of heliocentrism was prohibited, Galileo had never asserted its truth. But the pope and cardinals of the Roman Inquisition assumed that he had, and he was required to repudiate it. In contrast, Copernicus’s book was only lightly corrected and allowed to be read. Galileo continued his practice of not asserting the reality of heliocentrism in his Dialogue on the two world systems, but he was put on trial nevertheless, in 1633. However, instead of being charged with a crime to be proved, as required by canon law, he was subjected to pre-trial interrogation and intimidation, and he confessed to a made-up crime. His conviction entailed another repudiation of the static sun, on pain of harsh punishment. In subsequent years, even though he was reckless in expressing preference for the condemned theory, he still did not advocate it. In fact, in writing to the Tuscan ambassador to Venice in 1641, he insisted that the Copernican system was false, because theologians said so. However, he went on to say that the opposing Ptolemaic view was actually erroneous, while the other was merely insufficient – because stellar parallax (which would prove the earth’s orbit) could not yet be measured.

papers.title: Armed Robberies in Colonial Asante: Official Denial, Private Speculation, and the Perpetuation of Stereotype, 1935–45
papers.abstract: Abstract Armed robberies that occurred in colonial Asante between 1935 and 1945 made life unbearable. This caused the colonial state and the restored Asante monarchy to try to find solutions to the growing insecurity. This article considers the various reactions to the armed robberies as a lens on the colonial state’s relationship with Asante society at the height of colonial power (1935–45). We argue that the colonial state was undercut by tensions, contradictions, and conflicts, which produced paralysis at times, rendering its approach inconsistent. This contention goes against the image of benevolence and goodwill presented by the colonial state in Asante historiography. This article draws on a previously unexplored set of records from the Kumase branch of Ghana’s Public Records and Archives Administration Department and the Manhyia Archives, newspaper articles, and state commission reports to make its case.

papers.title: Enduring Medical Knowledge in the Age of Slavery
papers.abstract: Abstract Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century slave management texts, plantation guidebooks, medical dissertations, and treatises on preserving health in hot climates functioned as authoritative sources on the specific traits, symptoms, and health complaints of enslaved Black people. That said, information found in these texts, especially specific physiological assertions about Black people’s bodies, were not always uniform. While doctors largely agreed that Black people had a high pain tolerance and ease during childbirth, there was less consensus around the amount of therapeutic bloodletting Black people should undergo, mainly owing to beliefs that their bodies were not so well suited for it. Scholars have done well to demonstrate the ways in which physicians and plantation doctors made and accepted claims about Black people’s susceptibility to disease, but less attention has been paid to how and why the need to bleed slaves sparingly failed to take hold as an unquestioned truth about Black people’s bodies in the way that Black people’s high tolerance to pain did. The broad question ‘what did doctors think a Black person’s body could withstand?’ provides an instructive framework for interrogating the selective acceptance of certain claims about Black people’s bodies and the factors that led plantation doctors to embrace or disregard them.

papers.title: Getting creative with medieval landscape fragments: the Hull Maritime Museum, late-medieval poetry, and digital availability
papers.abstract: Abstract In this article, I reflect on my creative practice in the poetry pamphlet Exhibits from the Maritime Museum & the City, an output of my poetry residency at the Hull Maritime Museum from 2020 to 2021. Exhibits is intended as an alternative creative guide to the museum. Drawing on an established tradition of contemporary poets who ‘revoice’ medieval texts and landscapes, these poems engage with the fragmentary layered aural, textual, and environmental medieval landscapes of Hull and the Humber estuary as they are mediated through the museum and its collection of objects or artefacts. They collect literary and historical fragments of a medieval landscape of Hull and the Humber to create a sense of place around the gaps in history. Crucially, there is also space for the contemporary reader/visitor to build a bi-directional relationship with medieval landscapes in these gaps. To widen general access to these poems, which is to diversify the revoiced medieval landscapes of Hull and the Humber, I have created a freely available digital version using a simple weebly website: https://exhibitsfromthemaritimemuseum.weebly.com. Influenced by the long tradition of digitizing medieval manuscripts, I discuss the digital materiality of this online version of the contemporary poetry pamphlet Exhibits and how the reader/visitor might use this to engage with and potentially contribute to medieval landscapes.

papers.title: Quantifying narrative structure: a study of implicit narration and intermittent revelation in The Sing-Song Girls of Shanghai
papers.abstract: Abstract The Sing-Song Girls of Shanghai marks the inception of urban modernity narrative in Chinese literature, and it features the narrative structure of the ‘implicit narration’ and ‘intermittent revelation’. This paper proposes a conceptual model and an operational methodology for dissecting and quantifying this narrative structure. Integrating narrative theory with quantitative text analysis, we identify and extract key markers across three dimensions: character, place, and event. In the character dimension, we analyse word frequency, distribution, and co-occurrence networks among characters. The spatial dimension is examined through kernel density analysis of plot movement, while the event dimension is investigated using character-event and place-event co-occurrence matrices. The results reveal three core mechanisms: (1) Key characters function as agents of ‘intermittent revelation’, bridging disparate narrative threads; (2) Spatial organization is strategically deployed, with the Fourth Avenue brothel district enabling the rapid scene shifts of ‘implicit narration’, and the Conical Hat Garden serving as a consolidated stage for the suspension and reactivation of multiple plots in ‘intermittent revelation’; (3) Drinking parties act as narrative springboards for ‘implicit narration’, while the strategic shift from private encounters to public conversations refines ‘intermittent revelation’ through controlled disclosure and sustained suspense. In summary, this study elucidates how Han Bangqing orchestrated these elements into a distinctive narrative architecture and provides a replicable quantitative framework for analysing narrative structure.

papers.title: Hans Zeiss and Thomas Müntzer: Strange Bedfellows during the German Peasants’ War of 1525
papers.abstract: Abstract The name of Thomas Müntzer is relatively well-known, but the names and lives of several of his contacts are not. Among these was Hans Zeiss, the tax-collector in the town of Allstedt where Müntzer was preacher for eighteen months. Caught between his responsibilities as the local representative of the princes of Saxony and his enthusiasm for Müntzer’s radical theology, as tensions grew between Müntzer and the local and regional nobility, Zeiss found himself obliged to procrastinate. And as discontent erupted into open rebellion, he – like many others – had to choose between his livelihood and the radical German Reformation.

papers.title: The literary and digitals otters of The Voyage of St. Brendan the Abbot and Brendan’s Voyage
papers.abstract: Abstract Composed in Anglo-Norman French during the 1120’s, The Voyage of St. Brendan the Abbot features a striking episode in which an island hermit named Paul recalls his reliance on an otter who brought fish to the ascetic for thirty years. This little studied passage is remarkable for the way in which the poet positions the otter as a humanlike source of technical skill and hospitality alongside a hermit who exhibits animal qualities in his rugged physiognomy far from human community. Such an arrangement of the otter and hermit suggests that vulnerability and hospitality are shared features of animality and humanity. This specific vision invites readers—both medieval and modern—to construe animals and humans as distinctive while sharing in a common identity rooted in bodily precarity as well as the possibility of extending aid. These dynamics recur in Brendan’s Voyage, a five-module video game prototype supported by the National Endowment for the Humanities with the aim of teaching basic features of Anglo-Norman French through the story of St. Brendan. By comparing the literary and digital otters of the medieval source poem and its video game adaptation, this article positions Brendan’s Voyage as an opportunity to remediate the original poem’s expansive vision of animals, humans, vulnerability, and hospitality for a modern audience.

papers.title: Contact zone, desertion, or endurance? A spatial digital humanities approach to interpreting Irish medieval settlements
papers.abstract: Abstract Following a successful pilot phase, the Human-Environmental Exchanges in the Landscapes of Medieval Ireland Project (HELM) has developed an interdisciplinary methodology to identify the location and features of heretofore thought vanished medieval settlements. This innovative methodology integrates evidence from historical accounts, archaeological fieldwork, and remote sensing data collected by Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV, or drone). Digital models created and analyzed during project workflows are used to identify the minute remnants of medieval vernacular building in the present-day landscape. This article highlights the project’s methodology, illustrating how its innate adaptability is used to generate research hypotheses. In the case study provided the medieval town of Fore in County Westmeath, Ireland, at first appeared to have few remnants of medieval vernacular activity. However, contextual analysis led to the development of a new theory to the overall project of endurance and resilience at many medieval settlement sites. Fore also allows the examination of how ordinary people negotiated life in a medieval contact zone between two ethnic identities.

papers.title: The Mandeville -author’s sense of space: a digital–ecological reading of Mandeville’s Travels
papers.abstract: Abstract Combining digital and eco-critical analyses, this essay argues that in the Middle English version of Mandeville’s Travels, authorial emphasis on the topographical and theological centrality of Jerusalem forms the ideological keynote. Nevertheless, the overarching tendency of constructing the Holy City within the framework of composing a Christocentric universal history coincides with occasional shifts of authorial attention to the prospering civilizations in the non-Christian East (e.g. Cathay, India, and Arabia), which corresponds to some temporary and local centres of the fourteenth-century world system. In the Travels, the Mandeville-author’s sentiments of Christocentric universalism are conveyed primarily through spatial narrative. But dialectically, authorial acknowledgement and veneration of the East as an economically, technologically, and morally more advanced existence can also be extrapolated from the Mandevillian descriptions of the world. Confronted with the dual discourse, this essay endeavours to conduct a four-dimensional digital analysis grounded in the use of Geographical Information System and Computational Linguistics. It aims to further investigate the Mandeville-author’s Janus-faced world-view, as embodied by and reflected from their interlaced centralizing and de-centralizing narratives of Latin Christendom throughout the Travels. Consisting of frequency analysis, geographical visualization, directionality analysis, and verb–preposition analysis, the case study here exemplifies the Mandeville-author’s deeply entangled geospatial and ecological concerns that are elusive to traditional close reading. It also renders a fine-grained picture of the dynamics between cosmopolitan and Christocentric sentiments in the Mandeville-author’s cognitive mapping of the world.

papers.title: Imperial Family Biographies and New Approaches to the Family in Histories of the British Empire, c.1650–c.1950
papers.abstract: Abstract Recently, there have been several histories of the British Empire written through the lens of a single family. These works – which this review refers to as imperial family biographies – trace the activities, ideas, and/or connections of a group of individuals from the same family, usually spanning more than one generation, as they roved across the time and space of empire. They facilitate an understanding of a networked, informal British Empire, held together by personal bonds and material goods, and an imperial politics shaped by emotions, affections, and identities. Currently, imperial family biographies tend to prioritize asking what families can reveal about empire, rather than what empire can reveal about families; family networks are used as case studies, dictating the bounds of study and illustrating wider imperial themes. This review argues that this genre of history writing is most successful when families are interpreted as imperial agents that drove historical change, rather than merely conduits for individual action or means by which individuals were connected across empire. This can be achieved through a thorough engagement with the historiography on families and through centralizing concepts such as family identity, family culture, family structure, and family function.

papers.title: Digital objects as translation: their digitization depth as a taxonomy for digital analogues
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital collections of historical objects are increasingly the first interface when setting up new academic enquiries in the Humanities. This influences how research questions are formed. The size of these collections is posited to grow even more as the costs of digitization decrease and access widens. Framing digital collections and their contents correctly is therefore of great importance. However, in many cases the conceptualization of digitized collections remains in practice tied to the mistaken notion that digital copies are surrogates for the analogue originals they represent, with serious implications for how these items are organized. This article builds from earlier seminal contributions to argue that digitized objects are a different entity altogether, neither copy nor surrogate. This difference can be captured more faithfully by the notion of ‘digital translation’: digital objects are a selective description of the physical original; this description is translated into digital language and written in symbols bound by rules. This structured information can be read algorithmically. From this definition, we can derive a taxonomy based on the depth of digitization, that is, how many layers of description exist about the object. These layers often include shape, colour, and recorded metadata. Adopting a by-depth taxonomy has ramifications for existing digital collections: if digital objects are individualized translations of an original, their digital collections are collections of commentaries in digital language reflecting specific ways of seeing the original. If digitization depth differentiates these sources, our archival and dissemination strategies must respond to this reality.

papers.title: Exploring textual features of Chinese online literature: a multi-level digital humanities framework for literary texts
papers.abstract: Abstract Chinese online literature has become a major contemporary literary phenomenon, yet its linguistic characteristics remain underexplored from a large-scale empirical perspective. To address this gap, this study adopts a digital humanities framework and conducts a corpus-based, multi-level quantitative analysis using a self-constructed large-scale corpus of Chinese online literature. The Qidian Online Literature Corpus (QOLC) was built through automated web scraping and stratified sampling, covering male-targeted, female-targeted, and light novels. Using computational linguistic methods, the study examines textual form, lexical usage, structural complexity, semantic organization, stylistic variation, and emotional dynamics. The results reveal that online literature exhibits distinctive linguistic patterns that differentiate it from traditional written and spoken forms, which this study characterizes as an Oralized Written Register. Its linguistic features include moderate lexical richness, low lexical density, Zipf’s law of lexical distributions, dialogue-driven narration with compact syntax, gender-invariant nMDD despite sentence-length variation, and a PCA-identified stylistic dichotomy. In addition, systematic stylistic differences are observed between male- and female-oriented novels. Overall, this research offers a data-driven taxonomy of the stylistic features of Chinese online literature, underscoring the effectiveness of computational methods in characterizing emerging literary forms and the value of quantitative analysis in digital humanities research.

papers.title: CONFISCATION AS GOVERNANCE IN THE OTTOMAN EMPIRE, 1750–1839
papers.abstract: Abstract Müsadere, the confiscation of the estates of dismissed or deceased officials in the Ottoman Empire, has been viewed as a marker of despotism, an impediment to capitalism, a legitimate form of punishment, and a useful fiscal and political instrument. However, beyond case studies, the empire-wide logic and dynamics behind this practice remain elusive. Using both qualitative evidence and a rich dataset of confiscation attempts informed by a historically-informed interpretative scheme, this article examines the dynamics that shaped the enforcement of müsadere and their broader implications. Focusing on the period from 1750 to 1839, which was marked by an unprecedented surge in confiscations amid wars, fiscal crises, and tensions with regional intermediaries, it shows that calculations of cost and benefit, the bargaining power of families, and competition among rival factions shaped the enforcement of müsadere. It also makes a broader argument that in an era of increased dependence on intermediaries, often interpreted as one of decentralization, the imperial government used these confiscations as a selective mechanism of governance to discipline its agents, redistribute offices and resources, and recalibrate centre–periphery relations without jeopardizing essential alliances. Viewed comparatively, the Ottoman experience reflects an organizational trade-off faced by early modern polities in managing the risks of delegated authority. It demonstrates how an early modern polity could tolerate, negotiate, or even rely on forms of inherited or appropriated office, while simultaneously reclaiming public resources, typically seen as two opposing paths of state formation.

papers.title: Special issue—Digital Humanities 2023: Collaboration as Opportunity
papers.abstract: The 2023 edition of ADHO’s annual global conference ‘Digital Humanities’ took place in Graz under the theme of ‘Collaboration as Opportunity’. DH2023 showcased transdisciplinary and transnational collaboration, with a special focus on the thriving South-Eastern European Digital Humanities community. It explored how mutual empowerment and collaboration of neighbouring countries—regardless of continent and geopolitical placement—can transform regional hubs of expertise into international networks of excellent research, to the benefit of the global DH community. The programme committee, chaired by Toma Tasovac and Anne Baillot, accepted 361 submissions (125 short papers, 108 long papers, 112 posters, and 16 panels). It was the first on-site conference since the COVID-19 pandemic. There are several records of this: video interviews with participants and snapshots from the event can be found on YouTube, as well as recordings of the sessions via the DH Graz channel (https://www.youtube.com/@dh_graz137), curated by Sina Krottmaier and Thea Schaaf. There is also the Book of Abstracts, archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7961821), in which you can find how all 1,369 authors made the case for their research before the event. This special issue now collects what they thought about their topics after the conference. In this volume, you will find research in many well-established fields of DH: data modelling, linked data, and ontologies are covered by Massari et al., Andrews, Langeloh, Sagi et al., Romein et al., and Junginger. Textual analysis, corpus linguistics, and computational literary studies are topics of the contributions by Hall et al., Angermaier et al., Rafaeli et al., Takeuchi and Ogiso, Korecky-Kröll et al., and Kavčič et al. Visual analysis is done by Vignoli et al. and Llewellyn et al. Creation of digital resources in digital scholarly editions, archives, and bibliographies is done by Stangl et al., Bleier et al., Li and Li, Clement and Wintermeier, and VanderHart and Weigl. Finally, Schreibman et al., Kizhner et al., Hu et al., Bocanegra Barbecho, Horvàth et al., Sichani et al., and Winters et al. target the social, cultural, ethical, and community dimensions of DH. However, taking the topic of the conference into account, the contributions go far beyond this rather traditional reading of DH: They discuss community building (Winters et al.), joint international activities (Schreibman et al., Sichani et al.), and interlinguistic and intercultural data representations in shared infrastructures (Sagi et al., Langeloh, Stangl et al., Junginger, Romein et al., Kavčič et al.). Hu et al., Kizhner et al., and Li and Li address international and intercultural topics. Collaboration with non-academics is studied by Bocanegra Barbecho and Clement and Wintermeier. Transdisciplinary cooperation leads to the introduction of new technologies into the humanities by VanderHart and Weigl and Vignoli et al., and is at the core of continuous work on more or less established digital methods of DH (Hall et al., Rafaeli et al., Angermeier et al., Takeuchi and Ogiso, Korecky-Kröll et al., Horváth et al., and Andrews). Talking about collaboration: Managing a special issue can only be achieved by a team. We were eight (Georg Vogeler, Christof Schöch, Diane Jakacky, Elisa Cugliana, Anne Ladyem McDivitt, Miriam Peña Pimentel, Nadezhda Povroznik, and Edward Vanhoutte) and asked countless reviewers for their evaluation of the contributions. According to the reviewing principles of DSH, they are kept anonymous, but it is important to stress their unseen labour: thorough engagement with the text submitted and the research on the topic, careful, constructive, and appreciative comments take time. Collaboration is an opportunity here.

papers.title: HISTORICAL REALITY: A MANIFESTO
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT From the times of Herodotus and Thucydides until deep into the eighteenth century, the eyewitness account (or “autopsy”) was the model for historical knowledge. The eighteenth‐century Historical Revolution replaced this emphasis on autopsy by introducing the notion of the point of view, as explicated in Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's Monadology . That notion radically separated the historian's present from the world of the eyewitness's past. Historical knowledge was, from this point on, essentially ex post facto , and autopsy was reduced to the status of that which offers essentially questionable historical evidence. This amounted to the greatest revolution in Western historical thought, and it led to the birth of historist professional writing as it still exists today. Unfortunately, after the 1850s, historist reflection on professional historical writing was abandoned for a neo‐Kantian approach. Since then, many other approaches have been tried out on professional historical writing; pragmatism is the most recent variant. None of these approaches produced lasting results, nor are any such results to be expected. Results were never cumulative: Each time the blackboard was wiped clean again in order to write a new attempt. This is because historical writing must be seen from its historist inside and not from an external perspective. This article is a manifesto that invites philosophers of history to recognize that historist professional historical writing was born from Leibniz's Monadology and that Leibniz's thought is, therefore, the inside of its inside. Accepting this is necessary in order to bring about a more fruitful and, above all, more interesting philosophy of history than we've had for almost two centuries.

papers.title: Medical Practitioners, The Archive, and the Making of Slavery in Early Modern Barbados
papers.abstract: Abstract In seventeenth-century Barbados medical practitioners abounded, frequently operated as planters and merchants, and amassed sizeable estates. Their wills and property deeds attest to the efficacy of their professional ambitions and their important role in the formation of colonial Barbadian society. They also testify, unambiguously, to the frequency with which medical practitioners owned enslaved individuals, whose names were as prominent and more numerous in medical wills than were the names of wives, children, siblings, and friends. How should we consider this question of slave-ownership, and how does it fit into broader scholarship on the professionalization of medicine and its relationship to slavery and race? Mapping the wills and deeds of roughly 121 of these individuals, this paper examines the presence of medical practitioners in seventeenth-century Barbados, the practice of enslavement by these colonial medical men, and the archival relationship between these two historical phenomena.

papers.title: George Wallace and Britain’s First Abolitionist Publication (1760)
papers.abstract: Abstract This article offers an in-depth analysis of a little-known work, George Wallace’s A s ystem of the principles of the law of Scotland (1760), which contains the first text in Britain that explicitly advocated total and immediate abolition of both slavery and the slave trade. Wallace’s demand was that the Scottish court immediately recognize the inalienable natural liberty of any person arriving from the American colonies, and he thus anticipated by over a decade the first court cases in Britain which did precisely that. But Wallace went even further, drawing on a wide range of ideas and theories to reject any possible justification for slavery in any form. This article discusses the ways in which he constructed his novel philosophical, political, and legal arguments, the intellectual context of his uncompromising antislavery position, and the surprisingly wide reception of his now-forgotten work. It focuses on Wallace’s nuanced engagements with his multiple sources, including his debts to Montesquieu and to his father, Robert Wallace, a freethinking Church of Scotland minister. Close attention is given to George Wallace’s radical appropriation of Roman law, as well as the laws of nature and nations – traditions that had previously been used to justify, rather than challenge, slavery.

papers.title: Campus-Based Digital Approaches to Making Visible the Hispanic Past and Latino Present of North Florida
papers.abstract: This article reflects on digital oral history and digital documentary editing as approaches to public history pedagogy that allow undergraduate students to engage with the past and present in ways that have implications for local communities. The authors look at these methods in the context of two projects at the University of North Florida that highlight the role that speakers of Spanish play in the history and culture of the region: Voces y Caras: Latinx Communities of North Florida and the Florida Series of the digital editing workshop coloniaLab. The authors are the faculty leaders of those projects and three student contributors. The article proposes that pedagogically focused digital public history projects such as Voces y Caras and coloniaLab’s Florida Series provide mechanisms for increasing awareness, on campus and beyond, of the area’s Hispanic roots and the contributions that Latino communities make to the region of North Florida today.

papers.title: “Sometimes a Kitchen, Sometimes a Zoom Call”
papers.abstract: During the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, two community archives—After Violence Project (AVP) and South Asian American Digital Archive (SAADA)—shifted their oral history programs online. Both organizations wanted to know if narrators felt differently about telling their stories via videoconferencing. To answer this question, we conducted research interviews with narrators after they shared their life stories with AVP or SAADA to assess their experiences. Our findings indicate that, despite a certain amount of technological ambivalence, narrators expressed that such software can create the conditions for a productive emotional distance between narrator and interviewer and a sense of virtual belonging. Despite these benefits, we urge archives to use some caution in adopting such technologies and critically evaluate their implications for privacy, ownership, and profit.

papers.title: Taking History Beyond the Classroom
papers.abstract: Shared authority has become a key tenet in the practice of public history, but how do we teach the idea of shared authority in the university classroom? In this co-authored essay by student and teacher, we unpackage how we have attempted to tackle this issue in a capstone undergraduate history unit called History Beyond the Classroom. The unit requires students to work with community organizations on an independent public history project that is of use to their partner-organization. In doing so, students not only begin to appreciate the historical skills they have learned throughout their degree, but also appreciate the work of public historians, become public historians themselves, and begin to understand history as a lifelong learning process.
