papers.title: “Play the Long Game”
papers.abstract: For the last five years, I have had the honor of serving as series editor for “Considering the Revolution,” a collaborative project between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Council on Public History (NCPH). Each year, a convenor has brought together a panel of scholars and practitioners to discuss themes related to the American Revolution for the purpose of helping NPS interpreters and other practitioners prepare for the upcoming Semiquincentennial. The topics of panels, which were also written up by panel conveners into articles published in The Public Historian, have been wide-ranging. Panels from “Indigenous Histories and Memory in Alaska, Hawaii, and the Indigenous Plateau” (2021) to “Citizenship and Sovereignty” (2024) substantially enlarged the field of possibility for programming about the histories and legacies, broadly conceived, of the American Revolution.1 As impressive—and as indicative of the creative and inventive ways that public historians had been imagining the interpretive opportunities surrounding the commemoration—is the list of topics generated at various brainstorming sessions between NPS and NCPH members: religion, belief and disbelief; disability and the Revolution; and climate and environment.2 I share these now because, together, this archive of preparation and planning depicts institutional investment in the potential of a Semiquincentennial that would meaningfully reshape the way that Americans understood the Revolutionary period.The upcoming 250th is significant because of the national scale of commemoration and also because the symbolic importance of the ideals and rhetoric of the American Revolution flows though all contemporary politics. It has been perceived by a variety of stakeholders—ranging from “official” federal planners to individual public historians—as an occasion to change how Americans understand democracy and their place within it. But beyond that, it will have substantial impact on public history writ-large: its methods, its practitioners, and its institutions. Over years of reflection, I have come to view commemorations—especially national ones—as accelerators and codifiers: wherein, because of attention and opportunity and resources, and through new or emergent forms of commemoration, insurgent but already-extant tendencies in historical interpretation and perspective tend to clarify, mature, and solidify. To wit: many of our current institutionalized forms of public history, from the emphasis on grassroots and community history approaches, to local and vernacular preservation initiatives, to institutions themselves (not coincidentally, formal public history education, and the National Council on Public History itself) come to us as a result of the 1976 Bicentennial, which brought with it a popular excitement about the past, a desire, from people, to see themselves within American history, and an enthusiasm for grassroots efforts, all of which encouraged robust funding and institution-building.3 In my capacity as series editor, and also as a public history scholar and educator, I saw the first four “Considering the Revolution” panels—alongside broader efforts across the field to tell more inclusive, representative stories, and to account for and grapple with the histories and legacies of exclusions and inequalities—as the seeds for a meaningful and impactful commemoration that would reflect the new directions in formal public history practice.4 The far-ranging conversation across each panel reflected and magnified efforts and initiatives across multiple arenas of public history—including, notably, and until recently, the National Park Service itself.5 Practitioners and publics have been, for several years now, reframing the American past and its remembrance and commemoration; the Semiquincentennial seemed to be an opportunity to reflect upon and further institutionalize these developments.6When planning began, at the end of 2024, for the final panel, which I was also asked to facilitate, the goal was to move from interpretive content to interpretive practice; we wanted to focus on how practitioners were applying the types of thematic frameworks that had been introduced in previous panels. But after January, and with each new month, it started to become increasingly apparent that the Semiquincentennial envisioned by the previous panels—as well as the very public history institutions and federal funders, including humanities councils and the Park Service itself, that would support and articulate the commemoration—were under existential threat. It seemed more urgent, then, to convene a panel in which practitioners and audience members could talk about how they were meeting the moment, but also, to reflect on the way that expectations had altered over the past year.In early June of 2025, our panel, “Considering the Revolution,” was convened online, where, we hoped, we could make it accessible to as many practitioners as possible.7 Together, planners decided to invite past panelists, so that their reflections on the commemoration would be framed by the series itself. Joining me were three panelists, all of whom are public history practitioners at institutions at the forefront of inclusive and impactful public history practice. Ista Clarke was part of the 2023 panel on “The Rhetoric of Freedom: A Conversation about the Conditions of Black Life in the American Revolution,” convened by historian Sylvea Hollis. With an extensive background in interpretation, Clarke is Cultural History Interpretation Specialist at Charleston County Parks. Clarke leads tours at International Site of Conscience McLeod Plantation Historic Site and works closely with descendent communities.8 Nicole Moore and Kristen Hayashi had both taken part in the 2024 panel on Citizenship and Sovereignty convened by NCPH President Gregory Smoak. Hayashi is Director of Collections Management and Access and Curator at the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles, and has worked with Los Angeles history organizations, including serving on the board of directors for the Little Tokyo Historical Society and Asian Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation (APIAHiP). Moore is Senior Director of Education at the National Museum for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta and serves on the board of directors of the Slave Dwelling Project and Old North Illuminated. Together, these panelists brought a wealth of experience to draw from and reflect upon in our conversation.The developments that are impacting ideas and initiatives around the Semiquincentennial are so far-reaching that it seems strange for me to spell them out here, for a readership comprised of people who—whether they are federal employees, educators at federally funded universities, or recipients of grants from funders such as the National Endowment for the Humanities or the Institute of Museum and Library Services—have first-hand experience of those very developments, part of an ideologically driven effort to reshape public understanding of history.9 But one thing we are learning very fast is that it is always good to leave a record, many records, and in as many places as possible. Additionally, although much public history happens far outside of the realm of federally backed institutions, current events offer a good reminder of the profound ways that federal investments in history have the power to shape the field. This is another reason why thinking about and watching the Semiquincentennial—instead of, as more people seem to be doing, hoping that it goes by, and then, away—remains important.And so, here are some of the immediate contexts that inform where public history practice is right now, that inform the shape of the conversation of the panel, the experiences and outlooks of the panelists and the audience, and how we are all thinking about the Semiquincentennial. First, the losses: material and operational cuts to the Institute of Museums and Library Service, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Wilson Center, federal museums and historic sites, federally subsidized student loans, Medicaid, and other funders of public history and of public historians.10 Second: attacks—some federal, some from the state level—in the form of firings, book banning, and threats of detention; to schools, universities, libraries, movements, and everywhere else that knowledge and knowledge communities reside.11The undercurrent running beneath this is a threat to organizations and people exploring and sharing the histories and experiences of nonwhite, nonbinary, non-able-bodied, non-Christian Americans—that is, those who are seeking to tell stories about our nation that are more complex, more nuanced; about times when the promises of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness fell short, or even when they were withheld or wrested away—and to use those stories to make claims for freedom, equality, and access for those who have unjustly been left out of the promises of the very founding moment that the Semiquincentennial will be commemorating. These stories are difficult but also hopeful and aspirational. And they are always critical—for understanding the United States then, the United States now, and the United States of the future. As Nicole Moore said of the Semiquincentennial that she had been imagining during her previous panel, “I felt like we would be able to really dive into commemorating those men, women, and children whose voices hadn’t been heard…and seeing what their legacy in shaping who we are and where we could go would be.” But now, she continued, “that headspace has changed a lot.”It is impossible to overstate the reactionary nature of these attacks and silencings, as well as the degree to which they operate within the commemorative realm: the 1776 Project to counter the 1619 project, the renaming of forts and sites, the National Garden of American Heroes in response to contested statues.12 The Semiquincentennial that was envisioned by the first four panels of this series—a commemoration borne out of these inquiries and efforts—was precisely what is now being stripped away. The Semiquincentennial that is arising in its place is going to look very different: sponsored by funders like Palantir, Coinbase, and UFC, staffed by individuals closely connected to the current administration, and flanked by actions such as the recent executive order “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” which purports to combat a “revisionist movement [that] seeks to undermine the remarkable achievements of the United States by casting its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light.”13 Accordingly, institutional foundations for commemoration are changing. For example, the newly revised NEH grant guidelines state “[we] will only accept projects that promote a deeper understanding of our nation’s extraordinary heritage, including our record of advancing liberty, prosperity, and human flourishing.”14 At the National Park Service, rangers and visitors are being asked to flag interpretive content deemed “inappropriate”: signs mentioning climate change, enslavement, and forced assimilation of Native Americans have all been tagged.15 In June of 2025, the White House announced an extensive of all museums in of the It is difficult to see a place within these formal institutional for inclusive and impactful public But it is up to us to make the of the panel, and Clarke were asked to reflect on these and what they for practitioners who are planning projects and for the upcoming Semiquincentennial. that of these are new developments, and that the histories of the experiences of people, of and of have been to and in the contexts of that, like the are to be Ista to the way that experience historical the American Revolution well as how history be to for some is for For the past several years, have been efforts by state history institutions, and by historians themselves to or efforts at history that contested or of the founding moment and its has been for example, to the of from public the of the histories of in schools, the of the desire, by to some history those the to all of this was a about or historians contemporary and when thinking or about the I that a part of what was at for the historians who were during this was an about and a of how a historian be in For practitioners, of the of interpretation for the public in this panelists the importance of the past to the for visitors who are and in of the the of public historians in the at that with Revolutionary history, we be commemorating. papers.title: Digital heritage and fashion: preserving cultural identity through AI and virtual archives
papers.abstract: Abstract The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generation presents both opportunities and challenges for preserving fashion heritage and cultural identity. This study aims to evaluate AI’s capacity to replicate historical fashion by introducing the Multi-Dimensional Fidelity Assessment (MDFA) framework, which combines computational perceptual similarity (LPIPS) with expert-scored cultural feature concordance (CFC). Applying MDFA to 15 ensembles generated by Gemini and ChatGPT, findings reveal a divergence between automated metrics and human judgment. While AI often achieves high perceptual similarity, fidelity to culturally significant details is inconsistent. Consequently, these tools risk cultural flattening and misrepresentation, especially for non-Western attire. For example, AI struggled with symbolic motifs on a Qing Dynasty robe and Indonesian batik textures. The paper argues for ethical mediation in virtual archives by emphasizing transparency, contextualization, and expert oversight to ensure AI serves as a responsible tool in safeguarding diverse fashion legacies. In turn, the findings provide insights into identifying and addressing falsifications and outline directions for future research in digital heritage forensics.

papers.title: AI-assisted hermeneutics: validating a large language model for the rhetorical analysis of the book of revelation
papers.abstract: Abstract This article introduces and validates a framework for the computational analysis of rhetorically complex texts, moving beyond generic sentiment analysis to enable nuanced, large-scale hermeneutic inquiry. As a case study, we analyse the Greek text of Revelation, using the Gemini-2.5-Pro LLM to quantify its rhetoric against a bespoke, theologically-grounded eight-vector lexicon. The framework’s validity is established through strong correlation (mean Pearson’s r = 0.82) with a reliable human-expert baseline (Fleiss’ κ = 0.825), confirming its capacity to map the text’s salient features. The analysis provides quantifiable evidence for key exegetical claims—including the liturgical framing of divine judgment and a 12:1 deception-to-violence ratio for the Beast’s threat—and shows how AI-human divergences can map a text’s implicit theology. This study offers a reproducible and validated heuristic for mapping complex foundational texts, demonstrating a critically-aware partnership between computational analysis and expert exegesis.

papers.title: Cinematic adaptations of theatrical plays: an investigation into the transition from stage to screen
papers.abstract: Abstract The objective of this article is grounded in the examination of the peculiarities involved in adapting theatrical plays into contemporary cinematic productions. To achieve this goal, analytical, comparative, and weighting coefficient calculations and statistical analyses of Cronbach’s and McDonald’s coefficients methods are employed. Initially, the authors identified potential challenges in the cinematization of theatrical plays, including the preservation of the theatrical atmosphere (0.38), the search for additional details for a more vivid expression (0.36), dialogue adaptation (0.31), maintaining the artistic essence of the play (0.33), and varied approaches to material presentation (0.29). The analysis of the film adaptations of “The Peony Pavilion” and “Incomparable Mulan” revealed differences in graphic quality, portrayal of characters, plot accuracy, and their alignment with the theatrical production. It was established that the film “The Peony Pavilion” most accurately corresponds to the theatrical production, attributed to the use of music and the preservation of the main characters’ images. Conversely, the film “Incomparable Mulan” is more closely linked to graphic quality and the depiction of the main characters, contributing to the vibrancy and beauty of the artistic depiction. Respondents opined that the film “Incomparable Mulan” (0.37) is of higher quality, as it is oriented toward preserving Chinese values. Consequently, it can be inferred that for audiences, the storyline holds greater significance than logical gaps in information presentation.

papers.title: Indigenous Rights, Philanthropy and Humanitarian Governance across the Anglo World, 1837–1951
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines how three nineteenth- and twentieth-century philanthropic organizations – the British Aborigines’ Protection Society (APS), the American Indian Rights Association (IRA), and the Australian Association for the Protection of Native Races (APNR) – functioned simultaneously as opponents of colonial violence as well as instruments of colonial governance. These groups were vociferous advocates for Indigenous rights and welfare, yet they also directly contributed to building administrative structures of empire. The APS worked to generate metropolitan interest in Indigenous affairs, framing protectorates as both economically beneficial and a matter of national security. The IRA positioned itself as a fact-finding body, supplying the US government with on-the-ground surveillance that enabled more precise administrative control. The APNR acted as a public relations arm for Australian settler governments, deflecting criticism of state violence while promoting assimilationist policies. All three organizations reinforced colonial authority by outsourcing key governmental functions to private actors, and their reliance on voluntary labour and philanthropic donations underscores the contingency of imperial rule on non-state institutions. Bridging historiographies of humanitarian activism and colonial governance, this article argues that these groups were not merely critics or collaborators but infrastructural components of empire.

papers.title: Research on graph-retrieval augmented generation based on historical text knowledge graphs
papers.abstract: Abstract This article addresses domain knowledge gaps in general large language models for historical text analysis in the context of computational humanities and AIGC technology. We propose the GraphRAG framework, combining chain-of-thought prompting, self-instruction generation, and process supervision to create a “The First Four Histories” character relationship dataset with minimal manual annotation. This dataset supports automated historical knowledge extraction, reducing labor costs. In the graph-augmented generation phase, we introduce a collaborative mechanism between knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation, improving the alignment of general models with historical knowledge. Experiments show that the domain-specific model Xunzi-Qwen1.5-14B, with Simplified Chinese input and chain-of-thought prompting, achieves optimal performance in relation extraction (F1 = 0.68). The DeepSeek-R1 model integrated with GraphRAG achieves an absolute F1 increase of 0.11 (0.08 → 0.19) on the open-domain C-CLUE relation extraction dataset, surpassing the F1 value of Xunzi-Qwen1.5-14B (0.12), effectively alleviating “hallucinations,” and improving interpretability. This framework offers a low-resource solution for classical text knowledge extraction, advancing historical knowledge services and humanities research.

papers.title: ON HISTORICAL (ANTI‐)REALISM
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The problem of historical realism has gained some new momentum recently, with a fresh challenge to what is taken to be an anti‐realist hegemony in the theory and philosophy of history. Unfortunately, this has also provided the opportunity for the reheating of old polemics and lazy scholarship that characterized the 1990s reaction to “postmodernism.” Ill‐defined questions distract us from more important issues. Here, I offer a map that aims to clarify the conceptual space. I distinguish between a metaphysical problem, which is the problem of historical realism proper, and an epistemological problem, which is sometimes treated under the same phrase but is more adequately called the problem of historical skepticism . I then consider what the targets of each of these discussions are and map the conceptual space of possibilities in them.

papers.title: ‘But Their Mouths are Sealed’: Medical Practitioners in French Colonial Courtrooms, 1828–1848
papers.abstract: Abstract This article sheds light on a previously overlooked aspect of medical practice in colonial contexts: the involvement of medical practitioners in legal proceedings. It emphasizes that medical expertise was not solely utilized for diagnosing and treating patients in the disease-ridden environment of the Caribbean colonies, but also for explaining sudden and/or violent deaths. From the late 1820s onwards, driven by the abolitionist movement and legal reforms, there was a notable surge in trials where enslavers faced accusations of mistreating and killing enslaved individuals. This article investigates the role of medical practitioners and testimony within these trials. Examining French colonial trial records together with abolitionist writings reveals that medical expertise went beyond mere healing practices, instead serving as a tool to legitimize violent punishments based on racialized descriptions and perceptions of enslaved bodies.

papers.title: REALISM OR IDEALISM? PERSPECTIVES ON THE PHILOSOPHY OF HISTORY FROM A PRACTICING HISTORIAN
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This review essay argues that the realist philosophy of history, as represented by Adam Timmins in Towards a Realist Philosophy of History , raises interesting questions about the nature of historical writing and challenges some of the foundations of idealist philosophy of history. A basic problem with Timmins's book is the conflation of “constructivism” with “idealism” when there are, indeed, quite a few “realists” who are also “constructivists.” After summarizing the main arguments of the book and critically examining them, this essay argues that realism, if combined with constructivism, is appealing for many practicing historians, but it also warns that there can be no foundationalism regarding the institutionalization of professional historiography. Furthermore, it emphasizes skepticism regarding trust in specialization, and it cautions that idealist philosophy of history has had more of an impact on practicing historians than Timmins's book suggests. Because I am not a philosopher of history, I must leave the finer points of philosophy to other reviewers; instead, I focus on the perspective of a practicing historian with an interest in historical theory.

papers.title: UNIVERSALITY IN THE CLIMATE CATASTROPHE: RETHINKING CHAKRABARTY'S ANTHROPOCENE PHILOSOPHY OF HISTORY WITH MERLEAU‐PONTY'S PHILOSOPHY OF NATURE
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article critically examines Dipesh Chakrabarty's concept of Anthropocene history, a philosophy of history that is designed to respond to the universal challenge of the Anthropocene. It uses the work of Maurice Merleau‐Ponty to mitigate the pitfalls of Chakrabarty's concept and to propose an alternative relation between nature and history. I argue that the problem of Chakrabarty's Anthropocene history resides not in its use of the category of the universal per se but in its insufficient articulation of the particular. Even if he is correct in asserting that it is impossible to conceptualize the ecological crisis within the modern logic of history and that it is necessary to conceptualize the ecological crisis from a non‐Eurocentric perspective, Anthropocene history still leaves the modern structure of history untouched, resulting in a structure that is unable to meaningfully articulate particularity and universality because of its reliance on teleology and phenomenological emptiness. With this in mind, I show how Merleau‐Ponty's conceptual redefinition of nature as a foundational universality, when combined with the chiasmic intertwining of history and nature and a reflection on the concept of the institution as a point of passage between nature and history, enables us to rearticulate universality and particularity in the face of the ecological crisis. This in turn enables a freer conceptual navigation between the existential and political dimensions of the ecological crisis with which environmental philosophy is concerned.

papers.title: Race, Medicine, and Causation in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World
papers.abstract: Abstract In December 1753, the South Carolinian physician, John Lining, wrote a letter to Dr Robert Whytt, Professor of Medicine at the University of Edinburgh, offering ‘A Description of the American Yellow fever’. ‘[T]his dreadful malady, which so frequently rages like the plague in the southern parts of America’, Lining observed, seemed to strike almost everyone: ‘both sexes of the white colour, especially strangers lately arrived from cold climates, Indian, Mistees, Mulattoes of all ages, excepting young children and of those only such as had formerly escaped the infection’. Peculiarly, however, one group of people was spared. ‘There is something very singular in the constitution of the Negroes’, he claimed, ‘which renders them not liable to this fever; for though many of these were as much exposed as the nurses to the infection, yet I never knew of one instance of this fever amongst them, though they are equally subject with the white people to the bilious fever’. My aim in this article is twofold. First, I want to show how unusual a position like Lining’s was in the eighteenth century. Very, very few of those who committed their ideas to print made the claim that susceptibility or immunity to disease was a racial trait. This almost complete absence puts a point on the subsequent question: in what contexts did Lining and others develop their ideas? In answer, I divide the small handful of examples into two categories. The first may be the least surprising, for a number of authors invoked ‘Negro’ immunities to disease as a justification for African slavery in the warm climates that proved so seemingly inimical to Europeans. The second set of cases, which includes Lining, is more surprising: as we shall see, Lining’s location in South Carolina— and other writers’ connections to that state —would prove crucial.

papers.title: Grassroots Officials, Worker Wrongdoings, and Masculinity in the Nantong Municipal Steel Rolling Mill, c. 1970
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines how competing ideals of masculinity were negotiated in the everyday life of a steel mill community in the People’s Republic of China during the early 1970s. Using the personnel dossier of a male worker from the Nantong Municipal Steel Rolling Mill, contextualized within a framework of archival sources, operational manuals, industry periodicals, textbooks, and newspapers, it explores how workshop culture, homosocial interactions, and heterosexual relationships shaped gendered norms. Within the mill, the state promoted an ideal of disciplined, self-controlled masculinity tied to productive labour and socialist values. Yet, among workers, an alternative ‘rough’ manhood expressed through fighting, bravado, and sexual assertiveness persisted, reinforced by homosocial bonds and everyday practices. These conflicting visions of manhood were embedded in ordinary disputes, disciplinary hearings, social interactions, and everyday work culture, where official expectations frequently clashed with entrenched shop-floor norms. Because of life tenure and the ubiquity of minor infractions, the state struggled to enforce its ideals fully, making everyday transgressions powerful arenas of negotiation. By examining everyday life alongside the state’s social engineering efforts, this article sheds fresh light on how masculinities were reworked through societal and industrial practices, enriching wider comparative debates on working-class manhood under industrialization.

papers.title: A Task-Oriented Approach to Human and Equine Health and Ability in Early Modern Sweden
papers.abstract: Abstract Taking its departure from the dependence on human and equine bodies to be healthy and capable of performing their various tasks in early modern societies, the article studies what notions of human and equine health and ability ordinary people embraced, by using a large sample of court cases from Sweden. It is shown that people made sense of human and equine illness as physical weaknesses or as bodily subjugations by disease entities, and that it was not meaningful to differentiate between illness and injury, since a diminished capacity for work was at the core. Particular yardsticks of capability are also identified, in relation to which people’s and horses’ abilities to carry out alternative tasks were assessed. Importantly, it is shown that people did not depart from universal categories of human or equine physiology, but from how individual men, women, and horses used to be and be able to perform certain tasks. An implicit framework of a task-oriented functionality for working bodies is identified, which, it is finally suggested, shows similarities with and predates mechanistic physiology. It is thus suggested that working people’s task-oriented ways of understanding working bodies should be considered in historical studies of the rise of mechanism.

papers.title: Aetiological Politics, Mental Illness, and Affective Neuroscience in British Slave Trade Abolition
papers.abstract: Abstract The role of medical science, including testimony from medical practitioners during Britain’s parliamentary inquiry into the slave trade, has eluded sustained scrutiny in the historiography. Through a close reading of parliamentary hearings, doctors’ clinical reasoning, diagnostic practices, and therapeutic protocols emerge as key forensic evidence in the abolition movement. This article traces the politics of medical diagnosis by studying mental illnesses such as melancholia, hysteria, and insanity on British slave ships and as they were debated in parliament. Building upon the historiography of science in the context of British abolition, it offers a rereading of Britain’s slave trade debates by way of emergent eighteenth-century neuroscience, particularly the neurophysiology of feelings. I argue that evidence concerning the emotional capacity of African people was a key point of deliberation during parliamentary hearings and was embedded in a neuroscientific discourse that privileged idealized notions of British femininity. The article demonstrates how the diagnosis of mental illness overturned proto-racial theories of neurophysiology and the developing science of race, temporarily confirming the neurological fitness of African people. It concludes with the suggestion that these parliamentary disputes reveal the early racialization of mental healthcare with residual legacies in healthcare today.

papers.title: Navigating artificial intelligence narratives in Chinese media: a mixed-methods discourse analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract With the deepening social penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, mainstream media’s role in shaping public cognition through news framing has become increasingly prominent. However, existing research has long been constrained by Western-centric perspectives, leaving significant gaps in exploring the discourse construction mechanism related to AI in non-Western contexts. This study seeks to systematically deconstruct the mainstream media narrative strategies on AI technology in the Chinese context, by employing a hybrid methodology combining Analysis of Topic Model Networks, Moral Foundation Analysis, and linguistic analysis and using AI-related news reports from 2017 to 2024 in Chinese mainstream media as a corpus. The findings suggest that, first, the media have constructed four frames of “Politics and Economy,” “Society,” “Revolution,” and “Cooperation,” whose structural details reflect the deep coupling between technological discourse and national strategies. Second, moral discourse demonstrates Chinese characteristics prioritizing dimensions of Authority/Subversion and Loyalty/Betrayal, whose diachronic growth correlates with contextual factors such as pandemic governance and nationalist reinforcement. Third, through the combined linguistic strategies of predication and metaphor, media narrate AI as a manipulable national development tool while downplaying technological complexity and threats. This study not only reveals the mutual-construction mechanism between ideology and discursive strategies in technological socialization, but also provides Chinese empirical references for global AI governance research through a non-Western perspective.

papers.title: Exploring the applicability of digital humanities tools to Ottoman and Turkish languages
papers.abstract: Abstract The first known computerised language and literature analysis was carried out by Father Roberto Busa in 1949; such studies have increased greatly after 1980, and today the tools are diversified with artificial intelligence. Unfortunately, except for a few minor studies, this development cannot be seen in the fields of Turkish and Ottoman languages. Therefore, as the first step in producing tools for Turkish and Ottoman, it is necessary to understand the algorithms of existing English-based tools and determine the applicability of these algorithms to the Turkish and Ottoman languages. In this study, twelve tools based on text and network analysis will be examined in terms of their suitability for Turkish and Ottoman. Tests on the tools will be evaluated under the headings of Corpus, Visualisation, Word Count, N-Grams, Structure Analysis, Network Analysis, and Labelling. The data obtained will be evaluated in terms of the suitability of the algorithms of the tools, and suggestions will be made for the algorithms that seem suitable for the Turkish and Ottoman language and literature analysis tool or tools to be developed in the future.

papers.title: Digital memory research in Chinese and English literature: a DTM-based topic evolution and comparative analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract With the deepening integration of digital technology and humanities research, digital memory has gradually become a research hotspot in the field of digital humanities in recent years. However, current digital memory research suffers from fragmented theoretical systems and a lack of cross-cultural comparative studies, making systematic review of existing research both theoretically and practically significant. This study draws on research findings on digital memory from Chinese and English databases over the past two decades. Using the Dynamic Topic Model (DTM), it identifies research hotspots and analyzes their temporal evolution. From the three dimensions of cultural tradition, institutional environment, and academic paradigm, the study reveals cross-cultural differences in digital memory research within Chinese and English scholarly contexts and further proposes potential pathways for future development. The results indicate that research hotspots on digital memory exhibit a distinct pattern: Chinese studies emphasize system construction, whereas English studies focus more on cultural critique. Specifically, digital memory research in Chinese literature tends to strengthen cultural integration under policy-driven frameworks, while English literature highlights the political tensions of memory through technological criticism. Looking ahead, digital memory research should aim to build a more open and inclusive global digital memory ecosystem through subject collaboration, mechanism innovation, and contextual practice. This study innovatively constructs a cross-cultural research framework for digital memory, comprehensively uncovering its topic evolution and contextual differences over time, thereby providing a theoretical reference for future research in this field.

papers.title: Traveling Histories of Abortion
papers.abstract: Recent events have thrust abortion histories into the limelight. The US Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, dramatically ending the constitutional right to abortion, has prompted questions about how we got here and mobilized legions of activists to chart new ways forward. But in the urgency of our post-Dobbs time, historical perspectives have narrowed. Too often commentators and pundits tell the story of abortion as a national saga of the recent past, a story of US women struggling for bodily autonomy since the late 1960s and the New Right emerging to oppose them. This story leaves out deeper and broader histories of gender inequality and racial dispossession. It also overlooks imperial ambitions and transnational influences. This forum challenges that narrow view by foregrounding traveling histories of abortion over fractured domestic landscapes and across international borders. We highlight three forms of travel. The first is by abortion seekers and providers, people who moved to access and enable services. They traveled to skirt legal restrictions and obtain or provide safer and more affordable procedures. The second is the globetrotting beliefs, ideas, and social movements that, especially from the mid-nineteenth century onward, sculpted the landscapes that abortion seekers and providers traversed. These included Catholicism, racial nationalism, and biomedicine and, later, socialism, eugenics, family planning, feminism, population control, and conservative forms of Protestantism and Islam. We consider how religious and secular perspectives landed in different places, blending with local, national, and regional particularities to reshape the many meanings of abortion. Finally, we argue that traveling technologies have been vital to border-crossing struggles over abortion. Four essays consider the international development and circulation of vacuum aspiration technologies for performing abortions, and one examines US reformers’ promotion of a birth control foam to curb population growth in Brown and Black communities at home and abroad. Rather than analyzing these technologies as determinative of historical outcomes, we track their movements and varied appropriations to elucidate connections and disjunctures between different locales.

papers.title: Pathology, Heredity, and the Varieties of Man, 1650–1800
papers.abstract: Abstract When Enlightenment thinkers debated the so-called ‘Varieties of Man’ they relied to a surprising degree on claims about disease. This article seeks to explain why disease was so useful to eighteenth-century theorists of race. It argues that several major strands of early modern medical thought conceptualized disease as a force that could change the body in lasting and even heritable ways. These include close interaction between conceptions of contagion and early theories of generation, understandings of immunity and susceptibility, as well as the mechanics of hereditary disease. Physicians often presented disease not as a brief episode through which one passed but as a stubborn, durable force that left permanent marks which could linger even over multiple generations. It was this power to change bodies in lasting ways, which I refer to as disease’s ‘formativity’, that gave pathology such utility for Enlightenment-era race-theorists. Enlightenment theorists of human variety needed to explain how physiological differences had developed over time. Disease offered them a force that could account for such evolution. This study seeks to fill in the relationship between medicine as a field with practical application, and medicine as a conceptual apparatus within the pursuit of anthropology.

papers.title: Numeracy, Otherness, and the Invention of ‘Civilization’ in Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Anglo-European Travel Writing
papers.abstract: Abstract Depictions of numeracy among non-Europeans were a prominent feature of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Anglo-European travel writing, but remain largely overlooked in the extensive scholarship on travel, knowledge, and empire. This article shifts attention from traditionally ‘scientific’ forms of numeracy such as mathematics and astronomy towards more fundamental counting, calculation, and communication skills, to examine the way in which mutually reinforcing hierarchies of otherness and numerical knowledge were constructed in travel accounts. Focusing particularly on writings about China and the Americas, it demonstrates the way in which European written and mathematically precise numeracy was perceived as superior to oral, embodied, and object-based practices observed elsewhere. Exploring the reception of these ideas in eighteenth-century Britain reveals that numeracy became integral to emergent notions of European modernity and civilization. The example of numeracy, this article suggests, demonstrates the interrelationship between social relations in national context and global power structures.

papers.title: From Tragic Life to Tragic Death: Negotiating the Emotions of Suicide in Finnish Youth Press, 1967–89
papers.abstract: Abstract The meaning of suicide in any given community reveals attitudes about its acceptability, which might influence its occurrence. This article explores young people’s understanding of suicide during a time of high but fluctuating suicide rates in Finland in the 1970s and 1980s. Drawing from the history of emotions and treating suicidality as a feeling, this article shows how suicidal feelings were embraced and limited. I argue that during these two decades, young people went from viewing youth suicide and suicidality as pitiable yet ultimately understandable phenomena to seeing suicides as highly sentimental, exceptional tragedies. By analyzing young people’s writings in youth media, this article focuses on the age group in which suicide rates rose rapidly in the 1970s and remained high in the 1980s. It proposes another viewpoint on explaining suicidality by examining the processes through which suicidal feelings were adopted, challenged, and restricted.

papers.title: Domesticity in Precarity
papers.abstract: Abstract Histories of child removal have primarily focused on settler colonies, rather than other kinds of colonies. In British India, the separation of children from the Sansi population—a socially marginalized, low-caste, and itinerant group that was designated under colonial law as a “criminal tribe”—has not yet received the attention of historians. The story of Sansi child removal suggests that precarity can be both disruptive andproductive of domesticity, and furthermore, that precarity is often an ordinary part of domestic life. Methodologically, this article proposes the framework of “domesticity in precarity.” Histories of domesticity need to hold together the structural constraints on domestic life with the efforts of people to make many and varied relationships and households in conditions of precarity. Above all, interrogating the relationship between domesticity and precarity widens our view of the relationships and spaces that historically constituted the “domestic.”

papers.title: Exchanging the Pen for the Camera
papers.abstract: Abstract Does form affect the way people create meaning out of history? In 2023, the author—after a career as traditional text-bound scholar—undertook the project of making a documentary short. Cowboy Strikeexplores a labor conflict in late nineteenth-century Texas, but it also begot a collaboration with a contemporary songwriter. The process of filmmaking raised a series of dilemmas and opportunities for historical interpretation distinct from the traditional task of written scholarship. It generated new ideas about the power of collective memory, the role of mythmaking in historical understanding, and the malleability of time. These ideas, I suggest, were unlikely to have emerged from work on the same topic as a traditional scholarly article. The production of nonfiction film, therefore, offers scholars a powerful exercise through which they might rethink their subjects, and even the nature of the past itself.

papers.title: Nakba
papers.abstract: Abstract Contrary to the prevailing assumption, the genealogy of nakbadoes not begin in 1948 Palestine but stretches far back into the Ottoman past. This study examines the formation of nakba in Arabic as a concept of disaster and a social practice of catastrophic ideation. In the nineteenth century, intellectual constructions of nakba referred to famed medieval episodes of downfall. Diverse Arab intellectuals and the genre of social science redeployed these centuries-old constructions during the Hamidian massacres of 1894–97 and the Armenian Genocide of 1915 as well as subsequent colonial wars, including the Great Syrian Revolt of 1925 and the Great Arab Revolt of 1936–39. These events, among others, entrenched a malleable image, a mode of interpellation, and a structure of catastrophic ideation profoundly shaping how nakba became enmeshed with social formation and political action in echo with a wider conceptual landscape. The Nakba of 1948 Palestine prompted a generation of Arab intellectuals to redefine standards of selfhood, sovereignty, and objectivity. The layered genealogy of nakba prior to 1948 reveals how catastrophic ideation foregrounded persistent idioms in Arabic, Turkish, Armenian, and English beginning in the nineteenth century to mark varying degrees of political urgency and exceptionality.

papers.title: Living with Drought in the Long Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: Abstract The 1893 drought will, according to the science journal Nature in July, ‘unquestionably take its place among the recorded events of history, if regard be had to its intensity [and] the length of time during which it has lasted’. Communities reported being stretched beyond endurance. Rivers ran dry, reservoirs dropped to record lows, wells failed, and domestic water supplies were restricted to a few hours per day. But while the 1893 drought was severe, it was not unusual. As this article reveals, urban and rural communities faced regular droughts of varying intensity and duration during the long nineteenth century. What did this mean for them? Where previous interest in extreme weather events has focused on recovering historic patterns, or examined resilience or adaption, this article explores the lived experiences of drought to offer a new perspective on the impact of weather shocks and water scarcity on people’s lives. By combining evidence from meteorological reports, newspapers, official reports, and local government archives, the article undercovers the fragility of urban and rural water supplies and examines how behaviours were adapted in response to water scarcity and precarity.

papers.title: Sectarian Conflicts, Ideological Biases, and Professional Standards
papers.abstract: Abstract This article is about politics, history, and the politics of history. It centers on the Dominican friar Abraham Bzowski, or Bzovius (1567–1637). Born in Poland, Bzovius in the early seventeenth century moved to Rome, where Pope Paul V entrusted him with the task of continuing Cesare Baronio’s Annales Ecclesiastici. Baronio’s last volume was published in 1607, the same year as Baronio’s death, and reached the year 1198. Bzovius was supposed to pick up where Baronio had left off, ideally taking the Annalesup to the seventeenth century. Bzovius produced twelve additional volumes in his life: Virtually all of them were controversial; most of them had to undergo several rounds of revisions and emendations; and a few of them were never authorized for publication, thus remaining in manuscript. This article discusses the conflicts that Bzovius’s work provoked. Even though Bzovius’s name might be unknown even to the majority of early modern historians today, his case is well worth studying because it elucidates crucial aspects of the relationship between history writing and politics in seventeenth-century Catholicism. Understanding this relationship, in turn, provides insightful considerations on the ways in which history writing and politics are intertwined today.

papers.title: Trafficked into Oblivion
papers.abstract: Abstract This article recovers the lived experiences of trafficked Indigenous women in nineteenth-century Buenos Aires, Argentina. From 1878 through 1885, the Argentine Army carried out a series of campaigns in the Pampas and Patagonia, imprisoning and displacing thousands of formerly autonomous Indigenous people. Hundreds of prisoners, mostly women and children, were sent to Buenos Aires and placed under the jurisdiction of a women’s charity organization called the Sociedad de Beneficencia (SdB). In conjunction with Argentina’s Ministry of War, the SdB sent Indigenous women to live in the homes of wealthy Buenos Aires families as unfree domestic laborers. The SdB employed a racialized and gendered discourse of moral uplift to justify coercive treatment and sanitize ongoing frontier violence. This article reveals that some Indigenous women, unable to access protection under the law, attempted to shape their circumstances by publicly calling attention to mistreatment and neglect. These resistant actions forced Argentina’s political elites to question the meaning of Argentine citizenship and national belonging. Ultimately, this article provides insights into the complex relationship among gender, race, and social class in the construction of settler colonial nation-states, highlighting the possibilities for Indigenous resistance under settler colonialism.

papers.title: Exploring the application of artificial intelligence in English literary criticism: a Delphi and AHP-based thematic analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in various fields has revolutionized traditional methods, introducing innovative tools and approaches. In the realm of English literary criticism (ELC), AI offers novel possibilities for textual analysis, authorship attribution, thematic exploration, and more. Despite its potential, there is a significant paucity of robust studies that systematically explore these applications through structured methodologies. This article aims to fill this gap by employing the Delphi method and analytic hierarchy process (AHP) to identify and prioritize the key applications and components of AI in English literary criticism. To this end, the applications of AI in ELC were initially extracted through thematic analysis of previous literature. The Delphi method was then used to refine and finalize this list by consulting a panel of experts. Following this, the AHP was employed to determine the importance and prioritize each application based on expert evaluations. The applied method identified eleven key applications of AI in ELC, each with its own set of critical components. The AHP analysis provided a hierarchical structure, prioritizing these applications and components based on their importance and feasibility. The top applications identified include textual analysis, authorship attribution, and digital humanities. Within these applications, specific components such as sentiment analysis, stylometry, and thematic detection were highlighted as highly impactful. These findings offer valuable insights for researchers and practitioners, guiding future developments and implementations of AI technologies in literary criticism.

papers.title: Digital storytelling in India: from theory to praxis
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital storytelling, as the name suggests, refers to the production and dissemination of stories across various digital platforms. The study builds on the existing scholarship on digital storytelling and defines its characteristic elements, which make it stand out in the plethora of current digital content. The objective is to closely study the digital storytelling landscape of India with case studies of major projects from 2010 to 2021, like Indian Memory Project, Daak, and Talking Myths Project, to name a few that retrieve and digitize stories of the country’s history and cultural heritage. The systematic literature review follows a bibliometric and content analysis of the existing research and projects to study the current praxis in India. The results reveal that though there is an active participation in digital storytelling in India, there is a lack of representation on a global scale, and hence the need to create our own digital cultural record through stories. The concluding arguments identify the gaps and draw upon the ‘banzome’ model of transmedia digital storytelling that suits the diverse nature of Indian storytelling, contributing to creating the country’s own unique cultural record.

papers.title: Sydney Nathans. Freedom’s Mirage: Virgil Bennehan’s Odyssey from Emancipation to Exile
papers.abstract: Freedom’s Mirage tells the remarkable true story of Virgil Bennehan, born into slavery in 1808 on a North Carolina plantation. Bennehan was articulate and literate, and possessed professional skills that were highly sought after. He grew up connected to esteemed and wealthy family relations, even inheriting money through his father’s last will. Under these unusual circumstances, he received education and training, rising to the roles of plantation accountant and medical practitioner. In this book, author Sydney Nathans carefully traces Bennehan’s life journey, revealing a powerful and complex narrative of identity and resilience within the brutal realities of slavery. The first part of the book contextualizes Bennehan as a favored enslaved servant. It connects to an important strand of literature that complicates our understanding of the diverse social relations and experiences of the enslaved. These experiences might include people who were both victims and enablers of the system of slavery. This part of the book also addresses the question of why many enslaved people chose to seek freedom when presented with the right opportunities, while others did not. Much older historiography would have conceptualized the family who owned Bennehan as “benevolent slaveholders,” who tried to reconcile slave ownership and unpaid labor with—what they regarded as—moderate violence and medical care. In a way, Bennehan was the embodiment of this irreconcilable contradiction: A friend to both Black and white people (12), as the author presents him with some reservation, Bennehan tried to navigate two worlds without ever fully belonging in either

papers.title: Reconsidering Violence Against Women through the History of a Refuge for Trans Women
papers.abstract: Abstract Both right-wing forces and gender-critical feminists currently frame cis and trans women’s needs as fundamentally different and conflicting. Violence against women is a particular flashpoint: trans women are construed as a threat to women’s spaces, including refuges. In this article I use the history of Tiresias House, a refuge established in Sydney, Australia in 1983, to demonstrate women’s shared experiences of violence across the spectrum of cis and trans, to highlight shared histories of solidarity against male violence by feminists and trans women, and to explore what is at stake when we use history to answer contemporary political questions.

papers.title: Early modern translation and the digital humanities. Hilary Brown, Regina Toepfer, and Jörg Wesche (eds.)
papers.abstract: As digital databases evolve from simple bibliographies into complex analytical engines, the field of Translation Studies faces a critical juncture. Early Modern Translation and the Digital Humanities (Brown et al., 2025) arrives as a timely roadmap for this transition. Originating from a 2021 roundtable on European Translation Databases, the volume confronts the central challenge of the discipline: how to unify a fragmented landscape of isolated projects into a coherent, pan-European infrastructure. By surveying key projects developed in the early 2020s, the volume offers researchers not only a catalogue of available tools but a critical assessment of the digital methods now shaping the study of early modern translation. The volume Early Modern Translation and the Digital Humanities comprises ten chapters organized into four parts. The first part (Chapter 1) is an introduction to the volume, describing the application of digital technologies within the context of translation studies. It outlines seven ongoing database projects focused on translations in the Early Modern Period, which form the core of the subsequent chapters. It also explores possible interactions of translation studies and digital tools, such as data visualization, distant reading, network analysis, and stylometry. This discussion highlights the interdisciplinary nature of digital humanities and its potential to enhance traditional translation studies.

papers.title: Persuasion, Recruitment, and Repression in the Czechoslovak Campaign for Collectivization
papers.abstract: Abstract This article analyzes the relationship between persuasion and repression in Czechoslovakia’s Stalinist-era campaign for collectivization, challenging the widespread assumption that Communist leaders and local party activists abandoned an unsuccessful strategy of persuasion for a successful strategy of coercion. Rather, Czechoslovak Communists maintained both a commitment to farmers’ voluntary participation and confidence in their popular support in the countryside, leading local party activists and government officials to attribute difficulties in the collectivization campaign to deliberate sabotage on the part of hidden class enemies. Vague definitions of the rural class enemy placed extraordinary power in the hands of district and village authorities, but also afforded the accused opportunities to defend themselves by appealing to Communist Party doctrine and by drawing on their personal connections. Repression exacerbated tension within local party branches and among collective farm members, while failing to disrupt traditional village social bonds and structures of authority. This article demonstrates both how the Czechoslovak Communists’ continued commitment to persuasion enabled repression and how this repression hindered official efforts to transform the countryside along ideological lines.

papers.title: Infanticide, Infant Mortality, and the Racialized Construction of Fordist Motherhood: Household Surveillance, Suspicious Death Investigations, and “Neglectful” Mothers in Progressive Era Chicago
papers.abstract: Abstract This article traces how growing concerns with infant mortality shaped the interpretation and policing of infanticide in turn-of-the-century Chicago. At the heart of the article are 1,270 suspicious infant death investigations from the Cook County Coroner between 1872 and 1911. We analyze two major shifts in the inquest language: the rise of increasingly professionalized medical language and changes in the inquest language of “neglect.” In the 1870s, coroners typically used “neglect” to suggest a mother’s ignorance or lack of access to essential resources for childcare. By the early twentieth century, a more punitive conception of “willful neglect” arose, which attributed infant death to mothers who failed to adequately care for newborns. Infanticide—the private practice and public response to it—reveals a new institutional order with enhanced biopolitical power in Fordist capitalism: household surveillance, the expanding authority of emerging professions, and elevated expectations for working-class mothers. In this context, politicians and new professionals focused on conserving infants as a valuable national asset through education and public health campaigns that aimed to eliminate “ignorant” motherhood. We argue these new initiatives to conserve infant life were racialized, and we explore segregated campaigns to train white and Black mothers. While white professionals’ endeavors were well supported, efforts on behalf of Black motherhood and infants solely came from within Chicago’s African American community, led mostly by Black women reformers who struggled with limited funding and a lack of outside interest.

papers.title: “Carried to the Swamp”: Race, Place, and Geographies of Infant Death in the Post-Emancipation American South
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines infant abandonment, death, and burial in the late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century American South, predominantly in South Carolina. It investigates the physical and imaginary geographies associated with infant death, exploring how southerners navigated local landscapes to conceal infant deaths. It links physical spaces to geographies of power and control in a postbellum southern world still defined by racism and violence, arguing that places of infant abandonment or burial were deeply meaningful to both Black and white communities. This research also demonstrates how the spaces of infant disposal or burial could serve as sites of Black resistance even as they remained spaces of marginalization and death. Through an interrogation of infant death, this article uncovers the ways in which Black people in South Carolina and beyond negotiated, disrupted, and resisted the white domination of the landscape that persisted well after emancipation.

papers.title: Bureaucratic Ambitions and Indigenous Defendants in Nineteenth-Century Huajuapan
papers.abstract: Abstract As was true in many parts of Mexico, judicial prosecutions for reproductive crimes increased in the last third of the nineteenth century in the small communities of Huajuapan, Oaxaca. This article examines why community members and local officials denounced and investigated Indigenous women in these Mixtec communities for the crime of infanticide in this period. It suggests that local bureaucrats empowered by the positions, practices, and procedures of republican government engaged in the policing of the sexual and reproductive practices of women in their communities to publicize their commitment to the functioning of the modern liberal state before the audience of judicial functionaries who occupied positions above them in state government and the judiciary. Ironically, however, this effort often backfired. The Huajuapan cases show that local bureaucrats exhibited greater zeal in their intent to prosecute female community members than did judicial officers who occupied more powerful offices than they and who were further removed geographically from the small rural communities in which the cases originated.

papers.abstract: Abstract The penal conceptualization of infanticide (understood as the murder of a newborn) in the 1871 Federal Penal Code resulted from the construction of the liberal patriarchal state. Two interrelated phenomena justified the inclusion of infanticide in Mexican criminal law: the legal value of female sexual honor and the differentiated legal protection of the newborn’s life, depending on its legitimate or illegitimate quality. The offense of infanticide remained very similar in its definition and penalties in subsequent federal codes (1929 and 1931) until its repeal in 1994. During this period, alongside that conceptual stability, there were changes in criminological, judicial, and social views about infanticide, motherhood, and female sexuality. The repeal in 1994 was the result of a series of social and political changes rather than judicial interest. The focus of this article is to analyze legal conceptions of infanticide in various criminological and legal texts to show how they changed from the Siete Partidas to 1994. It is possible to observe that the ideas about newborn life and their relation to female honor and, ultimately, to ideals of motherhood were compatible with the interests defended by the liberal state that resisted social transformations.

papers.title: Re-reading the Infanticide Narrative: Enslaved Death, Plantation Medicine, and the Law in Cuba after 1820
papers.abstract: Abstract In 1837, a 30-year-old enslaved African woman known as Teresa Lucumí faced charges of criminal infanticide following the gruesome death of her son. Local authorities in her small western Cuban town received news of the crime from Teresa’s enslaver, who recounted a harrowing story of an enslaved mother turned violent murderer. Extracting a confession, authorities took Teresa into custody. Subsequent court records suggest that this confession was likely fabricated. When an appeals judge asked Teresa to ratify her account, she declared that local authorities had silenced her. She then recounted a version of events that not only challenged the story her enslavers told, but also implicated them in chronic physical abuse, rape, attempted murder against her, and murder of her son, likely sired by her enslaver. With its two diametrically opposed explanations of the child’s death, Teresa’s case allows a rare exploration of the way enslavers constructed narratives of infanticide, how police and judges interacted with them, and why they apparently proved so compelling. Tracing their medical and legal logics, I question the extent to which the infanticide narrative that so captivated judges reflected the enslaved woman’s experience. I propose that the stories ratified by criminal infanticide cases like Teresa’s more accurately reflect enslavers’ strategies for navigating evolving medical, legal, and moral frameworks governing slavery after the legal abolition of the slave trade to Cuba. The label “infanticide” does more to obscure than to explain how this woman negotiated the complexities of motherhood in Cuba’s nineteenth-century slave society.

papers.title: To Punish and Protect: Communal Responses to Infanticide in the Early Venezuelan Republic, 1830s–1860s
papers.abstract: Abstract Following independence (1830), there was a surge of court cases regarding infanticide in the Venezuelan province of Mérida. The defendants in all these cases were the mothers of the deceased; all were poor, illiterate, single women. Civilians initiated all of these cases, by informing the authorities that they had found a cadaver, helping to identify the mother, and then providing witness testimony. Though the judicial system dramatically increased prosecution of this crime, officials typically arranged to acquit the defendant even when there was abundant evidence that she was guilty. This article investigates the responses by the civilian community to the infant and mother, and finds that civilian responses were diverse and inconsistent. Responses varied: sometimes families or neighbors denounced the mother to the authorities and then assisted the prosecution, sometimes they denounced her but then endeavored to ensure her acquittal, and sometimes they shielded her from arrest and prosecution. Typically, community members did not themselves punish the mother but rather relied on the judicial system to provide justice. The only instances in which community members threatened or hurt the mother were cases in which the mother’s parents punished her for harming the family’s honor or cases in which the mother attempted to identify publicly the father of the child. These varied responses arose from a mix of honor culture, religion, family ties, sympathy for the mother’s plight, and a sense that the pursuit of justice required mercy.

papers.title: Race and the Politics of Infanticide in Post-Emancipation Virginia
papers.abstract: Abstract Although emancipation promised freedwomen greater control over their reproductive and familial lives, it also introduced new risks of state punishment for crimes related to reproduction, including infanticide. This article demonstrates that Black women and girls accused of infanticide in post-emancipation Virginia were subject to disproportionately harsh punishment, including lengthy periods of penitentiary incarceration. Drawing on court records, coroner’s reports, penitentiary records, medical literature, and popular media, this article reconstructs and contextualizes the story of Phillis Douglas, a young, Black woman convicted of killing her newborn infant and sentenced to 16 years in prison in 1869. Douglas’s fate was the product of both highly local dynamics and larger national struggles over the consequences of emancipation and new Constitutional guarantees of citizenship and equal protection. Competing accounts of how emancipation and the redefinition of citizenship had affected obligations between employers and workers, among kin, and between citizens and their governments, shaped conflicts around acts of infanticide, real and imagined, in the post-Civil War United States.

papers.title: Digital scholarship in education: multimodality as a window into learning. Brendan Jacobs
papers.abstract: As the boundaries between educational research and digital humanities continue to blur, Brendan Jacobs’ Digital Scholarship in Education: Multimodality as a Window into Learning offers a timely and insightful contribution to ongoing conversations about what constitutes scholarship in the digital age. Jacobs’s work situates itself within a rapidly evolving epistemic landscape, where text is no longer the sole vehicle of academic argument, and where the production and dissemination of knowledge increasingly rely on digital, visual, and interactive forms. This book, which focuses on multimodal theses and dissertations (MTDs), serves as both a theoretical reflection and a practical guide for those seeking to integrate digital media into scholarly inquiry. More importantly, it positions multimodal research not merely as an alternative mode of presentation but as a transformative framework for rethinking how knowledge is created, communicated, and evaluated within the academy. From the outset, Jacobs makes clear that the emergence of digital tools in education and research is not simply a matter of convenience or modernization. Rather, it reflects a paradigmatic shift in scholarly communication—a move from monomodality to multimodality, from static representation to dynamic, embodied, and interactive meaning-making. In Chapter 1, titled “Multimodal Theses and Dissertations,” Jacobs introduces the MTD as an epistemological innovation that challenges the linearity and textual dominance of conventional dissertations. He argues persuasively that integrating video, audio, and digital interactivity into academic writing allows researchers to represent the complexity of their data more authentically and holistically. This argument resonates deeply with current debates in digital humanities regarding the legitimacy of non-textual forms of scholarship and the necessity of expanding evaluative frameworks beyond written discourse.

papers.title: Sensing Heat, Finding Cool: The Search for Water in Summertime Paris, New York, and London, 1880–1930
papers.abstract: At the turn of the twentieth century, Paris, New York, and London were epicenters of urban modernity, but these cities and their inhabitants were ill-equipped to cope with summer heat. Urbanites experienced thermal discomfort directly through their personal sensory registers, and the search for cooling water was a major, although overlooked, aspect of collective urban life in summer. Drawing on sensory and environmental history, and on the archives of city authorities and popular depictions of social life, we find that obtaining watery relief from the heat was limited by inequitable access to cooling infrastructures, including municipal and philanthropic baths and pools, which were often insufficient to meet urbanites' needs. Instead, Parisians, New Yorkers, and Londoners turned to informal and often illicit methods to overcome the thermal inequalities that were baked into the brick and stone of their cities. Keeping cool in the melting metropolis was a challenge that demanded resourcefulness, bravery, and a willingness to disregard the rules and social norms that tried to regulate the use of other watery infrastructures, including ponds, fountains, hydrants, rivers, and canals. As present-day city authorities develop local adaptation plans in response to the global climate crisis, the fact that the coolness of water did not come easily or equally to turn-of-the-century urbanites should be at the forefront of our minds.

papers.title: Making trans-regional, cross-platform streaming catalogues a reality: Arguing for linked SVOD open data
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite a constant growth as a mainstream way of consuming media, subscription-based video on-demand (SVOD) platforms have remained under-studied in a specific yet core aspect of their service: their contents. Potential quantitative studies have been prevented by the unstable nature of their catalogues, both in time and space, and the lack of will to publish publicly accessible catalogues of these platforms’ works. This hinders many potential Digital Humanities projects pertaining to modern digital media, causing a lack of research by lack of data. After studying available data catalogues and their caveats, we suggest and detail the implementation of a simple model proposal to standardize, archive and eventually publish such metadata, proving that all technical aspects and benefits are already well-defined as well as commonly used, and that this kind of data would be particularly suited for Digital Humanities projects and Semantic Web standards. We thus further argue for more public initiatives to support work on open media catalogues, and push for more data releases from major SVOD platforms that would benefit both scholars and the general public without much burden for their service.

papers.title: Reading the unreadable: creating a dataset of 19th century English newspapers using image-to-text language models
papers.abstract: Abstract Oscar Wilde said, ‘The difference between literature and journalism is that journalism is unreadable, and literature is not read’. Unfortunately, the digitally archived journalism of Oscar Wilde’s 19th century often has no or poor quality Optical Character Recognition (OCR), reducing the accessibility of these archives and making them unreadable both figuratively and literally. This paper helps address the issue by performing OCR on ‘The Nineteenth Century Serials Edition’ (NCSE), an 84k-page collection of 19th-century English newspapers and periodicals, using Pixtral 12B, a pre-trained image-to-text language model. The OCR capability of Pixtral was compared to four other OCR approaches, achieving a median character error rate of 1%, 5x lower than the next best model. The resulting NCSE v2.0 dataset features improved article identification, high-quality OCR, and text classified into four types and seventeen topics. The dataset contains 1.4 million entries, and 321 million words. Example use cases demonstrate analysis of topic similarity, readability, and event tracking. NCSE v2.0 is freely available to encourage historical and sociological research. As a result, 21st-century readers can now share Oscar Wilde’s disappointment with 19th-century journalistic standards, reading the unreadable from the comfort of their own computers.

papers.title: Topic counts and quality in topic models for historic corpora
papers.abstract: Abstract Topic modelling methods enable the identification of potential topics within a corpus of historical texts; in particular, they enable the identification of latent topics that are not described just by a single word. Like so many computational methods for the automatic processing of historical text corpora, they come with a number of parameters with which the method can be tuned and adapted. Each change in the settings of any of these parameters will generate a new set of topics that will differ in larger or smaller ways and which may be qualitatively better or worse. One of the main parameters for tuning topic models is setting the number of topics to be generated. In this article, we present an analysis of the impact of the number of topics on the quality of topic models for two historical text corpora. Two manual evaluation approaches are combined with an automated evaluation metric, and based on the results, we propose a formalized process for choosing the final set of parameters for a topic model. The process ensures the quality of the final model, while minimizing the amount of manual evaluation work. The more structured process also allows for better documentation of the parameter choices and in that way enables better replicability of any research using topic models.

papers.title: EIGENSINN AND DOMINATION IN LIBERAL AND ILLIBERAL SOCIETIES
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article is a posthumously published text that was written by Alf Lüdtke and Alexandra Oeser but was left unfinished when Lüdtke died in February 2019. It examines two central notions—and their articulations—that Lüdtke and Oeser use differently in their work: domination and Eigensinn . Oeser has written an introduction to guide the reader through the text and to recall the conditions surrounding its production.

papers.title: From romance to reality: lexical and topic evolution in Chinese popular lyrics through digital humanities approaches
papers.abstract: Abstract This study explores the lexical and topic evolution of Chinese popular music lyrics from 2000 to 2025, reflecting changing public sentiments and broader socio-cultural transitions. While prior research has largely overlooked non-Western lyric corpora, this study addresses that gap by constructing the Chinese Popular Music Diachronic Corpus, comprising 1,560 representative popular songs sampled across twenty-five years. Using digital humanities approaches, it integrates word frequency analysis, readability metrics, and BERTopic-based topic modelling to trace lexical and topic evolution of lyrics over time. Findings reveal that high-frequency words consistently revolve around emotional expression, individual introspection, and interpersonal dynamics. Type-token ratio (TTR) has increased significantly, indicating growing lexical diversity, while textual complexity shows fluctuation, reflecting stylistic shifts in song writing. Topic analysis identifies twelve major topics, including romantic love, future aspirations, and urban life, with topic structures evolving from natural and temporal abstraction to emotional concreteness and psychological introspection. Recent years show a significant rise in negative emotional topics and self-referential artistic motifs. This study contributes a novel methodological framework for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of music, language, and society, and underscores the value of digital humanities tools in mapping collective emotions and cultural change through large-scale lyric analysis.

papers.title: Pre-digitally decoded alice’s adventures: an early record of readability computations
papers.abstract: Abstract This article offers a new reading of Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, proposing that Alice’s journey is an illustration of the process of learning to read.
