papers.title: Introduction
papers.abstract: This special issue of The Public Historian endeavors to situate places of burial, cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites within themes and methodologies of public history and historic preservation. Cemeteries and graveyards are sites that reflect the way a community memorializes its deceased and, in this sense, how it understands history in a profound and intimate way. There is purpose behind the placement of cemeteries. Many of these burial places were planned, not placed at random. Burial grounds allow for the public to see how families, friends, communities, and countries left a record of and paid their respects to the dead.What are the politics of preserving these sites? How do they change over time and vary over space? What is the role of the public historian in preserving and interpretating these sites? How can a consideration of the involvement of local community members, faith groups, historic societies, and professional caretakers in the creation and maintenance of burial sites help us reimagine community-based commemoration, preservation, and memory in understudied sites and communities? How might transnational comparisons help us understand practice, policy, and local history? What is the role of technology and digital history in documenting and preserving the history and legacy of our departed?The discovery of cemeteries, such as the African Burial Ground in New York City in 1991, has had a profound effect on public historical scholarship.1 The cemetery itself and the artifacts uncovered there have allowed collaboration among scholars in multiple fields such as history, archeology, and anthropology, and gave community members a window to interpret African life in New York City. What are the lessons of life and history that these spaces can offer, not only this example, but other cemeteries as well?2 This special issue considers subjects such as community reclaiming of unmarked graves and massacre sites; the politics of mining company motivations and the significance of land for Indigenous tribes; the response of communities in creating memorials when there are no remains to bury or when the colonial past overshadows the Native American story; and how massacres during wartime might be missed or overlooked by national institutions and their established methods of historic preservation. Research on cemetery sites simply takes a very long time because it requires extensive archival research as well as coordinated efforts between public historians, the local community, and descendants, who often need to be identified and located. These challenges, however, have not dissuaded scholars, nor reduced community interest in the topic.This special issue is intended to begin a conversation about cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites and the role of the public historian in researching and documenting those sites. These topics, and the role of cultural tradition in shaping rituals honoring the dead, have received popular attention, including from recent animated Disney films. Through box office hits Moana (2016) and Coco (2017), many people learned about ethnically specific rituals around death and remembrance for the first time. Although at best these films offered an incomplete portrayal of these traditions, the reality was that millions of people received introductory history lessons about the celebration of Dia de los Muertos (in Coco) or observed fictional Pacific Islanders caring for their dying family members and learning about their origins and their voyaging ancestors (Moana). As public historians, we recognize that further explorations on topics that examine everything from celebrations and cemeteries deserve our research attention.Technology has been a boon to cemetery studies by increasing accessibility. Satellite imagery has captured aboveground details of burial areas, and digital sites such as FindAGrave.com allowed community members to photograph pictures of headstones and cemeteries and upload them to the site’s crowd-sourced online archives.3 Having an accessible record online is particularly helpful when researchers are unable to travel to the cemetery themselves. Digitizing documents and images have helped to democratize the archives allowing everyone from family genealogists to the public the ability to access more information about the deceased and their final resting place. The site FindAGrave.com works well where there are known cemeteries with physical grave markers with names. However, not all people had a proper burial, and the archival paper trail may have gone cold or be nonexistent.In cases of limited archival information and a lack of a burial due to violence, war, colonialism, or massacre, the ethics of remembering the dead become complicated. In these cases, people have urged governments to intervene in the repatriation of human remains. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), passed by Congress in 1990, is one important response to concerns by the public and descendants. NAGPRA was designed to address the problem of the many Native American cultural items that were in museums or other institutions, items over which the descendants and tribes associated with them no longer held ownership or control.4 The cultural items included human remains, sacred objects, and funerary items, among other examples of material culture. To close some of the gaps in the law and to address issues specific to California, in 2001, the state legislature of California passed the Cal NAGPRA Act (California Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act) creating more oversight and tackling the issue of human remains of native peoples whose bones were studied by scholars in California’s public universities. As institutions offered public apologies while repatriating the bones of indigenous peoples, the politics of these interactions required knowledge of the oppressive conditions in that historical moment. Despite the federal and state requirements, which have been in place for decades, as of this writing in 2025, some universities have yet to comply fully with the terms of the law.5Memorializing the deceased can be a private activity and simultaneously something to be experienced collectively. On the national level, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, DC, and the 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York City effectively captured the nation’s emotions and memories of those historic events by allowing the public to mourn the loss of lives through listing names of the individuals on a public memorial. For many, this provided a way for families and the country to heal.6 The elegance of these memorials lies in the simplicity of their design. National cemeteries have identical headstones for military veterans which allow visitors to take in the sweeping imagery of rows and rows of headstones against manicured grass.Often it is the smaller local cemeteries where family and community members are buried, however, that members of the public are most familiar with and connected to. One such local cemetery, the Japanese Cemetery of 1908, a county historic landmark in Ventura County, California (Historic Landmark #18), inspired me to research more about it, ultimately generating greater public support for its preservation.7 The cemetery and its location are well-known by the local community, but few are aware of its historical significance as one of the only known segregated Asian cemeteries in the US.I became interested in cemetery studies because of my training in history and ethnic studies and the intersection of my scholarly interests with the history of the people buried there as well as the community today. For many years, I attended community clean up events and met with community caretakers and some descendants. Through this work it became clear that the cemetery was a significant community space. My research incorporated digital archives as well as oral histories to piece together the cemetery’s history.8 Shreds of archival information and oral histories led to a fuller picture of the nearly 120 Japanese Americans buried in the cemetery. My research on this segregated cemetery centers a diverse community by elevating Asian American public history and historic preservation of an Asian American public space. Recognizing the need to put this research into conversation within public history was the next logical step.The special issue’s cover image comes from Cheryl Jiménez-Frei’s research on los desaparecidos (the disappeared) in Argentina. Jiménez-Frei’s article, “In the Absence of a Grave: Public Memory, Human Rights, and Argentina’s Disappeared,” examines two monuments, the May Pyramid and the Monument to the Victims of State Terror, and analyzes how the public memorialized the people who died from state sponsored violence. During the late 1970s to the early 1980s, the military dictatorship of Argentina murdered and disappeared nearly 30,000 people in what would later be known as Argentina’s Dirty War. Due to the disappearance of the individuals and lack of human remains to bury, most families did not get to participate in the communal practices of closure such as a funeral or burial at the end of their loved one’s life. These commemorative sites were important for the public to memorialize those who were denied justice and to provide a space for victim’s families to remember and mourn them. Jiménez-Frei’s analysis highlights monuments and how the public responded to violence when a traditional cemetery is absent, resulting in activism led by women.Twenty-five miles south of the Oregon-Nevada border in Humboldt County, Nevada, is Thacker Pass. This was the site of the 1865 Thacker Pass Massacre, and today is a contested mining site for lithium, an important component for electric batteries and green energy. Kelsey Hill’s article, “A Mine and a Massacre Site: Historicizing Violence at Thacker Pass/Peehee Mu’huh,” centers the politics of the site of a historic massacre of noncombatants of the Numu people by the Nevada Cavalry. Efforts to shift from fossil fuels to clean energy make lithium mining economically important locally and nationally. Native American groups of Numu, Newe, and Bannock descent and their allies, however, have protested the mine, contending that the Bureau of Land Management neither accurately evaluated the site according to the National Historic Preservation Act nor did they consult tribal nations meaningfully. The context of Thacker Pass provides insights for public historians at the crossroads of contested lands, Native communities, and the federal government.Kelsey Moore’s article, “Grave Matter(s): The Politics of Submersion in the Santee-Cooper Basin,” examines submerged Black cemeteries and “soiled archives” in a development in South Carolina. In 1934, as part of a New Deal era project to produce greater hydroelectric power and sites of leisure for recreation and tourism, the South Carolina Public Authority engineered two reservoirs. The decision to build a dam and divert the rivers flooded the basin where numerous known cemeteries and approximately eight thousand Black graves had been buried in the centuries prior. Some graves were exhumed and relocated; some were left behind and are still covered by water. Moore’s research juxtaposes the site ninety years later as a space of white leisure at the expense of Black memorials. Using a host of archives, reexamining the early surveyors’ methodology, and creating ArcGIS StoryMaps, the article addresses the erasure of Black graves and digital public history.Santa Clara University in California is the focus of Lee Panich, Amy Lueck, Lauren Baines and Isabella ‘Amne Gomez’s article, “We Are Here Because of Them: Co-Creating a Native Memorial at Mission Santa Clara,” which analyzes how to present Native American cemeteries within the history of the California missions. The university’s campus was built on the legacy of colonialism and enslavement of Native peoples in California. The authors presented the details of designing the interactive digital memorial exhibition which was co-created by the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe, Santa Clara University, and its students. The cemetery memorial allows visitors to learn about historic themes including labor, Native leaders, mission connections, resistance, and enslavement to contextualize the reality of colonial mission history that traditionally centers the Native Californios. Rather than focus on the university and the mission’s colonial past, with guidance from the Ohlone community, the process of co-creating the memorial reckoned with the over 7500 Native individuals whose burials were recorded in Mission Santa Clara from 1777 into the 1840s. This public facing educational memorial gave students the opportunity to engage directly with the community by incorporating rigorous research and digital methods to shape the memorial with respect and intentionality.Johnathan Thayer and Lori Wallach present the details of their research on the cemetery in Old Flushing, Queens, New York City, showcasing how cemetery research can be incorporated into classroom pedagogy and service-learning for public history students. The article, “Reclaiming the Olde Towne of Flushing Burial Ground Through Intergenerational Public History,” used the methodology of service learning to preserve community memory of a segregated and abandoned cemetery made up of primarily Black, Native American, and impoverished people from the 1840s to the early twentieth century. During the 1930s, the cemetery was eradicated to make a park for the growing city. While collaborating with community stakeholders and activists, the students used archival materials such as municipal death records to reclaim the burial ground and honor the deceased with a memorial wall imprinted with their names.In Elizabeth Clappin’s article, “Used to Good Advantage: The Challenges of Unearthing Atlanta’s History of Convict Leasing at the Chattahoochee Brick Company Site,” she examined the politics of the Chattahoochee Brick Company site today. Since the 1870s, Chattahoochee Brick company was one of the largest and still intact sites of leased convict labor. At its height, the brick company relied upon hundreds of mostly African American men to work in conditions nearly identical to antebellum slavery. Many were beaten, literally worked to death, and buried in unmarked graves on site.9 The article puts into conversation redevelopment and city politics, historic preservation, and environmental justice in the city of Atlanta.Desun Oka’s article, “The Mili Atoll Uprising and Massacre of March 1945: US Public History in the Marshall Islands and the Former Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands,” looks at the politics of historic preservation within Mili Atoll in the Marshall Islands. The article centers on the site of a World War II massacre of Korean conscripted laborers and Marshall Islanders by imperial Japanese forces. Due to the remote location of the atoll in the Pacific and the fact that it had changed hands from Japanese control during World War II to becoming part of the Trust Territories of the Pacific Islands in the postwar period, preservation of the site was complicated. Simply getting there from the mainland US to conduct research is difficult and costly. The Pacific is an underrepresented area in public history as evidenced by the National Park Service’s Asian American and Pacific Islander theme study.10 Noting that there are so few listed NRHP historic sites in the Pacific, Oka argues that the problems confounding historic preservation there are not just the distance from the US mainland, but also requirements that in order to overcome would necessitate examining public history guidelines and institutions and preservation law.Our final piece, Lynn Rainville’s “A National African American Cemetery Database Starts in Your Community,” advocates for a national database for African American cemeteries similar to the databases in place for Native American cemetery sites. Not surprisingly, Black cemeteries in the US have not received equal treatment to white cemeteries, particularly in places such as Virginia where Rainville’s research is based. It is clear that community advocacy is necessary in preserving and protecting these cemeteries, but infrastructure to support those community efforts is key. Preservation requires partnership. Based on her experience working with community organizations, Rainville argues for the importance of an online database to centralize information. This is multidisciplinary work that requires the collaboration of many people and entities including public historians, archaeologists, government, technology, local communities, and national organizations.With this special issue, we hope that the articles generate interest for public historians to consider the topic of cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites. This subject lends itself to incorporate methods to expand knowledge, collaborate with community stakeholders, and bring high impact teaching practices into the classroom to engage students. Further research on topics such as cultural commemorations such as All Saints Day and obon; the practice of picnics at cemeteries; the complex and ethnically necessary process of repatriating the bones of Indigenous peoples; and the tragic unearthing of graveyards of children in boarding schools, among others, still warrant our attention. Several authors in this special issue encourage readers by offering recommendations and a call to action.At each memorial site, specific details may have been lost, but historic memory, archives, and descendants fill the gaps. Historic cemeteries of formerly enslaved African Americans, colonial mission graveyards, and wartime massacre sites in the Pacific include both marked and unmarked graves. In some cases, during their lifetimes, the people in the burial grounds were brutalized, assumed to be disposable laborers, while those who were disappeared did not even receive a proper burial. The reasons for not marking a grave may be attributed to the lack of funding or duress, whether in wartime or peacetime. Each of the articles here reflects on the lives of the people and allows readers a window to view our common humanity. After reading this special issue, my hope is that you will come to the conclusion that cemeteries and burial grounds are not only about the people interred there, but also, like the rituals following someone’s death, they were just as much for the living as for the deceased.Thank you to Sarah Case, the editorial board of The Public Historian, and the reviewers who provided their input in improving the articles for this special issue. My gratitude goes to the authors of this special issue for your expertise and for your passion for this topic.

papers.title: Alexandra Kaloyanides. Baptizing Burma: Religious Change in the Last Buddhist Kingdom
papers.abstract: Alexandra Kaloyanides’s book Baptizing Burma: Religious Change in the Last Buddhist Kingdom is a fascinating study of the Baptist Christian community in colonial Burma. Weaving together histories of art, religion, colonialism, and American missionary traditions, Kaloyanides provides a refreshing investigation of the little-known story of Christianity among Burma’s Indigenous minorities, such as the Karen, Kachin, and Chin, who became Christians in large numbers in contrast to the majority Buddhist Bamar (or Burman) population. This book is an intriguing and vivid history of religious material culture and how objects have shaped Burmese, American, and Baptist communities. Through examining the role of four primary objects—the sacred book, the school, the pagoda, and the portrait—Kaloyanides highlights transcultural, transnational, and interreligious histories. As she notes, most studies of Burmese religious history have focused primarily on Buddhism and the Bamar majority, while American religious histories rarely address missionaries in Asia that are not centered on forms of western imperial domination or American cosmopolitanism. In contrast, Baptizing Burma uses the study of religious material culture to move beyond elite monastic or royal scriptures to examine the lives of ethnic and religious minority groups through objects at a time when Buddhism and Christianity comingled in nineteenth-century Burma.

papers.title: We Are Here Because of Them
papers.abstract: Tens of thousands of Native individuals perished in California’s twenty-one Franciscan missions that operated from the 1760s into the 1840s, but most public interpretive programs gloss over their lives and the cemeteries where they are interred. This has historically been the case at Mission Santa Clara, on the campus of Santa Clara University. In this article, we reflect on the process of co-creating an interactive memorial designed to honor the Native people buried in two colonial-era cemeteries related to the mission and link their lives to the descendant community today. Importantly, the co-creation process helped strengthen relationships in numerous directions, furthering the work of both commemoration and reconciliation.

papers.title: Protecting Soviet Muslims: Muhajir Activism and the Minority Treaties, 1917–1934
papers.abstract: Abstract It is a historiographical convention to view interwar debates over the protection of vulnerable populations through the prism of ‘minority rights’, a regime fashioned by European empires, emerging nation states and the League of Nations. This article challenges that convention by widening the lens to recover actors who, in the 1920s–30s, contested the premises of international protection. Taking the transnational debate over the fate of Soviet Muslims as its principal case study, the article brings together two histories. First, it examines the strategies of Muslim émigrés from the USSR— sometimes in concert with, sometimes against, co-religionists across South Asia and the Middle East —to appropriate, resist and navigate that order in defence of Muslims inside the Soviet state. Second, it foregrounds the Soviet Union’s attempt to re-engineer the post-Versailles minority protection regime by appealing to Muslims under colonial rule. Whether advanced on behalf of ‘minorities’ or ‘majorities’, the language of protection became entangled with claims to sovereignty, the management of religious and social difference, and anti-colonial struggle. More broadly, the article argues that protection— not minority rights alone —offers a sharper and more inclusive framework for understanding the interwar international order and the political-legal templates it bequeathed to the twentieth century.

papers.title: Reclaiming the Olde Towne of Flushing Burial Ground Through Intergenerational Public History
papers.abstract: Graduate public history students at Queens College, City University of New York, worked with Queens Public Library and the community archiving organization Queens Memory to collaborate with a local community memory group, the Olde Towne of Flushing Burial Ground Conservancy, to reclaim a segregated, deliberately erased, and forgotten site of Black and Indigenous history. Through intergenerational collaboration, faculty, students, library staff, and the Conservancy activated a public history classroom with community-engaged service-learning, producing research and digital class projects that contributed to New York City’s formal recognition and investment in the Burial Ground as a site of mourning, memorial, and celebration of Black, Indigenous, and marginalized lives.

papers.title: A National African American Cemetery Database Starts in Your Backyard
papers.abstract: In the United States, human remains are protected at the local, state, and federal levels. And yet, due to systemically racist residential, economic, and mortuary segregation, African American burials have not always received equal care and attention. One solution is a national database that encourages the rediscovery and protection of Black graveyards. Working in partnership with descendants, community kin, and interested citizens, public historians can contribute their skills to creating this resource. This article uses one southern state as a case study, but the patterns, problems, and solutions apply to northern and southern states, as well as around the world.1

papers.title: A Mine and a Massacre Site
papers.abstract: To some, the now-underway Thacker Pass Lithium Mine in Nevada is the key to America’s “green” energy future. For some local tribal members, however, the project is a desecration of the sacred, as Peehee mu’huh—its Numu name—is a massacre site and the unmarked burial ground of their ancestors. This article examines Thacker Pass as a microcosmic example of how Native participation in land-based controversies can platform their histories within the public sphere, and how tribes remain limited under the current federal apparatus to ensure those histories are considered in the decision-making process.

papers.title: In the Absence of a Grave
papers.abstract: From 1976 to 1983, a military dictatorship in Argentina murdered and disappeared thirty thousand victims, now known as “the disappeared.” Despite significant efforts towards justice, one factor has left many loved ones in a liminal space between hope and acceptance: the absence of a body. Mourners were denied a cemetery or gravesite—places intrinsically defined by the presence of remains—and the rituals and processes these memory sites allow. This article examines how the weight of this absence brought collective action that re-signified one existing monument and created another memory site for the disappeared: the May Pyramid and the Monument to the Victims of State Terrorism. Inaugurated nearly two hundred years apart and distinct in intention and iconography, these monuments connect as locations addressing the absence of a grave and provide spaces for both memory and human rights activism.

papers.title: Grave Matter(s)
papers.abstract: Lake Moultrie and Lake Marion in South Carolina have become popular recreational sites. Although local institutions have created and disseminated a teleological narrative about the engineered lakes, the reservoirs both symbolize and attest to submerged Black histories. To create these lakes, Black communities and their cemeteries faced inundation, or removal and reinterment. Through an examination of the Santee-Cooper Hydroelectric and Navigation Project, this essay argues that the project’s administrators articulated and effected historical value through their procedures of cemetery preservation (or lack thereof). papers.title: Rumour, Public Opinion and Print in Istanbul, 1780s–1830s
papers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on Ottoman official correspondence, an informer’s report, and palace-sponsored tracts and chronicles, this article challenges the widely-held notion that print is inherently linked to diversification, liberalization, and Enlightenment ideals. Against the background of rising tensions between the authorities and the Janissary army, Ottoman officials viewed rumours and political discussions in coffeehouses and other social hubs as threatening to their efforts towards centralization. To counter these perceived dangers, they sought to capture oral communication in written records and invalidate its credibility, relying on written and, later, printed texts. Government-sponsored tracts that targeted the Janissaries linked the supposedly unrestrained tongues of the common people with their unruly imagination, portraying both as antithetical to truth, reason, religion, and order. The Calendar of Events, the government gazette launched in 1831, was the culmination of this process. Rather than marking the emergence of an Ottoman ‘public sphere’, it reflected an effort to subjugate an already-existing realm of popular public opinion.

papers.title: Evan P. Sullivan. Constructing Disability after the Great War: Blind Veterans in the Progressive Era
papers.abstract: The past quarter century has witnessed an outpouring of interest in the welfare of disabled military veterans. In the United States, this concern can be chalked up to the nation’s latest wars in the Middle East, conflicts that resulted in more than 1.8 million disabled American veterans. To this day, organized veterans’ groups continue to raise alarms about the threats facing the latest generation of war-wounded troops. At the same time, American culture is awash in a kind of performative patriotism that prioritizes public ritual (such as “thanking” veterans for their service) over substantive action on vets’ behalf. None of this is new. Building upon David A. Gerber’s pathbreaking edited volume Disabled Veterans in History (2012), books like Beth Linker’s War’s Waste: Rehabilitation in World War I (2011), John M. Kinder’s Paying With Their Bodies: American War and the Problem of the Disabled Veteran (2015), and Sarah Handley-Cousins’s Bodies in Blue: Disability in the Civil War North (2019) reveal how Americans have always displayed complex attitudes toward disabled veterans, hailing them as icons of patriotic masculinity one minute, demonizing them as threats to national health the next. Often missing in this work, however, is a sense of how experiences of disability, stigma, and homecoming played out differently among various groups of disabled vets.

papers.title: Joshua Nygren. The State of Conservation: Rural America and the Conservation-Industrial Complex since 1920 .
papers.abstract: The steady exodus of farmers from rural America and the consolidation of their lands into fewer hands represent core transformations during the twentieth century. In The State of Conservation, Joshua Nygren explains those changes by analyzing a loose and decentralized coalition of well-positioned farmers, state actors, and industrial players that he calls the “conservation-industrial complex.” In a thoroughly researched and tightly argued narrative, Nygren shows how these public-private partnerships formed around soil and water conservation during the 1930s, became powerful social and economic forces after World War II, and persisted in the face of critiques from the 1960s through the end of the twentieth century. Nygren argues that the capital-intensive notions of conservation held by industry and wealthy farmers were tools of “social oppression and land confiscation” (7). As Nygren explains, the conservation-industrial complex formed in the wake of the 1927 Mississippi Flood and the Dust Bowl, when agricultural leaders such as Hugh Hammond Bennett argued that soil loss from erosion represented the single greatest threat to rural America. During the 1930s, agricultural leaders promoted cultivation strategies such as terracing and contour-strip cropping, embedding state-sponsored technical expertise into local soil conservation districts. While well-to-do farmers exercised a disproportionate share of control in these districts, Nygren argues that, prior to World War II, the social justice aims of New Deal thinkers such as Rex Tugwell held sway over purely developmentalist goals. Though Nygren’s argument is convincing, industry voices are absent in the first chapter.

papers.title: Jason L. Newton. Cutover Capitalism: The Industrialization of the Northern Forest
papers.abstract: As has happened to many of us, the book that Jason L. Newton originally planned to write is not the one he ended up writing. Newton originally turned to the history of timber workers in the Northern Forest—the forests stretching from upstate New York, through northern Vermont and New Hampshire, and up through Maine—hoping to tell a story about labor radicalism. He had good reason to expect there’d be a good history to tell. Radical unions, like the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), famously attracted thousands of members in the timber industries of the upper Midwest and Pacific Northwest, and Newton assumed, as just about any labor historian likely would, that those same radicals garnered a dedicated following in the woods of the northern Atlantic states. But rather than find stories of radical worker uprisings, Newton found almost no evidence of union activity at all. The IWW largely passed the Northern Forest over, and attempts to unionize the region’s loggers in the later twentieth century fizzled out just as soon as they started. Accordingly, Newton’s focus shifted, and his project became about trying to understand why labor radicalism was, more or less, nonexistent in the northern woods. While the labor sympathizers among us might mourn the lack of a sustained union presence in the Northern Forest, historians will be grateful that Newton did not find what he was originally looking for. That’s because, in trying to understand the dearth of union activity, Newton has written an innovative history of labor, environment, and capitalism that offers new ways of conceptualizing the relationship between work and nature that many historians—not just those who study the North American timber industry—will want to pay attention to.

papers.title: Sharing Stories from 1977
papers.abstract: The Sharing Stories from 1977 project offers teachers an innovative way to introduce tools of digital humanities scholarship into the classroom. papers.title: Contemporary Parliamentary History and Petitioners in the Long Parliament, c. 1640–1642
papers.abstract: Abstract Studies of petitioning activity in the early years of the Long Parliament (1640–2) have often focused on the large-scale petitions which engaged with issues of high politics and religion in the charged atmosphere prior to the outbreak of Civil War. However, many subjects were drawn to petition the Commons and the Lords for relief in much more particular economic disputes. Utilizing overlooked manuscript petitions in the parliamentary archives and papers of the MP Bulstrode Whitelocke, this article re-examines petitioning activity between 1640 and 1642. It finds that, despite the absence of parliament during the Personal Rule, subjects eagerly embraced the calling of a new parliament, their perceptions of it shaped by its contemporary history. As MPs and peers increasingly utilized and preserved records, petitioners too evoked and confronted the parliamentary past. While some like the Merchant Adventurers’ Company glossed its presentation tactically, others including London-based glassmakers and merchants were driven by ideological beliefs in the historic role of parliament as a protector against arbitrary fiscal policies. This article contributes to post-revisionism by showing that subjects viewed parliament not as an event, but as an institution, fostering connections between past and present sessions as they petitioned for redress.

papers.title: The Language of confiance and the French cahiers de doléances of 1789
papers.abstract: Abstract In the context of increasing historiographical attention to the emotional content of French revolutionary politics, the essentially unprecedented nationwide consultation that produced the cahiers de doléances of 1789, now available as a searchable digitised corpus, offers a route into exploring the hopes, fears, and concerns of thousands of French people who participated directly in the cahiers ’ composition. It also provides material to contemplate the implications of the highly centralized, top-down reform processes actually initiated from the summer of 1789 onwards, and the violent complexity of their reception.

papers.title: Seasonality and the Practices of Illegal Trade in the Faroe Islands and the Northern and Western Isles, 1775–1785
papers.abstract: Abstract By investigating 321 smuggling vessels that travelled between the Faroe Isles and the British Isles between 1775 and 1785, this article explores the regionality and seasonality of illegal trade in the north Atlantic. The article centres on a neglected oceanic region, thereby inverting historical geographies, shifting the focus from port centres like London and Copenhagen to the Scottish Northern and Western Isles, as well as the Faroe Islands. Epitomizing the ‘dichotomy of insularity’, in the eighteenth century these areas were located along maritime highways of global trade, and illegal trade flourished there, despite their challenging location. The article demonstrates that this illegal trade had different seasonal cycles from those of legal trade. While legal trade halted in the winter season, illegal trade continued throughout. Linking illegal maritime activities to more lawful ones, like fishing, the article suggests that the recurring nature of the contraband trade ought to be understood in relation to the broader coastal culture, in which maritime knowledge was circulated and the local relationship to the sea defined. The study suggests that illegal trade should be viewed not merely as an extension of globalization but as a rooted phenomenon, which developed in unison with the local environment.

papers.title: THE WIND THAT MELTS THE ICE: REFLECTIONS ON THE SCALE OF PHILOLOGY
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The global history of philology, like that of writing systems and other technologies, is characterized by diffusion and adaptation. These processes are made more difficult to grasp if we maintain a presentist focus on the Western philological tradition and its deeply Eurocentric legacy. Arguing against those who wish to resolve the problem by abandoning the term “philology” as irredeemably tainted, I propose that we introduce the notion of scale. Heuristically, it is helpful to think in terms of “small‐p” philology, the low‐level quotidian strategies and tools used by students and scholars to solve problems of textual interpretation, and “big‐P” Philology, a larger ideological edifice linked to metahistorical and transhistorical narratives about abstract concepts such as civilization, race, and religious truth. As a first step toward illuminating this issue of scale, this article excavates a highly specific moment of philological scholarship in twelfth‐century Japan and shows how a difficult word from a classical waka poem is explicated through the extension of an existing Chinese exegetical system. The example is taken from the Ōgishō , a pioneering treatise by the Heian period scholar Fujiwara no Kiyosuke (1104–1177).

papers.title: Slavery and Capitalism: A New Marxist History. By David McNally
papers.abstract: Slavery and Capitalism, by the political scientist David McNally, is not precisely a work of history. Rather, it is a revision to Marxist theory and its applicability to the study of enslaved labor in the Americas. McNally argues that transatlantic slavery played a pivotal role in the rise of capitalism, and that British and American plantations were capitalistic from their inception. His theoretical argument is that only Marxist analysis can provide the “concepts necessary to comprehensively theorizing [sic] capitalism and Atlantic slavery” (6). And yet, though history and theory cross-pollinate, historians and theorists ultimately have different scholarly projects, and different methodologies. Few historians commit to comprehensive theorising, at least to the watertightness on which McNally insists. The book is divided into two parts. In the first part, McNally analyses the careers of Richard Ligon, George Washington, and Edward Gibbon Wakefield. All three are well-known figures. Washington is universally familiar, and Ligon (a seventeenth-century colonist in Barbados, and the author of a history of English colonisation in the Caribbean), and Wakefield (a key figure in the British colonisation of South Australia) will be very familiar to specialists. The second part refutes claims about the place of enslaved labor and enslaved laborers in the history of capitalism that McNally considers evasions of, or challenges to, the applicability of Marx’s critique of political economy. For example, in one chapter, McNally argues that enslaved laborers, forced to work according to the industrial rhythms of clock-time, brutally and violented exploited, and wholly alienated from the products of their labor, ought to be considered "proletarians" despite not being wage-laborers. In another, McNally draws on histories of racial capitalism to insist that “racialization must be understood as, among other things, a modality of capitalist discipline” (83). These chapters are brisk and passionately argued, and McNally’s knowledge of Marx’s published work and correspondence is encyclopedic and impressive. Ironically, McNally often praises Marx’s own theoretical flexibility, quoting Engels, who wrote of Marx’s work, “It should go without saying that where things and their mutual relations are conceived not as fixed, but rather as changing … they are not to be encapsulated in rigid definitions, but rather to be developed in their process of historical or logical formation” (110).

papers.title: Curating New York’s “Raw Material”
papers.abstract: In 1997, the literary critic Hans Ulrich Gumbrecht mused, “The real question behind the question of what to do with our knowledge about the past is not only the—more or less technical—question of how to write or represent history. It is above all the question of what we imagine the past ‘to be’ (the question about the past as ‘raw material’), before we even begin to think about possible forms of representation.”1 Gumbrecht aimed to chart the quotidian totality of a single year, 1926, jumping between topics as disparate as airplanes and murder. His book In 1926: Living at the Edge of Time invites readers to consider the “raw material” of history to make the historical environment of that year immediate for them—to make them feel as if they are “in 1926.” Gumbrecht’s aim of immersing readers in the materiality of the past is shared by public historians and museum curators, who often employ a range of sensory experiences—visual, textural, sonic—to stimulate different planes of historical thinking and rouse in audiences a sense of curiosity. At the same time, public history, like In 1926, provokes us to think about how “we” imagine the past, in effect making audiences co-producers of historical knowledge. Put another way, a historical museum exhibition usually emphasizes “showing” over “telling,” encouraging visitors to interpret historical change for themselves and, in the process, provoking emotional responses. Yet this approach also exists in tension with the craft of curation itself, which requires making narrative choices to create a cohesive exhibition.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in cultural heritage: Constructing a domain-specific LLM series for Chinese local product heritage
papers.abstract: Abstract Chinese local product records in traditional gazetteers constitute a vital component of cultural heritage. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) have opened up new avenues for the preservation and utilization of such heritage. This article introduces the large language models (LLMs) tailored to Chinese local products, comprising a base model, a chat model, and a reasoning model collectively referred to as the Chinese local product LLM series. These models validate the feasibility of applying LLMs to the intelligent processing of Chinese local product knowledge and provide both a technical paradigm and toolset for cultural heritage research. This article first constructs a hybrid pre-training dataset containing one billion characters, drawn from historical texts on Chinese local products. Leveraging this dataset, the Qwen open-source base models underwent further pre-training for domain adaptation, leading to the development of specialized models for Chinese local product knowledge, including a base model, a chat model, and a reasoning model. These models are subsequently deployed as API endpoints and web applications to support automated textual processing and knowledge-based question answering services related to Chinese local products. This article marks the first attempt to develop LLMs specifically for the domain of cultural heritage with a focus on local products. It further demonstrates the effectiveness of continued pre-training, instruction tuning, data distillation, long-chain-of-thought fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation in improving the quality of local product information services. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs to advance both the preservation and protection of cultural heritage in the AI era.

papers.title: Proximity and Segregation in Industrial Manchester
papers.abstract: Abstract Manchester has long been a model for the class divisions characteristic of British Victorian cities, and this segregation has largely been attributed as a spatial phenomenon as informed by qualitative sources from the period. The digitization of historical source material, however, allows for quantitative assessments of residential differentiation. By analysing patterns of residential distribution using nineteenth-century, individual-level census data, it is revealed that early Victorian Manchester was characterized more by residential heterogeneity than segregation. In light of this finding, this article revisits the source base for early Victorian Manchester in order to reconcile the differences in the physical and social dimensions of segregation for a more accurate and holistic understanding of urban dynamics and the mechanisms of class formation. It explains this dissonance by exploring the city’s architectural, occupational, and cultural structures: while rich and poor lived cheek-by-jowl in the industrial city, temporal rhythms of employment, institutionalized cultures of class, and emerging modes of urban maintenance and discipline all produced practices which differentiated and isolated one class from another.

papers.title: Predicting the Past
papers.abstract: Absences pervade the historical record. The loss or destruction of material, redaction of documents, silence of participants, data embargoes, and poor record keeping present inherent difficulties to any understanding of the past. Gaps in the historical record pose significant challenges but they can also provide valuable opportunities. Instead of avoiding all gaps, historians can test the accuracy of some inferences about the past by carefully outlining their assumptions and explicitly predicting what they believe to have occurred in the absence of evidence. Subsequent discoveries or declassifications can then be used to assess the accuracy of these hypothesized explanations and, in turn, help us to evaluate the quality of historians’ thinking about the unknown past. Given enough examples, we can begin to learn more about how to make better predictions about the past or what we term “retrodictions.”1 The importance of prediction has been well documented across the social sciences for decades.2 Economists, political scientists, and psychologists regularly extol the virtues of making testable predictions for good scholarly practice and improved judgement. Although historians and historically minded scholars in the social sciences routinely rely on their own expert judgement when studying the past, few have considered making and testing explicit predictions when conducting historical research. Even fewer have considered the methodological demands and theoretical implications of retrodiction.3 This article considers why historians and social scientists should attempt to predict the past and explains how they can make and test retrodictions in a more rigorous manner. These conceptual and methodological insights are of considerable significance. Retrodiction is not an abstract or hypothetical subject. While some scholars may argue that accurate prediction of the past is irrelevant or impossible, many historians and social scientists regularly make inferences about undocumented history. Educated guesses occur across the discipline and beyond. There is nevertheless a tension between the widespread but often implicit employment of retrodiction, and the rarity with which it is deliberately considered and applied. Thinking more explicitly about retrodiction offers the chance to assess and refine historical interpretation. By understanding why some predictions about the past prove more or less accurate than others, we can think more clearly about how to manage empirical gaps, better adjudicate between competing interpretations, and gain greater confidence in our own retrodictions. This article proceeds in three parts before concluding. First, we introduce the concept of retrodiction and then reflect on the rewards and risks involved in making predictions about the past. Second, we consider different ways of making and testing predictions about the past, giving special attention to the important role of retrodiction tournaments. Third, we draw on key insights from research in the social sciences to inform the practice of retrodiction and highlight future avenues of research. Historical claims are built on evidence. From archival research and oral histories to archaeological investigations and satellite imaging, we have assembled much of our knowledge about the past from available data. Yet there are many gaps in the historical record and the pool of data available to experts is often very shallow. Experts who study the past rely on imperfect or incomplete information. In developing a broader interpretation of history, they may therefore need to speculate or “predict” the sort of picture that would emerge if or when more evidence ever became available. This attempt to predict the past—to engage in retrodiction—is thus one of the basic techniques that historians and social scientists use when they construct an interpretation of the past. Efforts to predict the past are commonplace. Scholars often make assumptions or reach conclusions about the past in the absence of direct evidence. Many historians and social scientists therefore already make retrodictions, albeit sometimes unknowingly or implicitly.4 For example, scholars have debated the status of the United Kingdom’s considerable war debts to the United States government following World War I. At least one historian has concluded that the war debt issue was effectively laid to rest in 1940 as a new and highly personal relationship emerged between Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt.5 In the absence of direct evidence, however, this conclusion represents an implicit prediction about what occurred in the past. Recent archival discoveries drawing on data from both sides of the Atlantic challenge this claim by showing that the United Kingdom’s war debts to the United States persisted as a source of diplomatic tension in the decades that followed and remain unpaid and outstanding.6 Some historians and social scientists advancing arguments about the past may seek to avoid making any explicit claims about gaps in the historical record and limit themselves to presenting the evidence they have found. Yet those scholars may have missed a valuable opportunity to test their historical judgement. Historians and historically minded scholars in the social sciences should instead accept that their interpretations of the past are often based on incomplete data and speculate about the sort of picture that would emerge if more evidence became available. They could then test their understanding of events by providing specific details about what we would expect to see if that missing evidence ever became public. Retrodiction does not alter the underlying logic of an historical argument but instead seeks only to make it clearer and more testable. Thinking more explicitly about retrodiction can therefore improve historical practice and our knowledge of the past. If historians and social scientists explain how they reach their conclusions, they and other scholars can better assess the quality of those arguments if new and important evidence ever comes to light. By making and testing enough examples, we may be able to determine how far the lessons of retrodiction can be generalized to other periods or fields of study. We accept that many scholars prefer to focus their attention on explanation rather than retrodiction. Analyzing what the available evidence says is a more familiar practice than speculating explicitly about what presently unavailable evidence might show.7 Yet explanation and retrodiction are cognate concepts.8 As an interpretation is developed—and historians and social scientists develop an interpretation by drawing on theories about how the world works—predictions are generated as a matter of course. “At any given point in an historical argument,” one of the authors of this article has previously explained, “the historian can ask, given what was said up to that point, whether it would be possible to predict how things would develop. This provides a useful test of the power of the argument: a strong interpretation should have a certain predictive force.”9 Retrodiction also provides the historian with a way to assess the validity of the interpretation taking shape in their mind. As historians or social scientists proceed with a project, they could ask themselves what might turn up when they read new material—whether material that has already been released, but which they have not seen yet, or material that is released later—if that tentative interpretation is correct. Those retrodictions about what new sources would show might be borne out, in which case the historian would have more confidence in the validity of that interpretation. Alternatively, the new sources might not be in line with what had been expected, in which case the historian might have to rethink their emerging interpretation, and maybe even question the assumptions or arguments on which it was based. We argue that it is important for scholars to consider and apply retrodiction consciously and thoughtfully, by explicitly stating what they would expect to see in as-yet-unexamined or unavailable sources. Historians and social scientists have advanced broader interpretations about what drove the collapse of the Soviet Union, for example, with a small number of scholars making educated guesses about the unknown past and what they would expect the archives to eventually reveal.10 The absence of evidence therefore serves as a way in which to test and potentially bolster a specific historical interpretation. Transforming explanations of past events into explicit, testable predictions enables historians and social scientists to shift from rationalizing events after they have occurred to formulating hypotheses in advance. Emphasizing a priori theorizing over post-hoc analysis can potentially lead to sharper, more robust historical narratives and help to strengthen the inferential power of interpretations or theories regarding causes of past events and historical trends.11 Retrodiction can also help scholars avoid hindsight bias—namely, the common tendency to incorrectly believe in retrospect that one correctly guessed how events would unfold.12 By making falsifiable claims, before new historical data comes to light, historians and social scientists can combat this tendency and increase accountability, thereby fostering scholarly rigor.13 Attempts to predict the past, however, do carry some risks. Retrodiction requires a degree of uncertainty about what has happened in the past. If we make educated guesses when the required evidence is unavailable to us, there is always the possibility that the missing data will never come to light. Assessments of historical judgement require the discovery of new, relevant evidence after a retrodiction has been made. Some predictions about the past, no matter how specific or well formulated, may be unverifiable. Crucial archival records have been destroyed in wars, for example, just as some individuals or organizations may have never written much down. Historians and social scientists should therefore try to focus their attention on areas where there is a reasonable possibility of testing their retrodictions. New data about the past can be anticipated in some cases. Some archives use “timed releases,” such as the National Archives in the United Kingdom, which embargoes many government documents for twenty years before releasing them to the public. We tend to know which government documents have been embargoed even if we do not know what they say. Not all government documents are released within twenty years, to be sure, but even in sensitive cases a release date is often agreed. Venturesome scholars can test their historical judgement by offering educated guesses about what these files contain and help us learn from their retrodictions by sharing how they reached these conclusions. Moreover, new data continues to emerge at a remarkable pace. Archives around the world regularly release new material. Previously closed archives have reopened, even if only temporarily, and archivists remain hard at work recovering lost data.14 Archival data represents one of many types of evidence that can emerge over time. Witnesses may eventually come forward, for example, just as leaked documents can shed light on the unknown past.15 Many exciting testing opportunities therefore exist for historians and social scientists. papers.title: MEHDIE: the Middle East Heritage Data Integration Endeavor
papers.abstract: Abstract Scholars in the Humanities often strive for depth and rigor in a single field or a small number of interconnected linguistic, cultural, and historical domains. This specialization and expertise, however, come at the cost of bodies of knowledge becoming isolated from each other. Digital tools that facilitate linking resources from disparate languages, a process known as multi-lingual entity resolution, can break down linguistic barriers between scholastic islands and enhance fertile cross-cultural collaboration. However, many contemporary multi-lingual tools and underlying technological resources are developed or trained on web data, that is, modern text contributed by Web users over the past few decades. Unsurprisingly, therefore, these tools’ efficacy has been limited when applied to text written in historical languages and dialects. To address these issues, in this paper, we present MEHDIE, the Middle East Heritage Data Integration Endeavor, a project dedicated to facilitating the semantic integration of knowledge sources related to the history of the Middle East using innovative data integration methods. The prototype multi-lingual entity resolution system we are currently developing utilizes spatial (geo-coordinates) and cross-lingual matching of textual information about a pair of place records to help identify their semantic relationship. This unique ability allows researchers to create bridges between collections of historical places from different languages, sources, and cultures. We present the motivation for MEHDIE, the tool’s current state, and some of the challenges we intend to address in the future.

papers.title: HISTORY AND THEORY AND PHILOLOGY NOW: TOGETHER IN THEORY
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In English‐speaking academe, philology has virtually disappeared as a defined discipline, although its traditional array of skills and techniques for reading, editing, and interpreting texts are indispensable to fields ranging from biblical studies through every language and literature and are central to historical research. Philology's status “now” seems to be that the analytic skills for dealing with texts, skills developed over centuries, have been appropriated by multiple academic specialties while the framework that used to contain them has been dismantled and nearly forgotten. From a historian's viewpoint, I track the lively resistance movement pressing for a return to philology and a turn to a “new” philology, a revived, recovered, restored discipline with its own coherent identity. This movement of renewal and restoration is complicated by the need to come to terms with philology's deep entanglement with racialist thought and anti‐Semitism, a past that has indelibly stained the reputation of philology as a discipline. The guiding intent of this article is to bring philology, with all its complications, back together with history, its formerly yoked companion discipline, and inquire where and how theory emerges—a metaphilology analogous to metahistory.

papers.title: The Plunder of Black America: How the Racial Wealth Gap Was Made . By Calvin Schermerhorn
papers.abstract: Numerous scholars have written about the racial wealth gap in the United States, often through social scientific approaches highlighting the ability of white families to transfer inheritance and other assets to their progeny across generations. In light of this existing literature, the critical contribution of Calvin Schermerhorn’s book, The Plunder of Black America: How the Racial Wealth Gap Was Made, is the intimate, poignant manner in which he bores into several Black families’ narratives across time and place to illustrate the fragility of African American household wealth and its interdependence with white racial domination and economic exploitation. Amid a surge of scholarly publications advocating reparatory justice for African American descendants of slavery, Schermerhorn also uniquely personalizes this demand. Built on discrete chapters spanning the colonial era to the present, the author depicts historical and contemporary families whose individual upward mobility foundered against “a new iteration of economic racism that emerged as they climbed” (2). Indeed, according to Schermerhorn, “[e]ach time Black Americans gained a little wealth, new policies or economic practices stripped a portion of that wealth and imposed new barriers to its creation and retention… peeling away assets in the present and obstructing opportunities for helping the next generation.” (2) Rather than constituting a parallel development to the acquisition of white wealth, the latter was premised on the former through successive periods of systemic dispossession, disinheritance, and decapitalization—a process that the nineteenth-century abolitionist Frederick Douglass identified as plunder. “Stolen Black labor value,” Schermerhorn argues, “became white wealth, passed down and increased in each generation, on average, while theft of African American work product became a loss that was compounded in each generation” (82). This dynamic developed in earnest between the 1640s and 1660s, when the initial possibilities for Black property ownership and wealth for colonial families like Mary and Anthony Johnson were eroded and African Americans “were forced out of places that held marginal opportunities to become free, generate income, and build resources and into places that held virtually no opportunities to do so” (73).

papers.title: The Colony and the Company: Haiti after the Mississippi Bubble. By Malick Ghachem
papers.abstract: Malick Ghachem’s first book, The Old Regime and the Haitian Revolution (2012), examined the violent end of the French colony of Saint-Domingue and of the highly stratified, extremely exploitative model of plantation slavery that had made it France’s most lucrative overseas possession. In The Colony and the Company, by contrast, Ghachem is interested in beginnings rather than endings. He argues that the years 1715-1725 were particularly critical in the emergence of a distinctive “military-planter state” based on “militant slavery,” which he links to the rise of a new kind of finance monopoly capitalism, which burst onto the scene in France in the second decade of the eighteenth century with the rapid rise and dramatic fall of the financial system of the Scottish financier and fugitive John Law. As a result of this process, Ghachem argues, Saint-Domingue, hitherto something of a backwater of the French Caribbean, settled by pirates seeking quick riches through the plunder of Spanish treasure fleets, was transformed into a “bubble colony,” fueled by dreams of easy riches from the burgeoning sugar trade. The result was a dynamic but particularly unstable colony, characterized by rapid growth, periodic crises, and brutal repression, which would ultimately explode into the Haitian Revolution.

papers.title: What Makes Transportation History
papers.abstract: Abstract The idea that societies progress from rickshaw to railroad has been ubiquitous in discourses of colonialism and technological determinism since the nineteenth century. While historians of colonialism have debunked these discourses in specific cases, the question of why transportation came to be such a common sense measure of historical change has been left untouched. This article argues that “transportation” has a history. From eighteenth- and nineteenth-century political-economic philosophy in Europe, Japan, and the United States, to rickshaw puller movements in early twentieth-century Japan, to the emergence of transport devices as museum objects in the 1960s, “What Makes Transportation History” shows how transportation came to be understood both as the foundation for economic life and as a measure and maker of linear and irreversible change over time. This process did not exclude those who approached transportation as a livelihood. Rather, battles with rickshaw pullers and other transportation workers naturalized the idea that the needs of transport’s producers must be subordinated to the needs of transport’s consumers for modern societies to progress.

papers.title: A Revolution of Letters
papers.abstract: Abstract Colonialism in Africa was a textual encounter, with writing operating as an essential tool for colonial governance as well as a visual embodiment of Western “rationality” and civilization. Somalis, a predominantly oral people spread out across five colonial territories in the Horn of Africa, resisted Latin-based orthographies for their language because of these associations, while anticolonial nationalism following the Second World War brought the orthography question to the forefront as Somalis vigorously debated the written form Somali should take. Following Somalia’s independence in 1960, the continued use of colonial languages for writing threatened the postcolonial nation-building project and its larger ambitions to unify the partitioned Somali territories into a Greater Somalia, a central objective of Pan-Somali nationalist politics. When General Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in 1969, the adoption of a Somali script became a priority for his socialist military government, as his authoritarian regime used visual practices of statecraft such as mass spectacles and textual production to establish a modern Pan-Somali nationalist identity. This article examines the history of the Somali orthography and the making of a nationalist discourse ecology that brought together text, sight, and spectacle in revolutionary Somalia at a time when the Somali state looked beyond its borders and mobilized for war.

papers.title: Paula Fredriksen. Ancient Christianities: The First Five Hundred Years
papers.abstract: Ancient Christianities is exactly the kind of general account of the early Christian centuries that we would expect from Paula Fredriksen: elegantly written, theologically rich, socially nuanced. Paul and Augustine loom large, as do intellectual histories of concepts like sin, salvation, god, and body. We are treated to Fredriksen’s cogent insights into the construction of “Jewish,” “Christian,” and “pagan” labels, not as fixed identities or groups, but as powerful rhetorical strategies that shift with time, situation, and audience. The plural “Christianities” of the title refers to diverse modes of religion and discourse just as much as to the diverse groups of Christ-followers that populate these centuries. The book consists of seven thematic chapters, organized more-or-less chronologically within each chapter. The first chapter, “The Idea of Israel,” and the last, “Pagan and Christian,” frame the book with the questions of religious transformation that shape the period we call late antiquity. In what ways does Christianity grow out of, appropriate, and/or reject both Judaism and the traditional Mediterranean religions of antiquity? How does a particular form of Christianity become the dominant religion of the Roman Mediterranean? The middle chapters address theological diversity (aka heresy and orthodoxy), persecution and martyrdom, apocalyptic eschatology, imperial Christology, and asceticism. This may sound like a lot of -isms and -ologies, but Fredriksen has a knack for making complex ideas clear and grounded in social realities. She treats each category as a capacious net for a variety of interrelated sub-topics.

papers.title: Revisiting the “Comfort Girls” of Report 49
papers.abstract: Abstract In 1944, a Japanese American intelligence officer stationed in Ledo, India, unwittingly composed a famous historical document: “Japanese Prisoner of War Interrogation Report No. 49,” which focused on twenty Korean comfort women captured near Myitkyina, Burma. In the decades since, most historians have regarded the report as evidence of the Japanese state’s responsibility for the comfort woman system, but it has also been embraced by revisionists arguing the opposing case. This essay reassesses the document to show how it emerged from a many-sided struggle over how women’s bodies should be used in the simultaneous conflicts of empire and decolonization that constituted World War II in Burma. Korean comfort women’s status as both Japan’s “own women” and colonized subjects meant that they could be exploited to a variety of ends—both on the battlefield and in the realm of information warfare—for audiences including Anglophone newspaper readers, American military officers, Japanese soldiers, and Burmese civilians. Removed from its specific geographical and temporal context, the document’s elevation as a generic piece of evidence has obscured a larger history in which concerns about “sex slavery,” a concept notably absent from this report, emerged, retreated, and reemerged over the course of the war.

papers.title: Writing Histories of Everyday Life in Authoritarian Regimes, from Europe to the Global South
papers.abstract: Abstract This article – arising from an ERC-funded project on the lived experiences of dictatorship – explores the development of and approaches to the history of everyday life under repressive political systems, presenting the historiographical, conceptual, and contextual points of contact, synergy, and divergence between historians working in and on Europe, Southern Africa, and Latin America. As a historiographical review article, this piece provides both a critical assessment of and novel intervention in these respective literatures, making the case for ‘decentring’ European histories and historiographies, to encourage greater engagement and collaboration between those working on different historical and geographical contexts.

papers.title: Glenn Dyer. The Era Was Lost: The Rise and Fall of New York City’s Rank-and-File Rebels
papers.abstract: Organized labor is often treated as a cohesive unit. Phrases like “the labor movement” imply not only that there is an organized force but that it is unified. While this sense of solidity is useful when trying to understand the myriad forces stacked against workers’ organizations, it often oversimplifies complex dynamics at work within labor unions throughout US history. Sometimes the rank and file’s goals are not those held by union leadership. This dichotomy has only begun to be studied, and Glenn Dyer’s new book is a welcome addition to this literature. The Era Was Lost is a case study on New York City workers’ militancy in the 1960s and 1970s. During this period, which is detailed in Jefferson Cowie’s Stayin’ Alive: The 1970s and the Last Days of the Working Class (2010) and Kim Phillips-Fein’s Fear City: New York’s Fiscal Crisis and the Rise of Austerity Politics (2017), the United States became more conservative, and labor unions became substantially less powerful. While many of the unions and events discussed in the book have been told by other historians, Dyer claims his approach “provides a novel interpretation by foregrounding rank-and-file struggles” rather than “labor writ large” in the working-class struggles during this period (4). Making a distinction between union leaders and the rank and file, Dyer argues that the rank and file remained committed to advancing their cause of higher wages, better benefits, and better working conditions, even as union leaders became more conservative.

papers.title: Self-Fashioning, Food, and Masculinity in George III’s Monarchy
papers.abstract: Abstract George III was a family man, a modest eater, and a thoughtful ruler who wrote about the big questions of the day, from royal sovereignty to the best methods of agriculture to feed a modern nation. His writings provide a glimpse of his version of monarchy, which placed him at the head of a national family, where he embodied the habits of self-regulation and temperance in keeping with the sensibilities of late eighteenth-century manhood. This article brings together George’s meals and his essays, considering the histories of food, masculinity, and self-fashioning, to argue that George was a monarch who embodied a new form of masculinity, as marked by his agricultural interests and insistence on a modest diet. His eating habits, along with his intellectual interests and public persona, bring us to the intersection between the private man and the public monarch. Drawing on newly digitized data, alongside contemporary caricatures and descriptions, and George’s own writing, we argue that moderation was central to George’s creation of an image that appealed to the emerging British nation of the late eighteenth century; food was central to this image, highlighting both his masculine self-control and his ability to be useful to the nation.

papers.title: Revolutionary Warfare: How the Algerian War Made Modern Counterinsurgency. By Terrence G. Peterson
papers.abstract: The Front de Libération National was not the only revolutionary belligerent in the Algerian War (1954-1962). At least, that is how the French military viewed it. Since the 1960s, very few Anglophone studies have examined the truly revolutionary tones of the French Army’s guerre révolutionnaire doctrine, employed by a politically and militarily radicalized French officer corps, reeling from exposure and defeat to the Marxist Viet Minh in Indochina. It is perhaps more accurate to describe guerre révolutionnaire as more of an ideology than a strictly-military doctrine. Its proponents viewed the conflicts in Indochina and Algeria not as traditional colonial wars, but as part of a global conflagration against communism, which sought, in their eyes, to outflank and subsume the West via the colonies. The doctrine and its many proponents suggested that the French take a few leaves out of the Marxist playbook, and employ the methods of their communist foe. This included (but was not limited to) the use of psychological warfare: brainwashing, struggle sessions (autocritique), ideological re-education and political commissars: all utilized in Algeria in a desperate attempt to remake Frenchmen out of captured rebels.

papers.title: The Colonial Metamorphosis of Egyptian Capital Punishment, 1884–1903
papers.abstract: Abstract This article analyses how colonial rule remade Egyptian capital punishment. Around the turn of the twentieth century, British officials deliberately overturned the strong protections for defendants that Islamic law once offered, paving the way for a steady and sustained increase in execution rates. More executions meant more opportunities for ordinary people to practise the distinctive forms of ‘popular legalism’ that flourished on execution days. In keeping with established custom, the families of perpetrator and victim played leading roles on gallows days, defending kin and negotiating punishment. Women often took charge of these occasions, demonstrating and enhancing their social power while simultaneously directing the affective responses of the assembled crowds. Such public displays of gendered authority were anathema to Egyptian elites and colonial officials alike, turning both decisively against public punishment. The abolition of public executions thus erased a prominent manifestation of the social embeddedness of Islamic law.

papers.title: Joseph A. Seeley. Border of Water and Ice: The Yalu River and Japan's Empire in Korea and Manchuria
papers.abstract: Joseph Seeley has produced an excellent book for historians interested in Sino-Korean border spaces, Japan’s 20th century continental empire and its infrastructure, and the entwined environmental legacies of both colonial Korea and Manchukuo. Border of Water and Ice: The Yalu River and Japan’s Empire in Korea and Manchuria is thematically ambitious but manages not to sprawl, in part through regular meditations on the tangible and environmental impacts of the seasonal changes on the Yalu River, the narrow watercourse flowing down for about 500 kilometers out into the Yellow Sea and separating the cities of Chinese Andong (today Dandong) and Korean Sinuiju. Seeley’s clear prose is carefully underpinned with sources in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese, and the book adds in-depth coverage of an important region to the increasingly transnational field of environmental history of Northeast Asia. Readers who wonder how the contemporary North Korean state managed to secure sovereignty over several strategic islands on the Chinese side of the Yalu estuary will find a fascinating origin story in Seeley’s first chapter. His detailed historical detective work demonstrates how Japanese efforts to harvest natural resources like reeds led to Korean (and then colonial Japanese) control being extended along the northern bank of the river. Seeley traces the emergence of one island from its origins in the upstream erosion and sedimentation flows of the late 1880s, moving through militia violence and an array of historical agents, including Chinese reed harvesters, Qing diplomats, Japanese local consular officials, Korean collaborators (Ilchinhoe), Japanese “continental adventurers,” and the ever-changing river itself.

papers.title: Colonizing Accra
papers.abstract: Abstract Between 1886 and 1888, a series of dramatic events took place in the West African town of Accra, marking an escalation of colonial control and imperial state formation. This essay investigates three previously unknown, but profoundly important, political events through the perspective of narrative history. It asks how does storytelling change the way that historians approach the archive? What critiques of time, state, and power might narrative history offer the historian? This essay interweaves narrative storytelling with a critique of writing and archival practice. It argues that the events that took place in Accra in 1886–88 suggest a far later timeline for colonization than historians have previously accepted, and that these events—which were so crucial to Accra’s colonization by Britain—have perhaps been omitted from the historical record because historians mine the archives for data, not for stories. By approaching the archive for its storytelling potential, this essay suggests that historians may unearth not just compelling facts or anecdotes but a novel framework for understanding the movement of history.
