papers.title: Alison L. LaCroix. The Interbellum Constitution: Union, Commerce, and Slavery in the Age of Federalisms .
papers.abstract: One major theme in histories of the American founding is imperium in imperio (sovereignty within sovereignty, government within government). This phrase is often treated as the framers’ original understanding of federalism: the new states sharing sovereignty with the new federal government. Before it was treated as a solution, it was the Latin name of a serious problem, an error, a contradiction, even an impossibility. Alison L. LaCroix and other American historians have cited Blackstone and eighteenth-century Whigs on sovereignty as “supreme,” “absolute,” unitary, and exclusive; and have quoted Alexander Hamilton’s famous description in 1774 of such attempts to split the sovereignty baby as a “solecism of politics,” an error. A year later, John Adams put the problem in theological terms: Two sovereigns could coexist in the same state no more than “two supreme beings in the same universe.” Nevertheless, the framers took the leap and embraced imperium in imperio as the solution to the same problem. However, it was just a new informal experimental solution, an abstract solution in theory. The problem would be how to solve the solecism in practice, and those practices from 1815 to 1861 are the deeply engaging stories in LaCroix’s The Interbellum Constitution: Union, Commerce, and Slavery in the Age of Federalisms. The last word in the subtitle is the most important: Each chapter shows how this formative era produced more complicated and more intriguing alternative models. Even if the framers had any single theory of federalism—which LaCroix rightly doubts—the theory soon multiplied into multiple doctrines and practices of federalisms, plural.

papers.title: Catherine Tatiana Dunlop. The Mistral: A Windswept History of Modern France
papers.abstract: Those of us who have lived, worked, or travelled to Provence will have encountered the mistral. When this wind blows, the sky above turns the deepest blue while trees, crops, houses, and people are pummeled by the wind that sweeps down from mountains through the Rhône Valley and out to the Mediterranean Sea. The Mistral, Catherine Tatiana Dunlop’s slim yet punchy book harnesses the mistral in fascinating and generative ways. Tracking the wind’s impact through maps, illustrations, personal accounts and state records, alongside the landscape itself (such as wind-battered trees), Dunlop succeeds in showing how the mistral has shaped, but not determined, human and nonhuman life in this renowned and storied region of France. Beginning in the postrevolutionary era, she shows how successive governments have attempted to control, understand, and tame the wind through such things as the judicious planting of trees and new meteorological observatories (most famously on the top of wind-battered Mont Ventoux). Yet state attempts to contain the mistral were most often no match for the wind’s force: “the mistral became a forceful and bone-chilling reminder that provincial environments were not so easily quelled” (12).

papers.title: Avner Ofrath. Colonial Algeria and the Politics of Citizenship
papers.abstract: Avner Ofrath’s scrupulously researched work focuses on the politics of citizenship in colonial Algeria. The book opens with the following quote from an official 1958 photo album produced by the French government in Algeria: “[n]ever, since 1830 did any measure of racial segregation exist in Algeria.” Ofrath thus embarks on demonstrating the inaccuracy of this “astonishingly unequivocal” French claim that no measure of racial segregation existed in the colony from 1830 onward. Algeria was France’s most important colony, with parts of it becoming an extension of the metropole. As such, the question of citizenship and empire is particularly pertinent in thinking about the relationship between the colonizer and the colonized. To begin, it is germane to point out that segregation is a highly charged word, which in the 1950s was still closely associated in the French language with apartheid in South Africa and with the US South. At no point in the work does Ofrath distinguish the marginalization of the colonized population in Algeria, which varied in degree depending on status, from the more rigid segregation existing in the two afore mentioned examples. That segregation along those lines might not have existed in Algeria, at least until the post–World War II period, is never broached.

papers.title: Natanya Duncan. An Efficient Womanhood: Women and the Making of the Universal Negro Improvement Association

papers.abstract: Freedom Soldiers: The Emancipation of Black Soldiers in Civil War Camps, Courts, and Prisons by Jonathan Lande examines the protracted process of emancipation that Black Civil War soldiers engaged in as they transitioned from enslaved labor to military labor on their path to freedom. In doing so, Lande makes a powerful argument for seeing Black soldiers’ use of mobility as a larger struggle for Black self-determination and as a tool for renegotiating labor rights with the federal government. In Freedom Soldiers, Lande builds upon the arguments made in recent years by historians who argue that emancipation was a process and not an event and stress the important role that forging contractual relationships with the state played in defining and securing rights for newly freed people. However, Lande breaks new ground as he seeks to reframe the revisionist history of Black Civil War soldiers, which often aggrandizes their heroic deeds and loyalty while downplaying their acts of rebellion and desertion. Instead, Lande argues that the road to freedom for Black soldiers was multidimensional and that their acts of rebellion were not a departure from their fight for freedom but were, in fact, a defining feature. Lande argues that Black soldiers “leaves of freedom” or unauthorized departures were, in reality, ways in which these once enslaved men voted with their feet in their continuing fight for rights to familial bonds, equal labor rights, and in protesting unequal and coercive military labor practices. As such, Lande’s argument provides a unique perspective on Black soldiers’ desertion as a tactic to secure further freedoms and negotiate labor contracts with the US Army.

papers.title: Richard Reid. The African Revolution: A History of the Long Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: With this ambitious intervention, Richard Reid seeks to decolonize our understanding of the Scramble for Africa and its impacts. Drawing on his extensive knowledge of modern African history, Reid contextualizes the Scramble in terms of the political reformism and global commercial engagements that characterized much of Africa’s innovative yet volatile nineteenth century. The result is an impressive work of synthesis with its own revisionist agenda: to upend our understanding of the Scramble as a definitive “rupture” in African history (19). Reid presents his argument in The African Revolution in five parts, bookended by a prologue and epilogue. In part 1, he lays out the aim, scope, and arguments of the book. In part 2, he explores how the growth in trans- and intercontinental exchanges intensified political challenges in Africa and spurred much of the creative but violent political inventiveness of this epoch. Reid outlines a reoccurring “pattern … of fusion followed by fission” as polities were made and unmade through insurrections and violent reformism (54). These political developments were often entangled with socioeconomic reforms, and in the third part, Reid examines how “Africans, whether extant elites or entrepreneurial upstarts, sought to grasp the opportunities presented by intensifying global interaction” (116). Coercion and extraction underpinned many of the political and economic developments of this period, and as individuals attempted to position themselves advantageously, they created new urban spaces, forms of identity, and economic infrastructures that “ironically, facilitated global intrusion” (150).

papers.title: La última guerra del Siglo de las Luces: Revolución Liberal y republicanismo popular en Ecuador (The Final War of the Age of Enlightenment: The Liberal Revolution and Popular Republicanism in Ecuador). By Valeria Coronel
papers.abstract: Valeria Coronel’s La última guerra del Siglo de las Luces is the masterful culmination of efforts by a generation of scholars to rethink the nineteenth century in Latin America. The nineteenth century had long been understood as a time when popular actors, be they Indigenous communities, artisans, campesinos (small farmers), slaves, and freed people were ignorant of, and had no interest in, the newly independent Latin American nations and only entered the political sphere as clients of powerful patrons or cannon fodder. Their lot was to endure exploitation by an all-powerful oligarchy, occasionally engage in an atavistic rebellion, and await their political awakening with either populism or socialism in the twentieth century. A new historiography has slowly but surely worked to transform our understanding of the nineteenth century, exploring how plebeian actors created a popular republicanism to claim citizenship in the new nations, demand rights, and protect their interests. Ecuador has been mostly ignored in the historiographic revolution. Partly this is a matter of timing—while democratic republicanism was being dismantled by coalitions of liberal and conservative elites in most of Latin America by the 1880s, such as in Colombia and Mexico, in Ecuador it was surging. However, Coronel’s book is not only valuable for its focus on Ecuador (although this alone would make it a worthy read), but also because it builds on and perhaps even perfects the nation and state formation literature; it is a true social history of politics, linking the social history of popular groups’ everyday lives to their political discourse and actions.

papers.title: Dispelling ‘ das Herbert Butterfieldproblem ’: A Rereading of The Whig Interpretation of History
papers.abstract: Abstract Herbert Butterfield’s The Whig Interpretation of History (1931) is universally received as sceptical of ‘whig’ teleology in historical accounts and, therefore, of politically charged narratives of history. This view stands in need of a basic correction. Butterfield’s work targets teleological accounts which involve a determinate conception of progress such as would arm a partisan politics. He calls this the politics of the ‘general proposition’. Nevertheless, he does defend a conception of progress involving an indeterminate concept. The historian finds, intimated in the detail of the past, that progress is the fruit of interactions between opposing parties. The imperative for the statesman in the present, then, is to facilitate such interactions. In short, The Whig Interpretation of History is a positive work of political thought. Looked at this way, Butterfield’s later, controversial work, The Englishman & His History , does not appear to be in contradiction with the earlier book so much as a polemical expression of it. The two books together present what may be called Butterfield’s politics of historiography. Histories which present progress as a straight line, to be co-opted by one party, encourage precisely the political action which impedes progress. Butterfield, in short, is still a kind of ‘whig’.

papers.title: Political Equality and Economic Inequality in Étienne-Géry Lenglet’s Recipe for the Modern Republic
papers.abstract: Abstract Reflections on the legacy of ‘Jacobin egalitarianism’ in post-Thermidorian France can be seen as following one of three strands: conservative, communist, or democratic. By shedding light on the democratic trajectory, this article addresses the historiographical imbalance that has disproportionately focused on conservative and communist perspectives. This study thereby pursues a renewed understanding of the relationship between the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and the evolution of political economy. Through an analysis of Étienne-Géry Lenglet’s treatise, De la propriété (1798), the contexts and content of democratic political economy during the revolutionary decade are identified. Lenglet’s politics formed an intervention in the debates during the Directory on the dynamics of property, morality, the franchise, and the principles of modern polities. His thought exemplifies a Condorcetian egalitarianism that grappled with the dilemmas posed by the rise of commerce and standing armies. This analysis of Lenglet’s work challenges the notion that the radicals of the French Revolution operated outside of Enlightenment political economy: De la propriété was deeply rooted in Enlightenment and revolutionary rhetoric. Lenglet’s politics emerges as a crucial component of diverse reform projects that contradicts reified depictions of Enlightenment political thought.

papers.title: Zamira Abman. Coerced Liberation: Muslim Women in Soviet Tajikistan
papers.abstract: In the 1920s and 1930s the Soviet government imposed a crash “liberation” campaign on the women of Central Asia, staging public shows of women burning their veils and putting husbands on trial for domestic violence. The literature on how women’s liberation unfolded in Uzbekistan is robust, but fewer historians have worked on other Central Asian republics, especially for the postwar decades. In Coerced Liberation, Zamira Abman makes a fine contribution to the field with her study, which considers the failure of women’s liberation in Tajikistan. Abman was born and raised in Tajikistan, and was able to gather dozens of oral histories in Tajik and Russian. She also gained unprecedented access to the Tajik Communist Party Archive, as well as state archives. She uses these archives to show not only why the liberation project in Tajikistan failed, but why the Tajik republic was anomalous within Soviet Central Asia. Abman’s argument rests on the sharp distinction between urban and rural life. Tajikistan’s capital, Dushanbe/Stalinobod, was built in the late 1920s; the only other town of note, Khujand/Leninobod, was much older but lacked political importance. The communists building revolutionary culture in the new capital were predominately Slavic, a situation that did not change until the 1960s. Meanwhile, more than 80 percent of the Tajik population lived in the countryside and did not speak Russian. A profound gap between urban and rural outlooks existed everywhere in the USSR, but the communists made less progress in overcoming it in Tajikistan than elsewhere in Central Asia. Abman does not spend much time investigating why this was, but it was partly rooted in the republic’s mountainous terrain that created very difficult conditions for industrial development. Tajikistan was consistently the poorest of the Soviet republics.

papers.title: Alan M. Stahl. The House of Condulmer: The Rise and Decline of a Venetian Family in the Century of the Black Death
papers.abstract: The relationship between economic and political power is a central question for historians of late medieval Italian cities. Scholars have combed the archives of Florence, Venice, Padua, and Pistoia to examine how commercial success and merchant wealth did or did not allow individuals and families to ascend into civic government and gain control of political institutions. In the Venetian context, the question has been shaped by the closing, or Serrata, of Venice’s political class into a restrictive, hereditary oligarchy that ruled until the fall of the Venetian republic in 1797. While scholars traditionally dated the Serrata to 1297, Gerhard Rösch has argued that a more fluid political elite was defined as a ruling class in the early decades of the fourteenth century, and Stanley Chojnacki has extended the timeline of the social and legal consolidation of the Venetian patriciate to the early fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, arguing that the self-fashioning of Venice’s ruling class was a process of renewal and redefinition that spanned generations. While many studies of the Venetian patriciate focus on alliances and power dynamics between the most important patrician families, Alan Stahl’s The House of Condulmer: The Rise and Decline of a Venetian Family in the Century of the Black Death examines the fortunes of a family on the fringes of the nobility and tells five interconnected stories about individuals’ social, political, and economic strategies to gain access to patrician society.

papers.title: Paul J. Kosmin. The Ancient Shore .
papers.abstract: As the second century CE geographer Strabo noted, “We (humans) are, in some sense, amphibious, belonging as much to dry land as to the sea” (Strabo 1.1.16). papers.title: Vernacular development, drought, and US technical assistance in postcolonial Lebanon
papers.abstract: Abstract Between 1951–55, the US Bureau of Reclamation conducted research in Lebanon to plan a hydroelectric and irrigation scheme using Lebanon's largest river, the Litani. Vernacular development was a mode of interaction that interrupted and subverted the technological and temporal framework animating midcentury international development. That framework promised elaborate works in the future, which almost never materialized. Through vernacular development strategies, Litani communities identified their own material needs and goals and experimented with strategies to enroll international researchers into attaining them. They derived these strategies from their experience with successive imperial and corporate planning missions that had come and gone in the decades prior to the postwar development era. papers.title: Lydia Walker. States-in-Waiting: A Counternarrative of Global Decolonization .
papers.abstract: States-in-Waiting is a nuanced and meticulously researched exploration of knowledge, power, and legitimacy in the era of decolonization. The monograph opens with the story of India’s Jawaharlal Nehru handing a blank check to the Naga nationalist leader, Angami Zapu Phizo, and the rumored existence of this check within the archives of Naga nationalists. The catch is that these archives, much like many Naga nationalist leaders themselves, are in exile. Once handed to an international advocate for safekeeping, they have yet to be returned to the descendants of these activists. This opening vignette reflects one of the key tensions of the book: International advocates have played a critical role in preserving and promoting the knowledge of national claimants, yet colonial and paternal dynamics nevertheless pervade their relationships with those for whom they advocate. States-in-Waiting is driven by a core question: What makes a nationalist claim legitimate? Through exploring a range of case studies, this monograph reveals that the criteria for gaining legitimacy were not fixed, but were politically and temporally contingent. Walker argues that “international recognition [of nationalist claims] favored communities that had mobilized earlier under empire” and were able to leverage either colonial power structures or military strength and regional alliances to emerge as legitimate national actors when European powers withdrew (23). Nationalist claimants from supposedly peripheral regions, who surfaced during later periods, were often denied these forms of intervention and faced numerous barriers to gaining international recognition of their claims. Consequently, many states-in-waiting turned to transnational advocacy networks to legitimize and promote their struggles for national independence within international forums. The monograph follows a range of different struggles for liberation that reached their zenith in the early 1960s. Walker describes it as a connective rather than comparative history (7). Its narrative is situated at the level of the individual—allowing Walker to draw novel connections between a range of seemingly unrelated nonstate, state, and transnational actors. Amongst its diverse cast of characters are nationalist-claimants, postcolonial statesmen, humanitarians, intellectuals, peace activists, mining executives, missionaries, international civil servants, and government officials. Walker’s case studies are methodically researched and presented accessibly for a global history audience who may not have the regional knowledge to contextualize these actors or their networks. The chapters are written to work in isolation with detailed introductions and conclusions that reintroduce key figures and reinforce overarching arguments.

papers.title: Chris Beneke. Free Exercise: Religion, the First Amendment, and the Making of America
papers.abstract: Chris Beneke’s latest work, Free Exercise: Religion, the First Amendment, and the Making of America, serves as an excellent and remarkably readable survey of the political, intellectual, and social context in which the Constitution’s religious clauses emerged. The narrative starts from the genesis of the Bill of Rights as a text to then investigate how pragmatic and principled considerations—from the memory of religious violence to new ideas about free markets, nation-building, and “civility”—factored into the early republic’s option for free exercise, shaping both its terms and limitations. Such a comprehensive analysis of the “original meaning” of the First Amendment inevitably leads Beneke to address the contemporary debate opposing “separationists,” who argue that disestablishment was meant to create a secular republic, to “accommodationists,” who argue that its goal was the equal distribution of government support for religion (“nonpreferentialism”) rather than its wholesale suppression. The author’s ultimate case for separationism is more nuanced than his dismissal of accommodationism, which he bases on the First Congress passing up an explicit opportunity to incorporate nonpreferentialist language into the Constitution and on scattered evidence suggesting that public days of thanksgiving and laws on mandatory Sunday rest—commonly invoked by accommodationists as proof that the founding generation did not have a secular agenda—were considered at odds with the “spirit” of the Constitution from the get-go (32, 53–54). While conceding that attributing a modern secular sensibility to the founders, not to mention the average early American, would be an anachronism, Beneke emphasizes that those seeds were indeed being planted.

papers.title: Rachel M. Petrocelli. Transactional Culture in Colonial Dakar, 1902–44
papers.abstract: How have cities worked? In one way or another, anyone working in urban studies tries to answer this question. For scholars working in the so-called Global South, one concept often haunts answers to this query: informality. Many observers deploy this term to describe often undocumented economic practices in postcolonial cities that defy the European and North American-based categories that experts use to plan cities and their economies. For decades, Africanists have pushed back against this characterization and the very concept of “informality.” Instead, scholars have explained the logics undergirding urban systems across the continent, calling into question the utility of deeming such complexly organized socioeconomic structures “informal.” However, most works present this alternative urbanism as a contemporary phenomenon or, at best, a product of the postcolonial era, a period that saw unprecedented urbanization across the continent as well as austerity imposed by international economic institutions like the World Bank. Rachel Petrocelli’s new book Transactional Culture deepens this history by looking at the colonial genesis of what she calls a “transactional culture.” In doing so, she reveals how people in colonial Dakar created urban economies rooted more in elaborately managed social relations than official plans.

papers.title: Kit Kowol. Blue Jerusalem: British Conservatism, Winston Churchill, and the Second World War
papers.abstract: The 1945 General Election has cast a long shadow over the history of contemporary Britain. In both popular and scholarly narratives, it is often evoked to tell a particular story about Britain’s wartime experience and the consequences that followed from it. At the center of this story is the idea of Conservative retreat. The apparent collapse of Conservative support at the hands of Clement Attlee’s Labour party, it seemed, signaled a rejection of the party’s assumptions and beliefs. As early as 1969, writers like Angus Calder referred to a “people’s war” that had been marked by a popular enthusiasm for collectivist change. It followed that Conservatism had only survived the 1940s by capitulating to a leftward turn that had rendered its traditional ideas redundant. Blue Jerusalem challenges this story. Prior to polling day in 1945, Kit Kowol argues, Conservatives had been remarkably successful in defending their beliefs and institutions. As well as reinvigorating their party with new ideas, Tories inculcated Britain from an ascendent socialism and introduced policies that had enduring legacies.

papers.title: Nick Lloyd. The Eastern Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918
papers.abstract: Nick Lloyd’s new book The Eastern Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918 is the second book in a trilogy covering the First World War, following the 2021 book The Western Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918, and to be followed by a subsequent volume on the wider war. As a result, the division of coverage across the three volumes is necessarily somewhat arbitrary. The Eastern Front naturally includes the Russian front, but in addition spends extensive time covering the Italian, Serbian, Salonika, and Romanian fronts. He begins with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and carries the narrative through the Russian Revolution, and up to the final collapse of Austria-Hungary in the final months of the war. The campaigns in Africa, the Caucasus, Mesopotamia, and Gallipoli are left for the next volume. In trying to encompass a conflict as enormous as the First World War, even with three volumes of space with which to work, Lloyd has to choose the themes and aspects to emphasize. This is not to criticize his work for not being comprehensive, but instead to identify what he cares about. The best way to summarize the task Lloyd has set for himself is a chronicle: a strongly chronological, narrative story of decision-making by the highest-level military and political leadership on all sides. He has admirably sought out the primary sources to cover the military leadership of all belligerents, not merely the relatively well-known leaders of, say, Germany, Austria, and Russia. Italy, Serbia, Bulgaria, and Romania are fully represented, as are the British and French commanders of the seemingly remote and obscure Salonika front. Lloyd’s characteristic method of composition is to present generals and political leaders in their own words as they lay out their tactical and operational thinking, deciding when and how to risk their scarce and war-weary soldiers in new offensives. As a result, his book presents a vivid portrait of the personalities, pathological or otherwise, of the key commanders of all parties. His extensive use of their testimony is vivid and compelling. Despite the emphasis on military calculations, the book does not offer a particularly clear operational narrative. While it includes a number of maps, they do not offer much in the way of tactical and operational insight, and the military narratives do not provide much clarity.

papers.title: Involuntary Investors in British State-Building: Seamen’s Tickets and the Financial Revolution c .1700–1760
papers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the relationship between government liquidity, personal credit, and state practices in eighteenth-century Britain, drawing on a case study of seamen’s tickets: promises on paper issued to sailors by the Royal Navy to collect their wages at a future date. Because it was normal for tickets to remain unpaid for years, mariners and their households often sold them. To do so, they relied on an industry akin to modern payday lending. Tickets circulated within maritime communities and beyond, forming a financial market that existed in the shadows of the formal commercial paper economy sanctioned by the state. This article traces the contours of the ticket market in terms of its value, its actors, and its dynamics, as a crucial part of the invention of financial capitalism. It argues that British state-building and imperial expansion depended upon the involuntary investments of maritime labourers, whose wage debts were one of the largest categories of public debt in the eighteenth century. Focusing on the ticket trade expands the peripheries of Britain’s Financial Revolution, but it also complicates the agency and aspirations of the investors involved.

Scott’s field-transforming and now ubiquitously cited article “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (American Historical Review 91, no. 5 [1986]: 1053–75), scholars still have a tendency to conceptualize patriarchy as monolithic, failing to account for historical variability. Moran attends to those specificities and nuances exceedingly well, in a richly documented way. Several of the book’s chapters build productively on well-established lines of inquiry in Italian history, adding new and valuable empirical evidence to our current knowledge bases. Chapter 1, on women’s networking in their various capacities as wives, mothers, and widows, and chapter 3, on women’s associational work regularly breaching convent walls, offer fabulous new protagonists for us to consider as we continue to explore women’s active and positive contributions even in the face of premodern gender norms and patriarchal legal and social structures. These chapters, as Moran robustly acknowledges, in a way retrace interpretive tracks found in (among many others) Heather Gregory’s pathbreaking work on the redoubtable Florentine merchant’s widow, relentless network builder, and grassroots politician Alessandra Strozzi. So, too, there has been a flood of research in recent years on cloistered women’s cultural, medical, and political production, with K. J. P. Lowe’s magisterial Nuns’ Chronicles and Convent Culture: Women and History Writing in Renaissance and Counter-Reformation Italy (2003) and Sharon T. Strocchia’s Forgotten Healers: Women and the Pursuit of Healing in Late Renaissance Italy (2019) as just two instances of that important trend. Moran does more than ornament on these lines of inquiry, however; Gender and Family Networks ultimately expands the types of family relationships we consider to be historically—and politically—significant. In particular, Moran draws innovative attention to brother-sister and stepfamily interactions, as well as women’s friendships with each other inside and outside kinship networks. These are brilliant moves, to my mind.

papers.title: Polly Zavadivker. A Nation of Refugees: Russia’s Jews in World War I
papers.abstract: During the Russian Civil War between 1917 and 1921, White Russian armies and Ukrainian and Polish troops massacred at least fifty thousand Jews in western Ukraine and eastern Poland. The degree and extent of the violence specifically directed against Jewish civilians appeared unprecedented. Jews were targeted as collaborators of different enemies and soldiers systematically raped Jewish women, killed Jewish children, and looted homes and stores, often encouraging bystanders to join in the violence. Another feature of these attacks stands out: the post-1917 pogroms were often instigated by representatives of newly founded states and warlords. Several scholars who have examined the pogroms during the Russian Civil War in recent years have drawn a line to the Holocaust. Curiously, apart from Semion Goldin’s The Russian Army and the Jewish Population, 1914–1917 (2022) little has been written about violent attacks the Russian military committed against Jewish civilians before 1918. Even less was known about Jewish life during the war.

papers.title: Ellen Hartigan-O’Connor. America Under the Hammer: Auctions and the Emergence of Market Values .
papers.abstract: In our age of tariffs and greedflation, prices have never been more newsworthy, at least since the 1970s. But what actually is a price? Is it a value? A signal? A fantasy? America Under the Hammer: Auctions and the Emergence of Market Values is a history of early American auctions, but it is also a history of price as seen through the lens of those auctions. In her exciting new book, Ellen Hartigan-O’Connor makes a timely contribution to a growing literature that aims to historicize the capitalist relations we take as givens, from enclosure and commodification to monetization. With a focus on price, and closely attentive to the changing dynamics of gender and race, Hartigan-O’Connor breaks new ground and troubles old myths about property, supply and demand, and the “freedom” of choice. As Hartigan-O’Connor illuminates across six chapters, the notion that the price of a thing is its value has not always been a hard-and-fast truth. Rather, Americans’ equation of value with price was the outcome of a 150-year struggle over the nature of value itself. Over time, competing regimes of value “that allowed some things to be fungible and others not” gave way to the belief that everything and every life was reducible to a number, an economic fact, as it were (7). Auctions dramatized this alchemy. A constant fixture and emblematic institution of American markets through the end of the nineteenth century, auctions, more so than other modes of exchange, made visible the complex ways that nature, objects, people, and labor came to be regarded as commodities. But commodification was neither inevitable nor uncontested. On the contrary, the author argues, auctions served as spaces where “communities could sort out their ideas about value” (10). Though instituted by law and authority, their fundamentally social dimension demanded public participation in the production of economic knowledge.

papers.title: Donald L. Fixico. The State of Sequoyah: Indigenous Sovereignty and the Quest for an Indian State
papers.abstract: Donald L. Fixico has penned a concise and well-argued analysis of a statehood movement that has received little scholarly attention despite its importance as an overt expression of tribal sovereignty in pre-statehood Oklahoma. In The State of Sequoyah, Fixico demonstrates that, although efforts to form an Indigenous state proved unsuccessful, much can be gained by examining the historical context that spawned the movement. Heretofore relegated to a footnote in the march toward Oklahoma statehood, in this volume the State of Sequoyah takes center stage as a unique union of Indian and non-Indian partners in an attempt to thwart the aims of state and federal forces bent on imposing statehood upon a largely unwilling (or at least ambivalent) Native populace. Fixico begins by tracing the removals of the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee, and Seminole nations to Indian Territory and the alterations each made to its political structure as a consequence of forced relocation. While all five tribes remained matrilineal culturally, they reoriented themselves to function as patriarchal political systems similar to those of American states. This shift in governmental systems coincided with a more collective mindset of the Five Tribes brought about by conflicts with Native nations already occupying Indian Territory and later by a need to resist non-Indian incursions onto their reservations. Ironically, the same federal government that ultimately quashed plans for a separate Indian polity helped foster Native solidarity by sponsoring a series of intertribal councils in Indian Territory beginning in the 1830s. Apparently, the Great Father encouraged Native unity only up to a certain point and no farther.

papers.title: Rachel Louise Moran. Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America
papers.abstract: In Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America, Rachel Louise Moran offers an illuminating cultural and political history of postpartum mental illness. As the author notes from the outset, the book’s title term refers to a specific depressive disorder as well as to a wider constellation of conditions that manifest after birth, including depression, anxiety, mania, and psychosis. The naming and grouping together of these illnesses under one umbrella term, Moran argues, was the culmination of decades of activism carried out by grassroots and professional advocates, clinicians, and researchers. Braiding together a wide range of sources, including women’s magazines, medical publications, media coverage, parenting guides, and over thirty oral histories, Moran skillfully narrates this story of women’s suffering, treatment, and advocacy across ten chapters spanning the 1950s to the 2020s. The book opens in the post–World War II years, when a psychoanalytic medical discourse largely infantilized women troubled with the “baby blues,” framing their distress as a sign of immaturity. Popular advice, reflecting an expanding consumer culture of the era, encouraged women that a quick shopping trip and taking prescription “mood brightening” drugs like Ritalin would ease their adjustment to motherhood (32). With the rise of the feminist movement in the 1960s and 1970s, more women spoke out about their painful childbirth and motherhood experiences, linking their frustrations to broader critiques of social conditions—medical sexism, inadequate public resources for parents, and prescribed gender roles—that demanded reimagining. Such pointed challenges fueled feminist activism around a host of issues, including abortion, birth control, and child-rearing, but it was not until the 1980s that a movement focused on raising awareness about postpartum mental illness gained ground. Women organized support groups across the country, and an international network of, mostly male, psychiatrists pushed their profession to recognize the hormonal basis of postpartum conditions. These overlapping campaigns were part of a larger “quest for legitimacy,” as Moran characterizes it, with women increasingly turning to medical language to articulate their suffering (14).

papers.title: Elise Franklin. Disintegrating Empire: Algerian Family Migration and the Limits of the Welfare State in France
papers.abstract: Elise Franklin’s book, Disintegrating Empire, speaks to the limitations of the post/colonial welfare state in France. She sets her sights on the French state’s ever-contradictory relationship toward Algerians—a formerly colonized people who had the unique distinction of possessing French nationality but not citizenship, a distinction that posed a host of challenges for the imperial and postimperial nation-state. While Amelia Lyons’s 2013 study on Algerian women showed that until 1962, the French welfare state aimed primarily to assimilate them into French society in order to “keep Algeria French,” Franklin notes a contradiction: why, then, did state-sponsored services for Algerians continue after independence? If you’re expecting an argument about French largesse or colorblind benevolence, however, you won’t find it here. Drawing primarily on state publications and social worker reports, among other archival sources, Franklin offers a forensic analysis of how empire, racism, and—critically—whiteness became inscribed on the heart of the French welfare state.

papers.title: Stefanie Fischer and Kim Wünschmann. Illustrated by Liz Clarke. Oberbrechen: A German Village Confronts its Nazi Past .
papers.abstract: Within the dense historiographical landscape of Holocaust studies, unexplored topics continue to come into focus alongside methodological innovations, the use of more visual and similarly accessible mediums, and a greater emphasis on inclusivity and contemporary relevance. Stefanie Fischer and Kim Wünschmann’s Oberbrechen: A German Village Confronts Its Nazi Past exemplifies all these developments. The newest title in Oxford University Press’s Graphic History Series is a significant contribution to Holocaust and German Jewish studies, employing a microhistorical approach to the graphic storytelling format. Using three distinct mediums, the book chronicles the events of the Holocaust and its aftermath in a small village in western Germany, largely through the everyday encounters of Jewish and non-Jewish (mostly Catholic) residents, across several decades and generations. Fischer and Wünschmann maintain that the history of the Holocaust is not solely a story of grand political narratives and centralized state actions but also one deeply embedded in the everyday lives and local dynamics of seemingly ordinary communities.

papers.title: Christin L. Hancock. Unmentionable Madness: Gender, Disability, and Shame in the Malaria Treatment of Neurosyphilis
papers.abstract: Christin L. Hancock’s Unmentionable Madness: Gender, Disability, and Shame in the Malaria Treatment of Neurosyphilis deftly explains why families and physicians, and sometimes patients, sought an excruciating, painful experimental procedure—malaria therapy—to try and cure neurosyphilis, which very rarely, if ever truly, led to success. Hancock brings a historical lens to questions that often feel impossible to answer because of their emotional weight: When and how do physicians recognize the failure of their proposed treatments for terminal illnesses? Why do families or patients consent to see out treatments that might prove more harmful than therapeutic? What qualifies as consent concerning patients with mental health issues? How do social meanings about abled and disabled bodies drive decisions? What role do perceptions of race and gender play in determining who gets what type of care and why? Hancock addresses these questions by studying a forgotten therapy of ultimately dubious efficacy at the Central State Hospital (CSH) in Indianapolis, Indiana, in the 1920s and 1930s. In doing so, she gives voice to the men and women, both white and Black, whose incarcerated bodies became research subjects and stitches their stories back into the historical record from which they were silenced.

papers.title: Jennifer Ngaire Heuer. The Soldier’s Reward: Love and War in the Age of the French Revolution and Napoleon
papers.abstract: Should soldiers marry? This question runs through The Soldier’s Reward, in which Jennifer Ngaire Heuer ably weaves political, social, and cultural histories of military service from the Old Regime to the Restoration. The issue was already under debate in enlightened circles in the decades preceding the Revolution, as discussed in chapter 1. The naturalist Jean-Baptiste Robinet argued that soldiering was incompatible with family life: “A bachelor soldier has married war” (33). He was opposed by Voltaire and Louis-Sébastien Mercier: Without someone to fight for, soldiers degenerated into vagabond mercenaries. As the former expressed it, “Tied to their families, they will also be tied to their patrie” (35). The Crown, worried about economic obligations to soldiers’ dependents, did not agree. The Revolution transformed the situation. Soldiers were now citizens who had rights including, once past their majority (reduced to twenty-one), the right to marry. The surge of “volunteers” in 1792–93 also brought thousands of married men into the armed forces. Given the republic’s inability to meet its own promises about supporting the families of absent soldiers, many volunteers’ wives accompanied them, sometimes in uniform themselves. Such women were, according to Lazare Carnot, a drain on resources and morale, and they were mostly expelled in April 1793, in what Heuer calls the “first demobilization” (65) of the revolutionary wars.

papers.title: J. Barton Scott. Slandering the Sacred: Blasphemy Law and Religious Affect in Colonial India
papers.abstract: The publication of the Arya Samaj tract Rangila Rasool (Merry Prophet) in 1924 caused a stir in colonial India and led to the promulgation of Article 295A in 1927 to protect not religion as much as “religious feelings.” In Slandering the Sacred, J. Barton Scott takes readers on a quest to unpack the law’s origins, which he argues are not antithetical to liberalism or secularism, but very much rooted in these ideas. In the process, he helps us understand the term “secularism” itself as not just religious freedom, but quite as much the regulation of religious feeling and affect by the state. Scott meticulously details the emergence of what it terms “governmental” or “penal” secularism in colonial India as a means to contain and manage interreligious discord rather than conferring religious rights. Postcolonial India, which adopted secularism as a constitutional principle, rendered blasphemy a crime not against religion, but against secularism. The colonial and postcolonial states, thus, provided the language for groups to “inhabit outrage as legally actionable feeling,” thereby exacerbating the very conflict that the law set out to regulate (75).

papers.title: Ana María Otero-Cleves. Plebeian Consumers: Global Connections, Local Trade, and Foreign Goods in Nineteenth-Century Colombia .
papers.abstract: There are many pleasures in reading Plebeian Consumers: Global Connections, Local Trade, and Foreign Goods in Nineteenth-Century Colombia. One is the writing. Ana María Otero-Cleves presents her arguments with clear and direct prose, even in sections touching on theory-driven social science literature. Another is that this is a material history grounded in considerations of political economy and social agency that does not drift into anthropomorphizing market forces, an unfortunate tendency in some works representing the new history of capital. Further, the study addresses a yawning historiographical gap. Though it has been decades since Benjamin Orlove’s The Allure of the Foreign: Imported Goods in Postcolonial Latin America (1997), few historians working on nineteenth-century Latin America have addressed the questions posed in that collection. There have been notable works on export commodities, cartography, and material culture, but little on imports and even less on people in Latin America as consumers with agency. Finally, the study contributes to the collective effort of moving beyond the conceptualization of Latin America as peripheral, a place subordinate to the core world regions that produced ideas, politics, and manufactured goods. Colombianists have made numerous contributions to this effort, but the focus has been on politics and ideas, not material culture. This examination of how Colombians—plebian, elite, and those somewhere in between—made choices as consumers based on their own tastes and understanding, and the implications of those choices for manufacturers in the United States, Great Britain, and France, is revelatory.

papers.title: Sarah Lewis. The Unseen Truth: When Race Changed Sight in America
papers.abstract: “How do we come to know what we think we know?” (99). This is the question at the heart of Sarah Lewis’s new book, The Unseen Truth: When Race Changed Sight in America. It is a question that can be addressed in case studies from countless times, places, and societies. Lewis tackles it across an extended moment of change in United States history: the period between the Civil War and World War I. In global history, this is a period known for its sharp rise in nationalist movements, usually forged in tandem with communal acts of “forgetting” pre-national pasts. Lewis tells us the story of another act of creation and forgetting at this time: in her words, the “transformation of vision that let obvious fictions remain at the basis of the [American] racial project and settle into a kind of truth” (2). Across five chapters, Lewis delves into topics including P. T. Barnum’s spectacles; Frederick Douglass’s lectures; elite museum curation; atlases, maps, and textbooks; and President Woodrow Wilson’s federal government files. She argues that an American public once understood that the Caucasus region—which German naturalist Johann Friedrich Blumenbach identified as the origin point of the white or “Caucasian” race in 1795—was in fact a territory of significant ethnic and religious diversity. She contends, for example, that Barnum’s famous Civil War–era “Circassian beauty” (who purportedly hailed from the Caucasus) was in fact a sideshow act meant to lampoon the idea of “Caucasian” whiteness. Barnum’s audience, Lewis explains, would have understood the evident mockery; they were familiar with the Caucasus through contemporary coverage of the Caucasian Wars (1817–1864), and they would have understood that Barnum’s “Circassian” was just another one of his fabricated, “freakish” figures meant for them to scrutinize and inspect. Put simply, Lewis asserts that Americans in the mid-nineteenth century did not take “Caucasian” whiteness seriously.

papers.title: Kate Merkel-Hess. Women and Their Warlords: Domesticating Militarism in Modern China
papers.abstract: Standard narratives of China’s twentieth century typically minimize the lasting influence of the men who dominated politics following the 1911 collapse of the imperial system and preceding the rise of the Leninist party-state in the late 1920s. When mentioned at all, these men—usually characterized as junfa in Chinese, or “warlords”—are caricatured in a variety of cartoonish ways: some honorable and heroic, others petty and vicious. One of their only unifying characteristics is that their actions villainously split the nation apart, in contrast to heroic leaders like Mao Zedong or Chiang Kai-shek, who (depending on the historian) are often portrayed as struggling to unify China. The only thing more overlooked and understudied in the historiography of these warlords might be women in their orbit. In Women and Their Warlords: Domesticating Militarism in Modern China, Kate Merkel-Hess weaves together a wide range of sources to reconstruct the impact of these figures, both in their own time and after. While the literature has commonly implied that these warlords were overly concerned with material and military matters, or might have been shortsighted in managing their public image, Merkel-Hess shows that this is not the case. Furthermore, her book makes the long-overdue intervention of showing how stories about these men and women capture the attention of the Chinese public, both then and now, as historical myth and popular fiction. In other words, Merkel-Hess paints an empathetic portrait of her elusive subjects’ lives while simultaneously illustrating how they resonate in the present day as symbols of national duty, romantic love, and filial piety.

papers.title: Seán Ó Hoireabhárd. The Medieval Irish Kings and the English Invasion
papers.abstract: Modern scholarship has turned the year 1169 into either the start or end date of all studies of medieval Ireland. Such is the main point of Seán Ó Hoireabhárd’s first book The Medieval Irish Kings and the English Invasion, and it is an endeavor to disrupt this practice. This massive tome’s focus is the political (regnal power and relations) histories of the three “major kingdoms or hegemonies” on Inis Fáil during the twelfth century, when the island was invaded and English settler colonists first established their hold. These hegemons are Munster (Mumu), Connacht (Connachta), and The North (An Túaiscert). His preferred sources are the Gaelic annals, of which there are many, and thus he argues that they should be the main source for the history of Gaelic regnal politics. The book begins with a short mise-en-scène of events from 1167–71, a methodology chapter, and a historiography chapter. Next is section 1, “Connacht and the Shannon,” giving minute details about the rise of the Uí Chonchobhair and then a brief overview about the transition from the most powerful overking to English vassals. The latter has been covered in fine detail by Helen Walton (“The English in Connacht, 1171–1333,” PhD thesis, Trinity College Dublin, 1980) and Freya Verstraten (“Both King and Vassal: Feidlim Ua Conchobair of Connacht, 1230–65,” GAHS 55 [2003]: 13–37), so he does not need to rehash it here, but he should have cited them. Then comes section 2, “The Uí Néill and the North,” where the author covers the “phoney war” of Muirchertach Úa Briain and Domnall Mac Lochlainn (1088–1114); the fall of Uí Néill supremacy and the splintering of Uí Néill hegemony into several parts; and John de Courcy’s difficulties expanding his new colony. Section 3, “Munster and Leth Moga,” begins with the origins and origin legends of the dramatis personae, then pushes the study back to Cennéitig mac Lorcáin in 944 and traces the several rises and falls of the Dál Cais, ending with an examination of the historiographical depiction of Úa Briain-Mac Carthaigh relations. As another scholar who believes in providing copious detail, I think that these sections greatly support the arguments in the rest of the book and even could benefit from more context for the nonexpert reader.

papers.title: Tom Smith. Word Across the Water: American Protestant Missionaries, Pacific Worlds, and the Making of Imperial Histories.
papers.abstract: In his first monograph, Word Across the Water, Tom Smith contributes greatly to our understanding of the work of American Protestant missionaries in Hawaiʻi and the Philippines in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. papers.title: Samuel Agbamu. Restorations of Empire in Africa: Ancient Rome and Modern Italy’s African Colonies.
papers.abstract: Romanità—a celebration of the memory of ancient Rome—was central to the self-image and ideology of Italy’s Fascist regime. In Restorations of Empire in Africa, Samuel Abgamu builds on the extensive scholarship on this topic and shapes it in two discrete directions. First, he focuses on how the ancient past was read specifically into Italian imperial ambitions in Africa, as the title of the book makes clear. Second, he begins his study in the late nineteenth century, demonstrating continuities in how Italians understood the connection between ancient Rome and the era of high imperialism between the liberal and fascist periods. A wide-ranging cultural history, this study infuses a combined history of romanità and the history of Italian imperialism with Agbamu’s deep understanding of the history of ancient Rome. The book is structured chronologically in nine substantive chapters and a brief conclusion. It starts with the early stirrings of Italian imperialism in East Africa immediately after national unification, but the main analysis begins with the invasion of Libya in 1911 and ends with reinterpretations of the ancient past in Italian connections with Africa in the postwar Italian republic. The chapters are generally divided by the various stages of Italian colonial expansion along the way. Each chapter also centers on the analysis of a set of cultural materials. The type of cultural materials under investigation shifts over the course of the book to reflect the changes in cultural production of the early twentieth century and the process of Italian imperial expansion. The early chapters of the book spotlight the literature of prominent figures like Enrico Corradini and Gabriele D’Annunzio, whose work imagined the future of Italian imperial expansion as a repetition of the ancient past. In 1914, we start to see cultural production shift to film, with Giovanni Pastrone’s Cabiria and, later in the book, Carmine Gallone’s highly influential 1937 film Scipione l’Africano. As the Fascist regime embraced grand public works programs and claimed greater control in the colonies, Agbamu turns his attention to physical manifestations of romanità in the cityscape of Rome, in colonial expositions on the peninsula, and—the one instance when the book actually takes us into the colonies—in the fascinating case of the Arco dei Fileni, a grand monument completed in 1937 at the halfway point of the road built to join together the Libyan colonies of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica. Throughout, Agbamu uses these cultural materials to demonstrate “how Roman discourses on Africa were appropriated and engaged with in the dominant cultures of imperial Italy” (5).

papers.title: Marianne Kamp. Collectivization Generation: Oral Histories of a Social Revolution in Uzbekistan
papers.abstract: Marianne Kamp’s book Collectivization Generation is a landmark contribution to the social history of Soviet Central Asia, particularly to our understanding of Uzbekistan during one of the most transformative and traumatic periods of the twentieth century. Drawing on 120 interviews, Kamp reconstructs how rural Uzbeks navigated and made sense of the upheavals brought by Stalinist agricultural policy. What sets this book apart is its grounding in memory. While previous scholarship has leaned on archival materials and state documents, Kamp foregrounds the testimonies of the “collectivization generation” men and women born between 1900 and 1925 who experienced collectivization not merely as a policy, but as a rupture that reshaped the social, political, and emotional foundations of their lives. Her ability to weave these stories into an accessible yet analytically rich narrative is remarkable. As someone with personal ties to this history—my grandfather survived collectivization in Kokand and witnessed the execution of his father (labeled a quloq)—I was particularly moved by the book’s nuanced engagement with the paradoxes of memory. Kamp’s account of collectivization in Uzbekistan offers a compelling reflection on how oral histories illuminate the lived experiences and long-term recollections of Soviet rural transformation. Strikingly, as in my grandfather’s case, some of Kamp’s narrators ultimately came to embrace aspects of the very system that had once victimized them. Interviewed in the early 2000s, during Uzbekistan’s gradual and uneven retreat from collectivized agriculture, these individuals spoke with a candor largely unmediated by political incentives. This stands in contrast to many post-Soviet Eastern European contexts, where the pressures of privatization and political reckoning often shaped and constrained retrospective accounts.

papers.title: Bethany Hughes. Redface: Race, Performance, and Indigeneity
papers.abstract: Even today, the image of a muscular, bare-chested man in a feathered headdress remains instantly recognizable as “Indian.” How has this racialized portrayal been constructed and sustained in American culture? Why can we so easily identify what is performed as Indian while overlooking the continued presence of Indigenous peoples, nations, and cultures? Bethany Hughes’s Redface: Race, Performance, and Indigeneity responds to these long-standing questions by examining nineteenth- and twentieth-century American theater as a central site via which theatrical artists and audiences collaboratively defined “Indianness” through redface. This racial impersonation produced the Stage Indian—a curated, repeatedly performed figure in Indian plays that trained audiences to recognize the “Indian” on and off stage. Hughes’s analysis builds on substantial scholarship, including Robert F. Berkhofer Jr.’s The White Man’s Indian: Images of the American Indian from Columbus to the Present (1978) and Philip J. Deloria’s Playing Indian (1998) examining how Euro-Americans defined themselves through constructing and circulating stereotypical representations of Native Americans. Hughes extends this tradition by incorporating Chickasaw scholar Jodi Byrd’s view of representation as an imperial project that racializes and regulates Indigenous bodies. She illustrates that redface is not merely about costume and makeup; it is a settler colonial mechanism that erases Indigeneity, denies Indigenous sovereignty, and enacts the belief that the “Indian” is a vanishing race. Her extensive archival research, including theatrical posters, choreographic notes, and legal cases, combined with interdisciplinary insights, results in Redface, a provocative study that exposes the political and cultural dynamics that delimit and discipline Indigenous presence.

papers.abstract: The relationship of the Jesuits with the American world began in the mid-sixteenth century when the first missionaries arrived in Brazil in 1549, with the approval of the Portuguese Crown. However, after a brief stay in that territory, the first Jesuits were able to arrive in the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1568, founding a province and initiating the main activities of the order in education and mission. Four years later, they did the same in the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Over the years, the Jesuits began to venture into peripheral regions, where they founded important missions with Indigenous people. They did the same in Paraguay, Araucanía, Chiloé, Moxos, Chiquitanía, Orinoco, Maynas, Sonora, Sinaloa, and Baja, California, among others. In all of them, with varying results, the missionaries made contributions not only from a religious point of view—their main objective—but also from ethnographic, political, economic, social, environmental, and scientific perspectives.

papers.title: Caitlin Keliiaa. Refusing Settler Domesticity: Native Women’s Labor and Resistance in the Bay Area Outing Program
papers.abstract: In Refusing Settler Domesticity: Native Women’s Labor and Resistance in the Bay Area Outing Program, Caitlin Keliiaa offers readers an intimate window into the lives of Native women who worked as domestic servants in the Bay Area in the early twentieth century. Analyzing over four thousand archival records, she pieces together the history of the Bay Area Outing Program (BAOP), which existed between 1918 and 1942. Outing programs worked with federal boarding schools to assimilate Native youth into settler culture and prepare them for work in the laboring classes. In consensus with recent scholarship on federal boarding schools and urban relocation, Keliiaa argues that, although these kinds of assimilation programs sought to eradicate Native culture and confine Native people to menial labor, participants resisted constraints on their lives and carved out futures for themselves while creating intertribal communities all over the United States. As a Yerington Paiute and Washoe tribal member who grew up in the Bay Area, Keliiaa approaches this project as a scholar and a descendent of women who participated in the BAOP. As such, the book connects the contemporary urban Indigenous community to the women who took up domestic work in the Bay in the early twentieth century in the homes of wealthy Bay Area families. The girls and women who took these posts did so for a variety of reasons. Some were teenage girls from boarding schools gaining experience in domestic labor, others were mothers who needed to earn wages for their families. In either case, the women who took these roles earned 47 percent less than the national average. They also navigated significant restrictions on their bodily autonomy, including curfews and sexual surveillance. Breaking expectations sometimes led to incarceration, child removal, and forced sterilization. Despite these challenges, women sought this work to earn wages for their families, experience the excitement of city life, and find community with other Native women. Keliiaa makes the case that these domestic workers were responsible for the first Native community organization in the Bay Area, the Four Winds Club, founded in the 1930s.

papers.title: Tamara Chaplin. Becoming Lesbian: A Queer History of Modern France
papers.abstract: It is time to put the notion of lesbian invisibility to rest. That is the primary take-away from Becoming Lesbian: A Queer History of Modern France, Tamara Chaplin’s outstanding history of lesbians in twentieth- and twenty-first-century France. The title of the book lets us know how this historian approaches the topic. In a wink to Simone de Beauvoir’s famous phrase, “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,”(Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, trans. Constance Borde, [2011], 330) the “becoming” in the title shows an attentiveness to the idea that while same-sex sexual acts between women have existed since the beginning of time, an identity built around those acts did not appear until the late nineteenth century at the earliest, and that identity was far from static, but rather continued to become. There are reasons why at times historians, including me to be honest, have fallen prey to the idea that lesbians have been relatively invisible. Although there was an awareness of romantic and sexual attraction between women in twentieth-century France, it generally did not trouble the moral authorities of the time, so legal and political discussions of homosexuality were mostly limited to male homosexuality. This indifference among legal and political actors was to some extent rooted in prevailing stereotypes about female homosexuality, which suggested it was merely a passing phase or inherently less intense than male homosexuality. Such views were not limited to mainstream culture—they were also echoed within homosexual communities. For instance, in 1952, the homosexual journal Futur asserted that “female homosexuality is something essentially different from male homosexuality. There is a temporary and extremely fluid quality to it. The flames of that love are pale” (Claudie Lesselier, “Formes de résistances et d’expression lesbiennes dans les années cinquante et soixante en France,” Homosexualités expression/répression, ed. Louis-Georges Tin [2000], 105, translated by reviewer).

papers.title: Mary Bridges. Dollars and Dominion: US Bankers and the Making of a Superpower
papers.abstract: Mary Bridges opens her excellent study of American global economic power by depicting the scholarship on this early twentieth-century period in binary terms—divided between people-centered and institutions-centered narratives. In a story of interwoven private and governmental authority, Bridges centers banks, tracing how their interactions with businesses and policymakers helped transform a British-dominated system into the American-led international financial order. As US economic interests muscled their way into China, Latin America, the Caribbean, and the Philippines, US businessmen and government officials initially relied on seasoned British banks to finance trade, pay Americans abroad, and hold government deposits. But reliance on British banks came with a price. For example, American firms had to open their books to overseas financiers, who could then leak their trade secrets to competitors. Additionally, British bankers frustrated American authorities by refusing to pay their overseas officials in dollars. And while US policymakers partnered with their Anglo forefathers under the gold standard, they looked to dethrone British sterling as the world’s reserve currency in favor of the dollar.

Indeed, I had rarely questioned why these documents adding heft to my footnotes had been created, collated, indexed, and stored. Even worse, I had never recognized the striking similarities between early modern administrators of the British Empire and present-day scholars of that same empire: both have used archival manuscripts to give their claims authority. papers.title: Emmanuel Destenay. America’s French Orphans: Mobilization, Humanitarianism, and the Protection of France, 1914–1921
papers.abstract: In Western humanitarianism, children have long enjoyed pride of place: quintessential subjects of innocence who tug at the heartstrings of distant spectators, their visuals and voices have prominently featured in myriad funding campaigns to help those in need in faraway lands. In America’s French Orphans: Mobilization, Humanitarianism, and the Protection of France, 1914–1921, Emmanuel Destenay illustrates this point by revealing how, during and after World War I, Americans became invested in helping children affected by the hostilities across the Atlantic. Told as a transnational story between the United States and France, but skewing heavily on the American perspective, the book focuses on two initiatives that have previously been relegated to the footnotes of humanitarianism: the Fatherless Children of France Society (FCFS) and the Committee Franco-American for the Protection of the Children of the Frontier (CFAPCF). Though short-lived, these groups raised enormous sums for French children who had lost their fathers during combat by matching them with American donors and safeguarded some 300,000 French children from conflict zones by sheltering, feeding, and educating them in so-called colonies throughout France. Combining American money and expertise with French local manpower, the FCFS and the CFAPCF were among the first to not only prominently feature children as recipients of aid but also, on the American side, draw on them as philanthropists. By thus mobilizing young citizens as active participants in the world of international relief even before America’s entry into the war in 1917, Destenay argues, they “paved the way for a new form of American humanitarian culture” (13).

papers.title: Lindsay M. Chervinsky. Making the Presidency: John Adams and the Precedents that Forged the Republic
papers.abstract: Law reviews, courts, and podiums in the United States are alive with the sound of unbridled presidential authority, asserting an ever more imperial and unitary executive vested with authority to make and unmake law on matters foreign and domestic. Often these claims gesture toward a historical foundation, dressing up a drive for power with purported original meanings. The distance between this presidentialism, in practice and in the constitutional stories it summons, and the beleaguered presidency of John Adams is yawning—a discontinuity that confronts readers throughout Lindsay M. Chervinsky’s engaging political biography, Making the Presidency: John Adams and the Precedents that Forged the Republic. Chervinsky presents a sympathetic examination of the first post-Washington president through close attention to the wrangling and scheming of early national statesmen. Often a defense of Adams’s choices and character, the book affords a striking vantage of this chief officer’s authority as exercised and challenged. It shows a president without a legislative agenda who deferred to Congress; who did not exercise exclusive control over foreign affairs; who did not assert former royal prerogatives beyond constitutional specification; who was not the leader of his party; who faced competing claims to executive authority by ostensible subordinates; whose most common tactic against those claimants was inaction and silence; who commissioned another (Washington) as commander in chief and conceded military control; who could expect little loyalty based on his office; and who could not supervise and control a lean executive branch. Indeed, with his continuous eight-month retreat to Qunicy, Massachusetts, away from his ambitious cabinet’s activities amid international turmoil, the isolated figure of Adams gives new meaning to a unitary executive.

papers.title: Alberto Esu. Divided Power in Ancient Greece: Decision-Making and Institutions in the Classical and Hellenistic Polis.
papers.abstract: It is no surprise that ancient Greece continues to inspire reflection on the nature and functioning of democracy. Alberto Esu has produced an excellent monograph that bridges the gap between traditional history and political science. Divided Power in Ancient Greece aims to explain how institutions were shaped by and, in turn, shaped the historical agents operating in Greek city-states. Esu deploys the methods of “new” historical institutionalism and shows us how an interdisciplinary approach to decision-making bodies in ancient Greece can achieve a nuanced yet simple way of accounting for historical change and continuity. Rather than reducing political regimes to stereotypes (i.e., “radical” Athenian democracy, iron-clad oligarchies), Esu provides convincing evidence and argumentation for a concept of “divided power” (itself a term borrowed from the work of P. Pasquino [“Democracy Ancient and Modern: Divided Power,” in Deémocratie Atheénienne—Deémocratie Moderne: Tradition et Influences, ed. Morgens H. Hansen (Fondation Hardt, 2010), 1–40]). “Divided power” refers to how political institutions delegated or shared respective deliberative and decision-making authority to/with different citizen bodies both as a safeguard to the stability of the particular constitution as well as its internal consistency. Unlike the modern notions of the “separation of powers” and “sovereignty” of one house or branch of government or another, divided power “is a constitutional order that distributes the power of making laws and binding norms among different institutions such as magistrates, assemblies, and courts” (11) in which no single institution had greater sway than another since it was “a form of decision-making that is the outcome of multi-institutional interaction between different bodies, each one playing a distinctive and relevant role in the shaping of decrees” (13–14).

papers.title: Jack Furniss. Between Extremes: Seeking the Political Center in the Civil War North
papers.abstract: Between Extremes is a notable addition to a reassessment of the politics of the Civil War era in the United States that has been underway for a decade. Jack Furniss examines the politics of centrism—or, in the parlance of the war period, conservatism—practiced by Northern governors. His main focus is on state governors who affiliated with Union parties, ad hoc amalgams of Republicans, Democrats, and former Whigs. He argues that their successes lay in an ability to frame their support for the Lincoln administration around restoration of the Union, avoiding the revolutionary implications of emancipation and a consolidation of federal power. Furniss contends that governors engaged in realpolitik, acknowledging an electorate with no appetite for radical change but deeply invested in preserving the American republican experiment. Furniss situates Between Extremes within a gathering body of scholarship that views the Civil War–era party system as messy, factionalized, and fluid. Invoking J. Matthew Gallman, Adam I. P. Smith, Elizabeth Varon, and others, Furniss sets aside tidy Republican vs. Democrat binaries. The Republican Party, he observes, was in its infancy in 1860, still in the process of party-building by absorbing fragments of earlier organizations. Remnants of the Whig Party and the American Party (Know-Nothings) retained independence, and many conservatives voted for the Constitutional Union Party in 1860. The Northern wing of the Democratic Party, which supported Stephen A. Douglas for president in 1860, had more in common with Abraham Lincoln and the Republicans than with Southern secessionist Democrats. During the winter of 1860–1861, he points out, Northern state legislators acted across party lines to stave off secession. After Fort Sumter in April 1861, all but ardent peace advocates unified to support Lincoln’s limited war aim: restoration of the Union. The political center held and became a rallying point for Republicans, Democrats, and conservative Whigs, often via Union parties that sprang up across the North.

papers.title: Sudev Sheth. Bankrolling Empire: Family Fortunes and Political Transformation in Mughal India

papers.title: Melissa Reynolds. Reading Practice: The Pursuit of Natural Knowledge from Manuscript to Print
papers.abstract: Melissa Reynolds’s book, Reading Practice: The Pursuit of Natural Knowledge from Manuscript to Print, is a study of practical manuscripts and printed texts from over a two-hundred-year period, 1375–1601, and the impact that reading these works had on ordinary people for their understanding of natural knowledge and the divine. From medical recipes and herbals to weather predictions and more, the “middling sort” in consulting and responding to practical works joined in the conversations of early science and medicine just as the English Reformation was forming. Reynolds’s basic argument is that by studying the changes in the presentation and reception of religious doctrine in these practical works, we can see the influence that print technology and the English Reformation had on ordinary English people. For example, ordinary folks collected medical recipes as part of practical manuscripts, and in collecting them sought a greater understanding of the natural world as the manifestation of God’s power. The success of some recipes, however, could not be explained by the divine virtues of herbs alone. To cure a fever, one might write holy words on three sage leaves and consume one a day for three days, or a woman in labor might list the names of holy mothers on parchment and bind it to her right thigh for a successful birth. In the sixteenth century, however, readers coming across such charms in a manuscript might cross it out or write “evil this” (171). Reynolds notes that while it was rare to find evidence that readers censored the contents of practical manuscripts, when it did occur, it was most often directed at women’s knowledge. Not only had the English Reformation “hardened readers’ attitudes toward ‘women’s secrets’ considerably,” but print became associated with the learned masculine sphere regardless of whether or not men were taking credit for the knowledge of women, while women continued to create recipe collections in manuscript with few exceptions (Hannah Woolley) printed (151, 162).

papers.title: Leanna Brinkley. Coastal Trade and Maritime Communities in Elizabethan England
papers.abstract: Six years after the accession of Elizabeth I, the crown agency responsible for collecting revenue ordered customs officers at England’s ports to record in blank books provided by the Exchequer Office all maritime trade that transpired in their coastal communities. Leanne Brinkley’s book Coastal Trade and Maritime Communities in Elizabethan England arises from her entering information from thirty-three surviving port books spanning the Elizabethan era into a database, which she subsequently analyzed with help of other quantitative and qualitative sources and the aid of a computer program. Brinkley’s careful study of the port books leads her to challenge the existing interpretation of the nature of coastal maritime trade in England in the period prior to the kingdom inserting itself into the global and imperial commercial markets. Late sixteenth-century coastal trade was, in fact, more vibrant and vigorous than previous scholarship allows. It was abundant, undertaken by rational actors who evinced flexible and adaptive patterns of action, and who often operated as both mariners and merchants.
