papers.title: Oliver Volckart. The Silver Empire: How Germany Created Its First Common Currency
papers.abstract: The Silver Empire begins with the story of a scandal. It was 1543, and Hans Appenfelder, the mint master of Kaufbeuren, was accused of “breaking coins,” that is, of dropping them into a crucible, melting them down, and reprocessing the metals to turn a profit. Before long, Appenfelder had implicated Augsburg’s mint master, Balthasar Hundertpfund. Both were arrested. Soon, many others were implicated, prosecuted, and arrested. Augsburg was in an uproar. “What was all this about?” asks Oliver Volckart. “How and why did Appenfelder and Hundertpfund make a profit from purchasing and making money?” (2). This anecdote about Appenfelder and Hundertpfund, which becomes a leitmotif throughout the next 250 pages or so, is well chosen, providing the reader with a concrete foothold in the complex and detailed discussions about imperial monetary policy that form the core of the book’s argument. The dazzling diversity of the Holy Roman Empire, with its counts and barons and archbishops peopling its endless duchies, cities, and electorates, found a mirror in its myriad coins and currencies—heller and taler and batzens, oh my! Volckart echoes the existing monetary history literature in his account of the early sixteenth century: it was full of confusion and disorder, even for contemporaries. What seems bewildering to us was indeed perplexing to them. That is the baseline and where we begin. But Volckart’s narrative breaks from most of the existing historiography in what follows, as we get a story of how order was imposed on chaos by the relentless efforts of the imperial diets and Münztage—or “currency conferences”—that convened over the years between 1549 and 1566. If we want to believe Volckart, by the time Saxony capitulated and adopted the common coinage in 1571, the Holy Roman Empire had been transformed from a babel of currencies into something more rational and standardized. For those of us who work in periods after 1570, this can come as something of a surprise. Speaking personally, I cannot say I have ever felt comfortably at home in the world of kreutzers and groschen and stiebers while negotiating my own primary sources; it is one of the great accomplishments of Volckart’s book that it infuses this apparent mishmash with meaning and structure.

papers.title: Seth Rockman. Plantation Goods: A Material History of American Slavery .
papers.abstract: “Negro cloth.” “Slave brogans.” “Planter’s hoes.” As Seth Rockman explains in Plantation Goods, the names of these humble artifacts reveal the complex political and moral economies that entangled Northern industrial capitalism with Southern plantation slavery during the antebellum era. Plantation goods like shoes and shovels were made by Northern industrialists, sold by traveling merchants, bought by Southern enslavers, and consumed by enslaved workers who in turn planted, harvested, and packaged cash crops—sugar, tobacco, cotton—for sale on the world market. By drawing our attention to the trade in plantation goods, and to the wide cast of people who made and used them, Rockman brings us extremely close to the texture of the everyday life of slavery’s capitalism while expanding our historical and ethical view on the range of things that “mediated the world” for Americans in the nineteenth century (4). Generations of historians have explored the relationship between slavery and capitalism by examining the commodities that made plantation slavery work. Histories of cotton, of the slave trade, and, most recently, of financial capital have convincingly condensed our view of slavery and capitalism into a single historiographical frame—slavery’s capitalism—a movement that Rockman himself has helped to lead. What distinguishes his approach is a commitment to material culture as an archive and category of historical analysis. More than mere instruments of labor, the everyday clothing and tools used on Southern plantations were themselves products of work and manufacture, and their use involved the enslaved in processes of marketing, industrial design, and technological development unfolding in the North. By unspooling their material histories, Rockman shows us the “countless relationships, near and far, human and not” that plantation goods mediated and “materialized” (6).

papers.title: Alastair McClure. Trials of Sovereignty: Mercy, Violence, and the Making of Criminal Law in British India, 1857–1922
papers.abstract: Alastair McClure’s book Trials of Sovereignty reinterprets sovereignty in colonial India. Exploring how mercy, violence, and criminal law were integral parts of the post-1857 colonial state, McClure makes a few significant interventions in South Asian historiography. He utilizes criminal law—and the decision to punish or pardon—as a way of newly understanding how colonial power was contested. And in doing so McClure documents unexamined forms of colonial resistance. He also sheds light on how the violence of 1857–8 and later anti-colonial (revolutionary) nationalism molded India’s modern criminal justice system. Approaching the subject through legal methodologies and rich primary sources, McClure argues that mercy was an overlooked—yet integral—aspect of the consolidation of the post-1857 colonial state. In Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s and Gandhi’s rejections of mercy, McClure draws attention to “crucial assertion[s] of Indian sovereignty in opposition to British rule” (29). Chapter 1 starts with violence of the 1857 Uprising. McClure demonstrates how the deployment of mercy—arresting the last Mughal Emperor Shah Zafar II and guaranteeing his life in exchange for his surrender (and forgone conviction)—set the foundation for legitimizing colonial sovereignty until the 1920s. Diligently delineating the Uprising’s effect on the codification of criminal law, McClure shows how court-martials were given sweeping, almost unlimited authority and emergency powers. This created a tension between the colonial state’s claims to sovereignty and its exercise—a tension that was eventually drawn out and exposed in the 1920s. Chapter 2 reinterprets Queen Victoria’s 1858 Proclamation as a post-conflict resolution, framing it as a bargain offered to the defeated, entailing the “full surrender of Indian political agency” (30). British mercy and discretion shaped the narrative of an 1857 “rebellion,” which had the effects of intensifying the state’s legal power across India. McClure argues that since post-1857 criminal punishment could never be dispensed strictly along racial lines, the colonial state had to organize itself “through the politics of discretion” (103). Loyal subjects were rewarded; rebels were punished; others were pardoned. Chapter 3 examines the Indian Penal Code (1860), tracking the overlooked ways that the 1857 crisis informed its codification; the Code referenced the Queen’s Proclamation and, crucially, made waging war against the colonial state a capital offense. McClure demonstrates how the Code (and eventually judges) ended up with greater jurisdiction than its orignial drafter, Thomas Macaulay, originally envisioned. Notions of colonial difference based upon caste, gender, and race shaped the Code’s punishments (whipping was for “lower castes”; women were punished harshly for abortion) and procedures (race determined Indians were “unfit” for juries).

papers.title: The Highest Stage of Nationalism
papers.abstract: Abstract The study of fascism has long been dominated by a Eurocentric perspective that dismisses the presence of fascist ideologies and movements outside the interwar European context. But existing scholarship has been trapped in a circular logic that inevitably disqualifies non-European cases for not fitting the criteria for fascism determined by specifically European historical experiences. The existence of nationalist discourses in postcolonial Korea—which vehemently emphasized the supremacy of the ethnic nation while calling for a third way beyond capitalism and communism—that strongly resembled European fascism, however, demonstrates the possibility that fascism can exist not just outside Europe but also even in anticolonial nationalisms. Through the study of fascistic nationalism in postcolonial Korea, this article argues for the need to rethink existing approaches to the concept of fascism and broaden its geographic and temporal applicability.

papers.title: Colin M. Coates. Political Culture in Louis XIV’s Canada: Majesty, Ritual, and Rhetoric
papers.abstract: In Political Culture in Louis XIV’s Canada: Majesty, Ritual, and Rhetoric, Colin M. Coates examines the political culture that the French established in a small overseas colony in the Saint Lawrence Valley during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, which came to be known as New France. French officials used cultural practices to construct and strengthen French colonial power. Beyond attempting to impose their political systems on Indigenous territories, French officials introduced recognizably French Catholicism, an agrarian economy, and trade practices. Although French settlers rarely returned to France or visited other French colonies, they maintained their connection to France through their identities as subjects of the French Crown. Their construction of state systems emphasized the reign of the “Sun King” Louis XIV, an absolutist monarch. This book does not celebrate the settler colonial state. Instead, it investigates how French colonial officials employed monarchical symbols and rituals to establish state legitimacy for their colonial settler subjects.

papers.title: Marcus Meer. Heraldry in Urban Society: Visual Culture and Communication in Late Medieval England and Germany
papers.abstract: For anyone still inclined to assume heraldry to be the preserve of nobles or its subject the province of antiquarians, the book’s title may come as a surprise. Its content, however, not only confounds such lingering assumptions but also demonstrates how essential heraldry was to late medieval urban society. Far from being a slavish imitation of practices derived from the nobility, heraldry became customized for civic purposes from the thirteenth century onward. Proof enough of this is the wealth of visual and textual evidence of the ubiquity of heraldic signs (individual, family, guild or municipal) assembled in every chapter, and their appearance in or on every conceivable space or object (from city gates, guild halls, churches and streets, to textiles, clothing, and even of beggars). But Heraldry in Urban Society: Visual Culture and Communication in Late Medieval England and Germany provides much more than evidence: the main achievement of this excellent book is its elucidation of the multiple ways in which heraldic signs were interpreted.

papers.title: Stephen Cummins. States of Enmity: The Politics of Hatred in the Early Modern Kingdom of Naples
papers.abstract: In States of Enmity, Stephen Cummins offers a significant contribution to the history of violence through the lens of enmity and hatred, focusing on the mid-seventeenth century in the Kingdom of Naples. Southern Italy has long had a reputation for being unusually violent in this period, and for that violence continuing and intensifying even when it was on the decline elsewhere in the peninsula. Cummins does not contradict this reputation, but provides greater nuance and context, and pushes back against the assumption that greater violence is a sign of societal backwardness. More broadly, he argues that the political and legal history of the Kingdom of Naples must include the history of emotions, because “love, friendship, forgiveness, and hatred were integral parts of state and legal processes of peace-making” (192). This is an ambitious but compact book, which attempts to cover a lot of ground through a case study approach, allowing Cummins to advance several arguments. As he acknowledges in the introduction, each could be expanded to a book-length project on its own, but he aimed to give a broader overview of the ways enmity functioned and drove different forms of violence in seventeenth-century Naples. At times this approach feels a bit disjointed, but each case study does contribute to a complex picture of violence and enmity in the kingdom. The conclusion draws the case studies together more, and ultimately provides a theory for why Naples was so violent. In Cummins’s understanding, it was particularly the combination of a nonresident Spanish monarch (and the Spanish regime’s interest in fiscal exploitation rather than “buon governo”) with Naples’s extensive feudal system that hindered the extension of justice and attempts at pacification (192).

papers.title: Karen M. Inouye. Mary Kitagawa: A Nikkei Canadian Life
papers.abstract: In Mary Kitagawa: A Nikkei Canadian Life, Karen M. Inouye presents a richly detailed description of the life of a legendary Japanese Canadian woman, Keiko Mary (Murakami) Kitagawa. Notwithstanding its title, however, Mary Kitagawa is not the story of one woman alone. Inouye sensitively and skillfully situates Mary’s life within that of her ancestors: the Murakamis and the Okanos, as they cross time and space in a racist, white settler colonial society. In chronicling the lives of the Murakamis and Okanos, Inouye also provides us with a glimpse into the chronological history of thousands upon thousands of Japanese Canadians—as early migrants to Canada, settlers arduously clearing land; as suspects who were forcibly dispersed, dispossessed, and dislocated during the Second World War; as racialized peoples navigating their identities and struggling for economic security after the war, haunted by memory. In this sense, the book presents the reader with both shared and distinctive and unique lived experiences of Japanese Canadians. It represents a valuable contribution to Nikkei history. As a sansei (third generation Japanese Canadian), I did not directly experience the injustices and violations of the Second World War. But my mother and her family, like Mary’s, were dislocated from their farm and forcibly moved to Rosebery, British Columbia. My father was taken from his home in Vancouver and put in a prisoner of war camp in the province of Ontario. And as I was growing up in Toronto, I closely watched my mother and father, both of whom were similarly haunted by memories of these events. Like so many other Nikkei, I experienced the war indirectly through the intergenerational transmission of memory.

papers.title: Fang Yu Hu. Good Wife, Wise Mother: Educating Han Taiwanese Girls Under Japanese Rule
papers.abstract: Japan’s fifty-year colonial rule (1895–1945) over Taiwan profoundly influenced Taiwanese culture. Numerous social customs and practices characteristic of Han society during the Qing dynasty underwent significant transformation during the Japanese period, shaped by both imperial policies and the intellectual currents in the early 20th century. Notably, many modernizing discourses and institutions were first refracted through Japanese interpretations before exerting renewed influence upon Taiwanese society. Fang Yu Hu’s book Good Wife, Wise Mother: Educating Han Taiwanese Girls Under Japanese Rule focuses on transformations in women’s education under Japanese rule, offering a Taiwanese case study of the “Good Wife, Wise Mother” ideal prevalent in East Asia and enabling comparative analysis alongside examples from Japan, Korea, and China. Focusing on Taiwan’s majority Han population, the book examines the institutionalization of girls’ education and the construction of gender ideals, analyzing how gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status shaped the implementation and effects of colonial education, highlighting Taiwan as a cultural crossroads between Han tradition and Japanese colonial influence. A central analytical thread is Japan’s dōka (assimilation) policy, which sought to transform colonial subjects into Japanese citizens through language, education, custom, and identity. While claiming cultural unification, the policy was deeply unequal and stratified, especially along gender and class lines. Hu argues that “gendered assimilation intensified colonial mimicry” (12) by simultaneously affirming traditional Han Taiwanese gender norms and drawing the colonized into the framework of the imperial nation, and this gave the illusion of achievable assimilation.

papers.title: Stefania Pastore. An Invisible Thread: Heresy, Mass Conversions, and the Inquisition in the Kingdom of Castile (1449–1559) , trans. Consuelo López-Morillas
papers.abstract: Stefania Pastore’s An Invisible Thread was originally written in Italian over twenty years ago, and was translated into Spanish in 2010. The English version under review is a translation by Consuelo López-Morillas of the Spanish edition, which had revised and expanded the Italian original. As Pastore explains, this English translation was desirable to speak to Anglophone, specifically American, scholarly insularity. It appends a new historiographical chapter that addresses scholarship published after the 2004 and 2010 versions. Pastore’s chief contention in An Invisible Thread is “the peculiarity, even the uniqueness, of the early modern Spanish religious experience” and its distinct spirituality (280). She emphasizes the import of the mass conversions of Jews (and Muslims) on a troubled spectrum from coercion to questionable volition, resulting from Dominican preaching and evangelism in the late fourteenth century. As Pastore points out, Iberia’s sudden sharp increase of new Christians and their attempted assimilation was unique in Europe. (However, the assertion that “During the Middle Ages, the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon were the only areas of Europe in which three religions and cultures coexisted” must be tempered by the mention of Sicily [1].) These mass conversions prompted theological arguments, as defenses of conversos meant insistence not only on the universal, unfailing efficacy of baptism but also on all Christians’ unity in God and the unmediated link between God and believer (the title’s “invisible thread”). Pastore contends that both “Old” and “New” Christian efforts and strategies to integrate the newly converted generally imprinted themselves on fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Spanish spirituality: a rejection of ritual; a prioritization of faith over works; the promise that Christ offered gentle salvation rather than impossible observance; Pauline inner piety over empty externals; revelation approaching antinomianism; and universalism and syncretism shaped by contacts with Judaism and Islam. And after Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand founded the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 to pursue supposedly backsliding conversos, its repression served as a foil, underscoring the theological validity of this free, open, and often radically subjective spirituality.

papers.title: D. Andrew Johnson. Enslaved Native Americans and the Making of Colonial South Carolina .
papers.abstract: The recent publication of Pekka Hämäläinen’s Indigenous Continent (2022), Ned Blackhawk’s The Rediscovery of America (2023), and Kathleen DuVal’s Native Nations (2025) would seem to indicate that we are currently in our “big book” era when it comes to Native American history. D. Andrew Johnson’s Enslaved Native Americans and the Making of Colonial South Carolina is not a big book, in the physical sense. It’s quite slim, in fact, but it’s definitely not slight. And the sophisticated questions it raises should influence the field for years to come. Johnson’s work demonstrates that Native American enslavement was at the heart of South Carolina’s early development as an English colony, and that because of the demographics of Native slavery and Indigenous gender roles, Native women’s labor, knowledge, and bodies were in the middle of that heart. At first glance, the story that Johnson tells appears timeworn. The English arrival on the coast of South Carolina dispossessed coastal peoples, initiated shock waves of violence that affected societies all the way to the Mississippi River within a few short years, even shattering some communities in the process. Herbert Bolton and Verner Crane knew this in the early twentieth century, and Chapman Milling’s Red Carolinians made a similar point, in its own way, back in 1940, and generations of scholars have elaborated upon it, complicated and nuanced it, and ultimately reinforced it. In the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, Alan Gallay, Robbie Ethridge, and Christina Snyder, among others, have added immensely to our understanding of Native enslavement, and Johnson has benefited from their more recent scholarship. Along a parallel track, pioneers like Peter Wood, Leland Ferguson, Philip Morgan, Ira Berlin, and Daniel C. Littlefield, and later Max Edelson and Judith Carney, have explored how Africans forced to labor in South Carolina influenced, and were influenced by, the rising rice economy. The significance of Johnson’s contribution lies in part in exploring the intersection between these two historiographical traditions.

papers.title: COSMOPOLITAN PHILOLOGY AND SACRED GRAMMAR
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Persian developed a formal grammatical tradition comparatively late in its thousand‐year history as a lingua franca. This article takes up the emergence of Persian grammar within the larger trajectory of Persian philology. It explores questions about why and when such a tradition developed in Persian by closely analyzing the earliest formal grammar of Persian in the language: Minhaj al‐Talab (Program of Study; ca. 1660), which was written by a Hui Muslim scholar in eastern Qing China. This text is contrasted with a more mature later work of Persian philology from Mughal India: Musmir (Fruition; 1750s). Through comparative study of these texts and by drawing comparisons to Arabic, Sanskrit, Chinese, and other languages, the article complicates characterizations of Persian and the Persianate as cosmopolitan and explores the complex relationship between cosmopolitan and vernacular and between Persian and Islam. Persian has a sacred dimension for many Chinese Muslims, despite its primarily cosmopolitan function in Mughal India. This article concludes with a historical materialist analysis of the role of philology in general, arguing that the discipline is neither fundamentally reactionary nor colonial but rather a tool that can be used for multiple ends.

papers.title: PHILOLOGY IN AFRICAN HISTORICAL INQUIRY: TROUBLING THE MEANING OF GIRLHOOD IN BANTU SPEECH COMMUNITIES
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Language and history are inextricably entangled with each other, but can one be used to illuminate the other? This article focuses on the generations of philologists and Bantu speakers who have collectively, in different ways, obscured and illuminated our understandings of such categories as gender and childhood. In particular, it challenges the antiquity of girlhood as a historical designation in eastern and central African Bantu speech communities. It addresses questions regarding philology's relevance in studying ancient Bantu speakers’ practices marking gender and generation as characteristics of childhood and identity. Rather than looking to written literature, this article draws on spoken word in a part of Africa where historians have long developed models of historical analysis through philological methods that forefront African intellectual trends over externally imposed ones. The words people develop reflect their ways of thinking about who they are and which categories matter to them. In this article, ancestry and familial generations act as both a subject of and method for reclaiming the past and understanding some of the processes through which identity categories were formed within ancient Bantu speech communities. It concludes by demonstrating that childhood and, specifically, girlhood are not innate and automatic categories that can be easily defined but are historically contingent identities that are forged in particular, identifiable circumstances.

papers.title: TEACHING SPANISH IN THE UNIVERSAL MONARCHY: TOMÁS PINPIN'S GRAMMAR FOR TAGALOGS (1610)
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In 1610, a Tagalog printer named Tomás Pinpin published a Spanish grammar in Tagalog that was intended to help natives avoid errors and misunderstandings in their interactions with Spanish colonizers. This article attempts to clarify the book's genesis and to contextualize it within the global expansion of Spanish. Pinpin exemplifies a pattern whereby Spanish was taught by colonial subjects on their own initiative and following their own criteria. At the same time, his grammar is associated with a missionary translation project in which the printers, among them Pinpin himself, were non‐Spanish. This text thus offers an opportunity to broaden understandings of early modern colonial translation and linguistic description by stressing the creations of native collaborators.

papers.title: Keith M. Finley. From Slavery to Segregation: Reckoning with White Supremacy in the American South .
papers.abstract: Keith M. Finley’s From Slavery to Segregation is an intellectual history of white supremacy in the South. As Finley notes, white supremacy as an idea and, more importantly, as an argument, is central to slavery, Jim Crow segregation, and the political history of the South throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. One thing the author wants to do is map out a long history of racial caste in America embodied with Jim Crow segregation and connect it from the history of slavery on through to its demise with the civil rights and Voting Rights Acts of the early 1960s. Finely challenges us to imagine a long history approach to this history of white supremacy in the South. He makes the case that there is a continuity between the early antebellum defense of slavery and the massive resistance to integration that followed in the wake of the Brown v. Board decision. Each chapter is thematic. The first chapter examines the origins of the defense of white supremacy and places it in the context of the politics of the expansion of slavery and after the politics of maintaining a racial caste system. Chapter 2 features an examination of white mythmaking for the South as a region that ignores African Americans or sees them primarily as a threat. Chapter 3 focuses on how the white South constructed intellectually and through the social sciences a defense of racial hierarchy. Chapter 4 examines how this racial intellectual tradition was supported by legal and constitutional interpretations of the founding documents into what we would come to know first as states’ rights and later political and judicial arguments for limited government. Finally, chapter 5 helps us understand how the South, as a region, coalesced around arguments for white supremacy in defiance to a nation and its institutions, becoming increasingly hostile to first slavery and later de jure racial segregation. Each chapter follows its theme or argument from the antebellum period until the end of the “legal” Jim Crow system in the South. Thus, covering the same history but narrowly focused on that chapter’s argument.

papers.title: Keidrick Roy. American Dark Age: Racial Feudalism and the Rise of Black Liberalism
papers.abstract: Feudalism has returned—or, at least, news outlets and punditry would have you believe. Terms like “techno-feudalism,” “neo-feudalism,” and “feudal capitalism” have become increasingly en vogue as we grapple with material inequalities, authoritarian politics, and corporate power in the twenty-first century. Yet these treatments often deploy the term “feudalism” as if all things feudal are necessarily alien to American politics and culture, an invasion of otherwise liberal, modern institutions. Keidrick Roy’s American Dark Age: Racial Feudalism and the Rise of Black Liberalism disabuses contemporary readers of such a static staging by tracing American thinkers’ entanglements with feudal ideology and the Black liberal refutation of feudal thinking. Weaving together readings of letters, narratives, pamphlets, and well-known treatises, Roy suggests that current political crises can be understood in relation to “racial feudal ideology” that originates in eighteenth-century American attempts to conserve social hierarchy while affirming ideals of universal freedom and equality. And extending the work of philosopher Charles Mills and others, American Dark Age contends that this Black liberalism, fashioned as a weapon against feudal ideology, provides resources to challenge racist power structures today. American Dark Age excels when exposing the entanglement of American liberalism and feudal ideology. The promotion of Black liberalism as a definitive response to persisting feudal ideas, however, warrants more discussion of the problem of economic domination.

papers.title: Jessica Lauren Taylor. Plain Paths and Dividing Lines: Navigating Native Land and Water in the Seventeenth-Century Chesapeake
papers.abstract: As the field of Native American history has matured in the twenty-first century, one major focus of the scholarship has involved spatial themes. Borderlands have been joined by shatter zones, spaces of power, common pots, and other useful frameworks, often drawing on Indigenous linguistic and cultural concepts. In Plain Paths and Dividing Lines: Navigating Native Land and Water in the Seventeenth-Century Chesapeake, Jessica Lauren Taylor makes a strong entry into this genre. The book focuses on the period from the late sixteenth century to the end of Bacon’s Rebellion in 1677, paired with an ambitious geographical approach, venturing far from Jamestown to the Eastern Shore and islands in the Chesapeake, and upriver to the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Taylor’s approach places the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries at the center of the action, serving both as conduits for travel and exchange and as contested boundaries for a diverse cast of actors. Taylor convincingly argues that struggles over possession and authority in the Chesapeake often centered on questions of mobility and the ability to control who had freedom of travel across land and waterways.

papers.title: Sheila Fitzpatrick. Lost Souls: Soviet Displaced Persons and the Birth of the Cold War .
papers.abstract: In Lost Souls, Sheila Fitzpatrick delivers a landmark study on the displaced persons (DPs) of the post–World War II era, masterfully combining narrative readability with analytical rigor. Through a dual-layered writing style, Fitzpatrick crafts a work that is equally compelling for informed general readers and seasoned scholars. At the heart of this book are the experiences of Soviet DPs, whose plight became emblematic of the early Cold War’s political and humanitarian struggles. Numbering about one million, these individuals—originally citizens of the Soviet Union or its newly annexed territories—found themselves in the West after WWII and, in most cases, refused repatriation to the USSR. This diverse group included Russians, Ukrainians, Belarusians, Balts, Jews, and many other ethnic and cultural groups who either fled or were taken to the Third Reich as forced laborers or prisoners. Fitzpatrick also includes often-overlooked groups such as Kalmyks and Turks, examining their racialization within the refugee system with scholarly attention and sensitivity.

papers.title: Tate Paulette. In the Land of Ninkasi: A History of Beer in Ancient Mesopotamia.
papers.abstract: Reading In the Land of Ninkasi: A History of Beer in Ancient Mesopotamia, one quickly gets a sense of the challenge the author set out for himself. Beer is a subject begging for lighthearted treatment, which Tate Paulette, to his credit, refuses to give it. He aims for a colloquial yet substantive exploration of Mesopotamian beer. And he succeeds, perhaps a bit more so than he appreciates. In the first two chapters, the author uses archaeological evidence to show that beer has twelve thousand-year-old origins, emerging independently across multiple regions in diverse styles. In Mesopotamia, beer was integral to state power, urban life, economic systems, and social hierarchies, appearing in everything from royal ceremonies and institutional breweries to private taverns and household production. The rest of the book resists quick summary. Paulette takes the reader deep into debates in the specialist literature to reconstruct the Mesopotamian evidence for beer ingredients, to assay the techniques for brewing beer (with an excellent analytical section on what he calls the “minimalist trap”), and to explore the archaeological and written evidence for brewing, brewers, and breweries. The final two chapters discuss how Mesopotamians drank beer, and then, how they manifested and dealt with the effects of it.

papers.title: Brycchan Carey. The Unnatural Trade: Slavery, Abolition and Environmental Writing, 1650–1807
papers.abstract: In his Natural History of Barbados (1750), the Welsh naturalist and clergyman Griffith Hughes made a striking observation about the island’s soil. On the tops of the hills, it was white. At middle altitudes, it was darker: a reddish color. On the lower plains of the island, where most of the sugar plantations were located, it was black. For Hughes, this was evidence that God had adapted the composition of the soil in Barbados especially to suit the cultivation of different kinds of plants. Yet, as Brycchan Carey notes in The Unnatural Trade, it is impossible to ignore the parallels between Hughes’ presentation of the Barbadian environment and the racialized social hierarchy of this white supremacist, slaveholding society. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that, for Hughes, “just as God adapted soils to fit the trees necessary to the colonists, so he adapted enslaved people to the tasks necessary to colonists,” and all the more so when he then described “the black soil as being most suitable to support the sugarcane” (73). Hughes’s attitude was typical of mid-eighteenth-century British environmental writing about the Caribbean, representing slavery as a natural feature of the island’s landscape: ideologically neutral, preordained by God, and thus, seemingly immutable. Yet half a century later, abolitionists drew on environmental writers, including Hughes, to make precisely the inverse argument: that slavery and the slave trade were not only artificial, but perversions of the divine natural order, and for some, environmentally catastrophic to boot.

papers.title: Bradley J. Dixon. Republic of Indians: Empires of Indigenous Law in the Early American South
papers.abstract: Bradley J. Dixon’s ambitiously conceived and engagingly written first book, Republic of Indians: Empires of Indigenous Law in the Early American South, offers a comparative history of how Indigenous people actively shaped the law within the Spanish and English colonies of the American South during the long seventeenth century. His title, Republic of Indians, first appears in an anecdote that centers Timucua Indian leaders—“the aristocracy at the head of Florida’s Indigenous commonwealth, la república de indios” (2). For them, the ideal república de indios was one of two equal commonwealths under the authority of the Spanish Crown. While local Spanish governors mediated that authority, Indigenous people expected to retain self-government and gain the Crown’s protection. English colonizers, jealous of Spanish success in securing Native tribute, also adopted the republic of Indians model. In both Florida and Virginia, Native people initially rejected invitations to subject themselves to European monarchs. But some Native rulers saw benefit in such a relationship. By the early seventeenth century, the Timucuans of Florida accepted subjection because it promised protection from their Native enemies and because benefits flowed from “training the presidio in the duties of a munificent paramount” (18). The Chickahominies of Virginia accepted subjection in order to escape Powhatan oppression. But Native expectations of what the Spanish and English empires owed them as vassals or subjects differed from Europeans. For instance, Virginia’s English had a limited, basically defensive, view of what “protection” of their Indigenous neighbors entailed. Native expectations were far more expansive, including protection from “drought, withered crops, hunger, and plague” (32). Indigenous people in both regions expected that their own leaders would be treated with the same respect Europeans demanded for their officers, and both expected “a measure of self-government. Once they paid, tributaries expected colonizers to leave them alone, free to obey their own laws and lords” (32). Dixon acknowledges that “the ideal of two republics, of equal commonwealths, poorly describes the reality in either colony” (131). The Spanish frequently made excessive demands for labor of tributary Indians or failed to treat them with respect; the English colonists increasingly saw Natives as barriers to their expansion and railed against what they saw as official favoritism for “Darling Indians” (95).

papers.title: Adelina Stefan. Vacationing in Dictatorships: International Tourism in Socialist Romania and Franco’s Spain.
papers.abstract: Despite being latecomers to the study of tourism, historians have increasingly explored the phenomenon over the past three decades. papers.title: Kathryn Jasper. Bounded Wilderness: Land and Reform at the Hermitage of Fonte Avellana, ca. 1035–1072
papers.abstract: Bounded Wilderness: Land and Reform at the Hermitage of Fonte Avellana, ca. 1035–1072 by Kathryn L. Jasper is a book devoted to the monastic experience of Fonte Avellana in central Italy, a reality intimately linked to the figure of Pier Damiani, one of the key figures of the eleventh-century ecclesiastical reforms. The author moves in a rich historiographical field, taking on a theme that has been the subject of numerous studies by Italian scholars in recent decades. But the importance of this book is not only that it is the first major monographic study in English on this topic, but also (and above all) lies in the approach chosen, which makes it original within the broader historiographical landscape. This is due to the specific objectives of the research, and the analytical strategy chosen by the author. At the center of the story is not Damiani, but the monastic network he built, the core of which was the monastery of Fonte Avellana. Specifically, the author focuses on the physical landscape where the reforms of Pier Damiani and the hermits and monks linked to him took place; a reality made up of, above all, Apennine woods, streams, and mountains, but it should not be considered a pure wilderness but rather a reality deeply marked by human presence. The author carries out a fine-grained analysis, whose main sources are the documentation on the Fonte Avellana and Damiani’s very rich epistolary records, supplemented by thorough and first-hand knowledge of the physical landscape in which the action takes place.

papers.title: Joseph John Viscomi. Migration at the End of Empire: Time and the Politics of Departure between Italy and Egypt
papers.abstract: In the aftermath of World War II, 40,000 Italians returned to Italy from Egypt—a story largely overlooked in the histories of Italian emigration. Migration at the End of Empire is a deeply researched, theoretically dense exploration of the history of Italians in Egypt, historical temporalities, notions of political and cultural belonging, the centrality of migration in foreign policy, and the ways in which memory, experience, and politics shape intimate and historical narratives. This microhistory centers on moments of conflict and collusion between migrants, state actors, and local institutions, tracing the changing contours of imaginary and physical political and social communities. Viscomi explores how the Italian state and Italians in Egypt created a relationship based on mutual need and differing dreams. Italy needed the Italian community to realize its foreign policy dreams, while the community needed the Italian state for protection and power. Their goals did not always align. Out of this often-contested relationship emerged different imaginings of departure and belonging tied to specific historical moments. The compelling theoretical dimensions of the book are Viscomi’s attention to time and space. The framing of historical temporalities and contingency is central to his work. This frame foregrounds ideas of departure, belonging, and community, but also challenges accepted periodization of the Mediterranean world and decolonization. Scholars of the Mediterranean Sea have described it as a cosmopolitan world that suddenly, in the 1950s, emerged as a nationalist one. Viscomi’s study of the Italians in Egypt makes clear that processes of nationalism and politics of nationalization had been in play since the 1870s, continuing to reverberate in the present. Viscomi also attends to the changing spatial dimensions underlying the meanings of nation, community, and home. He deftly keeps shifting imaginaries of place and time in focus as political conditions evolve.

papers.title: David Allen Harvey. Tropical Despotisms: Enlightened Reform in the French Caribbean
papers.abstract: Decades before Jacobins attempted to regenerate the French nation by stripping it of Old Regime institutions and customs, a group of Old Regime bureaucrats, administrators, and officials hoped to regenerate the French Caribbean colonies. papers.title: Stephanie Baker Opperman. Cold War Anthropologist: Isabel Kelly and Rural Development in Mexico .
papers.abstract: Isabel Kelly (1906–1983), who lived in Mexico from 1939 until her death in 1983, is the Cold War Anthropologist to whom Baker Opperman dedicates this book. Through five chapters, Opperman presents Kelly’s intellectual and diplomatic work, from arriving in Mexico in 1940 until her resignation from her employment at the US State Department in 1960. Each chapter unfolds a particular layer of her experience as an international expert on development programs. In 1945, we see her as a team leader and coordinator of the research and development programs launched by the Smithsonian Institution’s Institute of Social Anthropology (ISA) (created by Julian Steward) in Mexico. We also follow her and the ISA director’s intense negotiations with the newly created Institute of Inter-American Affairs (IIAA) to administer Truman’s Point IV projects (chapter 1). With the absorption of ISA by the IIAA (1952), we see Kelly now working for the latter institute as an evaluator of rural development projects between the IIAA and the Mexican government (chapter 2). After 1953, the new Foreign Operations Administration (FOA) centralized the previous international cooperation agencies, and Kelly worked with it to establish collaborations with Mexico’s Instituto Nacional Indigenista (INI). During that period, she developed an applied anthropology methodology to introduce biomedicine in Indigenous localities, studying and respecting native practices and beliefs about illness and healing (chapter 3). The different areas in which Kelly developed her expertise are also examined from her “gendered experiences,” whether in her relations with the anthropological and diplomatic milieu, in her role as a teacher and project leader, or even in her relationships with the women of the communities where she worked (chapter 4). Finally, Kelly took her practical knowledge to Bolivia in 1957, where she administered cooperation projects managed by the United States Operations Mission (USOM), and in 1959, to Pakistan to evaluate a “Village Agricultural–Industrial Development program.” Both experiences led her to resign from the State Department and to reevaluate the role of anthropology and development projects, considering that, ultimately, they privileged the alliances and interests of the United States over those of the neediest nations (chapter 5).

papers.title: Susana Sosenski. The Fear of Robachicos in Mexico: Media, Childhood and Child Kidnapping, 1900–1968 . Translated by Quentin Pope
papers.abstract: Mexican Spanish has a word for a person who kidnaps children: robachicos. For Susana Sosenski, the robachicos is the iconic villain of the Mexican twentieth century, and her book argues that the Mexican media were responsible for generating widespread public fear of kidnapping. Published in Spanish in 2021 and now translated into English by Quentin Pope, Sosenski’s research brings together the histories of crime, emotions, and childhood to guide readers through the contradictions of modernizing and urbanizing Mexico. This is a cultural history that focuses on narratives as much as the empirical reality of kidnapping, which is difficult to quantify accurately, though we know a great deal about certain cases. From the early to the mid-twentieth century, incessant depictions of kidnappings in the press and entertainment media nourished fears and prescribed actions. Deeply conservative, patriarchal media narratives absolved the Mexican state of the responsibility to protect children and placed that burden on families, who were taught to cloister their children and deny them the right to public space.

papers.title: Sarah L. H. Gronningsater. The Rising Generation: Gradual Abolition, Black Legal Culture, and the Making of National Freedom .
papers.abstract: The Rising Generation: Gradual Abolition, Black Legal Culture, and the Making of National Freedom follows an arc of African American legal and political organization, from the Revolutionary period to Reconstruction, and joins a burgeoning field of study. A venerable narrative in US history has long had it that by the middle of the nineteenth century, African Americans lived on the margins of civic life. More recent work, however, has documented the creative ways that Black Americans claimed their citizenship despite the challenges arrayed against them. Sarah L. H. Gronningsater joins this effort, with a book that is supple, revealing, and beautifully rendered. The broad sweep of her story is that African Americans in New York experienced the Revolution, gradual emancipation in the 1790s and 1810s, and both general emancipation and electoral exclusion in the 1820s, as a determined, vocal, active, and organized group. But rather than narrate this history as a story of natural determination, Gronningsater uses a generational model to show how layers of activism built Black New Yorkers up. Ultimately, for the author, it was in the patient work of uplift that progress was to be found. Building her argument around a layering of generational experiences, Gronningsater braids a history not of unbroken, whiggish success, but of creative adaptation and political pressure, trial, and error. Through the courts, in schools, on the pages of their newspapers, on the streets, and in the rich associational life of their own communities and that of their allies, Black New Yorkers pushed at the constrictions of legislative programs of gradual emancipation, as hard as they pushed for a political voice.

papers.title: Michael O’Malley. The Color of Family: History, Race, and the Politics of Ancestry
papers.abstract: The Color of Family: History, Race, and the Politics of Ancestry tells four intertwining stories. The first story is about historian Michael O’Malley’s engagement in an activity often viewed with derision by members of his profession, including himself: genealogy. The second story is that of the changing racial categorization and ethnic identity of Patrick O’Malley, the author’s great-great-grandfather, who migrated from Ireland to the United States in 1871. The third story examines the evolution over many centuries of government efforts to categorize individuals by race in the United States, with a particular focus on Virginia in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, but continuing into the twenty-first century. The fourth story chronicles the privatization of access to government documents essential to family history, which coincided with the rise of online genealogy services like ancestry.com. Each story addresses a different question: Does genealogy serve any useful purpose at either the individual or societal level? How successful were government efforts to compartmentalize individuals within distinct racial categories? What motivated state and federal lawmakers and administrators to categorize individuals by race and endow that categorization with legal ramifications? Has the rise of private online genealogy services contributed to the perpetuation of this now-discredited practice of racially categorizing individuals?

papers.title: Lisa Jacobson. Intoxicating Pleasures: The Reinvention of Wine, Beer, and Whiskey after Prohibition
papers.abstract: Did whiskey, wine, and beer really need to be reinvented after the fall of Prohibition in the United States? From a business and cultural perspective, they certainly did. While alcohol has been an integral part of human culture for thousands of years, in the wake of the Industrial Revolution, Prohibitionists began to vilify the intoxicating pleasures that had been so long enjoyed. The tide turned so far that between 1920 and 1933 the Eighteenth Amendment to the US Constitution outlawed the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors, which the Volstead Act subsequently defined as any beverage containing more than 0.5 percent alcohol. Lisa Jacobson’s excellent book Intoxicating Pleasures: The Reinvention of Wine, Beer, and Whiskey after Prohibition shows how these beverages—and the industries behind them—shook off the stigma of being an illicit product and regained respectability in the United States. By the 1950s, they had even become an emblem of a good middle-class life. While many historians have focused on Prohibition as the culmination of the century-long battle to destroy the alcohol industry, Jacobson casts her focus on repeal as a great reset toward an all-new set of values and attitudes pertaining to alcoholic beverages in America.

papers.title: PHILOLOGY NOW: EDITORS’ INTRODUCTION
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In this introduction to the “Philology Now” theme issue, we make a case for “philology” as a useful sign under which to consider the ways historians are already working with words in their efforts to understand the past. Doing so, we recognize that “philology” has been variously defined. Rather than being normative or prescriptive about what philology entails, we proceed from a historical awareness that, in many of its uses, the word binds interrelated concerns of language, history, and method. The articles featured in this issue take up this nexus as providing opportunities for theory of history. Together, they demonstrate how attention to philology's methods of treating words in history enables self‐reflective work on disciplinary formations and their political legacies, on the relationships between language and power, and on temporality itself. It also enables innovative new approaches to words and concepts.

papers.title: Lesley J. Gordon. Dread Danger: Cowardice and Combat in the American Civil War

papers.title: Anne Greenwood MacKinney. Nature on Paper: Documenting Science in Prussia, 1770–1850
papers.abstract: Can paperwork, especially particular kinds of documentary artifacts such as lists, change the world? The answer that Anne Greenwood MacKinney pursues in her insightful book Nature on Paper: Documenting Science in Prussia, 1770–1850 is a resounding yes. Although perhaps not the most exciting things to read and engage with at first glance, bureaucratic artifacts such as catalogs and lists, Greenwood MacKinney shows, “not only contain but also help create entire worlds” (4). They possess a kind of “multilayered complexity” that exists in relation to the individuals (people)—and institutions—who make and use them, the natural specimens (things) they record, and the larger historical developments (time) within which they emerge. Greenwood MacKinney’s ability to illustrate these entanglements between people, things, and time via a highly nuanced analysis of lists and other forms of paperwork is what makes this such a powerful piece of scholarship. In taking up the world-changing powers of lists, including catalogs, inventories, registers, and indices, Nature on Paper engages with recent work in the history of science on information management, collecting, and paper tools, such as groundbreaking work by Anke Te Heesen, Emma Spary, and Stefan Müller-Wille. Yet her study is also informed by media studies scholarship, which has drawn attention to how paper records associated with natural history objects in collections “have tended to remain invisible while at the same time allowing seemingly direct access to those objects they record” (7). There is an invisibility to the mediating function of paperwork, in other words, that makes it easy not to prioritize despite its centrality to understanding the material and institutional contexts in which it is embedded. Studying natural history paperwork allows us to access both the “movements and meanings of specimens” (9).

papers.title: Debórah Dwork. Saints and Liars: The Story of Americans Who Saved Refugees from the Nazis
papers.abstract: Debórah Dwork’s elegantly written book Saints and Liars: The Story of Americans Who Saved Refugees from the Nazis spotlights eight American relief workers whose responsibilities included selecting the petitioners who would receive permission and assistance to emigrate from Nazi Europe. Located in five European cities, these administrators worked for agencies religious in origin: the Unitarian Service Committee (USC), the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), and the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee (JDC). They chose petitioners among thousands of applicants, helped them procure necessary permissions, papers, and immigration routes, and sometimes even accompanied them to their next point of departure. Empowered to save thousands of lives, they were radically restricted by the number of individuals they possibly could rescue. Dwork’s book examines how these relief workers accomplished their tasks and the multiple variables that shaped their decision-making processes. Dwork centers her book on the messiness of relief efforts. Rescue initiatives were complex, resting on luck, chance, accidents, and irrational impulses. Attraction, social ties, sympathy, distaste, timing, ambition, and a penchant for (or an aversion to) adventure all influenced the choices relief workers made. One administrator might have been swayed by the quiet nature of a mother and her well-behaved children; another worker might have chosen the opposite—namely, a parent who had been relentless in their lobbying efforts. Only a particularly skillful author could focus on capriciousness and still produce an elegant monograph. Dwork, who has published a half dozen seminal works in Holocaust history, has a well-deserved reputation for utilizing creative narrative arcs and innovative methodologies, and Saints and Liars is beautifully argued and written.

papers.title: Shannon C. Eaves. Sexual Violence and American Slavery: The Making of a Rape Culture in the Antebellum South .
papers.abstract: There is a form of “knowing” that exists among historians of US slavery in the antebellum era regarding the systematic sexual exploitation of enslaved women. Since the 1980s, Black feminist scholars have been at the vanguard of historical studies unveiling routine sexual assaults of enslaved women by white slaveholders as US slavery’s “open secret.” In the late 1990s, the use of DNA technology settled the long-rumored and hotly debated topic of Founding Father Thomas Jefferson’s paternity of the children of Sally Hemings, a woman he owned. papers.title: Scott K. Taylor. Ambivalent Pleasures: Soft Drugs and Embodied Anxiety in Early Modern Europe
papers.abstract: Drugs are fun. Drugs are frightening. Drugs will cure what ails you, but they might sicken you afresh in the process. There’s nothing new about the myriad attractions of stimulants and intoxicants, or about people’s obsessive concern over their potential dangers, and the conundrums addressed by users 350 years ago were not so different from those we face today. The chief difference is the drugs themselves. Today we worry mostly about the damaging individual and societal effects of synthetically manufactured “hard” drugs such as heroin, cocaine, fentanyl, and methamphetamines. In early modern Europe, the menu of available psychotropics was gentler: chocolate, coffee, tea, tobacco, sugar, distilled spirits, and opium. While there is no question today that consuming opium and tobacco presents health risks, and alcoholism is a serious illness, we might raise an eyebrow at the thought of classifying innocuous things like sugar and chocolate as “drugs.” However, the unusual effects these substances exercised on European bodies and minds—and their sheer addictiveness—alarmed and excited many early modern commentators in equal measure, and often provoked a degree of anxiety that would be familiar to any critic of twenty-first-century hard drugs. In Ambivalent Pleasures: Soft Drugs and Embodied Anxiety in Early Modern Europe, Scott K. Taylor hews unwaveringly, through over two hundred pages of fascinating examples, to examining exactly these reactions as expressed by users, prescribers, and proscribers: ambivalence about the pleasure drugs offer, anxiety over their real and imagined effects on consumers’ bodies, and above all “the tensions between the self-discipline [Europeans] desired and the disorder—and freedom—fostered by the use of drugs and alcohol” (11).

papers.title: Brook Poston. The Founders’ Curse: James Monroe’s Struggle against Political Parties
papers.abstract: I sometimes wonder about James Monroe’s final reflections. The fifth president’s life spanned from 1758 until 1831, the entirety of the Age of Revolutions. Under the circumstances, I had always presumed that Monroe spent his last days placidly contemplating the stunning growth and development that the nation had experienced under his stewardship. Indeed, Poston convincingly argues that Monroe was obsessed with the potentially ruinous influence of parties and continually sought to subdue them. In that sense, The Founders’ Curse is a concise, well-researched, and well-crafted portrait of a statesman trying to stem an impossibly strong tide.

papers.title: Kathryn L. Brackney. Surreal Geographies: A New History of Holocaust Consciousness
papers.abstract: Surreal Geographies: A New History of Holocaust Consciousness is an exploration of the modalities of rapport with the dead constructed through their absence—absence both as bodies to bury and mourn, and as subjects of recognition. At the same time, the book investigates these spectral figures as entangled with distinct historical moments. These moments are defined by broader geopolitical, scientific, and technological reconfigurations, and by their impact on conceptions of the human and of humanity more broadly: from the chaos and displacement of the early postwar years, through the anxieties and wonders accompanying the space race of the Cold War, the emergence of the new genre of video testimony alongside advances in the psychoanalysis of trauma, to the current reality of the unfolding climate crisis and environmental apocalypse. These narrative elements of Palmares’s history, he reminds us, are limited by ambiguous historical documents, embellished and biased accounts, and the deafening archival silences about lives lived and lost. Untethered from archival sources (which he still uses extensively) and published historical texts (also used to great effect), Hertzman incorporates oral and environmental history, geography, and comparative historical linguistics into his study. The resulting book is a demanding text—readers unfamiliar with the history and historiographical fields he engages might find it challenging. papers.title: Minority’s History: Tracing an Equivocal Social Category through the Twentieth-Century United States
papers.abstract: Abstract This article traces the long career of the term “minority” in the United States, tracking both its continuities and its shapeshifting in the twentieth century American vernacular. I argue that the changing uses of minority reflected a protean politics of language that reflected changes in racial ideology across the twentieth century, which I explore by analyzing the evolving tension between ascriptive language and demands for self-description by Black and Latino Americans in particular. The earliest usage of minority as a social category emerged after the First World War, when Black journalists and advocates argued that African Americans needed protection as a “racial minority” in the U.S. Social scientists popularized a broader version of the term in the 1930s—which included immigrants and their offsprings—that held sway until a postwar shift in racial schema enabled second- and third-generation European ethnics to escape the minority category. The phrases “disadvantaged minority” and “underprivileged minority” gained currency around that time, entangling Black, Latino, and other “non-white” Americans in a shared but fragmented marginalized status. While the development of affirmative action policies in the late 1960s lent minority status an important form of leverage, the category continued to signal exclusions from the benefits of full citizenship. Even by the late twentieth century, members of groups labeled minorities still resided figuratively and often literally on the periphery of American society, a position from which many continued to critique and rework the language of minority to challenge its normative power.

For reasons ranging from public or scientific recognition in other fields to gendered discrimination to a lack of uptake of their ideas, all of these individuals have been underplayed as contributors to environmental thought and practice. Guha’s uniformly lucid and engaging pen-portraits amply rectify this situation. Combining close readings of each subject’s writings, a masterful command of political and intellectual contexts, and sympathetic accounts of lived experiences, the book combines accessibility to a wide audience with a wealth of original insights for even the most expert reader. Most revelatory of all, to my mind, is Guha’s critical analysis of the lawyer K. M. Munshi’s harnessing of afforestation to a Hindu nationalist agenda during his tenures as Minister for Food and Agriculture and then Governor of Uttar Pradesh in the 1950s and 1960s. Munshi acts both as a foil to the book’s more positive—if never adulatory—engagement with his other environmentalists, and as a warning—all too salient in our age of “fossil fascism”—that environmental schemes need not be attached to progressive politics.

papers.title: Women and Their Warlords. Domesticating Militarism in Modern China. By Kate Merkel-Hess
papers.abstract: During the Republican period (1912-1949), when China lacked a powerful central government, strongmen used their military forces to gain control of land bases of various sizes. These men, called “warlords” (junfa), were major pieces on the political chessboard, but they were also a rather heterogeneous group. Some were illiterate men who had emerged from banditry to impose their law only on a few dozen villages. Others had an elite background, graduates of the most prestigious military academies and in control of several provinces. Much has been written on China’s warlords. Past scholarship has shed light on the complexities of their personalities and actions. Their alleged backwardness is largely a product of narratives promoted by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the Guomindang, which insisted in seeing them as obstacles on the road toward a unified, modern and powerful China. Warlords should not be seen as reactionary figures antagonist to the deep changes taking place. On the contrary, they were part and parcel of the process of cultural and social modernization taking place in the Republican era.

papers.title: Words shape characters: a case study of correspondence analysis on characters’ words in The Tale of Genji
papers.abstract: Abstract The words produced by characters play a pivotal role in the narrative. They serve not only to elucidate the thoughts and feelings of characters but also to help understand gender ideology and social norms. This article examines emotive adjectives produced by the characters in The Tale of Genji, the oldest extant Japanese novel, exploring how they are used among the characters, particularly between genders as well as different social groups. In this study, we employ a quantitative method known as correspondence analysis, which is enabled by the recent release of the speaker information for the tale by the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics. The resulting correspondence plot that we obtain from analysis indicates that gender, as well as social groups, influence the linguistic choices made in expressing emotions and feelings. In addition, we find that the differences in the use of the emotive adjectives correspond to gender norms embodied in the short poems included in The Kokin Wakashuu, the first imperial anthology of poetry. This article thus presents a case study that illustrates how quantitative analysis can contribute to not only gaining insights into understanding the language in that time but also how word choices contribute to creating characters.

papers.title: Nina S. Studer. The Hour of Absinthe: A Cultural History of France’s Most Notorious Drink .
papers.abstract: Nina S. Studer’s book The Hour of Absinthe: A Cultural History of France’s Most Notorious Drink is a welcome and much-needed addition to the growing field of alcohol history. Studer tracks meticulously the social, cultural, and political ramifications of absinthe, starting from debates about its uncertain origins in the late eighteenth century and ending with an exploration of early twentieth-century bans. What Studer describes as “perhaps the most demonized drink in the world” (6) has yet to be given such holistic diligence in scholarly research until now. The book incorporates a wide range of primary source material, including newspapers, cultural texts, travel accounts, and psychiatric theses. Studer also engages frequently with existing scholarship, and it is evident how earlier research has informed this book. The book’s title arguably undersells its ambitious scope and downplays Studer’s most significant contribution to scholarship: absinthe drinking in French colonies, namely Algeria. The way that Studer interweaves the colonial context into this in-depth study of absinthe’s history is cogent and well versed. Such context is not included simply as a necessary nod to France’s past, as it sometimes has been in French historical scholarship. Instead, the colonization of North Africa by France is integral to understanding the history of absinthe. Studer compares colonial and metropolitan perspectives throughout, drawing important conclusions about attitudes toward absinthe. Notably, the dangers of absinthe in colonial contexts “predate the metropolitan focus on the dangers of alcohol” (171). After reading Studer’s book, I find it easy to agree with the introduction’s assertion that “the history of absinthe and the history of French imperialism are indivisible” (10). Class and gender are more familiar themes relating to absinthe, but both are entwined seamlessly throughout the book and appear as the primary themes of chapters 3, 4, and 5.

papers.title: Tanja Petrović. Utopia of the Uniform: Affective Afterlives of the Yugoslav People’s Army
papers.abstract: After more than a decade of thinking about and writing about memory, nostalgia, and afterlives in Yugoslavia, Tanja Petrović, the director of the Institute of Culture and Memory Studies of the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts, poignantly narrates how men who served in the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) experienced, perceived, and remembered their mandatory military service. The author interviewed over forty men, many of whom served in the 1970s and 1980s; paged through photographs and memory books; and visited online forums for former JNA conscripts. From these sources, Petrović recounts how the pre-1991 JNA trained young civilians to be soldiers. More importantly, she argues that given the peacetime conditions of socialist Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav military inculcated the Yugoslav state’s concepts of “brotherhood and unity” and comradeship, designed to build solidarities across ethnic and class divisions. The book’s first section approaches understanding socialism through “forms of life”—the repetitive, performative, and ritualized forms associated with mandatory military service. Petrović details how the JNA used the military base (a “barbed-wire compound” [53]), military routine, drill, uniforms, and rituals as ways of feeling, connecting with, expressing, and enacting socialist ideology. The uniform and its cap, adorned with the five-pointed star shaded with red, white, and blue and conceived during the World War II partisan struggle, symbolized the promise of an egalitarian community where difference—ethnicity, nation, class, and religion—did not matter. Through the “utopia of the uniform” and forms of life, a Yugoslav socialist identity emerged.

papers.title: Bodies, Tides, Timber, and the Global History of London’s Docks, 1860–1928
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines changes in the bodies and environment of labourers carrying timber imported into London’s docks in the 1860s to the 1920s to provide a history of global capitalism from the ground up. Moving between London and Sweden, it shows how microphysical alterations in the skeletons of dockers, the wood they carried, and rivers in both countries materialized and modified macro-level changes in tides, forestry, and shipping. Repurposing the concept ‘lines of force’ from nineteenth-century physics, the article argues that lines — material, temporal, and spatial — reveal hidden relations between bodies and environments. Lines etched into bones or running through wood grain show how humans and other-than-humans were exposed to one another across varying distances, and how this exposure became accentuated under industrial capitalism. Second, they show how this mutual exposure operated over multiple timescales, from a worker’s lifetime to century-long modifications in tree growth and river flows. Finally, such lines reveal how ‘the world’ was not simply a space which steamships crossed, but a predicament, unique to and made by the relationships that living beings had with one another.

papers.title: Charles G. Thomas. Ujamaa’s Army: The Creation and Evolution of the Tanzania People’s Defence Force, 1964–1979
papers.abstract: Charles Thomas’s book Ujamaa’s Army is a welcome addition to the history of East African military structures while also providing a necessary insight into the construction and formation of one of the more successful military institutions to emerge in the postcolonial era. Laser focused on the formation and reforms of the Tanzania People’s Defence Force (TPDF) from 1964 to 1978, Thomas illustrates the transformation of the TPDF from a small colonial infantry force to an effective modern military, all while being a part of Julius Nyerere’s vision of a “People’s Army” embedded within the social, cultural, and political life of the Tanzanian nation. And while Thomas admits the “TPDF proved to be an exceptional case,” its story helps illustrate the “extraordinary complexity involved in negotiating and balancing … postcolonial transitions” in this period of African history (5, 11). Hopefully, readers who have picked up this volume will already be aware of the general history that culminated in Nyerere and TANU’s victory and the achievement of uhuru (true self-government) in the early 1960s. However, Thomas makes a concerted effort from the outset to provide necessary historical background that helps place the TPDF in this environment of enormous change. After this moment, Nyerere sought “a Pan-African solution to his security dilemma” that would reflect the new nationalist vision of the new republic (45). How fitting that the first one thousand new soldiers of the TPDF were marched out at the same time as the announcement of the United Republic of Tanzania in September 1964. Subsequent chapters follow this moment and address topics ranging from questions of vision, manpower, training, and relationship with the state from 1964 to 1968, to the increased politicalization of the military, which drove the TPDF to prove themselves on the battlefield, eventually culminating in the climax of the book, the Kagera (or Uganda-Tanzania) War of 1979.

papers.title: Trish Kahle. Energy Citizenship: Coal and Democracy in the American Century .
papers.abstract: If you wanted to mark the peak of American coal, you could choose one of two very different points. Around 1920, coal provided roughly two-thirds of all American energy, and per capita use of the fuel was higher than at any point before or since. But if you instead wanted to use the peak of total coal use—the date when the largest total amount of coal was mined and burned—you would have to go all the way forward to 2005. Between these two dates was a long history of adaptation, changing supply lines, and a wild transformation in use patterns that is obscured by the more common framing of American history as a shift from a nineteenth-century “age of coal” to a twentieth-century “age of oil.” Instead, the story of American coal is one of a shift from a hegemonic fuel to coal as one of a mix of fuels, each matched to a particular purpose in the American economy.

papers.title: Stacy D. Fahrenthold. Unmentionables: Textiles, Garment Work, and the Syrian American Working Class
papers.abstract: Who are the unmentionables of American history? Taking the “unmentionable” undergarment as a metaphor, Stacy Fahrenthold leads the reader on a journey through the histories of Syrian migrants, the unmentioned people who were key to textile production in and for the US in the early 1900s. This journey stretches from Lowell to Madeira and from New York to Syria. It takes place in different scales, zooming in on the papers of an undocumented migrant on the Mexican border or the conditions on shop floors in New York, and zooming out to transformations in the global commodity chains that crossed the Atlantic. Most importantly, the story of the unmentionables powerfully demonstrates the intersectionality of race, gender, and class, as its protagonists—all Syrian migrants but from different walks of life—navigate new lands, borders, businesses, and material conditions. The history of the hundreds of thousands of Syrian migrants in the Americas, the mahjar, intervenes in different historiographies. It is a criticism of the history of the US working class, which rendered early twentieth-century Syrian migrant workers invisible, despite their participation in various labor movements alongside their white European coworkers. It is a criticism of the histories of the American–Syrian communities, too, which deified businessmen and free-spirited peddlers as champions of their successful migrant communities, while women and child workers, upon whose labor entire chains of production depended, remained unmentionable. This was a deliberate choice: their labor was not visible, as it was organized at home as much as on the factory floors. Labor politics was carried on through “Syrian spaces” (20) such as community organizations and under the leadership of Syrian migrants from the professional classes. Union membership and working-class leadership remained limited. In the face of these omissions, Fahrenthold provides us an immensely rich and multilayered, hitherto untold story of “collective action, strategic invisibility, effacement of origins, and a struggle between labor and capital that occurred within an ethnic community” (197). The book offers promising, but yet untrod paths for the study of many such migrant groups, from the Middle East to the mahjar.

Collusion was assumed among pornographers, financiers, politicians, and the justice system, and the career paths of certain louche publishers (such as Victor Vidal, who had numerous connections with the financial and political elite) did lend some plausibility to these theories.

papers.title: Assef Ashraf. Making and Remaking Empire in Early Qajar Iran
papers.abstract: In the early nineteenth century, as the Near East was turning into the theater of the Great Game, the Qajar tribe, who descended from the Qizilbash confederacy of the Safavid military, rose to power in Iran. Russian expansionism brought war to the newly established Qajar Dynasty, and after facing defeat by Russia, the Qajars conceded some of their prized territories in the Caucasus and paid hefty indemnities to their northern neighbor. Meanwhile, as the British strengthened their foothold in India and the Persian Gulf, they turned into notable adversaries of the Qajars. Napoleon also had some interest in Iran as he envisioned a plan to approach India via Iranian territories. Few studies focus on the Qajar Dynasty in the opening decades of the nineteenth century without prioritizing how the Great Game unfolded within and beyond Iranian borders or examining how the Qajars’ political inefficacy and military setbacks started the process of modernization, which presumably led to the Constitutional Revolution (1901–1911) in Iran. Current works predominantly use modernization theories, focusing on the state and the elite, the interplay between the state and the Shiʿa ulema, or the political relations between the Qajars and Europeans. Especially after the Iranian Revolution of 1979, many scholars became interested in the roots of revolution and modernization in Iran. In Making and Remaking Empire in Early Qajar Iran, Assef Ashraf avoids modernization, Marxist, and postmodernist theories. Instead, he focuses on early nineteenth-century Iranian history by prioritizing what the historical actors did in their own historical time without expecting revolutions and modernization in the long run. Ashraf examines the “practices, customs, and relationships” that helped the Qajars consolidate their political power and remake a tributary empire after the fashion of the Safavids (296). Drawing on an impressive array of Persian, English, French, Russian, and Arabic published sources, as well as unpublished and archival documents in Iran, England, Russia, and Türkiye, Ashraf adopts an innovative sociological and anthropological approach that complements existing political histories in the study of early nineteenth-century Iran.
