papers.title: Walter Scheidel. What Is Ancient History?
papers.abstract: How do you solve a problem like classics? In What is Ancient History, Walter Scheidel sees the problems of how (American) universities and academics define and approach ancient history as an outgrowth of the deeper rot at the heart of the tree; namely, the persistent existence of a field known as classics and of departments still dedicated, regardless of what they call themselves, to its traditional study. Today, Scheidel argues, Greco-Roman history (a wholly artificial construct) still functions as a synecdoche for ancient history, and that status is problematic not only for political reasons but also because it is a misdirect for those interested in asking how our collective humankind made its first major leaps. For Scheidel, ancient history is a “foundational phase of human development in which the earliest versions of our current lifeways were created, consolidated, and locked in” (6). “Ancient” does not in all cases gesture to the same time period; rather, it signifies a “phase of development” that took place at different moments in different places. It was this phase that gave us the versions of “hardware” we still run on today, when agriculture, cities, government, information systems, and infrastructure, money, text production, etc. emerged. Crucially, these kinds of things have been shown to develop and evolve as “bundles” in relation to each other. Since then, the rest has just been elaboration and tweaking, which is why global “ancient history” should be of such interest. It “set the scene” for everything since.
topics: Globalization, Historical Perspectives, and International Relations

papers.title: Patrick Spero. The Scientist Turned Spy: André Michaux, Thomas Jefferson, and the Conspiracy of 1793.
papers.abstract: In The Scientist Turned Spy: André Michaux, Thomas Jefferson, and the Conspiracy of 1793, Patrick Spero explores a fascinating chapter in the new nation’s history, one in which borderlands, alliances, emerging national identities, and America’s future in the West were all contested. Key to sorting out many of these issues was botanical and geographical discovery. Into the fray came André Michaux, a French émigré who came to the United States at the behest of Louis XVI to identify New World plants helpful to the French economy. Michaux remained in America for more than a decade studying, exploring, and organizing botanical collections and gardens. Though besotted by America’s rich landscape, Michaux remained loyal to France. In 1793, Michaux was engaged by the American Philosophical Society (APS) to conduct a broad botanical survey of the West, but the survey never started because Michaux fell in with Edmond-Charles Genêt, roguish diplomat of France’s Revolutionary government, who sought to raise a fighting unit of discontented western American settlers, chiefly Kentuckians, to assert French claims over critical strategic points of Spanish Louisiana, including New Orleans. Michaux chose to help. Spero demonstrates that this plot was more than a pipe dream for Genêt. There was broad general discontent among western settlers, who were short on pathways to prosperity (chiefly Spanish restrictions on navigating the Mississippi) and long on knowledge of rifles and small artillery. George Rogers Clark, the one-time Patriot officer, was also short on patience and long on enthusiasm for Genêt’s plan, even if it meant becoming a French citizen. Spero shows he was not alone. Prominent frontiersmen, even those in leadership positions in the new republic, embraced the perceived virtues of this scheme.

papers.title: Kellie Carter Jackson. We Refuse: A Forceful History of Black Resistance
papers.abstract: At various points every semester that I teach the African American History survey, students and I discuss resistance within the African American experience. Somewhere around the middle of the semester, our discussions lead us to nonviolence versus armed resistance as strategies in the Black freedom struggle.We discuss Martin Luther King Jr.’s call for nonviolence versus Malcolm X’s “by any means necessary” approach. Alongside my efforts to nuance these appraoches, students often debate the effectiveness of each strategy and sometimes think aloud about which one they would have embraced. Some also question why one strategy seems privileged over another. Kellie Carter Jackson’s rich new text We Refuse: A Forceful History of Black Resistance takes up these very questions. Through conversational prose, moving personal vignettes, and a collection of rich historical moments, Jackson joins scholars of Black resistance and armed self-defense to further complicate historiographical conversations about what resistance has historically looked like. As scholars have illustrated, resistance has never been static. Nor can it be measured in wins or losses. Black people have persistently and consistently deployed a range of strategies to protest and resist racism and all other forms of oppression. While the beautiful cover art for We Refuse, which pictures a Black woman holding a shotgun, might conjure up visions of a book solely about armed defense, Jackson’s goal is more expansive. The author’s concerns lie in politically motivated efforts to place nonviolence and violence on opposite ends of a moral spectrum and the impact of this binary on activists, contemporary resistance efforts, and understandings of the past. To combat this, Jackson portrays resistance as a range of individual and collective decisions and actions made by Black people across time and space to defend their humanity. In We Refuse, Jackson sees the violence that accompanies white supremacy as an ecosystem. The concept of refusal—or the moments where individual actors and whole communities refuse “dehumanization, theft, lies, mockery, second-class citizenship,” and anything else of the like—is how Black people navigate and survive that ecosystem (7). Challenging binaries further, We Refuse largely centers Black women’s efforts in order to disrupt any idea that resistance or the use of force is an expressly masculine endeavor.

papers.title: Alasdair C. Grant. Greek Captives and Mediterranean Slavery, 1260–1460
papers.abstract: Greek Captives and Mediterranean Slavery is the first comprehensive study of the captivity and enslavement of Greeks in the late medieval period. Why were Greeks captured and enslaved? Where did this happen and by whom? Where were these captives taken? What do we know about their experiences of captivity and slavery? What was the impact of captivity for the Greek Christian population in the Mediterranean? These are a few of the basic research questions that are examined in detail for the period from c. mid-thirteenth century to mid- –fifteenth century. But that is not all. What makes the book extremely fascinating is, first, the rich, comparative—and up to now unexplored—material, consisting of literary and documentary texts mostly in Greek and Latin but also in western European vernaculars, Arabic and Turkish, which cover a remarkably broad geographical area (from the Aegean to Egypt and from Cyprus to Catalonia). Second is the author’s approach, which combines empirical and social-historical elements. The author does not limit himself to a strict presentation of captivity and slavery of Greeks within this period, but he examines, for example, the impact that this situation had on wider relations between Greeks, Latins, and Turks, or the role that the Church played in the redemption of captives and slaves. The aim of the book is “to establish the causation, chronology, geographical reach, demographic impact and cultural significance of the crisis of captivity” (5). This all-around treatment of the subject makes this book valuable to a broad range of scholars who are interested in social, cultural, demographic, and political structures and influences in Byzantine, Crusader, Western Medieval, and Ottoman Studies.

papers.title: Edward Anthony Polanco. Healing Like Our Ancestors: The Nahua Tiçitl, Gender, and Settler Colonialism in Central Mexico, 1535–1660
papers.abstract: In this relatively new century with its curious social and political winds, Edward Anthony Polanco’s study Healing Like Our Ancestors is wonderfully direct in insisting that scholars can, and must, decolonize Indigenous histories, now. We have the means and the knowledge, he argues, and we know that our sources are flawed, skewed, and in need of reading not just against the grain in the ethnohistorical sense, but against the grain of multiple layers of unhelpful obfuscations that hide how Indigenous peoples lived their lives before and after the introduction of settler colonialism to the New Worlds of the Americas. As Polanco explains, healers worked before and during the first era of Spain’s conquests of Mexico and El Salvador, and points in between, on their own terms, but later operated under the unwanted gaze of colonial authorities who attempted to change the language and meanings of their work. Polanco insists, rightly, that too many lenses sit between the era he studies and the present, and everywhere, in so many ways, colonization thrives in the present: ways of naming, systems of knowledge, and profit made from that knowledge when it comes to the Nahua and Nawat pasts. This book does not suggest that we decolonize just the past. It actively decolonizes Indigenous knowledge while using the same sources that so many have used to understand a colonized past.

papers.title: Meredith L. McCoy. On Our Own Terms: Indigenous Histories of School Funding and Policy
papers.abstract: In the past forty years, historians have published a relatively large number of books and articles on the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century experiences of Indigenous peoples in the federal boarding schools. From there, McCoy adeptly moves on to discussions of the various settler colonial impositions, from religious mission schools to government boarding schools. But, as alluded to above, she does not stop there. Most of the rest of the book examines Native experiences with federal legislation in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, from the Johnson-O’Malley Act of the 1930s, into the landmark policies of the 1960s and 1970s, and culminating with a look at the No Child Left Behind Act and the Every Student Succeeds Act of the 2000s and 2010s, respectively. Throughout, the book’s view is not only expansive in terms of time but also geography. The northern plains get special attention, but there are also examples from as far west as Hawai’i to as far east as the Mohegans of Connecticut.

papers.title: Hunter Price. Sacred Capital: Methodism and Settler Colonialism in the Empire of Liberty
papers.abstract: Hunter Price’s Sacred Capital: Methodism and Settler Colonialism in the Empire of Liberty is the best book on the history of early American Methodism in nearly two decades. It offers a fresh reading of well-trod sources and new insights into the histories of religion, social networks, and westward expansion in the nineteenth-century United States. Methodism, Price convincingly shows, was a key player in the settler colonialism that expanded North America’s western frontier. In advancing this argument, Price hearkens back to the work of church historians like William Warren Sweet in the mid-twentieth century, borrowing from him and his contemporaries the conviction that the story of early American Methodism is intimately connected to the “chaos” of the western frontier and attempts to “bring order” to it. In contrast to Sweet, however, Price turns a critical eye to the memoirs, journals, and letters left behind by Methodist preachers, arguing that circuit riders were “much less self-sacrificing than historians have assumed and a fair amount more self-serving” (2). To make this argument, Price looks to recent work on settler colonialism, noting that Methodism’s itinerant preachers and lay migrants alike were key participants in the process. In this telling, “the Methodist Age and the Empire of Liberty converged.” He is careful to point out that Methodists were not often directly involved in “Indian removal, ethnic cleansing, or genocide.” Rather, Methodist networks were “easily adapted to core settler concerns,” including “land, work, marriage, [and] money.” Methodism thus “contributed institutionally to the phases of stabilizing and developing settler communities” (3–5).

papers.title: Robert L. Nelson. Frontiers of Empire: Max Sering, Inner Colonization, and the German East, 1871–1945
papers.abstract: Max Sering, professor at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin from 1889 to 1925, was one of the leading agrarian economists of his time, and he had both the ambition and the ability to influence politics. It is thus surprising that it took so long for an intellectual biography of Sering to appear, and it is at the same time fortunate that Robert L. Nelson is the author of the inspiring one at hand. Through the lens of Max Sering’s academic and political career, Nelson’s Frontiers of Empire follows the trajectory of Germany’s settlement policies in the so-called German East, from their inception with the establishment of the Royal Prussian Settlement Commission for Posen and West Prussia in the 1880s, through the settlement projects pursued in German-occupied Baltic territories during the First World War, to their genocidal culmination in the Nazis’ lebensraum politics during the Second World War. Nelson offers neither a simple linear story nor a purely German story. He presents Max Sering as an internationally renowned agrarian economist and expert of settler colonialism, who developed his fundamental convictions as to what kind of agrarian policy Germany ought to pursue during a research trip to Canada and the United States in 1883—“the journey of a lifetime,” as Nelson calls it (41). The trip turned Sering into an admirer of the United States and convinced him that North America was the model that Germany should follow. Like many of his colleagues among the so-called kathedersozialisten, or “Socialists of the Chair,” Sering did not oppose capitalism, industrialization, and urbanization per se, but he was convinced that an industrial nation also needed agriculture to avoid becoming dependent on food imports, to slow down the migration from the countryside to the city, and to ensure that farming families would continue to produce the healthy young soldiers a great power like Germany required. In addition, Sering feared the creeping Polonization of Germany’s eastern provinces if the government did not implement a program of “inner colonization.” This consisted of breaking up large aristocratic land estates and transforming them into the kind of midsize homesteads of North America.

papers.title: Christopher Stedman Parmenter. Racialized Commodities: Long-distance Trade, Mobility, and the Making of Race in Ancient Greece, c. 700–300 BCE
papers.abstract: This excellent monograph marshals an impressive range of evidence to investigate the “processes by which ancient Greeks came to ascribe meaning to human diversity” (2). Racialized Commodities joins recent contributions to the history and historiography of race that argue that the concept can be fruitfully applied to describe the thinking and realities of premodern societies, long before its most well-known iteration in the context of Atlantic modernity. It does so in an innovative way and at an opportune moment in the study of long-distance trade in the ancient Mediterranean, applying the model of commodity biography, which traces the “life story” and cultural impact of goods as they move across different (and often disconnected) contexts and people. Following WWII, classicists rejected race as a framework for understanding Greek conceptions of appearance and culture, replacing it with “ethnicity.” Yet, “ethnicity was transferred many of the same meanings that race held prior to the war” (9). Although recent non-essentialist approaches to ethnicity have yielded results, the concept fails to capture the power dynamics embedded in emic descriptions of outgroups. Here, Parmenter argues, race proves a more effective analytical tool. The book contends that long-distance trade routes, and the commodities that circulated along them, helped shape Greek ideas of blackness and whiteness, and that these ideas were used instrumentally to rationalize aspects of status as well as structures of economic exchange and exploitation. As a result, blackness became associated with the prestige of Egypt’s Saite Kingdom while whiteness was linked with the enslaveable nomads of the Black Sea.

papers.title: Timothy Brook. The Price of Collapse: The Little Ice Age and the Fall of Ming China
papers.abstract: Timothy Brook’s book The Price of Collapse is a significant and thought-provoking contribution to climate history, price history, and global history. At its core, the book revisits a long-debated question with new methodological tools: why did the Ming Empire (1368–1644) fall? Drawing on the quantifiable evidence of grain prices, paleoclimatic reconstructions, and shifts in global economic flows, Brook, a pioneering historian for situating early modern China in a global context, argues that the onset and intensification of the Little Ice Age played a triggering role in driving the Ming toward collapse. Brook brings to life a wide range of historical actors, ranging from emperors and officials to Jesuit missionaries, Buddhist monks, art collectors, and gazetteer writers. Chapter 1 introduces the late Ming crisis through the eyes of a local schoolteacher, Chen Qide, who witnessed it firsthand. Chapter 2 assesses the cost of necessities and standards of living in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Chapter 3 challenges the traditional explanation that an influx of New World silver caused a “price revolution” of high inflation. Brook maintains that the available price data does not support that conclusion, except in the luxury goods market. Chapters 4 and 5 offer his alternative interpretation: a sudden and dramatic grain price spike under the Chongzhen Emperor (1627–1644) coincided with the peak environmental volatility of the Little Ice Age in the mid-1600s.

papers.title: Christa Dierksheide. Beyond Jefferson: The Hemingses, the Randolphs, and the Making of Nineteenth-Century America .
papers.abstract: As a founding father, public servant, and political theorist, Thomas Jefferson’s impact on US history has long been the subject of discussion by scholars. Likewise, his personal life has attracted significant attention for embodying the grim realities of American slavery and freedom. Yet, rarely are these two worlds brought together to consider how the legacy of Jefferson’s family reflected and contributed to the complex realities of the nineteenth century. Christa Dierksheide’s engaging family biography, Beyond Jefferson: The Hemingses, the Randolphs, and the Making of Nineteenth-Century America, takes on that task by tracing the paths of Jefferson’s Black and white lineages to tell a deeply intimate account of the multiple histories of the United States. As she successfully demonstrates, Jefferson’s influence on early America was not simply political and intellectual but also personal and material through the actions of his descendants. For both branches of the Jefferson family tree, the patriarch’s death precipitated dramatic transformations. On the Hemings side, two of his four surviving children with Sally were manumitted in his will; Jefferson freed the other two several years prior. Freedom was thus hard earned, and neither the children nor Sally—who was herself never formally manumitted—had any substantial support from Jefferson’s estate after his death. This made life quite difficult for the Hemingses, not only due to financial limitations but also because of the challenges of navigating the color line in antebellum America. The children born from Jefferson’s marriage to Martha were also rocked by their father’s passing. The former president was in such terrible debt that many of his enslaved laborers were sold off, and eventually so too was the Monticello plantation. Desperate to recoup the family’s wealth and status, Jefferson’s white descendants undertook risky business endeavors that carried them across the world and into some of the most important geopolitical conflicts of the nineteenth century.

papers.title: Mapping the intersection of digital technologies and humanities: a multidisciplinary scoping review of the digital humanities movement in Thailand
papers.abstract: Abstract Although digital humanities (DH) lacks a universally accepted definition, its boundaries are often shaped by local contexts and cultural factors. In Thailand, no formal DH programs exist, and only a few publications explicitly address the term “digital humanities”. At the same time, it is speculated that works considered as DH research have been sporadically produced. To gain a nuanced understanding of the Thai DH landscape, this study conducted a scoping review of scholarly works published between 2010 and 2019, using broad operational definitions and frameworks, and integrating quantitative and qualitative analyses. We identified a wide range of publications, frequently anchored in computer science and related fields, yet also involving humanities scholars and emerging “born-digital” disciplines. Many works focus on applying or developing digital tools, while relatively few emphasize long-term data stewardship or critical humanities-oriented methods. Patterns of collaboration remain mostly within or across departments, and conference proceedings dominate as publication venues, reflecting scholarly communication practices of Thai DH scholars. These findings suggest that a DH movement exists in Thailand without formal institutionalization or a cohesive community. By mapping the field’s scope and boundaries before the widespread adoption of generative AI, this study provides baseline evidence that can inform future strategies, encourage interdisciplinary dialogue, and situate Thai DH research within a broader international context.

papers.title: The Utopia within Utopia (1516)
papers.abstract: Abstract The debate between Hythlodaeus and an English lawyer before Cardinal Morton in Book One of Utopia (1516) contains many proposals for socio-economic reforms. These have typically been interpreted as innovative proposals to counteract the corruption of Christendom which surrounds them. However, when placed into their legislative context, it is apparent not only that these reforms echo closely many socio-economic reforms passed in England in the decades preceding Utopia , but that corollaries for almost all of them were passed when Morton, in whose presence the debate took place, was lord chancellor. Recognizing this forces a reassessment of this debate, showing Hythlodaeus’s flaws, and reframing the contribution of the English lawyer. This very reassessment, however, realigns the entire dialogue before Cardinal Morton, which it is possible to identify as a mirror to the wider text. It is a Utopia within Utopia , or, a mise en abyme . By closing examining the reflection, it appears that this provides a structural indication of how Utopia should be read.

papers.title: Michelle Lynn Kahn. Foreign in Two Homelands: Racism, Return Migration, and Turkish–German Histor y
papers.abstract: With this engaging first monograph, Michelle Lynn Kahn delivers transnational history at its most insightful. Foreign in Two Homelands centers on return migration, broadly defined to include cross-border flows of remittances, goods, discourses, images, and people. At its core, the book offers a long-overdue historicization of the migration wave triggered by the 1983 West German “Law for the Promotion of the Voluntary Return of Foreigners,” which encouraged so-called “guest workers” and their families to return to Turkey. In response, 250,000 Turkish citizens returned to their former homeland—“kicked out,” as Kahn puts it (9). Complementing studies that root Turkish–German history in German politics of identity, race, or gender, Foreign in Two Homelands argues that these return migrations—especially the often-alienated experiences of “returnees” in Turkey after 1983—were shaped by entangled, transnational dynamics. Two factors stand out in Kahn’s account. First is the racism—both everyday and structural—faced by migrants in West Germany, especially in the early 1980s. Second is a widespread belief in Turkey, dating to the early years of labor recruitment, that migrants had Germanized in behavior, consumption, and values, thus losing their Turkishness. For Kahn, this sense is captured in the term Almancı, translated here as “Germanized Turk” (5, 25). Commonly applied pejoratively to migrants in the Federal Republic in Turkish media and everyday discourse, Almancı implied they had become overly integrated. While German policy and public rejection of Turkish–German belonging rested on ideas of a biologically defined nation, this use of Almancı conveyed a commonsense belief in Germanness as acquired behavior and values. This meaning attached to Almancı surfaced in the condescending treatment Turkish Germans received from the Turkish state, in mocking portrayals in media, and in fraught interactions during visits or after return. For Kahn, being treated as Almancı complicated migrants’ belonging in Turkey, echoing the alienation caused by racism in West Germany. The result was a sense of betweenness. Through these meanings and their impact in both countries, Kahn shows that even Anatolian villagers who mocked visiting migrants as overly Germanized were actors in German history—shaping, from afar, “the contours of West German national identity” (317).

papers.title: TOWARD A CONJECTURAL HISTORY OF CONJECTURAL HISTORIES
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Most intellectual historians use the term “conjectural history” to designate a new form of speculative history created in eighteenth‐century Scotland by Adam Smith and a few others. These writers traced the development of human society and culture through conjectural reasoning based on philosophers’ views about human nature and travelers’ accounts of “primitive” peoples. Their work had a deep impact on eighteenth‐century philology: it helped to shape such original and influential studies of the ancient world as Edward Gibbon's history of the fall of Rome, Johann Joachim Winckelmann's history of the rise of ancient art, and Friedrich August Wolf's demonstration that Homer was an oral poet. But the connection between conjectural history and classical philology began long before any of the varied Enlightenments conjured up by modern scholars came into being. Conjectures about the past were deeply rooted in the central humanistic discipline, rhetoric; this gave Lorenzo Valla the tools for his conjectural refutation of the legend of the Donation of Constantine. But these same tools were plied with similar skill and originality by many other humanists, from Valla's contemporary in the Roman curia, Leon Battista Alberti, to the Jesuit historian of the New World, José de Acosta, a century later. And they saw them not as an innovation but as part of the philological and historical tradition in which they were grounded. Valla, for example, saw Thucydides—whose histories he translated into Latin—as a conjectural historian and thus identified conjecture as a central feature of historiography in the classical tradition.

papers.title: Fallen from Heaven: The Enduring Tradition of Europeans as Gods in the Americas. By Nicholas Griffiths
papers.abstract: Nicholas Griffiths has produced a synthesis of the various myths and fantasies about Native people thinking Europeans were gods. No spoiler alert needed here. Griffiths makes it clear that he is aware that ethnohistory and the “new conquest history” of the last thirty years has debunked the idea that Hawaiians thought Captain Cook was Lono or that the Mexica thought that Hernando Cortés was the return of Quetzalcoatl or that New Guinea highlanders thought that twentieth-century Europeans were gods from heaven. Few readers will find these conclusions surprising. So what does this book offer? Fallen from Heaven purports to offer a synthetic overview of the myriad ways that Native peoples of the Americas made sense of European invaders and explorers. In reality, though, the book synthesizes the debates that Europeans had about themselves being or not being gods. Such an approach has the strange effect of reifying the counter-point—that, no, Natives did not believe the Europeans were gods. Here is a good example. Captain Cook is famous for having made it to the Hawaiian Islands, where the Hawaiians did or did not think he was a temporary manifestation of the god Lono. Griffiths claims that Native Hawaiians may very well have continued to believe in some version of this story because the Mo’olelo Hawaii, published in 1838, repeats some of this belief (239). But the devil is in the details. Griffiths credits the Calvinist missionary, Sheldon Dibble, for authorship, but it was probably David Malo who composed this early history. Malo was a Christian convert who was under pressure to produce a version palatable to his Calvinist overlords.

papers.title: Dame Janet L. Nelson (28 March 1942 – 14 October 2024)
papers.abstract: Jinty Nelson left a strong mark of her presence in every institution that she was ever a part of, and there is none which does not regard its association with her as a source of deep pride. Past and Present is no exception. She was an immensely valued member of the Editorial Board for nearly twenty years, starting in 1995 and leaving in 2013, when she reached the mandatory retirement age of seventy. 1. Jinty Nelson c.2019 (Phil Fisk). Jinty studied at Newnham College, Cambridge, where she was a star student, made the University Challenge team, and later wrote her Ph.D. dissertation under the direction of Walter Ullmann.1 Ullmann did not approve of the way the thesis turned out, and their relationship was a fraught one, though it was eventually repaired. When discussing him later in life, she would sometimes quote what he had reportedly fumed to someone praising her work, after they were no longer on speaking terms: ‘Do not speak to me of that girl!’ (she emphasised ‘girl’, which is probably revealing, whether he had originally done so himself or not). At the root of their clashes was her evolving sense of a need to approach early medieval royal rituals as something other than the top-down communication of political ideas; to her they were also about negotiation, about meeting unspoken expectations. In this she was under the influence of anthropology, which at the time was a particularly active force in French medievalist academic circles, and was gaining ground in Britain among a younger generation of scholars, and a few older ones — even though, or perhaps because, it meant breaking out of some established patterns of thought. Despite this strong streak of intellectual independence from the start, it took her about a decade to really find her voice. In 1970 she was hired as a lecturer in the Department of History at King’s College London, where she would remain for the rest of her long and distinguished career. Six out of her first seven articles came out in Studies in Church History, the proceedings of the annual conferences of the Ecclesiastical History Society, to which she remained characteristically loyal throughout her career, publishing in it twelve times between 1971 and 1994. The sixth of these early articles, ‘On the Limits of the Carolingian Renaissance’ (1977), was her first classic, landmark article, and others followed hot on its heels over the next couple of years: ‘Kingship, Law and Liturgy in the Political Thought of Hincmar of Rheims’ (1977); ‘Inauguration Rituals’ (1977); and ‘Queens as Jezebels: The Careers of Brunhild and Balthild in Merovingian History’ (1978).2 The latter heralded a new aspect of her research, which would remain a stable feature from then on: women and gender — at this point still restricted to queens, but soon to branch out from there. During the 1980s and 1990s her strong and long-standing personal commitment to feminism became a more intrinsic part of her historical practice. She played a key role in setting up the Women’s History Seminar at the Institute of Historical Research in 1986. She was interested in engaging in dialogue across periods, but strongly resisted giving the early Middle Ages any special periodization job to do. She did not see it through rose-tinted glasses as a golden age for women, as many did who felt their duty lay in using the Middle Ages to show up modernity. She never lost sight of, nor took for granted, the deep seam of gender-based injustice running through the period she studied. But she did not dismiss the importance of women during it, nor discount the way some of them managed to leverage the small range of roles and privileges granted to them in this world of ‘little patriarchs’ in order to make their voices, their sense of their own rights, heard.3 As she showed in many articles, women were never simply not there; and accordingly, from this point until the end of her career, they would always form a part of any historical picture she put together. This was also, of course, a battle that still needed to be fought in the present: it took gumption then simply to demand to be taken seriously as an academic and an intellectual at the same time as being the mother of two small children. During these years, feminism, and a sense that the personal really was political, that the distinction between public and private was something that needed to be questioned, began to supply an increasingly crucial angle of approach for her historical work — and, unusually for the time, in relation not only to female subjects, but also to male ones. Two key male subjects for Jinty were Charles the Bald and Alfred, two ninth-century figures traditionally credited with the creation of (respectively) France and England. She roundly dismissed ahistorically nationalistic readings of their place in history, but without diminishing their role within it: rather than cutting them down to size, she cast them in a more realistic and a more interesting light — as makers of new political communities on more unfamiliar, contingent, and above all non-national terms. The culmination of this recurrent thread in her work was the series of addresses which she gave as President of the Royal Historical Society, in which she made connections and comparisons between England and the Continent in the ninth century in the broadest cultural as well as political, social, and economic terms.4 These lectures were given during a decade of professional triumphs. Between the 1990s and the mid-2000s she gained practically every accolade that it is possible to get as a member of the historical profession. In 1990 she joined the History Workshop Journal collective; in 1993 she became a professor at King’s; in 1993–4 she was President of the Ecclesiastical History Society; in 1995 she joined the Editorial Board of Past and Present; in 1996 she was elected a Fellow of the British Academy, serving as Vice President for Research from 1999 to 2001; she became the first female President of the Royal Historical Society in 2001; and in 2006 was awarded a DBE in recognition of her services to history. From the point of view of Past and Present, the 1990s were an important decade: it, and she, came not a moment too soon. In 1977, when Jinty’s first major article came out, Joan Thirsk had been the first and for the previous twenty years the only woman on the editorial board. In the late 1970s she was joined by Olwen Hufton and Judith Herrin, so the 1980s started strong, with three whole women on the board (and twenty men). At some point during the early 1980s, a daring proposition was made that perhaps a fourth woman might be asked to join the board, and that this might be Jinty. The suggestion was rejected, and there would in fact be a near ten-year gap before another woman did join (Joanna Innes, in 1988). Despite some significant renewal in membership, the editorial board remained quite strongly patriarchal in flavour and character, and a number of its members were yet to be convinced that women’s history or gender history were worthwhile pursuits. In view of this, it is not altogether surprising that the journal never became the natural home for gender history that one would wish, looking back, it had been able to become.5 The 1990s saw this atmosphere start to change. In 1990 the gender ratio had barely altered, with four women (non-administrative) editorial board members and twenty-two men; by 2000, there were nine women and sixteen men. Jinty, alongside the other women on the board at the time, was part of bringing about that important change in the character of the journal. At meetings she was an engaging and charming presence: someone with strong views about new directions the journal should take (not least on the need to encourage more articles by women and about women, family, gender, or masculinity), but by all accounts also someone one would always feel lucky to be sitting next to at lunch. Her reports on article submissions reflected her fierce standards, but she was immensely supportive and constructive wherever she saw potential. Two things happened during that era which I think had a big influence on Jinty’s practice as a historian: one was a professional caesura, when she started to assume those various positions of genuine influence in academic leadership; and the other in her life cycle, when she first became a grandmother in 2000. The latter led her, at this most busy time of her professional life, to scale back, and to turn Thursdays into inviolable, work-free ‘Granny days’.6 These two concurrent and major developments in her life — grandmotherhood and academic leadership — pulled against each other, if only in competing for her time; and together, of course, pulled against her own research time. But they both also seem to me to have enriched her historical practice profoundly. 2. Jinty’s staff page photograph: on a ‘Granny Day’ with grandson Eli, c.2002. The ease with which she made friends, and her ability to feel genuine admiration and respect for people with quite different values from her own, translated, in more official settings, into real political skill. As she experienced academic leadership there was a subtle change — not, I think, coincidentally — in the way she thought about Carolingian government. Her early years as a historian had been spent fighting back against a top-down reading of history, where kings, states, and governments were the ones that got their way and made things happen. She wrote about the limits to their ambitions, about the distance between their aspirations and the reality of their power; she was sceptical about the ‘Carolingian Renaissance’ and the ability of kings to force through change. In time, though, she became more attentive and more sympathetic to the sheer act of striving; and she laid ever greater emphasis on, and appreciation for, working towards a common purpose, of reform being not a test of royal power, but something that was brought closer to reality through the work of many people, lay and ecclesiastical. Her attention to the individuality of historical actors, strong from the beginning, had always led her to question the power of abstract ideas on their own to effect change, and to focus more on individuals’ own sense of their place in the world and the work they had to do in it. At first this led her to stress their scope for resistance. By the time of her later writings, though, she had come to see the part that these same individuals, with complicated personal histories and entanglements, could play in building something lasting: in establishing values and building institutions and communities, even in the face of ineffectiveness and defeat. This will likely chime with many readers’ experience of academic life in the UK and elsewhere, and this growing emphasis in her work went hand in hand with the process of learning to wield power herself within that world (in a way that was surely even more limited than that of the Carolingians). Grandmotherhood enriched her work in other ways. Her treatment of people became richer and more intimate: she started listening out for the ‘voice of Charlemagne’ in his legislation, and stressed the importance of family and how it was experienced, especially calling attention to the importance of small children within it — what she once called la politique de la crèche. Her last book included a memorable discussion of a story about Charlemagne losing his first milk tooth.7 These developments all leaned towards the highly personal, but were not reductive: they were intended to enrich her subjects, to open them up, to show how the conditions and structures of personal intimacy interacted with ideas about the self, about power and about the right order of things, but also about its disruption, in other areas — all of which came together in a genuinely embodied history of political ideas. Situating Charlemagne within that context is one of the major achievements of her biography of him, which was to be her last great work. It is symptomatic of her attention to individual experience that the only two books she wrote were biographies, of Charles the Bald (1992) and of Charlemagne (2019).8 Those were the projects that made her feel the need to expand beyond the length of a research article, which was otherwise her preferred format, and the one in which she made her mark.9 Even in this shorter form, she always turned her subjects, male or female, into real people: famous figures including Nithard and Dhuoda, but also obscure ones, such as Erkanfrida and Agintrude, who in someone else’s hands might have remained bit players but in hers were given a star turn.10 Curiously, almost none of these research articles came out in journals. Discounting Studies in Church History (every issue of which is more like an edited volume on a particular theme), you could count on the fingers of one hand the journal articles in her enormous bibliography: one in the English Historical Review, one in Speculum, one in Past and Present; that is pretty much it.11 She did contribute to journals, but mainly review articles, or short contributions to debates, or to special issues, or every now and then a published version of an annual lecture: in other words, she contributed to them principally in their capacity as a forum for exchange and debate. The overwhelming majority of her most important articles were published in the context of collective enterprises, in a wide range of edited collections published in many different countries. This was the context in which she most enjoyed working, and it reflects the breadth of her personal and intellectual connections. Forster’s ‘Only connect!’ was one of her favourite phrases, and she managed to live by it more than most. In her early career she had been combative and iconoclastic, but never a loner: she forged strong relationships, remembered and took to heart every personal fact and confidence, and was a fiercely loyal friend, who also made people feel loyal towards her. In the 1990s the Transformation of the Roman World project, funded by the European Science Foundation, helped to create a much denser and better-connected network of European scholars; she thrived in that setting. International connections in Europe and North America were important to her, and she to them. The collection The Medieval World which she published with Routledge in 2001, co-edited with Peter Linehan, was unusually broad in its outlook for the time — long before the global turn, when not many textbooks about the medieval ‘world’ had a chapter about Timbuktu — and it included contributions from academics working in North America, in the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and in Japan.12 She was interested in creating links with many different people, and was famously supportive of junior scholars in particular: she supervised no fewer than thirty-two Ph.D. students herself, but a great many more who were supervised by others found her to be just as unstinting in her attention.13 Visiting scholars often stayed at her house, and her kitchen table was a key intellectual magnet for early medievalists in London. These collective enterprises sometimes had a human focus rather than an intellectual one: some of her most field-defining articles, for instance, came out in Festschrifts, of which she co-edited quite a few herself.14 She edited papers and brought projects to completion for friends and colleagues who died prematurely.15 In historians and in historical subjects she was strongly preoccupied with recognizing the human beings behind the works, and not letting their contributions be forgotten. She was also extremely faithful to institutions: to King’s College London, to the Ecclesiastical History Society, to Past and Present, to History Workshop Journal, to the Institute of Historical Research in London. (Sometimes she was loyal to a fault, as in the case of her unswerving fidelity — to others unfathomable — to Pizza Paradiso, the little Italian restaurant on Store Street where the Earlier Middle Ages seminar felt duty-bound to go every Wednesday after the paper, until even her unconditional support proved unequal to the task of keeping it in business.) I was surprised, even a little bit shocked, to discover her rebellious streak in stories I heard about her youth, some of which she told me herself. Walter Ullmann, for instance, always smoked cigars during doctoral supervisions, which rather annoyed Jinty; one day, after they had sat down and he had taken out and lit his usual cigar, she took out and lit one of her own. (I like to remember she said it was a bigger cigar, though that may be wishful thinking rather than an actual memory: the point was made all the same.) papers.title: History Workshop: A South African Movement
papers.abstract: Abstract In its nearly 50 years of existence, the History Workshop at the University of the Witwatersrand (Johannesburg) has played an influential role in the development of social history and public history in South Africa. This article provides an overview of the collective’s contributions to the production of new, counter-hegemonic histories from the mid-1970s, when popular resistance against apartheid gained momentum, to the early years of the transition to democracy and the more recent period of deepening structural crises. It has negotiated these historical periods while attempting to maintain a commitment to researching and writing histories of and with subaltern groups.

papers.title: Historic Failures, Failures of History: ‘Necessitous Gentlewomen’ Reconsidered
papers.abstract: Abstract A chance encounter with the records of a local charity has re-opened the question of middle-class female poverty and dependence in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, in ways which seem to have been ignored by many historians. Studies on topics ranging from financial speculation to the expansion of education for women have often left unexplored the extent of middle-class precarity, and the wreckage left in the wake of the myth of the male ‘provider’. Can stories of inactivity, non-achievement and unheroic failure among ‘necessitous gentlewomen’ become subjects of serious and sustained research?

papers.title: Culture War: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis?
papers.abstract: Abstract Now ubiquitous in public debate, the term ‘culture war’ has become increasingly unmoored from models that were developed when the concept first shot to popularity in the specific context of the United States in the 1990s. This article retraces the conceptual history of culture war over the long term, questions some of the assumptions about the normal course of history and politics that are often implicit in its usage, and reflects on the place of the American paradigm in discussions of the subject. It argues that historians could adopt a more explicitly Gramscian perspective to develop a robust historical concept of culture war.

papers.title: “The Rooster Says There Is Life in Fear”
papers.abstract: Abstract As a Togolese refugee who grew up in exile, I have an intimate relationship with Togo’s political history that shapes the ways I conduct research and approach my analysis. In this paper, I examine an oral history interview I conducted with a retired textile merchant in 2022 to illustrate how Togolese people’s fears about speaking about the country’s past constitute a unique epistemological orientation. This understanding emerged from a critical examination of my own complicated relationship with the country’s history. As I show, it was through interrogating how my experiences as a refugee shape my relationship to my scholarship that I was better able to theorize about the regime’s terror and the open silences it has produced in Togolese people’s collective memory.

papers.title: Transnational Whiteness and the Elite Backlash to Reforming the Australian Immigration Control System in the 1950s and 1960s
papers.abstract: Abstract In the 1950s and 1960s, changes in the international situation, such as decolonization in Asia, led some Australians to question the usefulness of keeping the ‘White Australia Policy’, the basis for the country’s immigration system since Federation in 1901. Some argued that Australia’s international reputation, especially with newly independent countries in Asia and Africa, could be harmed by the maintenance of this policy. Events such as the Sharpeville Massacre in apartheid South Africa in 1960 caused further introspection into Australia’s racialized system. However, as pushes to reform the policy grew, others used international events to resist reforms. Using speeches by politicians and documents produced by policymakers, this article will show how events, such as the Notting Hill riots in Britain, the Little Rock controversy in the United States, and the Sharpeville massacre, were used as warnings about Australia potentially introducing similar ‘racial problems’ if it allowed more non-white migration. This article argues that these concerns tapped into a transnational whiteness that shared anxieties about decolonization, civil rights and non-white immigration in the post-war period, bringing a racialized solidarity forged at the turn of the twentieth century into the Cold War era.

papers.title: A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to Public Black HBCUs. By Crystal R. Sanders
papers.abstract: In A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to Public Black HBCUs, Crystal Sanders presents a compelling study of the intersections between segregation and the development or underdevelopment of graduate and professional school opportunities for African Americans and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). She incorporates suggestive vocabulary like “intellectual warfare” to depict the determination of civil rights lawyers like Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall, and the courage of African American test plaintiffs like Lloyd Gaines, Ada Sipuel, and George McLaurin, who legally dismantled the focus of her book—segregation scholarships. The term “segregation scholarships” echoes the definitive ideological themes like slavery as a “peculiar institution” and Jim Crow having a “strange career.” Southern and border state governments defended their racially discriminatory decision to allocate significant funds for sending Black citizens out of state, primarily to the North, for graduate degrees by citing the United States Supreme Court’s 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson, which established the “separate but equal” doctrine. However, in 1938, the Gaines v. Canada Supreme Court case stipulated that “separate but equal” meant either admitting African Americans into white, in-state public graduate schools or establishing and funding a “separate but equal” graduate program for African American students within the state, often at a Negro college. Sanders’ book highlighted enforcement challenges, as states ignored the Gaines v. Canada ruling and continued to offer segregation scholarships, along with significantly inferior funding for graduate programs at HBCUs, leading to a wave of litigation. Ironically, in 1921, Walthall M. Moore, the first African American to serve in the Missouri General Assembly, introduced the original legislation for segregation scholarships as an attempt to help Black’s attain higher education. As noted in Sanders’ central contention that “the burdens Black southerners withstood in the quest for advanced study functioned as a double tax levied on account of racism,” meaning African Americans contributed taxwise to funding state and federal education but due to anti-Black racism were illegally penalized for attempting to access that same educational system, particularly on the graduate level (7).

papers.title: Three rings, one story? Reconstructing the Historical Connectivity of Religious Encounters within the OTRA Project (Ontology for the Transmission and Re-Use of Argumentative Patterns)
papers.abstract: Throughout history, Islam has posed a challenge to Christians. Theologically, the Qur’an was interpreted as superseding the Gospel. Politically, Muslim territorial expansion resulted in military conflict. Theological interactions were marked by fierce polemics (Daniel 1993; Tolan 2002; Burman 2007), in which references to the Bible, the Qur’an, and other authoritative scriptures played a key role in argumentation (Mann 2019). Accordingly, identifying how scripture was used in argumentation—both the particular passages cited and the kinds of argumentation employed—is crucial to our historical understanding of religious encounters. Yet this information is typically scattered across footnotes in older printed editions, which are often outdated and difficult to access or analyze in aggregate. This article presents a pilot project aimed at digitally representing these data, enabling systematic compilation, comparison, and large-scale analysis of scriptural argumentation in interreligious polemics. I extracted, standardized, and refined textual references from a selection of Christian–Muslim polemics and summarized their use in argumentation. The resulting data were formalized as Linked Data using an underlying Ontology for the Transmission and Re-Use of Argumentative Patterns (OTRA). In what follows, I outline the core steps of this process. First, I justify the choice of specifically model reference, re-use, and argumentation as Linked (Open) Data. Second, I introduce the corpus selected for analysis. Third, I discuss key modeling decisions. Finally, I outline future work that would render this approach a true “shared conceptualization” through which historical connections between religions could be shared and analyzed. Religious texts claim to present the truth. Nevertheless, they require interpretation. The three so-called Abrahamic religions—Christianity, Islam, and Judaism—all generated vast interpretive traditions in the form of Bible commentaries, Tafsīr, and Talmud. These traditions aim to elucidate the true content of a religion by quoting, contrasting, and explaining scripture and previous commentary (Calder 1993). Interreligious discourse works similarly. Arguments are supported by quotations from scriptures and—overtly or covertly—they build on previous works. Accordingly, I work from the premise that interreligious polemics can be characterized by the answers to two questions: What is cited, reused, or alluded to? What is being argued? From this perspective, religious argumentation can be imagined as a network spanning millennia, with passages of religious texts as the central nodes. Representing this network as actual data would facilitate research and enable scholars to reach novel conclusions across periods, cultural contexts, and languages that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with traditional means. Due to its flexibility and inherent interoperability, Linked Open Data appears to be the best format for modeling such knowledge. Carefully annotated digital text editions are an ideal candidate for providing such data (Müller et al. 2021), but generally, the whole range of manual and automated methods should be exploited. One way scholars document intertextual relationships is through the source notes of critical editions. For this study, I extracted references from the critical annotations of multiple texts that are connected by their reliance—sometimes explicit, sometimes unacknowledged—on a treatise by the Dominican missionary Riccoldo da Monte di Croce. Riccoldo traveled to the ‘East’ in 1288. He went on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land and then continued toward Baghdad to convert Muslims. Along the way, he learned Arabic, studied the Qur’an, and sought religious disputations with Muslim scholars. Around 1300, he returned to Italy and recorded his experiences (George-Tvrtković 2012). His most famous work, Contra legem Saracenorum (“Against the law of the Saracens,” hereafter CLS) (Mérigoux 1986), was based on close study of the Qur’an, the anonymous Liber denudationis (Burman 1994), and Hadith (sayings of the Prophet) traditions, among other sources. Riccoldo became an influential source for knowledge of “Islam” (or what was taken for it) in the Middle Ages and beyond (Jensen and Scotto 2024). CLS’s intertextual links to earlier and later works make it an optimal case study for the transmission of religious knowledge. The works analyzed here use CLS to varying degrees. John of Segovia (Johannes von Segovia 2012) only quotes selective passages, while John of Ragusa (in: Langeloh 2019) cites him extensively both as an expert source of Islamic customs and beliefs and as a means of refutation. The anonymous author of the Epitome bellorum sacrorum (Anonymus 1601–1604) and the slightly obscure Petrus de Pennis (Petrus de Pennis 2016), on the other hand, construct nearly their entire texts through excerpting, rearranging, and sometimes reformulating Riccoldo (Langeloh 2023). In the text edition of CLS performed by Jean-Marie Mérigoux, the “raw data” appear in the following form (Fig. 1). Excerpts from CLS, c. 6, p. 83, illustrating how a text is elucidated by the source apparatus. In this edition, text passages are linked to other materials through footnotes. In modern publications, one might instead provide the starting and end words, as well as the line numbers. For example, the target of footnote 4 would become et 9 … lumen 10], indicating that it concerns the passage from “et” in line 9 to “lumen” in line 10. The annotations convey a variety of meanings. Most notes have a “cf.” (confer, conferatur) to indicate that one should “compare” the edited text with the referenced text. However, this is omitted when the text is marked as a direct quotation (note 5). Interestingly, the note refers to both Qur’an 93:6–7 and the Liber denudationis (here called Alpholica), which quotes from these Quranic verses. Some references by the editor also point to contemporary research literature, such as Gardet in note 7. To model these connections as sustainable Linked Open Data, I reused terms from the Hypermedia Dante Network (HDN) (Bartalesi et al. 2022) and the Sharing Ancient Wisdoms (SAWS) project (Hedges et al. 2017). HDN, which is an extension of the DanteSources ontology (Bartalesi and Meghini 2017), provided the basic model and some classification of connections. I then adapted categories from SAWS to express intertextual connectivity in a more granular way. Finally, I added categories to facilitate the unique identification of textual elements and to annotate argumentation. Both SAWS and HDN are based on the CIDOC CRM ontology (https://cidoc-crm.org) and the bibliographical vocabulary from LRMoo (https://www.cidoc-crm.org/frbroo/ModelVersion/version-1.0-2), making them inherently compatible. However, they exhibit a crucial difference. SAWS models textual connections directly, so one would state that “the passage in CLS c. 8 from et … lumen” “isRelatedTo” “Qur’an 93:6–7.” HDN uses the concept of “Reference” as an intermediary. It would declare an individual of the class “Reference” that “hasRefSubject” “the passage in CLS c. 8 from et … lumen” and “hasRefObject” “Qur’an 93,6–7.” In the context of HDN, “Reference” is defined as: “A says that the knowledge about B can be enriched through C,” where A is the statement making the connection (source), B is the text being “clarified by the reference” (subject), and C is the “entity […] that the source considers useful for explaining the subject” (object) (Bartalesi et al. 2022, p. 4). HDN also allows specifying the exact position of a text fragment through the class “Position” and the predicates “fromPosition” and “toPosition” (Bartalesi et al. 2022, pp. 8–9), which I used to clearly locate text passages. I also followed HDN’s convention of indirect modeling (Fig. 2a). This approach offers several advantages. First, the reification of the claim makes it easier to add additional information. Second, some of the annotations appear more optional than others, so it might be more accurate to say “can be related to” than “isRelatedTo.” Finally, I believe it most accurately characterizes what is happening in the apparatus. The editor is formulating a claim that two things can be fruitfully related to each other, but the connection is not always a necessary one. Modeling the connection as an indirect one highlights that the apparatus represents scholarly choices and opinions. Connective claims are specified in three dimensions. (a) A Connective claim postulates a connection between a subject and an object. The subject is a text fragment, which is elucidated by pointing toward some object, usually also a text fragment. For example, in Fig. 1, claim R.6.5.1 (belonging to note 5) has the subject “CLS chapter 6, paragraph 5, words 26-42” and as one object among others “Qur’an 93:6-7.” (b) The Connective claim can be further specified through subclasses and types. The basic distinctions in HDN are refined through classes derived from SAWS’s classification of textual parallels. In R.6.5.1, a Qur’anic verse is quoted and translated into Latin, constituting a “Parallel in a different language” with type “Variant” (a close parallel). (c) A text may signal that it is referring to an external object. Here, the text is explicitly related to Muhammad through “Ipse etiam dicit” and therefore has the Signalling Type “Explicit.” Though not implausible, I believe the term ‘Reference’ can be improved upon. Even in this narrow context, it could mean three things: (1) the fact that words generally refer to the world, (2) the piece of text through which a scholar creates a reference, or (3) the act by which the author of a text refers to something, like when Riccoldo says that “he himself [Muhammad] said …” (ipse etiam dixit). To address this ambiguity, I propose calling statements that establish connections between textual fragments “Connective Claims.” This term reflects that scholars are essentially claiming that two texts are related by annotating a text, thereby articulating and establishing a connection between texts. I used vocabulary from SAWS to more precisely define intertextual connections. SAWS offers a detailed and agnostic way of describing textual relationships, ranging from “isVerbatimOf” for direct, unchanged quotations, to “isLooseRenderingOf,” which describes more remote connections. SAWS further differentiates between parallels in the same language and in another language (https://ancientwisdoms.ac.uk/media/ontology/SAWS_relationship_types.html). To fit them into the HDN model, I created “TextualParallel” as a subclass of “Connective Claim” and then converted the predicates from SAWS to subclasses or types. I also derived two more subclasses from HDN, namely, “Topical Parallel,” and “External Support,” which are mostly used for references to secondary sources. Annotations to the text can contain multiple claims, for example, one TextualParallel, two TopicalParallels, and one ExternalSupport (Fig. 3). Thus, I combined the underlying model of HDN with the detailed typology of SAWS (Fig. 2b). Exemplary analysis of one note. The fragment is identified by its block (B) and the word-offset inside the block (48–88). The note provides four different connective claims (R. 6.7.1–6.7.4), which are assigned different classes (TextualParallel, TopicalParallel, ExternalSupport) and have different RefObjects. The proximity of the TextualParallel could be further specified by a type (in this case, “Variant”). Finally, there is the third possible meaning of “Reference” mentioned above: whether the text itself intimates that it is quoting something. In HDN, this is handled as a type of Citation, namely “explicitCitation.” I propose that this should be a separate dimension added to a “Connective Claim.” A “Connective Claim” can, therefore, receive a SignallingType (subclass of E55 Type) which specifies whether and how it refers (Fig. 2c). The example above, “he himself said,” would be classified as personal (as it is ascribed to a person and not a work) and precise (as we know it specifically concerns Muhammad, rather than, say, what “Muslims say”). For modeling argumentation, I considered using existing argumentation ontologies such as the Argument Model Ontology (Vitale and Peroni 2011) or the Argument Interchange Format (Argumentation Research Group 2011). Both are based on Steven Toulmin’s model for practical arguments (Toulmin 2003). While highly influential, Toulmin’s classification of the parts of the argument as claim, evidence, warrant, backing, rebuttal, and qualifiers poses challenges in distinguishing the elements and their precise meaning (van Eemeren et al. 2014). Therefore, I chose to model “statements” as the basic currency of argumentation without committing to a deeper description, attaching them to text fragments by “Position.” Even on this small scale, the data allow insights into the transmission of knowledge that would take hours to compile by hand. If, for instance, Riccoldo cites the Liber denudationis, the text edition of a work based on CLS, such as the Epitome bellorum sacrorum, will often fail to note this dependency. However, it can easily be queried from the available data how the Epitome draws indirectly from the Liber denudationis. It is straightforward to determine which parts of Riccoldo’s work were most re-used quantitatively and which arguments were based on which parts of his work (see Langeloh 2025, forthcoming). To fully understand the relationship between religions, further work is needed. Additional corpora must be incorporated, raising the question of how to scale reference extraction and refinement. Data ingestion tends to be easier when editions are consistent and digital, yet all processed editions still contain errors and inconsistencies that require manual correction. Accurately identifying points of reference remains challenging—even highly standardized, canonical citations can be problematic (Romanello 2015). Finally, while the classification of Connective Claims could potentially be delegated to machine learning with sufficient annotations, the process still requires gold standards and expert oversight. Adding further corpora will necessitate revisions of OTRA so that it becomes a true “shared conceptualization” (Guarino et al. 2009). The modeling approach should also be extended to include other perspectives between religions—such as those between Judaism and Christianity, or a Muslim perspective on Christianity—and even debates within one religion. Representing these perspectives in a shared format promises a hitherto unattainable perspective on religious argumentation and engagement. papers.title: ON CONCEPTS AS HISTORICAL FORMS
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT What are the consequences of holding fast to the axiom that words are not the same thing as concepts? This article explores some of them in relation to the tensions between two different but overlapping approaches to the history of concepts: philology and computationally informed historical semantics. The methods utilized were developed in the Cambridge Concept Lab and essentially comprise a measurement for word associations that can then be exported into comparative frameworks for tracking the evolution of concepts over time. Some examples are provided using the dataset Eighteenth Century Collections Online that are intended to demonstrate the fecundity of computational approaches to the history of ideas and concepts. Throughout the article, a distinction is held between two interconnected terms: meanings and concepts—or to put that more pointedly, the hard case of distinguishing between a change in meaning of a word and a change in conceptual form is addressed. Although the article comes to the conclusion that hard‐and‐fast distinctions between words and concepts are extremely difficult to maintain, it nevertheless insists on the benefit of supposing that such distinctions can be held. This enables one to characterize concepts in terms of their functions rather than their meanings, and some examples of these functions are provided. In conclusion, the article returns to the issue of historical approaches to words and concepts and suggests that a conceptual history formulated through the lens of conceptual function complements philological accounts of how words and meanings inform us about the past.

papers.title: Quantifying the faithfulness of poetry translations in four closely related Slavic languages
papers.abstract: Abstract Translating poetry is notoriously difficult—some would claim impossible—because it inherently requires making triage decisions what to preserve and what to sacrifice if necessary. Both form and meaning contribute to the esthetic effects of the original, but translations that faithfully preserve the metrical versification principles of the original might struggle to fully preserve lexically conveyed meanings and connotations, and vice versa. Other esthetically relevant sound-related features (e.g. phonemic patterns) are particularly challenging to preserve. This paper presents a pilot study to empirically test this intuition by assessing the faithfulness of translations to their original. Quantifying aspects of the beauty of sound and meaning, that is, the sonority and the esthetic affective potential, of selected poems and their translations in/from Russian, Polish, Czech, and Slovak, that is, a sample controlled for linguistic and cultural context, we measure the degree to which translations correspond to their originals along these dimensions. The results suggest that, for the poems and languages considered, the beauty of sound and meaning are preserved to varying degrees, which can be sensibly interpreted against specific features of the poems, linguistic distances, and cultural prestige. The study thus serves as a proof of concept that demonstrates the basic feasibility of the method applied and foreshadows its potential for advancing empirical studies in the field of comparative poetics.

papers.title: Natural language processing as Digital Veda (डजटल वद): a humanistic framework for language, ethics, and AI
papers.abstract: Abstract This article conceptualizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) as the Digital Veda (डिजिटल वेद), framing it as a culturally rooted communicative infrastructure inspired by the Vedic tradition of structured knowledge preservation and ethical discourse. Drawing on India’s linguistic and philosophical heritage, it positions NLP not as a neutral tool, but as an evolving ecosystem shaped by human values, language ideologies, and socio-cultural narratives. By mapping the four Vedas to key NLP domains, Rigveda (language modelling), Yajurveda (syntax and pipelines), Samaveda (phonetics and speech), and Atharvaveda (applied AI), the study illustrates how contemporary language technologies mirror ancient systems of meaning-making. It offers a critical, decolonial lens on mainstream NLP, highlighting digital language hierarchies, the marginalization of low-resource Indian languages, and biases embedded in large language model (LLM) training data. The article further proposes a Vedic-inspired ethical AI framework, grounded in the principles of Dharma (righteous design), Ahimsa (non-harm), and Moksha (AI for truth and well-being). This interdisciplinary perspective contributes to a more inclusive, context-aware vision for language technologies, with practical applications in multilingual NLP, bias mitigation, and ethically aligned AI governance. It is particularly relevant for AI ethicists, digital humanists, NLP researchers, and policymakers committed to culturally informed, responsible innovation.

papers.title: Todd Presner. Ethics of the Algorithm: Digital Humanities and Holocaust Memory
papers.abstract: In Ethics of the Algorithm: Digital Humanities and Holocaust Memory, Todd Presner seeks to respond to what he sees as a “big problem”: how to use computational methods “in ethical” ways to distant read vast Holocaust testimony archives (vii). While the book is rich in discussions of a range of current digital humanities methods and tools, its focus is very much on a core set of ethical concerns that persist regardless of the precise, ever-changing technologies deployed. Although working with a particular source—collections of oral history interviews with tens of thousands of Holocaust survivors—the central question in the book is one of wider significance for humanists: “How can we think, listen, compose, and interpret ethically with algorithms and computational methods?” (19) While Presner is the main author, the book includes the words of others from the UCLA lab. Collaborative and interdisciplinary ways of working are the norm in the digital humanities, and the book draws on this wider team to good effect, mixing Presner’s overarching narrative with shorter, focused sections that delve into particular projects coauthored with or by others. These multiple texts are further enhanced by QR codes that enable further exploration of the data under discussion. Both signal new ways of working and publishing that are to be welcomed more widely in the discipline.

papers.title: Mark Duerksen. Waterhouses: Landscapes, Housing, and the Making of Modern Lagos
papers.abstract: Mark Duerksen’s book Waterhouses: Landscapes, Housing, and the Making of Modern Lagos is a spatial history of the meaning, usage, and forms of houses in Lagos over the course of two centuries. The questions that guide the book are “What is a house?” and “How can contemporary structures—from informal settlements to mansions in gated communities—be studied historically?” An ambitious and well-written study, Waterhouses argues that “in the coastlands from which Lagos rose, housing architectures were the single most important social, material, and political instrument for people hoping to contour the city’s landscape—both its ecology and its image—and its historical course” (10). In five chapters, the author illuminates how residents, colonial, and postcolonial policymakers imagined, inhabited, and struggled over diverse housing models. Duerksen situates his study against the backdrop of the rise of British colonial rule, the interwar years, Nigeria’s transition from colonial rule to independence, and the rise of the military regime alongside its reliance on oil extraction, and the neoliberal policies of the 1970s and 1980s. During these eras, ­Lagosians constructed houses to secure shelter, exude elite status, accrue wealth, claim power, and control labor and resources.

papers.abstract: Innovations in Teaching History: Eighteenth-­Century Studies in Higher Education consists of collected contributions from nine UK and Australian-based specialists of Britain’s “long eighteenth century” (1688–1832). When allowances for the educational terminology unique to the UK are made, readers will find that the lessons offered here have a wide and general application. A strength of this collection is that the contributions take the form of self-reflective accounts of a single experience in course design. This is a universal experience for history teachers, and it is here enhanced by the restraint the authors show in not descending into excessive detail about the century that they love. papers.title: Jennifer Bond. Dreaming the New Woman: An Oral History of Missionary Schoolgirls in Republican China
papers.abstract: Jennifer Bond brings a welcome perspective to the study of (mostly) American Protestant missionary educational activity in early twentieth century China. As Bond points out regarding studies of Christianity in China, while the trend has been to focus on the indigenization of the religion and move away from missionaries, with some notable exceptions, most studies have done so by replacing male missionaries with male Chinese Christian leaders. Bond, on the other hand, highlights the case of female students, focusing on the lives and experiences of students at five all-girls Christian middle schools in and around Shanghai, covering a period from the founding of the schools in the late 1800s through their dissolution in the early 1950s. Based on the close examination of student writings in yearbooks and other school publications and interviews with seventy-five alumnae, Bond argues that “in their experiments with gender, Christianity, and nationalism, girls advanced a form of gendered Christian modernity—that is, a vision of how highly educated Christian Chinese women, such as themselves, could transform and strengthen the nation, allowing China to stand up and eventually overtake encroaching imperialist powers, such as Japan” (4). Not only does Bond introduce the reader to the girls’ activities and thoughts; she also makes a series of intriguing points on other issues of interest for scholars of the period including religion and secularization, ambiguities around wartime patriotism, and the connections between Christianity and communism.
