papers.title: Holly Miowak Guise. Alaska Native Resilience: Voices from World War II.
papers.abstract: In Alaska Native Resilience: Voices from World War II, Holly Miowak Guise (Iñupiaq) provides readers with a crucial reframing of Indigenous-US relations and World War II in Alaska. Drawing on her extensive oral history work and interviews with Alaska Native elders, Guise joins the proliferation of recent scholarship that challenges “simplistic, incomplete, often nationalist U.S. portrayals” of the “Good War” (3). Following the 1942 Japanese invasion of the Aleutian Islands of Attu and Kiska, the US government executed the forced removal of over eight hundred Unangax̂ from their homelands and justified their internment in southeast Alaska as a necessity of wartime exigencies. Challenging this narrative, the book situates the militarization of Alaska as the expansion of US empire to which Alaska Natives from diverse tribal geographies responded as nations. Upending one-dimensional tropes that portray Indigenous peoples as the reactive recipients of colonialism, Alaska Native Resilience demands that Alaska Native actions throughout the war be understood as more than resistance. Rather, Guise brings into focus an Indigenous wartime political geography in which she demonstrates that the subversive strategies employed by Alaska Natives represent assertions and affirmations of Indigenous sovereignty, diplomacy, and nation-­­­­to-nation alliances.

papers.title: D. Fairchild Ruggles. Tree of Pearls: The Extraordinary Architectural Patronage of the 13th-Century Egyptian Slave-Queen Shajar al-Durr.
papers.abstract: With a frankness that characterizes Tree of Pearls: The Extraordinary Architectural Patronage of the 13th-Century Egyptian Slave-Queen Shajar al-Durr, D. Fairchild Ruggles muses, “In writing Shajar al-Durr’s story, I have often struggled with the problem of genre. Is this biography? Social history? Art history? Melodrama?” (146). Narrating the lives of premodern Islamic women poses unique challenges that can only be partially solved through reading sources against the grain and employing interdisciplinary methods. Often, as in the case of Shajar al-Durr, the written record of elite women is produced by men who are concerned with their lives only when they intersect with politics and, as I have argued, through motifs and tropes as a way to praise or critique the state. Ruggles contextualizes such sources, as well as the later legends and myths that surround this exceptional figure, by putting them in conversation with material culture. Writing the story of Shajar al-Durr is doubly challenging. Not only was she a woman, but she was enslaved. Therefore, biographical information about her family history is completely unknown because her slave status erased those relationships. She enters the historical record as concubine to the Ayyubid Sultan Salih (d. 1249), as Ruggles notes, “as an object of exchange between men” (19). Negotiating the diverse array of source material necessary for excavating a history of this woman is where her analysis shines. Translated excerpts from textual sources are juxtaposed with detailed descriptions of urban space and the exterior and interior of key buildings, including Salih’s madrasa (school), his tomb, and Shajar al-Durr’s tomb. Scattered through the pages of the book are images of buildings, manuscripts, coins, architectural plans, and reconstruction drawings as well as maps of Cairo, inviting the reader to traverse the city as Ruggles imagines that Shajar al-Durr might have done. What makes a biography of the slave-queen possible is the abundance of material culture that gives evidence to her political role, especially the coins minted in her name, one of the signs of leadership in the premodern Islamic world, and the commemorative architecture that she built for both her deceased husband Salih and, later, herself.

papers.title: Waitman Wade Beorn. Between the Wires: The Janowska Camp and the Holocaust in Lviv
papers.abstract: Waitman Wade Beorn is one of the best experts on the history of the Holocaust in the occupied territories of the Soviet Union. Beorn’s earlier work traced the murderous deeds of the Holocaust in Eastern Europe over large areas, but the work to be presented here is a microstudy. Between the Wires: The Janowska Camp and the Holocaust in Lviv examines the Janowska camp on the outskirts of Lwow, one of the largest cities in Galicia. It belonged to Austria-Hungary until 1918 and then became Polish in 1918, but in 1939, the territory fell into the Soviet occupation zone as a result of the ­­Hitler-Stalin Pact. Before the start of the Second World War, Lvov had just over 300,000 inhabitants, around 100,000 of whom belonged to the ­­Jewish minority. Due to the flight of Jewish people from the German-occupied area of Poland, however, there were probably 160,000 Jewish people in Lwow when the Wehrmacht occupied the city on June 30, 1941. An SD-Einsatzgruppe carried out a first pogrom in the city with the help of Ukrainian nationalists. But the National Socialists did not assign the city to occupied Ukraine. Rather, it was ceded to the Generalgouvernement under the leadership of Hans Frank.

papers.abstract: Lost Fatherland: Europeans between Empire and Nation-States, 1867–1939 is a broad tableau of lives and political-ideological lineages stemming from Habsburg Austria—dissolved in 1918 after it lost the First World War—to its successor states: Italy, Yugoslavia, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and Soviet Ukraine. Rather, the heritage of Austria-Hungary had a positive influence on how its successors were organized and how they operated.

papers.title: Laura Frances Goffman. Disorder and Diagnosis: Health and the Politics of Everyday Life in Modern Arabia
papers.abstract: In Disorder and Diagnosis: Health and the Politics of Everyday Life in Modern Arabia, Laura Frances Goffman offers a social and political history of how medicine, disease, and public health transformed the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf from the late 19th century until the 1973 oil boom: A behemoth undertaking, but not unsurmountable. The book is structured into six chapters, each exploring key themes through specific institutional or social settings: contagion, hospitals, childbirth, experiments, nurses, and folk medicine. Goffman’s research draws on a range of archival collections in India, Kuwait, the United States, and the United Kingdom, as well as online repositories, such as the Indian Foreign Office Records via the Qatar Digital Library and the Arabian Gulf Digital Archive. Early chapters focus on quarantine stations, hospitals, and childbirth practices, demonstrating how British and US medical interventions sought to define and regulate health. Quarantine stations, positioned within the framework of empire, exemplify the imposition of sanitary controls that sought to discipline bodies in transit, while the latter chapters showcase spaces of contested authority, where missionary doctors, regional experts, and local communities negotiated medical practice and gendered access to care. Hospitals, for example, contrast the quarantine stations discussed in earlier chapters to show how “ordinary people . . . played a powerful role in institutionalizing modern health services” (54). ­­Nonetheless, Goffman highlights how the persistence of home childbirth despite missionary efforts to medicalize the ­­process underscores the limits of institutional authority while showcasing the agency of local women.

papers.title: Paul Nugent. Race, Taste, and the Grape: South African Wine from a Global Perspective
papers.abstract: The twentieth century witnessed a profound transformation of the global wine industry when it collapsed the binary of Old World versus New World. In Race, Taste, and the Grape, Paul Nugent offers a compelling exploration of how South African wine played a pivotal role in this shift, situating itself at the intersection of cultural exchange, technological innovation, and sociopolitical reform. Nugent’s work deftly demonstrates how South African wine exemplified the global currents that redefined the industry. The book highlights how South Africa’s wine communities skillfully blended tradition with innovation, underscoring the centrality of terroir as a concept that intertwines ecological significance with cultural heritage. South African wines became emblematic of a new wave of winemaking that balanced terroir-driven authenticity with the technological advancements demanded by international markets. The concept of terroir, which encapsulates the intersection of soil, climate, and human tradition, became foundational to South Africa’s transformation. Nugent shows how the post-apartheid period marked a renaissance for South African wine, with exports skyrocketing from 24.5 million liters in 1993 to over 525 million liters by 2013. This remarkable growth was underpinned by a strategy that combined the preservation of traditional viticulture—rooted in terroir-driven practices and old vine cultivation—with aggressive market adaptation. South African winemakers emphasized the quality and diversity of their wines, leveraging the country’s unique climate and soil diversity to appeal to a global audience. The adoption of terroir as a branding and production philosophy allowed the wine industry to craft a narrative that resonated with international consumers, while simultaneously rooting itself in the cultural and ecological heritage of the Cape region.

papers.title: Marion R. Casey. The Green Space: The Transformation of the Irish Image
papers.abstract: The stock image of what it means to “be Irish” in the twenty-first century is on bright display every year on Saint Patrick’s Day. papers.title: Thomas W. Smith. Rewriting the First Crusade: Epistolary Culture in the Middle Ages
papers.abstract: Much of what we used to know about the First ­­Crusade is becoming complicated by ongoing research. What was the catalyst? What was the goal? Who was in charge? Where does it fit within a developing ideology of holy war? One thing is clear: The voluminous textual record produced during and after the events of 1096–1099 constitutes an unprecedented documentary response driven by intense contemporary interest, raising vital questions about why and how such texts were made, and what kinds of evidence can be distilled from them. Moreover, because they were shaped by the various material and embodied media through which news and (mis)information circulated, these texts are a tremendous resource for studying medieval modes of communication, regardless of their veracity. In Rewriting the First Crusade: Epistolary Culture in the Middle Ages, Thomas W. Smith makes an important contribution to our understanding of the manuscript milieu that conveyed these narratives, and to the process of reassessing how historians should be reading and teaching them now.

papers.title: Nora E. Jaffary. Abortion in Mexico: A History
papers.abstract: Abortion is a hot-button topic in US culture and politics. Politicians are made and unmade over the issue. Families are admonished to avoid the subject at Thanksgiving dinner. The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, and some states like my own (Arkansas) enacted some of the strictest abortion restrictions in the nation. Some might believe that nations like Mexico, rooted in Catholicism and stereotyped as steeped in machismo, would also severely restrict abortion. On the contrary, Abortion in Mexico reveals that tolerance and a more nuanced assessment have characterized Mexican abortion laws and prosecution. Indeed, Nora E. Jaffary convincingly demonstrates that continuity with small bumps and valleys rather than dramatic change has characterized the history of abortion in Mexico from 1519 to 2000. It was not until the mid-twentieth century that more Mexicans, including women, disapproved of abortion and lobbied for criminalization of the procedure. By the mid-1970s, Mexican society shifted to greater receptiveness, culminating in the 2023 federal decriminalization of abortion during the first twelve weeks of pregnancy. Mexico City had decriminalized abortion in the first trimester in 2003 and 2007. Only the United States among North American nations has moved the opposite way: from decriminalization to criminalization. Engaging a wide range of primary sources and literature, Jaffary provides a highly readable, concise, and intellectually compelling historical synthesis of abortion in Mexico.

papers.title: Hamid Dabashi. An Iranian Childhood: Rethinking History and Memory .
papers.abstract: Memoirs are effective sources in gaining rare insight into the history of peoples and places where typical primary sources or theoretical analyses lag. That’s why they have become a “house” of their own, to borrow from Anna Green and Kathleen Troup, beside the standard “houses of history,” such as the Annales, Marxist history, and others. Although most academically informed memoirs are useful, one can argue that they are especially valuable in demystifying aspects of non-Western societies. By historically contextualizing personal experiences, as Hamid Dabashi does in An Iranian Childhood: Rethinking History and Memory, memoirs can strengthen our ability to look from the bottom up. Written in four chapters and including a prelude and an epilogue, the book also shares paintings and film posters that contextualize the text better; it is a must-read for those interested in mid-twentieth-century provincial Iran and anyone who wants to take cues about how to successfully integrate scholarship into creative memoir writing.

papers.title: Douglas Pretsell. Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: In a few short years, Douglas Pretsell has made important contributions to nineteenth-century LGBTQ+ studies by publishing two incredibly useful primary source collections translated into English from German. Now he returns with his first full-length publication, Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, examining the ground-­­shaking discursive impact that the pioneering LGBTQ+ activist Karl Heinrich Ulrichs had when he coined this term in the 1860s to describe same-sex-attracted men. Somehow Ulrichs was missed by Michel Foucault when this French philosopher first observed that the concept of the homosexual only entered into Western discourse at the end of the nineteenth century. During the 1980s, however, a whole wave of historians helped to return Ulrichs to the spotlight. Even more recently, Robert Beachy featured Ulrichs quite prominently in the first chapter of his 2014 book Gay Berlin: Birthplace of a Modern Identity. With decades of research into the emergence of LGBTQ+ identities in Germany behind us, it is a little surprising that anyone could show us anything new about the topic. And yet even scholars familiar with Beachy’s book and other relevant literature will be pleasantly surprised at how much can be learned by a real in-depth study of Ulrichs’s work as a writer and an activist. Specifically, in the debate going back to Foucault about whether “the homosexual” was an identity created largely by psychiatrists or by LGBTQ+ peoples themselves, Pretsell makes a compelling case for the latter. He does this by mining the letters sent to Ulrichs by his readers, which together with Ulrichs’s pamphlets created a kind of “community of correspondence,” Pretsell argues. A close reading allows him to highlight the ways that their inner lives were utterly reconfigured by the exposure to the term “urning,” years before psychiatrists were injecting their own ideas into public discourse. In the process, he is successfully able to trace the transformation of the urning from being a “strategic identity,” crafted, Pretsell suggests, largely at first for rhetorical purposes, into a “new, sexually modern social identity” in the course of the decade (39).

papers.title: Anthony H. Minnema. The Last Ṭa’ifa: The Banu Hud and the Struggle for Political Legitimacy in al-Andalus
papers.abstract: Anthony H. Minnema’s book The Last Ṭa’ifa: The Banū Hūd and the Struggle for Political Legitimacy in al-Andalus offers a comprehensive exploration of the Andalusī dynasty’s political strategies and ideological claims to legitimacy in the turbulent landscape of medieval Iberia. The Last Ṭa’ifa argues that the Banū Hūd exhibited nuanced and adaptive political culture over multiple generations that responded creatively to the pressures of Almoravid, Almohad, and Christian dominance. Minnema’s close analysis of primary sources in Latin and Arabic, including chronicles, coins, and diplomatic documents, shows how the Banū Hūd balanced dynastic pride with strategic alliances to sustain their rule across generations. This meticulously researched work is essential reading for scholars of medieval Spain and al-Andalus, medieval Islamic political culture, and the broader Mediterranean. Minnema sets the stage by framing the Banū Hūd as a unique Andalusī dynasty with a “second act”—a recurring ability to reassert power through careful claims to lineage and allegiance. He critiques conventional historiographical views of the ta’ifa periods as chaotic or politically unsophisticated, as influenced by a preference for centralized imperial regimes. He instead suggests that these fragmented times allowed smaller polities, such as the Banū Hūd, to develop distinctive forms of statecraft. The central question for the book is how the Banū Hūd deployed their dynastic identity and claims to legitimacy to maintain power over three centuries in the face of multiple challenges.

papers.title: Chanelle Delameillieure. Abduction, Marriage, and Consent in the Late Medieval Low Countries
papers.abstract: Abduction, Marriage, and Consent in the Late Medieval Low Countries is a fascinating analysis of an intriguing medieval phenomenon: abduction with marital intent. Although its title claims to cover the entire Low Countries, this book has a narrower focus and deals with three cities in Flanders and Brabant—namely, Ghent, Leuven, and Antwerp. Nevertheless, Chanelle Delameillieure was able to trace no less than 650 abduction cases during the fifteenth century. A thorough analysis of this extensive corpus allows her to critique traditional narratives that portray abductions and clandestine marriages solely as acts of rebellion by young women seeking autonomy. Delameillieure convincingly challenges conventional views on medieval marital conflicts and highlights the unique sociolegal environment of the Southern Low Countries. In fact, Middle Dutch had a specific term to distinguish abduction with marital intent (schaec) from rape (vrouwencracht). Furthermore, the Southern Low Countries had a unique legal regime with a secular age of consent, strict anti-abduction laws, and a high age threshold for marriage without parental approval, setting it apart from other regions in late medieval Europe. ­Delameillieure also exposes the tension between the church’s consent-based marriage doctrine and traditional customs favoring family-controlled marriage strategies. This conflict led to legal disputes and family conflicts, showing that marriage choices were highly contested areas. This distinctive legal and social landscape made marriage a matter of negotiation, both within families and the broader social fabric of cities in the Southern Low Countries.

papers.title: Matthew Neufeld. Early Modern Naval Health Care in England, 1650–1750
papers.abstract: Historians write about the formation of the early modern English state in one of two ways. One group describes a fiscal-military state focused almost exclusively on money and war, implementing an increasingly intrusive and efficient system of taxation to fund the increasing expense of sustaining armies and, especially, navies. Others focus on the loose network of local elites who exercised most other responsibilities of governance, maintaining social control of a burgeoning population through the administration of justice and the delivery of poor relief. Matthew Neufeld’s Early Modern Naval Health Care in England, 1650–1750 identifies an instance where the state reached in to manage the customary practice, usually left to local authorities, of providing relief for the “deserving poor”: A small state bureaucracy emerged to provide health care for sick and wounded sailors, ensuring the navy could man its ships. Neufeld’s book explores the development of that system of care over the century between the civil wars and the War of Austrian Succession. He argues that the system, overseen by a handful of centrally appointed commissioners for sick and wounded seamen, embodied a “preservative ethos” with three objectives: “saving seamen’s lives, saving money, and keeping men in sea service” (11). The system grew to include three parts—care in the community, care in contracted hospitals, and care in navy-operated hospitals—each of which arose as the solution to a problem. This story is not simply about modernization, however; rather than replacing its predecessor, each new method simply augmented the existing system and operated in parallel, and the final transition to a fully “modern” system of state-run hospitals did not occur until long after the book closes.

papers.title: Sanjay Subrahmanyam. Across the Green Sea: Histories from the Western Indian Ocean, 1440–1640
papers.abstract: Sanjay Subrahmanyam’s Across the Green Sea studies the western Indian Ocean’s maritime-terrestrial space through polycentric views from different spatial units. The book juxtaposes a set of analytical incisions to discuss interstate relationships, political economy, social history, and cosmopolitanism in the western Indian Ocean from the 15th to the 17th century. There could be many readings of this book. My review explores how these incisions read together. The book’s approach is of connected histories—a methodology Subrahmanyam outlined in other works—whose crucial aspect is to grasp whether our current geographies are fit for our research questions. Drawing on the approach of French historian Jean Aubin, Subrahmanyam stresses the need to interrogate a wide gamut of European and non-European sources to study the western Indian Ocean. We might imagine this book as analogous to a musical polyphony, where multiple counterpoints produce a harmonic texture. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss interstate systems, political legitimacy, and transition in the western Indian Ocean between the 15th and 16th centuries, and ramifications of Portuguese violence on its political economy. Symbolic political legitimacy, a contentious issue in the 15th century, saw the Mamluks and the Timurids competing for control over the Kaaba’s rituals. Then, the Ottomans defeated the Safavids and the Mamluks and dispatched victory bulletins to western Indian Ocean powers including Gujarat, while the Portuguese Estado da India regularly attacked western Indian Ocean shipping and changed the scale of violence. Chapter 2 analyzes an Arabic text, Kitab Nail al-muna, produced by the Islamic scholar Jarullah ibn Fahd al-Makki (d. 1547), which described the impact of the 1530s Gujarati-Portuguese struggle in the Hijaz: The local Ottoman officials and the Ottoman top brass extorted the Gujarati court elite seeking refuge in Mecca during Bahadur Shah’s conflict with the Portuguese. The episode culminated in an unsuccessful Ottoman expedition against the Portuguese. So, Subrahmanyam argues, the complexity of the western Indian Ocean’s political balance in the early 16th century needs further consideration.

papers.title: Thomas M. Larkin. The China Firm: American Elites and the Making of British Colonial Society
papers.abstract: “In February 1784, little more than a month following the end of the War of Independence, the American ship Empress of China departed New York for Canton,” Thomas M. Larkin explains in the introduction to The China Firm: American Elites and the Making of British Colonial Society. “This voyage anticipated a century-long wave of American mercantile interest in China” (1). Over the next 100 years, US merchants joined the international push to expand foreign trade with the Qing Empire. First at Canton, and then at Hong Kong and treaty ports along China’s coast, US firms positioned themselves to capitalize on the further opening of China to foreign trade and influence. This experience brought these US companies into competition, but also into different forms of accommodation, with foreign and Chinese merchants and officials. Most important was the relationship with the British, whose colonial culture and authority heavily influenced the lives and commercial activities of Americans in China, along with their sense of national and racial identity, and their attitudes toward Chinese people.

papers.title: Jessica O’Leary. Renaissance Masculinities, Diplomacy, and Cultural Transfer: Federico and Ferrante Gonzaga in Italy and Beyond
papers.abstract: Federico Gonzaga (1500–1540) must count among the best-traveled children of the Italian Renaissance. Son of Mantuan rulers Francesco Gonzaga and ­Isabella d’Este, Federico became a bargaining chip in his parents’ dealings with allies and enemies alike during the Italian Wars (1494–1559). As a boy, Federico was coveted as a hostage by French King Louis XII, and he spent almost a quarter of his life as a guest-detainee at the courts of Pope Julius II and King Francis I before returning to Mantua as its lord. Effectively a resident teenage diplomat, Federico absorbed knowledge, language, habits, and perspectives in this youthful tour that served him well for the rest of his life. In this stimulating study of the Gonzaga dynasty’s diplomacy in the first half of the sixteenth century, Jessica O’Leary’s Renaissance Masculinities, Diplomacy, and Cultural Transfer examines Federico’s life alongside that of his younger brother Ferrante (1507–1557), whose status as a cadet child brought him to different European environs from his brother: first to the court of Emperor Charles V and then a series of imperial appointments in Milan and Sicily as an adult. The book sets the two brothers’ lives and careers in the context of the Italian Wars to demonstrate the nimble and imaginative adjustments the ruling family of Mantua—a well-connected but diminutive Italian principality—made to insulate themselves from the ensuing political tumult. The book proposes that the Gonzaga boys’ cultural immersion in foreign courts trained them in new forms of sixteenth-century manhood and cultural diplomacy. The lordly fifteenth-­century “bluster” (54) of the boys’ father Francesco had little effect at the courts of major European monarchs after 1500, nor could the “crisis diplomacy” (20) the house of Gonzaga practiced in the early Italian Wars function effectively in later decades. The book charts transformations between generations as the men of the dynasty confronted the wars’ new challenges over decades, and O’Leary’s analysis of these shifting political and cultural terrains is particularly insightful. In tracing the evolutions of familial strategies of clientage and statecraft between parents and children, the author outlines the limitations of ­fifteenth-century lordship in new political realities and suggests how the Gonzaga adapted their approaches to the next century.

papers.title: Sugata Bose. Asia After Europe: Imagining a Continent in the Long Twentieth Century .
papers.abstract: This is a heartfelt and thought-provoking book by a distinguished scholar of South Asian and Indian Ocean history. It shows how some of the best minds in East, South, and West Asia imagined “Asia as an abstract entity transcending the imperial and national frontiers … [that were] etched by colonial powers onto the physical and mental maps of the colonized” (3). It tracks the “intersecting journey of Asian intellectuals and subalterns alike” to ask under what conditions a distinctively non-European idea of Asia and Asian solidarity was “forged” and then, unfortunately, “fractured” (6). Sugata Bose emphasizes that for many Asians, the continent of Asia was far more than a mere product of western cartographic invention. Instead, it was a creative space infused with emotion. In other words, this book is about how, if Europeans imagined Asia as a space—a cartographic invention—many Asian intellectuals imagined it as a place. Bose argues that against significant odds, Asian intellectuals like Rabindranath Tagore, Benoy Kumar Sarkar, Okakura Tenshin, Yone Noguchi, Yokoyama Taikan, Ananda Commarasamy, Xu Beihong, and Liang Qichao—to name just a few—tried to realize an Asia that was radically different from European ideals of nationalism, unitary sovereignty, and regionalism. These imaginings were developed as part of a shared network of interactions that was not mediated by Europe. It is perhaps not important that the lofty ideals of this strand of Asianism failed to materialize. Indeed, Bose recognizes how the complicated relationship between Japan and China and China and India made such solidarities difficult to sustain. But what is important is that some of Asia’s finest minds spent considerable time and energy conceptualizing an Asianism based on principles of “Asian universalism”—an idea I wish was unpacked more explicitly in the book. One of Bose’s central contentions is that if a notion of a European or Western identity could survive the mayhem of the two world wars, then ­­Japanese imperialism and Chinese and Indian expansionism, too, should not mean that in the future, a larger Asian identity based putatively on Asian ideals cannot be forged. I am convinced by this argument. In fact, I would venture to say that it is this point—that Asian solidarity is possible and plausible even in the age of inter-Asian national conflicts, as long as Asians try to (re)activate non-­­European or precolonial modes of Asian universalism—is the most significant argument of this important book. Whether one agrees whether non-­­European, precolonial, or Asian universalism is imaginable or desirable is beside the point.

papers.title: José Antonio Piqueras. Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna: Los esclavos, la ley y la justicia entre Europa y el imperio español de América
papers.abstract: José Antonio Piqueras skillfully captures the reader’s attention with the title Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna. With polished precision, he formulates the subtitle: Los esclavos, la ley y la justicia entre Europa y el imperio español de América. This work can be viewed as a continuation of his book La esclavitud en las Españas: Un lazo transatlántico (2011); interrelated, both aim to reveal the reality of slavery in Spanish America, which sharply contradicts and disproves the official narrative. In Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna, the author expands his analysis to include the experiences of Indigenous people, who, while being protected as subjects of the Crown in discourse, were also subjected to slavery in practice. He also addresses the official disregard for the transatlantic slave trade that continued until the nineteenth century. Piqueras presents the ancient phenomenon of slavery in its entirety and temporality as the first form of appropriation of the labor capacity of others through the appropriation of the person, approaching the history of slavery not as a continuous narrative but rather as a fabric that undergoes continuous moments, ruptures, jumps, and recoveries, where slavery experiences phases of revitalization following phases of decline. He highlights that in the former phase, history was utilized to legitimize the new forms of domination, while in the latter, abolitionists believed slavery had ceased to correspond to the changing spirit of the age.

papers.title: Juan F. Cobo Betancourt. The Coming of the Kingdom: The Muisca, Catholic Reform, and Spanish Colonialism in the New Kingdom of Granada
papers.abstract: This insightful book explores a crucial aspect of Spain’s early colonialism: the Christianization of Indigenous communities in its overseas territories. Using the Muisca—inhabitants of the central highlands of New Granada (roughly present-day Colombia)—as a case study, the author sheds light on a colonial region often overlooked in historical narratives, especially compared to the better-documented areas of Mexico and Peru. These regions are frequently seen as models for the Spanish colonial project, an assumption that this book challenges. Focusing on the century following the first encounters between Spaniards and the Muisca, the study spans from the 1530s to the 1650s. During this period, particularly in the early seventeenth century, colonial officials, religious leaders, and Jesuit missionaries launched an ambitious reform effort aimed at Christianizing the Indigenous population, a process thoroughly examined in The Coming of the Kingdom. Drawing from a wide array of sources—including correspondence, ecclesiastical reports, petitions, legislation, legal documents, and related materials—found in archives and libraries both in Colombia and abroad (Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom, and the United States), the book traces the complex dynamics of Christianization. Cobo Betancourt reveals this process to be coercive yet deeply negotiated, contested, contingent, and uneven. Despite its shortcomings and obstacles, the Christianization effort was persistent, closely tied to Spain’s identity as a newly unified kingdom and reinforced by its use of Christian evangelization to justify the conquest, occupation, and control of colonial territories, with legal backing from the papacy. The preservation of Catholic orthodoxy in colonial enclaves was an additional driving force.

papers.title: Robert M. Owens. Killing over Land: Murder and Diplomacy on the Early American Frontier
papers.abstract: Imperialism, colonization, competition for land, and murder go hand in hand. With the arrival of ­­Europeans on North American shores, an adversarial mindset developed between Indigenous and settler colonial communities. These contentious relationships often led to miscommunication, conflict, and, in some cases, murder. From the Pequot Massacre in 1637 and colonial cross-cultural frontier raids to the terror of Pontiac’s Rebellion and the horrors of removal in the 1830s, Indigenous and early American communities searched for stability in an ever-­­changing world. Murder impacted communities across the racial divide on the early North American frontier. Murder, like trading relationships, created an avenue for both sides to seek redress, forced them to communicate with one another in the cause of justice, and produced a shared space where the parties could potentially find common ground. This is the main argument of ­­Robert M. Owens’s book Killing over Land: Murder and ­­Diplomacy on the Early American Frontier. Over the course of fourteen chapters, Owens methodically unpacks the nature of cross-racial murder in early American history and its connections to power, land, natural resources, and empire building in the ­­eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

papers.title: Charlotte Lydia Riley. Imperial Island: An Alternative History of the British Empire
papers.abstract: Critical histories of Britain’s relationship with its imperial past have become commonplace in recent years, which is hardly surprising given the ongoing position of the empire in the country’s rabid culture war discourses of recent years. Charlotte Lydia Riley’s Imperial Island (originally published in the UK by Penguin last year and now appearing in the US ­courtesy of Harvard University Press) joins other recent works—by the likes of Hakim Adi, Priyamvada Gopal, and Sathnam Sanghera—in providing a historically detailed, yet highly readable, riposte to unpleasant waves of imperial nostalgia and apologia promoted by a coalition of right-wing politicians and nonexpert academics. Taking readers on a journey from the throes of the Second World War to the ferocious contestations over Brexit, Imperial Island convincingly demonstrates the near-inescapable presence of imperialism in British society, politics, and culture since the 1930s. As this core argument suggests, the book is a history of empire in Britain over the last ninety-odd years and not a new history of the British Empire (as the rather misleading Harvard edition subtitle of An Alternative History of the British Empire might imply). Riley focuses particularly on ordinary people—a category that is acknowledged as imperfect in the introduction—and builds her case using a well-established canon of sources. Newspapers and political pamphlets rub shoulders with government documents, diaries, oral histories, and popular culture artifacts (ranging from BBC sitcoms to anarcho-punk songs). A brief historiographical discussion in the introduction helps situate Riley’s work within a broader movement toward decolonizing and repositioning modern British history.

papers.title: John Ma. Polis: A New History of the Ancient Greek City-State from the Early Iron Age to the End of Antiquity
papers.abstract: The city-state (polis) is undoubtedly one of the most fundamental aspects of Greek history. John Ma’s Polis: A New History of the Ancient Greek City-State from the Early Iron Age to the End of Antiquity is a monumental study of the history of the Greek polis in the very long term. It starts from the collapse of the Bronze Age palaces around 1200 BCE and takes the story to the end of ancient poleis around 600 CE; alongside the immense temporal extent, Ma impressively covers the whole of the Eastern Mediterranean. In my view, this is unquestionably the most significant contribution to the study of Greek history over the last two decades. Until the 1980s, the study of the Greek polis was dominated by a simple narrative: The polis emerged around 700 BCE as a result of major social, economic, and political transformations. The late archaic and the early classical period (600–400 BCE) constituted the golden age of the polis; during these centuries the polis provided the framework for all important achievements of Greek history. By the fourth century BCE, though, the polis could no longer cope with growing economic and social crises, or compete geopolitically with larger actors, like the Macedonian and Hellenistic kingdoms; accordingly, the postclassical polis was either dead, or in serious malaise. As a result of these assumptions, most studies of the polis have focused on the archaic and classical periods. In recent decades, Hellenistic historians have seriously challenged this narrative and have shown the vitality of the Hellenistic polis; furthermore, they have documented the remarkable phenomenon that Hellenistic poleis overwhelmingly described their political systems as democracies: Were Hellenistic poleis the golden age of democracy rather than classical Athens?

papers.title: Nathaniel Mathews. Zanzibar Was a Country: Exile and Citizenship Between East Africa and the Gulf .
papers.abstract: Zanzibar Was a Country is the best book written on Zanzibar political history in over a decade. Beyond that, this work clearly has larger implications for other histories by enriching historians’ understanding of diverse subjects such as identity, diaspora, memory, and the interplay between decolonization and national belonging in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Nathaniel Mathews tells the story of the muwalladūn, individuals of mixed Arab and African descent who were born in the Zanzibar Protectorate but who were forced to flee in the wake of the 1964 Zanzibar Revolution. Before the arrival of the British, the isles were ruled by an Omani Arab dynasty; when the British departed in December 1963, they left in place a constitutional monarchy that was quickly overthrown in a bloody revolution a month later by African nationalists who deposed the sultan and incited an anti-Arab pogrom. Mathews chronicles the lives of these exiles from the years leading up to the revolution until the present day. While parts of this narrative have been told by scholars of both East Africa and Oman, such as James Brennan and Abdel Razzaq Takriti, respectively, Mathews is the first scholar to center this history on the diasporic Zanzibaris themselves and comprehensively tell the story from their perspective—a retelling only made possible by Mathews’s mastery of both Arabic and Kiswahili, allowing him to draw on the rich source materials from both languages and regions. In the process, he has illumined the complicated phenomena of the untangling of empires and the re-entanglement of peoples across postcolonial borders.

papers.title: Baijayanti Roy. The Nazi Study of India and Indian Anti-Colonialism: Knowledge Providers and Propagandists in the ‘Third Reich.’
papers.abstract: That the Nazis had a special interest in India is immediately apparent. As part of their self-mythologization, they linked themselves to the Indian subcontinent—think of the swastika—within the framework of their pseudoscientific theories about the Aryan race. As is now well known and thoroughly researched, this Nazi appropriation of India was the culmination of a long German tradition of Indomania, which originated in German Romanticism and unfolded in multiple directions throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. We can even pinpoint quite precisely when this particular German-language interest in India began: with Friedrich Schlegel’s Über die Sprache und der Indier (1808). Schlegel’s treatise sparked an enduring interest in Indian thought, broadly construed—sometimes purely philosophical, religious, or spiritual; sometimes infused with colonial fantasies; and, most consequentially, giving rise to a radicalized, antisemitic vision of an Indo-Germanic bond that the Nazis eagerly adopted and expanded in their ideology. This long and complex chapter has been examined by numerous scholars, most notably Suzanne Marchand, Doug McGetchin, and Perry Myers, each of whom has explored different aspects of Germany’s intellectual engagement with India. Yet one key question remained unanswered: What did the Nazis actually know about India? Thanks to Baijayanti Roy’s new book titled The Nazi Study of India and Indian Anti-Colonialism: Knowledge Providers and Propagandists in the ‘Third Reich’, we now have an answer.

papers.title: Elizabeth R. Williams. States of Cultivation: Imperial Transition and Scientific Agriculture in the Eastern Mediterranean .
papers.abstract: What does it mean to talk about the “post-Ottoman” period? That is, when, how, and where have Ottoman legacies and antecedents shaped the modern Middle East? papers.title: David N. Livingstone. The Empire of Climate: A History of an Idea .
papers.abstract: Global warming has restored climate and weather as serious topics for historians and social scientists. Yet after decades of avoiding these subjects, are scholars now succumbing to the same crude climate determinism that seduced writers of the late 19th and early 20th centuries? Geographer David Livingstone believes they are, and in The Empire of Climate: A History of an Idea, he argues for a direct continuity of ideas about climate and society from ancient Hippocratic thinkers through the Enlightenment to apologists of slavery and imperialism and down to present-day pundits projecting catastrophic effects from global warming. Though erudite and forcefully written, Empire of Climate ultimately fails to persuade. If anything, the breadth and depth of Livingstone’s subject emphasizes the diversity of past and present ideas about climate and society and the inadequacy of the single label “climate determinism.” Following a substantial introduction, Livingstone’s monograph is structured around four themes. Part I (“Health”) traces ideas about climate’s influence on human constitutions. The first of its three chapters examines the humoral theory of medicine and the search for salubrious climates from Hippocrates to modern health tourism. The following chapters turn to tropical medicine, acclimatization theories, and fears of tropical disease in the context of 19th-century British imperialism, and then to the intersection of biometeorology, pseudoscientific racism, and eugenics in the United States at the turn of the 20th century. Part II (“Mind”) first discusses recent science and speculation about links between Pleistocene climatic variability and human evolution, while implying that these theories are little more than 19th-century “environmental determinism reborn” (156). It next situates concerns over the mental health impacts of global warming within a longer history of ideas about seasons and moods, from early modern notions of weather and “melancholy” to 20th-century theories about temperatures and temperaments. Part III (“Wealth”) examines ideas throughout the centuries associating economic success with temperate latitudes as well as theories associating tropical climates with poverty and servitude. Finally, in part IV (“War”) Livingstone compares present fears about global warming and global conflicts to 19th-century climate determinist explanations for the US Civil War.

papers.title: Patricia Cleary. Mound City: The Place of the Indigenous Past and Present in St. Louis
papers.abstract: Despite the fame of the Cahokia Mounds across the river from St. Louis, Missouri, few are aware that the city was itself built around and atop another mound site or that these mounds were once central to the city’s identity. papers.title: Richard Stone. Bristol and the Birth of the Atlantic Economy, 1500–1700.
papers.abstract: As its title suggests, Bristol and the Birth of the Atlantic Economy, 1500–1700 by Richard Stone contributes to the “Atlantic” turn in the study of the early modern world, including the revived debate regarding the role of slavery in fueling European, especially British, economic growth. papers.title: Surviving the Bomb in Diaspora
papers.abstract: Abstract Uncovering the voices of the Korean diasporic atomic bomb survivors across multilingual and transimperial spaces in archives and memories in East Asia and the Americas, this article explores the historical meaning of compensatory justice for those who have been deprived of their national right of redress. Their history exposes the fundamental limits of the postcolonial discourse on human rights that has privileged justice adjudicated by nation-states. In the United States, linguist R. Joe Campbell has played a key role in this process. The Nahua: Language and Culture from the Sixteenth Century to the Present pays fitting homage to Campbell’s life’s work. For historians who may be most familiar with James Lockhart’s “New Philology” developed at the University of California, Los Angeles, in the 1970s–90s, the volume is an exemplary guide to other schools of thought and disciplinary approaches, from several generations of leading scholars in the United States, Mexico, and Europe. The first two chapters lay the necessary groundwork and demystify the term “Classical Nahuatl,” which refers to the variant of the language dominant in central Mexico at the time of Spanish invasion and should not be confused with the archaeological “Classic” period of Teotihuacán and the Maya lowlands from 300–800 CE. As Galen Brokaw and Pablo García Loaeza explain, this variant formed the bedrock of a new standardization created by Nahua and Spanish intellectuals in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The stakes could not have been higher; in a context of religious repression, imperialism, and demographic disaster, ancient and unique writing systems that constituted rare examples in world history of the independent development of script were replaced by a single Latin-based standard that only partially succeeded in capturing the richness of Nahuatl and other Mesoamerican languages. Brokaw and García Loaeza survey this transition in the early Spanish colonial period from semasiographic Mesoamerican to alphabetic European writing. They also survey the major schools of Nahuatl studies in Mexico and the United States (Europe and other parts of the world are not addressed, although some of their practitioners are cited).

papers.title: James Barnaby. Religious Conflict at Canterbury Cathedral in the Late Twelfth Century: The Dispute between the Monks and the Archbishops, 1184–1200
papers.abstract: The history reconstructed in James Barnaby’s Religious Conflict at Canterbury Cathedral in the Late Twelfth Century, a fascinating exercise on monastic microhistory, is uniquely English—that is to say, it could only have occurred in medieval England because of the peculiar circumstance that some medieval English cathedrals were staffed not by chapters of canons, as was the case everywhere in continental Europe, but by Benedictine monks. This situation, which arose from the reforms of English monasticism in the tenth century, meant that some bishops were also exofficio abbots. Archbishops of Canterbury, whether they were themselves monks or not, were also abbots of Christ Church, the Benedictine community that served as a chapter for the cathedral. Tensions between bishops and their cathedral chapters were, of course, a regular feature of episcopal life, but when the chapter was a monastic community, the stakes could be higher and the fallout more serious. For one thing, the Rule of Benedict required abbots to be elected by the community, but few kings—or popes, for that matter—were willing to permit the head of the Church of England to be elected simply by the monks of Christ Church. Then there was the question of resources. As episcopal governance became increasingly sophisticated and demanding, bishops needed an increasingly specialist household, for whom provision had to be made from the resources of the bishopric. Whereas this could be done in a chapter of cathedral canons by using prebendaries, this was not possible in a monastic chapter. Disputes over the proper use of the community’s resources were inevitable. One twelfth-century bishop, Hugh de Nonant, bishop of Coventry, even expelled the monks of his chapter in 1186 and replaced them with regular canons, an act that occasioned an assault on his person by one of the monks wielding a crucifix.

papers.title: José Juan Pérez Meléndez. Peopling for Profit in Imperial Brazil: Directed Migrations and the Business of Nineteenth-Century Colonization.
papers.abstract: In 1974, the Brazilian federal government issued a postage stamp entitled “Migratory Streams.” The stamp, part of a larger set hailing diversity by using ostensibly historical illustrations of different ethnic groups, tells the official story of Brazilian identity as synonymous with the nation’s immigrants. The imagery includes a map with Brazil surrounded by faces that represent human movement from Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas, suggesting that people were central to the legislators who had crafted immigration policy. José Juan Pérez Meléndez’s excellent book, Peopling for Profit in Imperial Brazil: Directed Migrations and the Business of Nineteenth-Century Colonization, rejects that position, arguing that revenue buttressed the empire’s immigration policies leading up to mass immigration at the end of the century and beyond. Pérez Meléndez takes a different, and welcome, approach from many studies of migration in Latin America. He shows how, as empires waned, new ideas about commerce created global migration patterns critical to the transformation of the Brazilian state and economy. This “Global Brazil” approach is an important intervention since it presents Brazil neither as marginal nor as a country operating independently of the world around it. The book’s opening map is a visual representation of Pérez Meléndez’s position, showing Brazil as a geographical global center, just as the aforementioned stamp did. By focusing on themes like recruitment and transportation, Peopling for Profit reminds us that the nineteenth-century world was as deeply interconnected by ideas about state building as it was by people and goods.

papers.title: Deborah Sutton. Ruling Devotion: The Hindu Temple in the Imperial Imagination, 1800–1946
papers.abstract: Deborah Sutton’s Ruling Devotion: The Hindu Temple in the Imperial Imagination contributes to the growing literature on Hindu temples in historical, art historical, and political contexts. Sutton is not concerned, however, with Hindu temples and their complex archeology, intricate carvings, and plentiful devotees; nor does she address the range of rituals that take place therein (though, of course, she acknowledges their importance). Rather, it is how the temple—which was variously understood in colonial history as “a site of enviable wealth, compelling depravity, architectural wonder, political sensitivity, and aesthetic appeal” (2)—and how the idea of the temple was mobilized variously throughout colonial history that Sutton expertly explores through deep archival research. In other words, Sutton explores the idea of the Hindu temple as it appears in historic, literary, and academic discourses in order to demonstrate how this discourse was utilized to justify continued colonial rule in South Asia. Sutton’s history of the Hindu temple in colonial discourse begins in the years following the eighteenth-century Carnatic wars in south India. Focusing on three temples in particular—the Srirangam, Jambukeswarar, and Thayumanar temples, all located in present-day Tiruchirapalli district—Sutton demonstrates the way that the British East India Company’s failure to understand elements of the temple (such as the organizational structure, financial management, and rituals) affected their (mis)management of the temples. The ambivalence of British authorities toward Hindu temples, which both fascinated and disgusted them, resulted in an overall discomfort that comes across in the archives as racially coded malice toward local temple managers. Despite this discomfort, the Company still benefited from these very same temples until Evangelist missionary campaigns eventually succeeded in ending the Company’s support of “idolatry” (and thus, Company involvement in temple administration altogether) in 1841.

papers.title: Jane Ohlmeyer. Making Empire: Ireland, Imperialism, and the Early Modern World
papers.abstract: In December 2020, amid the Black Lives Matter and Rhodes Must Fall protests, Professor Jane Ohlmeyer published an article in The Irish Times arguing that Ireland had yet to come to terms with its imperial past, citing, among several examples, the ownership of enslaved persons by eighteenth-century philosopher George Berkeley, which occasioned a “denaming” and eventual renaming of a library by Ohlmeyer’s university, Trinity College Dublin. The article prompted much debate and some backlash, as a trawl of social media and the Times’ letter pages will show. In Making Empire: Ireland, Imperialism, and the Early Modern World, Ohlmeyer returns to these key questions of ­­Ireland’s place in early modern imperialism, in a sweeping and impressive account that spans four ­­centuries of global history. Based on her James Ford lectures in 2021, Ohlmeyer presents a compelling synthesis of current scholarship and approaches to Ireland and empire, while making some important interventions based on original research. The book is thus simultaneously a masterful overview of this broad field, while advancing some new insights for those already engaged in its intricacies. Using Brian Friel’s 1988 play Making History as the overarching frame, the book literally sets the stage for a discussion of the complexities of Ireland and the Irish relationship with empire: the ideological underpinnings that were tested and honed on the island; how its people went out—both willingly and unwillingly—to participate in it; and what effects early modern imperialism had “back home,” evocatively captured in a 1660s recipe that evoked “the world in a potato pie” (176). As Friel’s Archbishop Peter Lombard declaims, it is “the time for a critical assessment” and “another history”—something that Ohlmeyer evidently firmly believes in, demanding that historians “change the questions we ask” of Ireland’s past (19). This framing, while offering some interesting vignettes, also has its limitations: It feels as if there is no real introduction or conclusion, and this together with the book’s inconsistent approach to explaining and engaging with chronologies may be off-putting for the nonspecialist.

papers.abstract: Bernard F. Reilly (1925–2021) approached the history of the eleventh- and twelfth-century Castilian-Leonese monarchs with the storytelling finesse of a Hollywood screenwriter, skillfully crafting a saga that unfolded through sequels and prequels. In fact, this latest book, León and Galicia Under Queen Sancha and King Fernando I, published forty-two years after his first political biography of Queen Urraca—granddaughter of Sancha and Ferdinand—thirty-six years after his seminal study of Alfonso VI, their son, and twenty-six years after his examination of Alfonso VII’s reign, their great-grandson, acts as a prequel to his earlier works on the Castilian-Leonese dynasty. Reilly’s work has been instrumental in shedding light on the key reigns to understand the Iberian Peninsula at a crucial time. Now, with the decisive collaboration of Simon R. Doubleday, this book emerges as a significant addition to the understanding of that period, revisiting the reign of Sancha and Fernando I, a pivotal moment in the consolidation of the royal power in the western Iberian Peninsula.

papers.title: Jeffrey M. Pilcher. Hopped Up: How Travel, Trade, and Taste Made Beer a Global Commodity
papers.abstract: The relatively young field of alcohol studies is witnessing a growth in scholarship with a global scope. Truly global coverage is particularly scarce as viable points of comparison across cultures and time periods is difficult. Jeffrey M. Pilcher sets out to address this gap with his engaging and detailed book that examines the development of beer from the medieval period to the 21st century. In Hopped Up, Pilcher focuses particularly on the rise of lager, weaving together analyses of technological, economic, and cultural history, determined to show how all three worked together in the development of beer as a global commodity. It is an ambitious work. He sets the stage by exploring the development of fermented drinks from ancient times, including regional drinking cultures across the ancient Near East, Africa, China, and the Americas. He includes the almost universal role of women in brewing beer in ancient societies as well as how societies used beer styles as a means to claim status. From this background he analyzes the role of technology from the early modern period. Technological development is one of the dominant themes, and a particular strength, throughout the book. He provides detailed explanations of how the introduction of hops in the 13th century began to change both the taste of beer as well as add the stability necessary for long distance trade. German brewers were able to increase their scale of production as well as the breadth of their markets, which grew throughout Europe over the next 300 years.

papers.title: Andrés I. Prieto. The Theologian and the Empire: A Biography of José de Acosta (1540–1600)
papers.abstract: There is no need to repeat that José de Acosta (1540–1600) was one of the pioneering Jesuits who established the general missionary policy in colonial Spanish America during the second half of the sixteenth century, a policy that continued until the end of the eighteenth century. His “religious and intellectual significance is comparable only to that of the Dominican friar Bartolomé de Las Casas (1484–1566)” (1). He is also world renowned as a protoanthropologist and naturalist, primarily because of his publication Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590). However, The Theologian and the Empire written by Andrés I. Prieto focuses on a different aspect: Acosta’s role as a “colonial” or “imperial agent” (1, 5). In reality, “Acosta focused on the necessity to create and maintain an adequate colonial superstructure supported by native labor that would allow for a robust colonial church to emerge” (7). In other words, Prieto’s book is highly valuable for shedding light on Acosta’s political activism, particularly focusing on his other famous soteriological treatise on the Indigenous people of the Americas, De procuranda Indorum salute (1588). As Prieto notes in his book, the discussion in De procuranda was adopted beyond the Americas, in regions such as South Asia and Africa (1).

papers.title: Jorell Meléndez-Badillo. Puerto Rico: A National History
papers.abstract: Puerto Rico: A National History argues that recognizing the archipelago’s colonial reality is crucial to understanding its past. Central to this study is what the author deems the Puerto Rican nation’s “ambiguous nature” (xiii), which renders it difficult to delineate a beginning or an end to its story. The book’s narrative ranges from pre-Columbian times through the 2020s, highlighting the creation of “circuits of self-determination” that people use to “experiment with freedom practices” (xiv) to affirm the existence of a Puerto Rican nation. Though the author abstains from defining the nation, tales about Puerto Ricans who migrated to the United States suppose its diasporic character. The book’s length is short (217 pages of text) and its language semi-academic. Yet the author’s attempts to cater to both scholarly and popular audiences present significant trade-offs and their own ambiguities. Though the settlement of Borikén, the islands that became Puerto Rico, took thousands of years, the book’s contents heavily emphasize the period that followed the US invasion of 1898. Seven of the fifteen chapters cover the “American” twentieth century by tracing the shortcomings of colonial projects, their effects on Puerto Rican society, and their contestation by liberation movements. The last four chapters discuss the twenty-first century by focusing nearly entirely on the effects of austerity measures and the impact of Hurricane María, providing an incomplete assessment because of their glorification of antigovernment actions. Puerto Rico’s organization follows the traditional logic of Puerto Rican historiography, using political-economic development and profiles of imperial intervention as frames to outline elements that may fit the narrative of a single “national history.”

papers.title: Christoph Rosenmüller. Viceroy Güemes’s Mexico: Rituals, Religion, and Revenue.
papers.abstract: Since the 1980s, the Bourbon Reforms stood as a watershed in Spanish American history. Scholars debated the extent to which they were successful, their scope and reach, whether they formed a coherent project, and their relationship to Spanish American independence. But there was little disagreement that change began in the aftermath of the Seven Years’ War (1756–63) and that, culminating during the tenure of José de Gálvez as minister for the Indies (1776–87), Spanish authorities had embarked on an effort to significantly transform imperial governance, revenue collection, and naval and military structures in Spanish America. Bourbon reformism came to define the region’s history during the late eighteenth century. That consensus began to crumble as, from the mid-2000s, a growing volume of scholarship focusing on the earlier and largely ignored part of the century highlighted a long series of previous reforms. These have been characterized as precursors of, laying the foundations for, and often more effective and successful than those introduced after the 1760s. In Viceroy Güemes’s Mexico, Christoph Rosenmüller adds to this scholarship, boldly suggesting that “it is now hard to say what the term ‘Bourbon Reforms’ should mean, and when they began or ended” (148), inviting us instead to think about imperial reform as an ongoing process stretching as far back as the late seventeenth century.

papers.title: Malcolm Ebright and Rick Hendricks. Pablo Abeita: The Life and Times of a Native Statesman of Isleta Pueblo, 1870–1940.
papers.abstract: By the start of the twentieth century, three hundred years of settler colonialism in modern Canada and the United States reached an apogee. Conquest, capitulation, and genocide resulted in the wreckage of Indigenous economies, the reshaping of cultures and social relations, and the loss of political independence to direct colonial rule. Indigenous nations also faced a renewed, reorganized, and intense national program of cultural genocide, with federal schools and federally subsidized church-run schools as a centerpiece. Amid resistance and adaptation, a relatively small but growing class of Indigenous people with high levels of formal Western education emerged, and some of them went on to become national activists. Much of their voluminous writings survived and ultimately fed good biographical scholarship. Recent work includes David Martinez, My Heart Is Bound Up with Them: How Carlos Montezuma Became the Voice of a Generation (2023), and two biographies by the late Tadeusz Lewandowski: Red Bird, Red Power: The Life and Times of Zitakala Ša (2016) and The Life of Sherman Coolidge, Arapaho Activist (2022). More broadly, historians have spent decades studying the Society of American Indians (SAI) and other national Indigenous activist organizations from the early twentieth century.

papers.title: Gale L. Kenny. Christian Imperial Feminism: White Protestant Women and the Consecration of Empire
papers.abstract: A book with a title like Christian Imperial Feminism leans heavily on terms and definitions. Author Gale L. Kenny uses the three title words to describe an intersectional sensibility that arose in white American Protestant women’s missionary organizations in the late nineteenth century and carried through to (still mostly white) American Protestant churchwomen’s organizations in the middle twentieth century. Where other scholars have noted discontinuities in this institutional history—a shift from emphasis on evangelism to more of a social work orientation, or the addition of a few Black leaders—Kenny highlights continuities. Whether they were raising money for overseas evangelism or trying, vainly, to open US borders to Jewish refugees during World War II, the missionary women and churchwomen consistently labored to create “an appealing and modern Christian cosmopolitanism that linked the hierarchical power dynamics of White women’s rescue fantasies of liberating religiously oppressed women to their seemingly more egalitarian vision of a Protestant and transnational community of women” (9). Put bluntly, these women wanted to achieve the best of all possible worlds through management by the best of all possible women—themselves. “Christian” meant their specific type of Protestantism; “imperial” meant global, but with a clearly demarcated center and periphery; and “feminism” meant not liberationist activism but gendered moral authority.

papers.title: Kelly S. McDonough. Indigenous Science and Technology: Nahuas and the World Around Them.
papers.abstract: Kelly S. McDonough’s book Indigenous Science and Technology: Nahuas and the World Around Them is a captivating piece of ethnohistorical writing. Boldly extending the boundaries of the discipline, it leaves readers with ample food for thought. McDonough combines engaged scholarship with rigorous scrutiny of historical sources, as well as innovative (sometimes controversial) methods of retrieving data and interpreting them, in a way that would serve both history and modern Nahua communities. She paves the way for future works of those Western scholars who wish to design and write up their research with respect and gratitude to the societies whose pasts they are studying. The Nahua culture that is the subject of Indigenous Science and Technology is one that, in the fifteenth century, produced the famous Aztec Empire, which, a century later, was invaded by the Spaniards and turned into a colony called “New Spain” (part of today’s Mexico). Although in subsequent decades the vast majority of these territories’ Indigenous populations perished in wars, epidemics, and forced labor systems, the Nahua culture has survived to this day. Consequently, the scholarly discourse about the past (precontact and colonial) Nahua affects their living descendants. Mindful of that, McDonough describes her approach as “grounded in the interdisciplinary field of critical Native American and Indigenous studies” (19). Instead of writing about the Nahua, as the traditional scholarship tends to, she chooses to write with or for the Nahua.

papers.title: Brian Patrick McGuire. Bernard of Clairvaux: An Inner Life
papers.abstract: Brian Patrick McGuire’s Bernard of Clairvaux: An Inner Life promises to take up the “state of mind” or the “inner conviction[s]” of Cistercian monk and abbot Bernard of Clairvaux (1090-1153), who was among the most creative thinkers of the Middle Ages and who exerted unparalleled influence on the major intellectual and institutional developments that rocked 12th century Europe. His sharp, sensual, reasoned, and imaginative writings shaped centuries of Christian spirituality. Attuned to the extreme reactions Bernard elicits among modern readers, McGuire is committed to presenting a portrait of Bernard that neither dismisses him as “intolerant and unsympathetic” nor reduces him to a saint cast in saccharine hues and instead aims to unveil the monk in his complexity (2). McGuire’s commitment to holding together Bernard’s subtle and sublime insights with his frequently brusque and brutal interventions is much needed and commendable. The book is divided into two major sections. The first section travels through Bernard’s life in rough chronological order, and a second section, “Fifteen Questions,” provides what McGuire calls “the background” for this study (xv). The book also contains a chronological list of significant events in Bernard’s life, a bibliography, and two maps, one of Champagne and Burgundy (Bernard’s home territory) and one of Cistercian monasteries—whose number explored under Bernard’s influence—established by the time of the abbot’s death. It is a real misfortune that McGuire restricts notes to “Fifteen Questions,” an omission he explains as in service of maintaining “the integrity of the text” (xv).

papers.title: Kristen L. McCleary. Staging Buenos Aires: Theater, Society, and Politics in Argentina, 1860–1920
papers.abstract: Kristen L. McCleary’s Staging Buenos Aires: Theater, Society, and Politics in Argentina, 1860–1920 offers a well-researched study of Argentina’s popular theater from its origins to its golden age in the early twentieth century. This is a particularly important contribution for English-language readers, as few monographs on Argentine theater have focused on this time period. The book examines the development of popular theater in this era and argues that, as the city’s main form of leisurely activity, it was not only a reflection of Argentina’s political and social processes but also a key site for their unfolding—including the formation of a national identity; modernization; democratization; and, most importantly, as the author argues, the emergence of a middle-class consciousness. The book begins with a historical overview of the development of Argentine theater, from colonial times to the 1920s, tracing how colonial practices, such as censorship and proselytism (political or religious), were still in effect in the early twentieth century. Through the analysis of various cases of censorship—ranging from popular theater’s beginnings to its massification—the first chapter attempts to show how theater was seen and used as a tool to force and instill ideas of nationhood and citizenship. Interestingly, McCleary reveals throughout the book, that censorship was often accompanied and resisted by “democratic spaces” (84)—created by practitioners and audiences alike—from public exchanges and negotiations surrounding censorship, to the formation of writers’ and actors’ guilds that defended their rights, as well as the social critique and satire conveyed on the stage.

papers.title: Digital humanities and social justice: a case-based approach
papers.abstract: Abstract Issues of Social Justice, broadly conceived, are increasingly being included as a component in digital humanities (DH) scholarship or are the reason d’etre of the research itself. Equally, issues of ethics, privacy, and copyright are taking on greater prominence in DH scholarship. This article focuses on the creation of a course for the #dariahTeach platform, Social Justice in the DH. This case-based course features a variety of scholarship, methods, theories, and communities and practices from around the globe that do research at the intersections of social justice and the DH. The article problematizes some of the issues and challenges of working within a social justice framework, highlights existing best practice, and explores issues of ethics, privacy, and copyright within the projects which differ, depending, not only on legal, but on moral frameworks. The additional duty of care when developing and disseminating content created by or about marginalised, indigenous, or minority populations, and/or those whose ethics and traditions differ from dominant western values is also highlighted. And lastly, the importance of taking these factors into account when conducting research in reparative ways, particularly in the context of contested histories and/or material cultures is considered.

papers.title: Unpacking the History of Higher Education
papers.abstract: Histories of higher education offer students and teachers opportunities to study political, social, and cultural history in particularly engaging ways. This module introduces the use of college and university digital archives to capture the rich histories of women’s sports, LGBTQ+ student experiences, and Hispanic-Serving Institutions. Contributors to the module were all participants in a 2024 National Endowment for the Humanities summer institute on higher education history that used digital archives to explore issues such as student activism, the legacies of slavery, internationalization, gender and sexuality, and the experiences of incarcerated students. The histories they tell are immediate and relevant to students attending these institutions today, providing a chance to see themselves (or not) in the archives.

papers.title: Michael D. Hattem. The Memory of ‘76: The Revolution in American History
papers.abstract: Michael D. Hattem’s book The Memory of ‘76 offers a much-needed and timely account of the meaning and legacy of the American Revolution in American culture from the nation’s beginnings to the present. As Hattem notes, despite the importance of the Revolution to American national identity, the memory of the Revolution as a whole has received surprisingly little attention from scholars. While there have been studies of specific aspects of that memory, such as Sarah Purcell’s Sealed with Blood: War, Sacrifice, and Memory in Revolutionary America (2002) or Alfred Young’s The Shoemaker and the Tea Party (1999), the only other broadly synthetic account of the memory of the Revolution comparable to Hattem’s is Michael Kammen’s A Season of Youth: The American Revolution and the Historical Imagination (1978). But where Kammen emphasizes how the Revolution was “de-revolutionized” and given a conservative cast, Hattem highlights the contested meaning of the Revolution throughout the nation’s history, showing how it was used to at once uphold and challenge the established social order. Consequently, Hattem departs from Kammen’s focus on mostly high culture—art, literature, and theater—in favor of more overtly politicized areas of contention such as political rhetoric, commemorative activities, and historic preservation, with the aim of integrating public history, formal historical writing, and popular culture.

papers.title: Traversing Multiple Sites of Transit: Repatriating “Mentally Distressed” British Seamen, 1925–30
papers.abstract: Abstract: This article examines the management of Distressed British Seamen (DBS) using surviving British Board of Trade records from the 1920s. In doing so, it positions merchant seamen who became incapacitated at sea as part of a global workforce who went through alternating periods of (im)mobility. By focusing on “mentally distressed” seamen institutionalized in multiple locations—home and abroad—and confined on steamships, this research exposes the complex legalities involved. We meet historical actors operating at different global “transfer-points”tasked with managing the 'mentally distressed’ in practical, financial, and altruistic terms. While Board of Trade officials were tasked with recouping repatriation costs, correspondence with seamen’s dependents and their advocates shows the emotional and economic ramifications of these lives “in-transit.” Ultimately this article helps answer the need to learn more about how practices governing steam-age mobility meant that some seamen had to traverse multiple sites of transit. papers.title: Marion Turner. The Wife of Bath: A Biography .
papers.abstract: “Alison of Bath is a middle-aged woman—a reasonably happy older woman (even if she might prefer to be younger)—still sexually active, still attractive, someone who works, goes on holidays, and enjoys life.” So Marion Turner begins chapter 1 of The Wife of Bath: A Biography, an imaginative and learned “biography” of one of Chaucer’s most famous characters. Part biography, part microhistory, and part literary reception study, Turner first explores this famous pilgrim in Chaucer’s own late fourteenth-century milieu and then in her cultural longevity and popularity as a figure who migrates out of The Canterbury Tales and into other authors’ creative works. papers.title: Communications
papers.abstract: Dear colleague, I am writing in response to a review of my book, A Slave Between Empires, that a colleague, Odile Moreau, contributed to the March 2025 issue of your journal. Usually, I do not reply to reviews of my books in academic journals. But the problematic nature of this review compels me to do so; it is biased, misleading, and full of mistakes. The book was awarded the Alf Andrew Heggoy Book Prize (from the French Colonial Historical Society) in 2021 for the best volume published in the preceding year dealing with the modern French colonial experience. It was also a finalist for the 2021 African Studies Association Best Book Prize. Yet in this instance, either the author did not understand the argument of the book, or she did not have the proper historical expertise to engage it. The reviewer does not discuss at all the argument of the book: namely, how to interpret the colonial history of North Africa and more precisely the history of colonial Tunisia through its own Ottoman legacy. She insists instead on details that are not relevant to the book’s core argument and goals. For instance, Moreau writes that “In addition to being very vague, however, the title is misleading, by fixing the category of slave in a static manner, whereas the book shows that Husayn’s trajectory and his status were very dynamic.” Titles are by definition very broad, and in this case, the title precisely highlights the main figure’s “in-betweenness.”
