papers.title: Cecily N. Zander. The Army under Fire: The Politics of Antimilitarism in the Civil War Era
papers.abstract: In our modern world, it seems unfathomable that a political party would challenge the necessity of the US military, much less outrightly refuse to support it. Nineteenth-century Americans, though, were cut from a different cloth. The events of the period, including a major war and the rise of the newly established Republican Party, combined with the distrust of a standing army held over from the early republic days, led many to attempt to dismantle the US Army, believing it to be a symbol of slavery. It is this topic that Cecily Zander ably covers in The Army Under Fire: The Politics of Antimilitarism in the Civil War Era. While the armies of the Union and Confederacy are the usual topics for military historians in this era, Zander provides a necessary addition to those works. Covering the period from the 1850s to the 1870s, Zander examines how politicians argued about the size and use of the US Army. The ideological position assumed by the Republicans, that of antimilitarism, Zander contends, limited the effectiveness of the military during a period of great challenge for Americans: in the South during the Civil War and Reconstruction, and in the West during the settlement of the region and the many Native American wars.

papers.title: Ian Atherton. Britons and Their Battlefields: War, Memory, and Commemoration since the Fourteenth Century.
papers.abstract: With Britons and Their Battlefields: War, Memory, and Commemoration since the Fourteenth Century, Ian Atherton sets out to chart a longue durée history of British commemoration. Using battlefields across eight centuries, he argues that the traditions of Bri­tish remembrance, so intertwined in popular thought with the world wars of the twentieth century, not only predate Remembrance Day but also draw heavily on Britain’s long martial traditions, the politics of nation and empire, and religious reformation. Britons and Their Battlefields employs a broad definition for both its title categories. Britons here include, at various times, the English, Scots, British, and various populations across the empire. This big-tent approach is particularly intriguing in Atherton’s analysis of battlefields and commemoration traditions from the English Civil War, the Jacobite Rebellion (1745–1746), and other conflicts that spilled blood on the soil of the British Isles, where monuments and commemoration take on even more loaded political implications and rivalries than they normally do. The definition of “battlefields” is equally broad. Atherton does an excellent job of demonstrating how what makes a battlefield has changed over the centuries, along with the changes in commemorations tied to such events and locations. Some of these evolutions are due to changing societal and religious mores, of course, but they are also influenced by the nature and locations of Britain’s conflicts.

papers.abstract: Tamrala Swafford Bliss’s book Wilma Mankiller: A Life in American History examines how Wilma Mankiller’s life (1945–2010) intersected with some of the most significant policies and events in Indian Country in the latter half of the twentieth century. Much of the book is devoted to the characteristics of Mankiller’s leadership style. Mankiller’s skills in organizing and motivating her community members came both from an adherence to Cherokee beliefs and from on-the-ground training in grassroots organizing. Throughout the text, Bliss returns to the Cherokee practice of gadugi. Bliss notes that the “most current usage of the term” means “working together for the good of the community” (xiv). Gadugi can also refer to “work crews” of Cherokee people who perform services for the community—including building and maintaining churches and stomp grounds, supporting elderly and sick community members, and rebuilding homes damaged by fire or floods (66). Gadugi is thus an active term, and practicing interdependence means getting things done for the betterment of the community.

papers.title: Susannah Gibson. The Bluestockings: A History of the First Women’s Movement
papers.abstract: Susannah Gibson’s The Bluestockings: A History of the First Women’s Movement explores the lives of the renowned Bluestocking women—an informal association of mostly upper-class women whose shared pursuit of intellectual study challenged contemporary beliefs of appropriately gendered behavior and capabilities. For Gibson, the Bluestocking salons enabled these women to “prove […] that they were capable of so much more than anyone believed possible” (4). Gibson possesses a power of description that works to transport readers to the Bluestockings’ salons, leading the reader to feel as if they are dining and conversing with guests, as if the reader knows each woman—her thoughts, feelings, and character—­­on a most intimate level. This style makes Bluestockings both informative and delightful, and it is written in such a way as to appeal to any reader interested in eighteenth-century histories of women, gender, and intellectualism. Gibson deploys a number of thematic lenses across eleven chapters, with something to interest readers from a wide range of scholarly backgrounds. A significant proportion of Gibson’s research is ­­centered, for example, around contemporary medi­­cal thought and practice; Bluestockings frequently includes detailed descriptions of ailments with which eighteenth-century women contended and the treatments they applied to cure themselves, their families, and friends. The seventh chapter of Bluestockings, “Motherhood,” is especially rich with such detail, explicating the remedies and practices applied, often seemingly in vain, by Bluestocking Hester Thrale to heal herself and her family from myriad afflictions. From her many uncomfortable pregnancies and the frequently fatal illnesses her children suffered to the sexually transmitted infections repeatedly contracted by her husband, Thrale oversaw the family’s care and often personally administered the recommended treatments of the time (159, 174–75). Gibson’s work offers critical insights to researchers of eighteenth-century English society that extend far beyond the salons of the Bluestocking women, and draws us into their sickrooms, still-rooms, and bed-chambers.

papers.title: Nico Slate. The Art of Freedom: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Making of Modern India .
papers.abstract: In The Art of Freedom: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Making of Modern India, Nico Slate introduces his readers to one of the most important and influential South Asian women of the twentieth century. It is said that—until relatively recently—there were more autobiographical writings by South Asian women themselves than biographies written about them. (It has been the other way round for South Asian men.) The process of recovering and piecing together the life stories of individual women—whether well known or not—was slow to get going, though now there is a growing corpus of publications that collectively addresses this historical deficit. In many cases, the challenge for biographers has been how to reconstruct lives from what are often scant or fragmented materials, sometimes only discovered by family members after the subject herself is no longer alive. A paucity of sources, however, does not apply in the case of Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay (or Kamaladevi, as Slate decides to call her). Prior to the appearance of this well-crafted biography, there have been others, both in Hindi and in English, testifying to Kamaladevi as a woman of substance whose achievements demand that proper attention be paid to her. Moreover, there is no shortage of her own words on which to draw. During the course of a long and extremely active life (1903–88), Kamaladevi wrote prodigiously in the form of published articles and reports, letters, and her own memoirs, all of which provide direct access to her thoughts and actions on a myriad matters.

papers.title: Julia Rombough. A Veil of Silence: Women and Sound in Renaissance Italy
papers.abstract: Anyone who has visited an Italian city such as Florence has experienced its unique sonic ambience—a cacophony of voices, shouts, songs, bells, sirens, doors opening and shutting at all hours—whose echoes are made more poignant somehow by the architecture. This noisiness isn’t just confined to the modern moment, however. If anything, early modern Italians were noisier; from early modern sources, we know that they made a great deal of noise, shouting insults at one another, crying their wares, calling out gride or official government proclamations, serenading one another, shouting the news, and in general fare baccano, or making a din. Julia Rombough’s A Veil of Silence: Women and Sound in Renaissance Italy explores this world and is a well-researched, ably argued, and insightful investigation of an understudied topic: the intersections between soundscapes, gender, and space in early modern Florence. Rombough sets the stage in the first chapter by discussing the striking demographics of women’s ­religious institutions in early modern Florence—approximately 19 percent of the female population lived in an enclosed institution, and there was roughly one nun for every seventeen residents, according to the 1632 census, many of whom were unwilling residents or women who forcibly professed for familial and economic reasons. As Rombough points out, the networks of religious institutions were extensive, and many Florentines had a female relative in one of these houses. This was particularly true for women of the aristocracy, but grand ducal policies toward women of mala vita, or ill fame, also pushed women believed to be at risk for the sex trade or repentant prostitutes into the growing number of charitable reforming institutions. Interestingly, Rombough has found that institutions like the Convertite and the Malmaritate were surrounded by active sex work zones and working-class enclaves. In such an atmosphere, concerns about unruly behavior seeping inside institutional walls were perhaps inevitable. Moreover, post-Tridentine reform stressed women’s silence as a crucial component of religious practice.

papers.title: Karen Lystra. Love and the Working Class: The Inner Worlds of Nineteenth Century Americans
papers.abstract: In Love and the Working Class, Karen Lystra turns her attention to courtship among the majority of ordinary nineteenth-century Americans. Having established middle-class courtship norms in Searching the Heart: Men, Women, and Romantic in Nineteenth-Century America (1992), Lystra wondered whether working folks had similarly romantic ideals and patterns of courtship. More than five thousand letters later, she has a clear answer: no. Lystra crucially expanded her scope beyond correspondence between courting couples to include letters to family and friends, who frequently functioned as go-betweens. She assembled a “geographically and racially diverse population of free people below the middle class” and focused on three drivers of separation: westward migration, the Gold Rush, and the Civil War (4). In the first chapter, she demonstrates that working-class writers were “extremely self-conscious about their deficiencies, even in letters to loved ones” (23). The content and treatment of these laboriously produced missives were strikingly different from those of middle-class writers. Less affluent correspondents were primarily group oriented, with “a tribal etiquette of sharing letters that was completely antithetical to romantic standards of privacy” (38). Hence, the reliance on vernacular poetry discussed in chapter 7: short rhymes’ and song lyrics’ “familiarity and easy memorization were part of their authenticity and charm, not the opposite” (197). Working-class courting couples did not emulate the interiority or erudition middle-class couples prized and sought to avoid ridicule by their tribe.

papers.title: Bayley J. Marquez. Plantation Pedagogy: The Violence of Schooling Across Black and Indigenous Space
papers.abstract: Each generation since Reconstruction, it seems, rediscovers Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute. Established by Samuel Chapman Armstrong on the grounds of Virginia’s Little Scotland plantation in 1868, the school adapted pedagogies from missionaries in Hawai’i to teach emancipated African Americans. It extended these methods to Native polities in the western United States, ultimately achieving global influence throughout the twentieth century. Planation Pedagogy by Bayley J. Marquez (Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians) reassesses Hampton for the twenty-first century. Turning to cultural geography, critical theory, and archival history, Marquez examines how Armstrong and Richard Henry Pratt, founder of Carlisle Indian Industrial School, believed African slavery in the United States held civilizing lessons for conquered Indigenous nations. If slavery removed Africans from their homelands and detribalized, Anglicized, and evangelized them in North America, the same process might be systematized for Native Americans through schooling. Marquez distills this discourse into a heuristic she calls “plantation pedagogy” and its two tenets: 1) that proximity to whiteness promoted civilization, and 2) that manual labor transformed people into productive subjects who would, in turn, transform land into productive property. This pedagogy aimed to reform Black and Indigenous peoples by teaching both “slavery and settlement” (3).

papers.title: Bryan Banks. Write to Return: Huguenot Refugees on the Frontiers of the French Enlightenment
papers.abstract: In Write to Return: Huguenot Refugees on the Frontiers of the French Enlightenment, Bryan Banks has written a fascinating and significant study of how Huguenots formulated an identity as refugees and advocated for religious toleration. At the heart of Write to Return are three arguments. First, Banks contends that the concept of suffering in Huguenot writing drifted away from a principle of faith built on religious foundations. In its place, Huguenot writers increasingly explained suffering in terms of its political meaning. Second, Huguenot writers in dialogue with the French Enlightenment adopted arguments supporting religious toleration, often in terms of the metaphor of the body politic. While community and universality animated their writing, theology did not entirely fade, and the limits of toleration led—by 1789—to demands for religious liberty. Third, the visibility of Huguenot refugees made possible new forms of sentimentalism that influenced the French Enlightenment. In the context of the 18th century, the increased attention to Huguenot experiences fostered conversations about rights that were universal, sentimental, and religious.

papers.title: Nina Janz. Remnants of Wehrmacht Soldiers: Burial and Commemoration Practices of German Soldiers of the Second World War in Russia and Europe, 1941–2023
papers.abstract: Roughly eighteen million German men served in Hitler’s armies, the Wehrmacht and the Waffen-SS, in World War II. Five million of them did not survive the war and were buried across Europe and North Africa, most of them in the Nazi-occupied territories of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. At the beginning of the war, the Nazis went to great lengths to honor German war deaths individually and collectively through military ceremonies and intricate rituals of burials and commemoration, taking up the cult of the fallen soldiers that had started with the rise of nationalism, drafted armies, and the concept of the citizen-soldier around 1800. But the abundance of losses since 1943, especially on the Eastern Front, left most of the graves unattended and often purposefully neglected or destroyed as symbols of German aggression, crimes, and genocide—until the end of the Cold War. While the West German Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge (VDK), or German War Graves Commission, assumed authority to recover and ­­cultivate the remains of German soldier across the battlefields of Western Europe and North Africa, only the end of the Cold War and a German-Russian war grave agreement established in 1992 allowed for expanding these activities into the Eastern hemisphere, including Russia. The activities, which culminated in the recovery of the remains of one million German soldiers through 2023, are at the core of Nina Janz’s Remnants of Wehrmacht Soldiers.

papers.title: Timothy C. Hart. Beyond the River, Under the Eye of Rome
papers.abstract: Timothy C. Hart’s Beyond the River, Under the Eye of Rome, a welcome addition to the field of Roman borderland studies, skillfully combines close reading of Greco-Roman ethnographic texts with environmental analysis and new archaeological data. The book’s geographic focus is on the Danube River and its watershed, with special attention to the Hungarian Plain and Pontic Steppe. Its chronological range is primarily from the second through fifth centuries CE, with some forays back to classical Greece and the early principate. It raises compelling and timely questions about the destructive power of ethnic stereotypes and the persistent tendency of societies like Rome to build borders out of a perceived need to protect themselves from being overrun by outsiders seen as threatening or inferior. At its core, Hart’s argument is straightforward—the Romans repeatedly failed to recognize the environmental and cultural realities of the Danube borderlands they sought to dominate. Indigenous people who lived in the region before the Roman arrival didn’t see the river as a dividing line; rather, the Danube lay at the center of a unified ecological and cultural zone. Rome’s establishment of a militarized border along the river in the first century CE—the Danube limes—thus profoundly disturbed the region’s migratory patterns and rhythms. Although force and ideology enabled the empire to maintain its imposed boundary for centuries, Roman policy was ultimately self-­­defeating for two main reasons. First, the navigable tributaries and traversable plains that defined much of the region extended on both sides of the Danube and undermined its suitability as a barrier against north-south migration. Second, the dated and inaccurate ethnographic tropes that the Romans used to categorize the various “barbarian” peoples who lived beyond the river led them to make disastrous policy decisions when confronting groups such as the Tervingi Goths or Huns, whose behavior did not align with expectations. Roman blindness to the environmental realities of the Danube watershed and the actual characteristics of the people who occupied the region, especially during late antiquity, ultimately led to the destruction of the limes system.

papers.title: Charmian Mansell. Female Servants in Early Modern England

papers.title: Jessica Marie Otis. By the Numbers: Numeracy, Religion, and the Quantitative Transformation of Early Modern England
papers.abstract: “Numbers were a socially pervasive technology of knowledge,” writes Jessica Marie Otis in By the Numbers, “with the power to shape modes of thought” (158). Yet one of the key points of this excellent book is that numbers were no more a single technology than mills. As Otis carefully shows, the use of numbers was complex, multifaceted, and dynamic, involving a number (so to speak) of techniques; tools; media; and social, cultural, and intellectual commitments. Reading this book, one quickly begins to wonder whether numeracy itself is too broad and too blunt a concept to have much purchase in any such fine-grained historical analysis of early modern ideas and practices of counting, measuring, calculating, or recording. Like the “quantifying spirit” that haunts many studies of these topics but is not conjured here, it encompasses too much and explains too little. Otis, for her part, uses the introduction to make the case for “recogniz[ing] early modern English numeracies, plural, within the overarching formula of early modern numeracy, singular” (10). Important to this case is a set of distinctions maintained throughout the book between the various linked but separately moving parts that “numeracy” tends to collapse: numbers as symbolic systems, numerical practices, mathematical education, and the wider, dynamic contexts of literacy and communications technology. The first chapter enriches this immensely via an in-depth survey of different systems, from performative systems of hand-counting and oral numeration through object-based systems involving slates, tally sticks, and counting boards (lovingly explored and explained here), through to written systems, including number words and Roman and Arabic numerals.

papers.title: David Cowan. Politics of the Past: Inter-war Memories and the Making of British Popular Politics, 1939–2009
papers.abstract: How can we trace the histories of stories? This excellent monograph by David Cowan charts how the memories, histories, and stories of the interwar period in Britain have been shaped and have influenced politics and society since. Politics of the Past brings together history, politics, and the family in new and fascinating ways, making several important contributions to the field of modern British history. There are three key points made by the book: that stories have a history that must be interrogated; that politics is an everyday practice made in conversations between family members, workmates, and friends; and bringing those two points together—that the twentieth century was by no means a period of increasing political apathy, but one in which individuals were often deeply engaged in political matters. By looking beyond political parties and other institutions and instead delving into the intimate spaces of the family, Cowan shows a different way of thinking about individual politics. The home and family, as he puts it, “facilitated forms of political thinking rooted in everyday discussions” (103). Cowan forges an approach of not only bringing together but also better understanding the “reciprocal relationship between family and politics” (10). Through reused social research materials, Cowan gives many fascinating examples of how “recollections became mutual productions between family members” (153). It’s a convincing argument: that politics is less what happens in debates between MPs but is what is thrashed out, argued about, between relatives and friends, between different generations, over kitchen tables.

papers.title: Matthew Rowley. Godly Violence in the Puritan Atlantic World, 1636–1676
papers.abstract: Between the outbreak of the Pequot War in the mid-1630s and the conclusion of King Philip’s War four decades later, Puritans on both sides of the Atlantic perpetrated more than their fair share of violence. By the end of the 17th century, Native Americans, English royalists, Irish Catholics, and Scots Presbyterians had all experienced firsthand the brutality of which hot Protestants were capable when they unsheathed their swords. Matthew Rowley’s new monograph, Godly Violence in the Puritan Atlantic World, asks how this violence was justified and seeks to uncover the complex processes by which the godly imposed providential meaning on their experiences of warfare. If all Christians in the 17th century could agree that God spoke through dramatic military events, what exactly was he saying? Which biblical and theological resources were enlisted to help interpret the divine messages that were spelled out in blood? These are undoubtedly important questions, not least since historians over the past few decades have demonstrated just how central providentialism was to political decision-making during the 1640s and 1650s. After an opening section setting out the book’s structure and methodological approach, Godly Violence shows how Puritans went about establishing when conflict was legitimate and outlines some of the problems they contended with when doing so. As well as confronting countless New Testament injunctions to peace, charity, and mercy, the godly were consistently discomforted by the multivalence of providence. Was God on the side of victors in battle? Or was he merely using them as instruments to admonish his chosen, sinful people? Almost any event could be—and was—read as evidence of God’s continued favor. The Presbyterian minister Edward Gee recognized after the Battle of Dunbar in 1650 that each side would interpret the result “as the respective quarrel of each unto them hath led them” (182). However, there was also a broader Protestant anxiety about Christians claiming divine inspiration when taking up arms. Hence, as Rowley shows clearly, most Protestant theologians were eager to argue that a holy war was a just war and vice versa. Parliamentarians in the 1640s claimed that their campaign against the king was both defensive—and therefore just—and supported by the dictates of scripture and providence.

papers.title: Vince L. Bantu. Those for Whom the Lamp Shines. The Making of Egyptian Ethnic Identity in Late Antiquity .
papers.abstract: Vince Bantu’s Those for Whom the Lamp Shines reads Egyptian sources through the lens of ethnicity, arguing that a latent ethnic identity emerged immediately after the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) and reached maturity around 700 CE (126, 141). The study charts the collapse of ethnic and religious identities—hence, “Egyptian” became synonymous with “Miaphysite”—and it promotes ethnicity as the optimal paradigm for reading the sources of this era (10–12, 129). Chapter 1 introduces ethnicity as a methodology, while dismissing older nationalist readings. Chapter 2 explores the universal Christian ideal of community and empire that dominated until Chalcedon, after which “ethnic thinking” emerged, deepening the Chalcedonian Schism; chapters 3 to 5 detail this evolutionary process. The last chapter identifies ethnic consciousness as the source of tensions even between Syrian and Egyptian Miaphysites. The volume raises new questions and thoroughly employs its chosen methodology, though it also poses many interpretive challenges. Methodologically, it groups and analyzes texts pertaining to the same historical figure(s) to demonstrate continuity in ethnic rhetoric. Nonetheless, the focus is typically on the period when the historical figure lived, not when a source was drafted. This dilutes historical context and ideological shifts within each cluster of texts, which—not infrequently—contains documents separated by centuries (e.g., Samuel of Qalamun’s dossier in chapter 5). Inconsistent historiographic discussions exacerbate this problem across the volume. For example, the precursors to the History of the Patriarchs are not discussed, and the work is glossed as a 10th-century composition of Sawirus ibn al-Muqaffa‘ (101), though it should be read as a late-11th-century work by Mawhub ibn Mansur (see publications by Johannes den Heijer, Perrine Pilette, and Mark Swanson).

papers.title: Brian D. Laslie. Fighting from Above: A Combat History of the US Air Force
papers.abstract: Brian Laslie takes a long view in Fighting from Above, arguing that “an American air force existed long before the United States Air Force [USAF] became a separate and independent service.” He breaks this long view into just four epochs (compared to ten or even twenty-seven “propositions,” “attributes,” or “dicta” of airpower proposed by some scholars), enough to demonstrate significant trends, but not so many that readers lose track of meaningful conclusions. This is also more than just another chronological or topical survey of airpower or USAF history. Instead, Laslie asks: “is it possible to discern a unique ‘way of war’ for the Air Force?”(4). This question shapes both the periodization and content of his excellent study. Epoch 1, “Period of ­Discovery, 1907–1941,” begins when the US Army Signal Corps established its aeronautical branch and ends when the United States entered World War II. This section describes the fumbling invention of various roles for military aviation during World War I, along with the interwar ascendance of the yet-unproven concept of strategic bombing. Epoch 2, “Strategic Dominance, 1942–1975,” encompasses the costly evolution of US strategic bombing from optimistic theory to brutal practice during World War II, followed by decades of single-minded focus on this mission, with long-range bombers providing both nuclear deterrence and the raison d’être for an independent postwar USAF. ­Laslie aptly describes Korea and Vietnam—including the repeated need to reinvent tactical air support for ground troops—as “aberrations that the Air Force was not prepared to accept” (114). During Epoch 3, “Tactical Ascendancy, 1975–2019,” the “fighter generals,” who as junior officers had fought the air war over Vietnam, finally displaced the postwar “bomber mafia” stranglehold on USAF leadership (128). Under their direction, the USAF shifted to a tactical-strategic mix in which fighters and bombers filled both roles using a combination of air-to-air missiles, precision-guided munitions, and stealth technology. A chapter on Desert Storm and the Balkans campaigns, and another on US military intervention in Afghanistan and Iraq, highlight the capabilities, achievements, and limitations of USAF airpower in recent conflicts. Finally, “An Unmanned Future?” ventures into current events, speculating that “even now the Air Force is entering into or, at the very least, moving toward a fourth epoch that could fundamentally alter its current way of war: that being the era of the unmanned aerial vehicles and a second space age” (5).

papers.title: Jane Webster. Materializing the Middle Passage: A Historical Archaeology of British Slave Shipping, 1680–1807
papers.abstract: The year 2023 was good for historians of Britain’s Atlantic slave trade. It saw the publication of two important studies that have deepened and extended our knowledge of that grisly commerce. Jane Webster’s Materializing the Middle Passage is one of them. It is a handsomely produced volume that synthesizes an extensive literature in a clear, confident fashion. It should be read alongside Nicholas Radburn’s landmark Traders in Men: Merchants and the Transformation of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2023), which provides a bold overview of how British merchants ruthlessly streamlined the trafficking of Africans in the 18th century. Webster details the material underpinning of that transformation. She loses no time in laying her theoretical cards on the table. She does not see the Middle Passage as an instance of “social death” that “stripped transported Africans of their culture and identity” (12). Nor does she view the slave ship as “a conduit by which African ethnicities were transferred, virtually unmodified, to the Americas” (12). Following the lead of Stephanie E. Smallwood, whose book Saltwater Slavery: A Middle Passage from Africa to American Diaspora appeared in 2007, she invokes instead a “mid-Atlantic creolization” (12). Webster argues that the shipboard experience of enslaved Africans was formative.

papers.title: Shelby Johnson. The Rich Earth Between Us: The Intimate Grounds of Race and Sexuality in the Atlantic World, 1770–1840
papers.abstract: Burials haunt the narratives assembled in Shelby Johnson’s The Rich Earth Between Us: burials in earth and water, burials deferred or denied, burials of knowledge and subaltern desire beneath the weight of imperial records and ontologies. One that lingers with me still is a brief story about reburial in William Apess’s (Pequot) Eulogy on King Philip (1836), in which an unnamed Native man disinters his son’s body, carrying it 200 miles away after finding his white neighbors apathetic to his grief. Johnson presses on questions history cannot answer: What was this child’s name? How did he die? What paths did his heartbroken father take? And what else remains buried in colonial archives, either hidden or distorted beyond recognition? While much remains unknowable, Johnson reads the father’s journey north to an Indigenous community in Canada as an act of “worldmaking”: “the father must, impossibly, improvise a world out of a shattering loss and an unsettled grave” (107).

papers.title: Corey Ross. Liquid Empire: Water and Power in the Colonial World
papers.abstract: Liquid Empire is a wide-ranging and sweeping book covering the length and breadth of European colonial engagement with water. In Corey Ross’s words, the book tries to tell “the intertwined stories of water and Europe’s modern imperial enterprise” (6). Ross attempts to bring together what he labels terra-acques histories of the European empire across irrigation schemes, hydropower, fisheries, urban waterworks, navigation, floods, land reclamation, and groundwater exploitation, among other colonial technologies of improvement. When taken together, the imprint of European empire, technology, and power becomes apparent, and to bring together these disparate histories is no easy task, but one that Ross accomplishes in a complex yet highly readable account. The core argument of the book shows how colonialism was as exploitative as it was contradictory, frail, and yet also a remarkably resilient system that lived well past its official end date. Ross places water and hydro-systems at the center of European empires, emphasizing connectedness, both of water as a substance and colonialism as a project at large across geographies. As Ross notes, a 200-year sweep requires generalizations, and in this sense one can think of this book as a critical rethinking of classic works such as Daniel Headrick’s Tools of Empire (1981), but where the frailties of empire and the materialities of nature are as important as the power exerted by European imperialism.

papers.title: Kevin Padraic Donnelly. The Descent of Artificial Intelligence: A Deep History of an Idea 400 Years in the Making .
papers.abstract: Despite its title, The Descent of Artificial Intelligence is not really about what we think of today as AI. The author, an intellectual historian whose previous book was a study of influential nineteenth-century Belgian ­­statistician Adolphe Quetelet, is instead concerned with “the descent of the idea of artificial intelligence” (259, emphasis mine). The real focus of this genealogy is on constructions of human intelligence and agency that have “reduce[d] the complex thought and behavior of human beings to a level where they might be studied by a variety of tools and methodologies ­borrowed from the natural sciences.” In other words, this is not a history of computing technology or information theory, but rather of the preconditions for believing that thinking machines or artificial intelligence (AI) are possible or desirable. Over the course of nine chapters divided into three historical acts, Kevin Padraic Donnelly carefully traces a trajectory of mechanical and mathematical reasoning from 17th-century natural philosophers like René Descartes and Isaac Newton (Part I), through debates about education and social values in the French Enlightenment and post-revolutionary France (Part II), and into the construction of nineteenth- and twentieth-­­century approaches to the “sciences of man” grounded in positivism, quantification, and statistical prediction (Part III). The central argument of the book is that, ever since Descartes famously suggested that living beings are machines, a tension has existed between mechanical and mathematical accounts of human intelligence and behavior—a “geometric spirit”—and those who emphasize the inherent complexity and irreducibility of human thinking and action.

papers.title: Emily Conroy-Krutz. Missionary Diplomacy: Religion and Nineteenth-Century American Foreign Relations.
papers.abstract: In Missionary Diplomacy: Religion and Nineteenth-Century American Foreign Relations, Emily Conroy-Krutz offers a careful examination of the relationship between Protestant missionaries and the US State Department. Indeed, Conroy-Krutz demonstrates that in the 19th century, American “evangelistic work was deeply entwined with diplomatic work” (13). In this period, she shows, missionaries served as “trusted experts” about the world to a wide array of US audiences. They wrote about the “world and its people” for lay audiences and increasingly took on more official roles: as translators, consuls, and advisers, in some cases even “testifying before Congress about international affairs” (3). As Conroy-Krutz argues, the State Department and the US mission movement each powerfully shaped the other’s growth over this period. The book is divided into three parts, which allows Conroy-Krutz to trace the evolving and complicated connections between the US State Department and the Protestant mission movement. The book’s first part covers the period between 1810 and 1840, “when the United States diplomatic corps was small, weak, and focused on European and Latin American affairs” (11). Yet—as the author ably demonstrates—US missionaries in this period trained their attention on the world’s “heathen,” who resided in places that “mattered less” to the State Department: places like India, China, and Hawaii. In doing so, they positioned themselves in such a way as to become “experts” on these regions and their people. Protestant missionaries wrote prolifically about their labors around the world. If they primarily aimed to drum up support for their evangelistic efforts, they were also frequently “quite earthbound and concerned with practical and political questions about peoples, governments, and civilization” (41). Thus, in their works for US audiences, they wrote not just as missionaries, but as “historians, scientists, and explorers” and endeavored to persuade Americans about the kinds of “issues, places, and peoples they should care about” (41). Their writings and their roles as “experts” about the world’s people and places created a situation in which missionaries began to influence the course of US diplomacy.

papers.title: Marion Girard Dorsey. Holding Their Breath: How the Allies Confronted the Threat of Chemical Warfare in World War II .
papers.abstract: The Allies did not deploy poison gas during the Second World War, but its potential use is the subject of this fascinating work of comparative diplomatic and mili­­tary history. Despite international attempts to limit or ban the use of gas after 1918, the Western Allies (the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada) ­­continued to explore the ethical and practical use of gas on the battlefield. This is an important study with a rich archival foundation that details the complexities of creating a common policy among three democratic countries. It also shows that, despite the wider efforts to outlaw the use of poisonous gas, each country was sometimes prepared to use gas if deemed necessary. Marion Girard Dorsey’s Holding Their Breath begins in 1925, when signatories of the Geneva Gas Protocol agreed to ban the use of chemical weapons and biological weapons. Britain and Canada signed the Protocol; the United States did not. Even so, it still posed a powerful check on the use of gas for all three countries. International opinion mattered. Dorsey draws from Susan Grayzel’s work to detail how the British government tried to prepare for gas attacks that never came. Dorsey is on firmer ground when exploring how gas became a powerful diplomatic and propaganda tool. British diplomatic notes to belligerents (and less trustworthy Allies) were worded carefully to avoid any sense that, if a gas war ensued, the Allies were responsible. It was a delicate balancing act. As Dorsey notes, after 1941 “Would a warning [against the use of gas] deter Germany? Would the same announcement backfire and incite Russia, bringing about the very outcome—gas warfare—that Britain hoped to avoid? And, on top of this, what was Britain willing to promise a dubious ally?” (105). Ultimately, in May 1942, Winston Churchill promised publicly that if “we are satisfied” that the Germans had used poison gas against the Russians, the Allies would launch “gas warfare on the largest possible scale far and wide upon the towns and cities of Germany” (105). For their part, the Americans broadened ­­Churchill’s warning, promising “full and swift retaliation in kind” if the Axis deployed gas in Europe or Asia. As Dorsey concludes, the Americans “may have deterred or risked—a global gas war” (107).

papers.title: Chloe Wigston Smith. Novels, Needleworks, and Empire: Material Entanglements in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World
papers.abstract: Chole Wigston Smith brings the interior worlds of romantic fiction and the so-called low arts of domestic needlework—pictorial embroidery, marking, mending, the sewing of a shirt, samplers—and other objects long seen as outside the epicenter of “taste and commodity culture” to the forefront of 18th-century global conceptions of empire and colonialism in the Atlantic World in Novels, Needleworks, and Empire: Material Entanglements in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World (7). While these goods were made and used in the home, the words, images, and materials they were made of were part of broader conversations on national and racial identity in the global 18th century.

papers.title: Dorit Brixius. Creolised Science: Knowledge in the Eighteenth-Century Indo-Pacific.
papers.abstract: Dorit Brixius’s Creolised Science places the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius at the center of an analysis of how plants were transported and transplanted across the Francophone Indo-Pacific. Brixius succeeds in decentering French science by demonstrating that the quest for useful or profitable plants to cultivate on Mauritius extended from Madagascar to China and island Southeast Asia, and relied on experts ranging from Southeast Asian plant collectors to enslaved expert gardeners from Réunion and India. The book is based on extensive archival research, demonstrating one of the author’s key arguments; that the agency of diverse actors is best revealed through unpublished records. Mauritius was under French control from 1721, following a period of Dutch occupation. The island was originally administered by the Compagnie française pour le commerce des Indes orientales and became a possession of the French crown in 1763. French ambitions for the island ranged from using it as a naval base to support Pondicherry against British rivals in India, to a plantation that would break into the Dutch stranglehold on the nutmeg and clove trade from the Maluku Islands. These aspirations often clashed with the practical needs of the settlers in Mauritius to feed themselves and the large numbers of enslaved people, who came from Madagascar and East Africa, with smaller numbers from West Africa and South and Southeast Asia.

papers.title: Langston Hughes. I Wonder as I Wander: An Autobiographical Journey.
papers.abstract: The first volume of Langston Hughes’s memoir The Big Sea (1940) may be more widely known, but I Wonder as I Wander (1956) is its indispensable second half. Across eight gripping chapters, Hughes—that great American poet and scion of the Harlem Renaissance—recounts his wide-ranging international travels during the 1930s, when the world was sliding toward catastrophe. This kind of nonfiction belongs to a distinctive genre of memoir writing that thrived between the world wars: autobiographical travelogues by foreign correspondents and other globetrotting intellectuals who raced to bring first-person glimpses of faraway conflicts to the reading public. Recently, similar work by Hughes’s white American contemporaries, such as Dorothy Thompson and John Gunther, have drawn extensive interest from historians. Yet written by a Black social commentator, and written in retrospect, on the other side of World War II and amid an accelerating civil rights movement and a Cold War–era Red Scare, I Wonder as I Wander in many ways exceeds the bounds of the genre and emerges as a much more interesting and layered source.

papers.title: Jody Benjamin. The Texture of Change: Dress, Self-Fashioning, and History in Western Africa, 1700–1850
papers.abstract: The eighteenth to mid-nineteenth century witnessed transformations of the political and economic landscapes in West Africa. The Islamic reformist movement spread eastward from the Senegal River valley, establishing theocratic states. Meanwhile, the Atlantic slave trade peaked and gradually declined in response to the abolitionist movement in Western Europe and North America. Concurrently, the cash crop trade, or so-called “legitimate commerce,” expanded in response to the British industrial revolution. Historians and economic historians have demonstrated that the growth of West Africa’s maritime trade, whether in slaves or in other items, was intertwined with an increasing inflow of European and Indian textiles. Recent scholarship highlights the crucial role of African consumers’ taste in these trades, showing that demand for textiles was deeply embedded in local production as well as social and cultural contexts. However, more research is needed to vividly illustrate how both noble and non-noble individuals consumed textiles and to analyze the political and cultural significance of their choices.

papers.title: Javier Fernández-Galeano. Maricas: Queer Cultures and State Violence in Argentina and Spain, 1942–1982
papers.abstract: Maricas: Queer Cultures and State Violence in Argentina and Spain, 1942–1982, by the brilliant historian Javier Fernández-Galeano, covers queer cultures and state violence in Argentina and Spain in the second half of the 20th century and fills a gap in the historiography of LGBTQ+ people. National studies on these topics in Argentina and Spain already exist, but there was not yet a comparative study that included both countries. In this sense, Maricas is a welcome addition to the literature, but it will also be appreciated by a wider readership who may be interested in Spanish and Argentine LGBTQ+ cultures because the book is written in a pleasant and accessible style. Maricas also has an almost iconic cover design by artist Miguel de Molina, which will certainly help make this book a classic. The word maricas refers to working-class men who adopted a feminine attitude in their interactions in the queer subcultures of these spaces, which stood in contrast to the entendidos who tended to come from the wealthier upper classes of society and who did not adopt a feminine attitude, but rather the opposite. Based on Fernández-Galeano’s dissertation, this book uses a wide variety of sources, including correspondence, memoirs, and interviews, as well as judicial, police, medical, military, and literary records. However, the author acknowledges varied access to research sources in Argentina and Spain. For example, there were significant differences in the judicial archives of the vagrancy courts in Spain and the judicial records available in Argentina, located at the Classification Institute. Similarly, the military archives in Argentina are kept in a civilian archive because of projects to clarify the role of the army in crimes against humanity, while in Spain, these archives are held at military bases. Fernández-Galeano relates how the colonel in charge of a base archive he visited did not show much interest in assisting with access to sources related to the subject matter. Fernández-Galeano shows monumental work in archives on both sides of the Atlantic, in spite of the peculiarities of each country. In this sense, the archival research is outstanding.

papers.title: Omar Valerio-Jiménez . Remembering Conquest: Mexican Americans, Memory, and Citizenship
papers.abstract: In his new book Remembering Conquest, Omar Valerio-Jiménez powerfully illuminates how the US-Mexico War (1846–1848) and the dispossessions, displacements, and disenfranchisements that colored life for Mexican Americans in the postwar era are not distant historical events but living legacies that persist in contemporary struggles. In turn, he effectively argues how the war’s conquest, as part of ongoing colonial structures, continues to shape the identities, livelihoods, and citizenship rights of Mexican Americans. While this argument may not be entirely new to scholars and students of Mexican American and Chicana/o Studies, Valerio-Jiménez innovatively and effectively explores this argument through a rigorous analysis of collective memories of the US-Mexico War across multiple generations of Mexican Americans since 1848. To do so, he examines, among many other sources, transnational oral histories, Spanish and English language newspapers, and political organizations on both sides of the border, searching for alternative war memories. These memories, he shows, urgently challenge official narratives on the US-Mexico War and the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo that ended this conflict. In doing so, Remembering Conquest offers a remarkably comprehensive cultural and intellectual history on the politics of memory as it pertains to the US-Mexico War. The book’s driving concern, however, is not simply how Mexican Americans have remembered this war in shared, distinct, and varied ways; perhaps most importantly, it is concerned with “the role of collective memories in processing the trauma of war and fomenting social transformation through political involvement” (8). The book therefore importantly adds to the wealth of literature on the US-Mexico War, the many (deliberate) failures of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the living history of Mexican American political organizing in response to these failures.

papers.title: Panagiotis Delis. Notions of Violence and Ethnic Cleansing on the Eve of the First World War: The Balkan Wars of 1912–13
papers.abstract: The Balkan Wars, fought as two distinct but closely interrelated conflicts between October 1912 and August 1913, reshaped the political map of Southeastern Europe and led to the expulsion of the Ottoman Empire from most of the Balkan Peninsula. Unlike the nineteenth-century Balkan revolutionary wars of national liberation, waged by local notables, peasants, and brigands against Ottoman rule, the Balkan Wars were launched by independent, modernizing Balkan states, grouped together in the Balkan League (Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro, and Serbia) against an increasingly beleaguered Ottoman state. These conflicts were waged by modern armies, supported by paramilitaries and other irregular forces, and characterized by internecine violence that often targeted noncombatants. They reshaped borders, communities, and identities, and in many respects, these wars prefigured the mass violence that characterized European history in the first half of the twentieth century. The centenary of the Balkan Wars occasioned several academic conferences and monographs that revisited these two wars, their origins, course, and legacies. While earlier studies had focused on the high politics of the Balkan Wars and small-power imperialisms of the region’s states, these newer works have examined the dynamics of local violence and how communities in the multiethnic and multiconfessional Balkans navigated the contentious and increasingly violent state policies of irredentism, occupation, and assimilation. This is certainly no easy task, as it involves working in multiple languages across regional and national archives in several countries, as well as having a solid understanding of local historiographies. Panagiotis Delis’s Notions of Violence and Ethnic Cleansing on the Eve of the First World War is one of the most recent studies in this vein and builds on the earlier works by Dimitar Tasić, Ryan Gingeras, Eyal Ginio, John Paul Newman, and others.

Marco also notes that some proponents of this new “respectable masculinity” considered not drinking wine as a sign of weakness, a lack of virility, and, as a result, of homosexuality.

papers.title: Robert Shea Terrell. A Nation Fermented: Beer, Bavaria, and the Making of Modern Germany.
papers.abstract: Beer and German culture are closely linked in the ­popular imagination, both in Germany and abroad. ­Robert Terrell’s book A Nation Fermented explores the social construction of “German beer” and its changing ­cultural meaning since the late nineteenth century. The study builds on recent interest in commodity ­histories and the transnational history of brewing, but Terrell focuses on the political and cultural significance afforded to the beverage in an effort to write “a history of [modern] Germany revealed through beer” (4). In particular, he asks about the role of regional Bavarian influences in shaping German debates on beer and broader perceptions of Germany in the twentieth century. In doing so, Terrell contributes to an important strand in the current historiography of modern ­Germany, which seeks to understand the nation through its “provincialism” and regional diversity. Contemporary German understandings of what should count as proper beer, Terrell contends, were shaped prominently by Bavarian actors. Indeed, Bavarian-style lagers became popular across the nation during the second half of the nineteenth century, and while beer production grew in many regions, Bavarians led the nation in per capita consumption and production. In contrast to large industrial brewing concerns further north, the Bavarian brewing industry long remained decentralized with many smaller breweries. In addition, Bavaria early on codified the traditional Reinheitsgebot (a beer purity regulation dating back to the fifteenth century), which stipulated that beer could only be brewed with four ingredients: water, malted barley, hops, and yeast. The possible inclusion of additives such as sugar would become a bone of contention between Bavarian brewers and those further north throughout the twentieth century, particularly in times of shortages induced by crisis and war.

Turtio’s work offers deeply researched insights into these questions as they pertain to what was once known as French West Africa. One of the book’s themes is the impact of foreign military assistance (chiefly French and Soviet) on the character of national militaries and the political fragility of states. papers.title: Don H. Doyle. The Age of Reconstruction: How Lincoln’s New Birth of Freedom Remade the World
papers.abstract: Rumors of US diplomats “negotiating with Denmark over the sale of Greenland” and Canada “peacefully and cheerfully” joining the United States might sound exclusively like a fever dream of the ­twenty-first century (117–18). These anecdotes, however, appear in Don H. Doyle’s account of how many Europeans interpreted the United States’ purchase of Alaska from ­Russia in 1867 as betokening a rising tide of republicanism in the Western hemisphere and beyond that followed the US Civil War. A sequel to Doyle’s The Cause of All Nations: An International History of the American Civil War (2014), this book ­considers the international dimensions of a period in US history that until recently was most often discussed and taught within a purely national frame. Like most scholars of Reconstruction for half a century and more, Doyle acknowledges his indebtedness to W. E. B. Du Bois, suggesting that this present book is merely an outworking of Du Bois’s intuition a century ago that “America’s racial divide [w]as part of a global clash between European whites and the ‘colored’ races, African, Asian, and all non-whites” (6). Doyle’s thesis is that there were two Reconstructions: the familiar, domestic version focused on rooting out slavery politically and economically, as well an international version aimed at “creating a zone of friendly, independent, ideally republican nations” (6–7). To substantiate this argument, Doyle details how the ­legacy of the US Civil War and the concurrent developments of Reconstruction loomed large in some of the era’s most important events, ranging from the Second French Empire’s interventions in Mexico and the Ten Years’ War in Cuba to the Canadian confederation, Britain’s Reform Act of 1867, and Italian unification. In the Western hemisphere, Doyle contends, international Reconstruction amounted to a “muscular new version of the Monroe Doctrine” backed up by the military prowess that the United States demonstrated in the Civil War (7). Elsewhere, the desire to remake the world in America’s image was largely contained to “inspiration and indirect influence, not foreign policy or government propaganda” (9). In other words, a victorious Union became a canvas onto which foreign liberals, socialists, and other radicals projected their conflicting hopes. At the same time, Radical Republicans shoehorned seemingly every incoming headline from foreign capitals into their preferred narrative that the United States heralded the democratic future in store for all nations. For example, Americans and ­Russians plausibly compared Lincoln and Tsar Alexander II, who abolished serfdom in 1861, as great emancipators, but it strained credulity when Senator Charles Sumner lauded the tsar for overseeing a “program of Radical Reconstruction by elevating twenty million serfs to full citizenship” (106).

papers.title: Tana Li. A Maritime Vietnam: From Earliest Times to the Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: Tana Li’s book A Maritime Vietnam: From Earliest Times to the Nineteenth Century is a brilliant exploration of how the sea has long mattered in the history of a country too often thought of largely in terms of its terrestrial orientation. papers.title: Kalyani Ramnath. Boats in a Storm: Law, Migration, and Decolonization in South and Southeast Asia, 1942–1962.
papers.abstract: Twenty years of tumult across the Indian Ocean provide the backdrop for Kalyani Ramnath’s fascinating study of decolonization in South and Southeast Asia, Boats in a Storm. This region, as many historians have highlighted, was long defined by the circulation of labor, capital, people, and commodities. In 1942, this world of motion was shattered by the Japanese invasion of Burma. The end of the war offered little respite. The British Empire unraveled rapidly, a bloody Partition tore apart the subcontinent in 1947, and the colonial state launched a ferocious war in Malaya. Postcolonial states were established in this context of fatigue, trauma, and suspicion, and faced the monumental task of sorting the former empire’s subjects into national citizens. In a few years, the legal landscape of the region utterly transformed. How did ordinary people, whose lives and livelihoods had long stretched between intertwined and interconnected geographies, navigate these drastic and paradigmatic changes? Ramnath takes this question up in her first monograph. Set between the Japanese occupation of Burma in 1942 and General Ne Win’s coupe état there in 1962, the book describes the “banal encounters with law” of migrants navigating new legal frameworks in postimperial South and Southeast Asia (1). Ramnath mines a wealth of legal and administrative records from India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Singapore, and Burma to excavate stories of ordinary people as they applied for citizenship ­­certificates and passports, settled debt repayments, contested taxation schemes, claimed or disputed property, and tried to avoid detention and deportation.

papers.title: Joshua Clough. Resisting Oklahoma’s Reign of Terror: The Society of Oklahoma Indians and the Fight for Native Rights, 1923–1928
papers.abstract: Oklahoma embodies the best and worst of American history. On the one hand, it is a place of astonishing resilience and creativity, a successful experiment in multinational Indigeneity in which thirty-nine different tribes from nearly every corner of America have managed to build rich and growing communities. On the other hand, it is a place with an almost unimaginably macabre past: the endpoint of the Trail of Tears, the site of the 1921 Tulsa race massacre, and the setting for an orgy of anti-Indian fraud and violence in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In Resisting Oklahoma’s Reign of Terror, Joshua Clough puts Oklahoma’s duality on full display by telling the story of the Society of Oklahoma Indians (SOI), a multitribal organization formed in 1924 to confront racist oppression and celebrate Indigenous nationhood. The society’s fleeting success and ultimate failure provide a fitting window into America’s most quintessential state.

papers.title: Marc-William Palen. Pax Economica: Left-Wing Visions of a Free-Trade World.
papers.abstract: Who’s afraid of free trade? In Pax Economica, Marc-William Palen argues that the contemporary tendency to link free market and free-trade ideas with right-wing politics fails to recognize their roots in a very different context: the world of left-wing socialist, liberal, feminist, and internationalist peace activists. Between 1850 and 1950, he contends, such activists developed a theory that linked free trade with global interdependence and, consequently, world peace. They have been forgotten, but not because they failed: Palen argues that the supranational organizations set up to oversee a free-trade world after the Second World War represent their political and ideological triumph. However, that triumph would be overtaken by Cold War politics and then obscured by the ideological shifts that soldered free trade to neoliberalism in the guise of Reaganomics toward the century’s end. Pax Economica makes an important contribution to the emerging body of historiography reconsidering the roots of key concepts in contemporary economics. This work unsettles modern orthodoxies by demonstrating the diversity of past ideas and alliances.

papers.title: Jacob Dlamini. Dying for Freedom: Political Martyrdom in South Africa
papers.abstract: Dying for Freedom is an innovative and thought-provoking study that places important conversations about death on the intellectual table. Dlamini uses several historical examples to support his analysis. papers.title: Matthew H. Sommer. The Fox Spirit, the Stone Maiden, and Other Transgender Histories from Late Imperial China
papers.abstract: In The Fox Spirit, the Stone Maiden, and Other Transgender Histories from Late Imperial China, Matthew H. Methodologically, Sommer adopts a distinctive approach pioneered by Susan Stryker, who emphasizes transgender practices over the subjective construction of transgender identity in studying transgender history. By doing so, Sommer offers a more inclusive and nuanced account of gender nonconformity in imperial China, capturing the complexity of gendered behavior beyond modern categories.

papers.title: Melissa Teixeira. A Third Path: Corporatism in Brazil and Portugal .
papers.abstract: Prior to the 1990s, when a rebranded left presented itself as defending a Third Way between socialism and neoliberalism, corporatist ideas that strengthened the role of governmental regulations on capital-­­labor relations and advocated for a central role for the state as an economic actor guiding society toward a higher nationalist future helped reshape countries around world. One of the main contributions of the work is to decenter historical narratives on the corporatist experience by demonstrating how countries not assumed as central in the established historiographies were indeed protagonists in the development of Third Path ideas, and successfully implemented these ideas in ways that reshaped the institutional structures of their societies. A second main achievement of the book is showing how corporatism, even if it is less clearly defined than liberal capitalism or socialism—or perhaps, exactly because of this feature—needs to be better understood if one is to make sense of the ideological struggles and associated geopolitical disputes about free-market versus state-run economies that defined the past century. Corporatism had a logic of its own that, largely due to its own conceptual malleability, left lasting impacts on nations across the world.

papers.title: William Max Nelson. Enlightenment Biopolitics: A History of Race, Eugenics, and the Making of Citizens .
papers.abstract: Reading William Max Nelson’s masterful Enlightenment Biopolitics amid the portentous atmosphere of the 2024 US presidential election campaign was at once an alarming and revelatory experience. Nuancing ­­Foucault’s foundational studies, Enlightenment ­­Biopolitics argues that “life entered the sphere of political techniques through the concern with the qualities of individual and collective bodies and the conviction that it was possible to transform and improve these qualities” (2). Through the history of biopolitics Nelson opens a window into broader, ongoing historiographical debates about the nature of the Enlightenment itself. He urges historians to abandon a Manichean view of the 18th century as either exclusively emancipatory or totalitarian, pointing to the manifold ways in which “the Enlightenment was characterized by the formation of new conceptual and practical foundations on which modern inclusions and exclusions were built” (4). In sum, Enlightenment Biopolitics navigates the choppy waters of post–World War II reevaluations of the Enlightenment by doing what all good intellectual histories do—historicizing contemporary debates and categories.

papers.title: Maurice Isserman. Reds: The Tragedy of American Communism .
papers.abstract: The history of the US Communist Party has been the subject of historiographical debate since the early Cold War. papers.title: Gaines M. Foster. Limits of the Lost Cause: Essays on Civil War Memory
papers.abstract: In this collection of essays, four previously published and four original to this book, Gaines Foster offers a self-described “contrarian” view of the belief that the South is “still fighting the Civil War.” Foster finds instead that both scholars and popular understandings of the Civil War have overemphasized continuing Southern distinctiveness and allegiance to the Lost Cause, particularly in the years following World War I. These essays expand on Foster’s finding in his 1987 book Ghosts of the Confederacy that in the aftermath of the war, Southerners created the Lost Cause as a way to create a new, more positive memory of the war and Confederacy. This new identity, although celebrating Confederate heroism and mourning the end of slavery, also paved the way for regional reconciliation and reunion. In this new collection, Foster argues that across the twentieth and into the twenty-first century, Confederate symbols, including the flag, statues, and the fiery cross, are better understood as signifying a kind of nationalism based on white, Protestant, and to some degree, class identity rather than indications of or allegiance to the Confederate past.

papers.title: Beeta Baghoolizadeh. The Color Black: Enslavement and Erasure in Iran .
papers.abstract: Iranians enslaved East Africans too. That simple yet significant intervention made by Beeta Baghoolizadeh in The Color Black challenges both the historiographic erasure of slavery in Iran and the collective denial that slavery became distinctly racialized from the latter half of the 19th century until its abolition in 1929. ­­Ensla­­vement in what is now Iran stretches back to the Achaemenid Empire (550 BCE–330 BCE), and those ensnared in the trade came from bordering areas, including the Caucasus, Central Asia, South Asia, and East Africa. Baghoolizadeh shows how the expanded regional influence of Russia and Britain during the 19th century cut off most markets for trading enslaved people with the exception of East Africa, which continued to be a source for enslaved people into the 20th century largely because overland trade routes circumvented British efforts to abolish the Persian Gulf slave trade. As the number of enslaved people from areas outside of East Africa dwindled, the status of being enslaved in Iran became increasingly synonymous with being East African and Black, which, in turn, solidified the whiteness of non-Black Iranians.

papers.title: Shane Bobrycki. The Crowd in the Early Middle Ages
papers.abstract: Crowds are a universal phenomenon. Throughout history and across all societies, crowds have emerged and continue to do so, particularly in urban settings, where they serve as a prominent expression of public life. Crowd dynamics are deeply interwoven with social, political, cultural, economic, and religious developments, making them a subject of great interest to societal leaders. Effective crowd management and control remain crucial for authorities tasked with overseeing the organized or spontaneous activities of large gatherings. Traditional modern scholarship on the early medieval period (500–1000 CE) has often portrayed this era as devoid of crowds. While crowds were undeniably a prominent feature of the Roman world and reemerged noticeably in the High Middle Ages, they seem to have receded into the background, almost as if they had vanished in the period in between. In The Crowd in the Early Middle Ages, Shane Bobrycki challenges this conventional perspective, aiming to demonstrate that the Early Middle Ages were in fact full of crowds.

papers.title: Amanda Lanzillo. Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India
papers.abstract: Pious Labor reconstructs an important and largely untold history of Muslim labor in late colonial India (1858–1947). Lanzillo has assembled a remarkable archive of Urdu and Persian texts that she reads with acuity alongside colonial sources to show how north Indian Muslim karigars (artisans) in six trades—bookmaking, metalsmithing, tailoring, carpentry, boilermaking, and stonemasonry—contended with the rapid economic and social changes of British colonialism. The book focuses on how Muslim artisans (predominantly male, though Lanzillo addresses questions of female labor and the gendering of labor in a chapter on tailoring) adapted to changes in the materiality and technology of their trades, and to the transition from artisanal production to wage-labor precipitated by industrialization. The centrality of Urdu sources allows Lanzillo to tell this story largely from the perspective of artisans themselves. She adeptly uses a combination of technical manuals that explained how to do tasks such as electroplating, maintain a steam engine, or use new construction technologies, and histories of artisans in a particular trade, which she refers to as community histories. Both types of texts were written mostly by artisans themselves and published by small commercial presses across north India. Although the artisanal communities studied through these texts (barring scribes) were largely illiterate, Lanzillo shows how these texts were directed at such communities, who would have accessed them through their being read aloud—a practice common of vernacular literatures in India during this era.

papers.title: Luca Zenobi. Borders and the Politics of Space in Late Medieval Italy: Milan, Venice, and their Territories.
papers.abstract: A poor man spent the summer of 1457 harvesting crops in fields near Lodi. Perhaps a day’s walk from his home near Bergamo, he had petitioned a local official for safe passage to allow him to travel through lands that were subject to the Republic of Venice; however, his route also took him through areas bound to the Duchy of Milan. On his return home later that summer, ducal officials seized the wheat he was bringing back to his mother, as he had not secured similar approval to travel through Milanese lands. The Venetian governor intervened. His letter, now in Milan’s Archivio di Stato, emphasized the difficulties travelers faced, as this route frequently crossed territorial borders between the two states. This episode is completely ordinary in its details of an otherwise unknown peasant seeking to improve his family’s situation. At the same time, it reflects the ubiquity and complexity of medieval territoriality that Luca Zenobi excavates in Borders and the Politics of Space in Late Medieval Italy. Focusing on the frontier between Milan and Venice established by the Peace of Lodi (1454), he shows how territorial borders were clearly identified and controlled. This argument challenges earlier scholarship that has presumed premodern borders lacked precision and were at best porous, before states demarcated clear boundaries. Zenobi also emphasizes their contingent nature, which he argues was characteristic of medieval Italian spatial politics. Strongly grounded in documentary evidence and adopting insights from contemporary geography and international relations theories, his book reveals how medieval people from all classes created, reimagined, and negotiated political boundaries that were both spatial and social.

papers.title: Kate Imy. Losing Hearts and Minds: Race, War, and Empire in Singapore and Malaya, 1915–1960
papers.abstract: With the publication of her award-winning book Faithful Fighters in 2019—a study that addressed British attempts to maintain loyalty in the colonial Indian Army—Kate Imy established herself as not only an expert in British colonial military policy but also of the psychological, emotional, racial, and gendered dimensions of colonial militarism in general. Her second monograph, Losing Hearts and Minds, therefore promised to bring this expertise to bear on colonial militarism in Singapore and Malaya. It absolutely fulfills this promise. Losing Hearts and Minds examines the lives of soldiers and civilians in Singapore and Malaya from the 1915 Singapore Mutiny through to the end of the British colonial period during the 1948–1960 Malayan Emergency. Its central argument is that while colonial power and white supremacy rested upon racial and gendered hierarchies, they also relied on the loyalty and service of Asians and Eurasians, both in the military and civilian spheres. This contradiction meant that, despite the colonial state’s understanding that it needed to win the “hearts and minds” of its subjects, each conflict in the region resulted in a series of betrayals to reassert colonial hierarchies. Imy frames the book around the now-infamous “hearts and minds” expression used by Sir Gerald Templer during the Emergency to reinforce the futility of colonial attempts to inspire loyalty: the colonial state’s supremacist mandate ensured that its promises of belonging would inevitably result in betrayals. These betrayals are precisely what hastened the empire’s demise.

papers.title: Prachi Deshpande. Scripts of Power: Writing, Language Practices and Cultural History in Western India .
papers.abstract: Prachi Deshpande’s cultural history of the Modi script—a “visual symbol” of current Marathi identity and an “opaque text” within Marathi language historiography (2)—anchors it “within a field of writing and documentation” that straddles the “early-­­modern” and the “colonial modern” to explore the social, multilingual contexts of usage and deployment at critical junctures (5). Deshpande’s “middle durée” perspective on Marathi literate practice and regional linguistic formation reveals “multiscriptality” in documentary practices, and bi/multi-lingual oral and literate usage that overturns modern linguistic boundaries. Deshpande urges us to rethink the easy equation between an objectified, “natural” deshi (local) language and its uninterrupted connection with history, territoriality, and identity. Spread over two parts and six chapters, Scripts of Power offers a rich narrative of the multilayered intricacies of writing practices in a plurilingual world. The work tracks the tousled trajectories of scripts; the conflicted notions of “roots”; the evolving ideals of scribal comportment and correct writing; the imperatives and impact of administrative and devotional documentation; and the perennial multilingual, regional, and transregional entwining in quotidian practice of language and script that incited debates over etymology, orthography, grammar, and pedagogy. All this shaped current Marathi language and script.

papers.title: Julia F. Irwin. Catastrophic Diplomacy: US Foreign Disaster Assistance in the American Century
papers.abstract: Hurricane Flora churned through the Caribbean Sea in late September 1963, killing 7,193 people in the region, among them 1,750 Cubans. Almost exactly one year after the Cuban Missile Crisis, Flora opened another front in the Cold War struggle between the United States and Cuba: a contest over the meanings of a disaster and its implications for statecraft. One Kennedy administration official saw the chance to offer disaster aid as a route to gaining a “psychological advantage” among the distraught Cuban population. According to long-standing tradition, the American Red Cross (ARC) initiated aid, and was rebuffed by their Cuban Red Cross peers, who rejected out of hand this “hypocritical offer of assistance.” Recriminations, anger, and—at last—diplomacy followed when a small delegation of American Quakers were permitted to deliver $92,000 in food and medical supplies—a small win for the soft power catastrophe diplomats. This superbly strange tale of hurricane realpolitik is one among hundreds of local disaster cases across more than a century—from East to West and all points in between—animating Julia F. Irwin’s densely researched and fast-paced new book Catastrophic Diplomacy: US Foreign Disaster Assistance in the American Century. Disasters may emerge from the weather, geology, or technological failures, but they are fundamentally social phenomena, and therefore political, and in no way separable from the broader forces shaping US foreign policy since the founding of the nation.

papers.title: Michelle T. King. Chop Fry Watch Learn: Fu Pei-mei and the Making of Modern Chinese Food
papers.abstract: There is no such thing as food for food’s sake. For Fu Pei-mei, the most influential culinary guru in Taiwan over the past half century, cooking was a love for life, a devotion to family, and a vital part of traditional ­Chinese culture. But historian Michelle T. King sees more. In her new book Chop Fry Watch Learn, King weaves together the stories from her own family and many others to present a compelling argument for how understanding the life of Fu Pei-mei and her cooking enables us to see Chinese food as both an inheritance of tradition and a modern creation in the postwar era. This book is an excellent example of microhistory, revealing the modern history of Taiwan through the story of the woman who brought Chinese cooking to the world. As King convincingly demonstrates, Fu’s cookbooks “contain more than just the recipes and photos of a delicious, beloved cuisine—they also reflect a tumultuous modern history, a social revolution for women, technological changes in the kitchen, and multiple generation of families, connected across oceans by an abiding love of Chinese food” (xxi).
