papers.title: Eram Alam, Dorothy Roberts, and Natalie Shibley, eds. Ordering the Human: The Global Spread of Racial Science .
papers.abstract: When discussing the origins of race and racial science, historians regularly have looked to the Americas and the Anglo-Atlantic World. In this framework, slavery and the conquest of the Americas provided a laboratory for the construction of the scientific race concept, which naturalized the enslavement of Africans as healthy and the dying out of Native Americans as an inevitable consequences of their bodily weakness in the face of novel illnesses. What this narrative does not always emphasize is how racial science was a product of emergent globalization. Racial science’s global nature and consequences, though, are the subject of a compelling new collection of essays, Ordering the Human: The Global Spread of Racial Science, edited by Eram Alam, Dorothy Roberts, and Natalie Shibley. Including scholarship from anthropologists, historians, and public health scholars, Ordering the Human covers diverse locales, times periods, and disciplines, with chapters ranging from late 18th-century ­­German naturalism to the consequences of racial thinking during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States and India. Collectively, what emerges is a much larger and more complicated study of racial science, one where its practitioners are ethnically and disciplinarily diverse and engage with such populations as government officials, academics, and health care providers. In short, expanding to a global framework highlights the true horrors of racial science, a knowledge system uncritically adopted by a range of academic disciplines and nations.

papers.title: Geoff G. Burrows. The Puerto Rico Reconstruction Administration: New Deal Public Works, Modernization, and Colonial Reform.
papers.abstract: The Puerto Rico Reconstruction Administration (PRRA) was one of the most important New Deal agencies in Puerto Rico and, one could argue, one of the most influential institutions in the archipelago’s modern history. For decades, historians of Puerto Rico have recognized its significance, but no one had dedicated monograph-length research to the PRRA. With The Puerto Rico Reconstruction Administration, Geoff G. Burrows brings new insights and interpretations to the intersections among development, colonialism, and the formation of modern Puerto Rico. The book offers a deep dive into one of the most complex periods in Puerto Rican history, from the 1930s to the rise of the Popular Democratic Party in the 1940s. Instead of simply portraying the PRRA as part of the US colonial project—which it certainly was, as the author points out—Burrows also demonstrates how the PRRA became a New Deal agency run by Puerto Ricans. That is, while stemming from the federal government, it was locally run. And it also set the foundations of Puerto Rico’s industrialization along with the transformation of Puerto Rico’s polity in the 1940s and ’50s.

papers.title: Mateo Jarquín. The Sandinista Revolution: A Global Latin American History
papers.abstract: Every revolution is global in both its origins and its repercussions, and Nicaragua’s was no different. In The Sandinista Revolution: A Global Latin American History, Mateo Jarquín emphasizes the regional over the global, placing Latin American diplomacy at the center of the Nicaraguan Revolution and the counterrevolutionary struggle it set off. In foregrounding Latin American diplomatic efforts first to remove the Somoza dictatorship and then to manage the ensuing regional conflict, Jarquín contends that “the view from Washington can obscure the Nicaraguan Revolution’s global dimensions” (2). The book draws on thorough research in multiple archives across Latin America and interviews with many Nicaraguan and other Central American diplomats, reinforcing the importance of regional diplomacy in Latin America’s Cold War. A key question during the revolution and afterward has been not whether the Nicaraguan Revolution should be considered global but its polarity on the globe itself: Was the revolution primarily a North-South or East-West conflict? Jarquín argues that in its earliest stages, the Sandinistas embraced the East-West polarity of socialism versus capitalism even as they couched their demands in the North-South language of self-determination. Over the course of the decade following the successful revolution, the language of self-determination and democracy would crowd out the aspiration for socialism as the revolution moved away from its most radical demands for social transformation. International diplomacy played a key role in the transformation of revolutionary priorities, as Sandinista leaders fought for survival by shifting the revolution’s goals in response to both internal and external pressures.

papers.title: Jacob Blanc. The Prestes Column: An Interior History of Modern Brazil
papers.abstract: For nearly two and a half years, Luís Carlos Prestes led a column of rebels that peaked at nearly three thousand on a fifteen-thousand-mile trek throughout Brazil’s interior. The Prestes Column, as it came to be known, challenged Brazil’s First Republic (1889–1930) at a pivotal moment in the country’s history. Although the march is one of the most famous and commented-on events of Brazil’s twentieth century, Jacob Blanc’s book The Prestes Column: An Interior History of Modern Brazil is the first work in English to thoroughly capture the column and its legacies. Eschewing mere narrative, Blanc sets out on a herculean task: to peel back the myths and legends of one of the most famous incidents in Brazilian history in order to rehumanize its participants. Focusing on Brazil’s interior—and the various meanings and discourses around it—Blanc situates the column and the struggles over its meaning throughout the twentieth century, incorporating analysis of political unrest, regionalist discourse, race, gender, and development in Brazil. The result is an invaluable contribution to both Brazilian and English scholarship on the column, national mythmaking, and the Brazilian interior.

papers.title: Chloe L. Ireton. Slavery and Freedom in Black Thought in the Early Spanish Atlantic
papers.abstract: One of the most astounding statements about slavery and freedom comes from a Black slave named Diego de la Cruz in New Spain in 1651. De la Cruz declared to the Inquisition in Mexico that he had spent a night out with friends, playing music and having a late-night dinner before returning to work the next morning. The Inquisition later discovered it was all made up. Slaves in the early modern Americas did not simply go out like that. The interesting point, however, is that the issue of freedom is fundamental here: Diego fantasized about being free, and by telling the inquisitors, that fantasy became more real. It was not merely a case of picaresque behavior but rather escapism from reality. I initially considered the case of Diego de la Cruz an exception, presuming that there were few such individual testimonies—until I read Jennifer L. ­­Morgan’s book Reckoning with Slavery and now Chloe L. Ireton’s new book, Slavery and Freedom in Black Thought in the Early Spanish Atlantic. Both books reveal a vast amount of testimonial material on the daily lives and self-fashioning of slaves about whom we knew little. Until recently, we could count the ships on the Middle Passage and analyze plantation economies, but we lacked access to personal data. Ireton’s book fills this gap by weaving together countless ego-­documents, fragmentary testimonies, and case studies. As the author stresses: “From a free Black mother’s embarkation license to cross the Atlantic as a passenger on a ship, or an enslaved Sevillian woman’s letters to her freed husband in New Spain, or an enslaved man’s negotiations for credit arrangements with prospective buyers on the auction block in Mexico City, to a Black man’s petition to a royal court in an attempt to reclaim his liberty after his illegitimate enslavement, Africans and their descendants were important intellectual actors in the early modern Atlantic world” (16–17).

papers.title: Elisa Camiscioli. Selling French Sex: Prostitution, Trafficking, and Global Migrations .
papers.abstract: In Selling French Sex: Prostitution, Trafficking, and Global Migrations, Elisa Camiscioli tells a sweeping story of global migration in the early 20th century that centers the French sex worker. Camiscioli shows how French women were a hot commodity in brothels across the Americas, where they frequently outnumbered and outearned women of other nationalities, benefiting from an image of Parisian vice culture that underwrote the idea that French women were more likely to offer “perverse” sex acts. But if “French sex” seemed to be desired much like a luxury good with a certain je ne sais quoi, migration for the purposes of selling sex also made French women undesirable in a moment when American countries like the United States were working to bar immigrants intending to enter the country for “immoral purposes” (45). That is to say that individuals found French sex workers desirable. States did not. Thus, in the eyes of both clients and immigration officials across the Americas, the French sex worker did not look much like a trafficking victim, despite the widespread circulation of stories about French women kidnapped into sexual slavery in Buenos Aires and other destinations around the globe, which have been well-studied by historians. Breaking with historical and contemporary framings, Camiscioli rereads the archive of the “white slave trade” as one of migration and transforms women characterized as both trafficking victims and “undesirable” immigrants into individuals making informed—if always constrained—decisions about their working lives. Much like Philippa Hetherington and Julia Laite, in their introduction to a special issue of the Journal of Women’s History on “Migration, Sex, and Intimate Labor” (33, no. 4 [2021]: 7–39), Camiscioli finds trafficking to be—if not a “useless ­­category of historical analysis”—a category that masks more than it reveals about women’s movement to sell sex across national borders.

papers.title: Rafał B. Reichert. Wood, Trade, and Spanish Naval Power (c. 1740–1795) .
papers.abstract: How did Spain manage to become the second naval power in the world, just 20 years after its disastrous involvement, alongside France, in the Seven Years’ War? This is the big question that Rafał B. Reichert, a regarded scholar of the Spanish colonial empire, has chosen to place at the heart of his latest book Wood, Trade, and Spanish Naval Power (c. 1740–1795). To answer this question, the author draws on several of his recent publications on the issue of timber supplies for the Spanish Navy, which was sourced from two strategic regions: the Baltic Sea and the Caribbean. The book is highly interesting due to the wealth of perspectives it opens. Indeed, the issue of supplying royal navies has already been the subject of a very rich historiography, which the author masters thoroughly and of which he offers an exhaustive review at the end of the work (except for its French side, where he could find useful points of comparison in the recent work of David Plouviez and Caroline Le Mao). The main interest of the book lies in its ability to situate a classic topic in the historiography of the early modern period at the crossroads of various scientific debates, which have been particularly active in recent years. Through its focus on the descriptions of forest resources provided by various investigators dispatched by the Spanish crown to the relevant areas, the book aligns fully with the field of environmental history, and as such it is a fitting addition to Brill’s Environmental History series. In addition, the book is inspired by imperial history, as it places the Spanish-British rivalry at the center of its analysis. The comparative method it employs, meanwhile, is drawn from global history. The focus on the various forms of contracts established between the Spanish Navy and the merchants responsible for provisioning it, with the participation of other institutional actors enlisted to support it (notably ambassadors and consuls), is unquestionably an interesting contribution to the social history of institutions and commercial practices. Finally, Reichert’s overall conclusion—that the Baltic did better than New Spain because it was better integrated into the commercial circuits of early globalization and because it offered more advantageous services than America—constitutes an important contribution to the more general reflection on the dynamics of globalization in the early modern era.

papers.title: Wealth, Health, and the Transnational Pesticide System: Tense Entanglements between the USA and Germany at the End of the Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: Abstract: Conflict over pesticides, their benefits, and their dangers is as old as the use of the substances themselves. At the very least, it can be dated back to the use of arsenic as a pesticide in the last decades of the nineteenth century. The debate has taken place not only on a national but also on a transnational level, where trading is an essential element. This article examines “tense entanglements” between the United States and the German Empire at the end of the nineteenth century through analysis of public and scientific discourses and media circulation of knowledge, both of which were essential for the political evaluation of the economic benefits and health risks associated with arsenic-containing pesticides. The article shows that deferred domestic decisions (between health protection and food production), scientific uncertainty, and a profit-driven economy paved the way for a transnational pesticide system . Conversely, this system fueled the intensification of global capitalism and continues to shape the production, use, and perception of pesticides to the present day .

papers.title: Turkish Anticolonialism and Muslim Southeast Asia, 1923–1949: Vernacular Diplomacy “Under the Yoke of 3 and a Half Dutchmen”
papers.abstract: Abstract: This article traces the awkward relationship of the early Turkish Republic with European empires and Asian polities under European colonial domination. It has been argued that Turkey was largely disinterested in the non-Western world, as its primary goal was to be recognized as a state of equal stature to Western nations. We argue that certain segments of Turkish political society remained heavily invested in Asian affairs. We demonstrate this through a case study of Muslim Southeast Asia (the Malay-speaking world), a region that had traditionally held strong ties with the Ottoman Empire. Turkey found itself in the peculiar position of being held up as a beacon of emancipation from the West by independence movements elsewhere while also being committed to integrating itself into a Western-dominated global order. Thus, we argue that Turkey’s interactions with the non-European world were fragmented and characterized by ambiguity. Discourses of westernization and anti-colonial rhetoric were both widely deployed. Within these tensions, new subjectivities could be crafted by a patchwork of vernacular actors that paint a picture of the imaginative political discourses in the early Turkish Republic and in a world connected by transregional imperialism.

papers.title: Making Perfect Markets: The Demand for Global Numbers at the Origin of the International Institute of Agriculture
papers.abstract: Abstract: In the second half of the nineteenth century, markets for agricultural commodities became far more integrated than ever before, but they also created new sources of conflict. The same forces that drove trade integration also led to financialization, the monopoly power of transport companies, and speculation based on information asymmetries. Historiography has identified these issues as crucial in fueling various mixes of nationalist resentment, anti-globalization rhetoric, and protectionist demands among agriculturalists in North America and Europe. This article shows that, instead, in the early twentieth century, agriculturalists and governments across the Atlantic (and beyond) reacted to the emergence of the world market by fostering international cooperation to reorganize trade and make it more transparent and fair. Rejecting the proposal advanced by the American David Lubin to create an international farmers’ union (for farmers by farmers), governments of major world powers agreed to establish the International Institute of Agriculture as the provider of global crop reports. By looking at the early years of the Institute through the prism of the history of quantification, we show how information thus emerged as a global public good and a fundamental element in the infrastructure of world agricultural markets.

papers.title: The Peculiarities of Cambridge History: Some Comparative Thoughts on the Historical Tripos
papers.abstract: Abstract This study develops and expands some of the arguments of a lecture I delivered on the occasion of the 150th anniversary of the foundation of Cambridge’s Historical Tripos. Its central proposition – that it is meaningful to talk about ‘Cambridge History’ and to discuss its distinctiveness – remains central to this published version of the lecture, as does the idea that the Tripos has always embodied that distinctiveness as a form of social memory. Both the Tripos as a structure and the Faculty archive as a source come into play in helping to make sense of the Cambridge trajectory over the past half century. The lecture lays stress on some persistent legacies from the Cambridge tradition, identifies some strands that developed internally after 1945, and considers the impact of external influences on Cambridge History. Taking the story up to the ‘new’ Tripos of 2022, the lecture concludes that the legacy has exercised more control than has innovation and that the Historical Tripos is best understood as a continuing conversation with its own past.

papers.title: Unpaid Debts
papers.abstract: Abstract “Unpaid Debts” provides a novel account of the New International Economic Order (NIEO), from the economic crises of the 1970s to the lost development decade of the 1980s. It shows that it was not just the Thatchers, the Reagans, and the neoliberal economists that sank the NIEO; its failure also resulted from the limits of socialist internationalism. This article tracks how Jamaican activists—working with key individuals across the Caribbean, Africa, Latin America, and Asia—worked to build support for the NIEO by redefining “socialism” and “socialist internationalism” nationally, regionally, and globally. They tried to push European social democrats to embrace the NIEO and global wealth redistribution, and help build an alternative to a post-Bretton Woods economic order defined increasingly by financialization. But they came up against hard limits, and the endurance of both imperial and Cold War logics. Centering the struggle for the soul of democratic socialism sheds new light on the world-making visions of the 1970s, the real-world obstacles they faced, and their unexpected afterlives. It broadens the conversation around the NIEO, showing how even if the NIEO failed, it fostered new forms of South-South collaboration that endured beyond the 1970s.

papers.title: The Battles Over Addiction Treatment
papers.abstract: Abstract To the extent that it is remembered today, the controversial California commune Synanon is known for two things—(1) attempting to murder attorney Paul Morantz by putting a rattlesnake in his mailbox and (2) spawning an addiction treatment model with violent and totalizing tendencies: the therapeutic community (TC). My book, The Recovery Revolution: The Battle Over Addiction Treatment in the United States, omitted the rattlesnake in the mailbox and glossed over the details of Synanon’s spectacular decline. According to some critics, including Morantz himself, this was a major mistake, and a small but highly vocal cadre of activists went online to publicly question my historical objectivity and reframe what I had intended as a nonpartisan history of Synanon’s public relations campaigns as an endorsement of therapeutic violence. The omission led me, then a closeted person in long-term eating disorder recovery, to a mental breakdown, psychoanalytic psychotherapy to treat it, and, with this approach, fresh insight into the value of analysis as well as synthesis in the development of historical knowledge. I conclude by exploring “reparatory history” as both a method and a way forward for our impossible profession.

papers.title: Charles Wilkinson. Treaty Justice: The Northwest Tribes, the Boldt Decision, and the Recognition of Fishing Rights
papers.abstract: Charles Wilkinson’s Treaty Justice begins dramatically on the banks of Tacoma’s Puyallup River in the summer of 1964, where violent clashes erupted between Indigenous fishers and Washington State police. These confrontations marked the opening salvos of the “fish wars”—a period when Puget Sound tribes actively resisted state attempts to deny them access to waterways where they held treaty-protected fishing rights. papers.title: Whose Revolution?

papers.abstract: Nathan Perl-Rosenthal’s ambitious new synthesis makes a novel contribution to the crowded field of comparative revolutions. Attuned to the Tocquevillian continuities that lurk beneath dramatic ruptures, The Age of Revolutions: And the Generations Who Made It charts the “long tail of political turning points” (465) like the American Declaration of Independence. What makes the work especially innovative is the onus it places on generational transitions to explain why revolutionary movements across the Atlantic World played out in the halting and often illiberal ways they did. Privileging practices over principles, Perl-­­Rosenthal argues that “what makes a revolution happen” (3)—and then endure—is a movement’s ability to mobilize the masses by building inclusive communication networks, public spaces, and institutions like political clubs and conscript armies. The first cohort he identifies—“gentlemen revolutionaries” who grew up in fixed societies where “birth was usually destiny” (29)—proved incapable of establishing durable alliances with their social inferiors. Drawing on Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of “habitus” (4), Perl-Rosenthal attributes this generation’s “top-down” tendencies to their formative experiences in a hierarchical world. From Túpac Amaru’s doomed Andean rebellion to the Constitutional Convention’s elitist coup in Philadelphia, the book’s opening half contends that George Washington, Maximilien Robespierre, and even Toussaint Louverture lacked the “mobile social imaginary” (292) and practical skills to operate across class and caste lines, much less dismantle them.

papers.title: Henry Reece. The Fall: Last Days of the English Republic

This is in many ways the first book to take on as a distinct research topic the difficulty of explaining why England’s only experiment with non-­monarchical government came to such an abrupt and dramatic end. Sewell’s Logics of History and similar works might have approached the task of accounting for the fall of the republic by asking whether it was a Sewellian event in which an important structural transformation occurred, thereby avoiding the false dilemma between structure and agency present in both structuralist narratives of inevitability and histories premised on strong individual agency. Such a historian might have begun by delving systematically into the difficult but fascinating question of whether the revolutionary regime ever existed on a structural or institutional foundation, a question with implications for the nature of the regime’s downfall.

papers.title: Mistakes I Carried
papers.abstract: Abstract My critical mistake as a historian was ignoring the physical body as a site of knowledge production. For years, I analyzed fitness history in archives and images while overlooking the value of embodied experience. Recognizing this blind spot offers historians a powerful new lens—namely, that bodies can serve as historical archives that capture dimensions of the past inaccessible through traditional sources. In this article, I explore this approach by connecting my personal weight training journey with J. C. Hise, an American strength figure from the 1930s. By examining parallel experiences of extreme body transformation during periods of economic instability—Hise during the Great Depression and myself following the 2008 financial crisis—the article explores how masculine identity crises repeatedly manifest in physical culture. Through my own experience with Hise’s grueling twenty-rep squat program, I discuss how physical practices reshape both bodies and worldviews. This embodied knowledge explains, in part, how fitness cultures reinforce the very insecurities they claim to address while transforming masculine anxiety into profit. By positioning the transformed body as a site where personal metamorphosis intersects with broader social and economic forces, historians can access a more complete understanding of how physical culture has shaped masculine identities across generations.

Frankel delivers a keen, critical, and affectionate take on the themes of consumerism, race and ethnicity, and what he calls “ambivalence and resistance” (10), the latter being represented by fears over “being drawn too far, too quickly into the American orbit” (11). Certainly, the 1960s and early 1970s was a fertile period for Israel adopting US cultural reference points. On the heels of Israel’s stunning victory in the Six-Day War (1967), Israelis were primed to consider new ways of living. The Yom Kippur War (1973), which concludes the formal period under investigation in Frankel’s book, represented a failure of imagination (Israel’s security establishment was under the spell of what became known by analysts as the conceptzia—a false conception of their enemies’ resolve and capabi­­lities to try to undo what Israel had gained in 1967). The months after the Six-Day War was also when France turned away from Israel, and the United States became its main arms supplier. All this solidified what we today call the Israeli-American “special relationship.”

Secularization is the process through which a society transforms into the secular; implicit in such a transformation is the decentering of belief systems and cultural practices associated with religion(s). The secular, to put it inversely, is the outcome of secularization, or as Bilgrami writes, the secular is something “to have come out from under the shadow of religion” (39). The book is thus asking the parallel question: How religious is art (in South Asia today)?

papers.title: Jenny Shaw. The Women of Rendezvous: A Transatlantic Story of Family and Slavery .
papers.abstract: In the summer of 1686, a “great and numerous family” sailed from Barbados to London. They included 2 enslaved African women, an English female servant, 11 children, and the children’s father. John Peers, ­­Barbados’s largest landowner, member of the island’s council, enslaver of 180 people, and master of 8 white servants, had business to attend in London. Three years earlier, 9 of the children had been baptized on the same day in the same church, their names and the names of their parents duly recorded. Their mothers were the enslaved women Susannah Mingo and Elizabeth Ashcroft and the English servant Dorothy Spendlove; their father was Peers, who already had 5 older children, born to two English women whom he had married in succession and who had not survived. After first lodging in London’s fashionable West End, the group from Barbados took up residence in a grand, finely furnished manor house five miles away in the small village of Streatham. There, the enslaved and servant women and their children continued to serve the white members of the family in their new home. Peers’s Eurafrican son may have worn, with his fine livery coat, a locked metal collar similar to those on dogs, as did many enslaved boys at the time in England. In 1689, still in London, the ailing Peers drafted a will and then, three days later, died. Though the amounts bequeathed differed according to the race and status of the recipients, in an unusual move, Peers recognized his entire, multihued family. The will provided for all of the Peers children and all three of their living mothers.

papers.title: David Stefan Doddington. Old Age and American Slavery
papers.abstract: In 1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom’s Cabin. While Uncle Tom’s age is never clear, representative of the uncertainty that most enslaved people had about their age, he was not elderly. Still, scholars, writers, and activists over the years attributed his subservience and passivity to his aging. “His type of goodness,” wrote James Weldon Johnson in his 1912 autobiography, could be found in “lots of old Negroes as foolishly good as he” (The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man, 39). Older people and their treatment have always been part of the story of American enslavement, and yet their experiences within enslavement have most often been portrayed as similar to those felt by other enslaved peoples regardless of age. Experiences as aging enslavers have been largely overlooked as well. Although middle-aged and elderly “Aunties” and “Uncles” were consistent and influential presences within slave communities, treatments of the history of enslavement through age has been nearly absent from the literature. Only in recent decades, with the works of Wilma King, Mary Niall Mitchell, Anna Mae Duane, and Daina Ramey Berry, has age, albeit youth, become useful as an interpretive lens. In fairness, Berry also attended to the elderly, but her interpretations, like those of a handful of other scholars who paid attention to the aged, were more focused upon the support and respect granted them by other enslaved persons and their diminishing monetary value to enslavers. Few historians have sought to understand American enslavement through the physical decline, social isolation, and acquiescence to enslavement experienced by the aging.

papers.title: Adrienne D. deNoyelles. The Lung Block: Plagues, Parks, and Power in Progressive-Era New York
papers.abstract: In The Lung Block: Plagues, Parks, and Power in Progressive Era New York, Adrienne D. deNoyelles explores the failed 1903 park campaign in the so-called “lung block” neighborhood of New York City. The working-class immigrant neighborhood, “two blocks inland from the East River, bounded by Cherry, Catherine, Hamilton, and Market streets,” was well known in the city as an area of poverty overrun by tuberculosis infections (3). In her analysis, deNoyelles “reveals a more richly nuanced picture of Progressive Era social activists in moments of conflict and resistance” (3–4). In doing so, deNoyelles paints a complex portrait of activists, leaders, and residents in conflict over the meaning of citizenship, power, disease, and the nature of contested spaces. Across five chapters, deNoyelles explores—from start to finish—a single conflicted park campaign. Each chapter focuses on the perspective of one activist or faction involved in the park effort. These individuals include Hermann Biggs, the chief bacteriologist for the city’s Department of Health; Lawrence Vellier, an activist dedicated to housing regulation; statistician Lilian Brandt; journalists Ernest Poole and Jacob Riis; and local Catholic priest Father James Curry. This approach allows deNoyelles to explore various perspectives, focusing on the personal stories of those involved in the campaign while not losing focus on the larger story of the Progressive Era.

papers.title: Elizabeth O’Brien Ingleson. Made in China: When US-China Interests Converged to Transform Global Trade
papers.abstract: China is today the largest exporter in the world. China’s largest market is the United States, and the country has been one of the largest sources of US imports for years, with a handsome trade advantage in China’s favor for decades. Elizabeth O’Brien Ingleson’s book Made in China explores how this came about, examining the first decade of the People’s Republic of China’s official trade with the United States, the 1970s. The book makes a revisionist argument about the importance of that decade to the modern US–China trade relationship. For much of the two centuries before the 1970s, Americans had thought of China as a market with as many as 400 million customers. But knowing what we now know about trends in that relationship after the 1970s, Ingleson suggests the real importance of the 1970s was the growth of Chinese exports to the United States and the beginning of China as the home of 800 million workers manufacturing products made in China but sold to Americans.

papers.title: Renée Poznanski. Propaganda and Persecution: The French Resistance and the “Jewish Question . ” Translated by Lenn J. Schramm
papers.abstract: In this abridged and translated version of her original book, Renée Poznanski offers readers a unique opportunity to think about the French Resistance and its stance on Jewish persecution. The author is not concerned with the measure of antisemitism in France or within the French Resistance, but rather the French social imaginary as it elaborated various responses to the so-called “Jewish question.” Instead of a black or white approach to antisemitism in this period, Poznanski uses close reading of the underground press and broadcasts from London to discover how they dealt with Nazi and Vichy persecutions against Jews in France. In the opening of Propaganda and Persecution, the author argues that “[w]hat is at issue here is the Jews’ place in the French cultural imaginary—not among the overt antisemites but among those who committed themselves, at their mortal peril, to fighting against the camp that harbored the antisemites” (xv). Poznanski tackles this question in chronological order, by starting in the 1930s, where she highlights the centrality of the “Jewish question” to texts—so much so that this Judeophobic rhetoric appeared in the writings of people who were ostensibly opposed to antisemitism. Naturally, the proliferation of antisemitic literature was sped up by the creation of the Vichy regime, normalized by its many laws and decrees targeting Jews, and supported by the historical legacy of “reasonable antisemitism” in France. It was into this landscape that the early resistance organizations, both metropolitan and overseas, were forced to decide how they could, on the one hand, wage war on Nazi narratives, and on the other, win over French public opinion. To be clear, one did not need to oppose the antisemitic measures of the day to be opposed to Nazism—we know from decades of research, including Poznanski’s, that many resisters had no ethical issue with many of Vichy’s antisemitic laws, beyond the fact that they seemed to be imported from Nazi Germany; however, all resistance organizations felt the need to counter Nazi propaganda (and Vichy propaganda that seemed to support Nazi goals). Thus, we find early references to antisemitism in Resistance messaging, often couched in broader attacks on the Nazis.

papers.title: Crystal R. Sanders. A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to HBCUs .
papers.abstract: In A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to HBCUs, Crystal Sanders uses legal and policy documents from archives while also foregrounding biographies, memoirs, and interviews with recipients and surviving family members to discuss the use and reach of “segregation scholarships.” These scholarships were used by Southern and border states to maintain anti-Black segregation by diverting funding from public historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) to (under)fund Black graduate and professional study at institutions “elsewhere” between the 1920s and 1960s. Black middle-class students—most often public-school teachers and administrators—were the prototypical recipients of these funds. Law school students, however, were the most frequent test cases against segregation in higher education because it was easier to show material harm based on how the legal profession operated. Sanders contends that these graduate students engaged in “intellectual warfare,” or “the subversive act of acquiring knowledge,” in often better-ranked white graduate institutions outside the South (2). Graduates used this education to “literally remake the academy” and other fields/disciplines by pushing for the end of segregation and training a new generation of scholars and professionals who further resisted and proactively attacked anti-Black uses of decidedly integrated tax dollars in education, medicine, and law (12). The committed fight against segregation was an explicit rebellion against public tax-supported institutions being solely white spaces. Few of these institutions were solely white spaces anyway as they routinely admitted international and domestic non-white students.

papers.title: Kathleen DuVal. Native Nations: A Millennium in North America
papers.abstract: In the book Native Nations: A Millennium in North America, historian Kathleen DuVal attempts two herculean tasks. The first is tackling a thousand years of Indigenous North American history in a single monograph. The second, and far more challenging, is reshaping the general public’s perception of that history. Despite some blind spots, this well-written and engaging effort achieves the first goal; yet only time will tell if it can undo centuries of misinformation regarding Indigenous life on the continent before and after European invasion. Duval’s work contends with early American historiography’s reliance on well-familiar tropes regarding Indigenous America, such as Natives being changeless people outside of history with little power to stop the overwhelming tide of colonization and progress, whose story ends with the 1890 massacre at Wounded Knee. In traditional versions of US history, Indians play the dual role of the savage/victim, both terrifying and pitiable, depending on the immediate psychological needs of colonizers and their descendants. To combat these long-outdated frameworks, Native Nations emphasizes the existence of strong, stable, and diverse Indigenous cultures that existed long before, and crucially, long after Europeans invaded North America. DuVal demonstrates profound change over time, undermining those assumptions and revealing that European domination, be it from Dutch, Spanish, English, or French colonizers, was neither immediate nor inevitable.

papers.title: Javier Fernández-Galeano. Queer Obscenity: Erotic Archives in Dictatorial Spain
papers.abstract: Javier Fernández-Galeano is already recognized as a groundbreaking author and a source of inspiration for those studying the history of sexuality in Spain. He is one of the most promising historians in the field of modern sexuality. While his first book, Maricas (2024), delved into queer cultures and state violence in Argentina and Spain, Queer Obscenity: Erotic Archives in Dictatorial Spain explores the intricacies of the Spanish erotic archive between 1923 and the late 1970s. In six chapters, Fernández-Galeano examines the production and circulation of erotica and pornography in two authoritarian contexts: the Primo de Rivera dictatorship (1923–1930), which he explores in the first chapter, and the Franco regime (1939–1975). The book ends with the transition to democracy and the new tensions created by the liberalization of censorship and the normalization of pornography. Although each chapter stands well on its own, a common thread runs through the book, addressing the politics of preservation, archiving, and visibility of erotic and pornographic material.

papers.title: Sean Griffin. The Root and the Branch: Working-Class Reform and Antislavery, 1790–1860
papers.abstract: What few historians are successful in doing, Sean Griffin accomplishes masterfully: making sense of a complicated story by bridging studies in labor and antislavery and standing among those scholars—Bruce Laurie, Mark Lause, and Keri Leigh Merritt, to name a select few—who have explored the relationship between slavery, antislavery, and free labor. This book fits nicely with recent studies on the history of capitalism and slavery. Griffin’s book is also in conversation with classic works, such as Eric Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery, and David Brion Davis’s works. Without diminishing the “central insights,” he says, of Davis’s work, Griffin boldly challenges an aspect of the “Davis thesis” which continues to present the “conflict between labor and antislavery as irreconcilable” (15). The Root and the Branch should be seen as a welcome revision. Griffin grapples with the question of “why a more robust” opposition to slavery failed to emerge in the labor movement (3). He traces the “common origins and impulses” of both reform campaigns and why they were unable to forge a formidable political coalition to combat labor exploitation wherever it appeared. Reasons why such a strong reformist phalanx could not be generated, according to contemporary historians, included racism, disagreements over strategies, the effectiveness of political activism and religious institutions, and disagreements over which movement (abolition or labor reform) should take priority.

papers.title: Andrea Wright. Unruly Labor: A History of Oil in the Arabian Sea .
papers.abstract: Andrea Wright’s timely monograph traces the consolidation of the nation-state through labor struggles in the oil-producing countries encircling the Arabian Sea in the waning days of the ­­British Empire. Unruly Labor opens with a chapter on oil work and oilfield mobilization in 1930s and 1940s Iran, where the Tudeh, the Iranian communist party, held significant influence and an internationalist orientation. Wright notes the extent to which noncitizens—especially Indian migrant workers—took part in a 1946 Tudeh-led strike to improve the labor and living conditions they shared with Iranians. Confronted with an anti-imperialist form of class solidarity that crossed ethnonational lines, representatives of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company advanced a paternalistic form of national development for Iranians—the “cultivat[ion] of workers into good citizens” through education and noncommunist union membership—combined with the deportation of “undesirable,” often communist, Indian workers (32–34). From here, Wright’s argument tacks across the Arabian Sea, encompassing labor struggles in Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Yemen from the 1940s through the early 1970s. Chapter 2 traces how the Kuwaiti state’s attempts to advocate for Kuwaiti oil workers amid mobilizations by a diverse workforce comprising local and migrant workers prompted a more restrictive definition of Kuwaiti citizenship. Chapter 3 details efforts by highly skilled Indian chemists to protest their subordinate status within the racialized labor hierarchies established by a US-owned oil company in Bahrain, which spurred the intercession of the newly independent Indian state on behalf of its citizens in the late 1940s. ­­Chapter 4 examines a cross-class hunger strike by Indian workers at a British refinery under construction in Aden. This strike drew from a nationalist tradition of protest against racial and religious discrimination targeting Indians—especially Hindus—laboring abroad, prompting Indian state intervention to defend the new nation’s honor. Chapter 5 returns to Bahrain, tracing growing pan-Arab nationalism among Arabic-speaking local and migrant workers in the mid-1950s. Pan-Arab, pro-Palestine, and anti-imperialist organizing prompted a crackdown against labor organizers and the passage of a labor law that constrained unions’ ability to make international affiliations, placed restrictions on noncitizens’ union activities, and limited unions’ right to strike. Chapter 6 examines a series of strikes in 1960s Qatar that specifically aimed to increase the rights of Qatari workers vis-à-vis noncitizens—including other Arab workers—amid drives to Qatarize the workforce and restrict non-Qatari capital. But by the end of the decade, a large majority of the oilfield labor came to be performed by South Asian migrants, while Qataris themselves increasingly abandoned such work as they began to receive growing shares of the country’s oil wealth via patronage. Chapter 7 moves to Abu Dhabi, where strikes against a ruler regarded by his British patrons as ineffectual led to a British-backed coup and an increasingly securitized approach to oilfield labor, including a more ready recourse to police and military force to suppress strikes and the passage of a labor law that banned labor actions in the public sector that might pose risks to “persons and property” (187). By 1970, a recognition that national governments throughout the region would ultimately assert control over their petroleum industries led international oil companies to move toward contracting services rather than owning and operating assets. This final shift laid the groundwork for the labor regime that emerged across the oil industry in much of the region: state employment in nationalized oil companies for citizens of Arab Gulf states, lucrative contracting work for Europeans and ­­Americans, increasingly limited opportunities for non-Gulf Arabs, and highly securitized manual labor for South Asian migrant workers.

papers.title: David Carey Jr. Health in the Highlands: Indigenous Healing and Scientific Medicine in Guatemala and Ecuador.
papers.abstract: In 1996, Jennifer S. H. Brown and Elizabeth Vibert’s edited volume, Reading Beyond Words, argued that it takes patience to recover and communicate the experiences and perspectives of those for whom the historical record is lacking or limited by the interpretation of others. In his work Health in the Highlands, David Carey Jr. takes on this challenge through an examination of public health within Indigenous communities in Guatemala and Ecuador. The book positions at its center the experiences of indígenas, teasing out their perspectives and interactions from outsider sources during an intense period of labor coercion and land colonization between the 1870s and 1930s in Latin America. Although Indigenous experiences with health care have been difficult at best to ascertain, Guatemala and Ecuador provide critical case studies, as these two countries have high proportions of Indigenous populations that make their erasure from the national archives impossible. The book is organized thematically over six main chapters, weaving together the connections among modernization, indigeneity, and medicine. Through an examination of the interactions among an array of actors, Carey’s research like roots of a tree tap into social, economic, and political soils. Beginning with the assertion that conceptions of health were bound up with concepts of the nation, Carey pursues a transnational analysis that destabilizes states and corporate entities as interpretive lenses in favor of analyzing power dynamics through body experiences and Indigenous encounters with illness and healing, along with the circulation of theories of race and racial difference. This work draws from a variety of archives, including the Rockefeller Archive Center, the Archivo General de Centroamérica and Academia de Geografía, Revista Militar, Revista Agricola, Government and Public Health Memorias in Guatemala, and the Museo de Medicina and the Archivo Nacional del Ecuador in Ecuador.

papers.title: Andre Schmid. North Korea's Mundane Revolution: Socialist Living and the Rise of Kim Il Sung, 1953–1965 .
papers.abstract: In his new book North Korea’s Mundane Revolution, historian Andre Schmid tackles the subject of North Korean social history. Utilizing lesser-known North Korean newspapers and magazines, Schmid uncovers fascinating details of North Korean socialism in the 1950s and 1960s. While analyses of North Korean print media can be quite repetitive and boring, Schmid skillfully brings to life the postwar nation-building projects and narrative processes that came to dominate the public lives of normal North Koreans. From describing socialist work competitions in factories to the advice literature that pervaded the pages of party newspapers, Schmid illuminates the social order and urban rehabilitation of postwar North Korea. Rather than offering the typical chapter-by-chapter summary, I will use this book review to illuminate some of Schmid’s most interesting findings about the North Korean party-state that you likely won’t find in other English-language books dealing with this enigmatic regime. Schmid spends a large amount of time investigating the political economy of the early North Korean party-state. This examination of the North Korean economy is fascinating on a variety of fronts. First and foremost, it contests the Western caricature of communist economics as a strictly top-down enterprise that simply grinds down humanity with Stakhanovite brutality to meet ridiculous quotas. Schmid highlights how the workers of the nascent Kim family regime voiced their concerns and criticism of national economic policies. For instance, they criticized the party-state with their choice of living quarters. Despite Party pleas for rural workers to remain in the countryside, many from those regions moved to urban areas for higher wages and better job opportunities.

papers.title: Tanisha C. Ford. Our Secret Society: Mollie Moon and the Glamour, Money, and Power Behind the Civil Rights Movement.
papers.abstract: On February 26, 1964, philanthropists and activists gathered in the ball room of Rodman Rockefeller’s Westchester, New York estate to raise funds for civil rights movement efforts. The ornately decorated room was filled with dedicated white and Black donors, well known civil rights leaders including Whitney Young, Roy Wilkins, Dorothy Height, and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and one less well-known Black woman activist: Mollie Moon. With this scene Tanisha C. Ford welcomes readers to Our Secret Society: Mollie Moon and the Glamour, Money, and Power Behind the Civil Rights Movement. Ford has published on cultural history and fashion, social justice history, and Black women’s memoir, and in this fourth book-length publication she devotes her efforts to the political life and work of Mollie Moon, a critical behind-the-scenes fundraiser for civil rights organizations and activities. Written in an accessible, engaging manner, Our Secret Society intertwines a biography of Moon with discussions of the politics of philanthropy and premier civil rights institutions like the National Urban League (NUL). In sixteen succinct chapters, with photos, footnotes, and a rich bibliography, Ford invites readers behind “the veil” of movement strivings and challenges using Moon’s life as the vehicle (8).

papers.title: Jian Chen. Zhou Enlai: A Life .
papers.abstract: Zhou Enlai was probably the most important leader in the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) after Mao Zedong, his ill-fated successor, Liu Shaoqi, and his ultimate surviving leader, Deng Xiaoping. Together they formed the CCP and the new People’s Republic of China, founded by the party in 1949. Yet assessing Zhou’s life has been clouded not only by the secrecy that characterizes the lives of top Chinese party leaders but also by the enduring tension in Zhou’s life: Was he the “Grey Eminence” and “Duke of Zhou” so warmly remembered by survivors of the tumultuous Cultural Revolution for protecting many cadres and intellectuals, or was Zhou a tragic enabler of Mao Zedong’s tyranny who failed to stand up to the nation’s leader, who had become a vicious bully? Chen Jian’s biography faces this question squarely and gives the historian’s answer: It’s not so simple, Zhou was both. The seven hundred pages of text and a hundred pages of notes and appendixes explain why; it is a highly readable narrative account that walks the reader through the major stages of China’s modern revolutionary history and the growth and changes of the CCP from the 1920s until Zhou’s death in early 1976.

papers.title: Joel Cabrita. Written Out: The Silencing of Regina Gelana Twala .
papers.abstract: Regina Gelana Twala is resurrected through the mediumship of historian Joel Cabrita’s astonishing biography of a rich, complex, resilient life, rendered beautifully by the biographer. Reading it leaves one with a need for more books on the life and thought of R. G. Twala. She is an intellectual ancestor who was as human as they come, and we will honor ourselves by remembering her life’s work. The reader will delight in her spunk, despair at her sometimes puritanical approach to life, and yet glory in the evidence that hers was a generous and well-lived life. Here was a woman who knew her mind and was not afraid to own it. As bell hooks reminds us, “No black woman writer in this culture can write ‘too much’ [… .] Considering the centuries of silence […], more contributions by women writers should be encouraged and welcomed.” This biography joins other recent works chronicling the lives of South African women whose stories were silenced or have to be told, and many are cited at the beginning of this book.

papers.title: David Reeve. To Remain Myself: The History of Onghokham .
papers.abstract: Indonesian historian Onghokham was “the best guide to Indonesia,” and he could be “the serious historian, the public intellectual, the sexual being, the quiet lover, or the hedonist and party host” (298). He was also “a maverick, an eccentric, an alcoholic, and an outsider who became an insider, [with] a mischievous wit” (295), as David Reeve writes in his biography of Onghokham—which is extraordinary for exposing virtually everything about Ong. As Ong said to his family, “I want the family to tell David everything bad about me,” which in some ways could include everything bad about the family as well (287). Ong died in 2007, too late to see the book, but Reeve, an Australian researcher with deep connections to Indonesia, has done a marvelous job of fulfilling Ong’s wish to tell the full story. Reeve coedited Onze Ong, a posthumous recollection by Ong’s friends, which was a key source for reconstructing Ong’s life; Reeve also relies on interviews and letters Ong wrote to his Cornell friends, such as Benedict Anderson, Daniel Lev, and Herbert Feith. The result is an affective narrative with a multiplicity of voices speaking to Ong’s emotional life, his identity, his worldview, and his lifestyle. We cannot help but admire Ong, who shows us how to remain oneself in the time and space within which one is embedded. As such, Ong’s biography is a critical intervention into the political establishment and cultural assumptions of Indonesian society.

papers.title: Niels Eichhorn and Duncan A. Campbell. The Civil War in the Age of Nationalism.
papers.abstract: The Civil War in the Age of Nationalism offers an ambitious reframing of the American Civil War era, one targeting navel-gazing studies that assume the United States was the only country to deal with the dynamics that led to political fracture and reformation. Drawing inspiration from Carl Degler’s underappreciated One Among Many: the Civil War in Comparative Perspective (1990) and Thomas Bender’s A Nation Among Nations: America’s Place in World History (2006), Niels Eichhorn and Duncan A. Campbell offer a “comparative study of the Civil War era” that “explores how the American conflict fit into global trends and helped craft our own contemporary world” (1). Eleven densely packed chapters cover a range of topics including nationalism, liberalism, secession, imperialism, emancipation, and religious evangelism. The US experience is placed alongside similar developments elsewhere, most frequently in Europe and Latin America, but when relevant in Asia, Africa, and Australia. The impressive geographic and chronological scope (evidenced by an invaluable 45-page bibliography) sets this book apart from a growing corpus examining the Global Civil War.

papers.title: Mistakes I Dare Not Admit
papers.abstract: History Unclassified’s first special edition is dedicated to mistakes. That is fitting because History Unclassified began in failure and rejection. In 2017, Kate Brown submitted a screenplay to the American Historical Review. It was not necessarily a good play, but it was all history, footnoted with newly-unearthed archival sources. Why, Kate asked, does history in the AHR generally appear in the same format? Why can’t, for example, nonfiction take fictional form? She found the format of a screenplay useful to narrate actions that occurred in different times and places simultaneously on stage. The stage helped frame the Chernobyl tragedy more reliably than chronology, she argued, because one effect of radioactive contaminants was to both slow time and speed it up. The readers rejected the play, but what was meant as a provocation started a conversation between Kate and Alex Lichtenstein, then AHR editor, and led to the launch of the History Unclassified section in June 2018.

papers.title: John K. Bardes. The Carceral City: Slavery and the Making of Mass Incarceration in New Orleans, 1803–1930
papers.abstract: Scholars and students in a plethora of fields will benefit from John K. Bardes’s outstanding book The Carceral City: Slavery and the Making of Mass Incarceration in New Orleans, 1803–1930. Superbly researched and written, this study contends that the nation’s carceral crisis is more than two centuries in the making, with origins long predating the Jim Crow era. State power and the post-Civil War prison complex did not simply replace the institution of slavery and private plantations, as popularly understood; rather, the author argues, “many antebellum slaveholders were fiercely committed to and deeply reliant upon, the use of police and prisons to coerce enslaved and free labor” (3). Bardes’s introduction includes a thorough historiographical discussion of the myriad ways The Carceral City engages scholars past and present and works to steer various disciplinary debates. Prison histories, for instance, have been too focused on the Northern United States, northern Europe, and the post-Civil War and Emancipation South, excluding slave societies and their tangled “interplay of race, slavery, and the growth of state power” (6). Studies of urban slavery have overemphasized “the relative freedoms that enslaved people accessed within cities, rather than the particular policing and carceral systems that cities developed to counteract those freedoms” (5). The author also furthers ongoing efforts to inject slavery and the American South into histories of the state and capitalism. But most impressively, each of the seven chapters and the epilogue include numerous historiographic interventions that greatly enrich readers’ understanding of the content while not interrupting the flow and readability of the text.

papers.title: Phillip Burnham. The Education of Clarence Three Stars: A Lakota American Life .
papers.abstract: Phillip Burnham has produced another compelling biography of a significant Lakota figure. His previous work on Dewey Beard is widely recognized as an essential account of a Wounded Knee survivor’s life. In The Education of Clarence Three Stars, Burnham tackles another critical issue in Lakota—and broader Native American—history: assimilation through education. The forced enrollment of children in schools, whether local reservation day schools or distant boarding schools, profoundly impacted the Lakota way of life, both collectively and individually. To call it cultural genocide is no exaggeration. Burnham delves into Three Stars’s experiences at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, highlighting the broader implications of Native American education during that era. The narrative chronicles his journey from early life near the Black Hills to becoming a pioneering educator, lawyer, and president of the Oglala Sioux Tribe. The book provides a nuanced perspective on the challenges and transformations faced by Native Americans from the pre-reservation period through significant legislative changes like the Dawes Act of 1887.

papers.title: Lifesaving, Sovereignty, and the Place of the Late Ottoman Empire in the European International Order
papers.abstract: Abstract: This article analyzes the status of the late Ottoman Empire in the European international order through an actor of both local and global historical dimensions, the Black Sea Lifesaving Service. This service was established by European powers in 1866 to provide assistance in the event of shipwrecks at the entrance to the Bosporus and was administered by an international organization from 1881 on. The article argues that this form of interimperial intervention by an international organization into local Ottoman lifesaving structures can be seen as an instance of Western interference in the sovereign affairs of the Ottoman Empire, justified on humanitarian grounds. Western actors interpreted the Ottoman Empire’s inability or unwillingness to provide adequate lifesaving services as evidence of its inferior “civilizational” status and the need for intervention and modernization, a logic understood and acted upon by Ottoman authorities.

papers.title: The Monarchs’ History Men: What Has Changed over Three Centuries?
papers.abstract: Abstract Since its foundation in 1724, the regius chair has been held by twenty-two men. In this study, I consider a small selection of them, using a range of sources including a guard book in Cambridge University’s archives and portraits in order to reflect on their lives, works, and reputations and on ways of analysing the history of one specific post. Implicit is a measure of scepticism about ‘professionalization’ as an explanation for the nature of historical practice over three hundred years and about existing interpretations of past claims that history is a science.

papers.title: Barbra Streisand. My Name is Barbra .
papers.abstract: “What is so offensive about a woman taking control?” Barbra Streisand asks on page 472 of her 2023 memoir My Name is Barbra. Her context is the fierce opposition she encountered in her quest to direct a film rather than simply star in it, but the question is a broader one and sadly resonant today as top ranks of the United States Armed Forces are purged of hard-working, qualified, and talented female leaders on no basis other than their identity as women. Uncannily, even defiantly, sure of herself since, apparently, birth, Streisand hasn’t exactly gone unheralded. Her accomplishments are legendary and legion: she is a member of the highly exclusive EGOT club, meaning her trophy shelf includes an Emmy (5), a Grammy (5), an Oscar (2), and a Tony (1). She has received both the National Medal of the Arts (2000) and the Presidential Medal of Freedom (2015). Her performance as Fanny Brice in the movie of Funny Girl earned her an Oscar at age twenty-one; legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael titled her review of the movie simply “Bravo!”

papers.title: David R. M. Beck. Bribed with Our Own Money: Federal Abuse of American Indian Funds in the Termination Era
papers.abstract: Bribed with Our Own Money: Federal Abuse of American Indian Funds in the Termination Era by David R. M. Beck is a fine addition to a growing body of scholarly literature on the federal policy of termination. The policy to terminate Indian reservations, and hence end the treaty status of Native American nations, has been the subject of multiple manuscripts in the last decades, so the topic is not new to the field of Native American studies. What has not been sufficiently researched previously is how this termination was paid for, and how the federal officials and congressmen advocating for the policy got American Indian leaders to agree to their own termination, as Congress expected at least a minimal level of agreement on the policy. David R. M. Beck’s new book seeks to fill this void in the scholarship. He focuses on six reservations and how their leadership were pressured, or “bribed” as Beck puts it, to accept termination bills in order to receive congressional approval for the release of their own money, which was awarded as compensation for mismanaged forest lands, lands flooded by dammed rivers, or stolen lands.

Best, and Theresa Rajack-Talley, provides an in-depth examination of Black women’s roles in global food systems. In this volume, Black women’s lived experiences are the prism through which food justice, food security, and sustainable agricultural practices are evaluated and understood. The chapters of this book collectively articulate the intersections of the personal and political dimensions of food systems. This book draws on interdisciplinary research methods to amplify Black women’s often-overlooked voices and contributions to global food systems. This book is structured into three distinct parts: “From the Fields,” “Food and Social Justice,” and “Food Security, Health, and Well-Being.” These sections examine themes of labor, justice, and health and highlight the interconnectedness of race, gender, and socioeconomics. Each section illuminates women’s pivotal roles in simultaneously shaping food systems and addressing systemic inequities that have historically marginalized their contributions.

papers.title: Jacob Flaws. Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp .
papers.abstract: Among the countless sites of brutality and criminality associated with the Holocaust implemented by Nazi Germany, the extermination camps associated with Operation Reinhard are perhaps the most notorious and enigmatic. Jacob Flaws’s Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp offers insights into one of those camps. Located approximately eighty kilometers northeast of Warsaw in the German-occupied General Government district, the Treblinka extermination camp operated between July 1942 and October 1943. During that relatively short time, an unfathomable 700,000 to 900,000 men, women, and children, predominantly Polish Jews from occupied Polish territories, were murdered in Treblinka’s gas chambers and proximate spaces. Together with Operation Reinhard’s two other main extermination camps, Belźec and Sobibór, SS troopers and their auxiliaries carried out the murder of approximately 1.6 million people, the deadliest phase of Hitler’s Final Solution to exterminate Jews and other groups regarded as subhuman by Nazi ideology. Flaws delves into this dark chapter and takes readers beyond the shocking and mind-numbing numbers to explore how perpetrators, victims, survivors, and various types of witnesses experienced Treblinka and how those experiences extended far beyond the barbed wire, guard towers, and anti-tank obstacles that defined its perimeter.

papers.title: Robin Bernstein. Freeman’s Challenge: The Murder that Shook America’s Original Prison for Profit
papers.abstract: Robin Bernstein’s book, Freeman’s Challenge, centers on the life of William Freeman, an Afro-native man who lived in Auburn, New York, from the 1820s to the 1840s and served a prison sentence there. Its ten chapters are organized into three sections. The first section introduces readers to Freeman. We learn that his parents struggled with alcohol abuse, that he stole chickens as a child, and was later found with a stolen horse in a nearby town. As an alibi, the then sixteen-year-old said that he had been sent on an errand with the horse by a man named Jack Furman, a fellow Black resident of Auburn. Authorities cross-examined Furman and ultimately believed the latter’s testimony. Young Freeman was subsequently held in the nearby Cayuga County jail to await trial, but he escaped with another inmate before it commenced. This probably contributed to the longer-than-usual sentence he received after his capture: five years in Auburn State Penitentiary.

papers.title: 張娟芬 (Chang Chuan-fen). 流氓, 王信福 (Hooligan, Wang Xinfu) .
papers.abstract: In April 2024, the Constitutional Court of Taiwan heard arguments against the constitutionality of the death penalty. The case was initiated by Wang Xinfu, the oldest person currently detained on death row, and was supported by his thirty-seven fellow death-row inmates. Hooligan, Wang Xinfu describes how the system of martial law in Taiwan had criminalized Wang throughout his youth and eventually led to a conviction for a murder Wang did not commit. Although constructed around an individual life, Chang Chuan-fen’s genre-defying book is not a biography of a man so much as a scrupulous examination of a corrupt police investigation and a reconstruction of a trial convened over a decade after the crime. Through the example of Wang Xinfu, Chang Chuan-fen describes how the Guomindang regime disciplined the population of Taiwan and oversaw the creation of a stigmatized hooligan class: people who could be targeted by an extrajudicial system of punishment and labor extraction.

papers.title: Captive Cosmopolitans: Black Mariners and the World of South Atlantic Slavery. By Mary E. Hicks
papers.abstract: Captive Cosmopolitans: Black Mariners and the World of South Atlantic Slavery represents an outstanding contribution to the growing literature on the multifaceted lives of Africans and those of African descent as they dexterously navigated spaces of water during the trans-Atlantic slave trade. Mary E. Hicks follows the journeys of enslaved Black mariners who traversed the South Atlantic serving in multiple positions both aboard slave ships and at coastal ports, for instance, as cabin boys, carpenters, cooks, interpreters, healers and surgeons. Black mariners’ identities and social statuses frequently changed: Hicks shows how an enslaved African male might be taken from the West African littoral to Bahia, Brazil and shackled under deck in fetid conditions, perhaps to then return whence they came in the capacity of an enslaved mariner expected to work in translation and taking care of those chained, once more, below deck. Dubbed “captive cosmopolitans,” these Black mariners demonstrated how they were frequently cognizant of laws, which they might employ to secure their liberty from the bonds of slavery.

papers.title: Secrecy and sovereignty in the Age of Revolutions
papers.abstract: Abstract Transparency, or publicity as it was then called, became a fundamental value linked to popular sovereignty in the late eighteenth century. Those who advocated greater publicity, particularly of legislative deliberations, did so as part of an overarching vision of political representation as a process by which the popular will was to be continuously reflected in government. Publicity, in short, would make popular sovereignty possible. But when elected officials in the early United States and revolutionary France made claims to speak for the people, the use of secrecy actually strengthened those claims by temporally dislocating disagreement to after the passage of unpopular policies rather than during the deliberative process. This reality created a paradox at the heart of representative government: secrecy was bolstering a type of regime to which it was simultaneously deemed anathema. Placing procedural decisions about publicity and secrecy front and center, this article addresses questions long plaguing historians: how did the American framers secure what Edmund Morgan called the “fiction of popular sovereignty”? And why were French revolutionaries unable to do the same? One answer, which has long been neglected despite its significance, is the procedural practices of constituent bodies in each context. This article undertakes a comparison of the procedural decisions in the American Constitutional Convention and subsequent legislature and the establishment of the French National Assembly and successor legislatures. It argues that there is nothing mystical about the legitimacy of popular sovereignty through representative government: it was the result of deliberate decisions about the procedures of governance.

papers.title: The Vortex: An Environmental History of the Modern World. By Frank Uekötter
papers.abstract: The Vortex is an ambitious reinterpretation of modern history that foregrounds the natural world. Over the past five centuries, human societies have expanded, fought, oppressed, rebelled, traded, and built in ways that have profoundly shaped life on Earth. Throughout, the environment itself has been a dynamic sculptor of world history, etching or foreclosing paths often beyond the intentions of our species. The book captures this thesis in its title and central metaphor of a vortex: “The key is that the vortex highlights the powers of the nonhuman world and their unrelenting inclination to push humans around” (11). The Vortex is an unapologetically anthropocentric book in which the environment constitutes perhaps the most important player—one that humans seek to master at their peril and whose instability in the face of modernity threatens increasingly to lead to collective catastrophe. Frank Uekötter is the author of several important books about the environmental history of Germany. Here he broadens his canvas. This book’s temporal sweep concentrates on the years between 1500 and 1970. The geographic scope covers all of planet Earth, with particular areas of focus, backed up by original archival research, on Germany, the United States, and the United Kingdom. In prose running across forty chapters and more than six hundred pages, Uekötter combines the tools of global history and environmental history to weave a provocative argument about what we can and cannot know about the modern world. He places The Vortex in dialogue with several other major syntheses of global environmental history, most prominently J.R. McNeill’s Something New Under the Sun and Joachim Radkau’s Nature and Power. Uekötter’s principal intervention is to emphasize disorder. “The best one-sentence summary of this volume,” he writes, “would be that it is all a big mess, and we are stuck in the middle of it” (611). Against the comparatively neat narratives of McNeill and Radkau, Uekötter asserts a more chaotic vision.

papers.title: Metricizing diaspora dualities: a comparative quantitative analysis of poetry and prose in Southeast Asian Chinese literature
papers.abstract: Abstract The intersection of quantitative literary studies and diaspora research presents critical opportunities for examining linguistic divergence between immigrant literatures and their cultural origins. While digital humanities scholarship has increasingly embraced computational methods, systematic applications in comparative diaspora studies—particularly those focusing on Southeast Asian Chinese communities—remain underdeveloped. This study bridges this gap through a corpus-driven analysis of 372 literary works (comprising 240 poems and 132 prose pieces) using natural language processing pipelines, hierarchical clustering, and one-way analysis of variance. The common features we proposed have played a greater role in distinguishing Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora new poetry from Chinese mainland poetry. We found that the new poetry of Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora new poetry is not as natural as that of Chinese Mainland, showing greater freedom and diversity in vocabulary selection. Specifically, the vocabulary usage rate of Southeast Asian diaspora new poetry is relatively high, while the grammar usage rate is low. These computationally derived patterns not only establish measurable criteria for distinguishing diaspora literatures through machine-learning classifiers, but also challenge conventional assumptions about linguistic “naturalness” in cross-cultural contexts. Our methodology, which integrates computational stylistics with diaspora theory, provides a replicable analytical framework for studying literary migration phenomena, thereby advancing both digital humanities methodologies and Southeast Asian literary studies.

papers.title: “When all the liquid World was one extended Thames”: Early Modern British Prospects in West African Estuaries
papers.abstract: This essay examines how cross-cultural politics and local ecologies shaped early modern British imperial structures by focusing on the Royal African Company’s efforts to exploit West African estuaries for economic and political advantage. Company agents pursued two strategies to integrate these tropical estuaries into a mercantilist imperial framework: prospecting, which sought to render estuarine productivity legible from across the Atlantic, and settling, which involved manipulating local trade dynamics and mobilizing both human and nonhuman forces to serve company interests. Environmental obstacles and African and European competition, however, hampered these ambitions. The result was the formation of hybrid waterscapes that reflected the entanglement of British imperial aspirations with local power dynamics and estuarine ecologies. In response to these challenges, a grassroots coastal trade emerged in the late seventeenth century to offset the difficulty of controlling any single river system. This evolving structure strengthened Britain’s Atlantic slave trade by facilitating the movement of captives, improving access to labor, and reducing shipboard mortality. It also encouraged a shift toward an aggregate estuarine strategy centered on the more secure, nonestuarine outpost of Cape Coast Castle. Drawing on the company records, travel narratives, and environmental histories, this essay argues that attending to the political ecology of estuaries reveals the adaptive and contested nature of British imperial expansion in West Africa.

papers.title: Fixing Early Modern Identity in the Mobile Mediterranean
papers.abstract: What did it mean to have religious and spatial mobility serve as both a professional asset and a legal liability? This article addresses the question through the lens of an early seventeenth-century Venetian inquisitorial trial involving agents who served as brokers and interpreters for Ottoman and Persian merchants in the city. The brokers’ backgrounds were marked by geographical and religious mobility. Their profession required competence in Turkish and/or Persian, which many had acquired while living periods of their lives as Muslims in the eastern Mediterranean. Like other early modern European commercial hubs, Venetian policy was driven by twin imperatives: on the one hand, the imperative of facilitating the movement of people and goods across religious and jurisdictional boundaries for reasons of commerce, and, on the other, the imperative of ensuring the fixity of identity, particularly religious identity. The Venetian state was a complex bureaucratic entity, and each of these imperatives was pursued by different magistracies at different times. The case demonstrates that while the brokers were valued by certain state institutions for their perceived ability to move between the worlds of Latin Christendom and Islam, that mobility proved a liability before other institutions that insisted upon fixity of religious identity. The case points to a set of strategies the brokers employed to negotiate the tension between mobility as an asset and a liability.
