papers.title: Parallel Revolution: Hungarian Peasants during the Upheavals of 1918–1920
papers.abstract: This article is the first study of Hungarian peasant revolutionism during the political upheavals that immediately followed the First World War and the collapse of the Habsburg Empire. Historians of Hungary have charted the revolutionary movements that brought to power Mihály Károlyi’s liberal regime in November 1918 and Béla Kun’s communist regime in March 1919, but they have mostly neglected the rural revolution that unfolded in parallel with events in Budapest. Although peasants enacted their vision of a new society for just a brief period in November 1918, their experience decisively shaped their attitudes toward successive urban-based governments. Rural discontent stemming in large part from the peasants’ stillborn revolution contributed to the fall of both Károlyi and Kun and helped pave the way for the counterrevolutionary regime of Miklós Horthy. It also influenced interwar Hungarian political culture in important ways. Instead of seeing Hungarian peasants as mere consumers of revolution emanating from the capital, as either passive allies or opponents, this article reveals villagers’ autonomy in articulating and pursuing revolutionary demands of their own. Communist tactics vis-à-vis the countryside, which have preoccupied many Hungarian historians as well as scholars of revolution in other overwhelmingly agrarian societies, appear less significant than peasants’ own radical expectations. The evidence from Hungary in 1918–20 demonstrates the critical importance of wartime mobilization and the role of rural veterans as instigators of political unrest in triggering modern peasant uprisings.

papers.title: “A golden bridge for republican consciences”? The Simon-Gagern Pact and the Frankfurt Constitution of 1849
papers.abstract: The Simon-Gagern Pact of 1849 is mentioned by nearly every historian of the Frankfurt Parliament, but seldom with much explanatory detail. It is presented as a simple quid pro quo, which fulfilled its short-term function but failed to satisfy anyone. Under the pact, Heinrich Simon (1805–60) and his democratic supporters agreed to vote for a hereditary emperor as head of state in return for significant changes to the German constitution, which was then undergoing its second reading. It was only with the votes of Simon and his followers that the hereditary emperorship was narrowly approved on March 27, 1849, and with it the entire constitution. However, when King Friedrich Wilhelm IV declined the imperial title and the revolutionary flame of 1848–49 was extinguished, both centrist liberals and exiled radicals sought to downplay the significance of the pact, portraying it as an ignoble episode in an era otherwise characterized by high ideals and heroism. Even though the 1849 Frankfurt constitution would later be recognized as a significant milestone in German history and an important influence on both the Weimar constitution and the Basic Law of the Federal Republic, it was not until 1954 that the first detailed study of the pact was published; no new research has appeared in print since then. This article employs sources from British as well as German archives to shed new light on Heinrich Simon’s actions during the crucial months of 1849.

papers.title: Who wrote Els quaderns d’en Marc ? A stylometric inquiry into twentieth-century Catalan popular literature
papers.abstract: Abstract The anonymous erotic Catalan trilogy ‘Els quaderns d‘en Marc’ (1984–85) remains one of the most intriguing mysteries in twentieth-century Catalan popular imagination. While many in the literary circles attribute the work to the Catalan polygraph writer Manuel de Pedrolo (1918–90), there has never been a clear confirmation from the author himself, or any significant study dedicated to exploring the subject in detail. With the use of stylometry, in particular the Stylo package for R, the main objective of this short paper is to look at the authorial fingerprint in the first three volumes of ‘Els quaderns d’en Marc’ (1984–85), in the first instance, and at the sequel ‘Els Quaderns de la dona d’en Marc’ (1985), in the second. The aim is to examine whether this methodology can validate or demystify some of the existing theories surrounding these anonymous works’ authorship. The main contribution of this analysis has been to confirm—by the use of three separate approaches to stylometry as recommended by Juola—the high degree of similarity between the authorial fingerprint of Manuel de Pedrolo and that of the anonymous author of volumes I to III of this saga. As part of this authorship attribution exercise, a second finding has emerged; in the case of volume IV of this saga, ‘Els quaderns de la dona d‘en Marc’ (1985), the writer Manuel Joan i Arinyó, who was initially a suspected candidate, has been identified as a strong potential author of this volume.

papers.title: Who are the users in multilingual digital humanities?
papers.abstract: Abstract Building upon previous work on the study of the multilingual digital humanities (DH) community through user experience (UX) lens and the conclusions of a workshop held at the DH2023 conference, in this article, we argue that qualitative data about users helps us document the complex and rapidly growing communities of multilingual DH. We do so by considering a hitherto understudied perspective in this context—the composition of the users themselves. We underscore the importance of listening to voices from the community and call for further research to be done on this diverse multilingual DH community. Constructing user profiles allows us to focus on building infrastructure adapted to the needs of those users. Moreover, we discuss the intersectional challenges that arise during the creation of multilingual DH user profiles and provide recommendations that can be shared with many communities adjacent to the profession for consideration and further development. We emphasize the necessity of considering how intersectional identities have an impact on the user profiles, and how they too can be integrated into data-driven user profile design. Finally, we also suggest practical actionable steps for stakeholders in university libraries, DH instruction, hiring, evaluation, promotion and tenure committees, research computing communities, funding agencies, and transnational DH organizations for integrating a vision of a more linguistically inclusive digital scholarship into their own mandates.

papers.title: The War People: A Social History of Common Soldiers during the Era of the Thirty Years War. By Lucian Staiano-Daniels
papers.abstract: In recent decades the influence of social and cultural history has transformed the writing of war history. For both modern and pre-modern Europe, the study of politics, diplomacy and the military now sits alongside a new military history that explores the wartime experiences of ordinary soldiers and civilians, the material and psychological impact of conflict, and postwar memory and commemoration. As the title of a recent essay collection edited by Tryntje Helfferich and Howard Louthan suggests, historians of war now spend much—possibly even most—of their time “Beyond the Battlefield.” Staiano-Daniels’ The War People is a very welcome addition to this literature. It traces in microscopic detail the history of a regiment raised in Electoral Saxony in 1625 by Wolf von Mansfeld in the service of Philip IV of Spain. At its strongest the Mansfeld Regiment comprised 2,545 infantrymen and 979 horses. In the summer of 1625 it travelled from Dresden to northern Italy, but arrived too late to participate meaningfully in the conflict over the Valtellina that was resolved by the Treaty of Monzón in March 1626. Its members remained in northern Italy until 1627, when the regiment gradually mutinied and collapsed due to a lack of money. Staiano-Daniel’s study was made possible by the unusually rich collection of surviving archival sources relating to the regiment: muster rolls, records of passage and quartering, and, most importantly, court books containing all manner of legal records. In keeping with the traditions of microhistory that Staiano-Daniels cites, trial records play a key role in his study. The author has also done an impressive job of mining local printed and archival sources to examine the impact of the regiment’s presence on the communities through which it passed.

papers.title: On proximity—exploring experiences of bias and discrimination in digital humanities
papers.abstract: Abstract This article explores proximity as a critical feminist methodology in digital humanities, emphasizing its role in addressing bias in digital technologies. Drawing on the insights of Virginia Eubanks and Ruha Benjamin, this article argues that those closest to systemic issues possess essential knowledge for creating equitable solutions and advocates for community-led, inclusive approaches to digital humanities research. Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities (FSF) project, a UK–Ireland collaboration that employed proximity as both a methodological and ethical framework, is offered as a case study, and as such, the article draws on an analysis of semi-structured interviews, carried out by Full Stack Feminism. In line with the proximal approach, interviews were conducted with community groups and organizations as well as researchers, academics, artists, coders, activists, and software developers. By centring marginalized voices, the article proposes a proximal approach as a means to counteract digital bias and foster more just digital landscapes. It aligns with bell hooks’ (1989) and Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren Klein calls for counter-hegemonic practices rooted in the politics of location.

papers.title: Worlds of Labor on Georgetown’s Waterfront: Work, Freedom and the Labor Question in Guyana, c. 1890–1966
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines conflicts over the meaning and organization of work on the waterfront of Georgetown, Guyana. In the Anglophone Caribbean, “free” wage labor was a key component of the post-emancipation civilizing mission. Afro-Caribbean peoples, however, had their own ideas about the place of wage labor in their individual and collective lives. For many freed peoples and their descendants, wage labor was often one “livelihood strategy” among many, and it did not always take priority over other individual needs, or familial and communal concerns. This article investigates how these different understandings of wage labor shaped the multifaceted worlds of Georgetown’s Afro-Guianese waterfront workers. The first part examines the social relations and hierarchies that mediated the organization of work on the waterfront, influenced waterfront workers’ attitude toward wage labor and its relationship to other aspects of their lives, and facilitated episodes of industrial protest, including strikes when Afro-Guianese and Indo-Guianese workers co-operated in defiance of British Guiana’s racialized political economy. The second part focuses more narrowly on the workplace and the colonial authorities’ ongoing search for answers to the labor question. The article contends that decasualization—which complemented the wider post-1945 development and welfare agenda—represented a new iteration of the post-emancipation project to organize Afro-Guianese peoples’ lives around wage labor. Against the backdrop of rising anti-colonial sentiment and the subsequent split within the nationalist movement, the article demonstrates that although the colonial authorities had some success in creating a cohort of regular waterfront workers, decasualization was no panacea for the labor question.

papers.title: Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp By Jacob Flaws
papers.abstract: One of the most disturbing characteristics of the Treblinka extermination camp is what Gitta Sereny described in her book “Into That Darkness: An Examination of Conscience,” (New York, 1983) as the “terrible smallness of the place.” The Treblinka (II) camp was only 42 acres in size but was responsible for the mass murder of as many as 925,000 Jews. It was, perhaps, one of the deadliest places on earth. It is more than a little surprising, therefore, that more scholarly books have not appeared covering Treblinka. In this book, Flaws contributes to the so-called “spatial turn” in Holocaust studies that approaches the topic from a more geographical perspective, considering the meanings of space and place. He sets out to explore the spaces of the camp both literally and figuratively. Importantly, he examines not only the spaces within the camp but also the spaces around the camp. In this way, Flaws situates the camp in its surroundings, not a space completely sealed off from the outside world, but rather one deeply connected with it. For him, it is a space “in which ‘distinct trajectories’ of experience, ideology, and perception from any different people—Germans, Jews, and Poles—coalesced around the focal point that was the camp” (xix). Flaws, thus, also rises to Saul Friedländer’s challenge for Holocaust scholars to write an integrated history that includes all participants. The prominence of first-person Polish accounts is noteworthy and enlightening.

papers.title: The Coming of the Kingdom: The Muisca, the Catholic Reformation, and Spanish Colonialism in the New Kingdom of Granada By Juan Cobo Betancourt
papers.abstract: Juan Cobo Betancourt’s masterwork, The Coming of the Kingdom, is an important contribution to historical scholarship that will shape the study of the Catholic Church during the first century of Spanish colonization in America. We are also fortunate that Cambridge University Press provides an online version free of charge. Cobo Betancourt explores how the New Kingdom of Granada (modern-day Colombia) became integrated into Catholicism and the Spanish imperial system from the 1530s to the 1650s. He focuses on the experiences of Indigenous Muisca and colonial agents—especially clergy and administrators—to reveal unique historical processes in New Granada within the larger context of sixteenth-century Spanish colonialism and Church reforms. He argues that the Christianization of the Muisca was neither simple nor assured but complex and contested. He challenges previous portrayals of Indigenous submission to the Spanish Crown and Catholic faith as certain, highlighting instead the contingencies, uncertainties, conflicts, and setbacks involved. As he states, “Christianization was rooted in coercion: incorporation into Christianity… was an unavoidable imperative for people under Spanish rule” (5). However, this force did not lead to a straightforward transformation. Instead, the Muisca interacted with Catholicism in ways that reveal resistance, adaptation, and ingenuity, as well as their limitations.

papers.title: Revolution or evolution? AI-driven retrieval of nature representations in historical prints
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) opens new possibilities for processing and analysing large, heterogeneous historical data corpora in a semi-automated way. The Ottoman Nature in Travelogues (ONiT) project applies a fine-tuned Contrastive Language–Image Pre-Training (CLIP) model for retrieving images with nature representations in digitized early book prints based on embeddings of visual features rather than on textual metadata. In this article, we present results of our work, including a curated and annotated dataset of 8,042 images of nature representations, and the CLIP-based text–image exploration tool ONiT Explorer. An evaluation of the fine-tuned model comparing it to the zero-shot model confirms the potential of vision-language models for retrieving specific contents from large image collections in the cultural heritage and digital humanities domains. While in general our fine-tuned model can retrieve more correct examples per class compared to the zero-shot model, our analysis also reveals some limitations that need to be addressed in future explorations.

papers.title: Ghostly Past, Capitalist Presence: A Social History of Fear in Colonial Bengal By Tithi Bhattacharya
papers.abstract: Anyone who knows Bengal will be familiar with the world of bhuts (ghosts) and sankchunnis (spirits of married women). Tithi Bhattacharya uses this entry point to make an important intervention in the social history of India. Focusing on Bengal, she sheds light upon how colonialism intersected with the worlds of Indians and their ghosts. Bringing ghosts back to the heart of Bengali modernity, Bhattacharya argues that examining death provides a new method of interpreting the emergence of Indian nationalism. Drawing upon a variety of Bengali and English language sources, she argues that “a new imaginary of death was necessitated by a new regime of labor and capital” (157). Bhattacharya puts capitalism front and center in a process whereby upper-caste elites vanquished older ghosts and refashioned an emergent Indian nation along Hindu lines. Chapter 1 begins by investigating pre-colonial ghosts in Bengali cultural lives. Sharing physical and emotional spaces, ghost-human relations cut across class and caste lines. The bhadralok (“respectable folk”) Rajendralal Mitra and the poor fisherman (with canny abilities to trap bhuts in urns) could not have been socially farther apart. But for both, the ghostly world was part of their spiritual and social fabrics. Traditional Bengali ghosts were social beings, engendering ecumenical participation: both Hindus and Muslims warded off evil spirits, invoking Krishna and Allah. Importantly, stories of the poor and lower castes provided the “narrative bridge” which allowed these old ghosts to continue (albeit transformed) in a modern urban, bhadralok social milieu.

papers.title: Zanzibar Was a Country: Exile and Citizenship between East Africa and the Gulf By Nathaniel Mathews
papers.abstract: Tracing the lives, experiences, and ideas of Zanzibari Arabs through rich oral and written archives, Zanzibar Was a Country demonstrates the significance of “experiences in diaspora” to Indian Ocean postcolonial national belonging (2). Belonging, in Mathews’ rendering, refers to both “sentiment” —the idea of Zanzibar as a sovereign state and collective attachment to it—and citizenship—recognized political status and the infrastructures that produce it. The book makes two key intersecting interventions: first, by examining the political economy of citizenship from the era of developmental colonialism to the hydrocarbon-fueled developmentalism of the Arabian Gulf, Mathews presents an important analysis of decolonization as an economic process in which the tensions of the late colonial era continued. Second, he explores the complex and diverse articulations of Zanzibari-Omani belonging that emerged among diasporic Zanzibaris in this context, both in individual memory and through a vibrant vernacular historiography. This is a book that takes seriously not just the memories of its interlocutors, but their scholarship; their own endeavors in writing their history.

papers.title: Money, Value, and the State: Sovereignty and Citizenship in East Africa By Kevin P. Donovan
papers.abstract: In the first pages of Kevin Donovan’s thorough and thought-provoking book, he asks what is national (as in sovereign) about a national currency when its value is determined by the amount of foreign currency that nation holds? That foreign currency is procured with a rickety seesawing of national and international markets. African states sell cotton or coffee or sisal on the international for foreign currency; they convert that currency to local currency—taking a percentage for the costs of marketing—with which they pay local producers. Postcolonial African states, Donovan insists, are therefore moneychanger states, because they do not fully control the value of their own currencies. Just as states are canonically defined by the ability to monopolize violence within their borders, they are also defined by their ability to monopolize the power to establish the value of the money that is used within their borders. Postcolonial African states, not being fully capable of controlling the value of their currency, thus find that their sovereignty—postcolonial, economic, and in contrast to development—is limited. This hinders the ability of residents to practice “economic citizenship,” one of several kinds of citizenship described in this book.

papers.title: Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America By Rachel Louise Moran
papers.abstract: In this well-written and engaging monograph, Rachel Moran captures the struggles and triumphs to define, diagnose, and raise awareness about postpartum depression in the United States. Though a certain percentage of new mothers have undoubtedly experienced mood fluctuations since the ancient times, the term “baby blues” emerged during the postwar baby boom era, when motherhood was celebrated as the ultimate goal of womanhood. And yet, as exemplified by Betty Friedan’s bestselling The Problem that Has No Name, motherhood could be a struggle. Moran traces the condition’s evolution from the 1950s to the present, as various stakeholders attempted to frame the baby blues as a legitimate medical condition worthy of research and treatment. As Moran aptly demonstrates, suggesting that the experience of new motherhood could be anything other than pure joy was contentious enough (particularly in the 1950s); understanding the causes and determining treatment when things went wrong was even more so. If a new mother struggled to bond with her child, for example, was this a sign of selfishness and immaturity? An indication of a traumatic birth? An unhappy childhood? A rejection of gendered expectations? Or a psychiatric disorder? It could, of course, be any of these, depending upon who you asked, which accounts for the cacophony of voices weighing in on the matter. Moran walks us through the decades, demonstrating how cultural influences (from pronatalism to feminism to celebrities and social media) shaped the debate over time.

papers.title: Demos Rising: Democracy and the Popular Construction of Public Power in France, 1800-1850 By Stephen W. Sawyer
papers.abstract: The French Revolution created a democratic society, one in which all adult males were in principle equal before the law. The new state of affairs raised a novel question: what kind of political regime was best suited to govern such a society? The answer, it might be thought, would hinge on a range of political technologies—constitutions, representative bodies, electoral procedures—and how they were made to work together to reconcile the contrasting demands of freedom and stability. But, as it turns out, there is another way to conceptualize the problem. For the Revolution also created the modern state, and it had projects of its own, to develop or preserve the nation’s resources, the better to enhance its own power. Citizens might see the virtue of such schemes or experience them as an imposition. Citizens too, free and equal beings that they were, might have projects they wanted to pursue, coming together for this purpose or that, and the state had an interest in making sure that such associational initiatives dovetailed with its own ambitions. How the state and its citizens interacted required management, regulation in a word, and regulation, as Stephen Sawyer notes, might take all kinds of forms, some more top-down and expert-driven in nature, others more participatory with folks on the ground claiming a say over how rules were applied. That see-saw battle between the experts and what Sawyer calls the demos over the command of the state’s regulatory power was ground zero, as he sees it, in the struggle for democracy in France under the Restoration and July Monarchies. Given Sawyer’s angle of approach, the time frame is an apt one. This was a period when the state conceded a measure of liberty to its citizens but was at pains to circumscribe its practice through censorship and disenfranchisement. The people were excluded from public life but had some room to maneuver, to bang, that is, at the state’s regulatory gates and demand entry.

papers.title: Movers and haters: dynamic network visualization and analysis of an historical French controversy
papers.abstract: Abstract This article presents the results of a novel, mixed-methods project that studied an eighteenth-century French debate about education reform using approaches from Social Network Analysis and contemporary Controversy Mapping, alongside traditional humanities methodologies. Toggling between close reading of over 200 texts, and distant reading of the whole debate as a network, revealed that this little-known polemic—which we call the Querelle des collèges—was one of many early modern quarrels, and that its central actors were not straightforwardly those one might have expected. SNA uncovered the paradoxical role in the debate of the celebrity philosophe, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, as well as the previously overlooked participation of politicians, little-known teachers, and chronologically unexpected points of reference in this late-Enlightenment debate. Moreover, we underscore the value of analysing an historical controversy not just as a static network, considered at its end state, but as a dynamic entity that develops and changes over time. We show how a network can be dynamically visualized, to serve both exploratory and communicative ends. Ultimately, this article proposes a ‘bifocal reading’ method for historical controversy mapping, and identifies directions for future comparative research that might help us understand the dynamics of controversies from the past to the present.

papers.title: From theoretical texts to concept maps: an annotation approach for a distant reading of argumentative text structures
papers.abstract: Abstract Assuming that all theoretical texts are at least intentionally aimed at introducing, defining, or relating concepts to one another, we propose a system for categorizing the components of such texts: we argue that on an abstract level, all parts of a theoretical text can be assigned to the categories theses, arguments, and notions. papers.title: Richard Simon, Vernacular Biblical Scholarship, and the Last Early Modern Polyglot Bible
papers.abstract: Abstract Richard Simon has long presented an enigma for historians, as his status as a pathbreaking textual critic and the opposition his work engendered from contemporary ecclesiastical authorities has sat uncomfortably alongside his consistent advocacy of his Catholic credentials. This article approaches this problem via an analysis of two hitherto understudied parts of his scholarly corpus. It first elucidates Simon’s distinctive plan for a new polyglot Bible in the mid-1680s before shifting attention some fifteen years to consider his work in French vernacular biblical translation, bringing out how the confessionally inflected content of his work in that field contrasted with his earlier critical scholarship. By revealing how Simon negotiated the relationship between scholarship and religion during his working life, the article foregrounds the continued import of confessionalized erudition at the turn of the eighteenth century while also interrogating the limits of its explanatory power as a historical category.

papers.title: Age, Gender, and Agency in Juvenile Migration from England to Canada, 1850–1900
papers.abstract: Abstract This article makes two important contributions. Firstly, it provides valuable insights into the motivations of working-class migrants in the second half of the nineteenth century, adding a new dimension to a scholarship focused on studies of forced migration or middle-class empire building. Its analysis of a rich body of published and unpublished letters from former institutionalized children reveals the primacy of financial gain in the migration decision and shows that working-class Britons saw the world beyond the British Isles as a space of opportunity, where they could leverage their mobility in pursuit of profit. Secondly, by arguing that juvenile emigrants need to be viewed as a heterogeneous body where age and gender made a difference in terms of experience, the article provides an important new perspective on institutional migration that has implications for wider literatures on childhood and youth. The average age of the boys studied for this article was sixteen and the research shows that they were active participants in the emigration process, shaping their own futures through their diverse decisions. Recognizing this significantly undermines the modern discourses of blame and victimhood that dominate the historiography and encourages us to re-evaluate our approach to nineteenth-century juvenile migration.

papers.title: Empire, Conscience, and Another Independency in Thomas Hobbes’s Leviathan
papers.abstract: Abstract Leviathan ’s famous pronouncement that England had been ‘reduced to the Independency of the Primitive Christians’ has often been understood to signal support for the newly ascendant Cromwellian Independents in England. This article ventures an alternative reading of the passage by investigating the notion of ‘Independency’ with an eye to wider European political discourses. Scholars such as Francisco Suárez contended for the natural independence of temporal sovereigns while specifying the juridical rights and reach of imperial power. The fact that Christ and the Apostles had eschewed involvement in temporal affairs clarified this initial independency. This original state was especially important in French narratives aimed at securing autonomy against both empire and church. In light of this, Hobbes’s statement may be interpreted as endorsing a time-delimited notion of free conscience given England’s ruinous political state, but one looking forward to the unified rule of a sovereign with civil and ecclesiastical power.

papers.title: PREAMBULAR HISTORY: THE VIEW OF THE PAST IN KEY HUMAN RIGHTS INSTRUMENTS
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article claims that the preambles of foundational human rights instruments, taken together, articulate a consistent view of the past. This view is firmly rooted in historical processes, embedded in metaphysical truths, and enacted in service of the future. Part 1 assesses the strengths and weaknesses of the “preambular approach to history” and selects four instruments from a group of twenty‐two: the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Genocide Convention, and the International Criminal Court Statute. Part 2 reconstructs the discussions during which the historical recitals in the preambles of these instruments emerged. Part 3 analyzes these findings. In writing the historical recitals, the drafters of these key instruments opted for either the approach of the contemporary historian (the “recent history approach”) or the approach of the philosopher of history (“the holistic approach”). Both approaches are explained and compared. The conclusion contains a thought experiment in which the human rights view of the past embedded in these historical recitals is articulated.

papers.title: Text mining Nahdawi discourses: topic modeling Taha Hussein’s reformist legacy
papers.abstract: Abstract This study re-examines the intellectual, cultural, and literary legacy of Taha Hussein (1889–1973), a pivotal reformist thinker of the Arab Nahda (renaissance or awakening). Integrating computational methods from the digital humanities, specifically topic modeling applied to a 42-work corpus, with traditional close textual analysis, the study uncovers the structural and thematic patterns underpinning Hussein’s discourse on identity, modernization, and cultural reform. The analysis foregrounds on his syncretic humanism, which weaves together Egypt’s Pharaonic, Arab-Islamic, Mediterranean, and European inheritances into a pluralistic national vision. It highlights his critique of essentialist binaries, his advocacy for educational democratization, and his integrative approach to mediation, translation, and nation-building. Situated within the (post)colonial frameworks, the study critically engages debates around Hussein’s perceived Occidentalism while affirming his enduring relevance to contemporary discourses on intellectual sovereignty, cultural revival, and the humanistic foundations of reform. This research contributes to digital humanities by demonstrating the value of topic modeling for mapping the complex intellectual landscape of a major non-Western historical figure across a large corpus. It offers a scalable methodology for revealing latent thematic structures that complement traditional hermeneutic approaches in Arabic and Middle Eastern studies. By bridging digital methodologies with close reading, this study reframes Hussein’s reformism as a dynamic transcultural project that resists reductive polemics and illuminates postcolonial identity formation and the global positioning of Arab thought.

papers.title: Synergizing structure and semantics: a knowledge graph-transformer framework for narrator disambiguation in hadith networks
papers.abstract: Abstract Historical transmission chains (isnads) are fundamental to verifying authenticity in Hadith literature, yet narrator identity resolution is a persistent challenge due to onomastic ambiguity and complex naming conventions. While traditional methods lack scalability and modern language models overlook crucial network structures, this study bridges the gap by synergizing structural and semantic information. We introduce a novel hybrid framework that integrates a Knowledge Graph (KG) representing the narrator network topology with a Transformer-based model for deep contextual understanding. Our approach first leverages the KG to generate a high-probability set of candidate identities, then employs a hybrid scoring model to evaluate them based on both global network prominence and local semantic compatibility. Evaluated on the AR-Sanad 280K-v2 benchmark, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art, achieving 97.8% accuracy and significantly outperforming existing baselines. This work provides a scalable, high-fidelity solution for narrator disambiguation, advancing computational methods in Hadith studies and historical identity resolution.

papers.title: Opening the black box of EEBO
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital archives that cover extended historical periods can create a misleading impression of comprehensiveness while in truth providing access to only a part of what survives. While completeness may be a tall order, researchers at least require that digital archives be representative, that is, have the same distribution of items as whatever they are used as proxies for. If even this representativeness does not hold, any conclusions we draw from the archives may be biased. In this article, we analyse in depth an interlinked set of archives which are widely used but which have also had their comprehensiveness questioned: the images of Early English Books Online (EEBO), and the texts of its hand-transcribed subset, EEBO-TCP. Together, they represent the most comprehensive digital archives of printed early modern British documents. Applying statistical analysis, we compare the contents of these archives to the English Short Title Catalogue (ESTC), a comprehensive record of surviving books and pamphlets in major libraries. Specifically, we demonstrate the relative coverage of EEBO and EEBO-TCP along six key dimensions—publication types (i.e. books/pamphlets), temporal coverage, geographic location, language, topics, and authors—and discuss the implications of the imbalances identified using research examples from historical linguistics and book history. Our study finds EEBO to be surprisingly comprehensive in its coverage and finds EEBO-TCP—while not comprehensive—to be still broadly representative of what it models. However, both of these findings come with important caveats, which highlight the care with which researchers should approach all digital archives.

papers.title: The Morality of Revolution: Reeducation Camps and the Politics of Punishment in Socialist Mozambique, 1974–1990. By Benedito Luís Machava
papers.abstract: Benedito Machava’s The Morality of Revolution is an essential and engaging account of the post-colonial Mozambican government’s ill-fated attempts to impose a moral code via re-education camps to guide the revolution it sought to fulfill. Based on a tremendous depth of research, it provides a deep immersion into the creation of postcolonial Mozambique. It will be vital reading for anyone interested in Mozambican history or the wider story of postcolonial Africa. Machava’s introduction presents the book’s primary argument: that studying the intellectual history of public morality is essential in understanding postcolonial Mozambican politics. The introduction effectively shows that this history deserves to be read within African and global contexts, arguing that understanding Mozambican history contributes to a broader perspective on the interplay between morality and power in post-revolutionary political systems. The first chapter begins the intellectual history of Mozambique’s revolution, providing a background into the moral code of Samora Machel, Mozambique’s first President. It further shows how Machel’s moral code extended into his leadership of Frelimo (Mozambican Liberation Front), the rebel movement turned political party that fought for, and subsequently governed, independent Mozambique. The chapter convincingly locates Samora Machel’s ideology within religious ideals of salvation and rebirth as well as revolutionary (especially Chinese) ideas of complete social transformation. It also shows the depth of his commitment to this ideology; indeed, the book recounts Machel’s decision to sentence his younger sister and his children to moral reeducation, an astonishing illustration of his ideological devotion. Chapter 2 shows how Samora’s philosophy of revolutionary social redemption was put into practice soon after independence via the start of show trials and reeducation camps, initially targeting Frelimo’s political opponents. In the years following Frelimo’s takeover, the government dramatically expanded the camp system, as it began relocating hundreds of thousands of Mozambicans from urban to rural areas, both as a means of reforming morally suspect city dwellers and of furthering state-led development projects. Chapter 3 provides a detailed reconstruction of how the Frelimo government implemented this policy, culminating in the 1983 launch of Operation Production, a huge effort to dramatically expand the number of forced deportations; as the operation’s title made clear, the government’s objective was to further its goal of cleansing Mozambican society by remaking deportees into productive citizens who could contribute to the broader goal of national development. The enormous campaign transformed both the machinery of the Frelimo government and the lives of ordinary Mozambicans, as the forced migrations profoundly altered conceptions of citizenship in the reborn Mozambican state. Chapters 4 and 5 move beyond the ideologies and practices of high-ranking officials to examine how the deportation campaign shaped the actions and ideas of ordinary Mozambicans in their everyday lives. Chapter 4 is about how Mozambicans reproduced the ideology of moral cleansing and acted on that ideology by denouncing their neighbors. Chapter 5 explores the reeducation camps, to demonstrate how the lofty ambitions of social rebirth were totally divorced from the austere, isolated camps at which detainees arrived. Chapter 6 further pursues this analysis through an examination of the punishing daily life of camp inmates; cold, sick, and forgotten, they were the victims of widespread disease and terrible torture meted out by camp guards. Chapter 7 takes the history of the camps forward into the 1980s, when many camps were shut down and the detainees resettled into development villages, joined by a new wave of individuals sentenced under Operation Production. This history intersected with the expansion and intensification of the Mozambican Civil War—the country’s more well-known postcolonial tribulation—which brought even more tragic consequences for its citizens.

papers.title: New Generations and the Hopes of Empire: Youth Premilitary Training in Early-Twentieth Century Eurasia
papers.abstract: Abstract In the early-twentieth century, state institutions and voluntary associations in the Ottoman, Habsburg, and Romanov empires envisioned a “new generation” of imperial subjects to reinvigorate patriotism serving as the bond between state and society. Anxieties linked to military inadequacy vis-à-vis other empires combined with the fear of social unrest and moral disorder, which drew increased attention on the discipline of youth. In those three Eurasian empires, forms of premilitary training involving children and teenagers (mostly aged six to nineteen) emerged from private initiatives and were quickly coopted by imperial authorities. The article discusses institutions like Türk Gücü in the Ottoman Empire, the Poteshnye Roty in the Russian Empire, and the Reichsbund der Jugendwehren und Knabenhorte in the Habsburg monarchy. Although their visibility in illustrated magazines and other media grew rapidly in the early 1910s, those projects mirrored the empires’ difficulties in implementing activities throughout vast territories. Premilitary training caused frictions between ministries and raised new issues of belonging and loyalty in those multiethnic societies. Eventually, the envisioned militarized imperial youth did not prove particularly effective in the framework of the First World War. However, those initiatives reveal a crisis in politics of difference as they reinforced activism in the name of empire albeit mostly limited to the empire’s respective “dominant” group: Sunni Turks, Catholic Germans, and Orthodox Russians. In so doing, premilitary training tested forms of mass mobilizations and remained a reference with which post-imperial societies in the republics of Turkey and Austria as well as the Soviet Union had to reckon.

papers.title: Research on the authorship identification of The Tale of Genji based on quantitative analysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Numerous scholarly contributions have enriched our understanding of The Tale of Genji; however, the question of its authorship remains a subject of debate, with no definitive resolution to date. This study addresses this controversy by employing a rigorous quantitative statistical approach. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of various linguistic indicators within The Tale of Genji, encompassing aspects such as distribution of part-of-speech, function words, word length, N-Grams, and sentence-segments. These characteristic parameters were subsequently utilized to perform principal component analysis, perform non-parametric tests, calculate relative entropy, and assess relative distances. The findings of this analysis reveal a remarkable consistency in writing style between Chapters 43–54 and the preceding Chapters 1–42 of The Tale of Genji. Consequently, the quantitative statistical examination presented in this study provides robust evidence to support the conclusion that a single authorship underlies the entire text of The Tale of Genji, refuting the hypothesis of a second author.

papers.title: Empire of Rags and Bones: Waste and War in Nazi Germany. By Anne Berg
papers.abstract: Today, people value recycling as a public good—important both for environmental sustainability and as a way to demonstrate care for one’s community. In reality, such a view of recycling practices is idealistic at best. “Recycled” garbage largely goes to landfills; “donated” used clothing undermines local manufacturing in developing nations. Most people, however, prefer not to think about the waste they are creating, as long as it disappears weekly from the kerbside. The meanings and motivations behind waste management is thus a subject that warrants closer analysis. In the case of Nazi Germany, the topic speaks to three issues that have long captured the attention of scholars: the Nazi fixation on purity and hygiene; the regime’s support for initiatives that appear to anticipate the environmental movement; and its engagement of most citizens in ways that belie the ferocity of the dictatorship. Empire of Rags and Bones interrogates Nazi Germany as a “waste regime.” The book examines the myriad ways the German state and individual citizens sought to turn trash into usable resources, such as the collection of kitchen scraps to feed livestock or the abhorrent Müllwurst (trash “sausage’)—made from pulping waste—that was fed for a time to Mauthausen prisoners. It also offers a framework for understanding the nation’s leaders’ obsession with recycling, or as Berg puts it, the internal logic of the regime’s “quasi-religious hunt for junk” (3). Her argument unfolds over three roughly chronological sections, beginning in earnest with the Four-Year Plan in 1936 and ending with the first wave of post-defeat clean up. Berg maintains that the recycle-mania she describes reflects the regime’s “extractivist” imperial agenda fueled by an annihilationist worldview that pitted purity and order, represented by “Aryan” culture, against impurity and disorder, represented chiefly by Jews and Bolshevism.

papers.title: Report on the Development of Digital Humanities in China (first volume) （Zhongguo Shuzi Renwen Fazhan Baogao (Diyiji)). Huiling Feng
papers.abstract: In 2004, Susan Schreibman and colleagues first brought together a wide range of theorists and practitioners to consider the significance of digital humanities as an independent discipline and reflect on its relationship with traditional humanities (Schreibman et al. 2004). In 2009, the concept of “digital humanities”—an imported term—was first introduced to Chinese academia by Professor Wang Xiaoguang from Wuhan University. Although many scholars such as Chen Jing have pointed out that there were already numerous digital humanities practices in China before this, facing the need for innovative research methods in the humanities and social sciences, it is crucial to systematically disseminate the latest content, research directions, and emerging frontiers of international digital humanities to domestic scholars in the humanities and social sciences, so as to expedite the evolution and transformation of research paradigms in China’s humanities disciplines (Wang 2010). Combining the reality in Chinese academic research, “digital humanities” is defined as a set of approaches to formulating, redefining, and answering academic questions. That is, humanists can use digital technologies, especially computer databases, as external tools to address academic questions they have previously posed, or to explore new issues inspired by digital technologies, and even to develop new research paradigms (Xu and Chen 2017). Edited by Feng Huiling, with Xia Cuihong and Liang Jihong as associate editors, Report on the Development of Digital Humanities in China (First Volume) is a work that demonstrates Chinese academia’s response to the global trend of digital humanities and its successful transformation of academic research in the digital era. In addition to the preface and appendices, the book is divided into four main parts, aiming to showcase the “remarkable journey of China’s digital humanities in its infancy” (Feng 2024) to the academic community. Led by the Institute for Digital Humanities at Renmin University of China, the book’s authors come from a wide range of backgrounds, including forty-seven educators and researchers from eighteen universities or research institutions across China, representing diverse disciplines.

papers.title: The Two Princes of Mpfumo: An Early Eighteenth-Century Journey Into and Out of Slavery . By Lindsay O’Neill
papers.abstract: This book tells the story of two princes, James Chandos Maffoom and his brother John Twogood Maffoom, who came from the Mpfumo area of Maputo Bay in modern Mozambique. In 1716 they and six attendants bearing gifts boarded an English ship as honored guests, intending to go to England on a diplomatic trade mission. The ship sailed first to Madagascar to fill its large hold with slaves, then Jamaica. During the voyage, the captain enslaved the princes and sold them in Jamaica—not the only time this happened to princes in the eighteenth century. The English lawyer who “discovered” them was shocked that elite African princes were being enslaved like common Black people on Jamaica. He purchased and freed the princes, and together they sailed with other ships for London. After a terrible shipwreck on the coast of Cuba that cost hundreds of lives, the princes arrived and remained in England for six years, first in London and then in Middlesex, where they became celebrities, yet were treated as curiosities, not equals, as was often the case with African princes in England during the eighteenth century. Meanwhile, the Royal African Company, the East India Company, and the Society for the Propagation of Christian Knowledge jostled over plans to manipulate the princes into assisting their projects in southeast Africa. Eventually, English reporting noted that the two brothers were fighting. Their ship departed for Maputo Bay in 1722 but foundered in the English Channel in a storm, and during the subsequent extended stay in Exmouth for repairs, James tried to kill his brother and then hanged himself. When the ship reached the Cape of Good Hope, imperial rivalry with the Dutch threatened the mission. Nevertheless, upon arrival in Maputo Bay, the missionary-trade project began well, and the English outperformed the Dutch, with the assistance of John, the nephew of the local ruler. Eventually, however, John, his uncle, and others changed their minds and ejected the British from their lands.

papers.title: Colonial world-making and global knowledges at the early modern Cape of Good Hope
papers.abstract: Abstract As the Cape of Good Hope was integrated into early modern colonial world-making projects, it came to be regarded as ‘the western part of the East Indies’. The initial elaboration of this imaginary was contingent upon the contours of Dutch mobility in the Indian Ocean and material exigencies on the ground at the Cape. Early commanders sought to transform the colony’s environment, culture, and demographic constitution into a mirror of their productive East Indian colonies. Relatedly, some Indigenous Khoekhoe, forcibly transported to Java to train as colonial servants, came to understand Europeans — and the dangers they posed — in relation to the East Indies. This contingent colonial world-making soon gave rise to broader epistemic frameworks linking the southern African territory to Asia. European travellers began remarking on the purported similarities between the Cape’s plants, colonial customs and material culture, and Khoekhoe practices and those of the East Indies. By the end of the seventeenth century, some travellers even hypothesized that the Chinese had visited the Cape before the birth of Christ. Exploring the causes and consequences of the Cape’s integration into the East Indies, this article underlines how contingent geopolitical designations reshaped scholarly descriptions of natures and cultures in southern Africa.

papers.title: The Weak and the Powerful: Omar Torrijos, Panama, and the Non-Aligned Movement in the World. By Jonathan C. Brown
papers.abstract: Jonathan Brown has written an insightful study of Panamanian General Omar Torrijos’s long struggle to gain control of the Panama Canal Zone from the United States to make his country a truly sovereign nation. The central problem Torrijos faced upon seizing power in a 1968 military coup was confronting the world’s most powerful state—which had reduced Panama to a neo-colony for nearly seventy years though its mastery of the Canal and the enclave that surrounded it. Panama had a population of only 2 million and territory smaller than South Carolina. The ingenious strategy that Torrijos adopted was to take advantage of the international environment of the 1960s-1970s as smaller states in Africa, Asia, and Latin America broke free of imperial domination to chart their own independence. Brown focuses the bulk of his study on the personality and vision of Torrijos, who was born in obscurity, the son of rural schoolteachers. Through twenty years of service in the Panamanian National Guard, Torrijos developed a strong sense of solidarity with the majority of his country’s impoverished population. He adopted a center-left political stance contrary to most of the hard-right caudillos of Latin America during the Cold War. While certainly a dictator, Torrijos proved far less repressive than the bloody tyrants of his era and pushed for moderate land and labor reforms. He moved to construct a populist base in contrast to the oligarchic rule of Panamanian elites—the so-called rabiblancos—who generally accommodated the hegemonic U.S. presence on the isthmus.

papers.title: The Archive of Empire: Knowledge, Conquest, and the Making of the Early Modern British World. By Asheesh Kapur Siddique
papers.abstract: Government data and paperwork are so central to modern life that, even now, they are flashpoints of political action and struggles over political liberty. papers.title: The aesthetic nature of Chinese-inscribed poetry and painting texts—evidence from eye movements

papers.title: Papyrus Economies and the Experience of Early Medieval Papal Documents
papers.abstract: Abstract The medium of papyrus, a ubiquitous, state-sponsored product in the Roman world, was turned by the empire’s loss of Egypt in the 630s–640s into a comparatively rare, high-status good in the early medieval northern Mediterranean (though not in the early caliphate, where it continued to have more or less the same value and associations as it had in the Roman period). The papacy continued to use this now precious commodity for its written communications. This was a crucial strategy in projecting its unique claims to authority across Latin Europe through the changing world of the late seventh to early eleventh centuries. Consequently, the sudden decline and disappearance of the Egyptian papyrus industry in the 950s-970s had its role to play in the transformation of papal government of the following century.

papers.title: Beyond Keeping the Lights On
papers.abstract: This article reviews the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on public history sites and museums along the Lower Mississippi River Valley between 2020 and 2024. Constructed from interviews with sixty-seven sites across a four-year period, it uses a regional approach to examine how pandemic closures, reopening processes, and adaptations impacted public history sites and museums in the short-, medium-, and long-term, arguing that the pandemic created lasting changes through adaptation rather than large-scale closure of public history institutions. It concludes with an assessment of what can be learned from the pandemic period’s effect on public history.

papers.title: Integrating AI in historical research: a new method to analyzing national narratives
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a human-machine collaboration method to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into historical research, specifically in the analysis of national narratives. Using President Ronald Reagan’s portrayal of America as a case study, the paper demonstrates how AI tools like natural language processing, BERTopic., and generative large language models, when guided by historians, can streamline the analysis of national narratives, significantly enhancing research efficiency. While AI tools have been successfully implemented in social science research, historical research requires more nuanced methods due to its emphasis on language and imagery within narratives. This study seeks to address this gap. This paper also examines the potential impact of AI on historical methodology, while acknowledging the challenges and limitations of integrating AI into historical research. Despite its promising capabilities, the paper argues that AI should be viewed as a research partner that assists historians with repetitive tasks, but underscores that human interpretation remains crucial for producing meaningful historical analysis.

papers.title: Charting a Path Toward Historic Sites Sustainability
papers.abstract: In 2021, Connecticut Landmarks worked with Museum Insights to create a model for assessing its twelve historic houses and developing new operating models that met the organization’s commitment to preservation and its goal to tell more of Connecticut’s stories through dialogic interpretation. This report will review the status of historic house museums and the perception that they are a moribund type of museum before explaining the development of the assessment frameworks, how the results of the assessment have been implemented at Connecticut Landmarks, and how the assessment frameworks could be adapted at other historic house museums to improve their operations.

papers.title: An Unformed Map: Geographies of Belonging between Africa and the Caribbean By Philip Janzen
papers.abstract: Philip Janzen’s innovative, insightful book offers new perspectives on the modern Black Atlantic by foregrounding African diasporic exchanges heretofore occluded by official archives. An Unformed Map takes the form of a collective biography of some 500 individuals who were born in the Caribbean and served as colonial officials and administrators in French and British African colonies from the 1880s through the 1940s. Some of these officials are well-known to historians—the eventual governor of Chad, Félix Éboué, for example—while others were otherwise anonymous schoolteachers, sanitary inspectors, and railway employees. What bound them together was a shared experience as onsite intermediaries between European colonial administrations and African societies, inflected by these civil servants’ status as double outsiders: too Black and too Caribbean to be accepted as European; too foreign and too associated with colonial hierarchies to be accepted as African. The result was a class of individuals “isolated on two fronts” (32). Such isolation, Janzen demonstrates, led this group of Caribbean-born African officials to engage deeply with the contradictions of empire. In the process, they created new “geographies of belonging” that drew upon the interconnected histories and shared experiences of the Black Atlantic.

papers.title: EDITORS’ INTRODUCTION: TRANSLATION, MIGRATION, NARRATIVE
papers.abstract: Empirical, positivist approaches have long dominated migration history and migration studies and shaped these fields with their research questions, theoretical approaches, and methodologies. However, the data, interpretations, explanations, and narratives of migration and society produced in this framework have come under criticism in recent years. This critique includes challenges to methodological nationalism, the construction of migration as a problem requiring intervention and regulation, the production of sedentarism as the normal, the use of categories and concepts that place migranticized people in subaltern positions, and the reproduction of colonial knowledge structures by privileging Western perspectives.1 Decolonizing research on migration, mobility-induced social change, and diversity that considered migration societies (Migrationsgesellschaften) as the norm and understood mobility and migration as constitutive elements of the conditio humana took different forms and paces within different disciplines, in different academic communities in the Global North and South, and across the Atlantic and Pacific. It also led to a growing number of interdisciplinary initiatives. The reflexive turn in migration studies transformed vague critique at the margins into a dynamic drive for a paradigm shift at the center of migration research, demanding fundamental transformations to long-established epistemologies, power structures, and disciplinary traditions in this multidisciplinary, international, and often highly politicized field.2 Our own intellectual trajectories reflect these shifts. As historians of migration policies and societies, we began collaborating to explore connections between histories of labor migration in Europe (Christoph Rass's expertise) and in the United States (Julie M. Weise's expertise). As we worked, we realized that the largely empirical research methodologies on which we both usually relied left too much unexplained. We needed a better way to analyze the circulation of ideas about migration management around the Atlantic and beyond—not just among policymakers but also among migrants themselves. As we engaged with theories of translation on a broad register, we were better able to interpret the documents in front of us, but more than this, we were pushed to rethink the ways we narrated migration history as a whole.3 We were fortunate to enlist leading German and US historians and literary, cultural, and ethnic studies scholars to join us in this critical reflection and methodological and narrative experimentation in the interdisciplinary field of migration history. Our shared foundation is an understanding of “translation” as a broad theoretical umbrella that includes all activities transposing sensual data into tangible and communicable—that is, social and aesthetic—forms. Inspired by Alexandra Lianeri's June 2024 reading of Theo Hermans's Translation and History: A Textbook,4 we explore these concepts of translation as parts of a fundamental paradigm that can enrich migration research not just as a methodological tool but as a critical force in shaping social reality and producing the knowledge we study and perform. Reflexive migration research demands a critical assessment of our epistemologies, our methods, and our roles as authors coproducing migration—or migrantization—through the choices we make while creating translations of the world into text.5 In her work on the reflexive turn, cultural theorist Doris Bachmann-Medick has highlighted how sociocultural and disciplinary frameworks and research practices themselves eventually co-constitute and re-produce the categories of difference that they claim to merely describe.6 At the same time, Bachmann-Medick has conceptualized translation as a transformative cultural practice that includes, but is not limited to, linguistic transfer. Translation is a continuum of ongoing acts negotiating and reconfiguring contested and contingent meanings across cultural, disciplinary, and temporal boundaries. It reshapes not only the original “object” of translation but also its contexts of origin and destination. This view configures translation as an analytical tool and metaphor for understanding cultural contact zones, power differentials, and knowledge production. As a methodology in practice, this equips us with a pragmatic model for navigating the complexities of interdisciplinary and intercultural scholarship. Understanding knowledge production as a translational effort makes ambiguities, hybridity, and contested meaning-making legible within a productive space for dialogue. This changes how we, as scholars, approach and analyze our source materials, represent the knowledge we produce, and do interdisciplinary research.7 Overall, this “Translation, Migration, Narrative” forum uses the framework of translation studies to make two principal arguments. First, we argue that theories of translation can point the way toward a critical self-reflexive approach to understanding ourselves, historians of migration, as not merely interpreters but also translators of history. In this endeavor, our authors have particularly appreciated the work of Thomas Nail, Theo Hermans, and Andrew Abbott. Nail's concept of “kinopolitics” creating the “figure of the migrant” demonstrates how the production of such figures, including by scholars, generates subaltern positions in a hierarchical social order and points out how translation becomes materially and politically consequential.8 Additionally, Hermans merged historical scholarship and translation studies by arguing for the inherent translingual dimension of the sociohistorical process, the study of knowledge production, and our doing knowledge while translating the past into history.9 Abbott has gone further to challenge disciplinary traditions privileging narratives structured by dominant choices and institutionalized practices; his “lyrical sociology” advocates for epistemological emancipation through his search for alternative modes of translating complex social realities into knowledge.10 Second, we argue that greater attention to linguistic and cultural translations, as found within typical historical sources, can yield penetrating insights into migrant agency and experiences that would otherwise remain hidden. We have found it particularly fruitful to draw on theoretical reflections and scholarship at the intersection of translation studies and postcolonial studies (for example, Paul F. Bandia, Homi K. Bhabha, and Mary Louise Pratt) in interpreting migrant archives and experiences. Both Bandia11 and Bhabha12 expanded translation from a linguistic process to a broader cultural process of negotiating meaning and identity in asymmetric colonial and postcolonial power relations. Whereas Bhabha stressed the outcome by focusing on hybridity and ambivalence, Bandia conceptualized the diasporic struggle for agency between being translated and translating the self. Indeed, this tension between translation as a way that society's most powerful actors (including scholars) attempt to control mobile human beings and translation as a way for migrants to engage in creative self-invention marks both dimensions of our forum's argument. In the forum's opening intervention, literary scholar Laura A. Zander (University of Münster and Osnabrück University) theorizes from an analysis of Nigerian author Helon Habila's 2019 novel Travelers.13 She shows how Habila's novel brings to the fore the ways in which intellectuals (in this case, the novel's protagonists) translate lived human experience into a limited set of migrant “types”—or, in Nail's words, “figure[s] of the migrant”—that are legible to the surrounding society. Zander's essay challenges historians of migration to reflect on how our own practices inadvertently mimic this reductionism and to consider how our texts could instead function, like the literature she analyzes, as a “contact zone” between migrants’ creative self-translations and the legal narratives that objectify them.14 Building on Bachmann-Medick's conceptualization of translation as a cultural and analytical practice, ethnic studies scholar Catherine S. Ramírez (University of California, Santa Cruz) and historian Christoph Rass (Osnabrück University) explore in their forum contribution how “integration” is constructed, translated, and institutionalized in Germany and the US.15 Their approach, which combines translation theory with conceptual history, challenges the traditional understanding of the evolution of what “integration” means. They demonstrate how political, economic, and historical forces actively shape the meaning of integration, using it as a medium to translate individuals into “migranticized figures.” They also interrogate underlying processes of knowledge production and meaning-making as acts of translation that both regulate belonging and reinforce social hierarchies. Translation theory makes “integration” legible not as a neutral category but as embodying historical power relations that contribute to the reproduction of exclusionary mechanisms and the perpetuation of unequal power dynamics. Three forum contributions, two coauthored by German and US scholars, then engage in interdisciplinary analyses and methodological experiments that focus on moments of linguistic translation to situate migration history as a “contact zone” between migrant agency and discursive and structural control by states and capitalists. These pieces show how translation can be operationalized as a mode of interpreting typical historical sources: migrant political expressions, archival documents, and autobiographies. Historians Albert Manke (Ca’ Foscari University of Venice) and Fredy González (University of Illinois Chicago) use multiple theories of translation to reexamine the political self-representation of Chinese migrants’ sworn brotherhood organizations over a century and a half of diasporic evolution.16 In particular, the organizations’ strategy of self-representing as “masonic lodges,” and even shifting their visual iconography to reinforce this image, expanded their political space for operation and challenged outsiders’ representation of them as threatening. By following Hermans's thoughts on the fundamental power of translation to shape social reality, these moments of linguistic translation become, for Manke and González, ways of understanding the brotherhoods’ creative agency and the powerful constraints within which they operated in an era of overt anti-Chinese racism. Cultural studies scholar Peter Schneck (Osnabrück University) and historian Julie M. Weise (University of Oregon) focus on a single 1954 document from the archives of the labor recruitment agency for the South African Chamber of Mines to conceptualize the archives of migration as repositories of translation.17 They look beyond physical mobility to see the ways that linguistic translation implicated the Malawian migrants’ “left-behind” family members whose translated words appear in the document. Bandia's concept of migrants as “beings in translation” creates a unifying frame for understanding migrants and their family members as part of a single process, even as analyses of two contrasting works of literature from the Mexico–US border point to the ways that Malawian migrants themselves experienced creative agency through translation while, for their family members, translation was primarily a constraint. Historian Anand A. Yang (University of Washington) then reconsiders heavily cited migrant self-writings through the lens of translation.18 He shows how the testimonies of North Indian contract laborers Totaram Sanadhya and Munshi Rahman Khan disrupted official colonial accounts and highlighted migrants’ lived experiences as both “translated beings” (Bandia)19 and self-translators forging new identities (Bhabha). Language choices—especially in Hindi—and personal perspectives emerge as key to understanding how migrants translated experiences of suffering, their advocacy for abolition, and their diasporic selves into their life-writing. By complicating historians’ treatment of these rarely preserved voices, Yang underscores their significance for a deeper, noncolonial understanding of how marginalized communities shaped their own narratives and identities in global migration histories. Even as the four middle pieces apply translation as a methodology to rethink familiar topics and sources in migration history, they also point the way toward critical acts of self-reflection for the historian. Indeed, just as German and US scholars, politicians, and bureaucrats, Chinese sworn brotherhood leaders, mine labor recruitment agents, and former Indian contract laborers engaged in power-laden acts of translation, so too do we as scholars of history. In the forum's final piece, literary scholar Kirsten Silva Gruesz (University of California, Santa Cruz) offers yet another provocation to historians of migration and their audiences.20 Whereas Zander's opening essay asks us to engage in critical self-reflection to push against our tendencies to order migrants as capitalists and the state have done, Gruesz's closing intervention asks us to consider entirely new forms of scholarly communication. Drawing on literary inspiration and Abbott's demand to move from structured narrative to lyrical representations of knowledge, Gruesz presents list, interruption, and assemblage as alternate modes of translating the migrant experience beyond “story.” Indeed, if the “figure of the migrant” (as conceptualized by Nail) is produced by a constellation of discourses, then the stories that historians tell are surely among them. Methodological case studies work in concert with Gruesz's call for new forms of translating migrant experience, together challenging us to find new possibilities within the inextricable ambiguities of our archives, narratives, and interpretations.

papers.title: The First Amerasians: Mixed Race Koreans from Camptowns to America. By Yuri W. Doolan
papers.abstract: Once considered a personal and apolitical act, transnational adoption has been reconceptualized by scholars of U.S. history, gender, and postcolonialism as a practice whose origins lie in Cold War geopolitics, particularly as Asia became increasingly central to U.S. strategic interests in the mid-twentieth century. Yuri W. Doolan’s The First Amerasians: Mixed Race Koreans from Camptowns to America extends this line of inquiry by urging a critical reassessment of the term “Amerasian,” used to describe children of mixed parentage born to Asian women and U.S. soldiers, many of whom became among the first internationally adopted children. Doolan contends that the Amerasian is not a neutral racial category but “an important figure in U.S. political culture—a Cold War construct—that has helped Americans to explain and promote, both at home and in the world, the dominant ideas undergirding the Cold War” (2). In this thoroughly researched and attentively written book, Doolan traces the evolution of the Amerasian category from the onset of the Korean War in 1950, a pivotal moment that positioned South Korea as a key site of U.S. military and humanitarian intervention, to the passage of the Amerasian Homecoming Act in 1982, which legally defined Amerasians as primarily biracial children from Korea and Vietnam. In doing so, Doolan underscores Korea’s centrality to understanding U.S. postwar modernity (12).

papers.title: FROM HOFSTADTER TO LEPORE: NATIONAL HISTORY FOR THE AMERICAN PUBLIC
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Nick Witham's Popularizing the Past: Historians, Publishers, and Readers in Postwar America provides cogent and accurate accounts of the careers of five American academic historians of the post‐World War II era who won large popular audiences for national narratives: Richard Hofstadter, Daniel Boorstin, John Hope Franklin, Howard Zinn, and Gerda Lerner. Witham omits, without explanation, the highly relevant case of Oscar Handlin, author of the 1951 work The Uprooted: The Epic Story of the Great Migrations That Made America . He also fails to engage the heavily Jewish ethnoreligious matrix of popular American historiography of the postwar era. In Popularizing the Past , Witham is directly concerned with today's challenges for writing popular national histories, and he argues that the very idea of a single, national audience has been rendered anachronistic by ideological polarization and media fragmentation. Whereas Witham insists that works resembling Jill Lepore's 2018 book These Truths: A History of the United States should no longer be attempted, he upholds Ibram X. Kendi's 2016 volume, Stamped from the Beginning: The Definitive History of Racist Ideas in America , as an example of what is appropriate today: a narrative for a certain community of readers, and not for other readers. Witham's essentially sound account of major features of postwar American writings about history is marred by his jejune comments about the early twenty‐first century. He leaves us with only a shadow of the witness that each of Witham's subject‐historians bore with distinction to the mission of discovering and disseminating the truth about American history in the interests of a national community.

papers.title: The Eastern International: Arabs, Central Asians, and Jews in the Soviet Union’s Anticolonial Empire By Masha Kirasirova
papers.abstract: The Eastern International has been so long anticipated by historians of Central Asia, the Soviet Union, and the Middle East that it had already been cited widely in manuscript or dissertation form well before it appeared as a book. The long anticipation is warranted: this is the type of work that launches a thousand dissertations, and it speaks to the book’s importance that its lacunae present less as deficiencies than as opportunities. Kirasirova’s book is, at least on a surface level, a kind of begriffsgeschichte, a history of the idea of the “East” throughout the Soviet period and across its geographical span. Kirasirova’s analysis thus entails a sizable amount of intellectual and cultural history: for example, it parses the arguments of Old Bolshevik Konstantin Troianovskii about the “East” and its potential for revolution in the years immediately following 1917 (chapter 1) and analyzes the films of Uzbek actor and director Kamil Yarmatov in the Cold War era of postcolonial cultural diplomacy (chapter 6). Across the book’s chapters, which span the entire Soviet period in chronological order, Kirasirova foregrounds the constructed and contested nature of the “East,” a nebulousness that made the category both powerful and dangerous. For Troianovskii, writing in the years immediately following the 1917 revolution, the “East” held massive potential as a driver of world revolution beyond Europe: it could spearhead an “Eastern International,” bringing together the newly Soviet, but historically Muslim regions of the Caucasus and Central Asia with the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, of South Asia, and even of China and Southeast Asia. As ephemeral as Troianovskii’s career may have been, Kirasirova argues, his geopolitical ideas “run like a thread” through the Bolshevik institutions designed for promoting world revolution (57). By the time Kamil Yarmatov made his mature body of work in the 1960s, a new kind of geopolitics was at play, situating Yarmatov as a crucial Cold War intermediary for the many foreigners who visited Tashkent for the Afro-Asian Film Festival of 1968. Billed as a participant in the Revolution and an authentic Easterner, Yarmatov brought together the ideological and geopolitical priorities of his time, but he struggled to bridge the contradictions between Soviet ideas and global ideas of decolonization. Both of these case studies emphasize the constructedness of the category of the “East” and its malleability in the context of shifting geopolitical priorities and of the longer history of Orientalism in the Russian Empire.
