papers.title: ‘Liberal’ Virtues and Values, Women’s ‘Genius’, and the British Literary Reviews, c. 1750–1795
papers.abstract: Abstract In 1764, while discussing female authors one critic suggested that the views of ‘the liberal’ were normative. But what did it mean to be a ‘liberal’ at this time? This article examines the ‘liberal and enlightened’ patterns of thought popularized by reviewers who belonged to the network of friends and acquaintances of the founders of the Monthly Review , the dissenters Ralph Griffiths and William Rose. Opposing different forms of ‘tyranny’, or authoritarianism, critics promoted ‘liberal and rational’ political principles and a social morality comprising the values of open-mindedness, reason, toleration, and ‘equity’ or justice as fairness. Focusing in particular on issues relating to gender, this article shows how conceptions of the ‘liberal spirit’ informed accounts of women’s capabilities, of their ‘genius’ and rationality. By the 1780s, the language of ‘liberal sentiments’ had spread within print culture, appearing in the New Annual Register , founded by Andrew Kippis, a leading critic at the Monthly , and in the work of political and social theorists such as Major John Cartwright or James Mackintosh. Yet, defeating stereotypical notions of gender could be complicated even for men who aspired to a place within the elite of the ‘enlightened’ or ‘liberal and philosophical’.

papers.title: The Second Battle for Africa: Garveyism, the U.S. Heartland, and Global Black Freedom By Erik S. McDuffie
papers.abstract: “This book is a manifesto,” writes Erik S. McDuffie in the first sentence of his impressive new monograph, The Second Battle for Africa: Garveyism, the U.S. Heartland, and Global Black Freedom. McDuffie really means it! Drawing on research conducted over ten years, in nine countries, including interviews conducted with more than 100 subjects, The Second Battle for Africa sets out to fill in a number of gaps—some distressingly wide—that hamper our ability to understand the full scope of the Black liberation struggle. McDuffie makes a convincing case for the enduring significance of Garveyism specifically, and Black nationalism generally, as a political formation. He demonstrates the centrality of the U.S. Midwest as a place of Black politics-making. And he shows how these political threads were held together by the organizational genius of the Black women, many little-known, who populate his story. Despite a renewed scholarly focus on Garveyism in recent years, there remains a discordance between our awareness of the global importance of the movement and our understanding of what Garveyism’s political success tells us about the innumerable communities it mobilized. McDuffie shows that Black Midwesterners, like Black people everywhere, were captivated by Marcus Garvey’s message of deliverance: a call to Black people to resist the assimilationist premises and promises of the Eurocentric domestic (and global) order, to look to their own communities for the resources to survive, and to embrace the principles of Black pride, diasporic solidarity, and race-based organizing. Black Midwesterners pursued this vision by eagerly joining, and doggedly sustaining, local divisions of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), the organization founded by Garvey and Amy Ashwood (Garvey) in 1914. McDuffie’s book, which traces the work of the UNIA in the Midwest from World War I to the election of Ronald Reagan (and up to the present in the conclusion), is the first to tell the history of the organization from start to finish, and the first to show how the UNIA continued to shape Black liberation politics for several decades after the organization’s 1920s heyday. McDuffie also shows how the influence of Garveyism far outstripped the reach of the UNIA and became manifest in what he calls the “midwestern Garveyite front”: the labyrinth of political, religious, and cultural organizations that were influenced by—and gave new shape to—the Black nationalist politics propounded by Marcus Garvey and Garveyites, and that surged again during the Black Power era. This presentation of Garveyism reveals both its flexibility and its enduring appeal. McDuffie shows how Garveyism was mobilized, in different moments, toward radical and conservative ends; how, in the form of the “Garveyite front,” it could be refashioned to meet new needs and serve new political purposes. What remained consistent across the twentieth century was that, again and again, Garvey’s Black nationalist message succeeded in galvanizing Black people to action, spurring organizational growth, and shaping the contours of midwestern politics. “Garveyism,” writes McDuffie, “was the most potent political, cultural, and social force in the twentieth-century Black world.”

papers.title: No Country for Old Age: America's War on Aging from Valley Forge to Silicon Valley By Mischa Honeck
papers.abstract: The 2024 election cycle revived a longstanding American concern with old age. I don’t mean a concern with actually existing older people and their need for Social Security and adequate nursing care. That population remained, as usual, an afterthought. The concern, in 2024, was about the gerontocracy: the idea that older people have too much power, and need to make way for the young. That concern has been present in America since the founding. In No Country for Old Age, Mischa Honeck explores that long history—tracing, as the subtitle promises, a history of a prejudice from the eighteenth century to the present. This is a brisk book, moving in nine chapters and just over two hundred pages through a vast historical terrain. The first chapter, entitled “Phoenix Rising,” gives a flavor of Honeck’s method. It begins with William Barton’s quixotic attempt to make the phoenix, rather than the bald eagle, the symbol of the nation. America, Barton insisted, was a land of longevity—understood not as a celebration of old age, but as an extension of youthful dynamism, as represented by the phoenix. He attempted to prove this scientifically, too, participating in the new science of demographics to show the remarkable longevity of American citizens. Honeck starts the book with Barton because he perfectly encapsulates Honeck’s own method, which brings together cultural history and the history of science.

papers.title: Applying (semi-)automatic metadata to early modern normative texts. Annif and Policeygesetzgebung from the City-State of Bern (1528–1798)
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the application of modern digital tools to analyze handwritten normative texts from the City-State of Bern (1528-1798). By leveraging the Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS) and automatic metadata generation tools such as Transkribus for Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) and Annif for automated subject indexing, we aim to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of historical text analysis. Our methodology involves digitizing 4,550 police ordinances, manually segmenting them, and employing a hierarchical SKOS framework with 1,830 distinct labels (Rhonda Organisation 2024). Annif’s backends, including TF-IDF, Umikuji Parabel, Umikuji Bonsai, and Machine Learning Language Model, were evaluated using Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) metrics to generate relevant metadata. The results demonstrate that the Umikuji backends achieved high NDCG scores, highlighting their effectiveness. This research highlights the transformative potential of integrating digital tools in the humanities, providing a scalable solution for managing large historical datasets and enhancing access to historical texts. The findings advocate for broader adoption of these technologies in historical research, promoting greater collaboration and innovation. Future research will explore the application of these methods to other historical corpora and additional backend systems.

papers.title: The Poetry of Failure
papers.abstract: Abstract Institutional records and reports, letters, and logbook entries are often the bread and butter of historical research, and the experience of extracting the depth and texture of these resources draws us back to the archive. Still, creative inspiration can wax and wane throughout a long project. In this essay, Johnson explores the utility of poetic inquiry as a method for getting “unstuck” in the face of waning inspiration. Poetic inquiry relies on a close reading of the source material, followed by the extraction and artful rearrangement of words and phrases that highlight themes in the original text. Johnson deploys poetic inquiry to analyze the student records of influenza orphans at Girard College. Accentuating the original texture and color of the sources, Johnson assembles three short, haiku-style poems distilling the resilience of influenza survivors, whose relationships ably stretched across new geographies and institutions following separation in the pandemic aftermath. Ultimately, the practice underscores how poetry and historical analysis connect us to the depth of human experience.

papers.title: ENTANGLING KNOWLEDGE AND IGNORANCE
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This review essays situates Alain Corbin's Terra Incognita: A History of Ignorance in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries within current discussions of knowledge and ignorance related to intellectual history, the history of science, and the history of knowledge. These varying approaches have drawn the borderland between knowledge and ignorance divergently. After a brief critique of the Corbin's positivist approach in Terra Incognita , I sketch some well‐known ground in the history of science over the past two generations. I then point to how recent discussions of the relationships between intellectual history, the history of science, and the history of knowledge have tended to sidestep that history. I conclude by suggesting how indigenous studies and Corbin's own previous work might serve to better entangle knowledge and ignorance in ways that might draw on the strengths of all three fields.

papers.title: Taken for granted? Investigating constructivist principles with Bayes’ theorem in Digital Humanities scholarship
papers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the intersection of constructivist principles and statistical methods within Digital Humanities (DH) scholarship. While constructivist principles are foundational, albeit often implicit, in DH scholarship, the increasing use of statistical methods, especially Bayesian approaches, introduces epistemological tensions. Therefore, this article examines the latent constructivist assumptions in DH and explores how these principles resonate with or diverge from the epistemic premises of Bayesian statistics. It argues that there are interferences between Bayesian statistics and constructivism. The main aim is to reveal how epistemological assumptions shape knowledge production, in order to pave the way for a more reflective epistemology of DH scholarship.

papers.title: The ‘People of the Pagoda’ and the 1963 Buddhist Mobilization in Huế, Vietnam
papers.abstract: Abstract A new, ground-up narrative of the Buddhist Mobilization of Huế in central Vietnam in the summer of 1963 highlights the voices of its participants – the ‘People of the Pagoda’. Drawing on local records and personal narratives, the article explores the process of how the ‘People of the Pagoda’ forged a collective identity from daily activism and protests for religious equality. papers.title: Canoes in the Early English Caribbean: The Role of an Indigenous Technology in Making Mercantilism Work
papers.abstract: Abstract The Caribbean, with its focus on cash crop production, played a major role in the rise of England’s Atlantic trading system and the making of modern capitalism. Yet, there remains poor understanding of the processes by which the early colonizers built the economic and social capabilities necessary to extract wealth from an alien environment, and a common assumption that they relied overwhelmingly on metropolitan skills and knowledge. This article addresses these issues through a study of the canoe, an Indigenous transport technology. The first imperative of successful settlement was to construct robust regional supply networks and, although the colonizers were fortunate in that the fragmented Caribbean island-scape possesses abundant land and marine resources, they lacked the knowledge and tools necessary for effective extraction and distribution. The newcomers turned to native residents to develop the skills required to manage local geography and soon recognized the utility of canoes, dug out of single logs, with their low cost, shallow draft, speed, and agility, and learned how these boats should be made and used. Canoes in a range of sizes became objects in everyday use among the English colonists and played a central role in moving people, goods, and information around the region, with its shallows and tyrannical wind system; served as platforms for resource extraction; and provided a necessary defence capability. Understanding the challenges encountered in managing the Caribbean environment, and bringing canoes into the picture, pulls Indigenous people into sharper focus and highlights some of the transcultural exchanges that made mercantilism work.

papers.title: Landscaping Patagonia: Spatial History and Nation-Making in Chile and Argentina. By María de los Ángeles Picone
papers.abstract: María de los Ángeles Picone’s Landscaping Patagonia examines the myriad ways that people understood and experienced space, place, and nature in northern Patagonia, and the impacts of these spatial imaginaries on nation-state formation in both Argentina and Chile. On the contrary, the diverse populations who inhabited, governed, and traversed Patagonia developed different—and often clashing—perspectives on the region’s natural and built environment. These diverging experiences of Patagonian space inflected contemporary discourses on identity, citizenship, immigration, patriotism, and modernity. Landscaping Patagonia is part of a growing body of transnational scholarship on the Argentine-Chilean cordillera region and builds productively on English- and Spanish-language scholarship, such as that of Susana Bandieri, Alberto Harambour, and Kyle Harvey. Additionally, Picone’s work is in conversation with the theoretical frameworks of borderlands history and spatial history. Picone employs both of these theoretical frameworks in order to unsettle traditional narratives of national history, highlight alternative ways of conceptualizing space and place, and bring a diverse array of historical actors into the frame of vision. In doing so, Picone is able to tease out the fascinating ways in which borderlands populations (elite and non-elite, Argentine and foreign-born) experienced and sought to shape the natural world.

papers.title: Representing provenance and track changes of cultural heritage metadata in RDF: a survey of existing approaches
papers.abstract: Abstract In the realm of Digital Humanities, the management of cultural heritage metadata is pivotal for ensuring data trustworthiness. Provenance information—contextual metadata detailing the origin and history of data—plays a crucial role in this process. However, tracking provenance and changes in metadata using the Resource Description Framework (RDF) presents significant challenges due to the limitations of foundational Semantic Web technologies. This article offers a comprehensive review of existing models and approaches for representing provenance and tracking changes in RDF, with a specific focus on cultural heritage metadata. It examines W3C standard proposals such as RDF Reification and n-ary relations, along with various alternative systems. Through an in-depth analysis, the study identifies Named Graphs, RDF-star, the Provenance Ontology (PROV-O), Dublin Core (DC), Conjectural Graphs, and the OpenCitations Data Model (OCDM) as the most effective solutions. These models are evaluated based on their compliance with RDF standards, scalability, and applicability across different domains. The findings underscore the importance of selecting the appropriate model to ensure robust and reliable management of provenance in RDF datasets, thereby contributing to the ongoing discourse on provenance representation in the Digital Humanities.

papers.title: The Age of the Borderlands: Indians, Slaves, and the Limits of Manifest Destiny, 1790-1850. By Andrew C. Isenberg
papers.abstract: Was the early United States a confident, expansionist nation? That depends on where you look and who you ask. Certainly, many early federal leaders and ordinary people shared a vision of continental expansion that became increasingly providential over the first decades of the early nineteenth century. Expansion was baked into the revolutionary settlement, and federal officials imagined that Indigenous land reaching west to the Mississippi River (and soon beyond it) would underpin the financial stability of the new nation. And yet, they also knew that expansion was a source of instability. Expansionists they may have been, but confident they were not. Indigenous people thwarted land theft at every turn. Even in the earliest decades of the new republic, some white Americans who we might expect to have been invested in expansion were troubled by its implications. And by the 1830s Indigenous leaders were supported in their efforts to counter Indian removal by a vocal white and black minority. As many scholars have recently shown, expansion was never inevitable.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Between the early nineteenth century and the early twentieth century, over one million people from India served as indentured laborers in European‐dominated colonies scattered across the Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and Caribbean. papers.title: Surgery and Salvation: The Roots of Reproductive Injustice in Mexico, 1770-1940. By Elizabeth O’Brien
papers.abstract: Progress on reproductive health has never been linear or easy. Even under liberal governments, women have faced restrictive policies, and medical professionals have often exercised their authority in paternalistic—and at times harmful—ways. In Surgery and Salvation, Elizabeth O’Brien takes a long chronological view of reproductive injustice in Mexico, tracing the roots of what she calls “obstetric violence” from the end of Spanish colonial rule through the Mexican Revolution. Over more than two centuries, priests and physicians intervened surgically in the name of saving fetal souls, women’s honor, and the nation’s reputation. Religious ideology and discourse, far from being displaced by modern medicine, became deeply intertwined with forms of institutionalized medical violence against women, whose bodies were used both for clinical experimentation and social regeneration. The book is structured chronologically and thematically, divided into five sections. A 1749 royal decree mandated that priests throughout the Spanish empire perform caesarean operations on dead or dying women to save the fetus’s soul. This practice—especially common on missions of the Californias—was more widespread in the colonial period than previously understood and laid the groundwork for a medical culture that often prioritized the unborn fetus over the mother’s physical health. During the liberal Reforma era (1840s–1870s), physicians were trained in an environment in which Mexico City’s hospitals remained largely under the care of religious women. When they diagnosed conditions of hysteria and complications from pregnancies, they frequently located disease in the reproductive organs, leading to therapeutic abortions or, in some cases, the surgical removal of ovaries.

papers.title: British Colonial Rule over Littoral Space and Watercraft in Hong Kong, 1841–1898

Third is the contrast between colonial designs and actual negotiations regarding the use of littoral space.

papers.abstract: Letizia Osti’s History and Memory in the Abbasid Caliphate: Writing the Past in Medieval Arabic Literature is a tightly argued investigation of a court operative who flourished during the ʿAbbasid caliphate (r. 750–1258). The subject, Abū Bakr al-Ṣūlī (d. 947), often appears in scholarly treatments of the period, but rarely does he receive the spotlight. At court, with access to caliphs, and both as a participant and eyewitness to caliphal power, he was a courtier-­­scholar of many dimensions. Al-Ṣūlī wrote about the chancery, turned his hand to poetry (as a writer and collector who collated other poets’ works—including the caliphs’), and gained a reputation as a skilled chess player. He taught Abbasid princes. After decades supported by caliphal and courtly patrons—especially the caliph al-Rāḍī (r. 934–40)—the caliphate’s unraveling proved to be his own too. He ultimately finished his life in Baṣra, selling his notebooks to survive (“the written word, accumulated over long years” was “precious currency at the end of al-Ṣūlī’s life” [81]). He inspired no editor to collect his poetry. A personal story runs throughout this book: of a man striving to win payouts, proud of his connections and foresight and unhappy with a dumbing down of educational standards, who witnessed the caliphate’s financial troubles and rivalries, as well as the insecurity experienced by the population of Baghdad. Still, this is no “life and times” story. Rather, across five chapters Osti goes to unusual lengths to situate her work within scholarship relating to the Abbasid period as she uses a well-­­documented, but rarely remarked on, person to give a wider account of Arabic literature and historiography. Osti’s critical treatment introduces readers therefore not just to al-Ṣūlī and the ʿAbbasids, but to the many fields that encompass him. The book is therefore also an efficient introduction to court life under the Abbasids.

papers.title: Housing and the Peripheralization of Race Politics in Britain, 1948–1977
papers.abstract: Abstract The idea that there was a ratio of people of colour to white people that, if exceeded, would prompt a white backlash was a tenet of folk sociology in Britain. However, the housing market had the opposite effect. It ‘concentrated’ Black and Asian people in run-down parts of British cities. Later, as urban authorities began to demolish these neighbourhoods and to integrate public housing, some (most notably Birmingham) introduced formal dispersal programmes with racial quotas. City and regional authorities in France and West Germany pursued dispersal in parallel ways, despite the differences in the three countries’ migration histories and citizenship regimes. The similarities in the project of dispersal and its failure point to a common European history of the origins of multiculturalism.

papers.title: Classification of Saikaku’s works using topic modelling
papers.abstract: Abstract This study quantitatively analysed the thematic structure and temporal transitions in Saikaku Ihara’s ukiyo-zōshi using latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), dynamic topic modelling (DTM), and Word2Vec. The results confirmed previous research findings, showing that early works primarily focused on Kōshokumono (romantic novel), while later works covered broader themes. Additionally, LDA identified distinct topics within each chapter, subdividing Kōshokumono into emotions and love (Topic 3), pleasure quarters (Topic 4), and personal romantic history (Topic 5). By integrating LDA, DTM, and Word2Vec, this study’s quantitative examination of thematic transitions in Saikaku’s works provides new insights into the structural and lexical evolution of ukiyo-zōshi beyond conventional classifications.

papers.title: PRODUCING INTEGRATION: THE TRANSLATION OF NON/BELONGING IN GERMANY AND THE UNITED STATES
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This essay examines how the concept of integration has been produced, translated, and institutionalized in Germany and the United States as a key element of policy frameworks that migranticize some people and, thus, translate them as outsiders. By combining conceptual history and translation theory, we analyze how the meaning of integration has evolved within academic and political discourse, tracing its emergence as a key category in migration governance. We argue that the production of what integration means can be read via and as translation, resulting in an ambiguous medium that structures access to belonging in a way that facilitates the reproduction of exclusionary hierarchies. We begin by outlining our theoretical framework, linking cultural translation with conceptual history to examine how integration operates as a dynamic but historically contingent concept. We then explore integration in Germany, tracing its genealogy from racializing notions during the Nazi years to its institutionalization as a migration policy in a multicultural society during the twenty‐first century. Next, we turn our attention to the US, where integration remains undefined in official policy but is shaped through differential inclusion in the market and illegality. Focusing on Duldung and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, we argue that the German and US systems translate older forms of exclusion into contemporary governance structures. Far from a neutral or inclusive concept, integration becomes operative as a tool for regulating mobility and non/belonging through a twofold translation: the production of what integration means determines how the concept translates people.

papers.title: Linked Data for Digital Humanities. Terhi Nurmikko-Fuller
papers.abstract: In the contemporary era, the phenomenon of digital transformation is redefining the global landscape, dramatically altering the modalities through which information is accessed. While users benefit from the advancements in digital convenience, there persists a significant lack of awareness concerning the data structures that shape the accessibility and nature of information. Fundamental innovations such as graph technologies and the semantic web, though critical, are frequently overshadowed by more conspicuous online technologies such as social media and algorithmic processes. Consequently, these foundational elements have yet to fully permeate public discourse or establish themselves as interdisciplinary paradigms within the humanities and social sciences. Against this context, Linked Data for Digital Humanities provides a comprehensive guide, ushering readers through a process of critical evaluation and practical implementation of one of the most transformative information publication paradigms globally: Linked Data. This publication not only exposes the covert influences of data structures on human cognition but also introduces a pioneering solution for research in Digital Humanities.

papers.title: Theses on the Metaphor of Digital–Textual History. Martin Paul Eve
papers.abstract: “Metaphor is a poor metaphor for what needs to be done.” (Eve, 2024, p. 10) Martin Paul Eve’s (2024) Theses on the Metaphors of Digital–Textual History aligns with a tradition of meta-critical studies of digital tools in the humanities—why the tools we use in the humanities matter for them. This includes, for example, Kirschenbaum’s (2012, 2021) Mechanisms: New Media and the Forensic Imagination and Bitstreams: The Future of Digital Literary Heritage, both of which Eve (more or less explicitly) identifies as central influences. The book also belongs to a larger set of publications by Martin Paul Eve (2014a,b, 2019, 2021) that includes, for instance, Warez, Close Reading with Computers, Open Access and the Humanities, and Pynchon and Philosophy. All these works similarly interrogate the epistemic conditions of reading, writing, and scholarship in the digital age. Each of these books engages, in different ways, with how “frames”—computational, infrastructural, institutional, or philosophical—shape scholarly inquiry. Theses synthesizes Eve’s meta-critical impulse by focusing on metaphorical referentiality as a structuring principle across digital and textual domains. In a sense, it is the most distilled and conceptual of Eve’s works, offering a portable critique of the metaphors that underpin all the others.

papers.title: Merze Tate: Race and US Imperialism in the Pacific
papers.abstract: This book was not reviewed by the AHR upon its original publication and its review now is part of the journal’s reckoning with racist aspects of its work and influence. For most of the twentieth century, scholarly associations like this one were racially segregated and exclusionary; so too was academic publishing, including journals. Placing articles and books by women professors was also difficult at a time when the publishing industry remained a male-dominated bastion. When Professor Merze Tate of Howard University wrote to an academic publisher in 1961 asking for advice on the preferred length of a manuscript submission, she received this reply: “The only reasonable answer to that question was given by a man who said that the length of a manuscript should be like that of a woman’s skirt—short enough to be interesting, long enough to cover the subject.”1 Fortunately for us, Tate was not easily deterred despite the obstacles faced by her and other Black and women scholars of her generation who worked in what she aptly named a “sex and race discriminating world.” Born in 1905, Tate was the first Black American to receive a graduate degree from Oxford, a B. Litt. in international relations in 1935. After earning her doctorate in government from Harvard in 1941, she began a career in Howard’s history department that stretched from 1942 until her retirement in 1977. Blessed with a long life, she continued to research and write until her death in Washington, DC in 1996.2

papers.title: Slipping from the Podium
papers.abstract: Abstract Three authors, Michael Kugler, Kelli Y. Nakamura, and Julie M. Rancilio, teach at a community college or a small evangelical college. Their training in PhD-granting institutions did not prepare them to teach students who took history courses as a box to check on the way to a degree, students whose attendance in class was just one stop in a busy, daily itinerary that also included jobs, care for family members, and long commutes. They expected to have students who, like themselves, had an intrinsic desire to learn. Very little in their training gave them models for what to teach their students, how to reach and inspire them. Each author wrote History Unclassified independently describing in similar ways the mistakes they had made in the classroom. We connected them and asked them to compare notes. What follows are excerpts from their conversations.

papers.title: Digitization and the recreation of Yorùbá cultural moral tales
papers.abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of the widespread allegation that Yorùbá folk stories and cultural moral tales are faced with the threat of marginalization owing to persistent attacks on indigenous cultural forms by the forces of globalization, this study underscores the inherent value in the digitization of Yorùbá cultural moral tales and stories. Interestingly, technological and scientific innovations have always conditioned both the material and immaterial aspects of culture. The article is situated within the theoretical purview of intangible cultural heritage and the Yorùbá philosophy of innovation and change in cultural production, distribution, and consumption. Methodologically, the study derives its evidence from the analysis of the ethnographic data collected through an online survey of 373 respondents. This was complemented with findings from participants’ observations and qualitative interviews conducted across Yorùbáland as well as the textual analysis of relevant primary and secondary literature on Yorùbá cultural moral tales and digitization. Interestingly, the study finds out that apart from their unique moralizing, entertaining, and economic values, Yorùbá folk stories are veritable cultural artefacts that can be used to promote social cohesion, moral uprightness, and civil citizenship. The conclusion is that there is an urgent need for the expansion and recreation of Yorùbá cultural moral tales in digital formats to make them more accessible to both local and global viewers.

papers.title: Graph schema validation at last? Work towards a StemmaREST ontology with Neo4J, RDF-STAR, and SHACL
papers.abstract: Abstract As of 2023, there have been two intriguing developments in the Semantic Web world that are especially relevant to digital humanities projects that are anchored to graph technologies, such as the StemmaREST repository for variant text traditions. The first of these is RDF-STAR, an extension to RDF that allows an entire triple to be the subject or object in further triple statements. The second is Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), a language whose purpose Is to define a set of constraints against Ih RDF graphs can be validated. This language solves a problem that OWL never adequately addressed: a set of SHACL constraints can help ensure the consistency of data as it is created. This article reports on the results of a proof-of-concept implementation of a validation pipeline for StemmaREST graph data, through conversion to RDF-STAR, ontological enrichment to make superclass membership explicit, and validation with SHACL. Although there remain certain obstacles to putting this into practice for the case of StemmaREST, the proof of concept demonstrates that graph schema validation is a viable option for digital humanities projects in general.

papers.title: Museums and the Ethics of Restitution: Benin City at the Crossroads of DebateMuseums and the Ethics of Restitution: Benin City at the Crossroads of Debate
papers.abstract: In 2006, Neil MacGregor, the former Director of the British Museum, asserted that “repatriation is yesterday’s question.” But recent history has proven this declaration to be highly inaccurate. Repatriation and restitution have become hot topics in recent years, in part due to a revival of interest in two well-known cases: that of the Benin “bronzes” looted by the British in 1897 from the ancient kingdom of Benin in Nigeria, and the Parthenon marbles (still controversially referred to as the Elgin Marbles after their eponymous extractor, Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin). Not only have there been more public calls for restitution and repatriation in recent years; the rate of successful claims has increased exponentially. Bénédicte Savoy’s Africa’s Struggle for its Art, Dan Hicks’s The Brutish Museums, and Barnaby Phillips’s Loot: Britain and the Benin Bronzes all focus on marshaling historical evidence for the ethical necessity of restitution. While drawing her readers’ attention to the longue durée of repatriation and restitution struggles in Africa, Bénédicte Savoy suggests in Africa’s Struggle for Its Art that the current focus is in large part due to the report she published together with the Senegalese economist Felwine Sarr in 2018 at the behest of the French president Emmanuel Macron. More than this, she suggests that many current claims have been able to gain traction in ways that earlier demands failed largely due to their joint research and the moral arguments advanced in their report. In many ways, what has become known as the Sarr/Savoy report was indeed a milestone. However, I would argue that the report was part of an established trend, and that a much wider set of political and economic circumstances have contributed to the current resurgence of calls for the return of cultural property.

papers.title: Construction and application of knowledge graph in digital humanities: a case study of Qiaokan
papers.abstract: Abstract This study utilizes Knowledge Graph (KG) technology, taking Qiaoxiang Memory Heritage “Gu Zhai Yue Kan” and “Guang Yu Yue Bao” as examples, to analyze the contributions of overseas Chinese to the development of their hometown. By integrating multisource heterogeneous data, constructing datasets, and mining deep information, the practicality and efficiency of KG in managing Qiaoxiang Memory Heritage (Qiaokan) data are verified. KG not only provides data analysis capabilities but also offers precise data management tools for governments and research institutions through knowledge question answering and visualization technology. The research finds that overseas Chinese have made continuous investments in multiple fields, having a profound impact on their hometown’s development. KG demonstrates applications in information querying, knowledge reasoning, and discovery, capable of rapidly capturing donations and changes. The conclusion points out that KG is a preferred method for analyzing donation information, though it has limitations such as a limited sample size. Future improvements are needed in areas like automatic entity extraction and multimodal data mining. This study provides a new pathway for the storage, management, and utilization of cultural data in Overseas Chinese hometowns and offers technical support and a knowledge framework for scientific research.

papers.title: The Social Impact of Automating Translation: An Ethics of Care Perspective on Machine Translation. Esther Monzó-Nebot and Vicenta Tasa-Fuster
papers.abstract: In the contemporary era of rapid technological progress, machine translation (MT) has emerged as a transformative force in global communication. Recent research on MT has proliferated, with scholars examining its technical capabilities, efficiency, and applications across various domains (Burchardt et al., 2016; Killman 2024). However, much of the existing literature has predominantly concentrated on the technological dimensions, often neglecting the broader social, ethical, and cultural ramifications. This gap in research has left a significant void in our understanding of how MT affects different stakeholders, ranging from individual users and linguistic communities to global democratic systems. In response to this gap, The Social Impact of Automating Translation, edited by Esther Monzó-Nebot and Vicenta Tasa-Fuster, addresses the need for a more comprehensive examination by adopting an ethics of care perspective. This perspective emphasizes the interconnectedness of human experiences, the importance of empathy, and the responsibility to address the needs of all stakeholders impacted by MT. By foregrounding this approach, the book seeks to offer a more nuanced understanding of the social implications of MT and advocate for a more equitable and ethical framework for its development and implementation. The volume explores the complex interplay between MT, social hierarchies, and ethical considerations, challenging conventional narratives of technological progress and underscoring the need for a more inclusive and responsible approach to the development of language technologies.

papers.title: The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America. By Andrew W. Kahrl
papers.abstract: In The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America, Andrew W. Kahrl reveals the insidious ways that local tax systems have perpetuated racial inequality. Kahrl traces the evolution of property taxes from the nineteenth century to the present through the experiences of Black Americans. Consistently overtaxed on their land and their homes, chronically underserved by racist officials who siphoned funds to white neighborhoods, and unfairly targeted by tax delinquency laws, “Black people have paid the heaviest cost” for the dependence of local governments on property taxes (3). A sweeping indictment of structural racism, The Black Tax explains the intricacies of tax policy while never losing sight of the ordinary Black people who resisted exploitation and fought for tax justice. The book is organized chronologically and thematically. Fifteen chapters are divided into five sections on Reconstruction, the Great Migration, Jim Crow, civil rights and Black Power, and the contemporary age of neoliberalism. The sections include three chapters on tax administration, public spending, and tax enforcement during each period. At times this structure feels somewhat schematic, but the vast chronology and geography underscore the centrality of taxation to African American history. If land ownership symbolized freedom for the formerly enslaved and their descendants, the threat of dispossession remained ever-present. Following the collapse of Reconstruction, officials squeezed Black landowners with high tax assessments while diverting the revenues to pay for sidewalks, schools, and sewers in white neighborhoods. A single missed tax payment often led to properties being seized and auctioned off to the highest bidder. These injustices drove millions of Black Americans to northern cities during the twentieth century, but migrants found the same high tax bills and inferior public services in urban neighborhoods. In recent decades, federal tax cuts and state austerity have made local governments even more dependent on property taxes, with devastating consequences for Black communities.

papers.title: The making and unmaking of religious toleration in Spanish Manila, 1571–1755
papers.abstract: Abstract This article traces the rise and collapse of religious toleration of non-Christian Chinese merchants in Spanish Manila between 1571 and 1755, offering a case study in early modern global commerce and interfaith governance in European Asia. It demonstrates that Manila became the most religiously diverse and tolerant city in the Spanish Empire — and perhaps in the entire early modern Latin West — despite many hardline authorities’ and jurists’ insistence upon maintaining the widespread imperial practice of persecution of non-Christian ritual and belief. This deviation owed largely to coordinated efforts of non-Catholic Chinese merchants and sympathetic authorities — especially the Spanish governors and municipal aldermen. Jurists responded by formulating a theory of toleration rooted in scholastic contractualism, natural law, and voluntarism. Manila thus became a pioneer of the de facto and de jure toleration that underpinned Christian Asia — and whose arrangements resemble later developments in Dutch Batavia and French Pondichéry. Yet while Manila’s practices later became mainstream in many European-dominated entrepots, the risk of war between Manila and the Zheng maritime power in the early 1660s shattered the city’s tolerant alliance, setting the stage for a slow dismemberment of non-Christian institutions culminating in the 1755 expulsion of non-Catholics. As other regional European powers adopted toleration, the regional trailblazer thus abandoned it. Manila toleration’s unique trajectory compels a partial re-evaluation of the Spanish Empire’s reputation for religious intolerance, underscores the critical importance of toleration in the emergence of commerce and governance in Christian Asia, and provides further evidence against the widespread liberal narrative in which toleration emerges exclusively in Northern Europe among a handful of eminent Protestant and deist freethinkers.

papers.title: To Change in China
papers.abstract: Abstract This article brings together sources from China, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France to explore the rare and fraught cases of Americans and Europeans who attempted to become naturalized subjects in late-nineteenth-century Qing China. Decades before China established its first formal law on citizenship, foreigners, especially foreign military experts, were trying and occasionally succeeding in naturalizing as Chinese. I see naturalization as one of many ad hoc collaborations within the period’s Self-Strengthening movement. Yet the place of China in the nineteenth century’s global debates on naturalization remains little known. More than just a product of silences, I argue that this is the result of a deliberate erasure, primarily achieved through historic efforts by Euro-American powers to deny the legitimacy of white naturalization in China. Despite small numbers of applicants, these powers quickly came to perceive the possibility as a threat to broader racial hierarchies they were constructing in Asia. Reconstructing and contextualizing these cases serves to expand the story of modern nationality in China, and to reinsert China into a global history with present-day implications. Ultimately, I argue, it was the lines drawn around China here that most shaped the boundaries of modern naturalization.

papers.title: Derek Taira. Forward without Fear: Native Hawaiians and American Education in Territorial Hawaiʻi, 1900–1941 .
papers.abstract: Scholarship on Native Hawaiian activism has portrayed the territorial period (1900–1959) as a nadir between the vibrant efforts of the 1890s anti-annexation protests and the renaissance of Hawaiian language and culture in the 1970s. In Forward without Fear: Native Hawaiians and American Education in Territorial Hawai’i, 1900–1941, Derek Taira challenges the notion that Native Hawaiians acquiesced to American rule and lost their cultural identity during this period. Instead, he argues that many Native Hawaiians “resisted and challenged Americanization by finding avenues, spaces, and opportunities to perpetuate and preserve their culture, language, and identity in ways that involved public education” (5). Drawing on unique sources to uncover the voices of Native students, educators, parents, and legislators, Taira’s work makes a significant contribution to recent scholarship highlighting public school classrooms as spaces where competing interests contested colonial hegemony and maintained cultural identities in the face of sustained assimilation campaigns. Chapters 1 and 2 frame the islands as sites of explicit American colonization, elucidating the intent of American schoolmen whose power shaped, but did not entirely control, island classrooms. Taira carefully weaves the story of Hawai’i’s public schools and the Progressive education movement into that of the concurrent educational state-building across the American empire. Progressive educators ardently promoted civic democracy even as they reinforced social efficiency and structural hierarchies that prevented immigrant, Indigenous, and Black students from achieving their goals. Native Hawaiians had engaged with common schools since the 1840s, but American educators created a narrative erasing this participation in favor of one that highlighted inevitable American presence and progress. Taira uses the writings of eleven haole (white, American) schoolmen in the Hawaii Educational Review, the official publication of the Department of Public Instruction (DPI), to trace this narrative. In their efforts to “cultivate consent,” they emphasized a white, normative social structure that steered most Asian and Indigenous students to plantation jobs by stressing the dignity of agricultural labor. Taira’s relatively narrow set of sources supports his argument about these men’s vision for the islands’ society and economy but, as he briefly acknowledges, limits his ability to examine the more complicated reality that played out in the islands’ administrative offices and classrooms.

papers.title: The Political Ecology of Violence: Peasants and Pastoralists in the Last Ottoman Century. By Zozan Pehlivan
papers.abstract: What if the unraveling of a multiethnic rural society in Ottoman Kurdistan had as much to do with distant ocean currents in the Pacific as with imperial reforms or communal tensions? Could the breakdown of coexistence between Armenian peasants and Kurdish pastoralists be traced not only to sectarianism or nationalism, but also to the timing and intensity of El Niño and La Niña events? In The Political Ecology of Violence, Zozan Pehlivan opens new historiographical terrain by treating global climate as a key actor in the region’s history. Focusing on the environmental fallout of ENSO-linked weather anomalies, especially the droughts and cold spells of the late nineteenth century, she demonstrates how ecological disturbances reshaped the region’s diverse landscapes and destabilized both human and nonhuman life. These disruptions, she argues, were central to the erosion of intercommunal relations and the eventual escalation into violence. In this way, at its core, the book offers a radical rethinking of violence: not as episodic, irrational, or solely rooted in ethnic antagonism, but as the cumulative result of structural transformations that unfolded over decades.

papers.title: Yixin Chen. When Food Became Scarce: How Chinese Peasants Survived the Great Leap Forward Famine
papers.abstract: The Great Leap Forward and its consequences are explored in many scholarly works, by scholars including Jean-Luc Domenach, Thomas Bernstein, Ralph Thaxton, Frank Dikötter, and Felix Wemheuer. In addition, peasant resistance in the Maoist and post-Mao eras is examined by, among others, Bill Skinner, Kevin O’Brien, Lianjiang Li, Edward Friedman, Paul G. Pickowicz, and Mark Selden. However, When Food Became Scarce: How Chinese Peasants Survived the Great Leap Forward Famine is an impressive addition to the existing repertoire of works on the state and peasants in the People’s Republic of China. By recognizing the severity of the Great Leap Forward as a man-made disaster, Chen asks the questions of who survived, what survivors did to avoid death, and what conditions made their survival possible. Focusing on Anhui, a province in eastern China, Chen situates peasants’ struggle for survival in environments defined by localized combinations of natural environments, history, grassroots cadres’ relationships with peasants, and, most importantly, lineage structure. His research is based on a variety of materials—archival sources, genealogy, and especially interviews with individuals. According to Chen, most vital to his book are interviews with local ­­cadres, a group possessing comprehensive knowledge about the Great Famine.

papers.title: Millicent E. Brown. Another Sojourner Looking for Truth: My Journey from Civil Rights to Black Power and Beyond.
papers.abstract: Millicent E. Brown’s engaging memoir, Another Sojourner Looking for Truth: My Journey from Civil Rights to Black Power and Beyond, is drawn from her lifetime of experiences as one of the “first children” of South Carolina’s civil rights movement, a Black student activist and grassroots organizer, devoted educator, public historian, and museum consultant. Jackson, and “The Fonz,” coupled with reflections about how the civil rights generation was carefully taught and forged through nonviolent protest, the high costs of sacrifice, the uses and misuses of their legacy, and the unintended consequences of the change they inspired. papers.title: Historical parliamentary corpora: the Carniolan provincial assembly records
papers.abstract: Abstract Parliamentary debates provide an invaluable source of information for research in various fields, as they reflect the prevailing ideas and beliefs of the time. We have developed a corpus of Slovenian parliamentary records from 1861–1913, covering 694 sessions of the Carniolan Provincial Assembly and containing about 10 million words. This article describes the process of creating the first version of the corpus, which consisted of obtaining OCR processed stenographic notes of the parliamentary sessions, analysing the content to extract metadata, and developing a linguistically processed, metadata-rich and structurally encoded corpus in the Parla-CLARIN format. Transforming these records into more accessible and analysable resources will facilitate in-depth study and analysis of the historical development and change of political concepts and ideas. In addition, a brief analysis of the corpus vocabulary is provided, focusing on the use of Slovenian and German language. As language played a key role in shaping ethnic identity during this period, the results are also discussed in their historical context. To make the corpus accessible to the public, we have developed a web application that facilitates exploration of the corpus and enables efficient searching in an intuitive and user-friendly way.

papers.title: Theresa McCulla. Insatiable City: Food and Race in New Orleans
papers.abstract: In her incisive book Insatiable City, Theresa McCulla argues that the lasting appeal of New Orleans’s cuisine is inextricable from racial oppression rooted in “social, cultural, economic, and political systems of great violence” (3). Stretching from France’s 1718 founding of New Orleans to the civil rights movement, McCulla carefully documents the intertwined history of New Orleans cuisine, enslavement, and escapist tourism, as the city emerged as an antebellum marketplace where everything and everyone appeared for sale. Further, McCulla traces the process by which, over two hundred years of American occupation, municipal administrations and white residents reordered the city’s heterogeneous racial and ethnic origins, interracial spaces, and syncretic foodways to align with the nation’s bifurcated racial identity and hierarchy. However, even as white locals and visitors erased enslaved and Indigenous contributions to New Orleans’s Creole cuisine, McCulla argues that Black and Creole of color residents used food and foodways to resist oppression, provide for their families, and build community.

papers.title: Modelling uncertainty: a controlled vocabulary for feminist film history
papers.abstract: Abstract When researching the role of women in the silent film era, researchers are not only faced with the scarcity of surviving (film) material but also need to find ways to account for varying degrees of uncertainty, contradictions and ambiguity in data. The online platform Women Film Pioneers Project (WFPP), which publishes research on women who worked behind the scenes in the early film industries, has established its own strategies for this purpose. In so-called ‘credit reports’, researchers can reflect on the filmographies they have compiled, address contradictions in the sources, point out gaps where women have not been credited for their work or speculate about their careers. However, as the WFPP focuses on the publication of scholarly texts, the filmographies are not yet available in structured form. Therefore, this article outlines an approach for preparing WFPP’s filmographies as structured data in which uncertainties are preserved. For this purpose, I have developed a controlled vocabulary that addresses two different layers of uncertainty. On the one hand, there is the historical uncertainty described by the authors in the credit reports. On the other hand, there can also be interpretative uncertainty about how to correctly interpret the credit reports. To account for both layers, I propose a controlled vocabulary that comprises four terms: contradictory, uncredited, possible, and unconfirmed. By making the WFPP filmographies available as structured data, I aim to lay the groundwork for telling data-based counter-histories that challenge traditional film historiographical narratives, which often fail to mention the contributions of women in the early days of film history.

papers.title: Embracing the Untamed Garden
papers.abstract: Abstract The hand-drawn visual essay, “Embracing the Untamed Garden,” is a collaborative project by a mother-daughter team. Claire Schen is a college professor at University at Buffalo, SUNY and Maddy Cherr is a college graduate in illustration from Rhode Island School of Design. The visual essay grew out of conversations during and since the COVID-19 pandemic about professional growth that suggested an unexpected convergence of creativity and research. Told equally in words and visuals, the essay focuses on shaping an authentic narrative of the professional self. The subject is the tension between risk-taking and growth on the one hand and the pressure for results and productivity on the other. The pandemic and growing unease about the value and purpose of higher education exacerbated this tension for learners and faculty. How do students and scholars craft their narrative about risks taken and detours made in education and careers? How do they define parameters of educational and professional lives in relation to personal ones? Describing the working dynamic, Cherr illustrated the visual essay and both authors generated the text. In addition, the images grew from conversations about how each visualized their challenges and observations.

papers.title: Francisco Bethencourt. Strangers Within: The Rise and Fall of the New Christian Trading Elite
papers.abstract: Francisco Bethencourt’s new book, Strangers Within, traces the emergence and eventual dissolution of an ethnic category during the early modern period and the association of that category with a particular cultural and social group. In addition to his conclusions about the experiences and legacies of those individuals who were affected by such categorization, Bethencourt’s magisterial study demonstrates that racial and ethnic categories must be historicized, countering the naturalization of stereotypes that can lead to the persecution of minoritized groups. Bethencourt’s focus is on descendants of Iberian converts from Judaism to Catholicism. He describes the historical life cycle of the legally and socially potent category of “new Christian” through four broad periods: Transitions (1490s–1540s), Expansion (1550s–1600s), Resistance (1600s–1640s), and Decline (1650s–1770s). He begins in the 1390s, when pogroms and forced conversions created the first significant population of “new Christians” in Iberia, often called conversos in both historical sources and modern scholarship. The unexpected social ascencion of some conversos created resentments among so-called “old Christians,” fomenting demonstrations between the 1440s and 1550s. Blood-purity statutes and the Iberian Inquisitions (founded 1478 in Spain, 1536 in Portugal) emerged out of these violent movements. Early inquisitors assumed that all new Christians were apostates, codifying a long-standing stereotype in law and literature. Meanwhile, blood-purity statutes created the idea—highly contested during the fifteenth and early sixteenth century but eventually accepted by both religious and secular institutions—that such apostasy was hereditary. It was, Bethencourt argues, this tandem emergence of discriminatory laws and a judicial institution to enforce them that accelerated the racialization of new Christians. From this point onward, new Christians were a community apart—the “strangers within” who Bethencourt refers to in his title, drawing on Georg Simmel’s 1908 essay. Cycles of integration and persecution affected new Christians through the eighteenth century, when inquisitorial and political pressure continued to increase, dismantling the transregional networks of new Christian families. Eventually, the legal category was abolished in Portugal in 1773 as a basis for special taxation. In this period, increasing state interventionism in both Spanish and Portuguese Inquisitions shifted the tribunals’ priorities away from racialized categories, though Bethencourt notes that racialized thinking about new Christians endured, even after the abolition of the Spanish Inquisition in 1834.

papers.title: Chile Underground: The Santiago Metro and the Struggle for a Rational City. By Andra B. Chastain
papers.abstract: It would be difficult to spend any amount of time in Santiago and not interact with the Metro system in some way. And anyone paying attention to contemporary Chile would have seen the troublesome rollout of Transantiago in 2007 and then the estallido social in 2019, triggered in part by the increase in Metro fares. Despite its centrality to life in Santiago, the Metro has not received much attention from historians. Andra Chastain’s Chile Underground provides the first book-length study of the ideas behind the metro, the construction process, and its relation to national political processes and to the broader context of the Cold War. Chastain proposes three interrelated arguments on the Metro: that it was “riven by tensions between planning and practice”; that it has been a “microcosm of Chile at key moments in time”; and that “the Metro was not only a channel for existing tensions; it also had concrete consequences for Santiago and Chile as a whole” (4-5). In addition to these arguments, the Metro allows Chastain to build on recent work by Heidi Tinsman and Thomas Miller Klubock that stresses the continuities that link the Pinochet dictatorship to what came before and what followed (12-13, 124-125). papers.title: Fossil Energy and The Ecology of Everyday Life in The Low Countries During The Long Eighteenth Century

papers.title: CAN HISTORY ABSOLVE? CAN HISTORY JUDGE?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Appealing to history, rather than to God, to provide an ultimate judgment about human actions can have a justificatory or consolatory function. The former grants proleptic absolution for acts that may be morally dubious because of their benign consequences, while the latter enables victims in the present to gain a measure of relief by imagining they will be honored by posterity. In both cases, problematic assumptions about “history” and “judgment” call into question the belief that future generations will vindicate present‐day struggles. The first of these assumptions is that “history” conveys worth by what might be called “victors’ justice,” in which success proves that the winner was morally superior. The second is that “history” is an impersonal process that can be recounted in a single metanarrative rather than an ongoing series of different narratives that are themselves variable depending on who is doing the narrating. When “history” means the community of historians who recount and analyze the past, there is rarely, if ever, a grand consensus agreed upon by all. Finally, whereas the judgment of God is assumed to be qualitative and individualized, and thus perfect for each case, human judgment depends either on deontological rules, which may not be universal, or on analogies that are only roughly equivalent. In either case, the judgment can never transcend the fallibilities of those doing the judging and approach the perfection of a divine Last Judgment. Perhaps the most plausible version of “history will judge” is the realization that we are judged in the present by the still admirable aspirations of the past, which have yet to be realized.

papers.title: From Confucius to computational linguistics: quantifying cross-linguistic semantic similarity and semantic fidelity using large language models
papers.abstract: Abstract Translating The Analects from classical Chinese into English frequently results in semantic losses that obscure understanding and introduce ambiguities. By leveraging large language models from Baidu AI, Zhipu AI, and OpenAI, the study established a framework for cross-linguistic semantic similarity. Instances of high similarity demonstrate that, despite linguistic variations, the core messages and logical structures of the original can be effectively conveyed in English. This ensures an accurate representation of meanings and maintains structural integrity. Conversely, instances of low similarity highlight the translators’ challenges in maintaining semantic fidelity to the source text while ensuring readability. Finally, this study assigns semantic fidelity scores to the five translations of The Analects and offers a reference for the quantification of semantic fidelity in translation evaluation.

papers.title: Internationalism, Empire, and the Early Esperanto Movement in India

papers.title: The Revolutions that Consolidated Empire: A Reconsideration of 1830

papers.abstract: Abstract This research aims to explore the application of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) technology in traditional Chinese paper-cut design and promote the protection and inheritance of traditional Chinese paper-cut culture. First, the paper-cut works of paper-cut artist are analyzed to extract the characteristic factors of her design styles. Second, based on the characteristics of the paper-cut style, a dedicated dataset for model training is constructed and passed into the fine-tuning network to train and generate a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning model with the design style characteristics of the paper-cut artists. Finally, the paper-cut LoRA model is combined with the stable diffusion model to complete the intelligent design practice of traditional paper-cut. Through experimental verification, the paper-cut model trained in this research can effectively realize the migration design of traditional paper-cut artists’ design style and improve the efficiency of paper-cut design. This research proposes a paper-cut style generation method based on AIGC, which provides a new perspective for the protection and development of paper-cut culture. This method reduces the difficulty of paper-cut design, optimizes the design process, and improves design efficiency, providing technical support for the sustainable development of paper-cut art. At the same time, it also has important significance and value for the digital inheritance and innovation of other intangible cultural heritage.

papers.title: The art of positive reporting in media discourse: Time magazine’s linguistic positivity bias over the 20th century
papers.abstract: Abstract Linguistic positivity bias is widely examined in spoken communication and written academic communication. Existing research proposes that this trend of favoring positive language use is common and universal in human communication. However, to date, no existing study has confirmed this tendency to use more positive words than negative ones in media discourse. By examining a list of positive and negative words and how they are distributed in the Time Magazine Corpus of American English, a large diachronic corpus with nearly 100 million words, the study reveals a greater increase in the use of positive words compared to negative ones in journal articles published in Time magazine between the 1920s and the 1990s. Finally, such an increased use of positive words in media discourse may be a result of the general tendency for positive communication, the shift toward constructive journalism, the application of positive psychology in media discourse, and the post-war socio-economic and technological development coupled with media commercialization.

papers.title: ‘Due Diligence’ and the British Government’s Response to Confederate Ship Procurement in Britain during the American Civil War
papers.abstract: Abstract The British government’s stance towards the American Civil War belligerents, while professedly neutral, has often been seen by historians as leaning, more or less strongly, towards the Confederacy. Its failure to prevent the Confederates from procuring warships in Britain during the war is regularly cited as supporting this viewpoint. This article examines in detail Britain’s response to the vehement demands from the US government to shut down the Confederates’ ship procurement programme in the context of Britain’s administrative machinery in the 1860s. It concludes that the state apparatus at the time was not fit for purpose, and in particular that it lacked central direction, was hidebound in its procedures, and was too dependent on individuals’ competence and integrity to rise to meet the challenge to British law and governance mounted by a determined Confederacy. However, Britain did make considerable efforts to prevent the Confederates from obtaining warships and did not set out with the deliberate intent to aid and abet the Confederate States by providing them with a navy, did not turn a blind eye to Confederate activity, and did not demonstrate a negligent disregard for its own laws.

papers.title: Historical evolution of Chinese music aesthetics in the digital age
papers.abstract: Abstract The research aims to analyze the evolution of characteristics of Chinese music within the context of the digitization of the music sphere. The study encompasses an analysis of changes in composition, performance, and dissemination of Chinese music influenced by digital technologies, as well as the transformation of traditional musical genres. Key aspects of the transformation of China’s musical landscape are examined, including the evolution of popular genres, the impact of digitization on music creation and consumption, changes in musical characteristics, and the preservation of traditional “Chinese” elements in contemporary music. Based on statistical data and trend analysis, the dynamics of the popularity of various musical genres are investigated, notably the significant rise of rock music and electronic genres. Special attention is given to the influence of technological innovations on the music industry, from the advent of MP3 players to the use of artificial intelligence and NFTs. The study also analyzes changes in timbral, tonal, and emotional characteristics of Chinese music, as well as the evolution of traditional “Chinese” elements in modern musical contexts. The findings reveal transformations in Chinese music under the influence of globalization, technological progress, and changes in societal values, demonstrating both the preservation of cultural identity and adaptation to global musical trends.

papers.title: A Dunhuang mural restoration network based on mask guidance and Transformer architecture
papers.abstract: Abstract In the process of Dunhuang mural restoration, models often struggle to focus on damaged areas, leading to issues such as color deviation and blurred lines. To address these problems, we propose a Dunhuang mural restoration network based on mask guidance and Transformer architecture, named MGTNet. First, we design a mural focus attention module to dynamically optimize both channel and spatial information in an adaptive manner. Next, we introduce a mural enhancement module that leverages the long-range dependency capturing capability of Transformers to improve restoration quality. Finally, a mask-guided downsampling module is proposed, which fuses the mask image as prior knowledge with downsampled features, enhancing the model's ability to perceive damaged areas. Experiments on a publicly available Dunhuang mural dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms comparison algorithms in terms of objective evaluation metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, validating the effectiveness of the algorithm. This study demonstrates the practical application potential of the algorithm in Dunhuang mural restoration and contributes to the significant advancements of artificial intelligence in the field of digital humanities.

papers.title: Immobility
papers.abstract: Abstract Increasingly, since the early years of the twenty-first century, some have questioned the relevance of historians’ ‘fetishization of mobility’ in an era of closing borders. This has led to greater attention being placed on systems of ‘regulation and intervention’ that shape global migration. Shifting away from the narratives centred on movement and fluidity, we argue that immobility is not a mere lack of movement: it is about the power relations and barriers that enforce, experience, and resist stillness. By delving into the archives of Past and Present, we aim to construct a conversation around the processes of enforcing, experiencing, and challenging immobility. We have found that immobility shapes the experiences of both the historical actors found in the journal and the historians and scholars who write these histories. This issue explores immobility through three interconnected sections: ‘Spaces’ examines the physical and metaphorical places where movement is arrested, revealing the lived experiences within these confines and the technologies that facilitate and enforce stillness; ‘Shadows’ delves into the legal and administrative categorizations that produce and sustain immobility, focusing on the policies and ideologies that mark certain bodies as immobile; finally, ‘Aftermath’ reflects on the consequences of enforced immobility, exploring how displaced and immobilized individuals navigate and shape their identities and communities in the wake of restrictions.

papers.title: Anna Bonnell Freidin. Birthing Romans: Childbearing and Its Risks in Imperial Rome .
papers.abstract: Anna Bonnell Freidin’s Birthing Romans: Childbearing and Its Risks in Imperial Rome is a study of birthing, risks, expectations, and ideology surrounding births and procreation in the Roman Empire. The text is structured as follows: an introduction, five thematic chapters, followed by conclusions, bibliography, and index. The thematic chapters are: “Veturia at Scale: Kinship, Community, and Empire”; “Cornucopia and Rudder: Imagining Generation, Embodying Risk”; “Bodily and Social Order in Soranus’s Gynecology”; “Technologies of Hope: Amulets, Materiality, and Affect”; and “Fate and Fortune: Living with Uncertainty, Understanding Loss.” The period covered by the study is from the age of Augustus and roughly over the first three centuries CE (4). The focus is on the Latin-speaking West and North Africa, but the Greek-speaking East is not entirely left out. The text is accompanied by twenty illustrations. The broader picture takes its point of departure from a microhistory of a woman named Veturia. She is introduced in chapter 1 and is recurrently referred to throughout the book, in a mixture of facts and the author’s speculations. The facts are that Veturia lived and died in Acquincum, Pannonia, in the second century CE. She passed away at the age of twenty-seven and was commemorated by her husband Fortunatus, a Roman legionnaire, and buried in a sarcophagus with an inscription giving a brief outline of the life of Veturia (CIL 3.3572; fig.1.1; Hungarian National Museum, Budapest). From the inscription, we learn that Veturia died after sixteen years of marriage, during which she experienced at least six pregnancies, perhaps from the age of fourteen. At Veturia’s death, however, only one of her children was still alive. From this harsh reality, which was shared by many women in the Roman Empire, Bonnell Freidin contextualizes birthing over three centuries and exemplifies how Romans tried to handle and control risks and anxieties related to childbirth. A legal marriage (matrimonium iustum) was required for having legitimate children, and as such, marriage and childbirth were the most prominent social duties for Roman women. As surviving children were a necessity for the continuity of a family line and for society at large, it was an issue constantly present in the lives of women from a young age. A first marriage followed by pregnancy was a reality for Roman female teenagers. Sometimes it could occur at a very young age, as in the case of Veturia, who appears to have been married at eleven, which was early even for the Romans. Given the risks and high mortality rates of both pregnant women and of newborns, across social hierarchies, all kinds of assistance and support were vital to make a pregnancy end with the survival of both mother and child. Bonnell Freidin gives extensive examples of how birthing women and mothers were supported by networks of family and kin (chapter 1), and how protections for pregnant women and unborn children were sought in a variety of ways, spanning from material objects such as amulets (see fig. 2.2 and 2.3. for examples of uterine amulets; chapter 4), by divinities, especially Fortuna, the goddess of fortune and luck (especially in chapters 2 and 5), and oracles.
