papers.title: Vernacular Imaginaries of the Southern Seas
papers.abstract: Few people native to the contemporary nation-states that make up the region known in English today as “Southeast Asia” would call themselves “Southeast Asians.”1 The process by which “Southeast Asia” became a distinct region in the international system, separate from the broader East Asian region of which it is a part, as well as a separate disciplinary specialization in academia, has long been understood to be one rooted in external strategic interests dating roughly from the 1940s. Through the upheavals of mid-twentieth-century wars, the region was ascribed a common political and economic character exogenously and militarily. The establishment of the Allied South East Asia Command in 1943 defined it negatively, as a space from which Japan should be expelled: a regionalizing salvo against Japan’s positive identification of a Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere over which Japan should preside. After the defeat of Japan and the creation of an Anglo-American hegemonic compact over the wider East Asian region, it came to be understood variously as a space of concentrated political revolt against Western rule, of underdevelopment, of political instability, and of susceptibility to communism. Eventually, with the establishment of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 1967, it assumed its fullest geopolitical form as an anticommunist space ranged specifically against, and in some ways defined in opposition to, China, despite the long histories of connectivity that have shaped their interactions.2 A measure of its ideological character is that many countries we regard as “Southeast Asian” today—Burma, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos—were incorporated into ASEAN only at the end of the twentieth century, their successful divestiture of communist influence a condition of entry. Capital, particularly American capital, further defined the boundaries of the region as one requiring a particular expertise. In the years after the defeat of Japan, philanthropic foundations from Rockefeller to Carnegie poured funding into articulating the disciplinary boundaries of this space, establishing departments of “Southeast Asian studies” at Yale in 1947 and Cornell in 1950, among others. Meanwhile, the almost contemporaneous transition in Japanese- and Chinese-language descriptions of the region from the older nomenclature (shared in Sinitic script) of Nanyō and Nanyang (南洋) toward direct translations of the English term “Southeast Asia” (Tōnan Ajia and Dongnanya 東南亞, lit. “East-South Asia”), in common use from the mid-1950s, suggests a hegemonic convergence of epistemologies.3 What differentiated the earlier Sinitic names from “Southeast Asia” was, firstly, their maritime orientation and, secondly, their understanding of a region fundamentally connected to others. Where the English term “Southeast Asia” names a portion of the territorial continent of “Asia,” Nanyō or Nanyang—literally “the Southern Ocean”—retained the sense of this space as fundamentally connected by water. Since as early as the period of the Eastern Han (25–220 CE), the Chinese word Nanhai (南海, lit. “South Sea”) has named a range of waters around the southern and eastern Chinese seaboards. Initially, Chinese merchants played a much smaller role in these waters than those Persian and Arab sojourners who boarded seafaring dhows in Basra, braved the Indian Ocean, and used the Malacca Straits as a fulcrum to reach the great emporia of Guangzhou. To Arab geographers of the eleventh century, the region stretching from the coasts of southern India to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, the Gulf of Thailand, and the seas around Vietnam was known as the “Sea of Malayu”; the evidence points, as Leonard Andaya has shown, to the sea’s naming for a group of people known to both medieval Arabs and Chinese as the orang Malayu.4 Later Arabic speakers, Persian travelers, and Safavid diplomatic missions came to speak of this same space instead as bilād al-jāwā, the lands of the Jāwā people, and as Zīrbādāt, the lands below the winds—the contrapuntal rhythms of the monsoons that shaped movement across these waters. This was likely a phrase that traveled into Persian from Malay (negeri di bawah angin). As Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh (r. 1607–36) described himself in a letter to King James I of England in 1612: “I am the lord in power here below the winds [Zīrbādāt] who holds the throne of Aceh and Samudra and all the countries adjacent.”5 Only from the early 1000s did Chinese junks begin to join Arab dhows in these waters in significant numbers.6 Later Song, Ming, and Qing geographers sought to make further distinctions, following the logic of trade routes from China’s southern coast. One route passed through the place named Xiyang (西洋), or Western Ocean. This Western Ocean passage was one of great antiquity dating back to the Tang dynasty, known to Chinese and Indian merchant traders who plied trade in small vessels that cleaved nervously to the coast, edging from Guangzhou to Hainan and thenceforth to the Champa coast and the southern tip of today’s Vietnam. A second route wended eastward through the Dongyang (東洋), or Eastern Sea. This was a more recent passage. Emerging during the Song dynasty and prospering during the Yuan, it brought waves of enterprising Hokkien merchants who cast out from Quanzhou and other sea-facing ports of Fujian province, to Taiwan and the Philippines, and southward to the Celebes Sea and the Moluccas. Ming emperors knew this space as Hainan zhuguo (海南諸國) (various states of the south seas), lands of southern barbarians (nanman 南蠻) that lay “outside civilization” (huawai 化外) and indeed far beyond the four seas (sihai zhi wai 四海之外) that surrounded the Middle Kingdom. The existence of the Selden Map (Fig. 1), a maritime commercial navigation chart dating back to the late Ming era and almost certainly produced in Quanzhou, shows that at least some at the time sought to center these surrounding seas, rather than the “Middle Kingdom” itself.7 During the Qing era, other names emerged, circling cautiously around the encroachment of Europeans into China’s maritime frontiers. The Hakka mariner Xie Qinggao, writing in 1820 on the cusp of the Opium Wars, divided Qing China’s known waters into the Southwest Sea (西南海), comprising the waters of the Malay Peninsula, mainland Southeast Asia, and the Indian coast; the South Sea (南海), now understood to comprise just Sumatra and Java to Celebes; and the Northwest Sea (西北海), some distant place beyond Sumatra from which Westerners had come to nip at China’s maritime frontiers.8 It was a precocious attempt to begin to fit the growing European presence in Asia into the knowledge cartographies of the dynasty, a task that would be carried forward with greater scholarly industry and rigor by the Hunanese jinshi scholar of statecraft, Wei Yuan.9 Then there was the name Nanyang (南洋), which came into more frequent use and eventually replaced Nanhai over the course of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Originally an administrative category alongside its sister name Beiyang (北洋) for the Northern Ocean—including the northeastern coasts of Hebei, Liaoning, and Shandong—it signaled in the most general way the provinces, regions, and seas lying to the south of the Yangtze River, and, crucially, included the terrestrial portions of southern China’s Fujian, Guangdong, and Guangxi provinces, along with the nebulous lands and waters beyond it.10 It was only over the course of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that the name Nanyang was honed into ever greater specificity, given a second life as the Chinese name for an aspirational quasi-imperial project that emerged in direct competition with Meiji-Taishō Japan, as both gazed southward at new extractive prospects in a “Nanyang” now dominated by European commercial interests. By the middle of the twentieth century, Nanyang—morphing gradually into Dongnanya—had come to correspond almost exactly to the limited Anglophone regional construct we now call Southeast Asia, its older oceanic qualities reduced to a penumbra around a space now understood as primarily terrestrial, its implied historical relationships to China and Japan severed by the guillotines of area studies. The Selden Map, a late Ming watercolor map of East Asia dating roughly to the 1620s, depicting a conception of the region that privileges the sea, and includes China, Korea, Japan, Borneo, the Philippines, the Indonesian archipelago, and the Malay Peninsula. A panel of text on the left of the map near Calicut, its western extremity, gives directions for the sea routes to Aden and the Straits of Hormuz. Photo: © Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford. CC BY-NC 4.0. Other vernacular names recognize the importance of both land and water to the adequate naming of this space. It is no coincidence that the Malay word for “homeland,” tanah-air (lit. “land-water”), discloses an archipelagic or estuarine orientation. The earliest available records for the Javanese name Nusantara (lit. “islands between”) date back to copperplate inscriptions from the fourteenth century, and its most well-known reference is from the sixteenth-century Kawi poem Pararaton (Book of Kings), in which the Javanese imperial chieftain Gajah Mada is said to have used the term “Nusantara” to refer to the furthest fringes of the Majapahit Empire. This usage is affirmed in the oldest surviving manuscript of the Sejarah Melayu, which says of the king of Majapahit, Terlalu besar kerajaannya pada zaman itu, segala seluruh Jawa semuanya dalam hukumnya, segala raja-raja Nusantara pula, setengah takluk kepada baginda. [Great indeed was His Majesty’s kingdom in that era, for all of Java was under His law, and half the kings of Nusantara submitted to Him].11 Nusantara overlapped only partially with Nanyang, its outermost boundaries reaching only into the Sea of Sulawesi and into the archipelagos west of Guinea, as far up the Malay Peninsula as today’s southern Thailand, and the coastal regions of Borneo. Yet it was, like Nanyang, a fundamentally maritime concept, a name that accepted the centrality of water to this region’s connectedness. Nusantara faded with the end of Majapahit, and was resurrected only in the early twentieth century as part of an explicitly nationalist project seeking a name behind which to consolidate against the “Dutch East Indies.” Beginning with the Djuanda Declaration aimed at quelling regional rebellions in the outer islands of Indonesia in 1957, a “Wawasan Nusantara” (Nusantara Vision) began to be promulgated over subsequent decades to inculcate a national and civic vision of a united archipelagic Indonesia that, for some, signaled a resurgent Javanese neo-imperialism over the entire archipelago.12 Yet Nusantara retained its aura of anticolonial indigeneity through the twentieth century, and remains part of a fringe petitioner movement even today that advocates changing the name of Indonesia to one that was not given by foreigners (pemberian asing).13 To expose the politics of naming is to recognize that names like “ASEAN” and “Southeast Asia” might be as much historically constructed political projects as others that have fallen away through history. They are no less real for that constructedness—as Donald K. Emmerson observed, “Some names, like ‘rose,’ acknowledge what exists. Others, like ‘unicorn,’ create what otherwise would not exist. In between lie names that simultaneously describe and invent reality. ‘Southeast Asia’ is one of these.”14 Yet recognizing them as such may help alert us to other visions and alternative worldmaking projects embedded in names that sought to invent other realities, and that have long since fallen by history’s wayside. I offer two examples below that were contemporary with the emerging Anglo-American concept of “Southeast Asia,” but specifically opposed to it. We find one name-project in Chinese, Fengxia (風下, lit. “beneath the winds”), popularized in the political journalism of Hu Yuzhi (1896–1986). Hu was a Chinese communist intellectual exiled in Sumatra between 1942 and 1945, and his gravitation to this name drew directly from his experience and encounter with the Malay world. He had known this region as Nanyang, but in his enthused, world-opening encounters with Indonesian language, geography, and history during his period of exile, he transmuted the Chinese-oriented Nanyang into the Malay Fengxia, to better describe a region that he was coming to understand as “the strategic military center of the British empire” (英帝國的軍事重鎮) and thus the center (中心) of the antiaggression movement of eleven million Chinese compatriots. Fengxia, he said, recognized the fundamentally monsoonal orientation of Nanyang, as well as its dialectical origins as a name distinguishing its peoples from the “white-skinned blue-eyed strangers” who came to the coast of Malacca half a millennium earlier and, when asked where they came from, pointed westward to indicate that they had been blown to these lands by the southwest monsoon. “Therefore,” Hu wrote, “the Malays later called the general countries of Europe ‘the lands above the winds’ [風上之國], and their own lands ‘the lands beneath the winds’ [風下之國].” After centuries of domination by fengshang zhi guo, those who lived in these lands beneath the winds were no longer willing to be enslaved, and it was here, he wrote, that the future of war and peace would be decided. Critically, Fengxia recognized the political significance of ethnic Chinese in this world historical region, while also articulating the essential fluidity of ethnic belonging; in the evolving mental geography he was constructing, Hu came to advocate that the Chinese zuguo (homeland) might not be usefully thought of as “China,” but might evolve to be the place to which one felt linked, politically, economically, or culturally. He came to advocate the creation of a new race in Fengxia, an amalgamation of different racial groups across the region that might be brought together under the name Ma-lai-you (馬來由). A radical vision of region could, in this sense, transmute Chinese into Malays and unite them in a shared anti-imperial project—if one were able to mentally reconstitute those names from ethnoracial containers into, essentially, historical-geographical ones. A second name-project in Indonesian retains the sense of a site of world-historical importance in the battle between imperialist war and socialist peace. Tan Malaka (1897–1949), a Sumatran Marxist intellectual and Comintern representative, began in the late 1920s to imagine a partly geostrategic and partly cultural-linguistic regional concept he named “Aslia.” Aslia, for him, was an amorphous concept produced by a Marxist historical imperative, but also transcended its materialist basis to embrace a metaphysics of belief (kepercayaan). In some of his writings, Aslia is said to comprise a federation of all countries (negara) that are found on the bridge between (pada jambatan antara) Asia and Australia, and in fact should encompass not only Burma, Thailand, Annam, Kalimantan, and what he termed Indonesia sempit (narrow Indonesia) but also about a third of the total area of Australia. In others, he considered Aslia to constitute a continuous unity of race and geography (ilmu bumi dan ilmu bangsa), as well an area of shared belief (kepercayaan) in things that have natures of their own (kodrat), in the existence of a soul (jiwa), and in spirits and ghosts (hantu). He writes that during his travels across this space he was now naming Aslia, he had become convinced of a preexisting oneness imposed by bumi-iklim (earth-climate), kebangsaan (racialism or nationality), economy, and kejiwaan (which he glosses with the English term “psychology,” but is literally “soulness”). Above all, after the end of the Japanese occupation, he spoke of Aslia as the site of a “great conflict [pertentangan hebat] between the socialist and capitalist world.” These variegated elements and characteristics of Aslia, for him, were not in tension with each other but the only possible full realization of what it would take to resist the “ruthless politics” (politik mulus) of European imperial domination.15 Both Fengxia and Aslia were at core socialist utopian imaginaries of a world expunged of colonial rule: a politics of naming that sought to name spaces for political and mental revolution. Their similarities lie in their greatly expanded conceptions of what constituted this East Asian region: Fengxia, in its positing of an intimate relationship to China; Aslia, in its advocacy for unity with portions of the Australian continent. Both propositions became impossibilities in the geostrategic encirclements of the Cold War. Yet they are in a continuous tradition of vernacular names, only a fraction of which I have explored in this article, that have spoken for centuries of the historical continuities of this space and its connections to other regions now demarcated by disciplinary borders, narrow nationalisms, geostrategic interests, and interspecializational hostility. By placing them in dialogue with our more limited Anglophone idea of “Southeast Asia” today as a territorial postwar geopolitical construct, forged in the crucibles of decolonization and Cold War and thought of as a shorthand for ASEAN, I have hoped to show how the latter offers only a partial picture of the richer vernacular imaginaries of these Southern Seas as a historical region of mobility, movement, and an alternative politics. papers.title: Kathryn Taylor. Ordering Customs: Ethnographic Thought in Early Modern Venice .
papers.abstract: Francis Bacon’s trio of key early modern technologies—the compass, gunpowder, and print—famously underpinned the explosive growth of Europeans’ awareness of, access to, and power to influence the wider world from the late fifteenth century onward. That empire, new technology, and sustained direct contact with distant peoples new to Europeans were sufficient to explain the equally rapid transformation in the scale and structure of European ethnographic thought has longed seemed natural. Kathryn Taylor, however, in Ordering Customs: Ethnographic Thought in Early Modern Venice, challenges such unexamined assumptions by focusing on a parallel tradition that operated significantly in manuscript, followed old routes to familiar places, and was bound up with the sliding relative power of a slowly crumbling empire. In Taylor’s account, the practices and institutional forms that developed out of Venice’s attempts to navigate a newly hostile world that threatened to undermine its prosperity and cherished independence generated genres in which sustained engagement with the manners and customs of other peoples, which Taylor characterizes as ethnographic thought, was expected. The center of this vein of the history of ethnography, then, lies in another classic pair of early modern stories: the growth of the state and its increasingly formalized practices of diplomacy and information gathering. Based on these premises, Venice—famously cosmopolitan, a towering early center of print, and the leading exemplar of new diplomatic practices—emerges as a naturally central site for the development of ethnographic thought.

papers.title: Ana Lucia Araujo. The Gift: How Objects of Prestige Shaped the Atlantic Slave Trade and Colonialism .
papers.abstract: The Gift: How Objects of Prestige Shaped the Atlantic Slave Trade and Colonialism is the latest piece of dogged historical detective work from Ana Lucia Araujo, a prolific historian of slavery, memorialization, and material culture in the Afro-Atlantic World. Unique among Araujo’s many books, The Gift takes a single object as the basis of its investigations: a silver ceremonial sword that has been held at the Musée du Nouveau Monde in La Rochelle, France, since 2015. The Gift retraces this object’s journey over the course of a little more than a century. Likely smithed in 1776, only a few blocks from its current location in La Rochelle, the sword emulates the form of a kimpaba, a material insignia associated with rulership in West Central African polities like Kongo and Loango. By mid-1777, La Rochelle slave trader Daniel Garesché gifted the sword to mfuka (a kind of commerce minister) Andris Pukuta of Cabinda. By the book’s end, Araujo has convincingly argued that the silver kimpaba was transported back to La Rochelle following Andris Pukuta’s death in 1786 and then gifted once more to elites on the Bight of Benin before being seized by the forces of the Kingdom of Dahomey. The kimpaba remained in Dahomey’s capital city of Abomey until its 1892–94 conquest by the French and afterward was, once again, transported back to France.

papers.title: Reflecting on the Holocaust for Today
papers.abstract: After more than a decade of preparations, the National Holocaust Museum opened in Amsterdam on March 10, 2024, in the presence of the Dutch king and other dignitaries, including the Austrian and Israeli presidents. The event was broadcast live on national television while pro-Palestinian demonstrators near the museum loudly voiced their discontent with the attendance of President Isaac Herzog, accused of genocide in Gaza. The confrontation of past and present made emotions run high, even before anyone had had a chance to actually visit the brand-new exhibition in the city center. The Jewish community in the Netherlands was more severely affected during the Holocaust than that of any other Western European country. Of the 140,000 Jewish citizens, more than 102,000 would not survive the war. That their fate has not been forgotten is evidenced by Anne Frank’s iconic status. However, the legacy of Frank as an individual cannot possibly do justice to the diversity of experiences of the multifaceted Jewish community. Since the 1960s, attention to the Holocaust has grown in the Netherlands, in a memory culture of World War II that initially focused on the military and heroism and, longing for national unity, dwelled too little on civilian victim groups. War museums nowadays invariably engage with the Holocaust, mostly as an element in a broader national or regional story. The Anne Frank House in Amsterdam and the Memorial Center Camp Westerbork offer a view of the Holocaust in a Dutch context, but from the perspective of their own historical location.

papers.title: Elizabeth Campbell. Museum Worthy: Nazi Art Plunder in Postwar Western Europe .
papers.abstract: The Museum of Art and History of Judaism (mahJ) in Paris features multiple displays related to art looted from France during the Second World War, including an installation of works photographed for art dealer Paul Rosenberg’s gallery, which were crucial to the postwar restitution of hundreds of his stolen pieces. There is also a room dedicated to the looting of Chana Orloff’s Parisian home studio featuring a wooden sculpture of her son, finally returned to the Orloff family in 2022. Additionally, a self-portrait by Max Liebermann bears a stamp identifying it as MNR-978. In 1967, Liebermann’s portrait was entrusted to the French National Museums as an unclaimed artwork (MNR) recuperated after the Second World War. The portrait found its way from the Louvre to the Orsay Museum and the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Strasbourg before becoming a long-term loan to the mahJ. Elizabeth Campbell traces the history of looted pieces such as these in France, the Netherlands, and Belgium in Museum Worthy in order to demonstrate the lasting legacies of cultural theft and how institutions benefited from unclaimed artworks while “the dispossession of Jewish Holocaust victims is an injustice that has yet to be fully rectified” (9).

papers.title: Jennifer A. Yoder. World War II Memory and Contested Commemorations in Europe and Russia .
papers.abstract: The memory of World War II has assumed renewed significance and prominence within contemporary media and political discourse, extending well beyond the traditional confines of history classrooms and academic research. The ongoing conflict in Ukraine and Vladimir Putin’s attempts to justify the invasion through historical arguments have brought the manipulation of historical narratives to the forefront of public attention. In her book World War II Memory and Contested Commemorations in Europe and Russia, Jennifer A. Yoder analyzes these mechanisms of manipulation, emphasizing the crucial importance of understanding how wartime memory is contested and instrumentalized within various political contexts. She asserts that “the collective memory of groups, nations, or countries can be a tool or weapon wielded by anyone,” referring to this phenomenon as the “politicization of the past” (2). Yoder focuses on World War II as the central stage for her analysis because the war represents “a common European-wide defining moment” (18). She examines the contestation over the wartime past in Western and Eastern Europe and Russia, employing key concepts from the multidisciplinary field of memory studies. Her objective is to develop a framework for understanding the motivations of memory challengers and the mechanisms they use to manipulate historical narratives. Yoder seeks to identify the factors that facilitate or constrain these challengers and to determine their strategies for contesting the dominant wartime memory narrative. Additionally, she explores whether and how memory challenges in one country can influence memory politics in other countries (3). She particularly focuses on commemoration days, such as the Bombing of Dresden (February 13), Waffen SS Galician Day in Ukraine (April 15 and 23), Victory Europe Day (May 8), and the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (August 23). By examining these events, she investigates how memory challengers instrumentalize them to further their political agendas.

papers.title: Marcia Stephenson. Llamas beyond the Andes: Untold Histories of Camelids in the Modern World .
papers.abstract: In 1957, Life Magazine featured a photograph of Llinda Llee, the beloved llama who worked as a model for magazines and shows in New York City, riding a cab on Broadway Avenue. Llinda was a US-born llama, and her presence in NYC symbolized the long and tortuous history of domestication, acclimatization, and extraction that had brought camelids and other animals from their natural Andean habitat to urban places like New York. The image, which Marcia Stephenson uses as the cover photo for her book Llamas Beyond the Andes and is the topic of her last chapter (chapter 7), visually challenges traditional accounts that have focused exclusively on Llamas in the Andean region. Instead, Stephenson invites the reader to look “beyond the Andes” and explore “the animals that were removed from their native habitat and transported overseas,” including to remote places in Spain, France, Australia, and the United States (4). To trace the complex itinerary followed by camelids around the world, Stephenson draws from a rich collection of primary sources that include literary, natural history, and Spanish colonial texts, travel accounts, and visual and material artifacts, among others. The research reflects the interdisciplinary and global perspective of the book, and the author masterfully weaves together critical observations of skeletons and taxidermy collections with a more traditional analysis of texts. The book then offers a model on how to look at the history of non-human animals and a reminder of the importance of cross-disciplinary dialogues, methodologies, and exchanges.

papers.title: Father Pepe’s House of Cards: Jesuits, Cheap Print, and Material Devotion in Eighteenth-Century Catholicism
papers.abstract: This article examines the impact of the rise of cheap print on devotional practice in eighteenth-century Catholicism. It offers a case study of Francesco Pepe (1684–1759), a Jesuit missionary active in Naples from the 1730s through the 1750s, and the media empire he built to popularize a religious practice steeped in material objects among the city’s poor. Mobilizing the technology of the printing press and innovative labor arrangements, Pepe mass-produced paper-based devotional objects whose use he promoted through another cheap print: best-selling booklets touting the miraculous interventions effected by his devotional articles. Participating in the “war on books” that the church had declared on enlightened tomes, Pepe swamped the market with tracts that rekindled a belief in the mediating function of devotional objects as a way of addressing the problems besetting the poor and women in an increasingly overcrowded early modern metropolis. Borrowing the notion of cheap print from book historians, the article suggests that historians of religion treat books not as repositories of ideas inherently at odds with material religion, but as an integral part of a media ensemble in which the borders between inexpensive books and paper objects remained porous. In an age when prints of all sorts could be produced at unprecedented rates, books and portable objects mutually reinforced each other, laying the groundwork for a new material piety for the uneducated and women that would survive well into the twentieth century.

papers.title: Amy Harris. Being Single in Georgian England: Families, Households, and the Unmarried .
papers.abstract: Being single did not mean being alone in Georgian England. Or, at least, being single never meant being alone for the close-knit Sharp siblings of clerics, professionals, amateur musicians, and philanthropists, who serve as the collective subject of Amy Harris’s book Being Single in Georgian England: Families, Households, and the Unmarried. Although this is as much a history of the Sharps as it is a study of English adults who married late, never married, or became widows and widowers, Being Single provides important, original insights into family and social history. Harris argues that historians’ emphasis on eighteenth-century marital and parental relations has overshadowed other equally important emotional bonds—namely, that between single people within kin networks. Beginning with Lawrence Stone’s The Family, Sex, and Marriage in England, 1500–1800 (1977), historians have emphasized marriage as people’s primary emotional bond in adulthood. Yet marriage was far from a universal state: In the eighteenth century, one-fifth of English adults never married and, as Amy Froide emphasizes, at least one-third of urban women were single at any moment (Never Married: Singlewomen in Early Modern England, 2005). Harris bridges the gap between the marital household and the state of being single by analyzing the Sharp siblings and cousin networks, showing that “[f]amilies did not just adapt to or accommodate their single members; they were shaped by them” (6).

papers.title: Christian R. Burset. An Empire of Laws: Legal Pluralism in British Colonial Policy .
papers.abstract: Christian R. Burset’s deeply researched study, An Empire of Laws: Legal Pluralism in British Colonial Policy, is a notable addition to the legal history of the British Empire. While there is a rich historiography on the legal history of the early modern British Empire, the role of legal thought in the intellectual history of eighteenth-century British imperialism still remains understudied, especially compared with the prominence of Jeremy Bentham, Henry Maine, and James Fitzjames Stephen in histories of the Victorian empire. An Empire of Laws analyzes changing British policies toward colonial law in the 1760s and 1770s, revealing how questions about what kinds of legality were appropriate to different colonies became central to imperial political thought. The book also intervenes in historical debates about legal pluralism. Lauren Benton’s influential book Law and Colonial Legal Cultures: Legal Regimes in World History, 1400–1900 (2002) focused attention on the plural legal environments of early modern empires and on the role of jurisdictional politics in shaping new colonial forms of legal pluralism. Burset’s study defines legal pluralism in a different way than Benton, as a legal system allowing for radically distinct forms of law rather than one with multiple jurisdictions and varied sources of legal authority. In contrast to Benton’s more practice-oriented, colony-centered approach to legal change, Burset’s study explores how elite British policymakers in London and the colonies reimagined imperial law in territories conquered during the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763). It argues that British elites before the mid-eighteenth century aspired to an ideal of legal uniformity, a “common-law empire” in which English law provided the broad template for judicial administration in colonial spaces, though with regional variations. Imperial policymakers only embraced “strategic legal pluralism” (7) with the incorporation of French civil law by the Quebec Act (1774), and of colonial versions of Muslim and Hindu law in Bengal after 1772.

papers.title: Lauren Benton. They Called It Peace: Worlds of Imperial Violence .
papers.abstract: The title of Lauren Benton’s book They Called It Peace: Worlds of Imperial Violence is an allusion to Tacitus’s account of the Roman conquest of Britain, where the ancient historian has a Celtic tribal chief claim that where the Roman Empire “make[s] a desert, they call it peace.” The phrase highlights the timelessness of the book’s synthetic narrative, focused on the relationship between law and violence in five hundred years of European imperial conquest from 1400 to 1900. Most exploration of imperial violence has concentrated on the mechanized and modernized warfare against colonized peoples from the late nineteenth onward. Additionally, histories of the laws of war often begin with European and American theorization from the nineteenth century. While Benton combines histories of imperial violence with its legal regulation, her book examines a significantly broader and earlier swath of time, presenting a transimperial history that not only shifts emphasis away from Anglo-American imperial action and thinking, but embeds it in the worlds of Spanish and Portuguese imperial circuitry in which it operated. The book argues that the uneven warfare of imperialism formed a pattern of consistent violence so that war and peace were not functionally separate processes.

papers.title: Gendering the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere
papers.abstract: Asia has peoples and languages, mountains and rivers, religions and civilizations. In many historical conceptions, it also had a gender. This is not entirely surprising, since the idea of “Asia” was often imagined in opposition to the idea of “Europe,” and binaries invite gendered thinking. If “Asia is one,” as Okakura Kakuzō famously proclaimed, then it must also have had one gender. The question was, which one? For twentieth-century Japanese Pan-Asianists, whose visions of a unified Asia were inextricably linked to the state’s imperial ambition, the answer was clear: Asia was male. As the state extended its reach into Hokkaido and Okinawa, seized colonies in Taiwan and Korea, and expanded into Manchuria, they imagined Asia as an all-male patriarchal family with Japan at its head. Analogizing the order of colonial expansion to birth order, the state often told Okinawans, “Okinawa is the eldest son, Taiwan the second, and Korea the third.”1 During the Asia-Pacific War (1937–45), a book called China’s Children (Shina no kodomo) reimagined China—often constructed as a menacing, demonic threat—as a “younger brother country.” In this vision, China was a failed patriarch who required Japanese guidance to properly raise his own children.2 Elsewhere, the war created new sons for the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere (1940–45): Manchukuo, Indonesia, Burma, and the Philippines. A wartime foreign minister, Tani Masayuki, explained, “Relations between the empire and member nations are like relations among relatives. It is our ideal to bring them closer, like a big family, so there will be no need for so-called diplomacy.”3

papers.title: Aditya Balasubramanian. Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India .
papers.abstract: A critical, though somewhat underappreciated aspect of late colonial South Asian history is the fact that neither the anti-colonial movement nor the visions of postcoloniality that were routinely advanced by several leaders of this movement were synchronous or homogenous. Deep ideological and political differences characterized the debates not only about the colonial state but also about all aspects of Indian life, such as the bureaucracy, economy, culture, laws, and impact of foreign affairs, to mention only a few. While the dominant political force of late colonial and the early decades of postcolonial India remained the Indian National Congress (a political party founded in 1885), and the thought and legacy of its two towering leaders, Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948) and his political successor and India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964), the subcontinental landscape was actually dotted by innumerable “minor” figures who played a pathbreaking role in shaping the life of the country. In Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India, Aditya Balasubramanian masterfully traces the life and legacy of one such oppositional force in postcolonial India, which espoused a powerful economic alternative to state-led developmental projects of the Congress and instead advocated an economy that would be unfettered to individual economic pursuits. Balasubramanian documents their emergence and transformation into a political party, notes their brief electoral success and subsequent formal demise, and reflects on their enduring legacy in the twenty-first century. In doing so, he provides a detailed account of the promises and perils of a movement that challenged the orthodoxy and became a testament to the deepening roots of democracy in a fledgling republic.

papers.title: Diego Javier Luis. The First Asians in the Americas: A Transpacific History .
papers.abstract: Histories of Asians in the Americas largely begin with the experiences of free and coerced migration in the long nineteenth century, when empires and nations looked to Asia for laborers as replacements for emancipated Africans. From Indian indentured laborers on Caribbean sugar plantations to Chinese railroad workers in the American West, multiple streams of Asian migrations changed the racial composition of societies across the Americas and complicated understandings of race that largely operated along the lines of Indigenous, Black, and White populations. Diego Javier Luis’s book The First Asians in the Americas: A Transpacific History challenges this dominant framework to offer the most comprehensive analysis to date about the transnational migrations of approximately one hundred thousand Asians who traveled to the Americas from the late sixteenth century through the eighteenth century. While historiographies of colonial Latin America have incorporated the themes and methods of Afro–Latin American studies, the history of Asians in colonial Latin America is a relatively new and emerging field of study. Across six chapters, Luis follows free and enslaved Asians across the Spanish Empire, from diverse populations who were funneled through Spanish Manila (the Philippines) via Portugal’s Indian Ocean slave trade to Peru, Guatemala, California, and Spain. Central Mexico—from Acapulco to Mexico City—is at the center of this narrative. Since central Mexico was at the core of both the Spanish Pacific and the Spanish Atlantic, this region had the largest Asian population and second largest African population in the early colonial Americas, serving as an essential site of racial convergence and new forms of race making.

papers.title: Immanuel Etkes. The Invention of a Tradition: The Messianic Zionism of the Gaon of Vilna , Trans. Saadya Sternberg.
papers.abstract: The principal object of Immanuel Etkes’s inquiry in The Invention of a Tradition: The Messianic Zionism of the Gaon of Vilna is the “imagination” of Shlomo Zalman Rivlin (1884–1962), scion of a prominent Jerusalem clan, whose father, Joseph Rivlin (1837–1896), was “an articulate and passionate spokesman” (38) of the pious Jewish community of the Old Yishuv, long settled in Ottoman Palestine. According to Etkes, it was thanks to his prodigious faculty of invention that Rivlin fils single-handedly managed to concoct a credible alternative to the well-established consensus narrative of Zionist origins—a tale convincing enough, it seems, to enter scholarly literature under the unimpeachable imprint of Oxford University Press. Based largely on material authored by Rivlin himself, Arie Morgenstern’s Hastening Redemption: Messianism and the Resettlement of the Land of Israel, trans. Joel A. Linsider (2006), has lent institutional credibility to a fiction that, in Etkes’s trenchant retelling, began life as a family myth. For it was Morgenstern’s academic imprimatur that elevated Rivlin’s fable to the status of “revisionist” history, the upshot of which is that the Jewish national movement ostensibly fathered by Theodor Herzl at the beginning of the twentieth century was really inspired by the messianic “doctrine” of R. Elijah, the Gaon of Vilna (1720–1797), who imparted it directly to Rivlin’s own ancestors, who, in their turn, mobilized the students of the Gaon to emigrate and thus “laid the foundations for Zionism” (1) decades before the first secular “pioneers” established the New Yishuv. In Etkes’s dissection of Rivlin’s oeuvre, neither the first nor the second of these propositions stands up to serious scrutiny; however, the most remarkable thing about The Invention of a Tradition is not Etkes’s painstaking anatomy of Rivlin’s case for “messianic Zionism” but what the nature of the evidence suggests about the standard secular account of Zionism in defense of which Etkes has undertaken to expose Shlomo Zalman Rivlin as a pious fraud.

papers.title: Jamie L. Jones. Rendered Obsolete: Energy Culture and the Afterlife of US Whaling .
papers.abstract: The concept of an energy transition is a powerful and deceptively simple one that has captured the attention of energy and environmental historians writing amid climate crisis. The result has been a spate of excellent work on the economic, social, and political implications of the modern era’s major energy transition: the shift from a world defined by renewable flows of energy (muscle, sun, wind, and water) to one defined by the production and use of fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas). Many of these studies have offered nuanced accounts of transition, noting that it is always contested, uneven, and overlapping to such a degree that the term transition may not even be appropriate. But few scholars have approached the question in the compelling way that Jamie L. Jones does in Rendered Obsolete: Energy Culture and the Afterlife of US Whaling. Most accounts trace either the rise of new fuels or the persistence of old ones, but in this densely argued book, Jones focuses on a declining resource—whale oil—to explore the “cultural afterlife” of a fuel rapidly losing its original economic significance (5). The result is a history of energy that deepens our understanding of how energy transitions work culturally and politically. Jones’s overarching argument is that the representation, memory, and artifacts of US whaling helped mediate the nineteenth century’s bewildering transition to fossil fuels, functioning as a yardstick of modernity and a site of nostalgic longing for a fictive past that helped remake social and political life in the United States.

papers.title: Kristine Wirts. A Peddler’s Tale: Religious Exile and Community in Early Modern Switzerland .
papers.abstract: Jean Giraud was a Huguenot merchant-peddler who fled from his home in the French Dauphiné after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Kristine Wirts’s engaging account of life in the late seventeenth century, A Peddler’s Tale: Religious Exile and Community in Early Modern Switzerland, is based on Giraud’s account book, which combines a record of his business activities with a description of the persecution he experienced in France and his experiences as a refugee in Switzerland. A Peddler’s Tale is presented in five chapters. The first focuses on Giraud’s life and livelihood before the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. Located to the east of Grenoble, Giraud’s home of La Grave lay along a major trade route through the Alps. Wirts describes the business connections and types of trade common to peddling firms such as that headed by Giraud, which were often family partnerships cemented by marriage alliances. La Grave had a significant Huguenot minority, with its own church, consistory, and hospital in La Grave. In the next chapter, Wirts describes the persecution of French Huguenots over the later seventeenth century, culminating with the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Over the following months, many La Grave residents fled, which only increased pressure to convert on the Huguenots who remained. Giraud and his wife were both arrested and forced to abjure, but they were finally able to escape to Geneva in the summer of 1586.

papers.title: Lewis Wade. Privilege, Economy and State in Old Regime France: Marine Insurance, War and the Atlantic Empire under Louis XIV .
papers.abstract: The home page for Lloyd’s of London, an institution once at the core of mercantile risk management amid early modern England’s Financial Revolution, boasts a subsection entitled “Our past” that proudly claims ownership of “nearly 350 years of history … at the heart of making progress.” The early modern French marine insurance institutions explored in Lewis Wade’s Privilege, Economy and State in Old Regime France benefit from no such contemporary corporate hagiographies. The Chambre générale des assurances et grosses aventures (1668–1686, the “Chamber”) and the Compagnie générale des assurances et grosses aventures (1686–c. 1710, the “Company”) lasted for only a few decades in Louis XIV’s reign. Apart from a handful of mid-twentieth-century French-language works, they have been forgotten to early modern French scholars focused on state power in the age of “absolute” monarchy. Among economic historians, neoinstitutionalists—from Douglass North to Ron Harris—have focused their efforts on exploring the so-called “Little Divergence,” or why northern European countries like England and the Netherlands produced durable, supposedly modern economic institutions, and countries like France failed to do so. Per Harris, this owed to a lack of “credible commitment”: French shareholders avoided investment in commercial institutions—from insurance to trading companies—because they feared expropriation at the hands of a strong, meddling absolute monarchy. These institutions are reduced in this formula to overburdened agents of state power, rather than private ventures designed to maximize shareholder profit. But, as Wade points out, this neoinstitutional model ignores decades of scholarship (by William Beik, James Collins, and others) that undermined any possible notion that the louisquatorzien monarchy was indeed absolute, capable of imposing its will from above without negotiation with elites. It has similarly neglected the contentions of scholars like Philip Stern, Rupali Mishra, or Oscar Gelderblom, who have shown that supposedly free-market, Anglo-Dutch commercial institutions were political bodies in their own right, both benefitting from and subject to political winds in their home states.

papers.title: Comment by Cemil Aydın
papers.abstract: Contributions to the AHR History Lab on “Big Asia” collectively summarized the critical scholarly wisdom on the origins, achievements, internal contradictions, limitations, and futurity of the idea of Asian geocultural unity since the height of Western hegemony in the 1880s. While we have a rich critical literature among both the scholars of Asia and Asian intellectuals about the invented and constructed character of Asian unity and Asianism as a project, why do we still talk about Asian identity and projects of Asian civilizationism in the early twenty-first century? These History Lab essays show us how we need a similar critical inquiry of Europe and Western civilization to complement our reflection on the idea of Asia. As long as the European master narrative of civilization stays alive and politically mobilized, there will be some form of imagining “Big Asia.” As Nile Green notes, the term “Asia” entered from its European origins into vernacular languages from Ottoman intellectual circles to China as early as the sixteenth century, yet it was in the late nineteenth century that the idea of Asia spread more widely amid spaces and people it designated in Asia. A synchronization and convergence of epistemologies occurred by the turn of the twentieth century, when European etic ascription of Asia was embraced by Asians themselves as a capacious emic concept, strategically formulating a humanist discourse of civilization, internationalism, and globalism. Since then, there have been multiple ways to describe an Asia beyond the negative unity against the European colonial hegemony and Orientalist discourses, with references to shared Asian geography, religion, language, culture, and art. In the age of steam and print as well as transportation and communication infrastructure built by Western empires, proximity was felt among Chinese, Indians, and Arab populations due to inter-Asian connectivity of trade, travel, and anticolonial solidarity, similar to the proximity felt among different Asian activists today, as discussed by Jeffrey Wasserstrom. But proximity was also imagined because of the problem space of colonial racism, with Persian and Afghans seeing Japanese in very distant lands as fellow Asians compared to Russians next door.

papers.title: Thomas D. Conlan. Kings in All but Name: The Lost History of Ōuchi Rule in Japan, 1350–1569 .
papers.abstract: In Kings in All But Name: The Lost History of Ōuchi Rule in Japan, 1350–1569, Thomas D. Conlan does not shy away from posing provocative questions. He challenges the typical historical periodization of medieval Japan, which characterizes the sixteenth century as the “Warring States period” and Kyoto as the geopolitical capital. Instead, he argues for an earlier “Age of Yamaguchi,” a city in western Japan that was the seat of power for the Ōuchi family. Conlan makes thorough use of Japanese and Korean sources to piece together a timeline of nine Ōuchi leaders and their methods of rule. In doing so, he demonstrates the strong impact that the Ōuchi had not only in western Japan but also in Kyoto and even in interactions with Korea and China. The monograph follows the rise and fall of the successive Ōuchi leaders. Conlan’s main focus is on how each ruler consolidated his power and influence, and he highlights several key themes: the Ōuchi’s ethnic ties with Korea, the use of religious rituals to legitimize rulership, and waxing and waning connections with military and royal institutions in Kyoto. The first topic in particular has not previously been deeply explored in the English-language historiography. Conlan demonstrates how the Ōuchi leaders actually tended to flaunt their ancestral ties (both real and imagined) with Korean peninsular royalty and used those ties to legitimize their leadership in Japan, challenging historical ideas of ethnic homogeneity in Japanese rulership. He further delineates how the Ōuchi skillfully used their connections to promote trade with the mainland, sometimes usurping the role of official trade carried out by the central powers in Kyoto and using the profit to strengthen their own position. In particular, Conlan suggests that the Ōuchi leveraged their political authority to develop copper mining, as opposed to the typical narrative emphasizing agriculture as the main source of income.

papers.title: Neeti Nair. Hurt Sentiments: Secularism and Belonging in South Asia .
papers.abstract: What makes secularism an enduring idea and a catchall phrase in contemporary South Asia? In Hurt Sentiments, Neeti Nair ventures to answer this question through a historical study of secularism in most of South Asia in the twentieth century—particularly the postcolonial nation-states of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Nair’s book tells a terrific tale, excavating the multilayered lives of South Asian secularism. South Asian secularism, as Hurt Sentiments shows, is a contingent idea constructed and reconstructed through a wide range of political practices. In a painstakingly detailed narrative, Nair argues that in order to study secularism we need to return to the founding moment of the three postcolonial nation-states and trace how being secular was an iteration of belonging in twentieth-century South Asia. In an astounding achievement, Nair forges a connection between intellectual history and social history in tracking the career of secularism in modern South Asia. The book consists of four chapters that present multiple iterations of secularism in the wake of crucial turning points in the history of South Asia. Drawing on Partha Chatterjee’s suggestion, Nair shows that pitting secularism against “Hindu majoritarianism” is not a useful framework, in the case of South Asia. Rather, Nair argues, the “hurt Hindu” and the “hurt Muslim,” on the ascendant, has in fact shaped state ideologies of secularism in modern South Asia (6, 14).

papers.abstract: In Revolutionary State-Making in Dar es Salaam: African Liberation and the Global Cold War, 1961–1974, George Roberts studies the politics of Cold War rivalries, African liberation movements, and socialist state-building in Tanzania. This rush, Roberts notes, turned Dar es Salaam into a “revolutionary city,” “Cold War hotbed,” “city of hopes and dreams,” “mecca of liberation,” “a dangerous staging ground for communist penetration,” “city alive with grand visions of Africa’s postcolonial future,” “center of revolutionary subversion in Africa,” and “epicenter of [African] radical politics.” These descriptions provide a mosaic picture of a busy city with strong characters and whose interests intersected and diverged. After introducing the city, Roberts zooms in on Nkrumah Street, decorated with signs of African nationalist parties: ANC, PAC, SWAPO, ZANU, ZAPU, and FRELIMO. Dar es Salaam’s residents included journalists, guerrilla leaders, Cold War diplomats, foreign embassy staff, Chinese booksellers, radical academics, and Tanzania postcolonial elites.

papers.title: Rama Sundari Mantena. Provincial Democracy: Political Imaginaries at the End of Empire in Twentieth-Century South India .
papers.abstract: Rama Sundari Mantena’s Provincial Democracy: Political Imaginaries at the End of Empire in Twentieth-Century South India is a history of liberalism and anti-colonialism in South India primarily concerned with analyzing discourses of self-determination, federation, and civil liberties. By taking a regional approach and focusing on Telugu-language source material, Mantena seeks to decenter imperial and national frameworks by attending to the development of Indian democracy within a vernacular context. This regional approach also allows Mantena to explore how anti-colonialism grappled with and sought to transcend the boundaries between the princely state of Hyderabad and the British Indian province of Madras. Provincial Democracy consists of an introductory chapter on liberalism and anti-colonialism in South India followed by two chapters apiece on federation and civil liberties. The opening chapter on liberalism maps out the pre–World War I history of social reform movements in colonial Andhra, and the subsequent development of a regional political identity, public sphere, and civil society in the crucible of the interwar period. The main figure here is J. Gurunatham, a little-known but founding figure of the Andhra movement, who, Mantena argues, “understood the necessity of training people to become citizens” (35). In pursuit of preparing Telugu-speaking people for democracy, Gurunatham sought to couple late nineteenth-century social reformism with an explicitly political agenda. Mantena argues that early articulations of a separate Andhra state were the product of the “cultivation of public reason” (43) and that the interwar Andhra movement subsequently, and successfully, engaged in a deliberate project of extending “civic institutions for nurturing Telugu political life and public spirit” (53). Provincial Democracy offers a rich sense of the broad range of ideas and initiatives that were indeed recognizably liberal or, at the very least, liberal-adjacent. Mantena’s capacious understanding of liberalism includes nearly all shades of Indian political opinion, which has the advantage of illuminating shared liberal sentiments, but also the effect of muddling the ideological stakes and dissensions. The book deploys more contemporary terms to categorize its subjects: Individuals are often described as either “progressive” or “conservative.” Overall, the global expansion of liberalism, within a context defined by imperialism and nationalism, is understood as largely unidirectional. One wonders what unique contributions these regional figures may have added to a global history of liberalism and liberal ideas, or how their ideological innovations, to borrow from C. A. Bayly’s Recovering Liberties: Indian Thought in the Age of Liberalism and Empire (2012), “cannibalised, reconstructed and re-authored” (3) ideas from the Western liberal tradition.

papers.title: Adeeb Khalid. Central Asia: A New History from the Imperial Conquests to the Present .
papers.abstract: In an illustrious career spanning some four decades, Adeeb Khalid has explored the effects of Russian and then Soviet rule on Central Asian (especially Uzbekistani) Muslim societies. In the acknowledgments to this his fourth book, Central Asia: A New History, Khalid writes that it “synthesizes most of what I know about Central Asia.” He does this geographically by expanding his focus outside Uzbekistan—particularly including East Turkestan (the Uyghur homeland)—and conceptually by identifying how a range of political, intellectual, and religious ideas and movements impacted the region. Khalid begins his text with an insistence on the centrality of Central Asia. Growing up in the 1970s in Pakistan, he tells us, although his hometown of Lahore was only twelve hundred kilometers from Tashkent, “it might as well have been on a different planet” because travel was difficult and news in short supply (2). He provides other anecdotes about how, from US diplomatic practice to Japanese documentary makers and British comedians, Central Asia was seen as inscrutable, exotic, timeless and unknown. This general level of ignorance is arguably no longer the case, and an early-career scholar embarking on a similar project today would be less likely to place their argument in such a framework. But it makes sense of Khalid’s formative experiences, and he uses it to compelling effect to insist that Central Asia “has experienced every current of modern history, every achievement of modernity and every one of its disasters, and every extreme of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries” (3).

papers.title: Trevor Burnard. Writing the History of Global Slavery .
papers.abstract: Although the institution of slavery has been continuously practiced in the world since its ancient origins, enslavement lacks a comprehensive unifying model that includes most or all of the forms of slavery that exist or have ever existed. papers.title: Sergio Gutiérrez Negrón. Mexico, Interrupted: Labor, Idleness, and the Economic Imaginary of Independence .
papers.abstract: Exemplifying a recent trend among scholars of cultural studies to embrace the study of non-literary historical sources, this book analyzes the economic imaginaries of the Creole ruling class in the aftermath of Mexican independence in 1821. Spanish plunder of the resources of its pre-eminent colony, the Viceroyalty of New Spain, figured among the main grievances of the rebels fighting for independence. At the turn of the nineteenth century, based on his conversations with wealthy Creoles, the Prussian geographer and naturalist Alexander von Humboldt had described and exaggerated the country’s natural wealth, particularly with regard to agriculture. At the same time, silver—the colony’s leading export—symbolized the colonial exploitation of the Americas. This vision of abundant but exploited and underutilized natural wealth influenced Miguel Hidalgo, José María Morelos, Vicente Guerrero, and Agustín Iturbide, the last the erstwhile loyalist who switched his allegiance to Guerrero and helped the rebels claim victory. Despite the differences among them, all these independence leaders promised that independence would limit access to Mexico’s riches to the country’s own nationals. But over the next forty-six years, Mexico experienced a devastating conflict with the United States, which robbed it of half of its territory, and suffered three foreign invasions, one from Spain and two from France. Foreigners continued to control much of Mexico’s wealth. At the same time, and in part because of endemic political instability, the Mexican economy lagged behind that of the United States and also behind those of larger South American nations.

papers.title: Quito Swan. Pasifika Black: Oceania, Anti-colonialism, and the African World .
papers.abstract: The islands and peoples of Melanesia, a region that etymologically means “islands of Black people,” were racialized as Black by various European colonizers who violently conquered these communities. papers.title: Erin Pettigrew. Invoking the Invisible in the Sahara: Islam, Spiritual Mediation, and Social Change .
papers.abstract: How to write about the invisible, the esoteric, the magical in a place like Mauritania? As in many other contexts, both in the past and in our own times, people in Mauritania appear to either believe in, or at least find credible, the possibility that there are unseen forces that can act on the visible, or human, world. Efforts to control these forces, for good or for ill, are called l’ḥjāb in Hassaniya Arabic, a term that Erin Pettigrew translates as “Islamic esoteric sciences.” These include a wide range of systematic knowledge and techniques that specialists use to access powers of the unseen world in order to manipulate the visible world. In Invoking the Invisible in the Sahara, Pettigrew traces a history of these ideas and techniques in Mauritania using as her sources the Islamic literature written in Arabic in Mauritania since the 17th century, French colonial accounts, and her own ethnographic work in the postcolonial period. Not only does she clearly demonstrate that l’ḥjāb has long been understood to be extremely important by people in this region at least since the time that we have written records, but she also shows that there can be a history of l’ḥjāb, in that it has changed over time from a knowledge and practice embedded in Sufism to a postcolonial perception that esoteric knowledge is subject to abuse by those who claim mastery of it. In contemporary Mauritania, TV shows and media entrepreneurs regularly focus on the uses and misuses of l’ḥjāb.

papers.title: Choon Hwee Koh. The Sublime Post: How the Ottoman Imperial Post Became a Public Service .
papers.abstract: While as teachers we constantly advise our students to first think about the questions they want to ask of the past and then find the relevant sources that might answer them, it is no shame to admit that as researchers we often experience the opposite. It is based on archival documentation of the Ottoman postal or courier system in the 18th century, hundreds of registers produced by bureaucrats in the capital Istanbul and by postmasters at relay stations from Belgrade to Baghdad. These unnervingly factual registers meticulously record expenses ranging from horseshoes to barley; the comings and goings of horses, couriers, and other travelers; and fees collected and waived. This body of sources seems to contradict commonly held assumptions about the Ottoman Empire. It shows that the central government paid a lot of attention to an important imperial infrastructure during an era that is usually thought of as a time of decentralization and weakness of the center. In contrast, the scarcity of sources suggest that Istanbul wasn’t as focused on this infrastructure during the 16th century, a time when the central state was thought to be most powerful.

Even if they were not seen by their neighbors as white, they could still be on the white side of the color line because they were not Black.

papers.title: “Survival in an Age of Revolution”
papers.abstract: Abstract While great effort has been invested in analyzing the role of revolutionary intellectuals in history, much less attention has been paid to the counterrevolution and its guides. This is especially the case in the former colonial world in the era of decolonization, where anticolonial politics are often portrayed as having been the default position. Lebanese philosopher and statesman Charles Malik was a candid opponent of what he theorized as the “great Asian and African revolution” against imperial rule. Instead, he advocated consciously counterrevolutionary politics that sought to purify the corruptions of “collectivism, materialism, and secularism” brought forward by an age of anticolonial and socialist revolutions. Primarily known as a principal author of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, it was in the Lebanese arena that his global political commitments were most directly expressed. This included his decisive role in securing US military intervention during Lebanon’s 1958 civil war, and more fundamentally in his founding role in the Front for Freedom and Man in Lebanon (FFML), the counterrevolutionary, Christian-supremacist alliance in Lebanon’s international civil war (1975–90). Malik’s praxis highlights an overlooked philo-colonial trend in the era of decolonization: native advocates for continued imperial sovereignty over a dependent and rigidly stratified nation-state without equal citizenship. Malik’s ideological and material entanglements on multiple scales foreground the defining part of counterrevolutionary networks in shaping the global history of twentieth century and its inheritance.

papers.abstract: An ongoing predicament in the Native South centers on how to make sense of the political organization and governance of Creek Indians during the eighteenth century. papers.title: In Defense of the Search Bar
papers.abstract: Mass digitized archival databases are anarchic, rhizomatic places. The search bar makes them this way. This is not to say that large-scale digital libraries and archives have no structure. A human-created interface shapes how we as users approach the human-selected documents, including opportunities to browse by theme, location, and document type.1 And yet the existence and centrality of the search bar, which is built on full-text search capabilities, means that, in the digital archive, it is up to us to create search vocabulary and make connections between the things we find in a way that is quite different from finding books on a library shelf, working through an archival box or folder or, chronologically, through a run of a newspaper. If items are ordered for us in the digital realm, it is in a virtually endless series of permutations, rearranged with each new keyword search and with each new document uploaded.2 In the absence of the expert guiding hand of the archivist or librarian, the archival becomes non-hierarchical, “anarchival.”3

papers.title: Huang Pumin, Wei Hong, and Xiong Jianping. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science . Translated by Fan Hao.
papers.abstract: The field of Chinese military history in the West has grown considerably in the last couple of decades but remains extremely small. Consequently, despite the growing interest in the contemporary Chinese military and the history and culture that informs its thinking, there are no reliable overviews in English of Chinese military history, military thought, or military culture. This is not peculiar to scholarship in English, however, as the field is similarly limited in Chinese (which the authors note), Japanese, or any European language. The few academic studies that do exist are highly specialized, with most books or articles confined to research on narrow issues and very limited times and places. There are several brief overviews of Chinese military history or Chinese military thought available in Chinese as well as a few massive, broad, but unreliable surveys, but there are no high-quality general surveys. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science is therefore valuable if only because there isn’t much else. Its primary value is in presenting a Chinese view of the history of Chinese military thought. To some extent, it is a fair representation of what many Chinese scholars think about war in Chinese history and the history of Chinese military thought. It does not engage any scholarship outside China, or even much Chinese scholarship. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science does not attempt to present the state of knowledge of the academic field of Chinese military thought in China. It relies upon a very narrow set of modern Chinese scholarship and a selective use of primary sources. Indeed, most of the secondary Chinese works cited are at least twenty years old.

papers.title: Does the “Indo-Pacific” Have a History?
papers.abstract: The “Indo-Pacific” is supplanting the South China Sea as an arena of geostrategic concern among liberal democracies. The emergence of the “Quad”—the “Quadrilateral Security Dialogue” among Japan, Australia, India, and the United States—has led to a geographical pairing of the Indian and Pacific Oceans to spatially naturalize a new security community predicated on notions of a “rules-based maritime order” and “peace and stability” in the region, notions that ostensibly are threatened by a militarily aggressive China. This essay ponders whether this constructed geography has a history and whether that history will prove conducive to the forging of new political identifications. It will focus on the early modern and modern port polities of Southeast Asia, which served as vital nodes in trade networks that connected the vast, commercial economies of East and South Asia. papers.title: Integral Outside: The Financial Curb Market, the Electric Telegraph, and the Politics of Pricing in Second Empire France
papers.abstract: Financial markets in nineteenth-century France were far more complex than an analysis of the official Bourse or its state-authorized brokers would suggest. Most financial transactions occurred on an illegal yet tacitly tolerated curb market called the coulisse, which played a vital role in expanding market liquidity during the Second Empire while also attracting controversy as a site of complex speculative activity. Existing historiography attributes the 1859 suppression of the Paris coulisse to aggravated competition between state-authorized brokers and coulissiers following the market downturn of 1857–58. Based on police, ministerial, prefectoral, and judicial archives, I present an alternate account that stresses the twin roles of financial innovation and the telecommunications revolution in breaching the limits of the state’s tacit toleration for the coulisse. I emphasize the lesser known coulisse in Marseille, suppressed at the height of a bull market in 1855, to formulate an alternative explanation of the 1859 suppression of its counterpart in Paris. I conclude that the rising importance of the curb markets in both cities reflected the robust, short-term options market developing among coulissiers. Public attention given to the coulisse price lists—distributed via newly opened telegraph lines—challenged the legitimacy of official brokers as authoritative sources of price information and compromised the political interests of the Bonapartist state, which proved decisive in the crackdown.

papers.title: Kelly Lytle Hernández. Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands .
papers.abstract: Ricardo Flores Magón is a widely-known historical figure in Mexico, yet has been little-known in the United States, until now. Lytle Hernández describes the efforts of the magonistas at the turn of the twentieth century to resist and overthrow Mexican dictator Porfirio Díaz. During his administration, Díaz centralized his power over the Mexican government, aided in establishing American dominance over the economy, and suppressed labor and indigenous movements in the country. Rather than making this a Mexico-centric story, the author intertwines the role of the United States into this story of the magonista revolt. Bad Mexicans therefore argues that the magonistas are as important to the history of the US as they are to the history of Mexico. Lytle Hernández explains that it is impossible to understand the history of the US as a world superpower without understanding its imbalanced relationship with its neighbor to the south. She also states that one cannot understand the American West without comprehending the long-standing presence of Mexicans in the region. Lastly, she details how Mexican Americans resisted a racialized social order that white Americans imposed upon them. Lytle Hernández argues that “the magonista revolt threatened key sectors of U.S. society at the turn of the twentieth century. US authorities, agents, and settlers mobilized to stop them,” and as a result, “the campaign to crush the magonistas opened a new chapter of policing in the United States” (11).

papers.title: Jessica L. Lamont. In Blood and Ashes: Curse Tablets and Binding Spells in Ancient Greece .
papers.abstract: In Blood and Ashes: Curse Tablets and Binding Spells in Ancient Greece by Jessica L. Lamont is a study of curse tablets in ancient Greek religion and magic. As Lamont defines them, curse tablets are “small, thin sheets of lead inscribed with maledictions, spells, and prayers against rivals, lovers, wrongdoers, or otherwise threatening persons” (3). Numbering almost two thousand, curse tablets are ubiquitous across the Greco-Roman world; appear in a variety of contexts (for example, commercial, domestic, and competitive); and are inscribed in multiple languages, mostly Greek and later in Latin, often with references to local contexts or gods, especially Egyptian but also Judeo-Christian. This book closely examines the objects themselves, which combine invective speech with the ritual actions of transcription and placement in specific locations, and tells the history of curse practices more broadly in Greek antiquity from 750–250 BCE. The book also provides fairly comprehensive examples of individual curse tablets from published and forthcoming works. By juxtaposing actual images and drawings of curse tablets side by side as much as possible with their inscriptions and translations, Lamont allows the reader to consider not only the content of the curses but also visible features, material manipulations (such as folding or nailing), and findspots (for example, at graves sites, in wells, and in temple precincts) to build a full picture of how they were used and were meant to operate.

papers.title: Olufemi Vaughan. Letters, Kinship, and Social Mobility in Nigeria .
papers.abstract: Olufemi Vaughan’s book Letters, Kinship, and Social Mobility in Nigeria examines an important aspect of the social history of modern Nigeria. The book, which is part prosopography, uses the letters that were preserved by Abiodun Vaughan to provide a detailed empirical account of the emergence and consolidation of a Yoruba Western-educated elite in Ibadan who were members of the Christian Missionary Society (CMS). The book focuses on the letters written by four generations of Vaughan’s extended family at the national and transnational levels in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and the United Kingdom, as well as letters written by friends and professional colleagues. Virtually all of the letter writers were associated with the CMS Church and schools with the bulk of them connected with the CMS Church, Aremo, Ibadan, and Ibadan Grammar School. The idea of kinship, whether at the natal family level or friends and colleagues, dominates the letters. The themes discussed in the book show the complex ways that the newly emergent Yoruba Western-educated elites negotiated their position in society at the intersection between modernity and traditionalism. This was clearly demonstrated in Abiodun’s biological family. With the death of their father in 1930, Samuel Aribiyi Vaughan, the eldest son who graduated from the first secondary school in Nigeria, CMS Secondary Lagos, and was 20 years older than Abiodun, assumed the role of the head and provider for the family. His letters to Abiodun were mainly instructions on issues such as sharing remittances to other members of the family, paying the school fees and other financial needs of Samuel’s two children, and ensuring that his houses at Ibadan were well maintained and rents collected. On the other hand, Abiodun’s letters to Samuel were respectful. This type of relationship changed when Abiodun graduated from Ibadan Grammar School in the 1920s and secured a job with the department of agriculture. The letters became more transactional and collaborative. As the two most successful sons of the Vaughan family, they were responsible for providing for other family members, that is, their widowed mother, their brother who had severe health challenges, and two married sisters, as well as maintaining the family home. The situation in Abiodun’s nuclear family reflected the gendered nature of education, work, and status that was promoted by Christian and colonial modernity during the early colonial period in Nigeria. Apart from Dorcas Olayinka Brainerd, Abiodun’s eldest sister who had a secondary school education, Mariam O. Vaughan, Abiodun’s mother, and Jadesola Juliana Odebunmni, Abiodun’s elder sister, only had primary education. This therefore put most of the women, as family matriarchs, in the position of protecting the interests of the family and ensuring the promotion of kinship ties and interpersonal relations among various family members while also partly dependent on remittances from the male elites. Abiodun’s relationships and letters to his mother-in-law, Rachel Ayodele Akinloye, and brother-in-law, Adisa Akinloye, reflected “the moral order on which obligations are negotiated” in the Yoruba kinship system and “reciprocal marriage relations” during this time of social change (153).
