papers.title: Elizabeth Garner Masarik. The Sentimental State: How Women-Led Reform Built the American Welfare State .
papers.abstract: In The Sentimental State, Elizabeth Garner Masarik expands our understanding of sentimentalism from a cultural phenomenon to a crucial political tool wielded by white and Black reform-minded women in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. The language of grief and emotion served as the conduit through which American women could make demands on local and federal governments. By tracing the formation of private-run organizations and their connection to nascent legislation protecting the sanctity of children and motherhood, Masarik provides an alternative history of the formation of the modern welfare state. The voluntary, unpaid, and often unrecognized labor performed by middle-class white and Black women not only facilitated the creation of these national welfare programs but also continues to define modern debates over their impact. Throughout the book, Masarik demonstrates that private, local, and voluntary reform organizations have never been separate from the state-building process. Redefining infant mortality, grief, and sexuality as concerns central to the state allowed reformers to influence local policy, acquire funds, and participate in political debates. These issues emphasized the mother-child bond and intimately connected the personal to the political. Importantly, the book locates the origins of the modern welfare state well before the New Deal. Masarik describes the process through which voluntary organizations in the late nineteenth century constituted an “associative welfare state” that later merged with local and state governments (10). The grassroots work of middle-class women created the foundation for social policies but also provided emotional legitimacy for their implementation. Crucially, Masarik acknowledges and centers the experiences of African American women and the unique conditions under which they engaged in maternalism and social reform work at the turn of the century. Contributing to the new and growing field of the history of emotions, she utilizes a variety of institutional and governmental documents, newspaper records, and cultural artifacts like popular fiction to craft a narrative of sentimentalism.

papers.title: Andrew Laird. Aztec Latin: Renaissance Learning and Nahuatl Traditions in Early Colonial Mexico .
papers.abstract: Aztec Latin. Renaissance Learning and Nahuatl Traditions in Early Colonial Mexico portrays in detail the influence of Renaissance humanist education, particularly the Latin language, on the cultural development of New Spain. The book has nine chapters, some of which center around particular Latin texts written by missionaries. Others focus on rhetoric and Latin as important models for the development of written texts in indigenous languages, such as grammars, catechisms, and other evangelistic sources. At the same time, it is important to bear in mind that in the end, texts were molded to fit Nahua language, beliefs, and ways of thinking, not to preserve humanist principles or Latin models. The first chapter addresses the work of early missionaries such as Zumárraga, de Quiroga, and Garcés, while chapter 2 reviews other figures in relation to their works written in Latin, such as las Casas, Focher, Valadés, and Cabrera. Chapter 3 describes the grammatical Latin models employed in the creation of the Artes of Amerindian languages, although only two are presented in greater detail. The fourth chapter deals with the known facts about the Imperial College of Santa Cruz at Santiago de Tlatelolco, stressing that this was not a school to train Indigenous clergy but rather to furnish Indigenous nobility with a humanist education that missionaries believed would enable them to become leaders in their communities. Additionally, the school produced evangelistic texts, with many translated from Latin into Nahuatl, but there were others created directly in Nahuatl. With this in mind, it would seem that the assertion that “the active translations those Indigenous scholars helped to produce from Latin are by far the most important legacy of their training and led to the creation of a written literature in Nahuatl” goes a bit too far because it seems to imply that without Latin, the Nahuatl language would not have thrived (148). This chapter also neglects to mention that after completing their formal preparation, Indigenous scholars also performed other tasks in addition to collaborating with any of the priests. Indeed, they served as scribes, interpreters, teachers, litigants, mayors, councilors, and authors in their own right. It should also be emphasized that the claim that the Tlatelolco scholars were better versed in Latin than in Nahuatl is an overstatement.

papers.title: David C. Porter. Slaves of the Emperor: Service, Privilege, and Status in the Qing Eight Banners .
papers.abstract: In Slaves of the Emperor: Service, Privilege, and Status in the Qing Eight Banners, David Porter makes a significant contribution to the fields of Chinese history and early modern history. The thesis of this book is twofold: First, Porter argues that the Eight Banners of the Qing empire (1636–1912) was a status group. Through a case study of the Hanjun banners, Porter then presents status as the most important organizing principle of the Qing empire, where banner people and commoners formed the two most prominent examples. Second, he puts forward specific characteristics that made the banners “service elites,” which he defines as “groups that provided military and administrative service to a ruling dynasty and received in exchange institutionalized legal privileges” (14). As highly bureaucratized service elites, the banners helped meet Qing rulers’ demand for centralized bureaucracy and military service in their expanding empires. As Porter notes in chapter 1, Qing historians seldom employed status as an analytical category. Drawing on studies on status in Edo Japan, the Russian Empire, and the Ottoman Empire, Porter lists five characteristics of status: It is defined by law, has implications for rights and obligations, is linked in law to occupation, is heritable with hard inter-status boundaries, and is historically contingent. These characteristics make status distinct from—and for Porter, more useful than—other categories such as class, ethnicity, and caste. The rest of the chapter shows how status operated in Qing at the household level and functioned as a basic identifying feature in official documents.

papers.title: Joshua Ehrlich. The East India Company and the Politics of Knowledge .
papers.abstract: Joshua Ehrlich’s book The East India Company and the Politics of Knowledge offers an original and densely populated intellectual history of the changing ways that the East India Company’s sovereign obligations and its enduring interests as a merchant came to be tied to the cause of “enlightenment.” Ehrlich reminds readers that eighteenth-century Britons were committed to the Baconian “advancement of learning” as much as they were to the plundering conquest of foreign lands, and, consequently, that it is necessary to take the age’s appetite for knowledge seriously if we are to make sense of how officials of the “world’s most powerful corporation” saw themselves as members of “the world’s most enlightened one” (2). Attention to the wrangles surrounding the Company’s contested charter renewals allows Ehrlich to show that the relation of the Company to knowledge was not merely one of instrumental legitimization: Debates about the proper relationship of government and trade to the provision of learning helped to define the substantive content of the idea of knowledge itself. Similarly, fierce arguments about what kind of knowledge the Company ought to patronize implicated and called into question the hybrid nature of the company-state.

papers.abstract: Karen Auman’s book The Good Forest: The Salzburgers, Success, and the Plan for Georgia casts a spotlight on the experiences and contributions of an often-overlooked aspect of colonization in British North America: the role of non-British colonists. Auman argues that the Salzburgers’ example proved that Georgia’s transition to a slave economy was not inevitable, and that those communities thrived for several decades before Georgia adopted slavery and continued largely without a major reliance on slave labor in the years immediately afterward. Auman also contends that focusing only on economic factors in Georgia’s development underplays both the Salzburgers’ and the Trustees’ overriding concern with the moral character of Georgia’s citizens. Ultimately, a discussion of Georgia’s Trustee era needs to include its German citizens, and Auman’s book serves as a case study for other scholars seeking to grapple more seriously with other minority groups in colonial America.

papers.title: Dan Stone. Fate Unknown: Tracing the Missing after World War II and the Holocaust .
papers.abstract: Dan Stone has produced a work of high-quality scholarship that attempts, and largely succeeds, in the aims it sets out to achieve. The motivation for writing this volume, Fate Unknown: Tracing the Missing after World War II and the Holocaust, lay in the release of the documentation of the International Tracing Service (ITS), which emerged in the aftermath of the Second World War with the aim of establishing the fate of the millions of missing victims of the conflict, especially as a result of Nazi racial policies, whether persecution of the Jews, transportation of foreign workers to German territory during the conflict, or dislocation when the war came to an end. The documentation, as Stone demonstrates, provides a wealth of information, largely through the personal files produced on missing individuals, the vast majority of whom had a fate unknown, although the narrative largely moves forward through the stories of survivors, which Stone meticulously reconstructs. Stone has placed his account into the history of the Holocaust, largely because most of those never found consisted of Jewish victims of the Nazis, although those tackled both by Stone and the ITS documents included all racial victims of the Nazis.

papers.title: Xin Zhang. The Global in the Local: A Century of War, Commerce, and Technology in China .
papers.abstract: In the most dramatic passages of Xin Zhang’s The Global in the Local: A Century of War, Commerce, and Technology in China, we read of the panic within the city walls as British troops approached Zhenjiang in July 1842, near the culmination of the Opium War. The city-dwellers’ fear of the foreigners was based on rumors of atrocities they had already committed and experiences of marauding soldiers in earlier conflicts. Paranoid Qing officials further terrorized those trapped in the city, publicly executing innocent people—including children and a monk—for aiding the enemy. When the nine thousand British troops arrived, the largest force mustered thus far in the war, they saw a group of women drown their children before being drowned themselves by Chinese soldiers, who then committed suicide en masse rather than face the unknown horrors anticipated of the enemy. Protecting women’s chastity at the cost of their lives had a long tradition in China, but Zhang stresses that this kind of mass “mercy killing” (a problematic term, not problematized in the book) was “sui generis” here (76). The British then unleashed a wave of looting and burning on the city, joined by some Chinese opportunists. This kind of drama is not, however, typical of the book, which charts the interaction of Chinese society with foreign steamships beyond that initial shock of war to long-term commercial and technological changes. Zhang warns in the introduction that he pays “a significant amount of attention to specifics” (12), which reads more as a threat than a promise, but the details enrich the history.

papers.title: Andrea Benvenuti. Nehru’s Bandung: Non-Alignment and Regional Order in Indian Cold War Strategy .
papers.abstract: Upon his return from the first Asian-African conference in Bandung in 1955, Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister of India and one of the event’s prime movers, declared that the summit—ostensibly an assertion of anti-colonialism and Third World solidarity during the Cold War—“opened a new chapter not only in Asia and Africa, but in the world” (187). In Nehru’s Bandung, Andrea Benvenuti underscores Bandung’s significance through a diplomatic history of India’s reasoning behind, involvement in, and contribution to that historic meeting. Combing archives from India, Britain, the US, and Australia to fashion a narrative that darts between Asian and global capitals, the book seeks to remedy the paucity of scholarship on Nehru and the Indian government’s route to Bandung. Why did Nehru, initially cautious about even the idea of an Asian-African conference, change his mind to the extent that the Indian government would eventually become one of its main proponents? In eleven chronologically sequenced, impressively detailed, and carefully reasoned chapters, much of them devoted to the three years preceding the conference, Benvenuti painstakingly solves this “central puzzle” of Nehru’s journey from Bandung skeptic to architect (5). The book argues that the transformation was caused by three factors: The United States’ defense partnership with Pakistan and its anti-communist regional military alliance in Southeast Asia (seen by New Delhi as threatening and destabilizing respectively); China’s seeming abandonment of international revolution and apparent adoption of the principle of peaceful coexistence in 1954 (which Nehru viewed as propitious); and Nehru’s overarching aim of using the Asian-African conference (initially an Indonesian proposal) as a means to secure his vision of “areas of peace,” understood as a region of nonalignment amid the Cold War, bound together by the “Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.” Challenging the commonly held view of Nehru as a lofty idealist on the international stage, Benvenuti instead contends that “Cold War concerns—not Afro-Asian unity—drove his actions” (8). Viewed from New Delhi, Bandung was “first and foremost an exercise in regional security” (53).

papers.title: Matthijs Lok. Europe against Revolution: Conservatism, Enlightenment, and the Making of the Past .
papers.abstract: Matthijs Lok’s brilliant book, Europe against Revolution: Conservatism, Enlightenment, and the Making of the Past, fundamentally transforms our understanding of the intellectual legacy of the representatives of the counterrevolution in early nineteenth-century Europe. It focuses on the reinterpretation of the European past and the idea of Europe by critiques of the French Revolution. It reveals that these counterrevolutionary authors, who were critical of the Enlightenment, were at the same time indebted to its intellectual legacy: They were simultaneously conservative and cosmopolitan. As a consequence, parallels existed between how revolutionaries and counterrevolutionaries interpreted key concepts of European history, including those of freedom, pluralism, and spiritual revival. Counterrevolutionaries identified the intellectual foundations of the French Revolution with a distorted perception of freedom and democratic sovereignty, ideas that they believed triggered anarchy and despotism. They saw themselves as representatives of moderation against the universal principles of revolutionary extremism: This entailed gradual development made possible by a political order that relied on historical institutions to secure freedom, moderation, and diversity. The author draws another set of parallels between the uses and abuses of history and the great degree of polarization as part of the “culture wars” in the decades around 1800 and in contemporary Europe. Yet he also emphasizes the significant differences between the ideas of counterrevolutionary thinkers and their self-appointed successors in the twenty-first century: The former sought to protect European civilization from the attacks of nationalist revolutionaries, while the latter are ardent nationalists.

papers.title: Masha Kirasirova. The Eastern International: Arabs, Central Asians, and Jews in the Soviet Union’s Anticolonial Empire .
papers.abstract: In the first years after the Russian revolutions, the Bolsheviks came to imagine the “East” as an area of people once or still under imperial rule whose struggles for liberation were interconnected, and who required a particular non-European kind of revolutionary politics. This “East” encompassed the formerly Russian imperial territories in the Caucasus and Central Asia that would become part of the Soviet Union, Ottoman territories near the Soviet borders, and any “other parts of the colonial world” in Asia and Africa “that might eventually decolonize within the framework of a global transition to communism” (10). The Eastern International draws on an impressive range of archival sources from Russia and Uzbekistan, several Arabic-language newspapers, memoirs, and interviews to trace how intellectuals and communists from the Soviet peripheries and the Middle East crafted an anti-imperial politics that connected their regions, how the experience of decolonization put pressure on this ideal, and how its legacy resonates today.

papers.title: Melissa Estes Blair. Bringing Home the White House: The Hidden History of Women Who Shaped the Presidency in the Twentieth Century .
papers.abstract: Due to a production error, two reviews were simultaneously commissioned for the following book. Melissa Estes Blair’s book Bringing Home the White House: The Hidden History of Women Who Shaped the Presidency in the Twentieth Century focuses on five professional women who led the Women’s Divisions at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and Republican National Committee (RNC) from the 1930s through 1950s. In clear, compelling prose, Blair uncovers the women’s work for three US presidents—Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR), Harry S. Truman, and Dwight D. Eisenhower—and explains why their efforts were lost to history. The women—Molly Dewson (DNC, 1933–37), Dorothy McAllister (DNC, 1937–41), Gladys Tillett (DNC, 1941–47), India Edwards (DNC, 1948–53), and Bertha Adkins (RNC, 1953–60)—sought to integrate women into the leadership of the two major parties as well as engage female voters at the grassroots level in the decades when women became an important new swing vote. Blair notes that even though most of their political messaging in these decades generically addressed “voters,” not women directly—other than when men were away at war and women became an especially coveted swing vote in 1944—Women’s Divisions designed their campaigns with certain voters in mind: white suburban homemakers. Such women, they felt, were best able to fold voluntary political work into their everyday maternal and domestic responsibilities. By contrast, the Democratic Party separately reached working-class women and women of color by appealing to unions and Black voters.

papers.title: Joy Schulz. When Women Ruled the Pacific: Power and Politics in Nineteenth-Century Tahiti and Hawai‘i .
papers.abstract: When Women Ruled the Pacific is a consequential and instructive read for scholars of Pacific Island history. It provides a gendered history of female Polynesian queens in the context of a rapidly changing eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Pacific. Joy Schulz’s focus is Hawai‘i and Tahiti—two Polynesian chiefdoms that became sovereign nations. The queens—Purea and ‘Aimata in Tahiti, and Ka’ahumanu and Lili’uokalani in Hawai‘i—exercised female spiritual and strategic power to shape the first hundred years of encounter with the West. Past historians have written histories of contact focused on a male world of chiefs, kings, and visiting traders and missionaries; women of high chiefly status who also negotiated with Western visitors are downplayed as minor characters. Schulz turns this trope around by recounting the complex political histories of four Polynesian women who ruled Tahiti and Hawai‘i. Her novel examination of gendered political and spiritual power opens new possibilities for reexamination of Polynesian history.

papers.title: Elizabeth Gansen. Natural Designs: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo and the Invention of New World Nature .
papers.abstract: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1478–1557) is best known as the author of the Historia general y natural de las Indias (General and Natural History of the Indies), a path-breaking work that both celebrated the early achievements of Spain in the Americas and conveyed to a European audience one of the first accounts of the lands and peoples of the New World. Oviedo’s efforts to compile systematically a complete human and natural history of the Indies, mainly from first-hand experiences, forced him to forge new ways of incorporating the models of antiquity and the Renaissance into an encyclopedic presentation of plants, animals, and other phenomena that Europeans had never witnessed before. His writings, and the choices he made to organize, categorize, and present the subject matter, proved influential for generations of chroniclers and historians. Elizabeth Gansen’s book Natural Designs: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo and the Invention of New World Nature makes clear that Oviedo’s writings and drawings underwent nearly continuous revision over the course of his life as he struggled to convey as effectively as possible, using written text and visual representations, the abundance of constantly increasing new information about American plants and animals. Gansen argues that it is necessary, therefore, to trace each stage of Oviedo’s writings and examine the evolving contemporary influences in the world around him. Her book is a significant contribution to the scholarship on Oviedo specifically and sixteenth-century European encounters with the Americas more broadly.

papers.title: Andrew Denning. Automotive Empire: How Cars and Roads Fueled European Colonialism in Africa .
papers.abstract: Andrew Denning’s Automotive Empire is a rich and significant contribution to the comparative history of how colonial regimes conceived and implemented their policies on road construction in Africa. The concept of “automotive empire,” which underpins the book, is centered on how technology, infrastructure, and mobility shaped colonial policies and how these interventions transformed Africa in turn. Denning aims to develop a theoretical framework connecting European technopolitics development with imperial projects—French, Italian, British, and German. At the heart of his analysis lies the fixation of colonial regimes on road building and automotive culture. The author explores how colonial administrators envisioned their automotive empires, their inherent fragility and limitations, and their challenges in confronting Africa’s landscapes, particularly regarding resources, territorial extension, and labor. Although the issue of African forced labor is addressed only tangentially, Denning compellingly examines the intersection between colonial ambitions and the practical realities of roadbuilding, offering valuable insights into the technopolitical dimensions of European imperialism.

papers.title: Uğur Zekeriya Peçe. Island and Empire: How Civil War in Crete Mobilized the Ottoman World .
papers.abstract: In this book, Uğur Zekeriya Peçe considers a question of profound historical and contemporary significance: When, why, and under what circumstances do the displaced become displacers? To trace that process, Island and Empire follows the trajectories of some 70,000 Cretan Muslim refugees who, after fleeing conflict on the island in the 1890s, brought the “Cretan question” to the forefront of Ottoman mass politics following the Constitutional Revolution of 1908. The book sheds light on an underexamined episode in the mass displacements that forged the modern Middle East and models an approach to examining historical coexistence alongside intercommunal violence. Peçe’s discussion of violence and his success in narrating the political participation of nonelite refugees emerges through virtuosic use of published materials and archival collections located in seven countries. His interweaving of sources in English, French, German, Greek, Italian, and Ottoman Turkish/Turkish serves as a constant reminder of the shared Greek vernacular of Cretan Muslims and Christians and of the polyglot spaces Cretans inhabited in Ottoman cities from Hania to Izmir.

papers.title: Shellen Xiao Wu. Birth of the Geopolitical Age: Global Frontiers and the Making of Modern China .
papers.abstract: In China’s arid far western region of Xinjiang, there is no shortage of monuments commemorating the reclamation campaigns that transformed landscapes and bound this border region more closely to the state. One such monument in a leafy park in the capital city of Urumqi, located a distant 1,700 miles from China’s capital of Beijing, features two brawny men grappling with the earth and a quote from a Chinese Communist Party official who proclaimed that it was the labor of men like these that made Xinjiang green and, implicitly, connected it more closely to China. In her new book The Birth of the Geopolitical Age: Global Frontiers and the Making of Modern China, Shellen Xiao Wu offers a new global perspective on the campaigns that transformed this and other border regions in China—and indeed around the world. In it, she centralizes not the blood and sweat of settlers but rather the plans, maps, and surveys of geographers, agronomists, and other scientists who were charged with the task of recasting imperial frontiers into national borders.

papers.title: Tabitha Stanmore. Love Spells and Lost Treasure: Service Magic in England from the Later Middle Ages to the Early Modern Era .
papers.abstract: Tabitha Stanmore’s examination of late medieval and early modern English “service magicians” builds usefully upon the foundations established by several generations of scholars such as George Kittredge, Keith Thomas, Alan MacFarlane, and Owen Davies. The book concerns actual magic practitioners who were employed in their local communities for a variety of tasks. Like Davies, although in a narrower timeframe, Love Spells and Lost Treasure focuses on those who provided remunerated services. The book pursues a strategy similar to prior studies of common magic by assembling a large body of examples and treating them thematically. Thus, the overall orientation of the project is conventional, although Stanmore has collected a significant body of previously unexamined evidence. As Stanmore writes in the conclusion, the volume serves in broad strokes more to confirm what has been suggested about the subject by prior scholars than to break entirely new ground, although it significantly expands the number of known magicians, provides considerably more evidence and detail, and makes some quite significant contributions in more focused ways.

papers.title: Oscar Sanchez-Sibony. The Soviet Union and the Construction of the Global Market: Energy and the Ascent of Finance in Cold War Europe, 1964–1971 .
papers.abstract: He did it again. Oscar Sanchez-Sibony fundamentally challenges our understanding of the Soviet attitude toward the capitalist world economy—this time by looking at The Soviet Union and the Construction of the Global Market. Sanchez-Sibony convincingly argues that the Soviet Union played a crucial role in the gradual globalization of energy and financial markets since the early 1960s—that is, at the apex of the Cold War. Large-scale energy projects initiated by the Soviet Union with Western European countries catalyzed the emergence of international credit relations—with the Soviet Union becoming a virtuous player and taker of (international) credit. The link of energy and finance is crucial for Sanchez-Sibony’s argument since it was ultimately the pipeline deals that led the Soviet Union to effectively “helping” (9) to dismantle the system of Bretton Woods. This “help” consisted of undermining the relatively strict international barter and trading list system of Bretton Woods, which did not allow for much free circulating credit or internationally floating currency since this would have affected the fixed exchange rates between the US and the other major international currencies. The Soviets, however, who were excluded from the system of Bretton Woods, pushed their Western European partners for international long-term credits in order to finance its energy infrastructure in and to Europe. Thanks to the international Soviet deals of the 1960s, capital controls became something of the past, and the unleashing of the petrodollar became the future—such is Sanchez-Sibony’s bold argument.

papers.title: Alvita Akiboh. Imperial Material: National Symbols in the US Colonial Empire .
papers.abstract: What binds an imperial community? This question animates Alvita Akiboh’s Imperial Material: National Symbols in the US Colonial Empire. The book’s title suggests the answers it provides. Objects (flags, stamps, paper currency), Akiboh argues, mediated the fractious, uneven, and malleable process(es) of Americanization in the United States’ Caribbean, Pacific, and Southeast Asian colonies. In their pervasiveness, they served paradoxically as a circulatory system for communicating (Euro)American culture and as conduits for reimagining and rearranging colonization. By mapping the banal nationalism of these objects, the book illustrates how the “stuff” of everyday colonial life became a site for negotiating citizenship, subjecthood, and the spaces in between. Like in other notable works on US overseas colonies, Akiboh uses the 1901 Supreme Court’s so-called Insular Cases as a departure point. Unlike them, however, she shows how the distances and proximities produced in their wake were articulated through symbols of the United States. Imperial material produced the imperial immaterial that culturally constituted colonization. In staking these claims, the book dialogues with not only the robust scholarship on the US empire but also work on a host of other empires.

papers.title: Kelly L. Marino. Votes for College Women: Alumni, Students, and the Woman Suffrage Campaign .
papers.abstract: Just as the College Equal Suffrage League (CESL) sought to reinvigorate the fight for the vote in the early twentieth century by adding new players and new energy to a movement that had stagnated, Kelly Marino hopes to reinvigorate suffrage scholarship with her book Votes for College Women: Alumni, Students, and the Woman Suffrage Campaign. The little-studied CESL, established by Maud Wood Park and Inez Haynes Irwin in 1900, started as an effort to mobilize female college graduates before turning its attention to on-campus faculty and student recruitment. Eventually, about five thousand women became affiliated with the organization through roughly fifty chapters scattered across the county. Marino documents the CESL’s creation, expansion, and impact while also tracing how reluctant college administrators and students, male and female, came to embrace the cause by the 1910s. Rather than dismissing the early twentieth century as the doldrums of the suffrage fight as historians so often have, Marino deems this an essential period. As progress stalled, leaders sought new strategies and new constituencies, and the CESL fit well into these revitalization efforts. She argues that the CESL’s work to help pass a state suffrage amendment in California in 1911—an effort that won by less than four thousand votes but that doubled the number of women voting in the country—was especially crucial and deserves more attention. Aligning itself with the National American Woman Suffrage Association, the CESL was not flashy, and it did not draw the kind of headlines that followed the more radical National Woman’s Party, but the professional prestige and gravitas its members offered helped turned the tide to make ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment possible. During these years, suffrage became a mainstream cause, and Marino emphasizes that smart, articulate, and reasoned college women were essential to the transformation.

papers.title: Hannah Forsyth. Virtue Capitalists: The Rise and Fall of the Professional Class in the Anglophone World, 1870–2008 .
papers.abstract: Global history often renders down the histories of modern British settler colonies into generic settler colonialism. In works with a global scope, it’s easy to lose the particularities of the interactions between the social, cultural, and environmental circumstances of a place, especially when settlers seem to be broadly British in their cultural and political aspirations. In contrast, each modern former British settler nation’s local history-writing traditions deal with the consequences of the specific encounter between what settlers and immigrants bring, and Indigenous institutions and environments. Here, the opposite is at stake: national historiographies seek what marks them out from neighbors, antecedents, and the rest of the world. This contrast between a totalizing global history of modern settler colonialism and the parochial historiographical traditions of modern settler colonies is often frustrating for those of us with an interest in both. Because of this, Hannah Forsyth’s book Virtue Capitalists is a refreshing, fun, and interesting book that integrates the local with the global without losing track of what is important about local detail or global scope. Forsyth argues that, far from being extensions or the margins of fundamental changes in modern work and class structures, Australia, Aotearoa New Zealand, Canada, and the United States were where the modern professional-managerial class (defined broadly and vaguely) was born. This was not an accident or coincidence; in fact, Forsyth argues, setter colonialism was central to the processes that created modern work and class, because of the settler need to marginalize Native claims to sovereignty, autonomy, and stewardship. The experiences of Anglo settlers, the experiences of the Native and non-Native groups whom they exploited and alienated, and the process of settler colonialism, therefore, made the professional-managerial class and modern bureaucratic institutions. To understand the dominant class dynamics of the twentieth century, Forsyth suggests, historians must invert the traditional perspective and provincialize Britain.

papers.title: Navyug Gill. Labors of Division: Global Capitalism and the Emergence of the Peasant in Colonial Panjab .
papers.abstract: When formal British rule arrived in the province of the Panjab in 1849, the colonial state immediately directed its energies toward extracting land revenue. The effect of this endeavor on Panjabi society has often been viewed positively, but Navyug Gill challenges this narrative of “colonial benevolence” in his book Labors of Division: Global Capitalism and the Emergence of the Peasant in Colonial Panjab. Rejecting the claim that cultivators remained “largely unscathed if not deliberately empowered” (4) under British rule, Gill sets out to show how colonial technologies of rule instigated an “internal contest for social and economic primacy among different groups of Panjabis” (261). The book is divided into five chapters, flanked by an introduction and a conclusion. Chapter 1 begins Gill’s investigation into how the seemingly obvious category of the “peasant” was the contingent product of colonial governance. To maximize revenue, the state used mathematical methods to assess lands based on criteria such as their productive “capacity” and the quality of the labor working it. Usually, such assessments were greater than what the land produced and/or the revenue that cultivators had hitherto paid. Gill concludes that the “peasant” who emerged through colonial rule was “irreducibly distinct and modern” (65) and that colonial benevolence was a claim produced to “conceal the novelty of a discordant accumulation” (66).

papers.title: Lindsey Dodd. Feeling Memory: Remembering Wartime Childhoods in France .
papers.abstract: In Feeling Memory: Remembering Wartime Childhoods in France, Lindsey Dodd continues her inquiry into children’s experiences of war. In this new work, the author breathes new life into oral interviews she conducted previously for a different project, focused on reconstructing children’s memories of the Second World War. Right from the start, she makes it clear that this is not a book on the official or collective memory of the Second World War, nor is it a prosopography, nor even, she warns, a work of history in the canonical and academic sense of the term. Instead, Dodd focuses on two questions that guide her investigation: What does it mean to be a child during the war? How can oral sources be used to tell the story “from the inside out” (2)? Following what has been called the “affective turn,” Dodd has taken up the challenge of weaving together a sensitive, “affective” history of the war by paying attention to the multiplicity and heterogeneity of individual memories and childhood experiences of the war. She explains that the more traditional historical methods prevented her from seeing that all her interviews were saturated with emotions, feelings, and sensations. In this respect, she starts from the premise that “memories of experiences must be memories of feeling” (52). Using an “ideological positioning” (2) and an “affective methodology” (11), she advocates for a much more empathetic approach to witnesses, listening to them with renewed attention and without overlooking them. The focus is therefore on individuals and their singularities rather than on the collective or the analysis of structures. In her view, the usual methodological reflexes of historians are inadequate insofar as they too often impose a chronological ordering of memory, which does not sufficiently take into account the challenges of the disordered, multiple, and complex dimensions of memory. Her approach is therefore both critical and reflective, offering a revision of her own work as well as a rereading of her personal use of oral sources. She draws on an impressive corpus of 120 oral testimonies produced between 1982 and 2017, fifty-two of which she conducted herself. By choosing an “impressionist” methodology (17), which seeks to fit the blurred and complex contours of the oral source, the author justifies her choice not to adhere to the traditional methodologies of the historical discipline.

papers.title: Samuel Dolbee. Locusts of Power: Borders, Empire, and Environment in the Modern Middle East .
papers.abstract: The history of the Jazira, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, finds new expression and creative resuscitation in Samuel Dolbee’s book Locusts of Power. The toponym, Jazira, is not often found on contemporary maps, Dolbee notes. Yet, by tracing the movement of peoples and insects across this geographic region from 1858 to 1939, Dolbee reveals the Jazira’s place in Ottoman and Middle Eastern history while also describing the limits of state power, the increasing influence of market forces, and the productive and destructive qualities of borders. The first two chapters of Locusts of Power focus on Ottoman efforts to control and benefit from the Jazira, a region that grew in strategic and economic value from the mid-19th century due to the US Civil War and the construction of the Baghdad Railway. Dolbee explains how the Jazira’s aridity and nomadic groups’ mobility affected Ottoman visions for settlement and agricultural expansion. The Jazira’s ecologies and physical geography take a backseat in these discussions as Dolbee foregrounds the movements of the book’s primary actors. An impressive array of sources furnishes vibrant descriptions of nomads, Ottoman reformers, warlords, deported Armenians, and European imperialists. The analysis is at its best in moments of synthesis, when the Shammar herdsmen, the armies sent to subdue them, and the insects and starlings, all kinetic and moving in “a choreography of locusts and nomads,” come together (39). The examination of the locusts’ economic effects and their reverberation through politics and society is also excellent. Moreover, the careful juxtaposition of material and political borders produces paradoxes that help to illuminate intertwined human and insect fates, as when Dolbee notes, “Regions remained beyond settlement because that was where the locust laid their eggs, and locust eggs could not be destroyed because they were located in regions beyond settlement” (134). More information about the locust itself and its reproduction would have made these juxtapositions that much keener.

papers.title: Sheyda F. A. Jahanbani. The Poverty of the World: Rediscovering the Poor at Home and Abroad, 1941–1968 .
papers.abstract: “The Peace Corps and the War on Poverty are two sides of the same coin,” the director of both programs stated in 1965. “Together,” Sargent Shriver continued, “they comprise a national program to promote peace and end poverty, at home and abroad” (179). Sheyda F. A. Jahanbani explores this contention in The Poverty of the World: Rediscovering the Poor at Home and Abroad, 1941–1968, showing how a particular set of influential liberal thinkers and policymakers came to define global and domestic poverty—and their possible solutions—as inextricably linked by the mid-twentieth century. In the process, liberals promoted an alternative role for the United States in the world, one based in that which Jahanbani calls an “empire of affluence” rather than pure militarism. In its ambitious and compelling linkage of geographic areas, topics, and people that have often been treated separately by historians, The Poverty of the World is of interest for historians across varied subfields, including United States political, intellectual, and social history as well as diplomatic and global history, particularly related to international development and postwar decolonization.

papers.title: Lauren Braun-Strumfels. Partners in Gatekeeping: How Italy Shaped U.S. Immigration Policy over Ten Pivotal Years, 1891–1901 .
papers.abstract: US immigration historians have long demonstrated that antipathy toward Italian immigrants and opposition to widespread Italian immigration were key ingredients to both elite and working-class expressions of nativist politics in late Gilded Age America and proved central to restrictionists’ efforts to pass and implement increasingly harsh Progressive Era federal immigration measures. Italian authorities rarely occupy center stage in such tellings, more often appearing as major actors in (seemingly separate) scholarship on sending states’ responses to mass emigration. In Partners in Gatekeeping: How Italy Shaped U.S. Immigration Policy over Ten Pivotal Years, 1891–1901, Lauren Braun-Strumfels reveals the fundamental inseparability of these American and Italian histories of migration law and politics. Comprising five chapters (plus an introduction and epilogue), the book proceeds briskly. Chapter 1 identifies 1891 as the nadir of late nineteenth-century US-Italian relations, centering on the fallout of the mass lynching of eleven Italian migrants in New Orleans and the recall of Italy’s ambassador from Washington. Chapter 2 reveals how Italian diplomats and bureaucrats swiftly and successfully rebuilt relationships with American immigration officials, winning approval for the establishment of a unique office at Ellis Island—the Office of Labor Information and Protection for Italians—run by Italian representatives themselves. Chapters 3 and 4 emphasize the limits of Italian officials’ powers of persuasion, exemplified by the difficulties they encountered trying to direct migrants to and support them in rural settlements in the US South (through a case study of one such locale: Sunnyside, Arkansas), along with the repeated refusal of American lawmakers and bureaucrats to clearly define excludable categories of migrants such as “alien contract laborers” and those “likely to become a public charge.” Chapter 5 illustrates how lawmakers in Italy responded to these and related challenges (such as the forced closure of their government’s Ellis Island office) by adopting a range of emigration policies—most concretely the Italian Emigration Act of 1901—that sought to prevent the departure of those likely to be denied entry to the United States while offering increasingly tangible legal protections to would-be migrants vis-à-vis recruiters and shipping companies.

papers.title: M. T. Howard. Black Soldiers in the Rhodesian Army: Colonialism, Professionalism, and Race .
papers.abstract: Following the imposition of colonial control, European powers recruited local forces in Africa to maintain internal order within these colonies. Most of these forces were then involved in the larger and complex process of decolonization, and many then entered into a period of negotiation or protest with the new state—such as the Royal West African Frontier Force becoming the national armies of Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Gambia. However, the path to decolonization was not always a smooth one, and for those regions of southern Africa, such as the colonies of the Portuguese Empire and South Africa, the desire for local majority rule demanded the use of organized violence. In these cases, the locally raised military forces and gendarmeries had a much different path to walk, becoming part of the armed forces fighting to maintain white minority rule within their colonial states. M. T. Howard’s book Black Soldiers in the Rhodesian Army explores the challenging and contested history of the locally raised African forces of the state of Rhodesia, investigating their experiences serving a racist state and drawing out how and why these personnel served throughout the lengthy liberation war that birthed Zimbabwe, and ultimately why these soldiers of the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) became integrated into the state now run by their former enemies. To achieve this, Howard manages to weave together an impressive series of interviews with former members of the RAR with archival sources and current social theory undergirding military professionalism and identity. The ultimate product is an extraordinary book, one that offers a deep analysis of the experiences of Black soldiers in one of the last colonial states; the social structures that maintained their group identity; and the RAR’s conception of professionalism, which shaped their relationships with their peers, their government, and their enemies throughout the 15-year liberation war.

papers.title: The Death of Woman Guo Big Asia and the Anthropocene
papers.abstract: One chilly night in December 1937, somewhere in Keshan, a county in Japanese-occupied Manchukuo, Mrs. Guo (née Sun)—no given name recorded—woke up in her adobe farmhouse with crippling head and chest pains. As a 26-year-old with no prior history of serious illness, she should not have had such severe symptoms. When local clinicians examined her three days later, they noted that Guo was in so much distress that they could not ascertain her heart rate or blood pressure, only that her skin had turned white and her limbs blue from the lack of oxygen in her blood. By this point, she was vomiting yellow bile. Five hours later, she was dead. Guo only exists in the imperial archive because Japanese epidemiologists documented her autopsy in a medical journal, alongside those of several other casualties from this mysterious sickness.1 Her death had followed a sudden and terrifying outbreak that had killed over a hundred people in Keshan two years earlier. The alarmed doctors at first wondered if they had encountered a new variant of pneumonic plague but ultimately decided to classify the disorder as a “climatic disease,” implying that its cause lay in the interaction between the environmental setting and cultural practices of a particular area. They named the ailment Keshan Disease after its place of origin.2

papers.abstract: When Eric Foner’s Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution came out in 1988, reviewer Michael Perman wondered whether historians would have anything left to say about the post-Civil War era. papers.title: Susan Gaunt Stearns. Empire of Commerce: The Closing of the Mississippi and the Opening of Atlantic Trade .
papers.abstract: Empire of Commerce: The Closing of the Mississippi and the Opening of Atlantic Trade by Susan Gaunt Stearns gives a clear view into the complex history of the “Mississippi Question.” In 1784, Spain closed the Mississippi River to European Americans triggering a national crisis for the United States. Stearns divides her history of empire and commerce into three parts. The first explores economic activity along the Mississippi River prior to the American Revolution through 1783. Indigenous peoples, like the Chickasaws, had long used the river as a center for long distance trade. Meanwhile an influx of European American settlers into the trans-Appalachian west, whom Stearns calls “westerners,” hoped to access Atlantic markets via the Mississippi to finance the region’s developing land market. Part 2 centers on events following Spain’s closure of the Mississippi River until its eventual reopening in 1795. Though no single power, Indigenous or imperial, could fully command the river, the Chickasaw Nation’s strategic position at the Chickasaw Bluffs near modern-day Memphis and Spanish policies in New Orleans made traveling and trading on the Mississippi a daunting task. The ramifications of this nearly divided the newly founded United States. Stearns culminates her work with the integration of the trans-Appalachian west into the Atlantic World. Pinckney’s Treaty in 1795 opened the Mississippi to American trade, working to reinforce the bonds between westerners and the rest of the United States. The economic benefits this brought to the national economy cleared the way for the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, ensuring the Mississippi became an “American river.”

papers.title: Tomás Irish. Feeding the Mind: Humanitarianism and the Reconstruction of European Intellectual Life, 1919–1933 .
papers.abstract: Tomás Irish’s Feeding the Mind unearths a fascinating chapter in the post–World War I relief and reconstruction of Europe: the rescue and rehabilitation of intellectuals and intellectual life. This is a valuable account of how civilizational projects and intellectuals and knowledge production combine into a form of humanitarianism unlike most. The book is organized into six chapters plus an introduction and epilogue. The introduction and chapter 1 lay out the major twin themes of the argument. Once the war ended, Europe turned to the labor of repairing the physical and emotional damage wrought by the war. This was a period of introspection. Ideas of progress were central to the meaning of European civilization, but the very fact of the war and its immense destruction cratered such beliefs. Indeed, in many conflict zones, the armed parties aimed to destroy the pursuit of knowledge and the preservation of culture by burning books, libraries, academic institutions, and museums. Irish notes how civilizational discourse served multiple functions: It is what kept Europe from descending into conflict and collapse; it represented a form of universalism that transcended borders and nationalisms; and it placed an emphasis on high culture. papers.title: Anthony Gregory. New Deal Law and Order: How the War on Crime Built the Modern Liberal State .
papers.abstract: In fall of 2024, Americans are entering an unprecedented presidential election season. One reason, though far from the only one, that this election differs from recent historical convention can be found in the divergent visions of crime policy presented by the two mainstream parties. In this 2024 clash, we can see the breakdown of a bipartisan commitment to what historian Anthony Gregory calls a “war on crime” that has dominated American politics since the 1930s. Gregory’s book New Deal Law and Order: How the War on Crime Built the Modern Liberal State is a thorough and convincing explication of the process of building this framework that will prove essential to historians of the New Deal, political and legal historians, historians of the carceral state, and readers who wish to understand one of the central building blocks in the political order that preceded our contemporary moment. New Deal Law and Order is an ambitious political and legal history of the formative years of twentieth-century American liberalism at the federal level. Gregory argues that welfare liberalism and what he dubs war-on-crime liberalism developed together in the 1930s. He contends that “the New Deal war on crime delivered political legitimacy to the modern state through the transformation of liberal ideas, liberal governance, and constitutional structure” (5). In this argument, Gregory makes an important intervention in a growing historiographic subfield, exploring the relationship between liberalism and state mechanisms of imprisonment, policing, and punishment. Gregory methodically reframes the role of the war on crime in 1930s state building, contending that 1930s crime policies enabled the political alliances and expansions in federalism that made the New Deal possible. The author clearly shows that New Deal policies built carceral capacity at every government level, which is a useful point that other scholars have referenced but few have taken the time to systematically prove. Gregory’s most groundbreaking and unsettling argument is that support for war-on-crime policies, including the introduction of new federal crimes and a massive expansion of federal crime-fighting infrastructure, brought adversaries together in a coalition that generated important liberal political capital, some of which translated into support for New Deal policies.

Otim argues that the men who held these important positions as war leaders, royal messengers, royal healers, priests, and poet-musicians—most of these persons were indeed men—were not the ordinary or marginalized citizens that European colonizers and missionaries assumed them to be, but instead, sophisticated and highly trained members of the precolonial political elite. These intellectuals played “a pivotal yet overlooked role in the transition to, and spread of, Christianity and colonial rule” (7).

papers.title: How Mediterranean Economies Were Shaped in the Early Middle Ages
papers.abstract: The clichéd image of the premodern Mediterranean economy is stagnation until the twin forces of capitalism and Industrial Revolution kick-started growth and the modern world. Yet the premodern Mediterranean economy fluctuated significantly over time with two significant trade cycles. First, the Roman Empire united the Mediterranean together for the first four centuries CE before its political economy broke down. Second, people and states, starting around 1000 CE, wove together local trade networks into trans-Mediterranean connections, leading to a Commercial Revolution. Chris Wickham’s 2005 book, Framing the Early Middle Ages, explained how the first trade cycle ended and trade atrophied from 400 to 800 CE. Framing sketches out the workings of the late Roman Empire’s tax system, whose extracted revenues based largely on agricultural produce funneled wealth toward the imperial administration in a capital city and, above all, to pay standing armies on its frontiers. The elites controlling the tax system simultaneously used these economic networks to piggyback trade in bulk goods around the Mediterranean. Elites thus both administered the tax system as bureaucrats and used the system’s networks to create massive wealth for themselves, leading to a booming late Roman economy.

papers.title: Lauren Lassabe Shepherd. Resistance from the Right: Conservatives and the Campus Wars in Modern America .
papers.abstract: Lauren Lassabe Shepherd has joined a growing number of scholars reconsidering the history of US higher education in recent years. That work has offered critical reevaluations of landmark federal laws (such as the 1862 Land Grant College, or Morrill, Act and the 1965 Higher Education Act), proprietary schools, once-celebrated university presidents (including Southern liberal Frank Porter Graham and California pluralist Clark Kerr), and campus expansions into low-income Black and Brown neighborhoods. Much of that research has shown the darker side of the liberal policies behind the academy’s storied expansion, but Resistance from the Right: Conservatives and the Campus Wars in Modern America explores the links between campuses and the growth of modern conservatism, a topic that has dominated the field of twentieth-century US history since the mid-1990s. Shepherd focuses on conservative and far-right students. That group has received far less attention than the broad student left, some of whom became the tenured radicals writing the history of Berkeley’s Free Speech Movement, Students for a Democratic Society, and other radical groups. Shepherd’s short account of conservative campus activism between 1967 and 1970 helps explain why. Most undergraduate and graduate students went to class. Only a small subset protested the Vietnam War, demanded integration, tried to stop left-wing demonstrations, or mocked efforts to start Black Studies programs. Yet the Young Americans for Freedom, Intercollegiate Studies Institute, College Republicans, and Campus Crusade for Christ International proclaimed themselves the voice for a silent student majority who wanted to learn, not be indoctrinated. They had a lot of help from powerful conservative groups, including the Foundation for Economic Education, the Mount Pelerin Society, and National Review. As such, Shepherd argues the conservative movement on college campuses across the country was better understood as “an astroturf backlash” (189). Such top-down support provided fellowships, instruction manuals, and jobs after graduation, which led many into careers in politics and policymaking, not academia. Yet conservative alumni found themselves with a lot of power over colleges and universities, which relied on federal funding that declined in the decades after this set of conservative activists graduated.

papers.title: Mesopotamian Words for “Slave”
papers.abstract: Abstract The emergence of slavery in Mesopotamia is of crucial importance for historians who study ancient cultures as well as for comparativists interested in its influence on later societies. But the social, economic, and legal contexts in which “slaves” appear in cuneiform texts differ so widely not only between ancient and modern forms but also within intracultural contexts, such that the nature of the underlying concepts and practices are hardly clear. Given these indistinctions, the Mesopotamian terms for “slave(ry)” warrant closer scrutiny. Remarkably, the relevant words in both Sumerian and Akkadian are etymologically opaque and semantically uncertain, obscuring the precise status denoted by the words arad/ardu. This paper delves into philological problems in order to argue that the ambiguity of these terms was deliberately perpetuated by structured linguistic choices. Definitional vagueness generated and permitted nonspecific meanings for personal status, legal object, and economic institution, which enabled slavery to change and thrive across the ages. This deliberate ambiguity allowed slavery and mastery to persist in legal and commercial practice untroubled by social logic or critical definitions—as concepts whose protean meanings were transmitted to successive historical cultures as both profoundly ambivalent and natural.

papers.title: Big Asia
papers.abstract: In recent years, after decades of increasing specialization, new approaches have emerged in Asian studies that focus on larger units of analysis. Some are predicated on transnational or transimperial spaces, whether based around language (the “Persianate world” and “Sinosphere”), geography (the Indian Ocean or “Silk Road”), or networks (whether forged by commercial, political, or cultural actors). This attention to networks has in turn fostered interest in “inter-Asian” developments, and in methods that are at once micro and macro in scale by following small numbers of people, concepts, or commodities across the continent at large. Correspondingly, the rise of not only global history but also environmental and “big history” has encouraged studies of the entire continent, or large sections of it, by way of steppes and mountain ranges as much as river systems and seas. Such big spaces have in turn linked the study of individuals and communities in Asia to their associates or counterparts in the Americas, Europe, and the Pacific, framing Asia within the larger geography of the “Pacific Rim,” “Asia-Pacific,” “Indo-Pacific,” and “Eurasia”—concepts that have found political as much as scholarly purchase. “Big Asia,” then, begs big questions about not only the methodological how but also the fundamental where and who of Asia’s past, and their implications for the geopolitical present.

papers.title: Beyond Antisemitism: Rethinking Stalin’s Anti-Jewish Campaign, 1948–1953
papers.abstract: This article focuses on a single major affair within modern Jewish history whose antisemitic context is unequivocally recognized by most historical scholarship, namely, the murderous persecution of Soviet Jews during the final years of Joseph Stalin’s rule (1948–53). I argue that alongside events and actions on the part of the regime that appear obviously antisemitic in nature, one can point to a certain distinct trend in Stalin’s “Jewish” policy at the time that the concept “antisemitism” does not help to unravel or understand. Historians were unaware of this trend until the Soviet archives were opened following the collapse of the Soviet Union. I address it here for the first time after perusing relevant archival material that has yet to be assessed by scholarship. After presenting and analyzing this unknown stratum of Stalin’s policy toward Soviet Jewry during the time of the persecutions, I argue that both this element, which is unassociated with the phenomenon of antisemitism, and the familiar murderous components of Stalin’s ostensibly antisemitic policy should from now on be analyzed and interpreted against a phenomenological and theoretical backdrop other than the paradigm of antisemitism.

papers.title: Caleb Wellum. Energizing Neoliberalism: The 1970s Energy Crisis and the Making of Modern America .
papers.abstract: Energizing Neoliberalism is a provocation to those of us who think about the 1970s energy crisis. Caleb Wellum effectively connects the event to many strands of the new ways that energy history has guided us to reconsider and evaluate these events, which becomes essential as our energy story progresses to reveal that maybe something important did, in fact, transpire in humans’ approach to energy use after this critical decade. As a provocation, though, Wellum’s work introduces insights without necessarily carrying them to completion. With its emphasis on neoliberalism, Energizing Neoliberalism is best categorized as a work of political history even though it states its emphasis as the cultural story. Readers expecting a complete consideration of the politics of the era, though, might best be served by Meg Jacobs’s book Panic at the Pump and other titles that broadly source the events of the period. However, what Wellum offers is a most insightful consideration that will introduce many readers to the approach of the developing line of inquiry known as “petrocultures.”

papers.title: Jonathan Huener. The Polish Catholic Church under German Occupation: The Reichsgau Wartheland, 1939–1945 .
papers.abstract: Jonathan Huener’s The Polish Catholic Church Under German Occupation: The Reichsgau Wartheland, 1939–1945 is a significant scholarly achievement. Huener demonstrates a meticulous command of a wide variety of Polish and German sources to describe in harrowing detail the largely successful Nazi efforts to cripple the Catholic Church in annexed Polish territories as part of making a new “model Gau” of Wartheland. After their victory over Poland, the Nazis carved up much of western and central Poland to create the largest and most populous Gau in an expanded Third Reich. The Nazi official in charge of Wartheland, Gauleiter Arthur Greiser, who played a key role in initiating the Shoah with his assaults on Wartheland’s Jews, also facilitated the mass murder of the region’s Polish gentile cultural and spiritual leadership. In addition to these crimes, the Nazi authorities enslaved and expelled much of the remaining Polish population and began the colonization of this territory by Germans to change the face of the region—particularly religiously. This work is especially strong in its analysis of the impact of first two years of the occupation on both this pioneering Nazi administration and the fate of Poles whom it sought to subjugate spiritually as well as physically. As a thick description of how the Nazis tried—and failed—to enslave a people spiritually, this is a model of careful scholarship.

papers.title: Benjamin Carp. The Great New York Fire of 1776: A Lost Story of the American Revolution .
papers.abstract: Stories of wars and revolutions, when abstracted to their ideological impact, can elide the daily horrors experienced by people unable to escape the violence. Narratives of the American Revolution are particularly susceptible to this framing. Unbeknownst to rebels and patriots, the United States would become a global superpower whose present-day citizens find in the Revolution the source of their country’s “exceptional” character. But many revolutionary actions, when explored as microhistories, reveal new lessons about a tumultuous era. Benjamin Carp offers just such a careful and nuanced study in The Great New York Fire of 1776. Carp’s investigation demonstrates that patriots could be vindictive, destructive, and cruel. His conclusion is clear and convincing—in the fall of 1776, American rebels torched New York in a coordinated effort to burn the city to the ground before the British could take it. Carp’s thesis, which is supported by a careful reading of extant sources, is important because he settles a debate that animated citizens and officials in Britain and the rebellious colonies at the time but was subsequently written out of revolutionary history. His conclusion that patriots set fire to New York complicates the founding story of the United States by reminding contemporary Americans that patriots “skulked and deceived, burned and massacred, unleashed campaigns of terror, and denigrated people as less worthy of citizenship” (5). Over the course of fourteen tight chapters, Carp recreates the world of New York in 1776—describing its buildings and streetscapes, its inhabitants, and the city’s role as a character in the revolutionary drama. New York was divided along class, gender, and racial lines in ways that are unfortunately familiar today; it was also a city where violence was not uncommon. Fire was a constant threat in crowded settlements across North America, especially given the ease and economy of building structures of wood rather than stone. In 1776, patriots from George Washington to nameless sympathizers considered torching New York to keep it from falling into British hands. Washington himself later regretted not giving official orders to burn the city—Congress had instructed him not to—but he must have taken solace in the fact that his orders were unnecessary. Patriots set the fires nonetheless.

papers.title: Andrew Seaton. Our NHS: A History of Britain’s Best-Loved Institution .
papers.abstract: In the spring of 2024, theatergoers in London had a choice of two star-studded plays commemorating the birth of Britain’s National Health Service (NHS). One, The Human Body, told the story of the NHS’s foundation in 1948 through the eyes of a socialist woman doctor. The other, Nye, celebrated the politician commonly credited as its architect, the Labour Minister of Health Aneurin Bevan. The ovations greeting these performances were not for the actors alone but spoke also to the affection in which the public still holds the service. In a country fractured by fourteen years of populism, austerity economics, and the Brexit folly, the NHS remains a beacon of solidarity amid a sea of sauve qui peut. This compound of nostalgia and hope that attends the service today owes less to its current performance than to its talismanic features. These are universal population coverage, cradle-to-grave medical provision, and “free at the point of use” funding based largely on graduated general taxation. Emotional attachment is the starting point of Andrew Seaton’s new history, Our NHS, which sets out to explain how it became the country’s “best-loved institution.” This question differentiates the book from the other major NHS studies, such as those of Charles Webster and Rudolf Klein, which both concentrate on health system policymaking. In contrast, Seaton’s focus is on retrieving attitudes and feelings toward the service to establish its place in popular and political culture.

papers.title: Comment by Hyunhee Park
papers.abstract: In today’s academic landscape, the growing emphasis on globalization has amplified the demand for non-Western curricula, prompting a reexamination of how Asian history is framed. Increasingly, institutions incorporate Asian studies into broader world history frameworks, grouping diverse histories into regional surveys that highlight Asia’s cultural, political, and economic diversity while emphasizing its historical connections to global processes. These approaches challenge the outdated notion of Asia as a collection of isolated civilizations, presenting it instead as a dynamic, interconnected region. The think pieces in this forum expand on this shift, urging a reconsideration of Asia’s historical boundaries and interactions. This commentary contributes to that dialogue by exploring “Big Asia” as a framework to move beyond static portrayals and uncover the region’s diversity, fluidity, and integrative contributions to global history. To begin with, the concept of “Big Asia” compels us to rethink Asia’s boundaries and historical definitions. As Nile Green observes, Asia has never been a fixed entity; its meanings and contours have shifted across time and cultures, shaped by the priorities of those who conceptualized it. With regard to my own research, premodern societies like China and the Islamic caliphates developed “geoconcepts” that situated Asian regions within broader frameworks of world understanding. Building on flourishing trade connections across Asia, their scholars crafted geographical texts and maps that divided the world into vast regions rather than defining Asia as a distinct entity. This integrative approach is exemplified by Sima Qian’s (145–86 BCE) official histories, which categorized foreign societies and described them in relation to China, as well as in the geographic works in the Islamic world, which synthesized knowledge into comprehensive worldviews, centered on their respective societies.1

papers.title: Amy Godine. The Black Woods: Pursuing Racial Justice on the Adirondack Frontier .
papers.abstract: Since its founding, the American nation has predominately been an agricultural society infused with notions of freedom, independence, and economic advancement through farming labor. The small independent farmer became a romantic symbol, which was most popularly referenced by Thomas Jefferson, to epitomize the ideal American citizen. However, such agrarian traditions were often denied to millions of African Americans and their descendants. The “forty acres and a mule” became the symbol of this obstructed promise of mass landownership after freedom. As the preeminent scholar W. E. B. Du Bois once wrote, “The vision of ‘forty acres and a mule’ . . . was destined in most cases to a bitter disappointment” (The Souls of Black Folk [1903], 26). Amy Godine explores an earlier short-lived pursuit of this Black agrarian vision in The Black Woods: Pursuing Racial Justice on the Adirondack Frontier. The Black Woods examines a little-known history of a land giveaway project of forty-acre plots to Black New Yorkers. Implemented from 1846 to 1853, this project was created by the abolitionist and large landowner Gerrit Smith, who broke up 120,000 acres of his land located in the remote northern New York wilderness of Adirondack. This land was intended for farming and gifted to three thousand Black people. Though eventually viewed as a failure, an analysis of this land giveaway reveals the earlier aspirations of Black agrarian pursuits.

papers.title: Ari Şekeryan. The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire: After Genocide, 1918–1932 .
papers.abstract: The challenges of understanding the road(s) to mass atrocity, the dynamics of the crime, and its prevention continue to engender a regular stream of multidisciplinary scholarly output. Less attention is focused on what comes after, even though it is no less compelling a subject, combining the complications inherent to genocide with the questions the preposition after introduces. Ari Şekeryan takes up this challenge for the Armenian Genocide in The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire: After Genocide, 1918–1923. Şekeryan is not entirely in uncharted waters. Two monographs in particular illuminate the path for him: Talin Suciyan’s The Armenians in Modern Turkey: Post-Genocide Society, Politics and History (2015) and Lerna Ekmekçioğlu’s Recovering Armenia: The Limits of Belonging in Post-Genocide Turkey (2016). Both compellingly explore—through different theoretical lenses, archival pools, and spatiotemporal focus—how genocide survivors who remained in Turkey tried to navigate the crime’s aftermath. Şekeryan’s interest in sociopolitical history and ethnic relations overlaps with the former, and the period he covers overlaps with the latter. However, The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire surveys larger territory—the length and breadth of a crumbling empire from where a resurgent republic emerges in 1924—and offers new insights into the political maneuvers of the decimated Ottoman Armenian community.

papers.title: Abigail Krasner Balbale. The Wolf King: Ibn Mardanīsh and the Construction of Power in al-Andalus .
papers.abstract: This stimulating book, The Wolf King: Ibn Mardanīsh and the Construction of Power in al-Andalus, by Abigail Krasner Balbale, focuses on the political significance of Muḥammad ibn Mardanīsh, the fascinating Andalusī leader of the Taifa state of Murcia, who resisted the Almohad Empire. In 1147, after defeating the Almoravids and seizing Marrakesh, their capital, the Berber Almohad confederation crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and began the conquest of the other side. Yet their newly proclaimed caliph, ῾Abd al-Mu’min (1130–1163), faced fierce resistance from local populations. Ibn Mardanīsh, their most powerful opponent, negotiated alliances with the northern Christian kingdoms and repelled assaults against his capital and maintained his rule over the southeastern lands (Alicante, Cartagena, Lorca, Baza, etc.) until his death. The author does not mention that the Almoravid emirate of the Banū Ghāniyya remained autonomous in the Balearic Islands, until their conquest by the Almohad fleet in 1203. For a better understanding of this complex situation, it would have been helpful to insert a short chronology at the end of the volume and visualize more precisely the political divisions on the map (36).

papers.title: Jürgen Buchenau. The Sonoran Dynasty in Mexico: Revolution, Reform, and Repression .
papers.abstract: In The Sonoran Dynasty in Mexico, Jürgen Buchenau explores how eleven politicians from the northern state of Sonora significantly influenced national politics during and after the Mexican Revolution (1910–20). The literature on the revolution has tended to cast this group, known as the Sonorenses, in a negative light. “Winning the revolution,” writes Buchenau, “came at the price of blame for its shortcomings, including the persistence of authoritarian governance and widespread corruption; the failure to achieve social justice; and the inability to diminish the influence of the United States” (9). Consequently, historians initially avoided in-depth analyses of the Sonorenses, preferring to focus on the revolution’s defeated agrarian forces and their leaders. Weaving together biography, political history, intrigue, and superb storytelling, Buchenau has crafted the first comprehensive and archivally based study on the Sonorenses and its members—a regional dynasty that dominated Mexican politics from 1920 to the mid-1930s. This work represents the “culminating synthesis” of a senior scholar who has established himself as the premiere authority on the political lives of Sonoran Presidents Álvaro Obregón (1920–24) and Plutarco Elías Calles (1924–28) (ix). In this latest book, however, Buchenau expands his analysis beyond these two patriarchs and considers the political rise and fall of the larger and influential Sonorense group. This group hailed from a state with “less than 2 percent of Mexico’s population [but] accounted for an estimated 11.4 percent of the governing elite” (4). Buchenau contends that the personal relationships and rivalries within this group contributed to Mexico’s process of centralization through institutionalization but also led to the formation of opposing “social and political movements” that fueled successive bloody civil wars and rebellions (6–8). The group “also brought about important reforms and innovations, in addition to defending Mexican sovereignty and political stability” (13).
