papers.title: Sam Ottewill-Soulsby. The Emperor and the Elephant: Christians and Muslims in the Age of Charlemagne .
papers.abstract: Sam Ottewill-Soulsby’s The Emperor and the Elephant: Christians and Muslims in the Age of Charlemagne reflects the global turn in Carolingian studies, focusing on the diplomatic interactions between Carolingians and different Muslim rulers during the eighth and ninth centuries. After a detailed exposition of the concept of diplomacy during the early Middle Ages, the general political context, as well as the Latin and Arabic sources in the first chapter, the author turns to a general consideration of diplomatic practice in the period, discussing perceptions of the other, envoys, and problems of traveling and gifts. The third chapter deals with Carolingian-Abbasid relations, involving the most famous episode, alluded to in the title, the Indian elephant sent by the Abbasid caliph to Aachen. Christian Arabic apocalyptic writings, discussed by the author in this context, are a welcome addition to the usual sources taken into account for the reconstruction of this episode. The author is an expert on Carolingian-Umayyad relations, which are discussed in two chapters. Treatment of these relations involves a detailed consideration of the Frankish frontier with al-Andalus, involving the border lords on both sides; shifting constellations in Catalonia as well as in the three marches controlled from Mérida, Toledo, and Zaragoza; and the varying strength of the Umayyad emirs in Córdoba, who were frequently faced with rivals and rebellions. The last chapter turns its attention to the central Mediterranean, comprising Muslim polities in Northern Africa, Sicily, and on the Italian mainland.

papers.title: Matthew D. Lassiter. The Suburban Crisis: White America and the War on Drugs .
papers.abstract: For a subject as well-trodden as race and the drug war, framing new work within the existing literature can be a challenge. Numerous studies have explored the US war on drugs as a system of social control targeting urban minority populations through the expansion of aggressive policing and the carceral state. As the story goes, Republicans, obsessed with law and order, designed punitive antidrug policies while Democrats kept their focus on treatment and rehabilitation. By focusing on white suburbia and the drug war, Matthew D. Lassiter offers a revision to the conventional narrative, demonstrating that the war on drugs operated through a reciprocal paradigm of criminalizing blackness (and foreignness) while decriminalizing whiteness. White middle-class youths consumed illegal drugs, to be sure. Lassiter’s aim though is to examine how the government helped them maintain clean criminal records. He argues that the government saw them as “victims,” creating strict laws and crime control measures that instead targeted nonwhite and foreign “predators” (4, 15). The racial state-building project chronicled in The Suburban Crisis intensified from the 1950s to the 1980s through policies enacted at the local, state, and national levels.

papers.title: Paul Hillmer and Ryan Bean. Inappropriation: The Contested Legacy of Y-Indian Guides .
papers.abstract: While many cultures have been subjected to cultural appropriation, Native American communities have been a primary target in the United States. Some might dismiss critiques of cultural appropriation as “mere identity politics,” or, in an effort to stem discussion, they might point out—rightly—that cultures are not static, and that people have always adopted ideas, practices, and objects from others. However, the structures and ideologies that facilitate cultural appropriation as such reflect unequal power dynamics and engender significant historical and material consequences. This is underscored in an excellent new contribution to this conversation, Inappropriation: The Contested Legacy of Y-Indian Guides by Paul Hillmer and Ryan Bean. Inappropriation is the first book-length study of the YMCA’s popular Y-Indian Guides program. Initially developed as a program for fathers and sons, a large portion of its participants were historically white and from middle-class families. As a core component of the program, participants “played Indian,” a longstanding practice described by Phil Deloria in his important 1998 book Playing Indian. As Hillmer and Bean document, non-Native participants in the Y-Indian Guides program organized themselves into “tribes,” adopted “Indian” names, crafted and wore clothing that was meant to mirror Native garb, and engaged in rituals and ceremonies that, whether or not they actually resembled any, were inspired by Indigenous beliefs and practices. The authors describe the cultural context out of which the program emerged, recount its (somewhat mythic) origin story, trace its growth and demise, and consider its legacy. Their intention is to offer a complex picture of the program—to account for its development and popularity while highlighting the damaging aspects of the forms of cultural appropriation perpetuated (or perpetrated) by the Y-Indian Guides.

papers.title: Ian Milligan. Averting the Digital Dark Age: How Archivists, Librarians, and Technologists Built the Web a Memory .
papers.abstract: Ian Milligan’s latest book, Averting the Digital Dark Age, traces the people and projects that made significant contributions to early web archiving. It builds on his own histories of the web and its value as a historical source, including Transformations of Historical Research in the Digital Age (2022) and History in the Age of Abundance (2019). This book is not a technical manual, but a social and entrepreneurial history of the web. As such, it does not cover practical web archiving nor the peculiarities of working with WARC (web archive) files, both of which can be learned elsewhere. The book starts by painting a frightening picture of a lost generation of early internet users whose web-based experiences were at risk of disappearing. Milligan’s opening includes a tribute to the importance of collecting and preserving, giving homage to archivists and the work they do to keep us collectively remembering, before considering the inherent fragility of technology and digital data, and the challenges of preserving and making readable information that cannot be seen with the naked eye.

papers.title: Max Fraser. Hillbilly Highway: The Transappalachian Migration and the Making of a White Working Class .
papers.abstract: “Hillbilly Highway” is the first track on Steve Earle’s 1986 debut album Guitar Town. Co-written with Jimbeau Hinson, the song chronicles a common migration experience for those in Appalachia who were looking for a job or a better life in the North. Max Fraser sees Earle’s song as a sort of collective history, which just so happened to connect to Earle’s own childhood spent moving around the South. “Spanning three generations in the life of the singer’s family,” writes Fraser, “the song moves from an unnamed Appalachian coal camp, to Detroit, to Houston, before ending up back on the road, ‘that old hillbilly highway’” (12). Fraser’s Hillbilly Highway: The Transappalachian Migration and the Making of a White Working Class is an illuminating history of one of the most significant mass migrations in the modern United States. Millions of poor whites in the rural South made the move north for industrial work, much of it in the auto industry, as the agricultural job economy dried up. Fraser focuses much of his attention on the ways that Transappalachian migrants shaped the cultural, political, and social life of the country.

papers.title: Simon Devereaux. Execution, State and Society in England, 1660–1900 .
papers.abstract: In 1706, Roger Lowen’s corpse was gibbeted (hung in chains post-execution) in Turnham Green, a suburb southwest of London. The decaying corpse swung in chains in view of the house where Lowen’s victim had lived, a practice that underlined the retributive force of execution and post-execution punishment. Any sense that this proximity gave succor or satisfaction to relatives of Lowen’s victim was undercut by a petition from the victim’s widow and her neighbors asking for the gibbet’s removal, as it was causing nuisance to the local area. Simon Devereaux offers this example in Execution, State and Society in England, 1660–1900 as perhaps constituting the first surviving recorded example of a suburban “not in my backyard” attitude in England. The disturbance caused by Lowen’s gibbeted corpse is just one illustration of how what Devereaux terms “urbane” culture was important to driving changes in English execution culture. As cities expanded, better-off suburban residents voiced their discomfort with or distaste for the sight (and, indeed, sound and smell) of the gallows and the gibbet. These residents were not from the ruling class, but in a constitutional monarchy like England, their views and feelings mattered.

papers.title: Ella Fratantuono. Governing Migration in the Late Ottoman Empire .
papers.abstract: Governing Migration in the Late Ottoman Empire by Ella Fratantuono explores the Ottoman migration regime and the history of the past six decades of the Ottoman state from the perspective of mobility. This is an original and timely work given the recent and growing interest in the history of migration in the Ottoman Empire. The book makes several important contributions: It highlights the crucial connection between migration and state-building in the late Ottoman context, it explores the pivotal period of Ottoman reforms from the perspective of mobility, it demonstrates how migration contributed to the way the Ottoman state managed and understood its populations, and it makes a compelling case for studying the Ottoman migration regime alongside other better-known cases. The Ottoman experience becomes quite notable as the author brings out figures about migrations in the 19th and early 20th centuries. They demonstrate that the Ottoman state was in many ways comparable to other countries or regions in the world commonly associated with immigration. According to certain estimates, between the 1850s and the aftermath of the Balkan Wars (1912–13) more than 5 million people, mainly Muslims, arrived and settled in the Ottoman domains. Of course, it should be noted that only a fraction of them came from regions that had not been part of the empire, and most of them or their ancestors were Ottoman subjects who migrated from former Ottoman territories. In comparison, in the period 1820–1932 about 6.5 million Europeans settled in Argentina, more than 4 million moved to Brazil, and 5 million immigrated to Canada. Throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, 6 million peasants resettled in Siberia. About 2 million Europeans moved to Cuba, Australia, and South Africa. In spite of comparable numbers, so far the Ottoman experience has remained largely overlooked in histories of migration and state-building. Fratantuono’s work aspires to fill this gap.

papers.title: Robert K. D. Colby. An Unholy Traffic: Slave Trading in the Civil War South .
papers.abstract: Drawing on the tools of political, economic, social, and military history, Robert K. D. Colby’s An Unholy Traffic: Slave Trading in the Civil War South sets out to uncover the commerce in enslaved people during the American Civil War. Through a creative patchwork of documentary evidence that accounts for over two thousand wartime sales of enslaved people, Colby manages to pair a sophisticated study of Confederate political economy with a careful social history of the enslaved people caught up in the wartime slave trade. The book rests on a crucial but easily overlooked observation: the domestic slave trade gave slavery its economic power, characterizing it as a property relation rather than just a labor relation. “The power of purchase and sale,” Colby writes, “fueled slavery’s viability and strengthened enslavers’ political and psychological hold over the South” (7). This means that his study is not an examination of one isolated aspect of slavery during the Civil War but rather of the proslavery struggle to maintain the viability of the transactions that formed the institution’s foundation.

papers.title: Arang Keshavarzian. Making Space For the Gulf: Histories of Regionalism and the Middle East .
papers.abstract: The study of the Persian Gulf has been invigorated over the past two decades. A flourish of studies and histories of labor, social movements, the environment, migration, cultures, and political economies of the region have proliferated, breathing scholarly life into a part of the world that, with the exception of a handful of earlier pioneering scholars such as Fred Halliday, had mostly been the preoccupation of security studies, students of and advocates for Western power, and those enamored with the region’s oil. Newfound interest in the Gulf’s complexities has been critical to rethinking the fields of Middle East studies and southwest Asia. Even so, the Gulf—including the name itself—remains somewhat inscrutable. The communities around it, as well as those connected to it and one another, are complex, varied, and, most importantly, have changed over time, rendering the Gulf historically contingent and ever-shifting. How should we think about the interconnections, forces, and histories that have shaped the making of the Gulf, including the very idea that it possesses the kind of territorial coherence that makes it a place and space?

papers.title: Gabriella Romano. Italian Fascism’s Forgotten LGBT Victims: Asylums and Internment, 1922–1943 .
papers.abstract: Gabriella Romano’s Italian Fascism’s Forgotten LGBT Victims is a fascinating and original book. It covers a vast amount of ground but does it with great care. The book is focused on LGBT patients in Italian psychiatric hospitals during the years of fascism in Italy. But, in reality, it also touches on a number of other crucial issues of history, medical history, and queer history. These include: the history of psychiatry in Italy and Europe; the understanding of homosexuality by psychiatrists and others in Italy, Europe, and elsewhere; the impact of fascism on psychiatry and psychiatric hospitals; the persecution of homosexuality in Italy (and elsewhere) by fascism but also before fascism; the management and institutional culture inside Italian psychiatric hospitals and the differences between various psychiatric hospitals and their cultures (also geographically); and personnel and psychiatric management. Moreover, the book is extremely reflective in terms of methodology and archival access, and it draws a number of interesting conclusions around its sources and the use of sources of this kind in the general and specific. It would not be an exaggeration to call this a pathbreaking work, which breaks new ground in a whole series of areas.

papers.title: Jane Mumby. Dismantling the League of Nations: The Quiet Death of an International Organization, 1945–48 .
papers.abstract: Jane Mumby’s book Dismantling the League of Nations: The Quiet Death of an International Organization, 1945–48 places itself in a broader body of literature that has emerged over the last decade or so, looking at this first experiment in global governance and institutionalized international cooperation from the perspective of its staff. Just within the last couple of years, Emil Seidenfaden has published the first study of the Information Section of the League, Benjamin Auberer has written a monograph on the Australian and New Zealander officials of the Secretariat, and Myriam Piguet defended a thesis on the integration of women in the League and UN Secretariats. This is a relatively new chapter in the historiographical saga, which first saw the League as a failure, then as a mere stage upon which great powers locked horns, then as an important node in broader transnational networks of embryonic global governance, and now as a bureaucratized multilateral organization with its own dynamics and history. These perspectives are, of course, both overlapping and complementary—and there are many more to come.

papers.title: Say Burgin. Organizing Your Own: The White Fight for Black Power in Detroit .
papers.abstract: The last two decades have seen a plethora of new studies on the history of the Black Power movement. Gone are the days when scholars largely dismissed Black Power as the civil rights movement’s evil twin. Since then, historians have thoroughly revised one-dimensional views of the African American freedom struggle of the 1960s and 1970s. While popular understandings of the movement continue to focus on the Black Panther Party (BPP) and armed self-defense, for instance, more recent studies have demonstrated that guns were frequently secondary to local organizing and to the concrete social changes members of the BPP and other organizations wanted to bring about in Black communities. They initiated social service programs, protested against police brutality, and devised political and cultural strategies both to empower people of color and to counteract white supremacy. New scholarship has also shed fresh light on the roots of Black Power, African American women’s significant contributions to the movement, and its global dimensions.

papers.title: Proximity Matters
papers.abstract: The activist was devoted to doing all he could to improve the situation in the Asian country that was his homeland. He felt it was on the wrong path. It was being ruled in too autocratic a fashion, and he wanted to do what he could to move it in the right direction. He followed the news about other parts of the world hoping to find models that could be adopted and adapted to further this end. While he was open to discovering inspiring or useful ideas in the work of all kinds of foreign thinkers and the histories of all kinds of foreign movements, he took particular interest in things happening in other parts of Asia. He found it especially valuable to pay attention to events in relatively nearby places even when the political situation there was very different from that in his own country. When activists in bordering lands or even ones that were a bit farther away managed to score a victory, this fascinated him. It gave him hope. And proximity made it easier for him to interact with people who had taken part in those struggles rather than in similar ones unfolding farther away. At an important point in his life, thanks partly to proximity, he was able to meet up with some of the activists from another part of Asia whose actions had inspired him. And even though there were major cultural differences between their homelands, and one was in East Asia and the other in Southeast Asia, he convinced some of these people that he and they had much in common and should collaborate.

papers.title: Caryn Cossé Bell. Creole New Orleans in the Revolutionary Atlantic, 1775–1877 .
papers.abstract: Caryn Cossé Bell’s new book is an interesting, smart, at times truly original—if at other times rather flawed—work that serves as a potent and meaningful follow-up to her excellent first book, Revolution, Romanticism, and the Afro-Creole Protest Tradition in Louisiana (1997). The first part of the book, “Revolutions,” follows a band of “itinerant revolutionaries aspiring to a new world order” who, displaced by the Haitian Revolution and inspired by republican independence movements across the circum-Caribbean, formed “an influential interracial refugee coalition” based in New Orleans by the 1830s (34). Sowed by their participation in, yet the denial of citizenship after, the Battle of New Orleans and a shared dedication to revolutionary spirit throughout the wider gulf area, this coalition took up the mantle of republican revolution and equal rights in the decades that followed. Importantly, and certainly historiographically novel, New Orleans becomes part of something bigger than the francophone circum-Caribbean. It becomes a waypoint for Atlantic radicalism—the same revolutionary ideas that gave rise to names like Pétain, Bolívar, and Lafayette.

papers.title: Leyla Amzi-Erdogdular. The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe: Muslims in Habsburg Bosnia Herzegovina .
papers.abstract: Leyla Amzi-Erdogdular’s new book, The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe: Muslims in Habsburg Bosnia Herzegovina, begins with a simple premise: The end of the Ottoman Empire’s rule over its Balkan provinces did not mean the end of an Ottoman presence. The radical remapping of the Ottoman Balkans at the end of the 1877–1878 Russian-Ottoman war created independent states, such as Romania and Serbia, the quasi-states of the vassal Bulgarian principality and autonomous province of Eastern Rumelia and Bosnia Herzegovina, which was placed in a novel legal limbo: The Ottoman sultan remained officially sovereign, but the Habsburg monarchy assumed administrative rights and responsibilities. It took a year to hammer out the details, but the essential feature was already fixed by the 1878 Treaty of Berlin: An Ottoman presence would be maintained not through the informal momentum of local practice but was to be formally guaranteed by international law. The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe offers a fresh perspective on what happened next by concentrating on Bosnia’s Muslim population who, unlike their Catholic and Orthodox neighbors, remained uniquely tethered to the Ottoman sultan as both sovereign and caliph. The province’s status left Bosnian Muslims trying to maintain their close relationship to Istanbul while adjusting to the Habsburg’s increasingly thorough and definitively Christian administration. For Austria, the occupation was a preliminary to annexation; the Ottomans viewed it as a temporary anomaly requiring innovative support for people who continued to be Ottoman subjects; and while Bosnian Muslims hoped for a provincial repatriation, they also seized all available tools to determine their future. “To the Habsburgs,” writes Amzi-Erdogdular, Bosnian Muslims “insisted on the execution of Ottoman laws and practices and ties with the sultan-caliph. To the Ottomans, they appealed for protection as Ottoman subjects and as part of the umma, stimulating Ottoman diplomatic activity in their direction and often trying to attract international attention” (166).

papers.title: Ian Delahanty. Embracing Emancipation: A Transatlantic History of Irish Americans, Slavery, and the American Union .
papers.abstract: Part of Fordham University Press’s Reconstructing America series, Embracing Emancipation provides a valuable reconstruction of the often-tortured relationship between Irish immigrants and American slavery. Ian Delahanty seeks to revise the scholarly consensus that, for the most part, Irish immigrants and their immediate offspring in America were relentless supporters of slavery. Whether it was an attempt to assert “whiteness,” or a severe dislike of evangelical abolitionists, the politically active Irish remained firmly on the pro-slavery side in antebellum America. Delahanty begins by going over the familiar ground of Irish opposition to the abolition movement as it grew to significance through the 1830s and 1840s. He emphasizes, however, that the Irish were not really motivated by an overt pro-slavery ideology but more a desire to protect the Union of the United States, a union which had provided them shelter from British misrule in Ireland. The fact that some prominent abolitionists saw the Roman Catholic Church as equally dangerous to America as the institution of slavery only enhanced Irish opposition to the anti-slavery movement.

papers.title: Benjamin E. Park. American Zion: A New History of Mormonism .
papers.abstract: As Benjamin E. Park points out in his magnificent book American Zion: A New History of Mormonism, it was only in 2012 when America had its latest “Mormon moment” (4). Then, the main catalyst of Americans’ obsession with all things Mormon was the first ever-major party nomination of a Mormon for president, followed by a viral reality TV show chronicling the ups and downs of modern-day Mormon polygamists and a Broadway musical gingerly satirizing Mormon missionary culture. Twelve years later, Mitt Romney has become persona non grata within the Republican Party because of his criticism of the current GOP standard-bearer. Three of the four “sister wives” from the TV show have divorced their husband. The Book of Mormon musical, however, still packs houses during its never-ending national tour. American Zion is the first one-volume history of Mormonism since that last Mormon moment. Park’s book benefits from more time. Between Romney’s nomination in 2012 and the fall campaign, another prominent scholar of Mormonism Matthew Bowman researched and wrote The Mormon People: The Making of an American Faith (2012) in just four months! Park also draws from the last decade of scholarship on Mormonism, highlighting the diversity of race, gender, and nationality in Mormon history—a challenge to the stereotype that Mormonism is a religion created (solely) by and for white US American men. Park also draws from newly available ecclesiastical sources, many of which the archivists of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—the biggest branch of the Mormon movement headquartered in Salt Lake City—kept under lock and key for decades. The recognition of Mormonism’s diverse influences, along with church’s reticence to open its books to outsiders and its current impulses to do so, reflect Park’s thesis: “The modern Latter-day Saint community is a product of two centuries of proving contraries” (10).

papers.title: Abby Smith Rumsey. Memory, Edited: Taking Liberties with History .
papers.abstract: In her book Memory, Edited: Taking Liberties with History, Abby Smith Rumsey seeks to answer the question, “Does a nation need a shared past to have a shared future,” and it does so by “examining the price paid when the answer has to be yes” (3). Rumsey promises to “look at the consequences of regimes that treat history not as an archive of self-knowledge but as mere prologue to the future” and to show “what happens when generations grow up ignorant of their true history, therefore not knowing who they are” (3). The author probes her material to understand the consequences of historical lies and cover-ups to entities she refers to intermittently as “nations” or “societies.” Chapter 1, titled “Making the Past Make Sense,” ends with a statement that reflects the author’s interests and style: “History doesn’t teach lessons, but if we consider it as an instrument of self-knowledge, we see the hidden dangers of taking liberties with history. If history tells lies, then the foundation we build our lives on is no more stable than quicksand. If we don’t know our true origins, we live in ignorance of our true character and capabilities. History is not a court of law, and pleading ignorance cannot protect us. In other words, what we don’t know will kill us. We cannot always anticipate what the past holds in store for us. But if we choose to ignore it, we stumble blindly into the future and encounter the past there, waiting for us” (14).

papers.title: Elijah Doro. Plunder for Profit: A Socio-Environmental History of Tobacco Farming in Southern Rhodesia and Zimbabwe .
papers.abstract: In a June 2019 episode of Edge Effects, a podcast from the University of Wisconsin, environmental thinkers Donna Haraway and Anna Tsing discuss the plantationocene as a concept for understanding environment and society. They highlight how the Anthropocene, as a named epoch where humans have become the main catalysts for changing Earth’s systems, often obscures the vastly different experiences that humans have had in creating these changes, and that they now have in dealing with everything from global warming, soil erosion, air pollution, and flooding to health hazards in homes and workplaces. There is rich potential in framing historical problems within these terms, but these big concepts must also be grounded in detailed stories of human and nonhuman experiences in creating this world where plantations have had such profound impact. Elijah Doro offers readers exactly that in Plunder for Profit: A Socio-Environmental History of Tobacco Farming in Southern Rhodesia and Zimbabwe, although he mentions Anthropocene once and plantationocene not at all.

papers.title: Writing My Seven Mothers Back Together
papers.abstract: Abstract Stories are the glue that hold families and communities together. Confronting past difficulties honestly can have a healing, strengthening effect on relations. But narrating an intimate history of people you love is risky. In this essay, I detail my experience writing and publishing a collective memoir of the seven feminists I called mother during my childhood in Denmark in the early 1970s. My mothers met in the Danish women’s liberation movement in 1971, and together four of them started the lesbian movement in 1974. The stakes in writing my mothers’ story were high. Their movement years are central to their sense of place in history. Their shared history has held them together despite the conflicts that tore our commune apart in the mid-1970s—conflicts about the role of lesbian feminism in the larger women’s movement. For me, their daughter, truth-telling was a way to honor their legacy and their spirit. I held up our mutual past, intimate heartaches and conflicts included, to remind my mothers that honest feminist alliances across difference are the way to go. It was not as easy as I thought.

papers.title: Catherine Volpilhac-Auger. Montesquieu: Let There be Enlightenment .
papers.abstract: In “The Translator’s Task,” Walter Benjamin remarks that the “history of great works of art knows about their descent from their sources, their shaping in the age of the artists, and the periods of their basically eternal continuing life in later generations” (154). Catherine Volpilhac-Auger’s biography, Montesquieu: Let There be Enlightenment, and her ongoing reproduction of Montesquieu’s complete works do precisely this. She injects new life into our understanding of Montesquieu and his writings. Her biography is a product of the monumental study of Montesquieu’s life and archive that includes his published and unpublished writings, correspondence, and library. Together these have brought to light new information and created a fresh, yet classic, portrayal of Montesquieu’s life, writings, intellectual and historical contexts. This biography does not seek to replace earlier ones produced by Robert Shackleton (1961) and Louis Desgraves (1986). Rather, it aims to fill in gaps, to rethink his ideas based on evidence that has recently come to light and to dispel false or embellished narratives. As such, her biography ought to be read in conjunction with these earlier ones.

papers.title: Maximilian C. G. Lau. Emperor John II Komnenos: Rebuilding New Rome, 1118–1143 .
papers.abstract: John II Komnenos (r. 1118–1143) had a grand plan. He aimed to rebuild “New Rome,” securing and substantially expanding its territory from Dalmatia across the Danube frontier to Northern Syria. John built on his father’s achievements, and his son Manuel continued his. He built a vast network of fortresses for ideological and logistical purposes. As far as he can be considered a “crusader,” John wished to visit Jerusalem as a pilgrim and appear as a legitimate overlord of all Christians of the East. But John’s premature death hindered him from reuniting a universal church. His results required a lot of effort for little gain or long-lasting effect. Lau describes John as having a dynamic personality: He was ambitious, family-centred, and merciful, and he promoted the cult of the Theotokos as a crucial element of his religiosity. Lau’s work is welcome, being the first monographic discussion of John II’s reign since Ferdinand Chalandon’s second volume from 1912, part of his volumes on Komnenian Byzantium (Chalandon, Ferdinand, Les Comnène : études sur l’empire byzantin au XIe et au XIIe siècles. 2, Jean II Comnène (1118–1143) et Manuel I Comnène (1143–1180), 1912). The author successfully tackles two significant challenges: First, John II’s reign is attested by the Byzantine historians John Kinnamos and Nicetas Choniates, whose narratives were written from a distance of four decades after the events with a specific authorial agenda. Second, Choniates described John as a second Marcus Aurelius and a soldier-emperor in favorable terms. Choniates’s positive portrayal has been echoed by scholars, who accepted this image of John with varying degrees. This volume, by contrast, attempts to make a holistic approach to the internal (Byzantine) source material, considering all available sources and genres. More importantly, Lau examines John’s reign in a Mediterranean context, considering various non-Byzantine sources. Lau’s use of Syriac and Armenian sources is a case in point, providing a more nuanced understanding of John’s roles. After preparatory research trips to the Balkans and Anatolia, Lau complemented his study of the written testimonies with archaeological case studies. The book is well structured, according to chronology, which is a justified approach, as it serves the purpose of a more profound analysis. The transitions within and between chapters are well crafted, enhancing the reading experience. I find the index helpful, and the key terms are well defined. Maps occur to the reader when visual explanation is needed. In this review, I want to assess Lau’s attempt to present a more complex image of John than a soldier-emperor by focusing on three chapters dealing with John’s education, his military profile, and church policy.

papers.title: Doriane Andrade Meyer. Bahian Recôncavo Plantations: Spaces of Power and Resistance .
papers.abstract: In Bahian Recôncavo Plantations: Spaces of Power and Resistance, Doriane Andrade Meyer examines the history of slavery and its afterlives on the plantations of the Brazilian Northeast through the lens of the built environment. Specifically, she focuses on the Bahian Recôncavo, a region encompassing the Bay of All Saints, historically one of Brazil’s most important sugar producing regions. Africans were trafficked to the Recôncavo to do the grueling labor of agricultural production on the imposing and immense sugar plantations known in Portuguese as engenhos. While slavery in this region of Brazil has been well studied, fewer works have focused on the experiences of enslaved people through the lens of architecture, Meyer’s scholarly and professional area of expertise. Published in the Studies in Latin America series by the Institute for the Study of the Americas at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, which features open access and interdisciplinary works, Meyer’s book sets out to understand “how architecture participated in the foundations of an unequal Brazilian society that continues to this day” (2).

papers.title: Cristina Stanciu. The Makings and Unmakings of Americans: Indians and Immigrants in American Literature and Culture, 1879–1924 .
papers.abstract: Students of American Indian history quickly learn that no aspect of US history is unconnected to the lives, politics, cultures, and struggles of the Indigenous peoples of these lands. In her book The Makings and Unmakings of Americans: Indians and Immigrants in American Literature and Culture, 1879–1924, Cristina Stanciu applies this insight to analyze literatures produced by immigrants from eastern and southern Europe alongside Native peoples’ self-representations during these same years. Stanciu poses immigrants and Native peoples as co-constitutive in the face of exclusions, of the meaning and boundaries of American identity, focusing on, in particular, themes of national belonging, citizenship, and literary and cultural production in relation to an overarching theme of Americanization during these periods. Reading the print and film production of Native people and European immigrants, Stanciu asks questions about the legal and cultural dynamics of “Americanization” and the visions of national belonging that arise out of these distinct perspectives. Examining these literatures in relation to each other, she argues, can underscore Indigeneity and immigration as “conditions central to American identity.”

papers.title: Kristalyn Marie Shefveland. Selling Vero Beach: Settler Myths in the Land of the Aís and Seminole .
papers.abstract: When US country music singer John Anderson wanted to draw attention to an environmental catastrophe brewing in Florida’s Everglades, he turned to a familiar figure in Florida history: Osceola. A Creek/Seminole leader treacherously captured under a flag of truce and woefully abused after death, Osceola has been—for white settlers and their descendants, at least—a romantic figure representing an authentic Florida untouched by modern development. In the song “Seminole Wind,” the narrator, sitting “on a cypress stump,” hears “the ghost of Osceola cry” at the damage wrought by the drainage of the Everglades. That Osceola never once set foot that far south in Florida hardly mattered: the song hit a nerve. It reached the number two position on Billboard magazine’s Hot Country chart and was one of the top-selling country records of 1992. Kristalyn Marie Shefveland’s creative new book does not include “Seminole Wind,” but her examination of the power of settler memories of Native Floridians helps explain why it and similar artifacts retain significant cultural power.

papers.title: Eric R. Schlereth. Quitting the Nation: Emigrant Rights in North America .
papers.abstract: Eric R. Schlereth’s book Quitting the Nation: Emigrant Rights in North America is a borderlands history of citizenship. American settlers in Spanish Louisiana, Mexican Texas, and British Canada may have been filibusterers and colonizers, but they were also expatriates who demanded freedom of movement and naturalization. Schlereth traces their struggles for “Emigration Right Citizenship” from the American Revolution to the eve of the Civil War (5). Across eight chapters and countless court cases and legislative battles, he recounts the stories of Norfolk sailors who swore oaths to Revolutionary France, Alabama slaveholders who pledged loyalty to the Mexican republic, and fugitive enslaved people who claimed rights in Upper Canada as the subjects of the British King. Historians usually separate these migrations into discrete contexts like Manifest Destiny and the Underground Railroad. Yet as Schlereth shows, diverse expatriates created a “common transnational legal culture” which defined citizenship as a volitional allegiance dependent on rights rather than a privilege of ethnic or religious belonging (65).

papers.title: Olivia Chilcote. Unrecognized in California: Federal Acknowledgment and the San Luis Rey Band of Mission Indians .
papers.abstract: Why are the San Luis Rey Band of Mission Indians the only Luiseño band in San Diego County not federally recognized by the United States? This question is asked by Olivia Chilcote in Unrecognized in California Federal Acknowledgement and the San Luis Rey Band of Mission Indians. Chilcote, a tribal member of the San Luis Rey tribe, tackles the topic of US federal recognition of California Indians and takes a personal journey to attempt to understand how her tribe fits into the fabric of federal recognition of the San Diego County tribes. She argues that her book is intended to draw attention to the topic of tribal legal status as a critical issue that impacts non-federally recognized California Indian tribes, and to show that California is the state with the most unrecognized tribes in the United States. Included in her study, then, is a discussion of San Luis Rey Band of Mission Indians’ legal status and its pursuit for federal recognition from the United States government through a historical lens (16).

papers.title: Patricio Simonetto. A Body of One’s Own: A Trans History of Argentina .
papers.abstract: In 1929, Virginia Woolf published two lectures in a book titled A Room of One’s Own, which has since become a classic of feminist thought. In it, the British author wrote the celebrated sentence “a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.” In other words, she asserted that women (in her case, cisgender women) could only write fiction if they had the material conditions to do so. The title of Patricio Simonetto’s masterful study, A Body of One’s Own: A Trans History of Argentina is a play on the title of Woolf’s work, changing “room” for “body”—the most important space of autonomy for those who, throughout Argentinian history, have not been afraid to challenge the sex they were assigned at birth. Woolf claimed, on behalf of other cisgender women, a room and money so they could write their books; the transgender women and men who dwell in Simonetto’s pages have to fight daily for the right to produce their bodies, to write their own lives as works of art worthy of respect and admiration.

papers.title: The Opiated Ocean
papers.abstract: Abstract In December 1853, British officials at Hong Kong amended the Passenger Acts to allow the substitution of “opium for tobacco” on voyages taking indentured laborers, or “coolies,” from China to the Caribbean. Authorities in the US, Cuba, and Peru followed suit by legalizing and mandating opium in what became known as la trata amarilla. By using fresh evidence to explore the genesis of this little-known cluster of regulations, this article explains the process through which Western officials authorized the provision of opium as a prophylactic against shipborne contagions, linking the circulation of opium with the global movement of Chinese labor. Whereas scholars have tended to present smoking opium either as a harmless restorative or as a tool of social control, this study calls attention to the prevalence of comorbidities between opium dependence and infectious illnesses such as cholera and typhoid to suggest that, above all, the drug served as a volatile resource necessitated by the exigencies of epidemic risk.

papers.title: Comment by Sebastian Conrad
papers.abstract: In April 1881, the Hawaiian King Kalākaua visited the mighty empire of the Qing. He attempted to convince Li Hongzhang, the minister of the Office of Foreign Affairs (Zongli Yamen), of their shared Asianness, despite their many differences. “We are Asian, as are you,” the surprised Li heard, and Kalākaua went on to explain the necessity of a common front against European imperialism. As related by Rebecca E. Karl, Li did not take either the warning or its carrier seriously. Allegedly, he had only learned from his secretary, on the morning of Kalākaua’s visit, that a country named Hawaii even existed. Li Hongzhang operated within the notion of a Chinese cultural sphere, a “common civilization” (tongwen) defined by script, Confucianism, and cultural tradition. Between the Great Middle Kingdom and the small, geographically and culturally distant Hawaii, there could be no similarities. But Kalākaua was unfazed. “[I] have warned the Japanese emperor, and now [I] am cautioning you, Li: if we were able to unite so as not to leave foreigners a single opening, would this not be the best way to arouse our brown Asian peoples? I eagerly await for this to happen.”

papers.title: Plume de nom: an experimental approach to handwriting analysis using OCR technology
papers.abstract: Abstract The following article presents a case study using neural-network-based Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology to revisit an unresolved problem regarding several manuscripts ascribed to the eminent Humanist Poggio Bracciolini. Granted OCR software is designed for the automatic transcription of text in a digital image, the experiment uses a side product produced by the OCR engine, the confidence score, to aid the comparison between different scripts or hands. The article first provides an outline of the conceptual background behind the technological approach and demonstrates the methodology on a set of medieval manuscripts; it then offers a description of the scholarly debate surrounding the exponents central to the case study, several manuscripts ascribed to the Humanist Poggio Bracciolini; and a report on the experiments conducted.

papers.title: Shaping Imperial Youth: French Youth and the Ligue Coloniale de la Jeunesse in the Late Nineteenth Century
papers.abstract: Abstract This article analyses the existence of an imperial youth in late-nineteenth-century France through the study of an association created for and by French young men in 1897, the Ligue coloniale de la jeunesse. Thanks to a thorough examination of a booklet edited by the Ligue comprising the names and information of 288 members, combined with other archival sources, it aims at writing a social history of the French imperial youth. In order to retrace the mindset and socialization of this youth, the article first scrutinizes the place of the Ligue in the colonial associative landscape and its recruitment, underlining the various profiles of its members. Second, it analyses the activities offered by the Ligue, divided into three main categories following its motto: propaganda, education, assistance. Lastly, it confronts the Ligue’s aim to shape colonial careers with the colonial prospects formulated by its members and their completion. In doing so, this article highlights the importance of the colonial world in the projections of French young men regarding their place in society, their training, and their professional future. More generally, it contributes to a better understanding of what youth meant during a time of thriving imperialism.

papers.title: The “Golden Age of Social Mobility” in Postwar Europe: Class Relations, Educational Expansion, and Political Stability in East and West
papers.abstract: Abstract This article seeks to shed fresh light on the “golden age of social mobility,” which lasted roughly from the mid-1940s to the early 1970s, in postwar Eastern and Western Europe. While much mythologized as a lost era of steadily increasing life chances and equality of opportunity in present-day Europe, historical research into social mobility in the postwar decades has only gotten off the ground in recent years. This article aims to formulate some general hypotheses for this budding research field by taking a pan-European approach, integrating the histories of social mobility in the communist East and the capitalist West. It focuses on three central dimensions of the golden age of social mobility. First, it analyzes how the golden age affected class relations, observing middle-class resilience and peasant advancement at the expense of the working class. Second, it explores how postwar educational expansion mostly benefited the same groups, while undercutting traditional working-class forms of training. Third, it questions the links between social mobility and postwar political stability, pointing to the dislocating effects that the golden age had even on some of its main beneficiaries. In doing so, the article challenges conventional wisdom on the consequences of the “drying up” of social mobility in Europe from the 1970s onwards.

papers.title: The Lives and Legacies of the British Gay Liberation Front Badge, 1970–2024
papers.abstract: Abstract The original and most commonly worn British Gay Liberation Front (GLF) badge often features in archives holding material on GLF, yet there is limited scholarship on why and with what effect this badge was worn. By combining archival research and oral histories, this article uses this badge to explore the experience and identity of GLF members both during GLF’s formal existence and in its afterlife. During GLF’s initial existence, between 1970 and 1973, the badge was a means of coming out to oneself and others. In turn, wearing the badge helped to construct and reinforce a new and distinct gay community. After the breakup of GLF, the badge continued to be worn and its imagery evoked to demonstrate allegiance to GLF and its ethos, whilst a tradition of gay badge-wearing emerged as a legacy of GLF. Overall, this badge was a major tool to signify identity and build community, not just during GLF’s initial existence, but up to the present day. Through its combination of extensive oral histories and archival research, this article provides new insights into how material culture can be used to understand social movements and their long-term impacts.

papers.title: Love and the Working Class: The Inner Worlds of Nineteenth Century Americans. By Karen Lystra
papers.abstract: This is a remarkable book; the product of decades-long research into archives (physical and digitized) to cast the widest net possible, it is a working-class counterpart to Lystra’s earlier study, Searching the Heart, which unearthed the “hidden world” of intimacy and romantic love revealed in middle-class love letters. Drawing upon over 5,000 letters produced by ordinary Americans from every region of the country between 1830 and 1880, the current book aims to illuminate the “intimate emotional lives of Americans who were poor, undereducated, and totally obscure” (5). Worried about a potential scarcity of sources, Lystra made an early decision to include in her research not only readily recognizable love letters, but other family letters and letters between friends, a decision that helps her avoid imposing middle-class emotional norms and “romantic intention[s]” (11) on the material while affording a broad view of the emotional landscape of working-class courtship, love and marriage. Focusing mainly on what David Henkin calls “the postal age,” a period marked by the rise of universally cheap mail that accompanied passage of the 1845 Post Office Act, Lystra takes up an era when “letters were written in a quantity never before seen in American history (5). Civil War correspondence is her most extensive body of evidence, since the war was a major catalyst for letter writing but also because letters from Civil War soldiers (unlike most letters) were preserved by families and found their way into institutional collections. Given the breadth of its archive, the study is localized less in large cities than in face-to-face communities of small villages and towns where most Americans (still 70% in 1880) lived, elaborating forms of “tribal” affiliation and collective attachment that, Lystra contends, defined ordinary Americans’ everyday lives and feelings. She extends her previous book by focusing centrally on race, including letters written by free African American as well as white working-class writers, highlighting some differences and many similarities in these groups’ epistolary efforts and forms of communal belonging. She is mindful of collection biases (e.g., those privileging soldiers’ letters over those written by their wives) that necessarily impact the story she tells.

papers.title: Digital humanities approach to analyzing the roles and military power of Supreme Commanders and Grand Coordinators in the Ming Dynasty: a computational analysis of Ming Shilu
papers.abstract: Abstract This article represents a digital humanities research endeavor that attempts to explore the roles and military power of Supreme Commanders and Grand Coordinators in the Ming Dynasty, employing computational analysis of the Ming Shilu. By leveraging a semi-supervised text classification framework to identify military paragraphs without needing prior annotation and generating heat maps based on location entities identified in the text, we discerned patterns correlating the presence of these officials with the incidence of military conflicts. We acknowledge the study's limitations, including potential misinterpretations due to the complexity of events and language used in the Ming Shilu. Despite these, our research illuminates the value of computational techniques in historical inquiries. The results underscore the complexity of Supreme Commanders' and Grand Coordinators' roles within local administration and military power structures and their impact on the political environment of the Ming Dynasty. This article advocates for future research to integrate diverse textual and data sources and incorporate additional digital methodologies, aiming for a deeper understanding of the Ming Dynasty's political landscape. This research significantly propels the utilization of digital analytical tools in historical research, offering a richer, more nuanced understanding of the past.

papers.title: The Political Crisis of British Keynesianism, 1973–1983
papers.abstract: Abstract In histories of Western political economy in the 1970s–1980s, Keynesianism is conventionally depicted as a victim of neoliberal ascendancy. Building on revisionist scholarship, this article looks beyond neoliberalism to explain the fate of Keynesianism in the transforming political economy of the United Kingdom in its global contexts. It explores a neglected case study: the intense controversies sparked by the Keynesian policy makers Wynne Godley and Francis Cripps. Responding to stagflation and strikes, Godley and Cripps demanded sweeping import controls to forestall mass unemployment and reverse Britain’s ‘decline’. They became celebrity economists, attracting admiration and opprobrium from government ministers and officials, political parties, journalists, and the City. Their arguments raised thorny questions, not just over economic policy, but also over Britain’s domestic statecraft and geopolitical relations after empire, during the Cold War, and inside the European Community. Revisiting these debates underscores the destabilizing impact of de-industrialization. It also reveals that (geo)political calculation determined the fate of Keynesian policy making more directly than neoliberal ideology. Godley and Cripps’s failure therefore illuminates a deeper political dilemma for fin-de-siècle Keynesians across Europe: upon which territorial order could they, and should they, exercise demand management as globalization accelerated? This question continues to shape Western politics in the twenty-first century.

papers.title: The Sacrifice of Thomas Cromwell
papers.abstract: Abstract The arrest of Thomas Cromwell in June 1540 and his inescapable execution on 28 July offered a chance for the Catholic powers of Christendom to hope and work for the end of the English schism. In 1540, Charles V proposed colloquies between the different confessions in his empire and in the same spirit conceived an alliance with Henry VIII. Both Charles and Henry practised to deceive, but two mysterious Imperial missions to England in July 1540, which the removal of Cromwell made possible, and the manner of Henry’s welcome of them, provide proof of the seriousness of their intent. The brief period between Cromwell’s arrest and his death was exploited by both Henry VIII and European powers to attempt reconciliation, or, at least, to temporize. This article analyses complex diplomatic reports to show how Cromwell’s fall assumed significance far beyond England, as new evidence of an abrupt realignment at a climacteric of European dynastic politics and Reformation diplomacy reveals.

papers.title: Sibling-texts keyword analysis: exploring topic and register keywords
papers.abstract: Abstract This article introduces a novel method for refining approaches to distant reading by proposing a procedure that categorizes prominent units (keywords) into two types: those pertinent to the topic and those associated with the genre/register of a text. This differentiation holds significant potential for more accurate modeling of topics and further applications in various domains of digital humanities. For example, register-related keywords may assist in various stylometric tasks, such as functional understanding of text groups (formed through clustering) that exhibit common stylistic traits, thus differentiating themselves from other groups or clusters within the discourse under scrutiny. In the initial step of the procedure, a set of texts with similar genre and register characteristics is identified; we term them ‘sibling texts’, and their similarity is determined using a model derived from multidimensional analysis. The next step involves conducting multiple parallel keyword analyses on these sibling texts and comparing them for keyword overlaps which mark the register relatedness. The test study on a corpus of Czech parliamentary speeches (Parlcorp) underscores the method’s ability to distinguish register-related and topic-related keywords, even in highly homogeneous corpora. The register-related keywords proved to be analytically very useful in substantiating the interpretation of parliamentary subregisters and advancing the understanding of the types of activities (administrative and procedural, deliberating and debating, and government policies) involved in parliamentary discourse.

papers.title: Making sugar out of opium: A narco-plantation regime in early modern Southeast Asia
papers.abstract: Abstract In the early modern period, while slavery became firmly entrenched in the Atlantic’s sugar economies, Southeast Asia witnessed the rise of distinct plantation regimes. Unlike their Atlantic counterparts, these Asian plantation regimes relied not on enslavement but on addiction — particularly to opium smoking — as a means to control and exploit plantation labour. Existing research has highlighted how such opium-driven regimes, along with Asian ‘coolie’ labour, proliferated globally in the nineteenth century following the abolitionist movement. Yet, their early modern origins in Southeast Asia remain largely unexplored. As a result, a deep plantation labour history outside the Atlantic World is still lacking, and researchers often continue to essentialize early modern plantation capitalism as inherently tied to slavery, while overlooking other, often more insidious, forms of plantation labour control that existed beyond the Atlantic. This article seeks to address this gap by examining the emergence and development of a narco-plantation regime on the sugar frontier of rural Batavia (Jakarta) from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth centuries.

papers.title: The purposeful workhouse of England’s Old Poor Law
papers.abstract: Abstract It has long been recognized that the English workhouses of the Old Poor Law era (1601-1834) were important precursors to institutions of the modern social services, but what kind of places were they? Characterized by eighteenth-century humanitarians as ‘pauper prisons’, and by early nineteenth-century political economists as ‘pauper palaces’, workhouses were undoubtedly varied institutions with hybrid regimes that included both care and work, nurture and discipline. Integrating recent work that has revealed much about material conditions and the agency of workhouse inmates, this article reassesses work in Old Poor Law workhouses, focusing especially on houses of industry in the county of Norfolk. We find a new perspective on these poor law institutions by recognizing their serious and sustained efforts to keep inmates working productively. Simply put, workhouses worked in the long eighteenth century. To house the infirm, embed work habits in the young, provide temporary shelter and confinement for the able-bodied or unsettled poor, parishes poured time and resources into their local and regional workhouses. In their multifaceted nature, workhouses most resembled not the prisons or hospitals to which they are sometimes compared, but rather the institution of the household-family that was the bedrock of society in the long eighteenth century.

papers.title: Virginia Prince, Robert Stoller and the Trans Feminist Intellectual History of the Sex/Gender Distinction
papers.abstract: Abstract Scholars have begun to genealogize the sex/gender distinction, pointing out that it was not a second-wave feminist invention, but in fact has its roots in the clinical research of US sexologists. Revisiting Prince’s rationale for distinguishing between sex and gender historicizes the inbuilt conservatism and weaponizable currency of the heuristic.

papers.abstract: Abstract This study explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in the preservation and innovation of intangible cultural heritage. papers.title: Connections and Community in Sixteenth-Century Verona
papers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the multiplicity of connections that were made between individuals from different trades and across the social hierarchy in sixteenth-century Verona. In the sixteenth century, Verona was a constituent part of the Venetian Empire with a large, diverse population. Each of the different neighborhoods of the city contained a heterogeneous mix of individuals, from the indigent poor to artisans, professionals, and the traditional elite, often living side by side. Through an exploration of three separate case studies from the courts of Verona, this article explores some of the ways in which these individuals socialized: at a card game, a dance, and a lottery. It is argued that connections were often made in spaces that transcended the public and private spheres, with domestic and workshop spaces being used to gather people from across the community. Despite concern from the authorities about the dangers of illicit gatherings, evidence within these cases suggests that there was an appetite among artisans of Verona to hold social occasions to earn extra income and to make new connections. Communities and culture were built among these wide and varied networks, and to understand more about everyday life and social ties in Renaissance Italy, it is important to look beyond traditional socio-economic and cultural boundaries.

papers.title: Improving text collations by local text resegmentation
papers.abstract: Abstract In almost all current approaches, the collation of large texts is applied to a fixed given segmentation of the two texts witnesses to be compared and consists of two consecutive steps. First, the segments of the two texts are aligned, and then the aligned segments are compared in detail. For larger manuscripts or books consisting of many pages, the segments are usually the paragraphs of the texts. When comparing two texts, where the second text is a revised version of the first, poor local alignments can arise. This occurs in places where paragraphs have been split into two smaller paragraphs to insert a new paragraph in between, or where several consecutive sentences have been moved from one paragraph to the previous or next paragraph. Most paragraph collation tools cannot handle these scenarios properly because they align each paragraph with at most one paragraph of the other text. In this paper, we discuss this problem in detail and present a heuristic for resegmenting the two texts to be compared in order to achieve a better collation.

papers.title: People’s Control and the Morality Quest of the Late Soviet Economy
papers.abstract: Abstract “People’s Control” was a centrally controlled institution of economic and social regulation widespread in state socialist countries and, particularly, in the Soviet Union between 1965 and 1991. The ideology underpinning the institution, however, insisted on its vernacular nature and framed its actions in terms of a democratic approach to economic problems. The offices of people’s control proliferated as part of a system that covered the whole country, empowering controllers with an impressive array of rights codified in high-level legislation. Endorsed by the system as moral and honest citizens, controllers inspected factories, farms, grocery shops, and other production and management units to reveal acts of crime, fraud, and low-quality work. Controllers denoted these phenomena as deviations from “normal” economic behavior and explained them in terms of a purported lack of morality. This article examines the place of morality in the late Soviet Union through the lens of political regulation of socio-economic relationships. People’s control, it argues, exposed a particular notion of morality as a range of norms and obligations for revealing and struggling against what the state deemed improper individual economic behavior. It served as one political attempt to mobilize society and tackle growing problems of the planned economy, which came to be described in terms of deviation. In the end, however, the ambit of people’s control remained largely limited to nominal public criticism.

papers.title: Patriots and Traitors in Revolutionary Cuba, 1961-1981 By Lillian Guerra
papers.abstract: In Patriots and Traitors in Revolutionary Cuba, 1961-1981, Lillian Guerra extends her long-term project to explain the post-1959 Cuban government’s authoritarian trajectory and to describe the political culture that enabled and emerged from it. Guerra attributes this process primarily to the leaders and agents of the Cuban government while attending to roles that ordinary Cubans played in facilitating and contesting it. papers.title: The Solidarity Economy: Nonprofits and the Making of Neoliberalism after Empire By Tehila Sasson
papers.abstract: Histories of humanitarianism have seen rapid development over the past two decades. papers.title: FROM ETERNITY TO APOCALYPSE: TIME, NEWS, AND HISTORY BETWEEN THE MUGHAL AND BRITISH EMPIRES, 1556–1785
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The eighteenth‐century origins of colonial orientalism in India spurred not just the translation of Indian texts but the production of interstitial histories, works that were forged in the intellectual culture of the Mughal Empire and created by individuals who explicitly sought to inform and influence their new colonial patrons. Turning to one such interstitial text, Muhammad Bakhsh Ashob's History of the Martyrdom of Farrukh Siyar and the Reign of Muhammad Shah (1782), which was produced at the behest of the East India Company orientalist Captain Jonathan Scott, this article explores the origins of the pervasive misconception that Mughal historical thought had faded to insignificance in the eighteenth century. It examines Ashob's representation of Mughal historiography for Scott in order to propose the existence of three discrete modes of historical writing over the course of the empire, modes that were each marked by a distinct temporal imagination. The article briefly discusses the first two modes—the “millenarian” mode of the late sixteenth century and the “eternal” mode of the seventeenth century—before focusing on the “apocalyptic” mode that became widespread in the early eighteenth century. This article argues that, against the influential and still widespread sense of the decline of historical production in that era, the Mughal bureaucracy (particularly its intelligence infrastructure) spurred the elaboration and efflorescence of historical writing outside the traditional ambit of the imperial court in a period of political turbulence. This article concludes by reflecting on the recasting of the apocalyptic sensibility of late‐Mughal historical thought into a vision of imperial decline by men, such as Scott, who were involved in the foundation of British colonial rule in India.

papers.title: Hungarian Refugees in the United States between Cold War Politics, Economic Growth, and Labour Demands, 1956–1958
papers.abstract: Abstract The resettlement of Hungarian refugees who had fled the Soviet invasion in 1956, from Austria to the United States, is generally perceived as a success story. Austria received extensive international support and most of the refugees were integrated quickly into American society. It thereby locates the movement of Hungarians within the broader context of Cold War history, economic growth, labour demand, and international relief.

papers.abstract: Abstract: Recent scholarship on the “rise of the West” has expanded in scope to military matters. On one side, traditionalists argue that Europe experienced more sustained innovations in “gunpowder technologies.” On the other, revisionists refute that developed areas of Eurasia—especially East Asia—were just as capable of deploying the same technologies. Valuable as the debate is, it has been waged without properly understanding the historical context of early modern technologies. This article draws on the history of technology and recognizes the “interpretive flexibility” of guns and ballistics science. First, it challenges existing comparative, quantitative indices of technological “productivity” by showing contextual differences in firearms use and production. papers.title: Beating the Odds: A Survival Story of Chinese Immigrants in Nicaragua
papers.abstract: Abstract: After the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was passed in the United States, anti-Chinese sentiment swept the Americas. Taking advantage of domestic and foreign assistanc, they avoided the grim fate that the Chinese elsewhere experienced. Drawing on archival documents in Managua and Taipei and oral histories from descendants of Chinese Nicaraguans, this paper traces the early development of the Chinese communities in Nicaragua. papers.title: The Refugee Political in the Age of Imperial Crisis, Decolonization, and Cold War, 1930s–1950s
papers.abstract: Abstract The three decades spanning the 1930s, '40s, and '50s witnessed the birth of the modern global state system, characterized by a protracted and tortuous transition from a world of empires to a world of nation-states. The demise of Nazi, British, and Japanese empires emancipated millions of people across the world. However, as old empires dissolved, new post-imperial states continued older colonial-origin forms of ethno-religious discrimination and ruling-class dominance, or invented novel hierarchies. Hence, this epoch was marked by catastrophic outbursts of racial violence, sectarian war, and genocide. If majoritarian nation-states were the privileged offspring of this transformation, then refugees were the unwanted issue. The national citizen and the refugee were co-created. Against their forced displacement and subalternization, refugees re-politicized their selves. We define this as ‘the refugee political’: refugees constructing themselves as political beings and building wide-ranging alliances – with churches, politicians, and entrepreneurs; with peasants, industrial workers, and feminists. They became ‘subaltern internationalists’, linking the Dachen Islands to the United States, and maritime Southeast Asia to India; connecting central European Jews to Australian women, or impoverished Indians to Soviet and Chinese communists. They created new forms of ‘refugee polis’ – political communities which were simultaneously local and daringly transnational.

papers.title: Enemy Alien Internment, Decolonization, and the Uprooted Elite of Treaty Port China under Japanese Occupation, 1941–1945
papers.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the process of decolonization carried out by wartime Japanese occupation authorities, exemplifying how it played out on the ground in 1940s China with a focus on the ‘uprooted elite’ – that is, the former Western colonists of the treaty ports. This culminated in a far-reaching general internment policy from early 1943 until mid- to late 1945, when a bittersweet Allied liberation shut Japan’s ‘Civil Assembly Centres’ down. Despite Western imperialists’ desires to resurrect racial privilege and recapture a modicum of their colonial possessions, the process of ethno-political and socio-economic relegation and replacement initiated loosely under the political schema of Imperial Japan’s ‘Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere’ proved to be largely irreversible as post-imperial domestic regimes advanced nationalization agendas. The uprooted elite were not merely passive objects enduring racial upheaval, removal, and ‘repatriation’. They navigated a complex and changing reality, exercising what rights they could in order to try to improve their lot. They benefited from humanitarian aid, administered by neutral Swedish and Swiss consular networks and the International Committee of the Red Cross operating on a global scale.

papers.abstract: Abstract The British Raj formally ended on 15 August 1947. Theorizing from their experiences of proletarianization, East Bengali refugees argued that decolonization had been incomplete. The postcolonial Indian state was a neocolonial state allied to Western imperialism. Refugees imagined themselves as part of a worldwide struggle between Anglo-American imperialism and Sino-Soviet-led socialist anti-imperialism. Refugees assembled in hundreds and thousands across the Indian state of West Bengal to overthrow regimes of big private property. They condemned the operations of money economy. They aimed to overcome capitalism. Inspired by Chinese communists, they built a vast confederal democracy uniting refugee camps and colonies – a ‘refugee polis’. This article offers a socially-contextualized intellectual history of this epic transformation, which delegitimized the postcolonial Indian state and dramatically drew the country, through struggles waged by refugees, into the tumult of the Cold War. papers.title: La fiesta de los negros: Una historia del antiguo carnaval de Buenos Aires y su legado en la cultura popular By Ezequiel Adamovsky
papers.abstract: Ezequiel Adamovsky’s La fiesta de los negros is a welcome addition to the flourishing literature on race in Argentina. Set in the city of Buenos Aires and drawing extensively on its rich periodical literature and visual archives, the book demonstrates how public festivities surrounding pre-Lenten Carnival in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries served “to process the acute class, gender, and ethno-racial tensions” accompanying the formation of modern Argentina, especially in the wake of mass European immigration. Carnival’s playful irreverence provided a space for Porteños (residents of the capital) of various backgrounds to bridge differences: men dressing as women, the rich as paupers, city-dwellers as rural gauchos, and whites as Indigenous or Black people. With its leveling impulses, the author argues, Carnival slowly eroded social boundaries and helped “forge a sense of belonging” that endured beyond the festivities. La fiesta de los negros focuses on the performances of Blackness that became a central feature of Carnival comparsas (troupes) by the late nineteenth century. Racial masquerade began in the mid-1860s with upper-class comparsas, whose members blackened their faces with burnt cork or makeup and sang songs in an Africanized form of Spanish with allusions to slavery (but whose costumes and musical styles remained European). The “mask of Blackness” was quickly adopted and modified by working-class comparsas that played stylized forms of candombe, an Afro-Argentine music and dance, and dressed in styles that evoked Africa or the slave past. These groups, which exploded in popularity in the 1880s and early 1890s, were typically comprised of either whites or Afro-Porteños, but the author suggests many were interracial. Building on the literature about what scholars have called “blackface” comparsas, but paying closer attention to the meanings of racial impersonation in these working-class troupes, Adamovsky offers a polemical argument: in Carnival’s spirit of unity and leveling, revelers used the “mask of Blackness” heretically (to reject dominant strictures of propriety or masculinity) and in an antiracist way (to affirm Black peoples and cultures, subvert racial hierarchy, or invoke interracial love).

Next, the article systematically analyses the course, extent and locations of technological unemployment produced by mechanization using more than 200 detailed qualitative sources. papers.title: Reckoning and Economic Life in Late Medieval England
papers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the practice of ‘reckoning’, a means of reciprocal accounting that becomes prominent in late-medieval England. Despite its critical importance to everyday exchange in this period, the practice has not received much attention from historians. The article argues that reckoning should be understood as a kind of economic infrastructure, one that performed some of the same functions as formal markets; and that as a concept, it was critical to the way that contemporaries delineated different forms of economic exchange. I proceed by tracing the emergence of reckoning from a convergence of institutional accounting, increasing technical literacy, and the proliferation of written accounts from the thirteenth century onwards. I go on to argue that as a tool of economic exchange, reckoning was particularly well-suited to the straitened economic conditions of the fifteenth century, in particular the shortage of coin, the retrenchment of formal markets, and the pervasive use of credit. I then examine three case studies in which reckoning went ‘wrong’, in order to explore the ideals of exchange relations on which it drew. In conclusion, I suggest that reckoning can help us to frame some of the broader transformations in economic culture in post-plague England.

papers.title: Black Elders: The Meaning of Age in American Slavery and Freedom By Frederick C. Knight
papers.abstract: In this engaging and timely study, Frederick C. Knight explores the meanings of old age, and the lived experiences of Black elders, in American slavery and freedom. It is, in some senses, an expansive study, taking readers from coastal West and West Central Africa in the age of the Atlantic slave trade, through antebellum slavery to Reconstruction and post-emancipation struggles in the U.S. But it is also a tightly focused one. Chapter one has a wide-ranging treatment of West and West Central Africa, but other chapters tend to prioritize a particular region, with Virginia and North Carolina particularly well represented in the sections on antebellum slavery (chapters two and three); others revolve around or return to select case studies, as with the focus on Philadelphia’s free Black communities when examining post-emancipation developments (chapters four and five). The book makes important contributions on age and generational power dynamics within West and West Central African polities, and Knight considers how age affected the wider structures of, and experiences in, Atlantic and colonial slavery. There are nuanced observations about the extractive violence of antebellum enslavers and the multi-generational support networks enslaved people crafted to navigate this hostile environment, and Knight provides original insight into the complex politics of emancipation and Reconstruction through the lens of age and generation.
