papers.title: Claire Bourhis-Mariotti. Wanted! A Nation! Black Americans and Haiti, 1804–1893 .
papers.abstract: Wanted! A Nation! Black Americans and Haiti, 1804–1893, authored by Claire Bourhis-Mariotti and translated by C. Jon Delogu, offers an extensive exploration of the complex relationship between Black Americans and Haiti during the 19th century. Originally published in French in 2016 as L’union fait la force: les Noirs américains et Haïti, 1804–1893, this translated edition sheds light on Haiti’s pivotal role in the formation of Black American identity amid a tumultuous era of racial oppression and revolutionary fervor. We have Ronald Angelo Johnson, who recently coedited In Search of Liberty: African American Internationalism in the Nineteenth-Century Atlantic World (2021), to thank for this translation, as he recognized Bourhis-Mariotti’s important contributions to the historiography with this monograph. It is then no surprise that he wrote the forward for the translation, published by the University of Georgia Press in 2023. Bourhis-Mariotti, a distinguished professor of African American history in France, brings to light the significance of Haiti as a symbol of hope and liberation for Black Americans. Amid the backdrop of white fear stemming from Haiti’s revolutionary history and strategic location for the “New World” colonial project, Haiti emerged as a beacon of Black independence and self-governance. The author meticulously examines how Haiti served as not only a physical refuge but also a source of political inspiration and cultural exchange for Black Americans. Namely, the author shows how Haiti served as “a promised land,” an example of Black liberation and self-government to follow, a source of political inspiration, or the very place where the “political regeneration” of the “Black race” would happen (xiv). Even for Black Americans who were never able to travel to Haiti, the knowledge of its existence as a free Black republic was enough to inspire both free and enslaved Black Americans to hold on to the possibility of Black freedom in the West, which was built off the interrelated dispossession and genocide of Indigenous groups and violent enslavement of Black bodies.

papers.title: Ned Blackhawk. The Rediscovery of America: Native Peoples and the Unmaking of U.S. History .
papers.abstract: Ned Blackhawk seeks to lay the foundation for a new paradigm of both Native American history and American history. He intends this new model to demonstrate how these histories are inextricably linked and how “it is impossible to understand the United States without understanding its Indigenous history” (4). Likewise, settler colonial policies and practices have deeply shaped Native American societies. Indigenous people have always been central to American history, Blackhawk argues, but scholars of American history have often ignored the significance of Native American nations in the shaping of US history. Blackhawk also works to break down common mythologies about American history and Indigenous peoples. The Rediscovery of America: Native Peoples and the Unmaking of U.S. History is a broad, ambitious project that excels in its task. A work of synthesis of the last few decades of scholarship in Native-newcomer relations, Native American and Indigenous studies, and settler colonial studies, The Rediscovery of America lends a critical eye to this work while also attending to the erasures common in American history. Covering five hundred years of history from the 1490s to the end of the twentieth century, Blackhawk splits his narrative into two parts composed of six chapters each. Part 1 examines the extreme violence in the making of early America to the foundation of the United States. Part 2 focuses on the fight of Indigenous nations to maintain their sovereignty in the face of ongoing violence and detrimental federal policies.

papers.title: David Parrott. 1652: The Cardinal, the Prince, and the Crisis of the ‘Fronde’ .
papers.abstract: French historian Denis Richet wrote that the Fronde was “an infantile disease of absolutism.” He thus placed this episode of civil unrest, which shook the Kingdom of France from 1648 to 1652, within an inexorable chain of events leading up to the reign of Louis XIV. The frondeurs, as its instigators were called, have generally been portrayed as either representatives of retrograde forces concerned first and foremost with defending their privileges against the rise of the state, or as visionaries anticipating the revolutionary chaos of the late eighteenth century. It is also clear that they were doomed to fail in light of the French government’s march toward modernity initiated by Cardinal Richelieu and then continued by Cardinal Mazarin, Anne of Austria’s chief minister when she served as regent for her young son Louis XIV. This failure perhaps explains why historians have shown little interest in the latter stages of the revolt. And yet, according to David Parrott, the year 1652 was a “distinct historical moment with decisive and lasting consequences” that recalls to mind the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire. Neither Mazarin nor the great nobles who led the struggle against him were driven by a deep concern for the values that had guided France for centuries or for the future of France and its people, starting with the king and members of his nobility. Rather, much like Augustus and his adversaries, they “systematically hollowed out the values and ideas of the Republic, maintaining only a veneer of outward constitutional forms under which factional and personal interests dominated political decision-making and the allocation of power and resources” (9). The Fronde essentially died out in 1652, giving way to a newfound stability, but the words and actions that characterized those four tumultuous years continued to make their influence felt. And not in a good way, for they were words and actions “from which the recourse to service, loyalty, and obligation was notably absent” (10).

papers.title: Ran Segev. Sacred Habitat: Nature and Catholicism in the Early Modern Spanish Atlantic .
papers.abstract: In Sacred Habitat: Nature and Catholicism in the Early Modern Spanish Atlantic, Ran Segev challenges the view that Catholic clerics of the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Spanish Empire were close-minded fanatics hostile to science. In this intellectual history, Segev finds friars, monks, and one nun who were curious about the natural world, intent on systematically understanding it, and creative in advancing interpretations of it. Segev focuses on three fields over four chapters: cosmography, descriptive geography, and zoology. The final chapter on zoology shows the intellectual stakes most clearly with the most convincing evidence. In it, Segev examines how Jesuit José de Acosta and Dominican Gregorio de Garcia squared the existence of previously unknown species from the Americas with their belief in the biblical account of Noah’s ark. Acosta in Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590) argued that the endemic species of animals in the Americas that were saved in the ark later migrated to the New World over a land bridge. The implication was that they became extinct in the Old World, an innovative idea to explain natural processes but one that contradicted Thomas de Aquinas’s assertion that the natural world reflected perfect divine providence (a place for every animal and every animal in its place). Realizing this shortcoming, Garcia in Origen de los Indios (1607) defended fellow Dominican Aquinas by positing instead that angels transported the animals. These creatures later diverged from Old World varieties, Garcia wrote, “due to the disposition of the land, and the particular influences and constellation of the heavens” (147). This conclusion pioneered an explanation for speciation. Here, as with the rest of the book, Segev demonstrates that these clerics were mostly concerned with upholding received theology. Nonetheless, even as orthodox Catholics, they considered some natural evidence and advanced new scientific reasoning.

papers.title: Adrian Masters. We, the King: Creating Royal Legislation in the Sixteenth-Century Spanish New World .
papers.abstract: In We, the King: Creating Royal Legislation in the Sixteenth-Century Spanish New World, Adrian Masters provides a fine example of the renewed interest in legal history and the working of the imperial government. While Masters examines the production of laws in the Spanish Empire, he also casts light on the origins of the caste system and the creation of the racial group composed of mestizas and mestizos (those of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent). Masters converses with significant literature and combines many illuminating examples into a stimulating analysis. He starts out by telling the fascinating protest of the Peruvian mestizos. Originally, the Augustinian friar Rodrigo de Loaysa helped to define this group by suggesting in 1578 that the crown should ban the ordination of mestizos in Peru. The crown approved the petition in the same year. An outcry ensued in Peru. In 1582, mestizo candidates for the priesthood began gathering signatures to rescind the policy; 149 students in Lima, Cuzco, and elsewhere signed off on the petition. Subsequently, the scribe-notary Pedro Rengifo was put in charge, and he claimed hyperbolically, as was common in the empire, that he had the power of attorney to represent ten thousand mestizos of various kingdoms in this matter. Yet not all petitioners were fully aboard to be labeled “mestizos” because of the term’s discriminatory overtones. Students in Arequipa, for instance, rather called themselves montañeses (those from the mountains), akin to the regional and influential group from Burgos in northern Spain. Rengifo also collected documents from bishops, clergymen, and local elites to strengthen the petition. He left Peru and probably arrived in Panama late in May 1584, catching the fleet sailing to Spain, which escaped French and Ottoman-allied pirates near Portugal. After arriving in Seville in September, the Council of the Indies heard him in February of the next year. Then Rengifo was summoned into the palace and “perhaps the bedchamber itself” for a personal audience with King Philip II. Rengifo continued to move the petition along, and finally the king signed off on a new communication in 1588, ordering equal treatment of mestizas and mestizos with Spaniards.

papers.title: Tobias Becker. Yesterday: A New History of Nostalgia .
papers.abstract: Nostalgia, we all know, comes dressed in sepia. In Yesterday: A New History of Nostalgia, Tobias Becker uncovers it for us in black and white, like a photo negative: not the thing itself—emotion, disease, style, or whatever it may be—but rather a sprawling “nostalgia discourse,” or what is said about nostalgia. This is a book about “how and why the term nostalgia is used” (232), or has been used since the 1960s in the United States, United Kingdom, and, to a lesser extent, Germany and France. These uses have also tended to be negative, but in the pejorative sense of the word, bordering on insult. Few proudly claim to be nostalgic or like to be labeled as such; on the contrary, many are experts at telling others that they are stuck in the past. Herein lies the originality of Becker’s approach: Nostalgia is like modernity’s black hole, the “counterpart or antithesis to progress” (5) that we all need, whether to quietly comfort ourselves in the face of change or imply that we, unlike others, can still change for the better. (No wonder Derrida was interested in it). Its gravitational pull has been hard to ignore since the 1960s, Becker argues, when the teleology of progress came under intense scrutiny. It is not so much the History that is New here, but Nostalgia itself: The thing is in fact older and harks back to the late 17th century, when the term was first coined and defined as a deadly form of homesickness. Nostalgia has always been in dialectical tension with capitalist modernity and for 200 years people succumbed to it when forced to leave their homes (by war, migration, enslavement). But between the 19th and 20th centuries we learned to cope with nostalgic yearning and rearticulate it in time—as a lost past—rather than space. Cope with, and eventually indulge, for as Becker points out, nostalgia became a household word after the Second World War—its success rivaled only by the vitriol of its detractors.

papers.title: Christopher Perreira. Archiving Medical Violence: Consent and the Carceral State .
papers.abstract: In his illuminating book Archiving Medical Violence, Christopher Perreira examines racialized forms of state-sanctioned medical violence in US colonial, imperial, and national contexts. He reads US racial formations through medicine and public health and criminalized bodies and diseases to highlight the fault lines of scientific and national progress in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, arguing that public health and security have borrowed from each other to “inform the production of racialized discourses that give meaning to the figure of the prisoner-patient” (22). Perreira understands medicine and public health as foundational to US settler colonialism, racial capitalism, and cultural politics. He insists that the devaluation and continual (un)making of criminalized, racialized prisoner-patients create the conditions for their necromantic revival and revaluation in triumphalist medicine and public health. The book lies at the intersection of Indigenous, race, ethnic, gender, carceral, and science and technology studies, and cultural theory. Perreira contributes to these fields not just by scrutinizing criminality in a eugenic register (a longstanding approach in historical scholarship) but by tracing how criminality has been defined and activated in medicine and public health and how the meanings of violence in these venues have changed and become normalized over time. Cast in the mold of “the anachronistic (re)turn” in many recent history-informed interdisciplinary studies, Archiving Medical Violence has no qualms about darting back and forth between past and present. Such an approach offers entry points to think about the undercurrents structuring historical racial inequalities, harmful legacies, and contemporary national reckonings (2, 20–21).

papers.title: Daren E. Ray. Ethnicity, Identity, and Conceptualizing Community in Indian Ocean East Africa .
papers.abstract: Ethnicity looms large over East African history and scholarship. While scholars reinventing the discipline of African history after the fall of European colonialism sought to prove that African ethnicities—rendered as “tribes”—were colonial inventions, the lived legacies of colonial tribalism have ensured the endurance of ethnicity as a category of inquiry. This is particularly true of scholarship on Kenya, where “ethnic politics” continues to define election cycles in the twenty-first century. Yet Daren E. Ray’s book, Ethnicity, Identity, and Conceptualizing Community in Indian Ocean East Africa, takes a novel approach to this familiar topic. Most impressive is Ray’s commitment to a longue durée approach; extending its analysis over at least two millennia, the book is an important corrective to a historiography primarily concerned with the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Interested in a pre-ethnic past, Ray turns to historical linguistics to frame his project around speech communities—specifically those who would come to speak Sabaki languages (including Kiswahili and Chimijikenda)—and the “schemas” that they assembled. Schemas, for Ray, are a dynamic alternative to the more static category of cultures, “shared mental maps” that provide a “reservoir of concepts, ideas, and resources” from which historical actors build categorizations, communities, and political claims (20, 50). By framing his book around Sabaki schemas, Ray seeks not only to conceptualize modern ethnicities as the result of “the incremental elaboration of ancestral strategies” but also to advance a “cis-Oceanic” approach that, by incorporating the hinterland into a broader “littoral” society, challenges coastal exceptionalism (5). Temporally and spatially ambitious in scope, then, a major strength of the book is the interdisciplinary method it necessarily employs.

papers.title: Enrique Rodríguez-Alegría. How to Make a New Spain: The Material Worlds of Colonial Mexico City .
papers.abstract: It is common knowledge that the encounter between Europeans and Indigenous groups in the Americas in the sixteenth century had disastrous consequences for local populations. Indigenous people were killed in great numbers, and colonialism led to a considerable loss of Indigenous languages, customs, and systems of knowledge. Yet despite this unprecedented destruction, a functioning society and new capital city were established soon after the fall of Tenochtitlan, the seat of the Mexica Empire, and we know considerably less about how this happened. It is this gap in our knowledge that Enrique Rodríguez-Alegría wishes to fill with his thought-provoking new monograph, How to Make a New Spain: The Material Worlds of Colonial Mexico City, which focuses on the first eighty years of colonial rule in Mexico (ca. 1521–1600). In this book, instead of centering the obvious conflicts that existed in colonial society, Rodríguez-Alegría shifts our attention to the interethnic alliances that made it possible to establish systems of exchange, build infrastructure, and create domestic livelihoods in the aftermath of the fall of the Mexica Empire. The work follows in the footsteps of scholars like James Lockhart, Matthew Restall, and Barbara Mundy, among others.

papers.title: Paula S. DeVos. Compound Remedies: Galenic Pharmacy From the Ancient Mediterranean to New Spain .
papers.abstract: This is an ambitious book and the program that it sets out is laudable. It opens with an account of a pharmacy in Mexico City from 1775 (the inventory, translated in an appendix, is a fascinating source for the history of medicine). Paula DeVos then relies on the inventory’s list of simples (singular natural substances), compounds (remedies from multiple substances), and distillations (remedies derived from chemical processing) to launch an exploration of pharmaceutical theory and practice—in terms of materials, techniques, and textual authorities—from the Roman period up through the 18th century. In one sense, the book is a reception history of Galen’s thought; in another sense, Compound Remedies is a global history, examining the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East before shifting focus to the early modern Spanish Empire and the changes (or lack thereof) to the medical landscape wrought by colonial apothecaries. DeVos argues successfully that pharmacy offers a compelling example of both continuity and malleability of thought—indeed, that as a tradition, it was particularly unusual in being constantly “in transit” across regions, cultures, and empires (15). Few monographs have attempted a longue durée study of herbal remedies or of Galenic transformation through to the modern period (Owsei Temkin’s 1973 Galenism appears on page 16 as the still-authoritative work). The great strength of the book is that it frames Mexican apothecaries as simply yet another peak in a long trajectory of the adaptation of pharmaceutical knowledge, calling out historians of science for frequently treating colonial medicine solely in terms of its derivation from, or challenge to, European norms.

papers.title: Said Amir Arjomand. Messianism and Sociopolitical Revolution in Medieval Islam .
papers.abstract: Messianism and Sociopolitical Revolution in Medieval Islam is a fascinating and ambitious book. Said Amir Arjomand, who several decades ago produced insightful and historically grounded studies of the Islamic Revolution in Iran and its intellectual roots in Persian political thought and Shi′i notions of religious authority, recently turned to the classical Islamic period and early Islamic political institutions. His goal is “to enrich political theory and the sociology of revolution by a historicized analysis of messianism” (1) from its roots in pre-Islamic developments through the fourteenth century of the Common Era. The study is timely, he suggests, because Islamism, shaped by an apocalyptic and millennial worldview, has replaced the revolutionary model of 1789 and its subsequent refinement in Marxism-Leninism as the dominant revolutionary ideology of our time and “the engine of [contemporary] history” (4). After an introductory chapter that discusses theories of revolution and provides a summary of the book’s narratives and arguments, Arjomand turns to his topic. Recent scholarship on early Islamic history has argued that Islam must be understood not as a sudden break, as the startling eruption of a new historical force, as an earlier generation of Orientalists had assumed; rather, it should be viewed as a continuation of ideas, practices, and trends already present in the Mediterranean and Iranian worlds in Late Antiquity. The caliphate, for example, has been recast as the culmination of late Roman and Iranian caesaropapism. Arjomand worries that this approach has “minimized the distinctiveness of the emerging Islamic civilization and denied the revolutionary break it constituted in world history” (24). On the contrary, he says, we should consider “the rise of Islam as the great apocalyptic revolution of Late Antiquity” (24).

papers.title: Chris Manias. The Age of Mammals: Nature, Development, & Paleontology in the Long Nineteenth Century .
papers.abstract: Dinosaurs play an exaggerated role in the modern psyche, and one can certainly understand why. They are fearsome, mysterious, and charismatic creatures, and they are seemingly ubiquitous. From Saturday morning cartoons to summer blockbusters, dinosaurs have captured the public imagination like few other categories of life. Little surprise that many of the best works in the history of paleontology examine this vibrant interface between dinosaurs and the public, including Caitlyn Wylie’s recent volume on fossil preparators and Elizabeth D. Jones’s work on ancient DNA. In his new book, The Age of Mammals: Nature, Development, & Paleontology in the Long Nineteenth Century, historian Chris Manias writes that while the focus on dinosaurs has borne considerable fruit, it has also resulted in a dearth of scholarship on the equally fascinating role that mammals have played in the history of paleontology. In contrast to our modern obsession with dinosaurs, visitors to metropolitan museums and readers of popular science books were primarily interested in mammals in the 19th century. Like dinosaurs, prehistoric mammals were distant and inaccessible, but, unlike dinosaurs, they were simultaneously proximate and coeval, and thus uniquely instructive. Constructing the history of mammals required diverse bodies of knowledge and expertise, and scientists and scholars from a variety of fields and disciplines worked to excavate deep time in general, and the Age of Mammals in particular. As a measure of geological time, the Age of Mammals spans the Tertiary and Quaternary periods, which corresponds to the past 65 million years or so. As the author astutely notes, this novel timeframe necessarily entails different narrative beats from other chronological frameworks, including the Age of Dinosaurs or the Age of Humans, and it thus offers different lessons.

papers.title: Muriam Haleh Davis. Markets of Civilization: Islam and Racial Capitalism in Algeria .
papers.abstract: Among its other achievements, colonialism was—and remains—adept at explaining away the effects of the violence and immiseration it inflicted as the natural, racial defects of the populations it subjugated and dispossessed. The “lazy native,” inclined to do no more work than was necessary for survival, and the “imprudent native,” incapable of hedging against the vicissitudes of nature or appreciating the benefits of credit, were stock images of colonial common sense. The belief that something inherent to Islam predetermined Muslims to such recalcitrance in the face of colonial capitalism would prove enduring. In this short but ambitiously wide-ranging book, Markets of Civilization, Muriam Haleh Davis shows how, from the mid-nineteenth century onward, Algeria’s economy was imagined, written about, governed, and planned with reference to a pervasive “racial regime of religion” that saw Algerians’ lives and livelihoods as determined by their being Muslim. Such Muslim-ness had less to do with belief or ritual practice than with a putative orientation to time, labor, and value that was inherited and immutable, dyed into culture, psychology, and physiognomy. The condition of homo islamicus was thus racialized: Racial capitalism in Algeria rested on a conception of religion that, Davis argues, was “a particular expression of racial thought.” According to this durable body of French thought, homo islamicus was all but impervious to the improving and value-creating efforts of commerce, civilization, and capitalism. Homo islamicus, of course, has never actually existed: But actually-existing Muslims would find themselves, for over a century, defined and objectified by a wide range of French technologies of rule—from legislation and welfare provision to the social sciences and psychological warfare—as the binary opposite of an equally imaginary Western homo economicus, whose rational, future-oriented pursuit of progress they were summoned to share while at the same time being denied the means of access to it.

By the mid-nineteenth century, the enslaved population had reached over four hundred thousand people, almost half of the island’s inhabitants. papers.title: Patricia Fortini Brown. The Venetian Bride: Bloodlines and Blood Feuds in Venice and its Empire .
papers.abstract: For more than four decades Patricia Fortini Brown has been one of the leading scholars of early modern Venice. An art historian by trade, she has produced a steady stream of important works that have fundamentally shaped our understanding of the history of Venetian art, from Venetian Narrative Painting in the Age of Carpaccio (1987) to Venice and Antiquity: The Venetian Sense of the Past (1996) to Private Lives in Renaissance Venice: Art, Architecture and the Family (2004). Her interdisciplinary explorations of Venetian art during its early modern highpoint have always overlayed deeply with their cultural and social historical milieus, and with The Venetian Bride, history moves to center stage. The bride at the center of the book is Giulia Bembo, who in 1549, at age eighteen, married Count Girolamo Della Torre. Giulia belonged to one of the most illustrious Venetian patrician families, whose most noteworthy sixteenth-century member was Giulia’s great-uncle, the distinguished Venetian humanist, historian, and cardinal, Pietro Bembo (1470–1547). Her husband came from an important feudal family from the region of Friuli, the often-restive northeastern frontier of the Terraferma, the Venetian mainland state. The marriage was celebrated against the backdrop of the decades-long vendetta between the Della Torre and another powerful Friulian feudal family, the Savorgnan. Indeed, the marriage was a rushed affair because the bridegroom was under a sentence of exile for his role in avenging the murder of his father, and immediately after the ceremony, the couple set sail for the island of Crete, one of the jewels of Venice’s maritime territories, the Stato da mar. With this union, the Della Torre gained kinship ties to a powerful and influential Venetian family that might assist them in their rivalries, and the Bembo gained an alliance with a wealthy Terraferma family with an established noble pedigree.

papers.title: Daniel H. Usner. Native American Women and the Burdens of Southern History .
papers.abstract: Readers are introduced to several “burdens” in Daniel H. Usner’s book Native American Women and the Burdens of Southern History. Among these are the literal burdens that Indigenous women carried as they moved through the Lower Mississippi Valley. Women held their burdens in rivercane baskets they had crafted themselves. Even as the reasons for women’s mobility changed from the colonial period through the early twentieth century—they were traders, migrants, refugees, itinerant laborers, peddlers, craftswomen, travelers, and diplomats—their baskets remained a constant. Traditionally, Usner explains, both Southern observers and Southern historians have pointed to women’s production, use, and sale of rivercane baskets as a sign of their diminished status within Indigenous communities (i.e., drudgery). Similarly, Southerners saw the persistence of Indigenous women’s basketmaking into the twentieth century as evidence of the decline and eventual extinction of Indigenous nations. Usner emphatically disagrees with these interpretations. To him, rivercane baskets represent neither drudgery nor decline but “the role that Indigenous women’s work and knowledge has played in shaping and reshaping relations with non-native southerners across centuries of time” (6).

papers.title: Yunxiang Gao. Arise, Africa! Roar, China! Black and Chinese Citizens of the World in the Twentieth Century .
papers.abstract: Arise, Africa! Roar, China! is an original, intelligent, and deeply researched book. In five rich chapters, it traces the lives and interactions of three well-known 20th-century African American towering figures—the scholar W. E. B. Du Bois, the singer Paul Robeson, and the poet and novelist Langston Hughes (as well as Du Bois and Robeson’s wives, Shirley Graham and Eslanda)—and of two much less known, yet remarkable, Chinese individuals, the journalist and musician Liu Liangmo and the Sino-Afro-Caribbean Sylvia Si-lan Chen (with whom Hughes had a tormented on-and-off sentimental relationship). Five “citizens of the world” (1), as the author Yunxiang Gao rightly defines them, whose travels, loves, dramas, and sometimes political and intellectual inconsistencies are colorfully and precisely reconstructed and narrated. The book possesses at least four significant merits. First, it exemplifies transnational history at its finest. The central theme of the narrative is of course race, serving as the pivotal element around which the story revolves. The five (plus two) protagonists, each in their own way, endeavored to represent and cultivate a global, anti-imperialist alliance among people of color. This pan-racial ambition underpinned their actions and shaped their interactions and collaborations. Si-lan Chen, with her distinctive biography, epitomized and embodied this ideal. During his legendary visit to Beijing University in 1959, for example, Du Bois urged China to recognize its status as “colored” and to understand “what a colored skin in this modern world subjects its owner” (11). In his final years, Du Bois extended his well-known philosophy of Pan-Africanism to encompass a Chinese-centered Pan-Asianism. This represented a significant shift for a man whose pan-racial ambitions had, in the 1930s, led him to uncritically embrace Japan’s regional hegemonic designs, blinding him to Tokyo’s imperial policies and inter-Asian racial hierarchies. Robeson’s enthusiasm for Chinese history and culture led him to diligently study the language. With the assistance of Liu Liangmo, he recorded an album in 1941 featuring Chinese resistance and folk songs, which included “Chee Lai,” the future national anthem of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), later renamed “March of the Volunteers.” Strongly inspired by his experience in segregated Shanghai, where “he felt he belonged with the Chinese as fellow ‘colored people’” (253), Hughes’s radical turn in the 1930s was enthusiastically acclaimed within Chinese leftist intellectual and academic circles. His works were translated in prominent journals, reflecting an effort to draw a new, global color line that connected Black internationalism with Sino–African American collaboration. This effort found an ideal environment during the Cold War, with the PRC emerging as a receptive partner and interlocutor.

papers.title: David Maxwell. Religious Entanglements: Central African Pentecostalism, the Creation of Cultural Knowledge, and the Making of the Luba Katanga .
papers.abstract: In a 1994 article, the missiologist Dana Robert explained phases of missions history scholarship and identified various scholarly strategies to disrupt a prior focus on changes initiated by Western Protestant authorities. Robert’s article lays out the context for the movement now known as World Christianity and the academic challenge behind David Maxwell’s newest book. Religious Entanglements: Central African Pentecostalism, the Creation of Cultural Knowledge, and the Making of the Luba Katanga explores the historical roots of World Christianity through the dramatic expansion of Pentecostalism in the Belgian Congo. He analyzes factors in this religious process that did not originate with the Western missionaries and were not controlled by colonial authorities. Maxwell also demonstrates research strategies that are not constricted by dichotomies of success or failure in terms of Christian evangelization. As the subtitle indicates, the chapters examine contested definitions of what it meant to call oneself “Luba” and what type of lifestyle that entailed. Yet Maxwell also explores shifts in how the Pentecostal leaders of the early twentieth-century Congo Evangelistic Mission (CEM) were perceived by regional Africans, by other missionaries, and by Belgian officials. The book sets innovative models of how religious histories can analyze Africans’ impacts on Christian ministries during the colonial period.

papers.title: Reshaad Durgahee. The Indentured Archipelago: Experiences of Indian Labour in Mauritius and Fiji, 1871–1916 .
papers.abstract: Reshaad Durgahee’s book The Indentured Archipelago is an excellent and superbly researched addition to the global historical scholarship on indenture. Indenture is most often studied in the context of the rapidly expanding British Empire in the nineteenth century. Initial scholarly conversations about indenture focused on whether indenture was a “new system of slavery.” In this book, the conversation is reframed from the perspective of historical geography, attending to questions of spatiality, mobility, and agency. Introducing the idea of “subaltern careering,” Durgahee traces how indentured laborers and colonial administrators moved between Britain and its colonies, and also between colonies in Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. These are “remigrants” whose lives and careers the book maps. They were indentured laborers who chose to re-indenture themselves to go to a different colony, and those who were “term-expired” and were entitled to return to India or receive a piece of land in the colony. The result is a sweeping account of what Durgahee terms “the wider geographies of Indian indenture.” It successfully reveals both the real and imagined extent of the indenture experiment in the long nineteenth century.

papers.title: Lucia Carminati. Seeking Bread and Fortune in Port Said: Labor Migration and the Making of the Suez Canal, 1859–1906 .
papers.abstract: In Seeking Bread and Fortune in Port Said, Lucia Carminati offers an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of the laborers, loiterers, migrants, and transients who passed through the city starting in the middle of the nineteenth century, some held there by choice, imprisonment, or death, and others merely stopping for a few days or weeks before moving on once more to other nodes in the networks of mobility that crisscrossed the Mediterranean. Carminati’s book traces “the successive metamorphoses, from the halcyon days in the early 1860s to the twilight of the 1890s and beyond, of the ‘small nook, remote and neglected’ that Port Said originally was and that, at some point, it reverted to being” (458–9). It does so by paying close attention to a multitude of incidents recorded in various archives, reports, or travelogues, involving coalheavers, prostitutes, unwed couples, and unaccompanied children. These otherwise unremarkable individuals are brought to light vividly as Carminati dwells on the details of their lives that the historical record brings into sharp focus for a moment. Such details were usually made salient by a disruption of the moral, legal, urban, or productive regimen the authorities wished to impose: an incident of public drunkenness, an accusation of theft, forged identity papers, a murder, workers absconding from their posts, or complaints about the rowdy behavior of a café’s patrons. Carminati teases from a host of minor events the texture of life in a city made of and by people on the move: “The migrant labor roaming Egypt and the Mediterranean in the second half of the nineteenth century had disparate and uneven modes of mobility to hand. These, and the attendant formation of an unequal migrant society in Port Said, undergirded the Suez Canal’s genesis and its first half century of operation” (471).

papers.title: Jamie Martin. The Meddlers: Sovereignty, Empire and the Birth of Global Economic Governance .
papers.abstract: Jamie Martin’s book The Meddlers has a straightforward premise: to correct a common misperception. The history of “global economic governance”—initiatives to control and guide political economies justified by international cooperation—tends to be viewed as an outcome of the Second World War. Our collective memory in economic history jumps forward from coercive gunboat diplomacy for debt repayment in the late 19th century, supposedly outlawed by the 1907 Drago Porter Doctrine, to John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White negotiating principles for the Bretton Woods institutions in 1944. Not so, demonstrates Martin in this thoroughly researched and convincing work. Rather, the antecedents of what we today call global economic governance can be found in a range of initiatives from Anglophone and French “meddlers” who concocted schemes to manage debt repayments, international payment transfers, commodity pricing, and what we currently refer to as critical infrastructure. In the wake of the First World War, elite technocrats established a series of organizations, or repurposed earlier imperial and colonial schemes, to act as “political buffers” (83) that could effectively meet the interests of private financial and trading cartels. Such organizations and arrangements ushered in a new institutional order that justified interventions into sovereign states on economic grounds.

papers.title: Agnes Gehbald. A Colonial Book Market: Peruvian Print Culture in the Age of Enlightenment .
papers.abstract: A Colonial Book Market is a study of great interest that deals with printed cultural consumption in Peru during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. It is a well-conceived and solidly developed study that begins with pertinent questions about the impact of the world of books, seeking to answer how the colonial book market was shaped. It is a venture of remarkable interest (and some risk), but the author manages to find the common thread in a social history of the book that addresses the book as a material object in everyday life. In some previous studies, other authors have partially addressed some of these issues. We have studies on the supply circuit of imports in the Hispanic Atlantic, such as Carlos A. González Sánchez’s work, and a study by Pedro Guibovich on the arrival of prohibited books and the production of Lima’s printing presses, but these aspects had not been connected in Peru. Other recent studies have dealt with relations with the British and French empires, such as Francesco A. Morriello’s Messengers of Empire: Print and Revolution in the Atlantic World (2023). Agnes Gehbald’s book deals with global networks of Atlantic cultural supply and is very attentive to the practices, access, and use of print, both in Lima and in the Peruvian viceroyalty.

papers.title: Adam Mestyan. Modern Arab Kingship: Remaking the Ottoman Political Order in the Interwar Middle East .
papers.abstract: How are new political orders built on the ruins of destroyed ones? Historians, sociologists, political theorists, and other disciplines have tussled with this question from the moment empires began to die. In Modern Arab Kingship, Adam Mestyan takes up this question again, focusing on the former Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire and entering a nascent historiography of the “post-Ottoman world.” By bridging legal history and political theory, the book elegantly constructs articulations of postimperial politics that will serve as building blocks for a paradigm across post-Ottoman space; in renarrating the eruption of Arab kingdoms following World War I, it offers a fresh take on how various stakeholders utilized the ruins of Ottoman order to contest for power and shape the post-Ottoman Arab world from the top-down and the middle-out. Mestyan is concerned not merely with an Ottoman “legacy” nor the postimperial careers of its nobility, but rather their “recycling” of the content or form of the ancien regime to colonial, national, or, monarchical ends. He borrows (or recycles) Richard Brilliant’s distinction between types of spolia—spolia in se (reusing material) and spolia in re (reusing form). By focusing on spolia, Mestyan contends that in the creation of post-Ottoman Arab mandates from a European imperial or local Arab standpoint, no party involved could dispense with certain legal, genealogical, religious, and social vestiges of the Ottoman’s unique making. Thus, the book roots the creation of the mandates and local states that evolved in their wake in the Ottoman Empire’s own legal and political refashioning in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century.

papers.title: Carla Roth. The Talk of the Town: Information and Community in Sixteenth-Century Switzerland .
papers.abstract: Combining a microhistorical approach with extensive archival research, The Talk of the Town by Carla Roth is a brilliant example of how a social history of early modern communication and information should be written. This is a book about the talk of a small Protestant town in sixteenth-century Switzerland, Saint Gall, focusing on the role played by orality in the circulation of information within early modern urban communities. The analytical framework that serves as a backdrop for this book is the history of information in the sixteenth century, a time in which new social actors entered the scene and new media coexisted and interacted with traditional forms of communication. From the impact of printing to the new postal services, the sixteenth century was a time of great innovations and revolutions in communication. One of the merits of this book is to analyze the effects of the communications revolution on the periphery of Europe’s communication system and main information hubs: Saint Gall did not enjoy the effects of these innovations, as it was excluded from the imperial mail services and did not have a printing press. In this peripheral town, face-to-face communication, orality, and sociability played a central role in the circulation of news.

papers.title: Rose Miron. Indigenous Archival Activism: Mohican Interventions in Public History and Memory .
papers.abstract: In Indigenous Archival Activism: Mohican Interventions in Public History and Memory, Rose Miron documents the creation of the largest collection of Mohican materials in the world, the Arvid E. Miller Memorial Library and Museum at Stockbridge Munsee Community located near Bowler, Wisconsin. Miron is the Vice President for Research and Education and former director of the D’Arcy McNickle Center for American Indian and Indigenous Studiesat the Newberry Library, a substantial library and archives in Chicago that houses material of special relevance to Indigenous peoples of the Great Lakes area. Miron centers Indigenous Archival Activism on the story of how, why, and to what ends the Mohican Nation Historical Committee created an archive and use it to change the way historical knowledge about Mohican Nation is produced. The committee, substantially led by Bernice Miller, Dorothy Davids, and other women of the Stockbridge-Munsee community starting in the late 1960s, has had profound impacts on the teaching and learning of the history about Indigenous people. The story of the archive is inspirational and instructional for other nations who do similar work.

papers.title: Challenging Abstraction
papers.abstract: Abstract Working with never-published agricultural data collected for Mexico’s pavilion at the 1900 Paris Exposition, this article argues that manuscript and published statistics represent a space to see state making as a multisided, ongoing process. Whereas historians have largely looked at statistics from the perspective of the state, highlighting bureaucrats’ projections of desired realities and political projects, here I show how local enumerators’ investment in statistical undertakings asserted space for conversations and arguments about the nature and composition of the political or economic whole being represented. I present a methodology for working with historical statistics that takes aberrations, anomalies, and unruly data as signposts to be followed rather than errors to be corrected. In doing so, I argue for seeing not only the frustrated yet durable aspirations of statesmen but also the ways those beyond the central state reforged, reinforced, and remade representations of their homes through engagement with and investment in statistical practices.

papers.title: Simon Partner. Koume’s World: The Life and Work of a Samurai Woman Before and After the Meiji Restoration .
papers.abstract: For a good portion of her adult life Kawai Koume (1804–89), a woman born into the lower ranks of the samurai class in central-western Japan, kept a diary. With long gaps in between, the surviving entries cover 18 years between 1837 and 1885. Simon Partner uses this diary as the main primary source for the highly readable and informative book Koume’s World: The Life and Work of a Samurai Woman Before and After the Meiji Restoration. The book proceeds chronologically, beginning with Koume’s upbringing in Wakayama, the castle town of Kishū domain. Her father and grandfather were scholars and advisers to the daimyo, a position that accorded them high prestige but middling to low income. Making ends meet within limited means was a constant challenge, one that fell primarily on women as household managers. In contrast to the image of samurai women as objects of patriarchal domination, Partner points out that Koume had considerable authority in her family not only because of her active role in household governance, but also because she was an only daughter whose husband married into the family as its heir and took the Kawai name—this was a quite common practice among samurai and commoners at the time. Koume’s own father had done the same, and so both Koume and her mother lived their lives in their natal homes rather than marrying “out” and being subject to the wishes of their husbands and in-laws as was the norm in much of Japan. (As a small criticism of an otherwise smooth narrative, Partner repeatedly renders the term for an adopted son-in-law and heir as a “muko [husband] husband,” an odd redundancy when he could simply say “adopted husband” or “husband adoptee,” both far better translations for the commonly used Japanese term for such men, muko yōshi.)

papers.title: Graphic Narratives and History in the Americas
papers.abstract: Detail from Ghost River: The Fall and Rise of the Conestoga. In recent years, graphic narratives have gained greater recognition within the historical profession. University presses publish series of graphic histories, conferences include regular contributions from historians studying various kinds of sequential graphic narration, and an increasing number of historians are collaborating with artists in the production of graphic histories. In a profession struggling with job precarity, falling budgets, and the attacks of state officials, graphic narratives seem to represent reason for optimism: a medium through which historians might reach broader audiences, increase collaborations across industries, and support our work with students. While it is easy to notice the graphic boom in the historical profession, it is not so easy to fully comprehend its implications. In the Graphic Narratives and History project, we, a comics scholar and two historians, enter into conversation with dozens of scholars working on comics and history in various regional contexts to try and figure out the relationship between history and graphic narratives. As we thought about our approach to the project, we saw our role as that of convenors and facilitators; we wanted to learn from the many comics scholars and historians who have thought about the seam between history and comics for a long time. Our initial idea was to hold a plenary conversation on graphic histories and what academic historians can do with them before embarking on a range of regional conversations that examine questions of history and comics in a particular area of the world. In reality, conversations proved more fluid—regional examples were used in the plenary discussion, and the regional conversations contain insights on graphic narratives as a medium and historians’ relationship to that medium. What we have here, then, is not a polished nor a comprehensive almanac of history and comics, but rather an effort to take stock of what experts on graphic histories in various regions consider to be some of the most relevant questions about the relationship between graphic history and history. This first installment includes our first three conversations: a plenary discussion on comics and history, a conversation on comics and Latin American history, and a conversation on comics and North American history. Some of the questions we ask focus on the methodological end: What kind of history does the graphic narrative do? How do historians research, teach with, and produce graphic narratives, and how can we do it better? And how do scholars studying graphic narratives see the relationship between their work and history? By contrast, some of our other questions focus on the history of graphic narratives as a cultural industry: What can historians learn by paying close attention to the production, distribution, and consumption of comics? How have imperial and national contexts defined the production of graphic narratives? And how do these contexts still shape and constrain our approach and access to various kinds of graphic narratives? No definitive answers await here. Instead, this project compiles a series of conversations where scholars who have studied the problems of graphic narratives and history in various contexts share their expertise, ideas, how-to tips on teaching and research, and advice to historians who are interested in producing graphic histories. papers.title: Fragments of Failure? An Unfinished History of Colonial America in the Scottish Enlightenment
papers.abstract: The subject of this article is an unfinished history of colonial America written from within the heartland of Scotland’s Enlightenment. The author of that history was the Reverend Andrew Brown (1763–1834), a Scottish Presbyterian minister, a former student at the universities of Glasgow and Edinburgh, one-time colonist in Nova Scotia, and holder of the Regius Chair in Rhetoric and Belles Lettres in Edinburgh. Brown’s career took shape under the patronage and guidance of William Robertson (1721–93), Historiographer Royal and Principal of the University of Edinburgh. It was Robertson who directed Brown to Nova Scotia and to a life’s work in pursuit of a history of colonial America. Throughout his career, Brown struggled with what he learned, wrestling with the moral and historical implications of colonization. At his death, his monumental history was incomplete. It remained unpublished and lies today in a fragmentary and highly disorganized state. Despite that, I will argue here that the archive allows valuable insight into the struggles of a historian schooled in Scottish stadial history who sought to do what others of his kind did not: to confront directly the brutal realities of colonial violence. For that reason, his archive affords a rare opportunity to trace the ideological and colonial limits of Enlightened history in its own time and place.

papers.title: Mark Santow. Saul Alinsky and the Dilemmas of Race: Community Organizing in the Postwar City .
papers.abstract: In the half century since his death, the community organizer and author Saul Alinsky has become something of a legend. His organizing model was coopted by conservatives in the Tea Party movement and also disparaged by conservatives as radicalism and Marxism. He influenced liberal giants such as Barack Obama, who learned about Alinsky as a neighborhood organizer in Chicago in the 1980s, and Hilary Clinton, who wrote an undergraduate thesis on him. Several popular and academic books have assessed his impact on organizing and the postwar left. Mark Santow’s book Saul Alinsky and the Dilemmas of Race seeks to fill a gap in the literature by analyzing Alinsky’s efforts to integrate the Southside of Chicago from the 1930s through the 1960s and placing them within the broader context of the urban political economy of the postwar era. Santow explains that the book is an attempt to use Alinsky’s strategies and perspectives to better understand the modern struggle for social justice in an era of renewed interested in how race and place shape identity and opportunity. The book is a series of case studies that highlight how incredibly difficult it is to create meaningful change through local organizing and activism, especially regarding race, segregation, and inequity. In my estimation, Alinsky’s attempts to integrate the Southside largely mirror the successes and failures of his other organizing efforts.

papers.title: Understanding Competing Agendas through a Love Triangle
papers.abstract: Countless commemorations, news reports, and scholarship have underscored the Vietnam wars’ significance in the global history of the twentieth century. However, stories, analyses, and memories appearing in the United States, in Vietnam, and in Vietnamese overseas communities all tell a widely different story. As a result, students who are just learning about Vietnam, Asia, the Cold War, or American foreign policy might feel overwhelmed by the monumental nature of the Vietnam wars. This is where The Quiet American, which the Australian filmmaker Phillip Noyce adapted from Graham Greene’s 1955 novel, becomes a useful tool.1 Starred by familiar faces like Michael Caine and Brendan Fraser, the movie offers an accessible storyline that suggests the multiple scales and dimensions of the wars. The Quiet American intertwines a war story with a murder mystery and a love triangle. The movie opens on a criminal case to elucidate the assassination of an Alden Pyle, an American aid worker. A French inspector in charge interrogates an old British correspondent, Thomas Fowler, through whom the movie uses flashbacks to understand what happened. Covering the war from Saigon in the 1950s, Fowler enjoys this time away from England in the company of a young Vietnamese woman named Phượng. He befriends a young American aid worker, Pyle, and introduces him to Phượng. However, the old man sees the two getting closer together. In the following weeks, Fowler covers battles and political meetings. He keeps seeing the young aid worker in the most unexpected situations. Blinded by his jealousy, Fowler does not realize that Pyle is not the “quiet American” he claims to be. It is only once a terrorist attack hits Saigon that he realizes the American is in fact a secret agent who had planned the bombing to blame the Vietminh and inspire a renewed mobilization against communist expansion in Asia. Fowler eventually agrees to arrange a dinner with Pyle, helping the Vietminh organize an ambush and assassinate the American agent.

papers.title: Wei Yu Wayne Tan. Blind in Early Modern Japan: Disability, Medicine, and Identity .
papers.abstract: An observant visitor to Japan will quickly notice the many accommodations in cities and towns around the country made for visually impaired people. In Tokyo, for example, one routinely encounters braille on elevator panels, audible pedestrian crossing signals, and tactile paving on sidewalks to aid those with vision issues in navigating the city. Such developments are noteworthy given that people with mobility issues still have considerable difficulty accessing even major subway and train stations in Japan due to the lack of elevators and wheelchair lifts. Wei Yu Wayne Tan’s book Blind in Early Modern Japan sheds light on the deep history of blind people in Japan by exploring the social and political conditions that shaped the lives of visually impaired people in the early modern period. Building on the work of musicologist Gerald Groemer, much of this work centers on the “guild of the blind,” an organization that integrated those with vision impairment into the Tokugawa status system. Significantly, this was the only social group for people with a disability that benefited from this form of institutional protection, problematic though it was. Tan goes beyond Groemer’s important body of work by exploring the medical discourse surrounding blindness, as well as the involvement of blind people in other occupations including moneylending, acupuncture, and massage. Consisting of six brief chapters, this clearly written and well-illustrated book offers an important window into conceptions of disability and the lives of people who are disabled.

papers.title: Guillaume Blanc, trans. Helen Morrison. The Invention of Green Colonialism .
papers.abstract: In The Invention of Green Colonialism, Guillaume Blanc investigates place-based conservation injustices in Ethiopia against a broader analysis of the unrelentingly colonial character of conservation work and thought across Africa. The Simien Mountains in Ethiopia might seem a curious place to start a work on “green colonialism”: Ethiopia was notably spared all but a brief occupation during Europe’s colonization of Africa. But Blanc argues that the broader colonial era saw the crafting of a set of narratives about Africa and its nature that endured, expanded, and perpetually renewed themselves after formal decolonization. Their reductive treatment of Africa meant that even Ethiopia was not spared their consequences. Blanc documents the origins of colonial conservation and then traces the broad persistence of the framework, and its particular Ethiopian iterations, across the period of decolonization, through significant changes in Ethiopia’s own political economy, and into an era of “sustainable development.” It is this long arc that gives The Invention of Green Colonialism much of its power for readers new to dimensions of this story, but which might frustrate others. Chapters 1 and 2 are based on existing scholarly literature and retell how Western visions of and assumptions about Africa and its landscapes amounted to the “naturalization” or “dehumanization” of Africa, with “catastrophic consequences” for people (1–2).

papers.title: Natasha Erlank. Convening Black Intimacy: Christianity, Gender, and Tradition in Early Twentieth-Century South Africa .
papers.abstract: Natasha Erlank’s Convening Black Intimacy explores how Black South African Christians (largely, but not exclusively, Xhosa from the Eastern Cape) understood, practiced, and articulated their emotional and sexual relationships, roughly in the period between the creation of the Union of South Africa in 1910 and the victory of the National Party in 1948. The book covers a range of issues: conceptions of masculinity as revealed in Xhosa circumcision rituals, the importance of kinship, the fluid and changing boundaries between public and private as conceived in traditional African and in African Christian circles; the role of women, who carried “the privilege and burden of lineage reproduction” (4); issues of polygamy, lobola (the gift/payment of cattle to the parents of the bride), church weddings, and the status that such ceremonies entailed. By its nature, a historical investigation of these matters is sensitive and elusive. The author uses a rich variety of sources: church pronouncements and disciplinary procedures, civil court records, a vigorous African press, in both English and isiXhosa, where articles and the letter pages are replete with diverse opinions on these issues. The book also introduces the importance of intimate letter writing, one of the consequences of Christian education and literacy.

papers.title: James R. Fichter. Tea: Consumption, Politics, and Revolution, 1773–1776 .
papers.abstract: Tea is an obvious candidate for the genre of global commodity history. Linking China, India, and European empires, both directly and through its diverse accoutrements from porcelain to sugar, it evokes emerging early modern capitalism in all its barefaced imperial violence, geopolitical intrigue, and cosmopolitan cultural pretensions. But Tea, James Fichter’s deeply researched second monograph, is not that kind of book. It is, instead, a book about the politics of boycotts, and an account of the revolutionary shift in public authority that took place in parts of British North America during the two-and-a-half years between the famous destruction of the tea in Boston harbor and the United States’ declaration of independence. The ill-fated tea aboard the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver was not the only East India Company tea to reach the mainland colonies in 1773 (that year’s Tea Act having allowed the Company to sell directly to colonial consignees for the first time). Fichter traces the fates of the Polly, triumphantly turned back from Philadelphia by patriot crowds; the William, wrecked off Cape Cod only for its cargo of tea to be rescued and, eventually, consumed by Loyalists and soldiers during the 1776 siege of Boston; and the London, whose tea was seized and landed by the Charleston customs officers and, in the end, sold off for the benefit of revolutionary South Carolina. Their stories show how differently things might have gone in Boston and, thus, how contingent the tea party moment was.

papers.title: Kith and Kin
papers.abstract: As a scholar and teacher of the Vietnam War, I have long been dissatisfied with Vietnam War textbooks. Some of the best-known textbooks on the market—such as George C. Herring’s classic America’s Longest War—treat the war primarily as an episode in American history, while paying little or no attention to the Vietnamese dimensions of the conflict. In response, several authors have recently produced textbooks that focus on Vietnamese actors and perspectives. One notable example is Pierre Asselin’s Vietnam’s American War, which teaches the history of the war through the ambitions and decisions of one Vietnamese group: the senior leaders of the Vietnamese Communist Party. To date, however, I have yet to find a textbook that successfully situates the war within the broader frame of modern Vietnamese history while still giving due weight to the US military intervention in the conflict. In lieu of using a textbook in my Vietnam War course at Dartmouth College, I ask my students to read Duong Van Mai Elliott’s The Sacred Willow: Four Generations in the Life of a Vietnamese Family.1 Published in 1999, The Sacred Willow is a brilliantly written family saga that details the lives and experiences of Elliott and her relatives over the course of the twentieth century. But the book is much more than just a compilation of family lore. Elliott carefully locates herself and her family members within the Vietnamese political, social, and cultural contexts in which they lived. Along the way, she provides readers with a wealth of insights about how Vietnamese perceived and experienced the war. At the same time, as someone who is Vietnamese, who was born and raised in Vietnam but studied in the United States, worked with Americans, and eventually became a US citizen, Elliott is unusually well equipped to provide students with a critical perspective on the American involvement in the conflict.

papers.title: Sarah Percy. Forgotten Warriors: The Long History of Women in Combat .
papers.abstract: Sarah Percy’s new book, Forgotten Warriors, issues a call to arms against a fresh generation of authoritarians and patriarchists who have targeted women’s newly gained rights (at least in Western militaries) to engage in combat. Partly for this reason, the book has already been reviewed widely. Percy, an academic at the University of Queensland, makes her case by appealing to history, although this history is not the stuff of conventional wisdom. Rather, the author takes a revisionist approach to military history, arguing that women in the past had “survived and even thrived as part of a machine of war” (xv), although news of this realty was suppressed and has still not been conceded by many military historians (John Keegan is the author’s main target). Percy does not frame this erasure as a conspiracy, but rather the consequence of long-standing chauvinist patterns of authority, which she describes as “the playbook of patriarchy” (xvi). As Percy notes, the manifest ability of women to succeed in combat has only recently been acknowledged, allowed, and valorized. She admits that historically women have not “fought in the same numbers and in the same ways as men” (xiv), but she attributes this mainly to men preventing them from getting a chance to perform in combat, especially after the 19th century. The takeaway, according to Percy, is that through the longue durée women did succeed in proving their ability in combat, and consistent examples of their presence on the battlefield made female warriors more than exceptions to a general rule. She also condemns political and military establishments for trying—not always successfully—to keep women out of combat, thereby denying them a way to demonstrate “the virtues that we associate with success in society, politics and . . . just about every field of human endeavour” (284–85).

papers.title: Steve Hindle. The Social Topography of a Rural Community: Scenes of Labouring Life in Seventeenth-Century England .
papers.abstract: Steve Hindle’s The Social Topography of a Rural Community is an unusual contribution to the genre of local studies; rather than thematic or chronological organization, Hindle explores the Warwickshire parish of Chilvers Coton in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries via thirteen residences. The basis for this approach lies in the survival of an unusual census conducted over three days in 1684 when the local lord, Sir Richard Newdigate, tasked jurors with collecting information on the residents of his lands, including a census of all households. Supplemented by traditional archival sources, such as parish registers and probate inventories, and a map drawn only months before the inquiry, Hindle argues that “it is possible to walk the streets of Chilvers Coton in the imagination” (407) and catch a glimpse of some of the nearly eight hundred individuals and how they lived in 1684. Sir Richard devised the plan, but as Hindle demonstrates, this was a survey compiled from below and offers modern scholars a chance to see the parish through its inhabitants’ eyes.

papers.title: Christopher F. Minty. Unfriendly to Liberty: Loyalist Networks and the Coming of the American Revolution in New York City .
papers.abstract: Christopher F. Minty’s Unfriendly to Liberty: Loyalist Networks and the Coming of the American Revolution in New York City provides an innovative, well-written, and meticulously detailed new look at the city in the years leading to the Revolutionary War and how the imperial crisis became entangled with New York’s bitter partisan politics. By examining voter lists, assembly and committee compositions, tavern culture, and the city’s vibrant print media from 1768 to the outbreak of the conflict, Minty offers a convincing argument that political affiliations and social networks “shaped, and in some cases, determined political allegiance in the Revolutionary War” (5). Through eight chronological chapters, Minty tells a story of political polarization and factionalism in New York City. The narrative centers on the rivalry between the wealthy DeLancey and Livingston families and their supporters, who dominated New York politics. Though Minty’s primary concern is tracing the development of loyalist support that emerged largely from the DeLancey faction, his book provides a compelling and balanced account of the twists and turns that transformed partisan politics into revolutionary violence.

papers.title: Victor Petrov. Balkan Cyberia: Cold War Computing, Bulgarian Modernization, and the Information Age behind the Iron Curtain .
papers.abstract: The study of the information age beyond the Anglosphere is now a robust and dynamic field. Instead of returning to milestones such as Colossus, Arpanet, Silicon Valley, and Apple, a generation of historians have written rich technological, political, and cultural histories of information processing from Chile to China. Victor Petrov’s Balkan Cyberia joins this line of inquiry with spectacular results. Prior scholars have depicted Cold War computing in the Eastern Bloc as an endeavor that had major cultural and political impacts, but that ultimately failed technologically. Cybernetics created a new language of social critique in the Soviet Union, but it did not create an all-union computer network. Socialist dreams of automating individual factories, let alone entire planned economies, never came to fruition. Petrov breaks from this mold by arguing that on technological and economic levels the Bulgarian computer industry was a success. By 1980, he reports, Bulgaria was responsible for 45 percent of electronic exports within the Eastern Bloc, employed over 10 percent of all industrial workers in ICT, and was intellectually involved in debates over the meaning of the information age.

papers.title: Samuel Moyn. Liberalism Against Itself: Cold War Intellectuals and the Making of Our Times .
papers.abstract: “Cold War liberalism was a catastrophe—for liberalism.” That is how Samuel Moyn opens his latest book, Liberalism Against Itself, pithily summarizing its main message. In the following pages, Moyn gives us a swift overview of Cold War liberalism’s key thinkers, with chapters on Judith Shklar, Isaiah Berlin, and Karl Popper, as well as on lesser lights like Gertrude Himmelfarb and Lionel Trilling. This cast of characters is used to illuminate key aspects of Cold War liberalism, most notably its rejection of any belief in collective emancipation as dangerously proto-totalitarian. Moyn also makes a surprise addition by including a chapter on Hannah Arendt. Arendt herself of course rejected the label “liberal,” but, as Moyn convincingly shows, she might nevertheless be described as a “fellow traveller,” being equally skeptical of the possibility to institutionalize an emancipatory politics. Moyn’s book contributes to a burgeoning literature on Cold War liberalism. But while much of the recent literature has been written by fanboys, Moyn strikes a very different tone. In his account, thinkers like Berlin and Popper remade the liberal tradition for the worse. Their liberalism was drained of any commitment to perfectionism or progressivism, starting instead from a quasi-Augustinian emphasis on the sinfulness of man. (Ironically so, since all protagonists of Moyn’s book were Jewish). Cold War liberals lionized thinkers like Lord Acton and Sigmund Freud, who shared their bleak view on human nature, “yoking liberalism to original sin as well as psychic bestiality” (5). At the same time, they rejected the legacy of theorists committed to the possibility of true human emancipation such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau, G. W. F. Hegel and Karl Marx, and, in Berlin’s case, the entire Enlightenment. Thus, they turned liberalism from a doctrine wedded to hope to one centered on fear.

papers.title: Alfred Peredo Flores. Tip of the Spear: Land, Labor, and US Settler Militarism in Guåhan, 1944–1962 .
papers.abstract: Numerous books, magazine and newspaper articles, blogs, and vlogs refer to Guam as the US military’s “tip of the spear.” This disturbing discourse proliferated after 2017, when North Korean leader Kim Jong Un publicly considered launching a missile test toward this US territory located in the western Pacific, not far from Korea, the North China Sea, and Taiwan, all hot spots on the US military’s radar. Yet the uber-militarization of Guam began long before this recent string of events, and these origins form the foundation of Alfred Peredo Flores’s Tip of the Spear: Land, Labor, and US Settler Militarism in Guåhan, 1944–1962. Guahan, the Indigenous name for Guam, is currently occupied by more than twenty thousand members of the US armed services and their dependents, alongside an Indigenous population of roughly sixty-two thousand and a multiethnic immigrant population of eighty-seven thousand, the majority of whom are ethnically Filipino. Flores’s work documents the growth of the military and Filipino populations, tying them directly to the reshaping of the island after the physical devastation of World War II in ways that promoted American military might in the Asia-Pacific region.

papers.title: Eline van Ommen. Nicaragua Must Survive: Sandinista Revolutionary Diplomacy in the Global Cold War .
papers.abstract: In Nicaragua Must Survive: Sandinista Revolutionary Diplomacy in the Global Cold War, Eline van Ommen brilliantly examines Nicaragua’s international diplomacy from 1977 to 1991 during the Sandinista Revolution. Moving beyond the well-trodden narrative of the Reagan administration’s overt—and at times, illegal—support of the Contras and the teleological perspective that this alone brought about the demise of the Frente Sandinista de Liberación Nacional (FSLN), van Ommen instead frames this story as one deeply embedded in the global Cold War and of carefully calculated decisions, not one of inevitable failure. Sandinista diplomats reckoned with a changing Cold War climate while they confronted unforeseen domestic pressures. As a result, they adjusted their strategies and made concessions that eventually undermined their regime. Rather than consider this a failure, van Ommen argues that we take seriously Sandinista diplomats’ creative use of solidarity networks, relations with European Community (EC) countries, and participation in Latin American initiatives and consider how their diplomatic strategy impacted the late Cold War well beyond Nicaragua’s borders.

papers.title: Introducing AfriWetu
papers.abstract: History in Focus, a podcast by the American Historical Review, recently released the latest entry in its podcast collaboration series. AfriWetu offers a thoughtful and accessible entrypoint to African history for all kinds of listeners with the hope, as Mona says at the top of each episode, that listeners will be inspired to find out more for themselves. In this collaboration, host Daniel Story speaks with Mona Nyambura Muchemi, the host and producer of a terrific and thoughtful African history podcast called AfriWetu. The following transcript of their conversation has been minimally edited for length and clarity. The full episode can be found at https://www.historians.org/podcast/afriwetu-host-mona-nyambura-muchemi. Daniel Story: Hi Mona. To begin, can I get you to introduce yourself, say your name, and maybe a line or two about who you are? Mona Nyambura Muchemi: Sure, my name is Mona Nyambura Muchemi. I am a storyteller—an African storyteller—and I tell the story of our ancient African ancestors. And I tell these stories in order to bring them back to life, and in order to inspire generations of Africans with the stories of their past and to know where they’re coming from. I should add that our tagline is “rooted in our story,” because I would like people to think about where it is that they come from and feel a sense of pride as to their ancestral history.

papers.title: Laura K. Muñoz. Desert Dreams: Mexican Arizona and the Politics of Educational Equality .
papers.abstract: Contributing to the rich historiography on schools and schooling as sites of liberation and community affirmation that has emerged in the last twenty years, Laura K. papers.title: Ellen Malenas Ledoux. Laboring Mothers: Reproducing Women and Work in the Eighteenth Century .
papers.abstract: Enlightenment ideology created categories for motherhood: those who were “good” mothers cared for and nurtured their children, while “bad” ones were neglectful or poor providers. papers.title: Diya Gupta. India in the Second World War: An Emotional History .
papers.abstract: Diya Gupta’s book India in the Second World War has assumed the daunting task of revealing the emotional impact on Indian subjects as they crossed the physical and mental terrain of global war. This is no mean feat, as the conflict’s effects on the socially and culturally diverse “Indian” subject defy any sort of blanket description. The war was felt in vastly different ways depending on one’s perspective, whether a hungry Bengali peasant, a Parsi woman in Bombay, an English educated member of the literati, or a sepoy, those myriad soldiers who fought for the empire. Indeed, the author summons them all in the service of this compelling work. Gupta’s broad approach points to a salient fact: There was no singular Indian experience, no commonly understood national narrative of victory or defeat despite the shared economic depravations the war brought to the subcontinent. In the wake of World War I, B. R. Ambedkar, the Dalit barrister and author of the country’s 1949 constitution, inadvertently argued as much in suggesting that India lacked nationhood since those who held no caste status, such as himself, by no means enjoyed the equality that enabled a population to imagine a common community. As he put it, “a government for the people, but not by the people, is sure to educate some to be Masters and others to be subjects.” Ambedkar saw the end of the British Raj as somewhat moot if it were merely swapped for an elite Brahmin Raj. Even the staid Indian Army, home of the traditionally recruited “martial races” of northern India, was highly stratified in terms of region and language. The Sikh solider, or sepoy, would have no way of communicating with a Gurkha from Nepal. Building an emotional history of wartime India then, as Gupta has done, is especially challenging.
