papers.title: Ryosuke Yokoe. Alcohol and Liver Cirrhosis in Twentieth-Century Britain .
papers.abstract: The idea that alcohol consumption could damage the liver has been around for a century or more. In Edwardian Britain, a “hobnailed” or “gin drinker’s” liver was widely recognized as a possible consequence of heavy drinking. Cirrhosis, indicated by scarring of the liver that significantly impairs its function, is now understood to be a late stage of liver disease, which begins with the development of a fatty liver, and then often leading to hepatitis, before reaching cirrhosis. Although medical practitioners had long suspected that alcohol played a part in causing cirrhosis, the establishment of a causal link between drinking and cirrhosis was not straightforward. In Alcohol and Liver Cirrhosis in Twentieth-Century Britain, Ryosuke Yokoe explores the crooked path taken by the medical science of cirrhosis from the early 1900s to the 1980s. This journey encompasses not only the ins and outs of scientific debate but also the impact that this had on the political, socioeconomic, and policy response to alcohol. Alcohol consumption fluctuated over the course of the twentieth century, and although Britain never introduced prohibition, alcohol was more or less restricted at different times, and the political space that drink occupied also varied.

papers.title: Robin Judd. Between Two Worlds: Jewish War Brides After the Holocaust .
papers.abstract: Robin Judd’s book Between Two Worlds: Jewish War Brides After the Holocaust centers the figure of the Jewish war bride, a previously all but neglected subject in modern Jewish- and 20th-century US and European historiography. Judd deftly intertwines biographical accounts of her fascinating subjects (including, in the conclusion, the stunning story of her own grandparents) and their often epic struggles with the legal, political, religious, and social situation in allied occupied Europe in the immediate aftermath of the war, making this book at once intensely human and rigorously scholarly, shifting back and forth, as it does, between individual narratives and broader social and political forces. papers.title: Ashkan Rezvani Naraghi. A Social History of Modern Tehran: Space, Power, and the City .
papers.abstract: Ashkan Rezvani Naraghi’s book, A Social History of Modern Tehran: Space, Power, and the City, takes us on a journey through the transformation of the urban environment of Iran’s capital from the nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century. This book is an incredibly rich mine of information for anyone interested in social history. As a scholar working on political contention and mobilizations, I appreciated Naraghi’s mastery in explaining that the socially embedded knowledge of how and where to protest builds upon existing spatial practices of communal life and how such knowledge has changed across the decades as a reflection of the meaning of “living together”. Intertwining cultural history, human and political geography, economic, gender, and class analysis, A Social History of Modern Tehran is a must-read for any scholar interested in Iran and an extremely beneficial reading for social scientists in general. Written with flair, the volume includes six chapters through which the “ontological shift in the conceptualization and representation of the spatiality of Tehran” during the centuries (1) is examined in depth. Engaging in the analysis of such a shift, chapters 1 and 2 focus on the Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1906 and the period preceding it. The chapters explain how Tehran moved from being a city of fragmented urban communities, divided by profession and other identity markers, who lived in segregated space—the coffeehouses of professional guilds, the zurkhaneh or traditional gyms with their strict hierarchies of belonging, among the others—to become a city with an emerging public and cross-communal space, thanks to the pressure of religion and protest politics, which acted as unifying forces. Mosques, in particular those that were not linked to a specific community but served larger portions of the population (Friday mosques, for instance), transformed into political spaces open to different communities and played an important role in the logistics of the revolution. Naraghi argues that this ignited a process of secularization and gender diversification in how urban spatiality was understood and experienced in Tehran. While women did not live segregated and without contact with communal, outer urban geographies, they existed in separated spaces, the andaruni (the “within”), with sporadic free access to the outer space. The revolution changed this differential access, also thanks to a new urban knowledge that contextually emerged in nineteenth-century Iran.

papers.title: Sebastián Gil-Riaño. The Remnants of Race Science: UNESCO and Economic Development in the Global South .
papers.abstract: Reframing the race campaigns of the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organizations (UNESCO) from the perspective of the Global South, The Remnants of Race Science reveals the surprising extent to which ideas about racial difference persisted within the organization and, significantly, how these ideas informed postwar development projects in the non-Western world. Although UNESCO’s famous, controversial 1950 Statement on Race rejected strict biological determinism, Sebastián Gil-Riaño provides a rich analysis of other hierarchical views of human diversity that remained. While UNESCO social scientists embraced plasticity and the benefits of race mixing—ideas that reflected the heavy influence of Latin American and Polynesian scholarship, he argues—they nevertheless retained an old, imperialist view of the world’s people as divided between those living in modern, Western civilization and those who remained “primitive” and in need of uplift. Indeed, scientific arguments about human equipotentiality, Gil-Riaño argues, gave new life to the equivalent of old—and overtly racist—colonial civilizing missions by recasting them into the “seemingly nonracial discourse of ‘international development’” (7). Rejection of innate biological hierarchy, in other words, did not dislodge the idea that Indigenous people were “backward” obstacles to modern, productive economies. Rather, it provided new ostensibly colorblind rationales for assimilation.

papers.title: Neil A. Knapp. Making Machines of Animals: The International Livestock Exposition .
papers.abstract: Sampson, a four-year-old steer that stood over six feet tall and weighed more than three thousand pounds, attracted crowds at the 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis. He was massive by any standards and seemed to dwarf his steer counterparts at the show as well as the humans who stood nearby. In Making Machines of Animals: The International Livestock Exposition, Neal Knapp demonstrates that Sampson’s extraordinary and prizewinning size was not a genetic oddity. Instead, Sampson and thousands of other steers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century were envisioned by a seemingly odd pairing of land-grant university professors, meatpackers, and farmers. Their traits were selectively bred into the population, and more importantly, unwanted characteristics were aggressively bred out of cattle populations. But Sampson’s aesthetic was ideal for a brief moment as the modern slaughter-bound steer emerged with a standard, compact body and less than half the age of Sampson.

papers.title: Geoffrey M. Hodgson. The Wealth of a Nation: Institutional Foundations of English Capitalism .
papers.abstract: Geoffrey M. Hodgson’s ambitiously titled book has several equally ambitious goals: to explain the rise of capitalism, to offer an account of English economic development from the Norman Conquest to the nineteenth century, to present Hodgson’s brand of legal institutionalism and institutional evolution, and to identify lessons from English economic development. Positively, Hodgson makes a good case that in thinking about capitalism, we should think about financial capital and not just about capital goods, and that in using the word “capital,” we should be careful not to conflate the two. His view that financial development is an important ingredient in economic growth (and that the absence of finance can constrain development) represents one (arguably well-established) position in a debate that has been running for some decades. His description of generalized Darwinism is a digestible summary of an approach to historical and societal development that should allow readers to take a view on its utility. papers.title: Susan C. I. Grunewald. From Incarceration to Repatriation: German Prisoners of War in the Soviet Union .
papers.abstract: Susan C. I. Grunewald’s book From Incarceration to Repatriation examines Soviet policy toward German soldiers captured during the Second World War. Of primary interest to the author are the motivations of Soviet leaders as they processed, accommodated, and exploited the large number of prisoners who entered Soviet custody beginning in early 1943. This compact volume is clearly argued and thoroughly documented using archives from Russia, Germany, and the United States. The primary contributions of the work are in three areas: the role of German prisoners in the economy, their importance to Soviet domestic and international politics, and their continuing legacy for Russian political and cultural affairs. Once the Soviet army began capturing large numbers of Germans in 1943, their potential economic contributions were paramount in Soviet officials’ minds. Prisoners of war landed under the jurisdiction of the People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs (NKVD), which had long experience managing forced labor in the notorious Gulag. It was common after the war, Grunewald points out, to consider the Germans just additional victims of Soviet brutality. While prisoners of war faced privations and restrictions similar to the inmates of the Gulag, however, the Germans often received attention and care not due to Soviet citizens, free or unfree, who faced starvation and political repression during the war and during the lean years that followed. German prisoners certainly suffered, but Soviet authorities labored to keep them alive—and working. Prisoners who became seriously ill or were otherwise incapable of work—whether due to wartime wounds, to the appalling transit arrangements, or the rigors of work and camp life—received priority for repatriation so as to spare the state the expense of their upkeep.

papers.title: Alexandria N. Ruble. Entangled Emancipation: Women’s Rights in Cold War Germany .
papers.abstract: By the late 1950s, the constitutional law of both East and West Germany included a clause that guaranteed equal rights between women and men. At that time, the constitutions of few West European countries explicitly incorporated the principle of gender equality under law. Thus, by the end of their first decade of existence, both Germanys look comparatively progressive on the question of “equal rights” for women. Yet, as Alexandria Ruble shows in her readable, meticulously researched, and evenhanded comparative study, Entangled Emancipation: Women’s Rights in Cold War Germany, this conclusion is simplistic and ahistorical. She does not deny the significance of the equal rights provisions but complicates their meaning by tracing their prehistory in political tensions and debates of the 1940s and 1950s, and by following their after-history in the family law of East and West Germany of the 1960s and 1970s. Her first great contribution to the literature on German women’s rights is to demonstrate convincingly that the process and the content of gendered legal change in each state was related to what was happening in the other German state. As do other feminist scholars, she sees gender relations as a major point of contention in the Cold War rivalry between the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) and German Democratic Republic (GDR). Applying this insight to the case of women’s legal rights, she shows that these rights did not evolve along parallel tracks in East and West but alternately diverged, converged, and crisscrossed as experts, government ministers, legislators, and ordinary citizens looked over their shoulders at debates and decisions in the other Germany—and aimed to prove that their state had more to offer women than did the other.

papers.title: Christopher Michael Blakley. Empire of Brutality: Enslaved People and Animals in the British Atlantic World .
papers.abstract: Empire of Brutality: Enslaved People and Animals in the British Atlantic World examines the “more than human world” of slavery (2). By analyzing the multiplicity of relationships between enslaved people and animals in the British Atlantic in the long 18th century, the book represents a much-needed addition to the existing scholarship. Building on Atlantic histories of slavery and the animal turn in history, Christopher Michael Blakley uses human-animal relations to complicate our understanding of slavery and systems of power. The book explores the so-called dreaded comparison of enslaved peoples to nonhuman animals, and how and why enslavers tried to reduce enslaved peoples socially and ethically to an animal-like position. Throughout the book, Blakley effectively argues that Atlantic slaving did not annihilate African cultures or the minds of African people and render human beings to animal-like subjects. The greatest strength of the book is how Blakley repeatedly acknowledges the agency of enslaved people within the empire of brutality that slavery created, exploring the myriad ways that “enslaved people retained their humanity” (15).

papers.title: Guo-Quan Seng. Strangers in the Family: Gender, Patriliny, and the Chinese in Colonial Indonesia .
papers.abstract: Guo-Quan Seng’s Strangers in the Family is a meticulously researched history of the formation of a settler Chinese community in Indonesia under Dutch colonial rule (1816–1942). Based on an impressive array of sources, including Dutch government records, the administrative and judicial documents of the Chinese Council of Batavia, and Sino-Malay vernacular press materials, it tackles a key question in the scholarship on Chinese migration and diaspora: How did the Chinese come to be essentialized as a patrilineal race and perpetual outsiders within? The book reflects a paradigm shift in the historiography on Asian mobility in the era of European colonial empires. In a departure from the conventional focus on the labor, capital, and intellect of men, Seng places women and gender at the center of his analysis and uncovers an obscured history of intimacies and estrangements between Asian migrant-to-settlers (his term, more on this later) and Indigenous and local-born women. He shows how profoundly these inter-Asian dynamics—and their regulation by the settler Chinese community—shaped modern ideas about identity and belonging. The result is a compelling challenge to the Eurocentrism of postcolonial studies that remains preoccupied with the European management of race, sex, and desire.

papers.title: Melvin L. Rogers. The Darkened Light of Faith: Race, Democracy, and Freedom in African American Political Thought .
papers.abstract: A renaissance has taken place in recent years regarding Black intellectual history. Thinking through the contributions of Black men and women to the larger streams of American, global, and intellectual history has marked some of the best-known works of history of late. The unique contribution of Black Americans to American political thought has especially seen an explosion, and Melvin L. Rogers’s book The Darkened Light of Faith: Race, Democracy, and Freedom in African American Political Thought is a tour-de-force in this field. For Rogers, reckoning with Black thinkers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries is not just a question of Black intellectual history. The Darkened Light of Faith is a valiant, and ultimately successful, attempt to recalibrate how we think about American democracy and its fraught relationship with both race and history. Melvin Rogers’s academic monographs, edited collections, and public essays in such forums as Dissent and The Atlantic magazines continually deal with the tensions inherent in American democracy. In The Darkened Light of Faith, Rogers points out how Black thinkers have wrestled with those tensions throughout the history of the United States. “What is it about democracy,” Rogers poses at the beginning of his book, “that justifies our faith, especially African Americans’ faith, in it?” (3). For Rogers, the answer is one that threads the needle between two traditions: the growth of Afro-Pessimism, on the one hand, and the ideal of the “American Creed” popularized by Gunnar Myrdal in his study An American Dilemma: The Negro Problem and American Democracy. It is a push to, in Rogers’s words, “deploy the principle of making and remaking” who and what constitutes the American body politic (5). While white supremacy may be at the heart of the building of American democracy, Rogers’s book reminds us that numerous Black thinkers never accepted that argument without trying to rethink and reimagine what American democracy could, potentially, be.

papers.title: Rachel Chrastil. Bismarck’s War: The Franco-Prussian War and the Making of Modern Europe .
papers.abstract: As Rachel Chrastil’s engaging new book, Bismarck’s War, demonstrates, the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 vividly combined modern and premodern elements. Like so many conflicts in the ancien regime, its immediate cause was a dynastic dispute—in this case, about the candidacy of a Hohenzollern prince for the Spanish throne. The war ended with a violent urban uprising that Karl Marx and his followers viewed as the model for the class struggles of the future. As they would in the twentieth century’s great wars, railways played a major role in transporting troops; the telegraph was used, albeit with imperfect success by both sides. But the same difficulties of movement and communication that had frustrated strategists for centuries remained; the Prussians won in part because they overcame these difficulties somewhat more successfully than the French. Soldiers fought with the breech-loading rifles that had transformed infantry tactics and even employed a rudimentary form of machine gun. The military use of hot air balloons hinted at the battlefield’s expansion into the air that would revolutionize warfare in the century ahead. At the same time, there were many familiar features from earlier wars, including a massive cavalry charge (perhaps the last in western Europe). As they had so often in the past, heads of state observed the battlefield and personally experienced the thrill of victory and the anguish of defeat. This would never happen again.

papers.title: Brooke Barbier. King Hancock: The Radical Influence of a Moderate Founding Father .
papers.abstract: King Hancock is not your typical founding father biography. Carefully avoiding the twin traps of hagiography and “myth-busting” that dominate the genre, Brooke Barbier brings careful nuance and deep historical context to a figure known by most Americans only for his larger-than-life signature on the Declaration of Independence. Rather than a paragon or a cautionary tale, John Hancock emerges as a fully fleshed-out human being, replete with virtues and flaws both typical and atypical for his time, and driven not just by high ideals and momentous events but also by the mundane trivialities, petty hardships, and simple pleasures of eighteenth-century life. Although written for a general audience, the book’s engaging prose, rich detail, and compelling narrative will assure it a readership among scholars of the revolutionary era from undergraduates to seasoned experts. With a knack for setting scenes, Barbier deftly takes the reader from Hancock’s origins in sleepy Braintree through his upbringing and adult life in bustling Boston, with stops in metropolitan London, congressional Philadelphia, war-starved Baltimore, and elsewhere. The city of Boston, where Hancock spent most of his life, becomes a character in the biography in its own right, with its wharves, streets, and denizens depicted in a type of contextualized detail that puts the reader in the place of a person on the street. We learn not only the size, furnishings, and architecture of Hancock’s Beacon Hill mansion, for example, but also how it commanded a wide view of Boston Common and the surrounding areas, how the family used it to receive visitors and engage in business and politicking, and how the servants and enslaved people who worked there interacted with neighbors both rich and poor. In describing Hancock’s mercantile empire, Barbier lingers on the area surrounding the merchant’s private wharf, stressing not just the vessels plying their trade but also the taverns, dram-shops, ropewalks, small retailers, and houses of ill repute that were as integral to Hancock’s enterprises as any mercantile firm. This eye for detail is not surprising from an author who also operates historical walking tours, but it is especially refreshing in a genre that too often trades the quotidian experiences that made up the vast majority of people’s lives for the high-flying oratory, intellectual debate, and political maneuverings of a relative instant.

papers.title: Thomas Blake Earle. The Liberty to Take Fish: Atlantic Fisheries and Federal Power in Nineteenth-Century America .
papers.abstract: Can the environment play an influential role in statecraft and diplomacy? In a new book examining fisheries as an effective lens for exploring nineteenth-century Anglo-US relations, Thomas Blake Earle answers in the affirmative. The Liberty to Take Fish derives its title from the Treaty of Paris (1783) that forever allowed the United States access to the fisheries on the Grand Banks and along the coasts of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Labrador (5). Earle argues that fisheries, fishermen, and fish were central to the diplomatic tension and turbulence between Britain and the United States from the years following independence until after the Civil War. In the nineteenth-century, the United States was a maritime power comparable to other maritime powers such as the British Empire and the Dutch Republic, and fish were a valuable resource requiring extraction. Long an integral part of US statecraft, Americans saw fishermen and fish as guarantors of US political and commercial independence until a desire for peace with Britain during Reconstruction made the fisheries a lesser priority for the federal government. “The history of fisheries,” Earle contends, “is the history of statecraft” (4).

papers.title: Gal Gvili. Imagining India in Modern China: Literary Decolonization and the Imperial Unconscious, 1895–1962 .
papers.abstract: China and India share a contested border and a complex modern history. Subject to colonial and imperialist violence, in widely different ways and time frames, both nations have occasionally looked to each other as an epistemic source of understanding their respective places in the modern world. In this bold and insightful study, Gal Gvili sheds light on Chinese perceptions of and engagement with India, from the Sino-Japanese War in 1895 to the Sino-Indian border conflict in 1962. Gvili’s study joins a small but growing body of research that brings into communication the histories of Asia’s largest nations, and contributes to the expanding field of global history, especially historical studies of the Global South. A literary scholar by training, Gvili draws primarily on literary and cultural texts to build her case, and is concerned first and foremost with perceptions and reception, and with the methodological and ethical implications of the act of comparison as a scholarly practice.

papers.title: Emmanuel Kwaku Akyeampong. Independent Africa: The First Generation of Nation Builders .
papers.abstract: In 1957, Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence, and the following year, Guinea, under Sékou Touré, said no to membership in the French community and gained independence from France. Two years later, in 1960, seventeen African nations obtained independence, and the wave of an independence movement continued for the rest of the twentieth century. Independence was marked by high hopes and excitement, but the fanfare and promises ended quickly. By the end of the 1960s, military takeovers occurred in rapid succession on the continent, as many nations tottered on the brink of economic and social collapse. At independence, writes Emmanuel Kwaku Akyeampong in Independent Africa: The First Generation of Nation Builders, one in every four people in sub-Saharan Africa could neither read nor write, life expectancy stood at forty-one years, and disease and poverty were rampant. Two examples illustrate this: At independence, the Republic of Congo had sixteen university graduates, and Tanzania had two trained engineers and three medical doctors. Those numbers were similar in other African nations. Akyeampong’s book is an in-depth analysis of the actions and challenges faced by the first-generation African leaders in their goal to provide solutions to the most urgent problems of their countries. Based on extensive primary and secondary sources, the author argues that postindependence African leaders believed industrialization was key to solving the problems of illiteracy, poverty, and disease. Though the author focuses on four leaders—Nkrumah, Touré, Leopold Senghor, and Julius Nyerere—the study also addressed the actions of others, many of whom were promoters of the ideas of modernization and development theories. By engaging the topic through a comparative lens, the book makes a significant contribution to modern African historiography. African leaders, though nonaligned in the Cold War, were determined “to reduce economic dependence on the West, industrialize, and increase the role of the state” (116). Their interactions with Communist nations put them on a collision course with the US. Nkrumah and Touré bore the brunt of America’s negative response to their anti-Western statements and actions. Unlike them, Nyerere was cautious in statements against capitalism, practicing what the author referred to as “soft ideology” (184), and Western nations reciprocated and sent more aid to Tanzania.

papers.title: Shira Lurie. The American Liberty Pole: Popular Politics and the Struggle for Democracy in the Early Republic .
papers.abstract: As Shira Lurie notes in the introduction to her excellent first book The American Liberty Pole, the scholarship on the political culture of the early American republic is exceedingly rich. One could argue, seriously, that it might be the most actively developed and thickly engaged subfield of historical inquiry over the last few decades. To add something genuinely new to such a field is an impressive feat, and Lurie has done exactly that. In clear and inviting prose, Lurie picks up the full weight of the scholarly tradition on early American political culture and distills it into a carefully researched narrative history of the liberty pole in the early Republic, with a special focus on the 1790s. Her argument shows us that there was no consensus of national identity and shared meaning at the founding that came apart in moments of crisis later, be they in the nineteenth century or the twenty-first. Rather, Americans have hotly contested their politics and tied their political identifications to the symbolic authority of the nation’s history from the beginning. The story of American political culture is the story of protest, contestation, and changing markers; it was that way from the beginning, and if Lurie is right, the liberty pole as a tool of opposition political symbolism was a founding element in that story. This book leaves little doubt that she is.

papers.title: Freedom in the Here and Now
papers.abstract: The efforts of 20th-century activists to achieve immediate freedom is the concern for Victoria Wolcott and Irvin Hunt. However, each scholar approaches the topic in drastically different ways, reflecting their respective disciplinary differences. In Living in the Future: Utopianism and the Long Civil Rights Movement, Wolcott, a historian of the 20th-century United States, traces the history of utopian communities, including worker education schools, cooperatives, and fellowship houses and churches, and spotlights their pivotal contributions to the long civil rights movement. In Dreaming the Present: Time, Aesthetics, and the Black Cooperative Movement, Hunt, a scholar of English and African American studies, reads Black cooperatives as an artistic practice that facilitated the creation of different temporalities of the present. In Living in the Future, an elegantly composed and meticulously researched book, Wolcott invites us to reconsider utopian practices and ideas within the long civil rights movement. (The long civil rights movement views the struggle for racial equality as extending before the 1950s and past the 1960s. Within this framework, the civil rights movement, spanning from 1954 to 1968, represents a pivotal chapter in this struggle.) Utopian ideals were quite popular from the 1920s through the Second World War, declined in popularity after the war and as the labor movement deteriorated, and resurged in the early 1960s when a fresh wave of visionaries emerged.

papers.title: Eric Klingelhofer, ed. Excavating the Lost Colony Mystery: The Map, the Search, the Discovery .
papers.abstract: In 2004, a group of scholars from diverse academic backgrounds met in Chapel Hill, North Carolina and organized the First Colony Foundation (FCF), an organization dedicated to researching the history of the sixteenth-century Roanoke colonies, especially the Lost Colony of 1587. Members included historians, archaeologists, curators, preservationists, and other specialists. Over the past two decades, these scholars have conducted fieldwork in North Carolina and documentary research in the United States and England. In Excavating the Lost Colony Mystery: The Map, the Search, the Discovery, edited by Eric Klingelhofer, nine authors, six of whom are members of FCF, summarize their findings to date. As the title suggests, much of the focus is on their methodology and the process of excavating, and they do not claim to have solved the mystery. But they do offer a hypothesis based on new evidence. They argue that after Governor John White left Roanoke, the remaining colonists split into smaller groups to search for food. Some ventured westward across the sound and onto the mainland where they settled, at least temporarily, near the head of the Albemarle Sound on modern day Salmon Creek, a location near the Algonquian town of Mettaquem.

papers.title: Philip Gooding. On the Frontiers of the Indian Ocean World: A History of Lake Tanganyika, c.1830–1890 .
papers.abstract: One of the most robust analytical debates within East African history and its historiography is the production and articulation of difference—difference between self and other, core and periphery, civilization and barbarism. At the heart of these frictions lays the divide between the salient conceptual metageographies of the region: Africa and the Indian Ocean World. Although intertwined for centuries, artists, intellectuals, and scholars alike have long shown that the regional production of social and cultural difference often relied on imbuing these geographies with meaning. Proximity to the coast and integration into the putative xenophilic and cosmopolitan worlds of the Indian Ocean signaled civilization and culture—ustaarabu and utamaduni, respectively. Alternatively, interior Africa was an archetypal hinterland—a static landscape that, through the trade in ivory, enslaved people, and the spread of Islam, was gradually pulled out of its insularity and into the dynamic and outward-facing coast. Scholars of all stripes have long shown, of course, how contingent, unstable, and violent these categories and characterizations often were. And indeed, the cultural divarication that these geospatial categories produced was often weaker and more porous than those who relied on it for wealth and power often needed it to be. Religious conversion, the appropriation of oceanic-spanning family genealogies, and strategies of consumption could allow for nominative outsiders to slip in and out the Indian Ocean worlds they encountered in coastal East Africa.

papers.title: Martín Bowen. The Age of Dissent: Revolution and the Power of Communication in Chile, 1780–1833 .
papers.abstract: The Age of Dissent: Revolution and the Power of Communication in Chile, 1780–1833, is not just another book on the history of the independence of Chile, nor is it about the “Age of Revolutions,” as might be assumed from its temporal scope (1780–1833). In this insightful, original, and informed study, Martín Bowen focuses on the marked continuity between late colonial and postcolonial Chile rather than the rupture between the new and old regimes. The focus is not on reiterating the well-known idea that colonial social and economic structures persisted well into the republican era nor on assessing how revolutionary the shift from the monarchical to a republican regime was. For Bowen, the “most revolutionary dimension” about the age of revolutions in Chile—and arguably in Spanish America—was “the opening of politics to radical political dissension” (2). To understand the nature of this revolution, the author casts doubt on the assumption that its roots are in the realm of ideas. In turn, he elaborates a sophisticated conceptual framework to demonstrate that the disclosure of politics to a wide range of social actors, such as women, Indigenous people, slaves, and Afro-descendants, was the result of a subtle and gradual transformation in the realm of communication. In this framework, communication is understood as an arena where different actors from the past “elaborated and discussed the worlds they shared” (8) as well as the interactions among them.

papers.title: Gregg Mitman. Empire of Rubber: Firestone’s Scramble for Land and Power in Liberia .
papers.abstract: The “empire” question—that is to say, the question of where independence projects in Africa took a wrong turn—decisively rose on the agenda of Africanists by the mid-1970s (again). This was no different in the state of Liberia, independent since 1847. Here, however, scholars began to take a more critical look at American intervention and influence, especially from the nineteenth century onward. And no other American entity, aside from the American Colonization Society, which founded the Colony of Liberia in 1822, has been as central to this historiography as the Akron-based Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, which developed its first rubber plantations in Liberia in 1926 and became the country’s largest employer and exporter by the 1940s. Into the 1960s and early 1970s, a generation of scholars, such as Marion Gartier, Caryl Roman, George L. Hall, and Franklin Neal, were still interpreting the formation of the world’s largest single rubber estate in largely positive terms—namely, as an economic boon for Liberia and as destroying the British (cartel)-controlled global rubber trade, to name just some examples. But then, anti-imperialist scholarship took root, challenging a system of economic domination that violated the sovereignty of African states. In the case of Liberia, some of the following scholars may come to mind: Jyotirmoy Pal Chaudhuri, J. Mills Jones, and Robtel Neajai Pailey. In his engaging study of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, the first book-length study of its kind, Gregg Mitman picks up this torch and uses it to illuminate a troubling entangled history between America and Africa. In doing so, he connects to literature on the formation of the “New South” in Africa through the “plantationization” of agriculture, featuring aspects of racialization, corporatization, the transfer of new values around work, and the growing comforts of consumer culture. He also engages with a historiography of Black internationalism. But readers who approach this narrative to make sense of sociopolitical circumstances on the local scene are hardly disappointed when learning about how Firestone’s policies exacerbated social divisions and weakened rural communal practices critical to survival. They also learn that it was especially groups falling into the reductive category of “native” who had to endure a series of epistemological, environmental, medical, and economic violences as the enterprise grew.

papers.title: Moe Taylor. North Korea, Tricontinentalism, and the Latin American Revolution, 1959–1970 .
papers.abstract: As research on the Cold War in the Global South—especially during the “Global Sixties”—has proliferated recently, the role North Korea played and the relationships Pyongyang had with other parts of the “Third World” have received only sporadic attention. Few works have detailed North Korea’s interactions with Latin America in depth. Moe Taylor’s monograph, North Korea, Tricontinentalism, and the Latin American Revolution, 1959–1970, fills that gap and so deserves the attention of historians of Korea, Latin America, and the Global Sixties. His work brings together source material in multiple languages and places scholars from Korea and Latin America into conversation with each other, further enhancing its value. Through seven chapters, plus an introduction and conclusion, Taylor describes the connections that existed between North Koreans and Latin American revolutionaries in the 1960s. State and nonstate actors on both sides of the Pacific recognized in each other common goals. The vision they shared had more to do with national self-determination in the face of US imperialism than with Marxist class revolution. Taylor emphasizes Latin America’s importance to North Koreans by analyzing the rhetoric of the Kim Il Sung regime and providing evidence of North Korean enthusiasm for assisting Latin America. Sources from Latin America, especially Cuba, suggest that some of the region’s revolutionaries viewed North Korea as a model of self-sufficient development.

papers.title: The Many Booms in Hong Kong’s Past—And the First Ever Hong Kong History Boom
papers.abstract: Unsettling Exiles is the second book—and second impressive book at that—by Angelina Chin. I am used to describing her as an up-and-coming specialist to watch if you are interested in the study of the history of gender and labor in China and Hong Kong. papers.title: Elizabeth Dore. How Things Fall Apart: What Happened to the Cuban Revolution .
papers.abstract: How Things Fall Apart: What Happened to the Cuban Revolution invites readers inside a Cuba typically unseen in historical work, relying almost exclusively on extended interviews with seven subjects interviewed between 2004 and 2018. Recently deceased historian Elizabeth Dore argues frankly that the Cuban Revolution has broken its promise to create an egalitarian society. The Cuba of the twenty-first century is one that has left socialism behind and bent to market forces even as propaganda continues to herald Cuban socialism. A warning to historians of Cuba and Latin America, to leftists who saw or continue to see Cuba as a beacon of hope in a landscape of hypercapitalist extraction: this book might break your heart. More happily, it might inspire new historical work on the second half of the twentieth century in Cuba. All seven of the primary interviewees in How Things Fall Apart grew up in the 1980s, coming of age just as the Soviet Union collapsed and sent Cuba into a decade of extreme scarcity. Because Dore and her team interviewed their subjects several times over a period of many years, the reader has rare and valuable access to the evolution of the interview subjects’ understanding of their own lives. Mario, an employee of Cuba’s Ministry of Industry, is initially reluctant to attribute any setbacks in his life—like his failure in art school—to racism. But as he speaks with Dore and her team again and again, he begins to see his life through the prism of anti-Black racism, despite having grown up in an environment that essentially prohibited acknowledgment of it.

papers.title: John H. Cable. Southern Enclosure: Settler Colonialism and the Postwar Transformation of Mississippi .
papers.abstract: In Southern Enclosure: Settler Colonialism and the Postwar Transformation of Mississippi, John H. Cable broadens the historiographical scope of enclosure by challenging the traditional Black-white binary approach. In this groundbreaking work, Cable argues that incorporating Native Americans, specifically Choctaws, not only strengthens our understanding of racial injustice but views the South through the transnational lens of settler colonialism. While convincingly comparing the South to other settler societies like South Africa and Rhodesia, he nevertheless maintains that a narrower focus—east-central Mississippi—allows him to analyze the land dispossession endured by Blacks, Choctaws, and poor whites. Concentrating primarily on the mid-twentieth century, he shows that despite the passage of civil rights legislation, sharecroppers and tenants continued to face eviction. Much like displaced people in other settler states, these two groups faced decades of ravenous exploitation followed by abrupt dismissal. In Cable’s words, the enclosure movement “was, in that sense, simply a new chapter in a very old story, of which Mississippi was as much a part as settler states elsewhere” (126).

papers.title: Owen Davies. Troubled by Faith: Insanity and the Supernatural in the Age of the Asylum .
papers.abstract: In Troubled by Faith: Insanity and the Supernatural in the Age of the Asylum, Owen Davies has conscientiously excavated a seam of medical history to investigate the relationship between religion, faith, and insanity in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Britain (and Europe). His research reveals how far the history of psychiatry has traveled since the single-minded focus on the Foucauldian fiction of the “total institution” in the 1980s. By placing religious belief about the supernatural—from the demonic through the orthodox to the spiritualist—at the center of his analysis, Davis shows how much of nineteenth-century psychiatry remained preoccupied by religion, even if these beliefs were often pejoratively explored as “superstition.” Well into the twentieth century, physicians found that religious ideas and fears remained important to a good proportion of their asylum inmates. He suggests how the period, rather than secularizing, became in many ways more seriously “religious,” with newly literate populations able to purchase commercially produced Bibles and prayer books. New forms of Christian worship and belief, such as the Pentecostals, believed ever more fervently in the presence of the Holy Spirit, while new movements—particularly theosophy and spiritualism—often stressed the presence of departed souls in the lives of the living. He is quite right to insist that the arrival of science and technology hardly erased fears of the supernatural. On the contrary, fluids and currents in telegraphy, telephones, and phonographs were often perceived as dangerous precisely because of their invisible and otherworldly capacity to invade and disrupt body and mind.

papers.title: Joseph E. Sanzo. Ritual Boundaries: Magic and Differentiation in Late Antique Christianity .
papers.abstract: The material turn in early Christian studies has led to robust investigation of how objects, bodies, built spaces, and environments interacted and shaped the lived experiences, beliefs, behaviors, and actions of ancient Mediterranean people. Joseph Sanzo’s Ritual Boundaries fruitfully adds to this conversation by exploring the complex relationship between rituals, texts, materials, images, traditions, and religious differentiation in late ancient Christianity. As Sanzo puts it, his goal is to explore how late ancient Christians “engaged through their everyday practices with notions of similarity and difference, good and evil, and propriety and impropriety” through ritual practice, religious belonging, texts, and objects (2). Rather than simply accepting ancient Christian writers’ claims that some magical objects weren’t Christian enough—or modern scholars’ claims that magical objects reveal a lack of interest in religious differentiation among the nonelite—Sanzo argues that late ancient magical objects might reveal something about how lived religious experiences materially and discursively shaped boundary formation between religious groups.

papers.title: John D. Garrigus. A Secret among the Blacks: Slave Resistance before the Haitian Revolution .
papers.abstract: Eighteenth-century Saint-Domingue was a place in great need of healing. On this Caribbean French colony ravaged by famine, drought, unexplained human and animal deaths, poison trials, and the Seven Years’ War, the path to revolution was paved by the responses of those who suffered most. This is the thrust of John D. Garrigus’s book A Secret among the Blacks: Slave Resistance before the Haitian Revolution. The study reaches back thirty years, from 1791, to chronicle the efforts of enslaved and freed men and women to forge bonds of solidarity in the sugar plain surrounding the port city of Cap-Français and the coffee hills of the North Province. Bearing the brunt of an environmental and political crisis of Atlantic proportions, Africans and their descendants drew on their own rituals and medical knowledge to address the collective ills that were exacerbated—and, in some cases, created—by colonialism and slavery. Here is the mystery that Garrigus unravels for the reader: rather than deriving from an articulated “overarching ideology” (174), the slave revolution in Haiti arose organically from the Afro-Atlantic spiritual world of healers, diviners, and their associated communities.

papers.title: Andrew W. Kahrl. The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America .
papers.abstract: In The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America, Andrew Kahrl, shows how “federated taxation” has been both a marker and a maker of racial inequality in the United States (3). Spanning the century and a half from emancipation through the early twenty-first century’s financial crisis, The Black Tax is a meticulously researched, compellingly argued, and often heartbreaking account of US history that centers “Black people’s struggles against local tax systems that forced them to pay more for less and subjected them to heavy financial penalties and the threat of dispossession” (4). Combining both a structural analysis of the broad political and economic forces that shaped the post-Civil War United States with archival accounts of how individual men and women, Black and white, upheld and resisted those same structures, The Black Tax shows how local tax systems have been used, exploited, and even designed to dispossess Black landowners, enrich white elites, and institutionalize racial inequality and injustice. By correctly insisting on seeing the tax system as built by and for white elites, this important and compelling book refutes the widely held—but historically inaccurate—belief that taxes are simply a way to transfer resources from white taxpayers to implicitly non-white “tax eaters” who feed at the public trough. This “makers and takers” narrative has been central to both the neoliberal project of shrinking the public sphere and the white supremacist project of rolling back the hard-won victories of the Black freedom movements. Kahrl’s work convincingly shows that Black Americans have not only paid their fair share in taxes; they have been overcharged for their share of the American dream.

papers.title: Paul Corner. Mussolini in Myth and Memory: The First Totalitarian Dictator .
papers.abstract: In Mussolini in Myth and Memory: The First Totalitarian Dictator, Paul Corner traces some of the key elements of the Fascist regime and the way it is represented in the national and international public sphere today. This concise volume is the historian’s response to, and an attempt to reflect on, the growing presence of memories of the Italian Fascist experience in Italy (and elsewhere). These are essentially positive and trivializing images of a dictatorship that, after twenty years of violent and disruptive authoritarian rule, led Italy into the political and economic disaster of the Second War World. Divided into six chapters—devoted respectively to Fascist violence, the relationship between consent and coercion, Fascist welfare, modernization and the modernity of Fascism, Mussolini’s role as a statesman, and the cult of the Duce—the volume moves effectively between the history of the regime and the public memory of it in recent decades. Mussolini in Myth and Memory thus allows us to explore some of the most significant and debated topics in the historiography of Fascism, as well as to recall some of the main events and processes associated with the regime and their place in the country’s public memory.

papers.title: H. Glenn Penny. German History Unbound: From 1750 to the Present .
papers.abstract: German History Unbound attempts to unshackle German history from the physical borders of the nation-state and the moral burden of the catastrophes it unleashed in the twentieth century. As a noted historian of German ethnology, H. Glenn Penny seeks to paint a new historical picture that abandons the vanishing point of Nazism to affirm a German past defined by polycentrism, mobility, hybridity, and tolerance, one that connects a deeper past defined by these traits to the newer German vanishing points of 1989, the 2006 World Cup, and the welcoming embrace of unprecedented waves of refugees since 2015. It does so by drawing on a large volume of recent transnational research on German migration, immigrant communities, and scientific and merchant networks beyond German borders in Eastern Europe, North America, and especially Central and South America. Penny’s book is a counterpoint to Helmut Smith’s The Continuities of German History (2008), which affirmed the vanishing point of 1941, when Nazi Germany began its genocidal war of destruction (312). Penny also takes issue with Reinhart Koselleck’s threshold period 1760–1860 (the so-called Sattelzeit), identified as pivotal for the emergence of the modern political order of secular nation-states. Instead, Penny views this era as one of accelerated German migration and connection made possible by “thickening networks of trade and travel” that made provincial Germans ever more worldly (57).

papers.title: A. Dirk Moses. The Problems of Genocide: Permanent Security and the Language of Transgression .
papers.abstract: Dirk Moses’s book The Problems of Genocide: Permanent Security and the Language of Transgression shows how genocide came to be distinguished from other mass atrocities. This masterful genealogy of the concept argues that the “crime of crimes” conceptualized at the 1948 Genocide Convention obscured the violence of aerial bombings, colonial atrocities, forced population displacement, or contemporary drone strikes in the age of what Samual Moyn called “humane war.” Moses begins by tracing the historical development of the term originally coined by Raphael Lemkin in the aftermath of the Holocaust. The first part of the book recapitulates the language of transgression—how lawyers, rulers, and thinkers conceptualized mass violence between 1500 and the 1930s—before the term genocide officially came into being. A turning point in this history, of course, is Lemkin’s separation of genocidal killing from other forms of atrocities. This first section already announces the main theme of the book: a more expansive framing of genocide—if not a definitive rejection of the term—that considers the multiple ways groups (in totality or in part) can be the targets of murder. The quest for universal principles of prevention and intervention, contends Moses, clashes with the need to account for the unique cultural, political, and historical circumstances of different genocidal events.

papers.title: Joshua Savala. Beyond Patriotic Phobias: Connections, Cooperation, and Solidarity in the Peruvian-Chilean Pacific World .
papers.abstract: In light of the increase in nationalist rhetoric and policies over the last decade throughout the world, including in Latin America, Joshua Savala’s Beyond Patriotic Phobias: Connections, Cooperation, and Solidarity in the Peruvian-Chilean Pacific World is a timely and welcome historiographical contribution. The book’s main objective is to understand Peruvian-Chilean relations starting from spaces of transnational solidarity and collaboration and not from conflict, as has been traditionally done by historians from the War of the Pacific until now. A central part of Savala’s proposal is that this solidarity and collaboration has occurred in a space that he calls the “South Pacific World”—a space that has promoted connections between Chileans and Peruvians, where individuals, for different reasons, have distanced themselves from nationalist rationales. Given the central role that war has had in defining the relations between both countries, Chilean and Peruvian readers who have been taught in educational systems that reinforce conflict as a part of national identity will find that Savala’s argument is counterintuitive. That is one of the book’s strengths and one of its challenges—the attempt to disarticulate visions that are profoundly rooted in nationalist discourses found on both sides of the border. Consisting of five chapters, an introduction, and an epilogue, the book starts from the middle of the nineteenth century and covers up until the first decades of the twentieth. It analyzes different instances of solidarity and cooperation among maritime and port workers, Chilean and Peruvian doctors during the cholera epidemic that occurred between 1886 and 1888, and between police from the Callo and Valparaiso ports in their law enforcement efforts.

papers.title: Arieh Saposnik. Zionism’s Redemptions: Images of the Past and Visions of the Future in Jewish Nationalism .
papers.abstract: Like other projects of national liberation, Zionism—the Jewish national movement that emerged in Europe in the late nineteenth century and founded the State of Israel in 1948—spent much of its intellectual energy on devising images of a better future for its people. Conceived as a remedy for a distressful present—sometimes as a metaphorical return to a glorious past—these visions often assumed a redemptive quality, offering collective and individual regeneration of the Jews in their homeland. In this penetrating and well-conceived book, Zionism’s Redemptions, Arieh Saposnik argues that redemptive ideas are indeed central to Zionism’s self-understanding and goals. He investigates expressions of these ideas in texts, political debates, relations with other political and religious entities, and in attempts to reshape the landscape of Palestine and later Israel—or, in other words, the impact of an intellectual discourse on historical and cultural realities. His study concentrates on narratives of redemption developed in the period before 1948, mainly in the Jewish community in Palestine (Yishuv) but also in the diaspora, with a few brief references to the post-statehood period.

papers.title: Michelle Tusan. The Last Treaty: Lausanne and the End of the First World War in the Middle East .
papers.abstract: During approximately the last 175 years, humanitarian groups have raced around the world trying to help civilian populations ravaged by war and other disasters. That this has become an accepted practice highlights one of the paradoxes of modern humanitarianism: Why does the world allow for the existence of war and other man-made conditions that necessitate humanitarianism in the first place? Perhaps, then, it is not surprising that modern humanitarianism, according to Michelle Tusan in her book The Last Treaty: Lausanne and the End of the First World War in the Middle East, “developed in concert with military and diplomatic concerns” during the largest war the world had yet seen. Analyzing the symbiosis between the “strange bedfellows” of war, peacemaking, and humanitarianism is the core of Tusan’s stimulating monograph (8). Tusan has two additional objectives for this book: First, she argues that historians must acknowledge the “centrality of the Middle East in Allied thinking about the war” and analyze its events as interdependent with the war’s other developments (11). Second, Tusan argues that the oft-repeated contention that the war ended in 1918 is false and misleading. Fighting continued in several places, including in various parts of Anatolia, long beyond 1918. She is not, however, simply arguing for a new end date for the war. Instead, Tusan focuses on the implications of “how the First World War ended,” with continuing violence influencing the way in which peace was negotiated (3, Tusan’s emphasis). To accomplish these tasks, she has employed political and diplomatic sources, as well as utilizing the voices of “refugees, aid-workers, and soldiers” for insight into “why and how those who offered aid did it and in whose name” they did it for (8–9). Reading the sources in this way makes the war in the Middle East seem more like a “strange defeat” for the Allies rather than a victory, as the peace “came at a heavy price for the now former subjects of the Ottoman Empire” (15). Tusan seeks to achieve these goals by interweaving chapters about the conflict, the peace negotiations, and humanitarianism.

papers.title: Catherine McNeur. Mischievous Creatures: The Forgotten Sisters Who Transformed Early American Science .
papers.abstract: Catherine McNeur’s book Mischievous Creatures: The Forgotten Sisters Who Transformed Early American Science explores how two sisters navigated the gendered discourses of nineteenth-century science. Elizabeth Carrington Morris (1795–1865), in accordance with ideals of feminine modesty, happily served behind the scenes as a collector, informant, and illustrator for male botanists. Margaretta Hare Morris (1797–1865), in contrast, fought to receive credit for her entomological discoveries. In this dual biography, McNeur traces how these women found ways of entering and contributing to scientific networks but argues that both were erased from the 1860s onward by the men who sought to professionalize American science. The sisters were immersed in the sciences early in life, as the first two chapters detail. Thanks to ideas of republican motherhood and the custom of educating elite young women in science, Elizabeth and Margaretta were schooled in natural history during their childhood in Germantown, Pennsylvania. They were connected through kinship or neighborhood to men involved with the American Philosophical Society (APS) and the Academy of Natural Sciences (ANS) in nearby Philadelphia and were privately tutored by several significant American naturalists.

papers.title: Noble David Cook and Alexandra Parma Cook. Luis Gerónimo de Oré: The World of an Andean Franciscan from the Frontiers to the Centers of Power .
papers.abstract: Friar Luis Gerónimo de Oré’s life is a thread that ties together many of the events of the early colonial period in Spanish America. As part of the first generation of Creole Peruvians born after the conquest, Oré’s trajectory weaves through events that would shape the Spanish colonial Andes: the Taki Onqoy movement, the third church council of Lima, and the rise of regular clergy in Indigenous parishes. Oré also traveled to the courts of Spain and Italy, to Florida and the Carolinas, and finally back to South America as bishop in Concepcion, Chile. Through all of this, he served as a translator, parish priest, author, inspector, and senior cleric, but was above all, a Franciscan. It is this narrative that Noble David Cook and Alexandra Parma Cook sew together through decades of exhaustive research and exceptionally readable prose to successfully reveal a piece of the complex tapestry of the first post-conquest Creole generation.

papers.title: Caroline Ritter. Imperial Encore: The Cultural Project of the Late British Empire .
papers.abstract: In Imperial Encore, Caroline Ritter significantly advances the study of Britain’s cultural project in the former colonies. The scope is both wider and narrower than the book’s title might suggest: wider, because it covers not just the late colonial era but also the postcolonial, with some chapters reaching until the 1980s; and narrower, because its focus is Africa rather than the entire British Empire. Even so, it is an ambitious book, based on archives from multiple institutions and various countries, and impressively drawing these sources together. The book focuses on three main institutions: the BBC, the British Council, and Oxford University Press. It is structured in two parts, with each containing a chapter on the three institutions. The first part focuses on the late colonial period; the second on the postindependence era. This structure makes clear the significance of the late colonial era in developing future trajectories. The book complements recent historiography, which recognizes that independence should not be seen simply as a moment of rupture, and highlights continuities of practice.

papers.title: On/ In the Ground with Vietnamese Communists
papers.abstract: Undergraduates often arrive in my classes convinced that great men, and a few exceptional women, are the ones who make history. Here, they think of power wielded by presidents, generals, and self-styled geniuses of strategy and diplomacy. (Henry Kissinger’s name invariably bubbles up in class discussions, like it or not.) Perhaps this happens elsewhere? In Singapore, this mindset likely takes root because the country’s record of benevolent authoritarianism underpins the legitimacy and influence of political elites. Equally, male citizens of Singapore perform compulsory military service before entering university and internalize, readily or grudgingly, that rank confers power—it is power—and that those of lower stations must fall in line. This is the lens through which many of my undergraduates initially viewed the Vietnam wars, certain that the conflict was orchestrated chiefly, even exclusively, by politico-military elites. Furthermore, those among my undergraduates who, in their middle or high school years, opted to study history probably absorbed from the national textbook that the Vietnam conflict was essentially a proxy war (though I know teachers take pains to emphasize nuances to this description contained within the same textbook). Hence, a fair number of my undergraduates will cursorily note that the struggle for Vietnam was local in some sense but resolve that the war was more properly an extension of the US-Soviet Cold War from Europe into Asia.1 Some are quick to even conclude that the big powers basically made puppets of the Vietnamese; indeed, they show little concern for the ground-level experiences of ordinary Vietnamese. From that vantage point, the Vietnam wars are a chess game played by powers at great remove from the board, or even a crater-riddled battlefield of tiny, faceless figures glimpsed as if from a high-altitude bomber.

papers.title: Mikkel Dack. Everyday Denazification in Postwar Germany: The Fragebogen and Political Screening during the Allied Occupation .
papers.abstract: The Allied occupation of Germany and the early years of the country’s Cold War division have long drawn interest from academic scholarship. From Robert Moeller’s exploration of narratives of suffering to Atina Grossmann’s focus on Jewish survivors to Monica Black’s cultural analysis of faith healers, the tumultuous postwar years have undergone a variety of interpretations of how Germans grappled with a violent past and transitioned into two new nation-states. In such a dense historiographical landscape, it is challenging to find an original approach. Mikkel Dack does so successfully with his focus on the Fragebogen and its underestimated impact on the denazification of Germany. By exploring the 131-question document completed by twenty million people from the mid-1940s until the early 1950s, Everyday Denazification in Postwar Germany assesses the policymaking process for eradicating National Socialism among the Allied powers, the implementation of denazification, and the ways Germans experienced the end of Nazi ideology.

papers.title: Selda Altan. Chinese Workers of the World: Colonialism, Chinese Labor, and the Yunnan-Indochina Railway .
papers.abstract: Some years ago, I wrote an article on the Yunnan-Burma railway. I discovered that British colonial authorities, Western investors, and Chinese and Burmese nationalists had different, and often conflicting, perceptions, imaginations, and plans for the railway. When the Chinese Nationalist government and the British authorities finally agreed to undertake this project on the eve of the Pacific War, the defiance and mass desertion of the Chinese construction workers, most of whom were from Yunnan, significantly delayed progress. Clearly, the British colonial authorities and Chinese nationalist elites had learned nothing from the Yunnan-Indochina railway case four decades earlier. In Chinese Workers of the World: Colonialism, Chinese Labor, and the Yunnan-Indochina Railway, Selda Altan finds that Chinese workers on the Yunnan-Indochina railway project employed various forms of “the art of not being governed” to challenge the agendas of French colonial authorities, capitalists, and Chinese nationalist elites alike. Altan argues that a working-class identity was cultivated among the Chinese workers through their daily interactions with racial capitalism. Altan interprets the mass desertion of workers from the exploitative worksite as a symbol of their class consciousness. The Chinese nationalist elites’ neglect of the potential of the workers’ new identity led to their failures in pursuing their political agendas.

papers.title: Fiscal Innovation Gone Bad: Comprehensive Business Censuses from the Florentine 1427, 1433, and 1458 Catasti
papers.abstract: The first descriptive purpose of this article is to document changes in the industrial composition of Renaissance Florence through business censuses that we have extracted from household-wealth declarations in the 1427, 1433, and 1458 Florentine catasti (tax censuses). These consecutive censuses reveal a decline in the number of businesses in many but not all of the industries in Florence over this thirty-year period. The second purpose of this article is to explain this economic decline. We find, through both quantitative and qualitative evidence, that the innovative tax catasti themselves were to blame: they all too effectively extracted enormous levels of taxes from the wealthy Florentine population in order to fund mercenary wars related to the emergence of Italian Renaissance regional or “territorial” states. The economic decline was due not only to the direct effect of heavy taxes but also to the indirect effect of default contagion among highly leveraged companies doing business with each other on credit. This case study contradicts the rosy portrait in the social science literature of a positive relationship between state formation and economic growth. We show that newly emergent Italian Renaissance regional states did not always produce positive economic gains for the capital cities that constructed them. This raises questions about economic self-interest explanations of that expansion. An important corollary for Florentine political history is our finding that this economic slump contributed structurally to the political rise of Cosimo de’ Medici through drastic contraction and concentration in the domestic banking industry.

papers.title: Paper Tracings in the Spectacularly Boisterous Archive of Slavery
papers.abstract: Everybody knew what she was called, but nobody anywhere knew her name. Disremembered and unaccounted for, she cannot be lost because no one is looking for her, and even if they were, how can they call her if they don’t know her name. Although she has claim, she is not claimed . . . It was not a story to pass on. Toni Morrison, Beloved . . . not all silences are equal and . . . they cannot be addressed—or redressed—in the same manner. To put it differently, any historical narrative is a particular bundle of silences, the result of a unique process, and the operation required to deconstruct these silences will vary accordingly. Michel-Ralph Trouillot, Silencing the Past In 1831, a will is recorded in South Carolina. The testatrix is Lucy Buchanan, a free Black woman. Like most wills, Buchanan’s included a request that her debts be “punctually paid out of such perishable property” that she might own at the time of her death. She left the remainder of her estate in real and personal property to a local white slaveholder, a man she described as a “friend” and who she named executor of her estate. She asked that he hold this property in guardianship for his son until such time as the son arrived at the age of twenty-one. At that point, the estate would fall to the son and in succession, his “heirs and assigns forever.” Her estate included, she stated, “my son William who is a Slave.” She further stated that she believed this decision represented “the best disposition that according to the laws of this state I can make for his welfare.”1 To date, I have found no other record of Lucy Buchanan or her son—no letters written by either of them or about them, no document created by the state. It is therefore with just the will that Lucy Buchanan and William enter the archive as far as I am aware. Moreover, it is not even clear that the will is a legal declaration. On the line that called for Buchanan’s signature, her name appears in typeset and inserted between her first and last name is the letter “X,” neither of which is unusual. An X-mark signature, typically a mark of handwriting illiteracy or disability made in lieu of an actual signature, is considered legally valid when properly witnessed, and there were witnesses to Buchanan’s will. But what exactly did they witness? Clearly, they did not witness Buchanan making an X signature as the X mark is, like her name, typeset. Was she even present for this non-signed but signed document? These problems notwithstanding, the will provides important insight into Lucy Buchanan’s life, including the violence of slavery that adhered to it. The lack of a signature represents but part of the violence of the system of human bondage that created and operationalized the spectacle of a free Black mother of an enslaved child. Lucy Buchanan’s attempt to extricate herself and her child from this spectacle commands my attention. I linger with her justification for remanding her child—a child enslaved to her—to the care of a white slaveholder. Perhaps the young man to whom she ultimately wills her son is the child’s biological father, but that is pure speculation. I focus on her statement that leaving her child enslaved with this man was the “best disposition” she could “make for his welfare” under the laws of the state in which she lived, South Carolina. It was not what she wanted for her son, only what she thought was best for him under the circumstances.2 It dawns on me that Buchanan used one of the master’s tools—a will—to protect her child the best way she knew how. With this decision, she also telegraphed the violence that attached to her, inserting her testimony into the archive of slavery.3 Entering the archive of slavery is to confront what Foucault calls “the jostling violence of the facts they tell” and Arlette Farge terms “the rustling voices of the population.”4 The archive of slavery is a boisterous place where the violence of slaveholders jostles against the resistance and “rustling voices” of the enslaved, of the kind that characterizes Buchanan’s will and so many documents in which enslaved people cry out despite the curatorial efforts embedded in the archive that aimed to silence them. The “jostling violence” appears in the papers of slaveholding women who talked about Rose, an enslaved woman who led a rebellion in South Carolina during the Civil War. papers.title: Teaching the History of the Vietnam Wars
papers.abstract: A visitor encountering a set of historical photographs that were part of the 2023 Vietnamese American Roundtable’s annual commemoration for the end of the Vietnam war in San Jose. Like the organizers of this event, many in the Vietnamese diasporic community in the United States commemorate the war’s end on April 30th as “Black April” (Tháng Tư Đen) in sharp contrast to the celebrations that mark official Vietnamese state commemorations where the anniversary is called Reunification Day (Ngày Thống nhất) or the Day of the Liberation of the South (Ngày Giải phòng miền Nam). Photo courtesy of the Vietnamese American Roundtable. Four high school teachers who were part of a National Endowment for the Humanities Summer Institute in 2022, “Contested Territory: America’s Involvement in Vietnam, 1945-75,” reflect on their teaching of the Vietnam wars and present an ensemble of classroom activities that have helped their students understand war in new ways. Master teachers who work in diverse classrooms across the United States, they offer innovative learning activities on the Vietnam wars that explore the everyday experiences of war; the roles of ideologies in shaping conflict; soundscapes of war; and the use of Geographical Information Systems (GIS) to study the complex geographies of war. Framing essays by the Institute’s co-leaders provide context on new Vietnam war scholarship and the design of inquiry-based practices that foster critical historical thinking. Three years into the official commemoration of the fiftieth anniversary of the first US combat mission in Vietnam, I happened to be teaching a course on the geography of modern Vietnam. On Memorial Day 2012, President Obama had proclaimed a “13-year program to honor and give thanks to a generation of proud Americans who saw our country through one of the most challenging missions we have ever faced.”1 In 2015, Obama’s proclamation was the first reading I assigned to twenty-four first-year students at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and it prompted a lively conversation. Asked to consider whom the document remembered, students praised how it “honored” American servicemen and servicewomen, some of whom were their grandparents. But some noted that it overlooked other Americans, including protesters who, one argued, had also stood up patriotically for democratic ideals. Moreover, many quickly grasped that the proclamation focused exclusively on American actors, mentioning nothing at all about the people of Vietnam. Why were they left out? How did they remember it? What were the war’s local causes and consequences? Evaluating the commemoration for whom it forgot and remembered introduced a critical pedagogy that integrated history with geography. First, it revealed to students fresh out of high school that not even popular, relatively progressive presidents were infallible. Their ready critique of his American-centric point of view recognized that such near-sightedness left out other points of view, especially Vietnamese perspectives. Then, their recognition opened a line of inquiry pointing to the course’s goal: to introduce a large, diverse country with long, complex histories that informed multiple perspectives on what, in Vietnam, is commonly called “the American War.” My course thus featured a bit of bait and switch: Hook students with a war, then argue for understanding it within a geographic context grounded in places and peoples too often left out of the picture. Significantly, the exercise meant it was the students who argued for shifting the gaze. Prepared for the leap from domestic to international perspective, I paired the presidential proclamation with another reading that foregrounded one of many Vietnamese points of view. In his aptly titled essay “The United States Isn’t the Only Country Still Trying to Figure Out the Vietnam War,” political scientist Tuong Vu starts with a different commemoration.2 In Vietnam, April 30, 2015, was celebrated as the fortieth anniversary of the American War’s dramatic conclusion, when People’s Army tanks crashed through the gates of the Presidential Palace in Saigon. “Ever since,” Vu argues, “Hanoi leaders have sought to capitalize on their military victory to legitimize their rule.” Indeed, official memory there, including public school curricula, cultivates a narrative papers.title: Digital Restoration and Historical Renovation in Vietnam
papers.abstract: In 1972, public intellectual Susan Sontag lamented the “image-choked” state of the world, which resulted in part from the overwhelming flood of Vietnam War photos then circulating.1 Over fifty years later, the visual landscape is even more saturated. The digital revolution, widespread smartphone use, and instant sharing via social media have inundated us with images. The advent of generative artificial intelligence and the deployment of deepfake and shallowfake technologies for disinformation are eroding confidence in the documentary authority of photographs as historical artifacts. These developments fundamentally transform how war is perceived and how history is shaped. They also deeply unsettle critical assumptions about the Vietnam War, which were widely accepted when I began teaching a few decades ago at a time when iconic Vietnam War photos became potent symbols, with some photographers even crediting them for helping end the war, and critics claiming that they set a template for portraying future conflicts.2 In Vietnam, socialist photographers crafted images to rally anticolonial support and inspire global solidarity. These images are currently displayed to commemorate the triumph of national liberation struggles.

papers.title: Deceptively “Easy”
papers.abstract: The book begins in a hospital in New York City; the first illustration is a tightly cropped image of a woman in labor, the frame drawing attention to her pregnant stomach, medical tubing, and spread legs. In the next panel, her husband stands beside her, but the text and the images spotlight an empty chair. Her mother has “disappeared.” Despite traveling across the country to assist, she “can’t bear to be in the same room” as her daughter1 (1–2). Thi Bui’s graphic memoir The Best We Could Do opens with this explicit childbirth scene, as it sets the stage for an immersive meditation on the fraught relationship between parents and their children, and on the consequences of colonialism and war across generations. The Best We Could Do’s powerful drawings and nonlinear narrative have seeped into my writing on refugee camps and provoked questions about historical method and form.2 It has also become a go-to book in my courses on the US War in Vietnam and US immigration history.
