papers.title: Michael H. Kater. After the Nazis: The Story of Culture in West Germany .
papers.abstract: Michael H. Kater’s book After the Nazis: The Story of Culture in West Germany falls into a rare historical genre. It deals with culture as the sum of cultural productions and their creators in the fields of literature, visual arts, music, film, theater, and journalism. Which is very different from the structural version of culture that shapes works like Axel Schildt’s and Detlef Siegfried’s 2009 compendium Deutsche Kulturgeschichte: Die Bundesrepublik von 1945 bis zur Gegenwart (Munich: Carl Hanser Verlag). In Kater’s book, by contrast, culture in the narrow sense is also itself a subject of history; it can have an “apotheosis,” be “in decline,” and “compromise,” (xiv) expressions the author uses to refer to the content of his two preceding books, Weimar: From Enlightenment to Present (2014) and Culture in Nazi Germany (2019). After the Nazis is a big narrative endeavor that aims at understanding culture’s role in the “relative success of the Federal Republic” (xiii). It is hard to argue with the assumption that democracy not only provides the possibility of free cultural expression but also needs enough cultural creations that use their aesthetic possibilities to critically react to oppressive political and social tendencies. After nearly four hundred pages, Kater concludes that West Germany’s culture was indeed “a check” in the checks and balances of the Federal Republic (382).

papers.title: Remembering the Fall of Phnom Penh to the Khmer Rouge
papers.abstract: “We will only execute seven people.” Prince Norodom Sihanouk, former Cambodian head of state, sought to calm fears as the Khmer Rouge closed in on the capital city of Phnom Penh in 1975. Deposed in a coup five years prior, Sihanouk in turn threw his support behind the Khmer Rouge and over the radio issued the group’s death list of seven high-ranking leaders of the US-supported Cambodian government.1 The Khmer Rouge captured the Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, in a collapse quickly overshadowed in the United States by the fall of Saigon two weeks later. Fifty years later, the following collection of images explores how violence in Southeast Asia extended in time and scope beyond American involvement in Vietnam. One photograph was taken by Samuel Jackson, the director of an English Language Center in Phnom Penh. International governments and organizations carried out evacuations throughout the spring of 1975. In the previously unpublished image (Fig. 6), Jackson captured the end of the American evacuation. He had spent the morning of April 12 arranging for the incineration of identifying student records before evacuating on the last US helicopter out of the city. His photograph shows John Gunther Dean, the US ambassador to Cambodia, as US officials flew out to the USS Okinawa waiting in the Gulf of Thailand. In two weeks’ time, the Okinawa would then go on to host evacuees from Vietnam.

papers.title: Lindsay Schakenbach Regele. Flowers, Guns, and Money: Joel Roberts Poinsett and the Paradoxes of American Patriotism .
papers.abstract: Lindsay Schakenbach Regele’s Flowers, Guns, and Money: Joel Roberts Poinsett and the Paradoxes of American Patriotism is a portrait of a self-interested man with significant power living through an era of dramatic historical change. Joel Roberts Poinsett (1779–1851) was a man of contradictions. He was the first US minister to Mexico who, despite the expansionist times, undermined the United States’ attempts to annex Texas. He was a South Carolinian who opposed protectionist tariffs and yet secretly mobilized military enforcement of federal tax collection in Charleston during Andrew Jackson’s Nullification Crisis. He was a Secretary of War who both introduced Cuban bloodhounds to kill Indigenous people in Florida and supported global exploration missions to obtain knowledge of Indigenous communities around the globe. He condemned US citizens fighting in foreign armies but had himself played a role in Chile’s independence fight. Enslaving many people to work in his several homes and on his wife’s rice fields, he also led the campaign to create the Smithsonian as a site of national enlightenment. He married late and only secretly acknowledged his only known child—a son born “out of wedlock” (58). His most lasting legacy is a Nahua plant marketed as a Christmas flower rechristened with his name: the Poinsettia.

papers.title: History(ies) of Authoritarianism(s) in the Philippines
papers.abstract: “My job is to go places where people die. I pack my bags, talk to the survivors, write my stories, then go home to wait for the next catastrophe. I don’t wait very long.” —Patricia Evangelista, Some People Need Killing, 5. How do we make sense of the history of and return to authoritarianism in the Philippines? This is one of the central questions that scholars and creatives working on the Philippines have engaged since the Marcos dictatorship in the 1970s. In recent years, there has been a renewed focus since the election of Rodrigo Roa Duterte to the presidency in 2016 and the return of the Marcos clan to Malacañang in 2022. There is a political urgency to work on Philippine authoritarianism as most people writing on the topic want to combat the resurgence of authoritarian rule in the Philippines and elsewhere. Four recent works, all dealing with the history and present of authoritarianism in the Philippines, provide insight into both the form and content of the study of dictatorship.

papers.title: Kidada E. Williams. I Saw Death Coming: A History of Terror and Survival in the War against Reconstruction .
papers.abstract: I Saw Death Coming is an incisive and moving analysis of freed people assaulted and murdered by the Ku Klux Klan and other groups across the South in the years following the Civil War, reframing this violence as “the war after the Civil War” (xxi, 222). Kidada E. Williams has crafted a unique contribution to the turn toward understanding the Civil War and Reconstruction at home and in daily life, drawing skillfully from survivors’ testimonies before the United States Congress’s Joint Select Committee to Inquire into the Condition of Affairs in the Late Insurrectionary States (published in 1872), narratives from the Works Progress Administration’s Federal Writers Project (1936–1938), and contemporary literature on trauma and human rights. By shifting our focus from individual office holders and voters to families, and from polling places to homes, Williams exposes the realities of lives caught within the “[f]issures between the letter and the fact of the law,” legislation including the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the Enforcement Acts of 1870–71, and the constitutional amendments for which Reconstruction is best known (54).

papers.title: Sarah Keyes. American Burial Ground: A New History of the Overland Trail .
papers.abstract: In the popular mythology that swirls around the expansion of the United States into the far West, the Overland Trail figures heavily in tales of victory: tenacious white pioneers pushing against tremendous odds to settle the land and claim it for the United States. It was a journey of progress, the story goes, one during which, if we are to believe Frederick Jackson Turner, both the emigrants and the land itself became ever more American with each step along the way. But contrary to cultural and even historical depictions of the movement westward through the romantic haze of white triumphalism, “the Trail was a treacherous, often deadly trek that left a string of burials” (2). Rather than seeing this history as one to celebrate, Sarah Keyes sees the story of the Trail as “a story of death” (9). In her newest book American Burial Ground: A New History of the Overland Trail, Keyes offers “a darker portrait of westward migration than we are used to, remembering, and uncovering the cultural significance of the dead” to the appropriation of the territory by the United States (2). Ironically, emigrant deaths and their graves along the Trail, Keyes argues, literally laid the groundwork for the seizure of these lands from Indigenous peoples. In other words, by remaking the Overland Trail into an American burial ground, “[d]ead emigrants eventually became an answer to another problem [they] hadn’t fully grappled with at the start of their journey: how to definitively claim the West for the United States” (5). Calling the failed emigrants who died on their long journey toward Oregon and California “as successful as those who reached” their destination, Keyes asserts that these dead emigrants became “traces of an expanding nation’s presence across the continent and, ultimately, the seeds of later white settlements” (6).

papers.title: Rebekah E. Pite. Sharing Yerba Mate: How South America’s Most Popular Drink Defined a Region .
papers.abstract: Whether consumed as an infusion or in some other form, stimulants are a common feature of human cultures across time and place. While some, like tea and coffee, have been adopted and embraced globally, others have remained largely regional and continue to define regional and national cultures. One example of the latter is yerba mate, a South American stimulant infusion typically consumed using a gourd or cup (mate) and a special straw (bombilla), and often shared and consumed collectively with others. Rebekah E. Pite’s book Sharing Yerba Mate: How South America’s Most Popular Drink Defined a Region is a well-researched, engaging, and important look at yerba mate’s history and geography of cultivation and consumption from the precolonial era to the present. While patterns of consumption and cultivation have evolved over time, yerba mate remains an important marker of culture and identity in parts of South America, even as it has gradually extended its global reach in recent decades. Pite traces mate’s production and consumption from what is now Paraguay to Peru and Chile, and later to Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. Using a variety of written and, perhaps most notably, visual sources, this study weaves this plant and drink into South America’s history in engaging and fascinating ways for regional and nonregional specialists alike.

papers.title: Rodney Hessinger. Smitten: Sex, Gender, and the Contest for Souls in the Second Great Awakening .
papers.abstract: During the Second Great Awakening, prophets, priests, and evangelists wooed their followers with divine revelations that often came with new conceptions of family, gender, and sexuality. These religious innovators also met with critics who denounced these men as false prophets intent on deceiving their “smitten” (mostly) female victims. In Smitten: Sex, Gender, and the Contest for Souls in the Second Great Awakening, Rodney Hessinger provides a gendered analysis of these debates over the authenticity and effects of religious enthusiasm. He demonstrates that the religious and gender dynamics of the Second Great Awakening were inextricable as the competition to win believers fueled debates about sexuality, consent, marriage, motherhood, and the power of male religious authorities. Religious groups further developed alternative sexual practices and gender norms to distinguish themselves and “strengthen the commitment of believers” while condemnations of such phenomena contributed to a coalescing white and middle-class Protestant establishment (7). Ultimately, Hessinger concludes that such efforts to stifle the sexual and gender experimentation that flourished as a part of religious innovation were also responsible for ending the Second Great Awakening. By the 1850s, both enthusiasm and sexual experimentations “had been tamed and contained” (13).

papers.title: Emma Day. In Her Hands: Women’s Fight against AIDS in the United States .
papers.abstract: Over the last fifteen years, a growing number of historians have described the impact of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the United States and the stories of activists who demanded education, services, and medical research to fight the disease. Many of these scholars have worked to diversify stories of HIV/AIDS activism by documenting work in and by communities of African, Asian, Latinx, and Native American descent. At the same time, sociologists such as Sabrina Marie Chase and Celeste Watkins-Hayes have studied the ways that HIV-positive women in the present day navigate systems of HIV care and services. Emma Day’s recent book In Her Hands: Women’s Fight against AIDS in the United States joins both bodies of scholarship. Day shows how women activists organized to make AIDS visible as a women’s health issue; created safer sex and AIDS education programs with women in mind; fought for medical care for incarcerated women with HIV and AIDS; and demanded medical research into the transmission of HIV between women during sex and women-specific HIV prevention tools, such as microbicides.

papers.title: Ayelet Brinn. A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press .
papers.abstract: In A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press, Ayelet Brinn analyzes the “vital, complex, and often unexpected ways that questions of women and gender” shaped the evolution of American Yiddish press (5). This study of Yiddish dailies in New York from their founding in the 1880s through their decline in circulation and influence in the mid-1920s centers newspaper features like advice columns and human-interest pieces described (and at times disparaged by critics) as “women’s content.” Though the Forverts’s long-running advice column the “Bintel brief” often appears in studies of American Jewish print culture, Yiddish women’s content broadly defined receives less scholarly attention than editorials, news reporting, and literary criticism. Interweaving the history of the rise of the American Yiddish newspaper industry with detailed portraits of editors, journalists, and readers, Brinn challenges the perspective that women’s content and those who produced or consumed it were “peripheral to the development of the Yiddish press” (14).

papers.title: Politics of War and Memory
papers.abstract: All wars are fought twice, according to Viet Thanh Nguyen, author of Nothing Ever Dies: the first time on the battlefield, the second time in memory. But maybe all wars are fought three times: the third time in the classroom.1 Nguyen—a professor of English, American studies, and comparative literature at the University of Southern California and winner of the Pulitzer Prize in Fiction for his novel The Sympathizer—gives student readers the opportunity to think about the Vietnam War from the vantage point of constructed memories and the formation of national identity. He argues that “garlands of euphemism and a fog of glorious myth shroud a bloody past,” and that such pretenses help states shape wars as necessary for defense of the country (5). He challenges this mythmaking, giving voice to the forgotten people, places, and memories that help us better understand the true cost of conflict. My students generally agree with Nguyen’s argument that memories of war are produced, cultivated, and empowered. They are particularly drawn to the way he links the commercialized and industrialized production of memory with the Vietnam War. Nguyen believes that a rich and fully developed country, like the United States, can create a “powerful industry of memory” that “makes it easy for people to access its products, delivered to their doors, their televisions, their screens, their shelves, their newspapers, even when they do not want these memories or seek them out” (167). Each of these intrusions tells an unjust war story, one that serves a larger and usually nationalistic cause. Nothing Ever Dies is a needed corrective, according to my students.

papers.title: F. Evan Nooe. Aggression and Sufferings: Settler Violence, Native Resistance, and the Coalescence of the Old South .
papers.abstract: In Aggression and Sufferings, F. Evan Nooe seeks to bring the tools of ethnohistory and the insights of Native history to the study of the white South. Specifically, the author wants to explore the question of how white Southerners came to identify as a distinct and coherent entity in the decades before the US Civil War. Nooe acknowledges the crucial and central role that the practice of slavery played in this process, deeply embedded as it was in the social and economic fabric of the white South. However, Nooe notes another dynamic that has received less scholarly attention: the shared experience of settler violence against the peoples of the Native South. Nooe distinguishes his work from that of scholars such as Patrick Griffin and Peter Silver, who argue that anti-Native violence was a formative component of American identity. He argues that perceived federal disinterest in aiding white Southerners’ colonizing ambitions created a rallying effect among them and a defiant attitude toward the rest of the country. When federal aid proved insufficient to match white Southerners’ expectations, states, cities, and volunteer organizations cultivated a siege mentality. They took it upon themselves to aid one another in promulgating settler violence and conquest, and defending newly conquered lands, sometimes in defiance of federal authority. These shared experiences begat a hagiography passed down by families and historical societies for generations, shaping how white Southerners viewed themselves, their ancestors, and their claims to colonized land.

papers.title: Rob Goldberg. Radical Play: Revolutionizing Children’s Toys in 1960s and 1970s America .
papers.abstract: In the early 1990s, I remember seeing Gene Wilder in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory (1971) on TBS and wondering why there would be a character like “Mike Teevee,” who was so addicted to Western films and shows on television that he couldn’t bother to speak with reporters about his golden ticket find. Being a gun-toting lawman of my grandmother’s favorite films and shows, especially John Wayne, seemed boring to me. As I’ve aged (as has the racial politics of 1950s and 1960s popular culture), I realized that Mike Teevee’s character was Roald Dahl’s commentary on the popularity of guns and violence in American television of the period and what happens to children that absorb all the gun-slinging action. Rob Goldberg’s Radical Play: Revolutionizing Children’s Toy’s in 1960s and 1970s America helps provide broader historical context for the material objects of play that I found boring but Roald Dahl and many other writers, parents, and policymakers of the period criticized.

papers.title: Robert A. Schneider. The Return of Resentment: The Rise and Decline and Rise Again of a Political Emotion .
papers.abstract: Early in The Return of Resentment, Robert A. Schneider quotes from a sermon by Samuel Parris, a Puritan who preached in Salem at the time of the witch trials. Parris had failed in a commercial venture in the Caribbean and now watched as farmers in the village succeeded and grew wealthy. His text was Mary and Joseph’s doomed search for lodgings in Bethlehem. He speculated why there was no room at the inn: “The Inne that it may be was full of rich folks” (36). Parris’s resentment was not exactly anger. It registered economic forces beyond his control and signaled a betrayal of the values that had impelled the community’s flight to the New World. The suspicion of harboring such traitors within, Schneider suggests, may have also fed persecution. Schneider’s encompassing and timely book is at once an intellectual history and archaeology of potent forces at work today. Unlike other emotions, resentment thrives from a complex dynamic involving both shared and personal experience. Its French expression, ressentiment—“to feel again”—conveys some of this complexity: Resentment is the memory of a wrong, and with memory comes lasting outrage that time doesn’t always heal. Resentment is relational; it carries a sense of victimization and sometimes humiliation; and it can dwell at length on hopes thwarted or denied. As a collective emotion, Schneider writes, it can also be used to powerful political effect. Unlike most other emotions, he argues persuasively, resentment has a history.

papers.title: Clark Davis. God’s Scrivener: The Madness and Meaning of Jones Very .
papers.abstract: In Transcendentalist circles, the poet Jones Very became briefly infamous in late 1838 for disrupting the refinements of Unitarian literary culture with an astonishing bout of religious enthusiasm. Arriving at Elizabeth Peabody’s door beside himself, he announced that he had come “to baptize you with the Holy Ghost & with fire” and then, sitting in her parlor, he revealed, “I am the Second Coming” (184–85). Just months earlier, Ralph Waldo Emerson had given his startling address at Harvard Divinity School in which he excoriated the dry formality of the New England ministry and extolled the intensity of immediate religious experience. Maybe this youthful enthusiast was exactly the “newborn bard of the Holy Ghost” that Emerson had been prophesying (175). Up to the time of his mystic transformation, Very had a reputation as a promising poet and ambitious literary student; after his Harvard graduation, he was serving effectively as a Greek tutor while also preparing for the Unitarian ministry. However, when he announced to one of his Greek classes that the Holy Spirt was speaking through him and commanded his students to “flee to the mountains, for the end of all things is at hand,” Harvard spared no time in dispatching him for his religious mania (177). His academic career over, he was briefly confined to McLean Asylum, but the implications of his artful ventriloquizing of God’s voice had only begun to be sorted out. In God’s Scrivener: The Madness and Meaning of Jones Very, Clark Davis provides the first major biography of the poet-prophet in over fifty years, placing this episode of dramatic spiritual awakening, which baffled so many of his contemporaries, within the full sweep of his life.

papers.title: Matthew Bowman. The Abduction of Betty and Barney Hill: Alien Encounters, Civil Rights, and the New Age in America .
papers.abstract: Betty and Barney Hill were an interracial couple from New Hampshire who, in 1961, reported the first ever abduction by extraterrestrial aliens. While accounts of alien abduction proliferated some decades later, the Hills’ account acts as a sort of foundational text in UFO studies, an inflection point in the longer history of belief in UFOs and extraterrestrials whereupon ETs were understood to shift focus from outer space to the inner space of human bodies and psyches. In his book The Abduction of Betty and Barney Hill: Alien Encounters, Civil Rights, and the New Age in America, religious historian Matthew Bowman acknowledges existing scholarship that has examined belief in alien abduction narratives as “an expression of anxiety and unease” (4). Bowman, however, is not fundamentally concerned with explaining or interpreting the belief in aliens or alien abduction. He seeks instead, through a close examination of the Hills themselves, including the social, cultural, and political forces that shaped them, to read their changing narrativization of their experience as a sort of vexing exercise in world building. Ultimately, Bowman’s reading of the Hills’ experience acts as a compelling case study of the history of the broader erosion of trust both in institutions and in the belief that citizens can work with and alongside those in power toward a greater good.

papers.title: Lydia Pelot-Hobbs. Prison Capital: Mass Incarceration and Struggles for Abolition Democracy in Louisiana .
papers.abstract: Louisiana posted the highest per capita incarceration rate in the nation and the world for every year except one between 1998 and 2020. Prison Capital: Mass Incarceration and Struggles for Abolition Democracy in Louisiana explores both how this came to be, and how Louisianans resisted their state’s carceral rise. In doing so, Lydia Pelot-Hobbs pursues academic and political goals. In addition to illuminating the innovations that nurtured Louisiana’s carceral state, she seeks “to highlight the conditions of possibility for dismantling carceral power in all its forms” (4). Pelot-Hobbs identifies the 1970s as a pivotal moment for Louisiana’s carceral state, and she argues that responses to local, national, and global crises moved the state from its prior “austerity approach to incarceration” (2). Louisiana’s imprisoned population, which barely exceeded four thousand in 1970, more than doubled during that pivotal decade, doubled again during the 1980s, and then doubled once more during the 1990s, before cresting at more than forty thousand in 2012. As was the case nationally, mass incarceration in Louisiana disproportionately affected Black people.

papers.title: Marlene Epp. Eating Like a Mennonite: Food and Community Across Borders .
papers.abstract: While cleaning out her parents’ house recently, my cousin found her mom’s well-worn copy of Frances Youngren’s Food for the Body, Food for the Soul, a cookbook first published by the Moody Bible Institute in 1943 and reprinted many times. Readers found spiritual inspiration as well as recipes inside: how to avoid wilting lettuce by turning on the faucet of “refreshing thoughts of love, duty, honor, sharing and kindness”; the importance of vitamin B, the Belief Vitamin, “essential to the development and normal functioning of the new life”; and advice on appropriate conduct for mothers and fathers that made no attempt to connect to the theme of food. My cousin’s unexpected discovery illustrates Marlene Epps’s central argument in her 2023 book Eating Like a Mennonite: Food and Community Across Borders that food is “imbued with cultural, religious, social, and political meaning,” but because it is “so ubiquitous and so everyday … we overlook its potential to offer meaning” (13). Epps is particularly interested in her own Mennonite tradition, a form of Anabaptist Protestant Christianity that has typically emphasized adult believer baptism, simple living, sharing possessions, and pacifism. The present global population of roughly 2 million Mennonites is spread across North America and, thanks to evangelism, countries in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Exploring what it means to “eat like a Mennonite” reveals important connections between ethnoreligious identity and immigration, colonization, gender, and memory.

papers.title: Max Deardorff. A Tale of Two Granadas. Custom, Community, and Citizenship in the Spanish Empire, 1568–1668 .
papers.abstract: Building on extensive archival research in Spain, Colombia, and Italy, A Tale of Two Granadas is a fantastic addition to the growing field of governance and citizenship in the multiethnic, composite Spanish Empire during the 16th and 17th centuries. The book explores how Indigenous and mestizo peoples in the New Kingdom of Granada (present-day Colombia) and moriscos (Muslim people who were forced to convert to Christianity) in the peninsular Kingdom of Granada negotiated a place in the political arena within the context of the religious transformations brought by the Council of Trent. The author, Max Deardorff, follows an encompassing comparison in which processes occurring on both sides of the Atlantic influence each other, share protagonists, and ultimately are part of a single, complex drive toward political organization across the Spanish Empire. The key element in the argument is the evolving conflict between two views of integration/segregation of new converts as Christianity expanded among the territories absorbed by the Spanish monarchy in Europe and the Americas. One segment of the political spectrum sought to use concepts of race and blood purity (limpieza de sangre), to exclude former Muslims, mestizos, and Indigenous peoples from power positions and urban governance. Another political posture drove for integration through what Deardorff calls “Christian citizenship,” a set of values and duties associated with community life shaped by church precepts such as marriage, mass attendance, and catechism. Even though the first stance ultimately prevailed, the wide array of case studies analyzed by the author shows how neophytes carved out urban privileges by taking advantage of the church’s role in the political cementation of the Spanish dominions. The result is a highly nuanced discussion that draws the reader deeply into the cultural and political milieu of two little-studied areas of the Spanish Empire.

papers.title: Henry Alexander Wiencek. Oil Cities: The Making of North Louisiana’s Boomtowns, 1901–1930 .
papers.abstract: When observers hear the term “boomtown,” they typically think of silver or gold rush communities in the West. Images of rowdy saloons full of newly flush drunken men spending their newfound wealth on whiskey and women form the centerpiece of thinking about boomtowns. The same reasoning often includes scenes of rampant speculation, corruption, unbridled violence, and the occasional hero who tames the lawlessness. One need only think of Tombstone, Arizona, with its infamous gang known as the “Cowboys” and their nemesis, Wyatt Earp, to get the idea. In American thought, boomtowns remain the very personification of the “wild West.” In Oil Cities, Henry Alexander Wiencek finds that boomtowns were far from monolithic and not always located in the West. Wiencek examines the boomtowns that emerged in north Louisiana when the fledgling oil industry targeted the region as the next hot spot for exploitation. In a matter of months, the territory surrounding Caddo Lake, along with the lake itself, experienced a comprehensive transformation that saw a sleepy farming region recast as an epicenter of industrial development. Desperate sharecroppers found higher paying jobs. Those fortunate enough to own land, including some Blacks who had to overcome the additional hurdle of ensconced racism, found themselves suddenly comparatively wealthy. According to Wiencek, the oil boomtowns offered a bridge to economic success for workers and landowners alike.

papers.title: Scott Ingram. Constitutional Inquisitors: The Origins and Practice of Early Federal Prosecutors .
papers.abstract: Given the tremendous power that federal prosecutors have in modern American society, it is remarkable that no historian has explored their origins. In a new book, Constitutional Inquisitors: The Origins and Practice of Early Federal Prosecutors, Scott Ingram argues that the first federal district attorneys were “unintentionally established” as the nation’s premier law enforcement officers (7). According to Ingram, public prosecutors were originally nothing like the investigator-cum-advocates we have today. At the founding, private parties (usually victims) instigated and directed criminal prosecutions. Government attorneys functioned more as clerks, drafting indictments and compiling evidence to aid grand juries in deciding whether prosecution should proceed (though at times they also questioned witnesses and provided legal advice). Most important, public prosecutors did not investigate crimes, and they did not have the authority to direct or decline prosecution. Befitting their minor role, the first federal attorneys were largely an afterthought. The Constitution’s drafters and ratifiers debated the scope of federal criminal jurisdiction but paid little attention to who would enforce it. The only requirement in the Judiciary Act of 1789 was that the president appoint a “meet person learned in the law” to serve as the government’s attorney in each federal judicial district. George Washington tried to appoint well-regarded lawyers who supported the new federal government, but he was more concerned with who would serve as federal judges. Potential candidates were similarly ambivalent; other positions were more prestigious (like judges), or more lucrative (like customs collectors), prompting leading nominees—including future Chief Justice John Marshall—to decline the position.

papers.title: Neil Roos. Ordinary Whites in Apartheid Society: Social Histories of Accommodation .
papers.abstract: As Neil Roos comments in the introductory chapter to Ordinary Whites in Apartheid Society: Social Histories of Accommodation, it is worth asking if historians should “bother” (20) with writing histories of whites in South Africa—about the category of people who benefited the most from apartheid rule and who were the least involved in the anti-apartheid movement. Indeed, it is especially striking that Ordinary Whites is grounded in Roos’s own autobiography: It “is set in the world [he] grew up in,” drawing on the stories of people “[he] grew up with” (11), including photographs of Roos’s family and of his parents, Sheila and Dick, and using their biographies as points of entry into the book’s key arguments. The category of “white” had to be made and constantly reinforced under apartheid, and tracing the experiences of “ordinary” white South Africans is revealing of those efforts to constitute and maintain “whiteness.” As a result, one of the key preoccupations of Ordinary Whites is the state’s management of white, working-class people, from efforts to raise their standard of living, to attempts to “improve” them morally.

papers.title: John McAleer. Atlantic Voyages: The East India Company and the British Route to the East in the Age of Sail .
papers.abstract: When an East Indiaman departed Britain, many passengers felt strong emotions, ranging from regret and sadness to a recognition that the voyage they were embarking on would be a dividing line in their lives. When the ship reached the Bay of Biscay, seasickness was common. Those who recovered eventually developed routines to pass the time. They celebrated the first sight of land after leaving the English Channel—usually Madeira or Tenerife. They witnessed flying fish landing on deck; they endured the heat of the tropics; they marveled at the ceremonies crossing the equator. Further south, Cape pigeons followed the ship in strong winds and cold weather, before it finally rounded the Cape of Good Hope and entered the Indian Ocean. As John McAleer admits toward the end of his introduction to Atlantic Voyages, this description applies to most voyages between Britain and India in the age of sail. Like Tolstoy’s happy families, most voyages were alike. But McAleer does not take that insight as a point of departure to emphasize the unhappy voyages—the mutinies, the hurricanes, the shipwrecks, or the encounters with French privateers. He recounts such happenings when appropriate, but he is most interested in “the quotidian experiences of those passengers who sailed the length of the Atlantic Ocean on their way to Asia” (6). He bounds his study in the age of sail, specifically on ships sailing to India (mostly but not exclusively East Indiamen), and specifically on the part of the voyage that took place in the Atlantic, both going and coming.

papers.title: Drew A. Swanson. A Man of Bad Reputation: The Murder of John Stephens and the Contested Landscape of North Carolina Reconstruction .
papers.abstract: On May 21, 1870, during the height of Congressional Reconstruction in North Carolina, Caswell County Democrats held a public political meeting in the local courthouse. Among the attendees was a man decidedly unwelcome there: Republican State Senator John W. Stephens. Like many so-called “scalawags” (white southern Republicans), Stephens drew the ire of Democrats, who viewed him as a traitor. On that day, Stephens sat in the courtroom taking notes on his opponents’ meeting. At some point, however, he left the room at the behest of a man who proposed to speak to him about the upcoming election. He never came home to his family. The next morning, a search party discovered Stephens lying dead with a rope around his neck in the courthouse basement. Although several men were arrested, no one was ever tried for Stephens’s murder. In A Man of Bad Reputation, Drew Swanson explores not the question of who killed John Stephens (it was a mob of local Ku Klux Klan, as most contemporaries well knew) but how Stephens’s assassination played an outsized role in the fall of Reconstruction and in the contested public memory of the era.

papers.title: Mary Fulbrook. Bystander Society: Conformity and Complicity in Nazi Germany and the Holocaust .
papers.abstract: Since the 1990s, “bystander” concepts have firmly been part of the conventional analytic frameworks in the field of Holocaust studies. As part of a triad with “perpetrator” and “victim,” this concept enabled scholars—in the words of Raul Hilberg, one of its key proponents—to “encompass everyone who stood on the [Shoah’s] stage” (The Politics of Memory [1996]). In recent years, historians have severely criticized the very notion of bystander as a misleading oversimplification, catchall concept or, as Mary Fulbrook stresses, integral part of Germans’ exculpatory postwar myth of innocence (6, 396). In her latest study, Bystander Society: Conformity and Complicity in Nazi Germany and the Holocaust, Fulbrook offers a far-reaching reevaluation of bystanding and its role in the Nazi dictatorship and genocide. Rightfully insisting that a sole focus on key individuals, elites, and institutions is insufficient to explain the Hitler state and its racial policies, Fulbrook turns to the actions of the “muddled middle”—her term for the majority of Germans who were neither committed Nazis nor part of the tiny minority of resisters nor the regime’s victims (18). Instead of discarding the bystander category and devising new concepts, Fulbrook seeks to turn it into a useful analytical concept at the center of a multilayered investigation that returns to the core question of how the Holocaust could happen (24).

papers.title: Joaquín Rivaya-Martínez, ed. Indigenous Borderlands: Native Agency, Resilience, and Power in the Americas .
papers.abstract: The inspiring book Indigenous Borderlands: Native Agency, Resilience, and Power in the Americas is the culmination of a project whose first step was a symposium held at Texas State University in 2018. In the words of the book’s editor, Joaquín Rivaya-Martínez, “such methodology involves situating the focus on the natives, incorporating indigenous sources and testimonies whenever possible, and trying to comprehend indigenous actions and perspectives through multidisciplinary approaches that often rely on nondocumentary archaeological, linguistic, ethnographic, environmental, or other sources” (22). papers.title: Pamela Voekel. For God and Liberty: Catholicism and Revolution in the Atlantic World, 1790–1861 .
papers.abstract: The genre of the book review may be notable for its use of superlatives, but in this case, it is no exaggeration to say that Pamela Voekel’s deeply researched, highly original study is one of the most important books in the field to appear this decade. She documents the impact of the schism inside the Catholic Church between Jansenist-inflected reform movements and ultramontane reactionaries and shows how it entirely permeated the Spanish American independence era and shaped its legacy political culture. Voekel’s For God and Liberty: Catholicism and Revolution in the Atlantic World, 1790–1861 effectively upends two generations of historiography on the nature of the civil strife that rent asunder the newly independent Latin American states during the 1810s–1830s. Focusing primarily on the experiences of Central America and the four states emerging out of the former Viceroyalty of New Granada—Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panamá—Voekel argues that “[at] the heart of the Age or Revolutions in Spanish America was a Catholic civil war . . . The traditional narrative of the transition from monarchy to independent republicanism as a process of secularization misses completely the warring factions in the church who vied to define humanity’s relation to God and, therefore, the proper order of temporal authority” (1). It’s the sort of forehead-slappingly obvious truth that, after reading the book, one wonders why no one has noticed it before. Generations whose research focused on the formation of the nation-state, or the buildup of economic resentments, or the appeal of Enlightenment political philosophy and constitution-writing have generally ignored or underestimated the ongoing relevance of religion and have tended to see the church as a monolithic entity. Voekel brilliantly resurrects the players and doctrinal positions to show how “[t]his was not a battle between modernizers and traditionalists, but between religious innovators” (251) as the Reform Catholic tradition of people like the abolitionists Abbé Grégoire and various Jansenists prompted an equally intense countermovement among ultramontane factions eager to shore up absolutist monarchies and papal authority.

Stokes tells this complex story through a fine-grained analysis of federal, state, and local regulations, which she supplements with media discourse and migrants’ experiences.

papers.title: Srirupa Roy. The Political Outsider: Indian Democracy and the Lineages of Populism .
papers.abstract: In recent years, we have witnessed the rise of populism across the world. Whether it is Donald Trump in the United States, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey, Viktor Orbán in Hungary, or Narendra Modi in India, populist leaders everywhere have followed a familiar script. They conjure up a division between a victimized “people” and the elite, and project themselves as political outsiders who alone are able to right the wrongs done to the powerless citizens. There is a burgeoning literature on the subject, analyzing populism and offering explanations. Srirupa Roy’s The Political Outsider acknowledges this literature but finds it inadequate, deeming it presentist and electoralist, and insufficiently attentive to the broader range of politics and history within which populism is embedded. Focusing on populism in India, the book argues that populism is a “project of democratic reform fueled by an imagination of democracy’s repairable lapses” (6). It relies on diagnosing what ails the political system, and its core mission is to cure and restore a flawed and diseased democracy. Populism is remedial rather than revolutionary. Unlike left-wing movements, populists do not try to overturn the unequal sociological and economic order, but only attempt to “cure” the political system of its disease, to restore its health. Such a project of restoration throws up political outsiders whose purported exteriority to the normal system of electoral representation allows them to cleanse it of its distortion and corruption. Roy elaborates this argument by her study of populism in India, which, she suggests, is part of an older and ongoing program of curative democracy that took shape in the long 1970s and gave rise to “outsider politics,” both of which can be witnessed in the present.

papers.abstract: Media technology today connects potential donors to sufferers of humanitarian crises across the globe. Like most other phenomena, this form of international philanthropy has a rich history. The groups’ identities are strikingly dissimilar: US American, English, and Irish; white and Black; middle class and enslaved. Shrout argues that the famine proved to be “the right catastrophe at the right time” that united multiple groups around a common cause. Scholars of philanthropy know well that the charitable impulse has existed as long as human beings and is embedded in all faith traditions. Studies of social movements, moreover, have linked resistance to authority and charitable purpose. Scholarship on the linkage of charities that meet basic needs with social justice advocacy spans abolition, settlement houses, immigrants’ burial societies, the Black church, and civil rights. The pathbreaking argument in this book is not that many different groups supported those in need, nor that social movement organizations fulfill basic needs, but that charity cloaked a variety of political uses to advance other agendas.

papers.title: Robert Hornsby. The Soviet Sixties .
papers.abstract: With The Soviet Sixties, Robert Hornsby aims to write the USSR into the story of the “global Sixties.” The book covers the years 1953 to 1968, an era bookended by the death of Joseph Stalin and the Soviet military intervention in Czechoslovakia. Over the course of nearly four hundred pages, Hornsby synthesizes the growing literature on the Thaw era into an easy-to-digest and often entertaining narrative. The book moves chronologically through the era, starting in 1953, when Stalin’s sudden death initiated a struggle for power among his top lieutenants. The victor, Nikita Khrushchev, immediately began to relax some of Stalin’s policies. In 1956, Khrushchev denounced the purges of 1937 and Stalin’s creation of a “cult of personality” in his famous “Secret Speech.” Hornsby traces the various small “freezes” and “thaws” that followed as the Soviet leadership sought to maintain control of the country—and its satellite states in Eastern Europe—while selectively repudiating elements of Stalinism.

papers.title: What Made the Levellers Revolutionary? Reconsidering Leveller Political Economy
papers.abstract: The article addresses the neglect of matters of political economy in Leveller scholarship, which for some time has focused on political and constitutional issues. It foregrounds Leveller approaches to trade and taxation, tithes and enclosure, and the relief of poverty before, during, and after the Leveller zenith of 1647–49. These concerns were as central to Leveller thinking as the issue of the parliamentary franchise, and the Levellers’ attention to such issues helps explain their contemporary appeal. Demanding the elimination of monopolies, tithes, and feudal land tenures, the Levellers projected a vision of flourishing English local and national economies built upon the work of the “laborious and industrious” people. Moreover, their approaches to poor relief were primarily intended not to control the poor but rather to assist them in returning to household independence. The Levellers’ attack on trade restrictions, their preference for taxation that fell predominantly on the wealthy, and their assault upon the tithe income of the state clergy and lay impropriators all struck at the resources of the social elite and at rationales for their predominance. Indeed, the Levellers were social revolutionaries: they both challenged contemporary institutions and practices that they found injurious to the “middling sort” and the “meaner sort” and proposed incompatible alternatives. Their emphasis on the country’s future as a trading and manufacturing nation anticipated the commercial revolution that accompanied the political revolution of 1688–89. Finally, the consistency over time of Leveller argumentation about matters of political economy suggests caution in imposing restrictive Leveller chronologies.

papers.title: The Kaleidoscopic Approach
papers.abstract: In teaching the Vietnam War—on the eve of the fiftieth anniversary of the war’s end and especially in Southern California, where I am based—I am most impressed by the diversity of student experiences and learning expectations compared with earlier generations of students. Thanks to Hollywood and a continuing stream of movies and television shows, there is a continuing “Vietnam mystique” that attracts students to Vietnam War classes; however, in the Southern California classroom, many students have diverse, personal connections to Vietnam and the conflict that transcend movie stereotypes. As teachers, we can use that initial curiosity—whatever prompts it—to challenge students to embrace a kaleidoscopic variety of experiences that range far beyond old assumed categories. For teachers, one of the best ways to do this is to use online, digital archives that now contain millions of digitized documents and other materials, all searchable with a few keywords and clicks. Considering wars globally, one of the most remarkable developments to come out of fifty-plus years of peace and reconciliation between the United States and Vietnam has been the declassification of millions of military and civilian records in state archives and increased opportunities for former combatants, refugees, and others to travel, meet, and jointly examine the war from different angles. This was America’s first television war, too, and besides preserved documents, photographs, and maps, we have worlds of other media, now digitized and archived, including television newsreeels, 8mm home movies, captured documents, personal diaries, personal photography, satellite photography, and consultant reports.

papers.title: More Than Meets the Eye
papers.abstract: I encountered Jonathan Schell’s 1967 New Yorker article “The Village of Ben Suc” as an enthusiastic if somewhat naïve undergraduate conducting research on American counterinsurgency in Vietnam.1 It was absorbing, dramatic, and poignant, and I remember devouring it late one night in a single sitting, then reading it again the following day. At 130 pages, “The Village of Ben Suc” is considerably longer than most of the research articles and book chapters I’m able to assign in my Global Vietnam War course at the University of Leeds. But with reading expectations everywhere wavering due to eroding attention spans if not work ethic, the piece has always been popular with my students, due in large part, I suspect, to Schell’s adept storytelling. Classroom discussions of the text are lively and engaged, and it is routinely listed in my end-of-year course evaluations as one of the readings that students enjoy most. “The Village of Ben Suc” presents a vivid eyewitness account of the 1967 Operation Cedar Falls campaign. This was a massive United States–South Vietnamese military exercise aimed at pacifying the so-called “Iron Triangle,” a rural Communist Party stronghold immediately northwest of Saigon. Schell recounts swooping into the titular village aboard a squadron of sixty helicopter gunships while he was embedded with a company of enthusiastic American soldiers primed for combat with a tenacious and cunning foe. The soldiers, teenagers outside the United States for the first time, find themselves instead deposited into a tranquil and bucolic community that regards them with bemusement, exasperation, or weary resignation. We observe the Americans’ bewilderment and frustration as they attempt the futile task of identifying enemy agents, equipped at best with a few words of broken Vietnamese. When communication proves hopeless, the soldiers instead cite the villagers’ demeanor or clothing in distinguishing friend from foe. A man riding a bicycle and a young couple enjoying a picnic are among the many shot and killed for wearing “the V.C. uniform,” the áo bà ba or “black pajamas” to the Americans, a loose-fitting ensemble ubiquitous in the rural South. “What are you going to do?” a US Army major later concedes to Schell. “We’ve got people in the kitchen at the base wearing those black pajamas” (120).

papers.title: When Elephants Fight, Flirt, or Make Love
papers.abstract: The end of the US wars in Indochina generated much circumspection across the Asia-Pacific region. In the United States, American officials and scholars debated who should be blamed for the American setback in Southeast Asia. In Vietnam, the fall of Saigon brought a close to the American War. In Southeast Asia, governments expressed their concerns that the victorious communists in Indochina and their comrades across the subregion might be inspired to attack or subvert their states.1 Southeast Asian leaders, however, also had broader concerns. With Sino-American ties thawing, Washington adjusting its policies toward Asia, and the Soviets intensifying their activities in the region after 1975, the member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) worried, as they regularly did, about the international politics of the region.2 As Singaporean Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew quipped: “When elephants fight, the grass suffers. The thought occurred to me that when elephants flirt, the grass also suffers. And when they make love, it is disastrous.”3 For me and for many of my students, April 30, 1975, brings into sharp focus these enduring challenges and dynamics in Asia. We address the conflict in Vietnam in that context. A work that generates such discussion in my classes is Michael J. Green’s study—By More Than Providence—of the US involvement in the Asia-Pacific since 1783.4

papers.title: Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India, By Amanda Lanzillo
papers.abstract: The historiography of artisanal labor in colonial India reflects a dynamic and evolving field. While traditional Marxist interpretations highlight the detrimental effects of colonialism on indigenous industries, revisionist scholars and recent research offer a more nuanced view, acknowledging the resilience and adaptability of certain sectors and the multifaceted nature of economic change during this period. Yet “De-industrialization versus Modernization” still dominates the academic debates of economic history in South Asian curricula. As a fresh breeze, in Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India, Amanda Lanzillo examines how Muslim artisans in northern India during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries integrated Islamic principles into their crafts amid colonial industrialization. This work is a meticulous exploration of the intersection between Islamic identity, artisanal work, and technological advancements in colonial northern India. Lanzillo argues that Muslim artisans positioned themselves as both technical experts and religiously grounded professionals, producing Urdu technical manuals that framed modern technologies within an Islamic intellectual tradition. This perspective diverges from most of the prior scholarship, which tends to separate religious identity from labor practices, primarily focusing on colonial policies and their effects on labor. Lanzillo’s turn to vernacular Urdu manuals and community histories shows how artisans themselves framed their labor as both economically and morally significant, creating an alternative discourse on labor that countered colonial narratives of progress. This approach challenges the assumption that technological change in colonial India was entirely dictated by British frameworks.

papers.title: Energy Policy and Climate Change in Europe during the Era of Neoliberalism
papers.abstract: Abstract This article shows how the European Community sought to become a global climate leader during the 1980s and 1990s, only to fail to make progress after Brussels was moved by globalization and by neoliberal ideas to pursue reforms that led the Community to burn more fossil fuels. European commissioners hoped to revive growth and fight global warming simultaneously by extending Europe’s internal market to energy in the belief that this would invigorate competition while also reducing carbon emissions. They bolstered their climate agenda with proposals for a carbon tax, which they envisioned as a model for the world. National politics, however, shaped this agenda and prevented Brussels from implementing its vision in the form imagined by Eurocrats. The growth component of their reforms prevailed because it found support from key states and business groups. This struggle, moreover, narrowed the scope for feasible climate action at a European level. For, as energy policy became entangled with the single market, European states departed from their earlier interest in directed investment and command-and-control measures, weakening efforts for a green industrial policy. Ultimately, as the energy landscape of Europe was transformed, globalization, market liberalization, and global warming became deeply intertwined processes, in which the former two accelerated the latter.

papers.title: Tech-empowered equity: advancing linguistic justice through digital scholarship
papers.abstract: Abstract This proposal addresses a critical yet often overlooked aspect within human rights, linguistics, and translation and interpreting studies by advocating for the integration of digital scholarship into the pursuit of linguistic justice. Focusing on court interpreting for migrants in Australia, the study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative accuracy assessments with qualitative discourse analysis to evaluate and improve interpreter-mediated communication in legal settings. By leveraging digital humanities (DH) methodologies such as corpus linguistics, natural language processing, and machine learning (ML), the proposal outlines three interdisciplinary research directions: (1) corpus-based analysis of courtroom interpreting performance, (2) development of ML-driven interpreter feedback systems, and (3) evaluation of linguistic rights and language equity within legal contexts. This research aims to bridge the gap between applied research insights and real-world legal applications, enhancing the accuracy and reliability of interpreting services, especially in technology-enabled remote hearings. Additionally, the proposal emphasizes the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in developing innovative solutions to systemic inequities in legal proceedings. By transforming specialized court interpreter training and practices through digital tools and data-driven approaches, this work seeks to ensure equitable access to justice for non-native speakers and promote a more inclusive legal system. Ultimately, this proposal demonstrates the potential of DH to not only advance academic understanding but also deliver tangible benefits in institutional settings, thereby reinforcing procedural justice and linguistic human rights in courtroom environments.

papers.title: Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, By Douglas Pretsell
papers.abstract: In their effort to bring queer history into mainstream consciousness, public history initiatives have often sought to find touchstones, exemplary figures who can act as historic rallying points. In Germany, one such figure is Karl Heinrich Ulrichs, a Hanoverian lawyer who, in 1867, addressed the Congress of German Jurists in Munich to argue for the rights of people he termed “urnings,” who now would fall under the category of gay men. The centering of “great men,” however, has come at a cost: a simplification of the complex human histories of such characters. Ulrichs has, in some quarters, been regarded as the “first gay man,” and his appearance at the Congress as the “first coming out.” Such characterizations are glib, reducing Ulrichs—and more ephemerally, the “meaning” of Ulrichs—to a handful of chartable moments. In Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, Douglas Pretsell seeks to do justice to Ulrichs by focusing specifically on the impact of his ideas and theories of what it meant to be an urning, before examining in a broader context how the urning concept populated itself in the German-speaking world. The result is a deeply interesting work that places Ulrichs at the center of an intellectual-identitarian cosmos while at the same time recognizing that, once Ulrichs’s arguments were taken up by a broader public, they exceeded the control and imagination of their originator. Rather than a biography of Ulrichs, Urning is thus a biography of an idea.

papers.title: Gay Student Services v. Texas A&M University: A Social History of the First Amendment in the Struggle for Equality
papers.abstract: Abstract In 1975, students at Texas A&M University created the campus’s first gay and lesbian student organization, Gay Student Services (GSS). When university administrators refused to recognize the group the following year, the student members filed a federal lawsuit claiming that the university had violated their First Amendment rights protecting speech, expression, and association. Nearly a decade later, the students won, and a federal appellate court ordered Texas A&M officials to recognize GSS. The students’ legal strategy differed remarkably from the one employed by the mainstream gay and lesbian rights movement of the era, which relied on a constitutional right to privacy to advance queer equality. In this article, I uncover a largely forgotten and discarded strategy in the national movement for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) equality. I argue that using the tools of social history to study the Texas A&M students’ legal struggle against the university reveals the ways that constitutional arguments about free speech, expression, and association had more liberating potential than arguments about sexual privacy. Although free speech, expression, and association eventually took a back seat to arguments about privacy in the larger movement, the First Amendment may yet hold a key to preserving the rights of queer people today.

papers.title: The Prestes Column: An Interior History of Modern Brazil, By Jacob Blanc
papers.abstract: Historians of Brazil have embraced region as an important category of analysis since at least the 1970s, a sensible strategy for the world’s fifth largest country, which occupies half a continent. We now have excellent English-language studies that compare Brazilian regional identities, from the São Paulo planters and industrialists who took credit for bringing modernity to Brazil to the Northeastern public intellectuals who represented the people of their region as the true backbone of their nation. Jacob Blanc’s historiographical aim is to bring attention to the “relational and imaginative category” of “the Brazilian interior,” zooming in to the regions that people from coastal and urban areas have imagined as “the space just beyond reach—far enough away so as to still pose risks, but close enough to offer the potential of settlement or extraction” (199, 14). To this end, Blanc’s first book, The Itaipu Dam and the Visibility of Rural Brazil (Duke, 2019), explored the competing efforts of Indigenous communities, landless peasants of mixed heritage, and farmers of European descent to defend their lands in the interior where Brazil meets Paraguay. This second monograph, like his co-edited volume, The Interior: Recentering Brazilian History (University of Texas, 2025), maintains the focus on interior peoples and spaces but expands the goal in time and in scope. Starting in the 1890s and stretching to 2022, Blanc analyzes how ideas about the interior were generated before, during, and after Army Captain Luís Carlos Prestes crisscrossed the hinterlands in thirteen of Brazil’s then-twenty states with his column of rebel soldiers and officers. The 1,000-person column engaged in some 150 skirmishes with federal, state, and local forces, marching the equivalent of “Los Angeles to New York and back again three times” from 1924 to 1927 before leaving for exile in Bolivia (1).

papers.title: Republican Kinship in the Society of Princes: The Dutch States General as Corporate Godparent, 1578–1732
papers.abstract: Abstract Throughout the early modern period, the Dutch States General, as if it were a natural person, frequently stood godfather over foreign children. Based on innovative archival research, this article investigates this unknown phenomenon as ‘corporate godparenthood’ and argues that it was an important tool of republican diplomacy in the Protestant society of princes, particularly in the Holy Roman Empire. Corporate godfatherhood allowed the Dutch Republic to partake, and assert its presence, in familial princely spheres to which it did not otherwise have access. The cultural practices of baptism, including the right of the godparents to name a child and baptismal gift-giving, allowed the States to form lasting kinship relations of mutual obligation in an economy of affection. Corporate godfatherhood had important and long-lasting effects: many of the dynasties with whom the States entered into a kinship relation remained allies for several generations, and supplied the States’ army with troops and officers, while the States assumed the role of benefactor, protector, educator, executor, or legal guardian of various of its princely godchildren.

papers.title: Digital debating cultures: communicative practices on Reddit
papers.abstract: Abstract Reddit as a platform for online forum interaction hosts various communities (subreddits), which give rise to specific digital communicative practices. Communication on Reddit is on the one hand unified by a set of common affordances, and on the other hand it is characterized by a great deal of variation in terms of topics, interactional patterns, and linguistic features. In this article, we aim to map the communicative space(s) of Reddit by means of vignettes of studies from four research groups, each of them describing a different approach to one or several subreddits. Study 1 examines concessive constructs in r/changemyview posts, Study 2 focuses on expert-lay communication on r/mountaineering, Study 3 addresses register variation within a large corpus of Reddit comments from many different communities, and Study 4 looks across different subreddits to explore the function of text-length. Drawing on these four vignettes, we show the range of discourses that Reddit has hosted in recent years, while also exploring the methodological tools as well as the insights that qualitative, text-based digital humanities, critical discourse analysis and computational text analysis can provide. The map to the Reddit language research space we create here can help digital humanities researchers to make sense of the variety of different theoretical vantage points and methodologies that are currently being employed to Reddit, and it can serve as a guideline when it comes to choosing research agendas and relevant literature on current forum interaction.

papers.title: Emotion and Ethics: The Conjoined Twins of Early Modern English Culture
papers.abstract: Abstract Passions and affections, notwithstanding their potential and capacity for disorder, were fundamental to the workings of the early modern world and lay at the centre of ethical life. Yet, most scholarship ignores the inseparability of emotion and ethics for early modern society. This article reviews the current state of scholarship in three fields: history of philosophy, history of emotions, and English society and governance, highlighting the assumptions and arguments which have led to the mistaken severance of affect from morality, the exclusion of ethics from histories of emotion, and the omission of emotion from studies of English power and authority. It argues that this separation is anachronistic and impairs our ability to understand governance in early modern England. This was a world of fused affect and morality which underpinned particular notions of power and authority. That governance was located within an ethical/emotive paradigm has been given insufficient attention.

papers.title: John Owen, Puritan Politics, and the Fall of the Cromwellian Protectorate
papers.abstract: Abstract The English protectorate began in 1653 with a conspiracy of politicians, army officers, and religious leaders against a theocratic strain of puritanism. Among the plotters was John Owen (1616–83), the leading religious authority of the Interregnum, vice-chancellor of Oxford University, and the ‘Cajoler of Cromwell’. When amid a military and republican coup parliament was dissolved and Richard Cromwell removed in 1659, Owen was again at the heart of events. But the narrative became that this time he had used his influence to oppose the Cromwells. As minister of a congregation at the centre of the nation’s halls of power composed of the military and political elite, Owen became seen as Richard Cromwell’s ‘instrument of ruine’. This article challenges that narrative and its appearance in histories of early 1659 and of Owen’s biography by utilizing new sources and re-evaluating known evidence within the broader context of religious and political divisions at the end of the protectorate. Owen supported whatever political form could best preserve the long-term safety of the English commonwealth and godly rule against the Stuarts. Yet Owen’s legacy became contested among the godly after the Restoration, as the agent of the protectorate’s fall and the failure of puritan politics.

papers.title: Starving Empire: A History of Famine in France’s Colonies, By Yan Slobodkin
papers.abstract: From Gaza to Sudan to Ukraine, our world’s ongoing wars have often sparked debates about one term: famine. Pundits and reporters have argued about whether famines have arisen amid these tragedies, as well as about whom to blame. Yan Slobodkin’s fascinating new book The Starving Empire shows the history behind these debates. By explaining the history of famine relief in France’s former empire, Slobodkin provides a new lens on the history of colonial governance, decolonization and humanitarianism. Trained as an historian of modern Europe and France’s Empire, Slobodkin reveals the global history behind the “French” way of managing famine. Slobodkin argues that from the mid-nineteenth century through the Second World War, “the French imperial state and an emerging international community took increasing responsibility for managing famines, and ultimately failed to fulfill this responsibility” (2). This shift occurred as new explanations of the causes of food shortages produced new ideas about who should manage their consequences. Slobodkin grounds these evolving famine policies in evolving ideas about “foresight” that colonial officials infused with racialized readings of non-European environments and practices. Over several decades, colonists’ liberal view of famine, which blamed “improvident” natives, morphed into a collective social model that made sustenance a government responsibility. However, by taking on the burden of famine prevention, Slobodkin convincingly argues, French experts laid the groundwork for the imperial collapse they sought to prevent. Starving Empire begins by explain the development of a detached liberal approach to famines before the First World War. Chapter One presents the 1867 famine in Algeria as foundational to this history. Settlers blamed the famine on an Arabophilic military regime that protected Arab land rights. Allied with Catholic leaders hoping to lift conversion bans, settlers argued that dispossession in favor of European settlers would foster a market-based agricultural economy that would predict and prevent future disasters. Out of this crisis emerged a humanitarian imperialism rooted in Christian charity, free-market liberalism, and an emphasis on provident individualism. In Chapter Two, Slobodkin argues that the French state’s reliance on a precolonial Vietnamese imperial apparatus partially mitigated the official disregard seen in the Algerian famine. However, officials’ commitment to laissez-faire economics as well as racialized ideas of indigenous impropriety prevented them from enacting policies to actually prevent famines. Chapter Three on the 1913 Sahelian drought shows the discursive forms this disregard took in less monitored corners of the Empire. By presenting famine as the inevitable result of improvident races and harsh environments, French administrators absolved themselves of responsibility. Instead, they created a reactive mode of governance rooted in either bureaucratic rationality or humanitarian horror. After World War I, however, reluctance yielded to responsibility. Chapter Four explains how new nutrition sciences and internationalist organizations made managing famines seem both possible and necessary. New scientific ideas about nutrition, as well as the rise of internationalist organizations focused on well-being, convinced experts that states could and should prevent famines. While these authorities critiqued older notions of improvident races, they held onto racial difference to justify European government’s right to manage how entire populations ate. Chapter Five returns to the Sahel to show the consequences of this newfound responsibility. Journalists, humanitarians and experts blamed poor administrators for famine. However, they did not critique the colonial economic dynamics that caused this disaster. Instead, observers argued that Africans’ inability to plan ahead for life in their harsh environments necessitated further European intervention. The final chapters argue that this responsive approach rested on an unsustainable tension between colonialism and care. Chapter Six explains how leaders across the empire made sustenance a government priority by the end of the Depression. France’s left-wing Popular Front government reinforced a growing belief in France’s responsibility for its colonial subjects’ well-being. However, a series of famines across the empire in the late 1930s revealed the government’s inability to reconcile this responsibility with colonialism’s dependence on extractive economies and thread-bare administration. Within a few years, this tension became unmanageable. The final chapter explains how, in the immediate aftermath of World War II, France’s empire faced its largest ever famine in Indochina. While the exiled French government could not immediately provide famine relief, authorities created plans to rebuff Allied skepticism towards their claim to Indochina. Meanwhile, leaders of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam claimed that the French government had failed in its self-appointed mission of preventing famine. In turn, they used their own mass food provisions to prove their legitimacy as Vietnam’s rightful ruler. Subsistence thus anchored competing sovereignty claims amidst decolonization. Slobodkin concludes by arguing that this French approach to famine fueled a postcolonial humanitarian governance without sovereignty that continues to occlude the structures determining who eats and who starves. Grounded in extensive archival work across the world, Slobodkin’s book reveals how responsibility, or its absence, fueled the rise and fall of European empires. Starving Empire connects intellectual debates with on the ground policies to show the linkages that produced changing, and ultimately unmanageable, burdens. Slobodkin thus challenges static histories of imperial rule by explaining when and why officials did or did not intervene. In doing so, he produces a new explanation of why Europe’s imperial regimes collapsed. To be sure, Slobodkin’s official and largely discursive approach has its limits. Above all, Slobodkin does not deal with non-elite colonized people. Did colonial rule change how Vietnamese peasants or Tuareg pastoralists viewed famines or whom they held responsible? Answering this question would do more than just expand the “voices” within this largely European colonial history. Combining Slobodkin’s empire-wide institutional analysis with the kind of on-the-ground focus taken by scholars like Laura Ann Twagira in Embodied Engineering would explain the role of popular responses to famine in conflicts over imperial and postimperial sovereignty. This comment reflects the rich questions Slobodkin powerfully provokes. In an era of growing resource scarcity and eroding faith in international or governmental agencies, Starving Empire shows how these institutions took on and failed to meet certain burdens. Tracing this history helps explain why unequal hunger continues to define our postcolonial present.

papers.title: Piracy and the Making of the Spanish Pacific World, By Kristie Patricia Flannery
papers.abstract: This provocative study examines Indigenous loyalty to the Spanish empire in the Philippines by examining how Hispano-Filipino military forces mobilized against external maritime attacks (conceptualized as piracy) and how these attacks shaped colonial policies in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In doing so, it challenges an Anglophone historiography that has predominantly located Indigenous agency in resistance to colonialism and emphasized the weakness of effective Spanish control, by demonstrating how this focus has obscured Indigenous (and particularly subaltern) loyalty to empire and failed to adequately explain the longevity and resilience of Spanish colonialism. Flannery argues that this older approach has erased the history of the many Indigenous people who, for the complex and shifting reasons she explores, found it in their interests to work with Spanish colonial agents and initiatives. She also explores how Indigenous and Sangley (resident Chinese) participation in Spanish-led military expeditions brought the empire into being, as this cooperation saw communities and individuals engage with colonial institutions. Flannery locates the primary reason for this collaboration in the need of the people living in the archipelago to defend themselves from maritime attacks. This is an effective perspective to examine the formation of communities of interest between Spanish colonial agents, Indigenous peoples, and Sangleyes, because raiding shaped the political economy of the Philippines before the arrival of the Spanish and, as Flannery demonstrates, influenced the specific policies and organization of their administration, powerfully highlighting the reactive nature of Spanish colonialism.

papers.title: Imperial Island: An Alternative History of the British Empire, By Charlotte Lydia Riley
papers.abstract: This is a briskly written narrative of British social history since 1945 seen through the lens of empire and decolonization. Released by a trade press in the U.K. and an academic press in the U.S., it is aimed primarily at a popular audience—and more particularly at the British public, which is navigating a period of often contentious debate about whether and how narratives of national history can be integrated with the story of empire. The inextricability of “metropole” and “colony”—to employ a useful if somewhat misleading shorthand—has been a commonplace of academic writing since the 1990s and the advent of what was then called the New Imperial History. Other forms of collective memory, though, have been slower to catch up. While bestsellers like Sathnam Sanghera’s Empireland (2021) have begun to close the gap between specialist knowledge and public discourse, the backlash from those uneasy with a critical approach to imperial history has been fierce. Right-wing outrage at the Rhodes Must Fall and Black Lives Matter protest movements, which targeted symbols of the imperial past, has been fanned by Conservative Party politicians. It also fueled the success of a very different bestseller, Nigel Biggar’s Colonialism: A Moral Reckoning (2021), which employed selective readings of evidence to make the case that the British Empire was often a force for good. (The Conservatives have since rewarded Biggar with a seat in the House of Lords.)
