papers.title: Contested Burial Grounds: African Religious Communities, Urban Displacement, and the Spatial Politics of Difference in Colonial Lagos, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Abstract This article uncovers how Black interfaith communities agitated to preserve public cemeteries on Lagos Island from the nineteenth century until the 1930s. As burial grounds became full during the 1920s, the British administration proposed closing Muslim and Christian cemeteries. The Black residents would be expected to bury the dead on Lagos mainland, which was connected to the island by the Carter Bridge. News of the cemetery closure galvanized Africans to successfully campaign for the expansion rather than the closing of public graveyards. Historians of mortuary politics and colonial planning have studied how European rulers mandated cemeteries and how Africans developed new burial rites in public burial grounds. This article demonstrates that the cemeteries were more than colonial instruments of dispossession. Interfaith practitioners developed new meanings for burial grounds that later motivated their struggles to ensure cemeteries’ accessibility. Despite their varying attitudes to burial grounds, as the traditional rulers maintained the precolonial practice of home burial, Lagosians claimed the right to inter their loved ones in the same area that they considered home. I argue that Black residents agitated against cemetery closure to challenge colonial residential segregation and maintain belonging to Lagos Island. The campaigns for burial grounds offer insight into Lagosians’ intervention in the built environment and resistance to colonial planning schemes.

papers.title: Bluecoated Terror: Jim Crow New Orleans and the Roots of Modern Police Brutality, By Jeffrey S. Adler
papers.abstract: Bluecoated Terror is a book about state-formation that does not announce itself as such. Just before the period this book analyzes, but thousands of miles from Louisiana, Max Weber outlined what made a state. His useful, but also bedeviling, definition became canonical: “a state is a human community that (successfully) claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.” Most who study the history of the carceral state focus on the achieved monopoly of legitimate use of force. But Weber’s definition includes a methodological prompt and challenge by conjoining the aside “(successfully)” and the verb “claims.” Weber thus invites scholars to investigate a monumental “how” question: how does a state make a claim to monopolize violence legitimately? This raises further questions. If the state pre-exists this monopolization, does the claiming fundamentally transform it? How does the monopolization process unfold? The approach that historians might take to answer these questions is necessarily processual. The monopoly claims–making process unfolds over time, in a delimited space. Bluecoated Terror admirably reveals what this process looked like: how lynch law enforced by “self-appointed white sentinels” became law and order enforced by white police officers (2). It also prompts a question we might turn back on Weber about the human community. What is legitimacy in a human community cleaved by the color line?

papers.title: (Un)Remembering Sexual Violence in South African History
papers.abstract: Abstract South Africa is a country known for its high rates of gender-based and sexual violence. Historical research demonstrates that such issues are not new to the post-apartheid era but have deep roots stretching into the country’s colonial and apartheid periods. Yet when asked to reflect on historic sexual violence, oral history interviewees — Black women in their sixties, seventies and eighties — largely recalled the apartheid past as a period devoid of sexual violence, describing the problem to researchers as something that only started happening ‘now, in your days’. This article unpacks such statements and argues that much rape perpetrated during apartheid, particularly within communities, has been subject to a collective unremembering. It highlights four central explanations for this: how rape was historically silenced by families, communities and the police; the refusal to name rape as such in the past, with sexual violence more commonly characterized as ‘force’; how histories of intra-communal sexual violence have been sidelined within dominant historical or political narratives of apartheid; and how discourse of South Africa’s present rape ‘crisis’ fosters historical amnesia and promotes nostalgia for a past believed to be without rape.

papers.title: Nationcraft and the Origins of Territory: Experiencing Romanía in the Medieval Empire of New Rome
papers.abstract: Abstract The modernism debate in the historiography of nationhood and nationalism has fizzled out to a curious détente: the idea that nationhood and nationalism are unique to ‘modernity’ remains dominant, but ‘premodern’ fields continue to research ethnonational phenomena while largely avoiding the vocabulary. Compelling research continues to be produced on both sides of the pre/modern divide, but there is little cross-fertilization between the two. This article returns to the modernism debate, to argue for the utility of political economy as a mode of analysis able to address the dynamics of nationcraft across a range of times and places. The case study is the production and experience of national territory in the medieval empire of New Rome, traditionally termed Byzantium. Between the eighth and thirteenth centuries East Roman political economy produced a national territory known as Romanía, ‘Romanland’, experienced for the most part in terms strikingly similar to the ‘countries’ produced by contemporary nation-states, including a kind of patriotism. The implication, fleshed out with comparative suggestions in the conclusion, is that similarities and differences between the nationcraft of different times and places should be situated in political and economic motions, rather than a pre/modern binary.

papers.title: Spanish Pistolerismo and Labour Violence in Post-War Europe, 1917–1923
papers.abstract: Abstract Political violence in Europe in 1917–23 has typically been associated with the destabilizing impact of the First World War. However, some forms of violence displayed continuities with the pre-1914 period and were not directly related to the war, as was the case with trade union violence. This article engages with debates about the character and causality of the convulsions that shook the continent in 1917–23 through the case study of labour violence in Spain. This country remained neutral throughout the conflagration but experienced episodes of intense social warfare connected to strikes that came to be known as pistolerismo (the rule of the gunman). Pistolerismo had a complex prehistory, but it crystallized in 1917–19 due to the economic fallout of the war and the radicalizing influence of the Russian Revolution. This study traces the evolution of labour violence in these years, exploring how neutrality shaped pistolerismo, the retaliatory logic of aggressions, the formation and professionalization of trade union armed detachments, and the entanglements between social and political violence. It does so by interweaving social and cultural approaches. Viewed through this prism, trade union violence stands out as an important driver of instability and polarization in post-war Europe.

papers.title: Migrants, Violence, and Discrimination in Early Modern Holland
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines the experiences of migrants in early modern Dutch cities, focusing on violence and indications of social tensions in criminal cases from 1680 to 1810. Despite the prevailing notion of harmonious coexistence, migrants, comprising a significant portion of urban residents, faced stigmatization and bias. The research focuses on Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Leiden, major economic centers witnessing high immigration rates. Whereas existing studies suggest migrants faced similar treatment in courts, this article challenges such notions. It explores tensions and conflicts in violence-related cases, revealing subtle forms of discrimination against immigrants. Through quantitative analysis and case studies, it uncovers differential treatment in the reporting of violence, court sentencing, and procedures. The findings reveal that while the overall patterns of violent crime were similar between local and immigrant offenders, immigrants were disproportionately accused of more serious offenses. Moreover, immigrants faced differential treatment in the judicial system, including harsher interrogation methods, limited opportunities for settlement, and a higher likelihood of expulsion and corporal punishment. The study highlights the complex interplay between immigration, social tensions, and discriminatory practices in early modern Dutch cities. It underscores the need for further research to fully understand the extent of discrimination against immigrants in historical criminal justice systems, advocating for a nuanced approach that combines quantitative analysis with qualitative examination of individual cases.

papers.title: The Promises and Perils of Periodization in Global History: Lessons from the Inter-War Era
papers.abstract: Abstract This article considers the role of periodization in global history through the lens of the inter-war era. The global turn has shifted the ‘metageographies’ of historical practice, focusing historians’ attention on the flows, mobilities and networks that connected peoples and places across the globe. Often left uninterrogated, however, are the ‘metatemporalities’ that structure historical inquiry, resulting in the perpetuation of Eurocentric definitions of historical epochs, particularly in the modern era. Periodizations are not objective or merely descriptive containers for historical events, but are themselves arguments that promote certain historical actors and dynamics from particular places, while relegating others to reactive roles, if not historiographical obscurity. The inter-war era offers a particularly compelling case study that shows how global history methodologies qualify, extend and dissolve inherited temporal frameworks. In place of singular, Eurocentric eras, polycentric global history presents the opportunity to elaborate polytemporal models that advance plural, overlapping periodizations. Aligning multiple global periodizations and becoming attuned to the rhythms they produced allows historians to reveal the particularity of historical eras.

papers.title: Capitalism in the Colonies: African Merchants in Lagos, 1851-1931, By A. G. Hopkins
papers.abstract: Did Europe underdevelop Africa, as Walter Rodney so famously put it? Or, as European imperialists argued, did colonialism bring vital capitalist transformation and economic growth, despite the shortcomings of African economic actors? This magisterial study of indigenous entrepreneurs in one colonial port city suggests that both formulations are overdrawn. In Capitalism in the Colonies, the eminent economic historian A. G. Hopkins assesses the fortunes of African entrepreneurs under colonial rule in Lagos, Nigeria, between the initial establishment of a British consulate and the onset of global depression. To do so, he supplements the often limited official records with a truly remarkable set of sources he collected at the start of his career more than half a century ago: oral histories of colonial-era merchants’ family members and privately held personal papers, including wonderful photographs. Many of these records, as well as some precious early court records, are no longer available, making Capitalism in the Colonies a vital work of recovery. But it is far more. Zooming in and out between larger-scale analysis and the lives and careers of some 116 merchants in Lagos, the book weaves together three key components: the economic history of a West African port city; a collection of professional biographies of Lagosian economic innovators, some of them not widely known; and an argument about the development of capitalism under British colonialism.

papers.title: HISTORICAL ANTIFASCISM AND THE GLOBAL LEFT
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Joseph Fronczak's Everything Is Possible: Antifascism and the Left in the Age of Fascism presents antifascism in the 1920s and 1930s as a universal cause that united people across social and ideological divides, creating the discursive framework for the global Left we know today. It revises standard accounts according to which the Left originated either with the Atlantic revolutions circa 1800 or with the international workers’ movement that took shape in the late nineteenth century. This article accepts the weak form of the book's argument that the antifascist era was remarkably creative and essential for understanding the development of today's Left. However, it rejects the strong form of the argument that dissociates the Left from any prior history in the revolutionary tradition or the workers’ movement. To complement the book's discursive analysis of languages of the Left, this article outlines a structural analysis of antisystemic opposition in the contexts of global capitalism, imperialism, and mass politics. What results is a long‐term concept of the Left that, among other things, highlights the promise and pitfalls of antifascist populism. The core problem of defining the Left is accounting for the historical disjuncture between unity of antisystemic consciousness and unity of organized action.

papers.title: Slavery, Prosperity, and Inequality in Roman Pompeii
papers.abstract: Abstract Historians of premodern economies, in contrast to modern ones, have only infrequently contemplated the economic contribution of slavery. Here, I suggest that quantitative and statistical tools allow us to evaluate the place of slavery in an early economy, using Roman Pompeii as a case study. At the time of its destruction in 79 ce, Pompeii appears prosperous, having benefitted from the economic development thought to have characterized the Roman world. Recent discoveries, meanwhile, shed new light on the conditions of working classes and slaves throughout the city. These narratives can be seen to form two sides to the same coin, as Pompeii’s prosperity was created in large part thanks to slave labour. The connection is supported by constructing a probabilistic model, which suggests some 6 million sesterces (HS) flowed every year to Pompeii’s masters through their exploitation of slaves. Slave owning probably formed the largest single income source for the urban economy. This scale of income is shown to be consistent with recent reconstructions of wealth and income inequality in the city. The results not only speak to slavery’s profound importance to Pompeii’s prosperity, but they encourage a recentring of labour and slavery in Roman economic history.

papers.title: The Disappearance of Self-Determination from the League of Nations Covenant, January–February 1919
papers.abstract: Abstract After Woodrow Wilson’s speech to Congress in February 1918, ‘self-determination’ was expected to be a guiding concept for a post-imperial order once the Great War had ended. Yet when the Covenant of the League of Nations was negotiated at the Paris Peace Conference, the phrase was removed. Why and by whom? The existing literature offers little answer. This article argues that Wilson fought for inclusion of both the phrase ‘self-determination’ and the substance of it but was convinced to remove both by his own advisers and members of the British delegation. These men had an agenda at variance with Wilson’s, one focused on solidifying wartime transatlantic co-operation into a post-war governance model that would strengthen the British imperial position and bring the US into support of it. That agenda could not accommodate Wilsonian self-determination. Its resulting disappearance effectively reversed the post-imperial sense of wartime statements on self-determination made by Wilson and David Lloyd George. Anti-colonial movements, as the Paris negotiators knew, had taken inspiration from those promises. Their hopes for an organized dismantling of the imperial order were disappointed. Only after four decades of political violence would the pre-war order be replaced by one that better resembled Wilson’s abandoned vision.

papers.title: DNA Technology and the Struggle for the Power to Declare Missing Soldiers Dead in the Post-Vietnam War United States
papers.abstract: Abstract The recovery of soldiers’ remains has been a major concern of the US military since the mid-nineteenth century. However, military defeats during the Cold War left the remains of US soldiers unattended for decades, which diminished the odds of their identification and created ambiguities about their fates. After the Vietnam War, some statespersons and soldiers’ families alleged that many missing soldiers had not been killed, but rather detained by the enemy and abandoned by US authorities. The US military strove to recover and identify as many missing soldiers as possible to debunk these allegations. Existing forensic methods failed to provide definitive conclusions, straining the relationship between the military and the American public. Consequently, the military turned to DNA profiling to identify missing personnel. Technical limitations and US society’s lingering distrust of authorities turned DNA profiling into a new battleground between the US military and prisoners of war/missing in action (POW/MIA) families. Despite the promise DNA technology seemed to offer for remains’ identification, this article argues that its success was reliant on POW/MIA families’ attitudes towards the military and politics, who demanded much more than identified remains as a means of achieving closure.

papers.title: Subtle Bodies: Networks and Corporeality in Philipp Hainhofer’s Pomeranian Cabinet
papers.abstract: Abstract The merchant and art agent Philipp Hainhofer (1578–1647) is best known for his extraordinary art cabinets. Collaborating closely with neighbouring Augsburg artisans, Hainhofer worked to compile, collate, and market these visually and materially astounding collections to a range of elite patrons. His first commission, the Pomeranian Cabinet, was for Duke Philipp of Pomerania-Stettin in 1610, and took around seven years to complete. This article adopts a body-centred approach, arguing that in doing so, new light is shed on the ways period actors enacted their relationships with materials, objects, and other bodies. It uncovers the process through which the body of the art-lover was constructed, convening with those engaged in a shared material community through the lens of health and bodily entanglements. Hainhofer, as a merchant, diplomat, and secret agent, occupied a dubious position. Through the staging of the shared, art-loving body, he was able to create and sustain friendships, while simultaneously raising the status of the merchant through his material identification with these practices.

papers.title: Virtual Tools for IRL Problems
papers.abstract: In a growing environment of censorship, in which the right and far right have targeted the study and teaching of queer history internationally as a scapegoat for political gain, the internet has become a refuge to those looking for information regarding queer history.1 Online, public history plays an important role in filling gaps of knowledge that cannot be filled easily anywhere else. The sharing of queer history on the internet is an important intervention against its censorship elsewhere. This essay is a review of queer public history on social media, especially Instagram (IG). I will center my attention on five Instagram pages that I consider to be part of a growing corpus of internet historiography focused on queer history.2 I use “queerness” here to signify the rejection of what lesbian-feminism has called compulsory heterosexuality, a challenge to the imposition of heterosexuality as an ideology, and not only a sexual orientation.3This review begins with The AIDS Memorial, an IG page dedicated to those who fell victim to the AIDS pandemic in the 1980s and 1990s that got some attention recently thanks to the Queen of Pop, Madonna.4 Madonna used some of the site’s photographs as part of her 2023–24 Celebration Tour as a tribute to those who died in the pandemic, heightening its visibility.5 The page has posted more than 11,000 stories of people who died during the global pandemic and aims to spread awareness through life stories. Most of the stories relate to gay men from the US and UK, but there are also some stories from various parts of the world, and some stories about women and straight people. The project is, at its core, a collective virtual grieving monument that allows users to enter a space where they can share their thoughts and emotions in relation to this traumatic event that marked a whole generation. Although the page has no explicit political agenda beyond memorializing and does not call for pressure on governments for more funding in treatments, research, or similar demands, its name creates an unavoidable connection with the AIDS Memorial Quilt project, a handmade quilt sewed with names of people who died of the virus, that activists and advocates used in several protests in the US during the late 1980s and 1990s.6Much like the Quilt, the AIDS Memorial IG page and its growing contributions function as a political statement about the systemic violence and marginalization that people suffer, made clear via life stories shared by users and the comments of solidarity and relatability posted by others. In this page and others, the lack of a singular author (or content curator, as it is also called) is fundamental in creating a direct connection between the users and the past, mediated through the archive (usually family photos) and a short biography (usually made by someone close to the person who died). Thus, the page relies solely on the emotional connection the users can make with history, a deeply empathetic approach to the past, which gives significant attention to marginalized communities. There are almost no citations to academic works related to the history of the AIDS pandemic, other than the ones shared in the comments by other users. This creates a different approach to the past, mediated only by the knowledge of the users and with no authoritative voice to create or incentivize a reflection on the subject.Similarly, Queer Love in History (QLH) is a project dedicated to sharing queer love, because, as the page asserts, queer love has “always existed.”7 This project, curated by a person who only identifies themselves as Kate, posts pictures and stories of queer couples, both male and female. The IG profile also includes a link to a drive of supplemental material on “Sapphic History Media Recs,” which is appropriate considering the amount of sapphic love stories featured in the posts of the page. This page echoes the notion that “history hates lovers,” an idea made popular by an internet song turned meme, meaning that in describing personal relationships, historians tend to favor a heterosexual explanation rather than contemplating the idea of complex queer relationships.8 The phrase used to describe the IG page hits at the core of the debate about queerness as a historical phenomenon. The idea of queer love in this case is used to refute the historiographical assumption imposed by the constructivist/existentialist debate of the eighties that was all but won by the constructivists in part thanks to the enormous influence that the work of Michelle Foucault had in the emergence of queer historiography. Foucault, in his first volume of History of Sexuality, established a division between act and identity that has since been prevalent in queer historiography all around the world, creating a chronological division used to understand queerness from the perspective of the institutions that prosecuted it. More recently, however, historians have taken seriously the role of emotions, such as love or lust, challenging that division and proposing that even though we cannot assume, or even know, how a person understood their own sexuality, we can come close to understanding their feelings and thus their personal relationships.9Thus, much like The AIDS Memorial, QLH seeks to underscore that mystery of love by sharing archival photos of couples and their stories, appealing to empathy via shared experiences and reducing the mediation of academia to reach the past. However, unlike The AIDS Memorial, this page uses citations in most of its posts to reference either the archival material or further reading to understand a particular love story. In this case the academic authority is used to underscore an already established principle and functions more as a complement to the past narrative than a guide.A more conventional approach to history sharing can be found on the page Yesterqueers.10 This page is made by self-described “accidental public historian” Amanda W. Timpson, a former television executive, who decided to dedicate herself to internet-based queer public history.11 She links her experience as a TV executive with her current work as a historian by highlighting the importance of storytelling in both jobs, an interesting approach, especially when engaging with nonprofessional publics. On this page, Timpson shares short video essays in which she discusses queer history, either via a specific event or a person, in a very charismatic yet thorough manner. On her own webpage she claims that the idea came from friends who insisted she should share the stories she told them through social media and thus the format has that kind of flavor, of a friend sharing curious historical facts with the user.12 However, Timpson is far from careless with the information she shares. All her videos come with accompanying bibliography (either cited or for further reading) as well as full scripts. The level of source management is commendable. She demonstrates an awareness of how historiography works in her videos and expresses a knowledge of the politics and limitations of history as a profession. Although the phrase used to describe her project, “We have always been here, and we have always been queer,” seems to indicate an essentialist perspective of queer history, her content distances itself from anachronistic approaches by recognizing in almost every video the transformation of our understanding of queerness, and at the same time highlighting, as the phrase asserts, that queerness is not new. Its content, although primarily US based, extends to most parts of the world via commemorations such as Hispanic Heritage Month, and she uses current events as a way to delve into the past, linking present interest with historical processes.Timpson has a clear political position, and she is not afraid of sharing it in her videos, something that makes the approachable aspect of her presentation more intimate, as that of a friend. She describes her work as bringing forward the stories so that “we engage in queer history together,” ultimately seeking to “[e]ducate, celebrate and spark conversations that create new meanings to the past.”13 This is a more traditional approach to public history, in which the professional is a mediator between the past and the people, unlike the previous pages which broaden authorship.A similar interface, but with a different political approach, can be seen on the Instagram page Working Class History, a cross-media project that seeks to “record and popularize our grassroots, people’s history, as opposed to the top-down account of most history books.”14 This project is heavily influenced by social and political history as understood by leftist historiography that can be traced back to British Marxism, Indian postcolonialism, and North American radicalism.15 The page works as a calendar of sorts, using public commemoration, or the lack of it, as a tool to share history; every day is remembered through an episode of what the anonymous authors call “working class history” and sheds light on political history, including queer history, such as the birthdays of Amelio Robles Ávlia and Oscar Wilde, the pie attack on anti-gay activist Anita Bryant, or the making of the first Pride celebration in South Africa. Episodes of radical political projects and actions are shared by a post with a significant archive photo and a short text about the event in discussion.This project uses its political orientation, a broad popular left, as a booster to frame queer history as part of a continuous struggle for a better world. In this case, much like in Yesterqueers, the author(s) frame queer history as part of a social process and share it with users who can engage with it as they see fit. All the posts are accompanied by source citations and supplementary material that also links to their other media projects. Aware of historiography, Working Class History frames queerness in a Marxist political context that gives meaning to the historical events in relation to the ongoing struggles today.Not surprisingly, queer public history sites appear in language other than English. Moléculas Malucas (Crazy Molecules) is an IG page dedicated to reconstructing queer history in Latin America and Spain, aiming to highlight archives and memories “that resisted the darkness of oblivion.”16 On this page, archival photos are posted by the anonymous editors with texts from various authors (researchers, activist or artists), highlighting episodes of queer Latin American history, including interactions with other countries such as Spain or the US. The project also runs a parallel blog that broadens the information of the post with full-length articles that include very well-organized citations.17 Unlike the previous examples, this page features continuous engagement of multiple academics as the posts are defined by academic articles or investigations that reach the editorial team of the page. In this case, the administrator functions as an intermediary between other academics and the users and creates a platform to share new findings and reconstructed stories made elsewhere. This is a direct extension of the editorial project of the parallel blog but also shows another approach of public history in which academic works are transformed so they can circulate in nonprofessional spaces. Thus the many debates included in these posts come from various historiographical perspectives and users engage with the academic authors. Also, the material that is shared on the page is related mostly to the LGBTIQ+ social movement, its protests or writings. In this sense, the project is aimed not only toward a general audience, but also toward progressives or leftists who might not know about the shared history of revolutionary and queer politics.Due to the lack of academic spaces for Latin American queer history, Moleculas Malucas sprouted two other Instagram public history projects that have come to have a life of their own: the sister page Archivos Desviados, under the control of editors who share documents of queer history; and Sexo Y Revolución, a subdivision of a digital archive project of Latin American leftist political history called CeDinCi.18Of all these pages, Working Class History holds the biggest follower count, with 779,000 as of October 24, 2024, and next are The AIDS Memorial with 296,000 and Queer Love In History with 87, 200. The remaining pages have considerably smaller followings with 4,446 for Moleculas Malucas and 1,686 for Yesterqueers, who nevertheless hold 141,900 followers on TikTok, a social network on which only two others of the sites reviewed have a presence and none as robust. The biggest page, in terms of content, is The Aids Memorial with 12,379 posts, followed not closely by Working Class History with 7,446, Queer Love in History with 576, Yesterqueers with 230, and Moleculas Malucas with 142 as of October 24, 2024.What all these pages have in common is the drive to share episodes of queer history obscured by either ignorance or malice. They thrive in sharing relatively unknown moments of the past (collective or personal), moments that are not learned either in schools or universities. What they do, at their core, is fight what some queer scholars have called the “cruelty of the archive,” the difficulty of re-constructing queer pasts in a dignified and positive manner, when most documents come from places or institutions set on persecuting queerness.19 Some decide to do this through empathy and without the mediation of historical analysis, appealing to human emotions and the familiarity of personal archives; others seek to use historical analysis as a tool to frame events so they can make sense of present struggles, sharing information as a political exercise toward social transformation. There are differences in their projects also, both ideological and methodological, yet all these pages have in common the awareness of the contentiousness of queerness and the fragility of current acceptance.Thus, through social media, activists and/or academics who understand either the peril of absence of information or the importance of access to it are trying to fill the gaps in knowledge of the queer past. In this case, the history that is being constructed online is one that recognizes the relevance of current events and the relationship between past, present, and future. Queer public history online is aiming to create tools: empathy, political consciousness, mobilization tactics, and strategies; and every tool could be used for change, if used correctly.

papers.title: Renting History
papers.abstract: House museums and historic sites have long functioned as unconventional providers of housing where employees who live onsite provide rental payments or exchange labor for housing. This article charts the growth of renting among house museums from the early twentieth century to the 1990s. House museums came to constitute a new class of landlord while tenants emerged as critical agents in the preservation of these sites. Whereas scholarship on the evolution of public history practice has focused on the public-facing labor of museum employees, shifting the focus to museum apartments reveals the intertwined nature of housing and labor in the growth of public history in the last century.

papers.title: Revolutionary History

papers.title: Motion Comics as Digital Public History
papers.abstract: Motion comics—animated picture stories on historical subjects—have received little attention as a format for presenting public history. Yet due to their literally moving multi-perspectivity, motion comics readily engage viewers, especially with contested and complex national histories. First, I provide a theoretical foundation for future analyses of motion comics as public history tools. papers.title: Conserving the Historic Stone Walls of New England
papers.abstract: Policies for conserving and interpreting historic sites in New England are well established. This is not the case for the region’s most salient historic feature: the extensive and nearly ubiquitous latticework of drystone walls dating mainly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. For these iconic structures, there is only a hodgepodge of extant laws, ordinances, zoning regulations, and management guides for public properties at the local, state, and federal levels. Regulations for private property are very limited. This article recommends a stepwise approach to the conservation and interpretation of New England’s stone walls that considers their historic, archaeologic, ecologic, aesthetic, and geologic values while remaining respectful of the presence of Indigenous stonework.

papers.title: Can machine translation of literary texts fool stylometry?
papers.abstract: Abstract This article uses standard authorship-attribution stylometry to tell machine translations made with DeepL and Google Translate from human translations. This is done using a Burrows-like distance measure procedure of cluster analysis, later visualized through network analysis. Using a corpus of French literary classics translated into English by humans and machines as illustration, this article shows that, in most cases, translations of each text were very similar irrespective of the type of translator. Discrepancies in this respect were only found between translations of authors writing in very complex style (Proust). On the other hand, sentence length distribution compared with the Dynamic Time Warping Distance method was much more indicative of whether translations were made by humans or by machines.

papers.title: Dams and the Deep Earth: The 1967 Koyna Earthquake and Human Agency in the Anthropocene
papers.abstract: Abstract On 11 December 1967, a large earthquake devastated the village of Koynanagar in Maharashtra, western India. Many blamed the new Koyna hydroelectric dam nearby. Prompting international inquests, Koyna became perhaps the world’s most famous case of reservoir-induced seismicity, a novel type of earthquake triggered by human activities. We use the dam’s history to explore the emergent consciousness of human geophysical agency that characterizes the Anthropocene, the putative new epoch when humans have become a planetary-scale ‘force of Nature’. The dam was explicitly designed as a geotechnical assemblage, a blending of technology, mountain topography, monsoon waters and rock. Striking a supposedly stable region, the 1967 earthquake revealed the more-than-human unpredictability of this composite. Scientists began to trace a radically new form of human agency at work, which owed its effects to complex chains of causality that extended deep underground and backward into deep history. Yet there was remarkably little policy fallout. Dam construction only accelerated in seismically active areas. The debates over reservoir-induced seismicity showed that human geotechnical agency could be read in diametrically opposed ways: as a source of anxiety or hubris, or simply irrelevant to practical policy making, thereby presaging today’s debates over human planetary stewardship in the Anthropocene.

papers.title: Orality, State Power, and the Labour of Policing in Colonial Bengal, c .1850–1947
papers.abstract: Abstract In colonial Bengal, the average police constable was largely unlettered. Nevertheless, constables were at the frontline in the enforcement of colonial law. This paradox of an unlettered constabulary enforcing the letter of law defies the familiar logic in the historical scholarship on British India that associates the written word with histories of state power and orality with histories of subaltern classes. In a departure from the existing literature on the significance of writing and documentary power for modern state-making, this article uncovers a world of orality at the heart of state power. To do this, the article deploys a labour history method to the vast archive of the colonial police and explores the play of orality in the labouring lives of police constables in colonial Bengal. In the nineteenth century, colonial officials responded to the illiteracy of their constabulary workforce by organizing oral instruction in law at police stations. The constable heard the law as speech rather than grasping it as text. In this aural space, his consciousness became a site for the reinterpretation of the law, refracted through the operation of the security labour market, his conditions of work, and the modes of constabulary training. Moreover, oral modalities structured how the police worked on the streets, and police officials, despite complaining about the illiteracy of constables, exploited this illiteracy to consolidate the violent power of the colonial police.

papers.title: PHILOSOPHY OF HISTORY AS A CRITIQUE OF VIOLENCE: HISTORY, THEOLOGY, AND POLITICS IN WALTER BENJAMIN'S EARLY WRITINGS
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Walter Benjamin's “Critique of Violence” became a classical work on revolutionary politics mainly due to influential political‐theological expositions of its arguments. The main challenge with the political‐theological understanding of the essay, however, is that Benjamin seemingly argued against any reconciliation of politics and theology. For this reason, this article develops a historical‐philosophical rather than a political‐theological interpretation of Benjamin's “Critique of Violence.” It demonstrates how Benjamin's essay on violence can be best understood if it is read as a text containing a speculative philosophy of history. In the essay, Benjamin indeed presented the role of violence in history as a historical “law of oscillation” between lawmaking and law‐preserving violence. The problem of violence transcends the framework of the political, which can witness only “administered” violence, not violence as such, and hence cannot escape the dialectical movement of this “law.” While Benjamin's philosophy of history is usually located in the final period of his philosophical activity and comprises a messianic‐Marxist complex, Benjamin's “Critique of Violence” suggests the existence of a more substantial philosophy of history in Benjamin's early writings than is usually assumed. The period between 1919 and 1922 especially shows a concentration of anarchistic and nihilistic texts devoted to developing this philosophy of history.

papers.title: Individualism and Emotional Attachment: An Evolving Tension in American History
papers.abstract: Abstract This article identifies and traces the rise of greater individualism in American history, from the early nineteenth century onward, and the corresponding effort to provide protective compensations, through associations, family ties, friendships, and sympathy for stresses such as homesickness and loneliness. The essay emphasizes several major stages in this often complex balancing act. Risks of tension increased in the twentieth century, with declining sympathy for some issues of adjustment, somewhat weaker family, and emotional ties. The situation deteriorated further after the 1950s, through a combination of new and more isolating forms of individualism, greater though diverse family instability and the now-familiar signs of growing loneliness. However, new forms of compensation must also be assessed, from the rise of pets to the unusually eager American reception of psychological therapy. The purpose of the article is to highlight an enduring basic theme in the nation’s emotional history—contributing to the growing interest in the history of emotions more generally—while also placing several urgent current problems in clearer historical context.

papers.title: Whitney Nell Stewart. This Is Our Home: Slavery and Struggle on Southern Plantations .
papers.abstract: In the fields of slavery and plantation studies, one of the greatest challenges is balancing a narrative between investigating the brutal, dehumanizing realities of slavery and celebrating the perseverance required to survive it, never mind explaining how enslaved people were able to find joy and hope in that bleak world. Whitney Nell Stewart’s book This Is Our Home: Slavery and Struggle on Southern Plantations navigates this balance impressively as she uses material culture from historic sites across the southern United States to illuminate how enslaved people made homes for themselves despite the precarity and inhumanity of the world in which they were forced to live. Stewart’s study focuses on five sites—Montpelier Plantation in Virginia, Stagville Plantation in North Carolina, Chatham Plantation in Alabama, Patton Place in Texas, and Redcliffe Plantation in South Carolina—that were created or operated during the antebellum period. At Montpelier, Stewart focuses on the swept yards that created a boundary around the dwellings of the enslaved. At Stagville, she shows us how enslaved people carved private spaces for spiritual practices or personal possessions into their and their enslavers’ homes. At Chatham, Stewart explains the importance of the slave cemetery in rooting the community and explores the sense of dislocation enslaved people felt at being forced to leave not only the place where they lived but the place where their people were buried. At Patton Place, she shows how an enslaved woman expressed domestic authority despite frequent challenges, and though it is certainly an exceptional example, in Rachel Patton we can see that the desire for domestic authority was not only the province of white plantation mistresses. Finally, at Redcliffe Plantation in South Carolina, Stewart demonstrates how enslaved people and their descendants used a plantation built as a monument to slavery and white supremacy to build their own legacy that would extend beyond slavery to the present.

papers.title: Decomposing dependency analysis: revisiting the relation between annotation scheme and structure-based textual measures
papers.abstract: Abstract Standardized quantitative measurement of texts lies at the heart of digital approaches to humanities. Structure-based textual measures are known to be influenced by the choice of syntactic annotation schemes. Building on previous research, the present article further explores the relation between annotation schemes and the index of mean dependency distance (MDD) by comparing the treebanks of seventeen languages, respectively, within a tree representation (basic universal dependencies, BUD) and within a graphic representation (enhanced universal dependencies, EUD). Following the idea of decomposing annotation schemes into the combinations of analyses of specific constructions (coordinate structures, control constructions, and relative clauses), we design algorithms to identify them in the CoNLL-U format treebanks and explore their influences. It is found that the overall MDD of the EUD representation is statistically higher than that of BUD at corpus level, primarily affected by the coordinate structure due to its high frequency. At sentence level, all three constructions might contribute to either increased or decreased MDD, with stochastically intervening words and word order being two important determinants of the values of the measure. Finally, we propose and argue for the view that MDDs calculated under different annotation schemes should be regarded as different textual measures in nature. In sum, the present study provides another case study to deepen our understanding of the nature of syntactic annotation schemes and its relation with textual indices, which paves the way for standard measurement of texts in future humanities research.

papers.title: The Making of Elixir: Ambergris, Emperor Jiajing, and the Portuguese Settlement at Macao in 1557
papers.abstract: Abstract: Focusing on the procurement and consumption of ambergris in sixteenth century China, this article illustrates how this marine product as the tipping point led to the Portuguese settlement at Macao in 1557. However, his ten-year effort to obtain ambergris proved futile until the Portuguese in Macao, the sole suppliers of this Indian Ocean substance, began to present it around the year 1555–1556. A scrutiny of both Chinese and Portuguese sources has illustrated the temporal and spatial junctures in which the Portuguese succeeded in squeezing their way in and putting down roots in maritime Asia. This study of ambergris sheds some fresh light on the conceptualization of maritime Asia, and exemplifies “the interactive emergence of European domination” in the region.

papers.title: Papuan Children, Catholic Missionaries, and the Formation of Transimperial Networks in Late Nineteenth-Century Europe
papers.abstract: Abstract: In 1890, the French Catholic Bishop Louis Couppé took Tolika to Kagai and Auguste to Kadalama from a mission station on German New Guinea on a tour to Europe. papers.title: The Japanese Eye on Latin America Through The Japan Times , 1926–1941
papers.abstract: Abstract: This paper examines the The Japan Times ’ uses of Latin America during the early Shōwa period up to the attack on Pearl Harbor (1926–1941); The Japan Times was tightly linked to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Gaimushō) and thus it was an important player in shaping public perception and manipulating Western public discourses in favor of the Japanese empire’s international ambitions. Against the general wisdom that migration-related images were the most common conceptualization of Latin America in the Japanese Press, we argue that the image of Latin America as expressed by The Japan Times reflects a strong political meaning as well, viewing the region in Imperial terms: either as a location for colonial expansion or as a continent dominated by the U.S.-led Monroe Doctrine and the Pan-American movement. In other words, Latin America became a polysemous term, aptly used by the press and the officials in Tokyo to convey various social and political meanings that could serve their own ideological stance. The paper presents a mix-method research, including the results a scoping review of all published information pertaining to Latin America between December 1926 and December 1941 in the web-based engine of The Japan Times Archives.

papers.title: Oceanic Wahhabism
papers.abstract: Abstract: At some point around 1810, a leading Wahhabi theologian in the capital of the First Saudi State fielded an intriguing question: Although Wahhabi leaders preached the ideals of enmity and violence toward non-Wahhabi peoples, could Wahhabi merchants travel to non-Wahhabi lands, do business with non-Wahhabi persons, and reside among them while pursuing commercial agendas? The theologian’s answer reveals how Arabia’s interior where Wahhabism emerged was enmeshed alongside Arabia’s coasts within the broader Afro-Asian Indian Ocean world. Oceanic Wahhabism thus situates Najd, the emergence of Wahhabism and the First Saudi State as parts of an inter-regional world in which Najdi peoples helped forge, consolidate, and sustain political, social, and commercial connections before and after Wahhabism’s emergence. An oceanic, world historical framework highlights individuals, agendas, and events that add new dynamics to the standard tribes-religion-oil framework for studying Arabia and its history, and helps to continue uncovering a portrait of Arabia—interior and all—as integral to modern world history.

papers.title: “Why Doest Thou Thus?”: Providence and Discourses of Difference in Two Nineteenth-Century Missionary Lives
papers.abstract: Abstract: Nineteenth-century missionaries interpreted the events of their lives through the lens of providence. The frequent suffering that challenged missionaries in global mission fields, including the threat of illness and death, the loss of family, and failure, were likewise understood through providential narration, but for some missionaries, confidence in a divine plan waned in the face of great pain. This article comparatively examines the lives of two relatively unknown missionaries: English Baptist Felix Carey, who worked in India and Burma, and Elizabeth Thomson, a black American woman who emigrated to Liberia as a missionary teacher. Both experienced lives of extraordinary hardship, but they—and the evangelical publications that described their struggles for worldwide readership—responded to their suffering in very distinctive ways. The different expectations Carey and Thomson navigated around their gender and race offer key insights into nineteenth-century narratives of evangelical providence and colonialism. papers.title: Cultural gene decoding: digital protection of intangible paper-cut and construction of gene bank
papers.abstract: Abstract With globalization and modernization accelerating, the protection of intangible cultural heritage faces significant challenges. Chinese paper-cutting, a cultural treasure, has become a key focus due to its unique value and exquisite craftsmanship. However, inheritance is threatened by aging practitioners, skill loss, and market decline. This highlights the urgent need for digital preservation and the creation of a cultural gene bank. This paper proposes a dual strategy: digital preservation and cultural gene decoding. High-precision data acquisition and image processing technologies enable detailed documentation and conservation of paper-cutting techniques and imagery. Additionally, artificial intelligence and machine learning are used to decode and classify cultural genes, systematically building a cultural gene bank to support continuity and innovation. A case study examines technical, resource, and ethical challenges in digital preservation, addressing data standardization, intellectual property protection, and cultural integrity. Looking ahead, this paper explores technological innovation and cross-cultural collaboration to enhance market applications and encourage social engagement with paper-cutting. These efforts provide a theoretical foundation and practical strategies for safeguarding live transmission and global cultural heritage.

papers.title: ETHICS FOR ARTIFICIAL HISTORIANS
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial historians do not need to have intentions to complete actions or to solve problems. Consequently, a revised approach to the ethics of history is needed. An approach to ethics for artificial historians can be proposed through the recognition of historiographical logic, which is a hybrid of modal, propositional, and erotetic (question‐based) types. Looking to examples of texts produced by artificial and human historians, I argue that this hybrid historiographical logic is seen at play in what Jo Guldi has called “signal” (which can denote both the focus and interpretation of historians) and I call “healthy noise,” or metadiscursive question‐begging and possible world generation. Together, the signal and noise of histories generate an ethical stance of openness toward the possibilities of new evidence from the past, new ways of interpreting that evidence, and new combinations of signal and noise. Recognizing the potential presence of this logic in modal‐propositional‐erotetic statements about the past in a wide range of texts, I argue for the recognition of historiographical logic as broadly useful for AI and specifically useful for the discipline. This historiographical and logical turn facilitates stepping beyond treating ethics as the generation of lists of principles that may fail in application and toward recognizing particular forms of logic as indicating ethically beneficent outcomes. This shift may facilitate the detection and deterrence of histories shaped by logics that indicate ethically maleficent outcomes.

papers.title: Fabian Baumann. Dynasty Divided: A Family History of Russian and Ukrainian Nationalism .
papers.abstract: When Ekaterina Shulgin moved to Western Europe after the civil war and the collapse of imperial Russia, she focused on writing her memoirs. It gave her a sense of purpose and some relief: Having lost both of her sons in World War I, she turned to writing for solace. Her children were dead, so was her state: The Russian Empire that she and her husband had endorsed and supported for decades before 1917 was gone too. The Bolshevik-riled Soviet Russia that replaced its imperial predecessor was as alien and unacceptable for her as for many others from her generation who moved into exile either after 1917, after the Bolshevik takeover in Russia, or during the civil war that followed. On her husband’s side, Ekaterina belonged to a large extended family of Shulgin/Shulhyn. Just as she was pouring her pain into writing, one of her relatives, Oleksander Shulhyn, also put his mind into writing. He was composing a work of different kind. He wrote the memoirs of the Ukrainian movement in the Russian Empire and the short-lived Ukrainian independent state that came out of that empire. That was his personal story too: He had earlier served as a foreign minister of an independent Ukraine. They both spent most of their pre-1914 lives in Kyiv under Russian rule. Both found themselves in emigration in Western Europe after the empire’s collapse. Ekaterina and Oleksander had an almost identical family name—barring the different spelling, the Russian and the Ukrainian, respectively: Shulgin versus Shulhyn. Sharing common predecessors, their family had split into two branches—one adopting a Russian imperial identity and supporting Russian autocracy; the other one supporting the Ukrainian national cause instead, becoming part of the pre-1918 Ukrainophile intelligentsia in Kyiv under Russian rule.

papers.title: The Indian National Army and the Making of Indian Nationalism in Japanese-Occupied Malaya
papers.abstract: Abstract From 1942 to 1945, the Indian National Army (INA) and its civilian wing, the Indian Independence League (IIL), operated in Japanese-occupied Asia to prepare for wars against Britain. Led by first Rash Behari Bose and then Subhas Chandra Bose, the INA recruited members from diverse Indian communities in Asia. This article examines the spiritual training that the INA launched in Malaya in 1943 to unite Indians outside the subcontinent. Through twenty-three lectures, the spiritual training taught a strand of Indian nationalism by creating a historical narrative, which helped reproduce the Indian National Congress’s vision for India. Contrasting with existing literature that attributes the lectures solely to Chandra Bose, this article traces the lectures to the works of Behari Bose, Mohandas Gandhi, and Jawaharlal Nehru. It further argues that Behari Bose’s leadership of the IIL and the INA and the spread of Nehru’s political ideas in Malaya shaped the lectures. Accordingly, the article restores the importance of the lesser-known Behari Bose in the INA and the Indian independence struggle. More broadly, it demonstrates the relationship between violent and non-violent movements, and questions the historical memory about the anti-colonialists who worked with the Axis powers.

papers.title: The Invention of Gay Community in San Francisco, 1960–1970
papers.abstract: Abstract Though historians have often traced the evolution of LGBT ‘communities’ in the United States, they have left the genealogy of queer ideas of ‘community’ underexamined. This article begins to address this lacuna by charting the bifurcated early history of these ideas in the nation’s ‘gay capital’, San Francisco. It identifies homophile activist José Sarria’s 1961 campaign for San Francisco city supervisor as the event that introduced the notion of a ‘gay community’ to lasting effect into local homophile organizing. Sarria’s camp mobilized the idea as a resistance tool for the fight against state repression. In the following years, the concept established itself across local homophile activism. Simultaneously with the rise of ‘gay community’, some homophile leaders also developed coalitional visions of ‘community’. These were inspired by Black freedom organizing and prioritized building community with other marginalized groups. Only a mid-1960s struggle over the orientation of the country’s first homophile community centre led to a lasting sidelining of this coalitional tradition. The reconstruction of this bipartite history challenges enduring myths of a monolithically conservative homophile movement, and helps explain the subsequent success of a homonormative gay politics in the late 1960s and 1970s.

papers.title: Economic Change, Silver, and the Plague of 664–687 in England
papers.abstract: Abstract Bede and other authors describe a destructive wave of plague sweeping across Britain and Ireland in the period 664–87. In the decades around and after this time, the English kingdoms saw rapid economic changes as urban settlements grew, monasteries were founded, and a large silver currency appeared. Here, it is proposed that these developments were influenced by the effects of the plague. Exact levels of mortality are uncertain, but the survivors may have had the capacity to produce more, and more diverse, goods. Relatively weak seigneurial powers on the part of landlords meant that non-elite cultivators became a more important economic constituency in these circumstances, while elites turned in two directions: to development of small but intensively worked central farms, and to liquidation of large stocks of silver, which enabled them to profit by engaging with a diverse body of partners. This liquidation took the form of a much expanded currency of silver pennies, which provides a case-study of monetization as an important yet comparatively short-term economic change.

papers.title: Decolonizing Vietnam War Syllabi
papers.abstract: The essence of this AHR History Lab forum was to identify a recent work of scholarship that proved to be a game-changer, either for teaching or researching about the Vietnam wars. Without question, the biggest shake-up in the field over the past dozen or so years has been the emergence of a measured, archivally based literature on various aspects of both South and North Vietnam’s conduct and experiences of their mid-twentieth century conflicts. The massive canon of work about the Vietnam wars, which has for too long danced to the beat of one outsized American hand clapping, is now fully cast (or much closer to it). Scholarship about South Vietnam by myself, Philip Catton (Diem’s Final Failure: Prelude to America’s War in Vietnam), Edward Miller (Misalliance: Ngo Dinh Diem, the United States, and the Fate of South Vietnam), Geoff Stewart (Vietnam’s Lost Revolution: Ngo Dinh Diem’s Failure to Build an Independent Nation, 1955-–1963), and Van Nguyen-Marshall (Between War and the State: Civil Society in South Vietnam, 1954-1975), among others, has illuminated the inner workings of the state with which the United States was so fatefully aligned from 1954 to 1975.1 This literature reveals South Vietnam’s autonomy, its infighting, its ideological currents, its deep flaws, and also at times its strength, legitimacy, and even nobility. And works about North Vietnam by Pierre Asselin, Lien-Hang T. Nguyen, Ang Cheng Guan, Tuong Vu, and others have enabled us to assess Hanoi’s war with the United States as a strategic contest between two legitimate—albeit asymmetrically powerful—states. This replaces the conventional view of the conflict as a war waged by a great power against a weak national entity, which has been rendered alternately, and two-dimensionally, as either a patriotic victim of neo-imperialist violence or a diabolical puppet of Sino-Soviet overlords.2 Taken together, this new body of work not only has helped to answer long-standing historiographical questions but, by focusing on the internal complexity of the two Vietnams, has shifted the very terms of scholarly debate away from questions related to the Cold War balance of power and toward issues of Vietnamese decolonization, sovereignty, nationalism, strategy, diplomacy, politics, and civil society. I find myself unable to single out any one of these paradigm-shifting works as more enlightening or influential to my scholarship than the rest, though in sum their influence is profound. Pierre Asselin’s Vietnam’s American War: A History, however, stands out as particularly transformative for teaching students about Vietnam’s war with the United States as a complex, multisided, and multisited conflict that defies pithy characterization.3 The book enables teachers to introduce students to some key elements of the scholarly turn discussed above in a clear, engaging, and digestible package.

papers.title: Improving topic modeling for literary studies: a hybrid model combined with Word2Vec visualization in the case of Robinson Crusoe
papers.abstract: Abstract Topic modeling techniques, initially developed for the analysis of short texts, often face challenges when applied to literary research due to the complexity of the literary language and length of the text. Algorithms that typically yield clear and distinct topics for concise informative or opinionated texts often produce ambiguous and overlapping results in literary contexts. This article explores the application of one of the most popular topic modeling techniques, latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), in the analysis of fiction and addresses these central questions regarding the effectiveness and interpretation of LDA topics through a case study of Robinson Crusoe. It proposes combining the Word2Vec method with LDA analysis to render topic modeling results more readable by mapping topics words in a three-dimensional space where semantically related words are placed close to each other. Furthermore, this integrated approach undergoes validation using various children’s editions of the novel and other works by the same author to assess its effectiveness. It is found that the combined method is capable of differentiating subtle changes in children’s editions and other novels. This study highlights the promising potential of LDA in literary research and underscores the importance of visualization techniques for nuanced interpretations of LDA topics.

papers.title: Stephen Robertson. Harlem in Disorder: A Spatial History of How Racial Violence Changed in 1935 .
papers.abstract: I cannot say that I have encountered a project that has inspired me to think as deeply about the form of a monograph and the many functions it can serve as Stephen Robertson’s Harlem in Disorder: A Spatial History of How Racial Violence Changed in 1935. More than an ebook, this digital project demonstrates the still untapped capacities of the internet to inform how we create knowledge, and how and why we present this knowledge in the ways we do. Additionally, it encourages this reader to think more audaciously about inviting audiences of different levels of preparation, varied curiosities, and diverse physical and cognitive abilities into the oftentimes opaque practices of professional historical production. In this book, Robertson echoes the historiographical refrain that the 1935 riot in Harlem indicates a transformation of the nature, motivations, and practices of “riots” in the United States precipitated by some racial event, in this case rumors that sixteen-year-old Lino Rivera, Puerto Rican and racialized as Black by observers, had been assaulted and killed at the Kress department store after being caught shoplifting. The resultant “disorder,” Robertson is more careful than others to call it, boiled over from persistent economic discrimination by white-owned businesses against Black Harlemites. The participants looted businesses, vandalized white- and Chinese-owned establishments while purposefully sparing Black-owned ones, and physically attacked some white people.

papers.title: Analysis of modern strategies for using artificial intelligence technologies in the creation of fantasy content
papers.abstract: Abstract This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the creation of fantasy narratives, examining the new possibilities AI offers for authors and readers and its impact on the genre’s evolution. The study used literature review, textual analysis, comparative analysis, data analysis, experimental methods, ethical and legal examination, and data processing methods using Natural Language Processing software. Through analysis of films, video games, and qualitative text review, the research found that modern technologies—particularly AI and computer graphics—have greatly enhanced the visualization of fantasy worlds, contributing to the genre’s growing popularity. Interactive AI-driven platforms enable customized experiences, increasing engagement and satisfaction among audiences. A significant finding is that contemporary fantasy works, while retaining traditional elements like the struggle between good and evil, magic, and adventure, are now incorporating modern socio-cultural and political themes. This blend preserves the genre’s appeal to diverse audiences while keeping it relevant in today’s context. Additionally, AI opens new avenues for authors by aiding in overcoming creative blocks, generating fresh ideas, and constructing interactive worlds where readers can shape the plot or create their own characters. This not only accelerates the creative process but also enriches storytelling with more varied narratives. The study concludes that fantasy remains a powerful tool for cultural and social expression and that AI holds great potential for the genre's future growth, promising more innovative and inclusive experiences for audiences.

papers.title: “They Do Not Have Physiognomies of Their Own”: Tracking Racialization of Maritime Professions in the Eighteenth-Century Portuguese Empire
papers.abstract: Abstract During the second half of the long eighteenth century, various nations and empires began keeping records of sailors arriving and departing certain ports. In Portugal, all sailors were required to register at the Junta do Comércio (the board of trade), a measure enacted in the wake of a ban on the importation of enslaved people into the kingdom in 1761; an exemption was later made for enslaved sailors or crew members. This article draws on a data set of 344 sailors registered in logs of the Junta’s Lisbon office, dating from 1767, when the board was formed, to 1788, when it was absorbed into the royal court. Our analysis shows how the Junta’s logbooks became a contested space in which enslaved and free sailors of color attempted to define their own occupations, racial identities, and legal status in terms that frequently conflicted with the increasingly homogenized racialization of the state. We link the patterns of increased racialization of sailor records in Portugal to wider Atlantic developments in Brazil, France, Britain, and elsewhere to show how, during a period of immense political, economic, and social change in the long eighteenth century, racial categories were created, expanded, and disseminated across empires. The racialized vocabulary and mechanisms of anti-Blackness were developed, tested, and implemented via maritime networks during an age of capitalist and imperialist growth.

papers.title: Love’s Next Meeting: The Forgotten History of Homosexuality and the Left in American Culture By Aaron S. Lecklider
papers.abstract: Thirty years after red and lavender scares washed over American politics, John D’Emilio revealed that the historical connection between homosexuality and communism was not just a figment of the imagination of early Cold War politicians. In Sexual Politics, Sexual Communities (1983), the first historical monograph on the American gay movement, D’Emilio observed that “the Communist party experience of some of the founders gave them organizational skills especially relevant to the situation of homosexuals and lesbians” (58). These same leftists were themselves soon purged when the organization they created, the Mattachine Society—like so many American unions, industries, and groups—banished actual and suspected communists from its ranks. Even as the field of LGBTQ history has flourished, few scholars have followed D’Emilio’s lead in analyzing how queer and Left U.S. history intersected and overlapped before the 1960s. In Love’s Next Meeting, Aaron Lecklider finally provides a full-scale, nuanced, and sophisticated account of the relationship between the American Left and homosexuality in the years between the Bolshevik Revolution and the 1950s. This book is anchored in the Popular Front era, when leftist activism and influence in the U.S. was at its height and there was not yet an organized gay movement. Lecklider notes accurately that much scholarship in queer history “discounts the Old Left due to its perceived homophobia;” his book replaces that stereotype with vivid, complicated portraits of leftists who “brought sexual dissidence and the Left into conversation” (6). Confronting the task of reconstructing people and communities who were deliberately cautious about leaving written traces, historians have often turned to records kept by state agents. Often, the repression itself becomes a key focus of our narratives. Lecklider, by contrast, keeps his attention squarely on the lives and especially the ideas of queer leftists in these decades, as well as their fellow travelers, sympathizers, and critics.

Writing about Colonial India, Christopher Pinney has used the term iatrogenic to describe state interventions that were intended as cures or solutions to anti-colonial speech, but made the original problem worse. In this astonishingly wide-ranging (thematically, chronologically, theoretically) book Scott repeatedly draws our attention to the iatrogenic nature of blasphemy law in India from the mid-1920s onwards; intended to regulate religious conflict, the laws in fact fueled it. Scott argues that this was because it gave social actors the vocabulary and the tools to employ law’s attention to their aggrieved sentiments. As he memorably puts it, “polemicists learned to speak law’s language, alleging that their ‘religious feelings’ had been outraged, and thus performatively constituting those feelings in the very act of transmitting them to others… Law contained the script for communal violence. It educated its subjects in outrage” (18). The central concern of the book is thus to illustrate the cultural production of law (taking blasphemy law as an exemplar) as well as the entanglements of law and religion as “technologies for the governance of emotion.” (27) Part I of the book focuses on the making of a specific law (section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, hereafter IPC) in the 1920s; Part II on the IPC’s draftsman, Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800-1859), his “private self-government” and its implications for a public law governing millions; Part III sketches in great detail the animating ideology and activities of the Arya Samaj from the 1870s through the 1920s, in order to better understand the context of the law’s application and utilization by non-state actors.

papers.title: Bystander Society: Conformity and Complicity in Nazi Germany and the Holocaust . By Mary Fulbrook
papers.abstract: This is an important book on a highly relevant topic. Author Mary Fulbrook makes a daring attempt to offer new insights to an already extensively explored field: the question of (ordinary) Germans’ complicity in the Nazi crimes of World War II and the Holocaust. While Fulbrook’s essential research question is not original, it remains crucial. What conditions and factors allowed the radical regime under Hitler to “kidnap” German society to go along with committing heinous crimes? To be clear, Fulbrook does not bother querying the degree of knowledge among ordinary Germans about the crimes committed in the name of their country. The perhaps stubborn postwar myth—upheld by many Germans post-1945—according to which most knew nothing or very little has long been debunked. But to ask what Germans knew, Fulbrook says, is to pose the wrong question. Instead, she urges the reader to investigate what Germans made of what they knew. The book thus concentrates not on the doings of German perpetrators and their collaborators but instead sets a clear focus on the silent majority of Germans, what Fulbrook refers to as a bystander society. Her argument is sobering. Conformity alone was sufficient for the regime to go unchecked (181). Popular perceptions and (in)actions were not shaped by a morally weak society but by the calculation of the relative risks versus the potential benefits of different forms of action (though the discussion of a balance sheet is quite one-sided and the discussion on how Germans benefitted from Hitler’s regime comes too short). Despite possible inner misgivings, most Germans went along with the system, played their allotted roles and in effect, helped the radicalization of the regime (341). These bystanders, according to Fulbrook, became over time and to varying degrees “complicit—whether through looking away, condoning violence or more actively sustaining the system.” (375).

papers.title: Managing Water Consumption in Colonial Hong Kong: Separate Water Metering, c. 1965–1980s
papers.abstract: Abstract Water troubled administrators of the colonial regime and residents in Hong Kong during the first three decades of the post-war period. The colonial regime attempted to remedy water shortages by exploiting additional water supplies and by improving its administration of water usage. Using archival records in Hong Kong and London, as well as unofficial sources such as local newspapers, this article studies an under-explored demand-side maneuver, separate water metering, introduced by the colonial government in Hong Kong in 1965, and its sociohistorical role in managing water usage. With an improved legibility of water consumption for both local households and the government, separate meterage prompted households to use water more wisely and economically. This article demonstrates that separate meterage expanded the state’s capacity to manage household water consumption and strengthened societal efforts in water conservation. The combination of technology, financial incentives and persuasion—a “pragmatic-persuasive” governing strategy—planted “save water” in the minds of residents which involved households in the water administration to a greater extent. Separate meterage transformed public perceptions of water consumption in the long run and fostered the emergence of civic obligation over water conservation in Hong Kong. This article thereby makes an original contribution to the political and social history of Hong Kong, colonial statecraft, and water management.

papers.title: The Capital City Murders: Black Women and Serial Murder in Interwar Era Washington, DC
papers.abstract: Abstract A series of horrific crimes rocked the nation’s capital during the interwar era. Taking advantage of the city’s socioeconomic and political conditions, as well as its racially segregated landscape, a serial killer preyed on a vulnerable community of urban citizens: Black women. Drawing from a myriad of archival materials, this essay highlights how pervasive patterns of race and gender exclusion left DC Black women susceptible to police brutality, serial murder, and municipal neglect.
